title: Illustration from Agrippa's *De Occulta Philosophia* (1651 edition)
work: The Book of Abramelin & the Magic Square Tradition
creator: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
summary:
An illustration from the 1651 English-language edition of Agrippa's *De Occulta Philosophia* (translated by J.F. and published in London) — a page from the most influential single compendium of Renaissance magical theory.

## Iconography
The 1651 edition's illustrations include magical figures, signs, and geometric diagrams derived from the 1531/1533 Latin originals. This particular plate (designated S3 in the Wikimedia Commons filing) belongs to Agrippa's system of magical characters — forms derived from letters, numbers, and celestial configurations that could be used as spirit-seals or inscribed on talismans.

## Significance
The 1651 English translation brought Agrippa to a new readership outside the Latin-literate scholarly world: it was read by cunning-folk, astrologers, and the growing literate urban class of Interregnum England. Francis Barrett's *The Magus* (1801) drew heavily on it; so did the grimoire tradition that would eventually produce the published Key of Solomon texts of the 19th century. The magic-square kameas that appear in Agrippa's Book II sit within this vast systematic framework: number, letter, planet, spirit, character, and talisman are all faces of the same underlying occult philosophy.

## For artists & game designers
A small engraving of a magical character or sign from Agrippa is the seed of an entire magic system: behind each image stands a planetary correspondence, a spirit name, a numerical value, and a human purpose.

title: Three Magical Alphabets from Agrippa's *De Occulta Philosophia*
work: The Book of Abramelin & the Magic Square Tradition
creator: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
date: 1531 (first ed.); plate here from a later facsimile
summary:
The three magical alphabets from Book III of Agrippa's *De Occulta Philosophia* (1531/1533) — the Celestial Script, the Malachim script, and the Passing of the River script — which provided the Renaissance occult tradition with its definitive system of encoded magical writing.

## Iconography
Three complete alphabets are laid out in parallel rows, with the standard Latin letters on one axis and their equivalents in each magical script across from them. The Celestial Script (*scriptura caelestis*) uses forms derived from constellations; the Malachim ('of the angels') uses forms based on a rationalisation of square Hebrew; the Passing of the River (*transitus fluvii*) is a further variant. These are the scripts in which, Agrippa argues, divine names and magical formulae can be written with particular efficacy.

## Significance
Agrippa's three alphabets became the standard reference for Renaissance and early modern occultists writing spirit-seals, talisman inscriptions, and magic circle letters. They appear in the Goetia (where the Theban alphabet, derived from these, is attributed to Honorius), in John Dee's angelic records, and in countless manuscript and printed grimoires. Their visual logic is closely related to the Abramelin letter-squares: both assume that the visible form of a letter is not arbitrary but carries intrinsic power, and that the power can be concentrated or encoded by using the 'true' form of the letter rather than its everyday equivalent.

## For artists & game designers
Three distinct magical scripts with full alphabets — a complete worldbuilding kit. Each script has a different aesthetic register: astronomical, angelic, riverine. A world-builder can assign each to a different tradition or period.

title: Human Proportions and Secret Numbers, *De Occulta Philosophia*
work: The Book of Abramelin & the Magic Square Tradition
creator: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim
date: 1531 (first ed.); plate here from 1533 Cologne edition
summary:
The famous human-proportions diagram from Agrippa's *De Occulta Philosophia* Book II — a man inscribed in a circle, arms and legs outstretched, with numerical annotations marking the sacred ratios of the human body, cousin to Leonardo's Vitruvian Man.

## Iconography
A standing human figure with arms spread horizontally and legs at shoulder width is enclosed in a circle. Numbers annotate the body's proportions according to ancient and Pythagorean-Neoplatonist number theory: the distance from crown to navel to foot, the span of the arms, the intervals of the face. The implicit claim is that the human body encodes the same mathematical relationships as the planetary kameas — that man is a microcosm whose proportions mirror cosmic numerical order.

## Significance
This diagram sits at the intersection of the Renaissance body-as-microcosm theory and the magic-square tradition. For Agrippa, the planetary kameas are not merely arithmetical curiosities but numerical expressions of the planetary spheres — and those spheres are mapped onto the human body via its sacred proportions. The magic square is thus a mediator between the macrocosm (planets) and the microcosm (human body): an image that captures a cosmic ratio and allows it to be inscribed on a talisman. This diagram makes that theoretical connection visible.

## For artists & game designers
A man inscribed in a circle with numbers marking his proportions is the most enduring image of the Renaissance magical worldview: the universe is mathematical; the body is the universe in miniature; and whoever knows the numbers knows the key to both.

title: Folio from Al-Buni's Treatise on the Ninety-Nine Names of God, Khalili Collection
work: The Book of Abramelin & the Magic Square Tradition
creator: Ahmad ibn Ali al-Buni (d. c. 1225); scribe unknown
repository: Khalili Collection of Islamic Art, London
rights: CC BY-SA 3.0 igo. Nasser D. Khalili Collection of Islamic Art. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A double-page spread from Al-Buni's treatise specifically on the *Asmā' Allāh al-Ḥusnā* (Ninety-Nine Names of God), one of the most copied texts in the Islamic occult corpus, here from a Khalili Collection manuscript.

## Iconography
The opening displays letter-grids and numerical tables keyed to the divine names. Each name of God in the Islamic tradition has a numerical value (via the *abjad* system, where each Arabic letter corresponds to a number) and a specific set of properties — for health, victory, protection, sustaining life, or defeating enemies. The grids here encode these properties into geometric forms suitable for transfer to amulets and talismans.

## Significance
The *wafq* system built around the ninety-nine names became one of the most widespread talismanic practices in the Islamic world, crossing sectarian lines and geographical boundaries. A *wafq* containing the letters of a divine name, inscribed on paper or metal and worn on the body, was believed to transmit that attribute of God directly to the bearer. This is structurally identical to the Abramelin method, where the letters of a spirit's name, inscribed in a word-square, confer that spirit's powers. The parallel — likely not coincidental given the medieval Hebrew-Arabic intellectual exchange — was noted by scholars including Moshe Idel.

## For artists & game designers
Letter-squares built from divine names provide a morally complex magic system: the talisman-maker is not commanding spirits but invoking divine attributes — making the magic prayerful rather than coercive, devotional rather than commanding.

title: Folio from Al-Buni's *Shams al-Ma'arif al-Kubra*, Khalili Collection
work: The Book of Abramelin & the Magic Square Tradition
creator: Ahmad ibn Ali al-Buni (d. c. 1225); scribe unknown
repository: Khalili Collection of Islamic Art, London
rights: CC BY-SA 3.0 igo. Nasser D. Khalili Collection of Islamic Art. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A double-page opening from a copy of Ahmad ibn Ali al-Buni's *Shams al-Ma'arif al-Kubra* (The Great Sun of Knowledge, 13th c.) — the single most important work in the Islamic occult science of letter and number magic.

## Iconography
The folio spreads show the dense geometric layouts characteristic of al-Buni's opus: letter-grids (*wafq*, plural *awfaq*), numerical tables, and inscribed squares arranged amid Arabic text. These are not decorations but operative instruments — pages designed to be copied exactly, or the book itself consulted while performing a working. The grids combine the ninety-nine names of God (*asmā' al-ḥusnā*), abjad letter-number correspondences, and planetary hours into precise talismanic configurations.

## Significance
Al-Buni (d. c. 1225, in Tunis or Cairo) synthesised Arabic, Greek, and possibly Indian numerical traditions into a comprehensive theory of the *wafq* — the magic square as an instrument of divine power, not mere numerical curiosity. His *Shams al-Ma'arif* was the root from which the Islamic magic-square tradition branched across the Ottoman, Persian, Mughal, and Malay worlds. The European planetary kameas in Agrippa are ultimately indebted to this same Arabo-Hellenistic synthesis via the Picatrix and other transmission routes.

## For artists & game designers
The densely packed letter-grids of al-Buni offer an aesthetic unavailable in European grimoire art: Arabic script in talismanic geometry, angular and cursive by turns, with a visual logic that game artists could adapt for any 'Arabic' or 'Islamicate' magic system.

title: 16th-Century Arabic Magic Square
work: The Book of Abramelin & the Magic Square Tradition
creator: Unknown
summary:
A compact manuscript page bearing a single Arabic magic square (*wafq*) — a concentrated example of the Islamic talismanic numerical tradition in its mature 16th-century form.

## Iconography
The grid is divided into cells each containing an Arabic numeral or letter. The rows, columns, and diagonals sum to the same constant — the 'magic constant' that marks the square as formally correct and therefore operationally valid. Surrounding text probably identifies the square by the name of God or the operation it performs. The script and layout suggest a practitioner's manual rather than a luxury presentation copy: a working document.

## Significance
The 16th century was the great age of *wafq* compilation in the Arabic-speaking world, as authors built on al-Buni's 13th-century foundations and absorbed Indian and Persian traditions of numerical magic. By this period every town with a literate population would have had access to *wafq* recipe books: printed or copied lists of squares keyed to specific human needs. The visual difference between this Islamic square and a European planetary kamea is primarily one of script and labelling convention; the underlying mathematical structure is identical.

## For artists & game designers
A single tightly ruled grid on yellowed paper, with each cell containing a numeral — the minimal expression of talismanic power. Works as a found-object clue, a magical component, or a page from a captured enemy wizard's codex.

title: Buduh Magic Square (Arabic Amulet Diagram)
work: The Book of Abramelin & the Magic Square Tradition
creator: Unknown
date: Modern diagram; tradition attested from medieval period
summary:
The *Buduh* square — the Arabic 3×3 magic square with the specific letter values **ب-د-و-ح** (ba, dal, waw, ha), corresponding to the numerals 2-4-6-8 in the *abjad* system — is one of the most widespread single talismanic objects in the Islamic world.

## Iconography
This small diagram shows the 3×3 grid containing the letters of *buduh* distributed so that each row, column, and diagonal sums to the same value. The name *buduh* itself has no independent meaning in Arabic; it is a technical term coined from the letter-values of this specific arrangement, attested in al-Buni and widely reproduced in talismanic manuals ever since.

## Significance
The *buduh* square was used across North Africa, the Near East, and into South and Southeast Asia as a general-purpose protective talisman — worn as an amulet, inscribed on doorposts, copied into personal prayer books. It is the Islamic analogue of the SATOR square in the Western tradition: a minimal letter-grid of such wide diffusion that its origin is untraceable, its meaning largely symbolic and protective rather than specific to any one operation. Its extraordinary longevity — attested from the 13th century to the present — demonstrates the deep human appetite for the talismanic letter-grid.

## For artists & game designers
The *buduh* square is a worldbuilding detail of high specificity: a 3×3 letter-grid that any character in an Islamicate setting would recognise immediately, worn like a cross in a Christian world — private piety made portable.

title: Magic Square from a Chetveroevangelie (Orthodox Gospel Book)
work: The Book of Abramelin & the Magic Square Tradition
creator: Unknown Orthodox scribe
medium: manuscript illumination, ink and pigment on parchment
summary:
A magic square incorporated into the decorative programme of an Eastern Orthodox *Chetveroevangelie* (Gospel Tetraevangelion) — a rare witness to the penetration of the magic-square tradition into Christian liturgical manuscript production.

## Iconography
The square appears amid the ornamented frames and canon tables characteristic of Slavic Gospel manuscripts. Its incorporation here is not incidental decoration: in Eastern Christian tradition, geometric grids with numerical or alphabetic properties were understood as expressions of divine order, akin to the Solomonic geometries of the Western grimoire tradition. The square's letters or numbers would have been read as sacred numerology reinforcing the text's authority.

## Significance
The Eastern Orthodox encounter with magic-square tradition was mediated differently from the Western Latin one: through Byzantine Greek sources, through Jewish communities in the Slavic lands, and through the same Arabic-Greek transmission that produced the Picatrix. The presence of a magic square in a Gospel book — the most sacred text in the Orthodox liturgical corpus — shows how thoroughly the talismanic grid had been naturalised into Christian devotional culture. This convergence makes the magic square one of the most cross-cultural artifacts in the pre-modern world.

## For artists & game designers
A magic square embedded in a holy book inverts the usual occult-vs-religion binary: here sacred text and talismanic number-grid are presented as complementary expressions of the same divine order.

title: Hebrew Manuscript Amulet for Protection from Plague (Wellcome Collection)
work: The Book of Abramelin & the Magic Square Tradition
creator: Unknown Jewish scribe
rights: CC BY 4.0. Wellcome Collection. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
An Ashkenazi Hebrew manuscript amulet for the protection of a named individual from plague — a personal talismanic document combining kabbalistic letter-magic with Psalm verses and divine names in the tradition that directly parallels the Abramelin word-squares.

## Iconography
The amulet is a sheet of paper inscribed in Hebrew with a combination of protective Psalm verses, divine names, and letter-grids or *kamea*-style arrangements. The name of the protected person is typically written into the formula ('for the protection of [name], son/daughter of [mother's name]'), personalising the talisman. The script is Ashkenazi square Hebrew with some cursive elements, suggesting a scribe who was a literate community specialist — possibly the local rabbi or a professional amulet-writer.

## Significance
The Wellcome Collection holds one of the largest holdings of Hebrew protective amulets in the world, acquired during the 19th and early 20th centuries when such documents were sold or donated from European Jewish communities. They document the living practice of Hebrew letter-magic — the same tradition that informs the Abramelin word-squares — in its everyday rather than grimoire form: not elite ritual magic but domestic protective practice, handwritten and personalised for ordinary people facing epidemic disease.

## For artists & game designers
A personalised plague amulet with a specific name written in Hebrew is a powerful narrative prop: it belongs to someone, it was made with urgency, and the person who commissioned it believed their life depended on the correct arrangement of letters on a page.

title: Kabbalistic Amulet for the Cure from Jaundice, 18th c. (Wellcome Collection)
work: The Book of Abramelin & the Magic Square Tradition
creator: Unknown Jewish scribe
rights: CC BY 4.0. Wellcome Collection. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A kabbalistic healing amulet written for Abraham Elijah son of a named mother, prescribing a cure from jaundice through the operative use of divine names and letter-grids — an 18th-century Ashkenazi document of vernacular Jewish magic.

## Iconography
The amulet combines Psalm fragments, angelic names (likely Raphael, the healing angel), divine names from the kabbalistic tradition, and potentially a small letter-grid *kamea* keyed to the healing operation. The combination of biblical text and magical formula is characteristic of the *kame'ot* (amulet) tradition: Scripture provides the authoritative matrix; the divine names and geometric arrangements are the operational technology layered within it.

## Significance
This amulet documents the interface between kabbalistic theory (the emanative power of divine names, the correspondence between letters and aspects of the divine) and folk medical practice. Jaundice was a serious condition in early modern Europe with limited effective treatment; the amulet was part of a therapeutic package that might also include herbal remedies and prayer. The Wellcome Collection's holdings from this tradition form a documentary archive of how kabbalistic ideas, ultimately sharing roots with the Abramelin letter-magic, were operationalised at the level of everyday life.

## For artists & game designers
A healing amulet written for a specific person, specifying the illness and the beneficiary's name, is the most intimate possible magical object. It implies a community of practice, a working relationship between scribe and patient, and a worldview in which the correct letters, correctly arranged, could alter the body's condition.

title: Kabbalistic Amulet for Safe Pregnancy and Delivery, 18th c. (Wellcome Collection)
work: The Book of Abramelin & the Magic Square Tradition
creator: Unknown Jewish scribe
rights: CC BY 4.0. Wellcome Collection. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A kabbalistic amulet for the safe pregnancy and delivery of Esther wife of a named husband — a standard genre of Ashkenazi protective magic, among the most commonly produced amulets in the Jewish world, here from the Wellcome Collection's 18th-century holdings.

## Iconography
Birth amulets typically invoke the angels Sanoi, Sansanoi, and Semangelaf (the three angels sent to retrieve Lilith from the sea in medieval legend) alongside Psalm 121 ('He who watches over Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep') and other texts. They commonly include letter-grids or magical names arranged in geometric patterns, and the name of the pregnant woman written explicitly into the formula. Some include illustrations of the angels, the menorah, or other iconic forms.

## Significance
The birth amulet (*kame'a* for *leidah*, for birth) is the most extensively documented type of Jewish protective talisman. Childbed was the most dangerous regular experience in a woman's pre-modern life; the amulet offered a form of spiritual protection that coexisted with midwifery skill. The invocation of Lilith's enemies (the three angels) in protective charms is a striking example of how apotropaic magic uses the names of threatening supernatural forces as deterrents. This is structurally identical to the Abramelin method: the names of spirits, correctly inscribed, control those spirits.

## For artists & game designers
A pregnancy protection amulet is a morally complex magic item: protective, not aggressive; gendered; tied to the most vulnerable moment of domestic life. It makes visible the magic system's social function — not power-seeking but care.

title: Islamic Magic Bowl (Khalili Collection)
work: The Book of Abramelin & the Magic Square Tradition
creator: Unknown Islamic craftsperson
repository: Khalili Collection of Islamic Art, London
rights: CC BY-SA 3.0 igo. Nasser D. Khalili Collection of Islamic Art. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
An engraved metal magic bowl from the Khalili Collection — a material object of operative Islamic magic, inscribed with divine names and *wafq* grids for healing or protective use through the medium of water consumed from the vessel.

## Iconography
The bowl's inner surface is covered with Arabic inscriptions: divine names, Quranic verses (particularly al-Fatiha and Ayat al-Kursi, the 'Throne Verse'), and compact numerical or letter-grids. The outer surface may carry further protective inscriptions. These bowls were used for healing: water, milk, or honey was poured in, allowed to absorb the inscribed power, then given to the patient to drink. The bowl itself could also be pressed against the body at the site of illness.

## Significance
Islamic medicine bowls (*kasa*) represent the intersection of the *wafq* tradition, Quranic healing practice, and material culture. They were produced throughout the Islamic world — Iran, Ottoman Anatolia, South Asia — and their production required both scribal literacy and metalworking skill. The practice of ingesting or touching a surface inscribed with divine names is directly analogous to the Hermetic idea (found in the Leyden Papyrus and in early Christian amulet practice) that sacred letters have physical as well as spiritual effects.

## For artists & game designers
A magic bowl that must be drunk from — where the power is transmitted through the inscription via liquid — is a striking mechanic. The magic is not worn, it is consumed; the letter-grid enters the body.

summary:
A double-sided polygonal metal talisman from the Khalili Collection — a physical object of protective and operative magic produced in the Ottoman or Qajar Islamic world, engraved on all faces with letter-grids and divine names.

## Iconography
The talisman's polygonal form (likely octagonal or twelve-sided) provides multiple faces for inscription, each panel carrying a different *wafq* grid or invocation. Metal talismans of this type were typically produced by specialist craftsmen working from recipe books like al-Buni's *Shams al-Ma'arif*: the client specified the operation (protection from enemies, success in business, safe travel), and the craftsman selected the appropriate divine names, numerical squares, and planetary correspondences, then engraved them under the correct astrological hours.

## Significance
The polygonal metal talisman is the highest-grade material form of the *wafq* tradition — more durable than paper, more complex than cloth, and requiring specialist engraving skill. Such objects circulated at courts and in wealthy households across the Ottoman, Safavid, and Mughal worlds. Their existence in museum collections (Khalili, V&A, Topkapi) demonstrates that the magic-square talisman was not a marginal practice but central to early modern Islamic material culture.

## For artists & game designers
A multi-faced engraved metal talisman is an ideal prop for an Islamicate fantasy setting — it implies a structured magical technology, craftsperson traditions, and an economy of protective devices comparable to a pharmaceutical industry.

title: Egyptian Ink-on-Paper Amulet, LACMA (M.2002.1.370)
work: The Book of Abramelin & the Magic Square Tradition
creator: Unknown Egyptian craftsperson
repository: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
rights: Public domain. Los Angeles County Museum of Art. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A Fatimid or Ayyubid-period Egyptian ink-on-paper amulet from LACMA's collection — one of the oldest surviving examples of the Islamic talismanic document tradition, predating al-Buni's systematisation but already displaying the letter-grid aesthetic.

## Iconography
The amulet is a piece of paper inscribed with Arabic script in a compact, grid-like arrangement — magical names, protective formulae, and possibly a numerical or letter square. Egyptian paper amulets of this period were folded and worn inside small leather cases suspended from the body. The ink-on-paper format made amulet production accessible: any literate person with access to the necessary texts could produce one.

## Significance
Fatimid Egypt (909–1171 CE) was a crucible of Ismaili esoteric thought and a centre of the letter-magic tradition that al-Buni would systematise a century later. These early amulets document the pre-al-Buni state of Islamic protective writing: already using divine names, Quranic verses, and geometric arrangements, but not yet with the elaborate numerical *wafq* grids that would later dominate. LACMA's collection of such objects is an important resource for tracing the evolution of Islamic talismanic practice.

## For artists & game designers
A small, folded, ink-on-paper amulet worn inside a leather case against the skin is the most intimate portable magic: invisible, personal, and constant. The idea that a piece of paper with the right words on it protects the wearer's life inverts the modern secular assumption that writing is merely communication.

creator: Unknown Egyptian craftsperson
repository: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)

summary:
A second Egyptian ink-on-paper amulet from LACMA's collection — a narrow scroll-format document inscribed with protective formulae, part of the same Fatimid-Ayyubid talismanic tradition but in a different physical format from the folded-sheet type.

## Iconography
This amulet is in scroll format: a long narrow strip of paper densely covered in small Arabic script arranged in columns and rows. Scroll amulets were typically worn rolled and inserted into cylindrical silver or copper cases (*hifaza*) suspended from a chain or cord. The narrow format concentrates the inscribed power into a portable object that can be worn against the heart or the upper arm.

## Significance
The scroll and the folded-sheet are the two principal formats for Egyptian Islamic paper amulets. Both formats were already in use by the Fatimid period, suggesting a well-established production tradition with workshop conventions. The scroll format has a long history in the ancient Egyptian magic tradition (hieratic papyrus amulets from the Ptolemaic period are its ancestors); the Islamic *hifaza* represents the continuity of this Egyptian talismanic practice through the Islamic period, absorbing new content (Quranic verses, Arabic divine names) while retaining the old material form.

## For artists & game designers
A rolled scroll carried in a silver case at the chest, its contents unknown to anyone but the person who commissioned and the scribe who wrote it — the most private form of magic, combining body, metal, and inscribed language in a single wearable object.

title: Lo Shu Magic Square (Chinese Mystic Table, from Paul Carus)
work: The Book of Abramelin & the Magic Square Tradition
creator: Paul Carus (ill.); traditional Chinese pattern
date: 1906 (from *The Monist*); tradition attested from Han dynasty
summary:
The Lo Shu (*Lò shū*, 洛書, 'Luo River Script') magic square — the 3×3 numerical grid whose rows, columns, and diagonals all sum to 15 — as illustrated by philosopher Paul Carus in a 1906 article for *The Monist*, demonstrating the square's cross-cultural significance.

## Iconography
The diagram presents the Lo Shu in its 'mystic knot' form: dots and lines (the traditional Chinese representation) on the left, and the corresponding Arabic numerals arranged in the 3×3 grid on the right. The same numerical arrangement appears in Chinese tradition as the map carried on the back of the cosmic tortoise that emerged from the Luo River, granting the legendary Emperor Yu the knowledge needed to order the universe.

## Significance
The Lo Shu is the 3×3 magic square — the smallest possible magic square with distinct positive integers — and it appears independently in Chinese mathematics (attested from the Han dynasty, 206 BCE–220 CE) and in the Arabic *wafq* tradition (where it is the *buduh* square or the Saturn kamea), and possibly in Indian Jain mathematics. Whether these represent independent discovery or transmission along trade routes (Silk Road, Indian Ocean) is debated. For the history of magic squares, the Lo Shu is ground zero: the mother-pattern from which all larger squares — including the 4×4 Jupiter kamea and the vast squares of the Abramelin — descend.

## For artists & game designers
The Lo Shu establishes that magic squares are not a Western or Islamic peculiarity but a near-universal human discovery. In a multicultural fantasy world, the fact that widely separated civilisations arrived at the same grid independently could serve as evidence of a shared underlying metaphysical reality.

title: Post-Medieval Copper Alloy Talismanic Pendant (FindID 755270)
work: The Book of Abramelin & the Magic Square Tradition
creator: Unknown craftsperson
rights: CC BY 2.0. Portable Antiquities Scheme. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A copper alloy talismanic pendant recovered through the UK Portable Antiquities Scheme — a physical survival of post-medieval English amulet practice, likely bearing magic squares or other protective inscriptions derived from the Renaissance grimoire tradition.

## Iconography
The pendant is a cast copper alloy medallion with engraved inscriptions on one or both faces. Post-medieval copper talismans of this type typically bear one or more of: the planetary kameas derived from Agrippa; fragments of Psalm text; divine names (IAO, AGLA, Tetragrammaton); magical characters or spirit-seals from the grimoire tradition; or simple geometric protective patterns. The copper medium and size suggest a wearable object intended for personal rather than domestic use.

## Significance
The Portable Antiquities Scheme has recorded hundreds of post-medieval talismanic pendants across England, demonstrating the wide circulation of grimoire-derived amulet practice outside elite manuscript culture. By the 16th–18th centuries, the planetary kameas and magical characters of Agrippa had been absorbed into vernacular protective magic practised at all social levels. A copper pendant sold or made locally and worn against the skin is the low-cost democratic version of the elaborate ritual magic documented in manuscripts like the Abramelin: the same underlying technology of letters, numbers, and divine names, packaged for everyday accessibility.

## For artists & game designers
A found metal pendant with obscure engraved symbols — the kind of thing pulled from an English field by a metal detectorist — is a perfect archaeological mystery object. What is it for? Whose power does it invoke? The answer connects to five centuries of grimoire tradition.

title: 17th-Century Picatrix Frontispiece, Hagia Sophia MS 2443
work: The Book of Abramelin & the Magic Square Tradition
creator: Unknown Ottoman scribe
date: 17th c. (copy of Arabic original, *Ghāyat al-Ḥakīm*, c. 11th c.)
summary:
The frontispiece of a 17th-century Ottoman copy of the *Ghāyat al-Ḥakīm* (*The Goal of the Wise*, known in Latin as the *Picatrix*) — the major Arabic text of astral magic and the key intermediary through which planetary kameas, magic squares, and spirit-images were transmitted from the Islamicate world to Renaissance Europe.

## Iconography
The frontispiece page bears the title of the work in ornate Arabic script, with decorative borders appropriate to a prestige copy. The *Ghāyat al-Ḥakīm* (compiled c. 11th century CE, probably in Andalusia) is a massive encyclopaedia of astral magic: how to attract planetary influences, manufacture astral talismans, and command spirits through the correct use of planetary images, suffumigations, prayers, and numeric grids.

## Significance
The *Picatrix* is the bridge between the Islamic *wafq* tradition and the European planetary-magic tradition. It was translated into Castilian and then Latin for Alfonso X of Castile in the 13th century, and from there circulated through European scholarly networks to reach Ficino, Agrippa, and ultimately the Renaissance Hermetic tradition. Agrippa's planetary kameas in *De Occulta Philosophia* derive their mathematical structures from material in the *Picatrix* milieu; the planetary images and spirit-names also trace back to it. Without the *Picatrix*, the Abramelin magic-square tradition would have no European grounding.

## For artists & game designers
The *Picatrix* is the sourcebook of sourcebooks: a magical encyclopaedia so comprehensive and systematic that it provided the building-blocks for European ceremonial magic for five centuries. A copy of it in a fantasy world would be the most dangerous library acquisition imaginable.

title: SATOR-AREPO Word Square (Acrostic Diagram)
work: The Book of Abramelin & the Magic Square Tradition
creator: Unknown (diagram from YDEA collection)
date: Modern diagram; inscription attested from 1st c. CE
summary:
The SATOR-AREPO word square — five words, five letters each, arranged so they read identically left-to-right, right-to-left, top-to-bottom, and bottom-to-top — is the earliest and most durable magic word-square in the Western tradition.

## Iconography
The five words are **SATOR / AREPO / TENET / OPERA / ROTAS**, forming a perfect reversible grid. The central word TENET forms a cross; the whole can be rearranged into a double PATERNOSTER cross with the letters A and O (Alpha and Omega) left over. Whether the original meaning was Latin prose ('the sower Arepo holds the wheels at work') or a cryptic anagram is still debated, but the visual impact — a self-similar grid that reads the same in every direction — was clearly understood as a sign of hidden power.

## Significance
First attested at Pompeii (before 79 CE) and found across Roman military sites in Britain, Germany, and Egypt, the SATOR square entered medieval Christian amulet practice as a protection against fire, disease, and evil spirits. It is the direct ancestor of the Abramelin letter-square tradition: a grid of letters whose geometric perfection implies cosmic order and naming power. Scholars debate whether it originated in Jewish, early Christian, or Mithraic milieux; its ubiquity suggests a pan-cultural talismanic logic rather than a single origin.

## For artists & game designers
The SATOR square is the ur-puzzle of the Western tradition — self-referential, palindromic, and spatially complete. It works as an in-world cipher, a glyph on a cursed object, or the solution to a mystery that reveals who created a magical working.

title: Rotas-Sator Amulet, Museu Monográfico de Conímbriga
work: The Book of Abramelin & the Magic Square Tradition
creator: Unknown Roman craftsperson
summary:
A physical survival: the SATOR-AREPO magic word-square engraved on an amulet-stone now in the Museu Monográfico de Conímbriga, Portugal — one of the most westerly Roman attestations of this ancient talisman.

## Iconography
The five-word square is incised in orderly Latin capitals on a flat stone. The medium itself — a portable inscribed object worn or carried — shows the square in its primary operational context: not an illustration but a tool. The grid reads ROTAS-OPERA-TENET-AREPO-SATOR in this presentation (the 'Rotas' variant), beginning with the word for 'wheels' rather than 'sower.'

## Significance
Conimbriga (near modern Coimbra) was a prosperous Roman city on the road from Olisipo (Lisbon) to Bracara Augusta. The amulet demonstrates that the magic square travelled with Roman soldiers, merchants, and settlers to the edges of the empire. Its presence in Portugal reinforces the theory that the square circulated within military and artisan communities rather than elite literary culture. The Museu Monográfico's collection of Roman amulets provides crucial material evidence for the lived practice of protective inscription magic.

## For artists & game designers
A graved stone inscribed with a word-square is the perfect prop for a historical RPG or dark fantasy setting — portable, mysterious, grammatically impossible to parse, and unmistakably the work of someone who believed letters themselves could hold power.

title: Adinkra Cloth (1825 Engraving)
work: African & Diaspora Divination, Sign-Systems & Power Objects
creator: Anonymous (engraver, after Bowdich)
summary:
An early-19th-century printed plate (1825) reproducing the layout of an Asante *adinkra* cloth, among the earliest European records of the textile.

## Iconography
The cloth is divided by hand-drawn lines into a grid of rectangular panels, each filled with a repeated stamped ideogram. The regular ruled blocks and the variety of symbols across them show the standard *adinkra* compositional scheme.

## Significance
This image descends from the era of Thomas Edward Bowdich's mission to Kumasi (1817), which first brought systematic European description of Asante material culture. *Adinkra* cloth — its name often glossed "farewell" — was worn at funerals, the stamped proverbs offering consolation and moral commentary. The 1825 plate documents the tradition before photography and is a key dating anchor for the practice.

## For artists & game designers
The ruled grid of stamped panels is a procedural tiling system: pick a symbol per cell from a meaning-tagged set and the whole cloth reads as a sentence.

title: Adinkra Symbol (Akan Ideogram)
work: African & Diaspora Divination, Sign-Systems & Power Objects
creator: Modern rendering (J. El Bouamraoui & K. P. Moletsane)
date: Modern rendering of a traditional Akan symbol
summary:
A clean modern rendering of an Adinkra symbol, the visual proverb-signs of the Akan peoples of Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire.

## Iconography
The ideogram is a bold, symmetrical black device of the kind block-printed onto cloth with calabash stamps and *badie*-bark dye. Each of the scores of canonical signs carries a name and an attached proverb or aphorism.

## Significance
Adinkra are not divinatory in the oracular sense but constitute a structured ritual sign-system: symbols such as *Gye Nyame* ("except God"), *Sankofa* ("return and fetch it"), and *Dwennimmen* (ram's horns / humility) encode Akan cosmology, ethics, and proverbs, and were historically worn at funerals and on mourning cloth. The corpus is a codified iconographic language of values, repeatedly catalogued since the 19th century (R. S. Rattray).

## For artists & game designers
A finite set of named glyphs each bound to a proverb is an ideal in-game writing system or sigil alphabet — meaning per symbol, not per letter.

title: Àgéré Ifá (Divination Vessel with Kneeling Woman)
work: African & Diaspora Divination, Sign-Systems & Power Objects
creator: Anonymous (Yoruba)
rights: CC0 (Metropolitan Museum of Art). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
An *àgéré Ifá*, the lidded or open carved bowl that holds the sixteen sacred palm-nuts (*ikin*) of an Ifá diviner, here supported by a kneeling female figure, in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

## Iconography
The cup rests on the head or hands of a carved kneeling woman, the dominant Yoruba figure of devotion and fertility. The vessel itself is the storehouse from which the *babalawo* draws the *ikin* to be cast between his palms.

## Significance
The sixteen palm-nuts are the holiest objects of Ifá; their manipulation (passing them between the hands and counting the residue) yields the marks that build an *odu*. A figural *àgéré* dignifies their keeping, and the kneeling caryatid binds the apparatus to ideals of piety, supplication, and the support women give the cult. Such vessels are central exhibits in surveys of Yoruba court and ritual carving.

## For artists & game designers
A container whose carved bearer embodies the virtue the contents demand — the object literally kneels in worship of what it holds.

citations.text: Henry John Drewal & John Pemberton III, *Yoruba: Nine Centuries of African Art and Thought* (1989).

title: Akan Goldweight (Figurative Brass)
work: African & Diaspora Divination, Sign-Systems & Power Objects
creator: Anonymous (Akan)
rights: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Muséum de Toulouse, Roger Culos). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A cast-brass Akan goldweight (*mrammuo*), from the Muséum de Toulouse, used to weigh gold dust and encoding a proverb.

## Iconography
The small lost-wax brass casting takes a figurative or geometric form. Akan weights range from abstract geometric devices to miniature scenes — animals, tools, human vignettes — each calibrated to a unit of the gold-dust currency.

## Significance
From roughly the 15th to the early 20th century the Akan weighed gold dust against these brass figures. Beyond their metrological use, the figurative weights illustrate proverbs and aphorisms — "it is the fool's sheep that breaks loose twice" — so that a merchant's set doubled as a portable anthology of [[motif:proverb object|Akan wisdom]]. Geometric weights also relate to a notional system of weight-names. Georges Niangoran-Bouah compiled them as a documentary corpus he termed *Akanology*.

## For artists & game designers
Currency objects that each carry a proverb turn an inventory of weights into a deck of moral aphorisms — economy and lore in the same item.

citations.text: Timothy F. Garrard, *Akan Weights and the Gold Trade* (1980).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Babalawo Akinropo (Ifá Diviner)
work: African & Diaspora Divination, Sign-Systems & Power Objects
creator: Photograph by Kehinde1234
summary:
A photographic portrait of Babalawo Akinropo, a living Ifá priest of Ibadan, in ritual dress.

## Iconography
The diviner is shown in the regalia of his office. The image documents the practitioner rather than an object — the human node of a system usually represented in museums only by its instruments.

## Significance
The *babalawo* ("father of secrets") is the trained custodian of Ifá: he memorises a vast body of *odu* verses, casts the palm-nuts or *ọpẹlẹ*, and interprets the result to prescribe sacrifice (*ebo*) and counsel. Ifá remains a living West African and diaspora practice, not a closed antiquity, which is why a contemporary portrait belongs alongside the historic apparatus. The role passes through long apprenticeship and ranks among the most prestigious of Yoruba religious offices.

## For artists & game designers
A reference for costuming and staging the diviner NPC — the human interface to the oracle, not just the props on the table.

citations.text: Wande Abimbola, *Ifa: An Exposition of Ifa Literary Corpus* (1976).

title: Divination Object with Cowrie Shells (Gbaule, We people)
work: African & Diaspora Divination, Sign-Systems & Power Objects
creator: Anonymous (We / Wè people)
rights: CC0 (Brooklyn Museum, photo Daderot). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A composite divination object (*gbaule*) of the We (Wè) people of Liberia, assembled from clay, feathers, porcupine quills, cloth, cowrie shells and other matter, in the Brooklyn Museum.

## Iconography
The object is a dense bundle: a clay core bristling with quills and feathers, wrapped in cloth and leather and set with cowrie shells and bright fragments. It is an accretive power-object rather than a smooth carved form.

## Significance
Cowrie shells are the most widespread African divinatory lot, cast and read by their up/down fall — the Yoruba *owo merindinlogun* (sixteen-cowrie oracle) is the best-documented system, but cowrie casting recurs across West Africa and the diaspora (Cuban *dilogún*). This Liberian *gbaule* shows cowries embedded in a charged ritual assemblage that both divines and protects, linking the [[motif:cowrie divination|cowrie oracle]] to the wider family of African power-objects such as the Kongo *minkisi*.

## For artists & game designers
Sixteen cowries that each read open or closed give a 16-bit oracle; bundled into a power-object, the dice and the talisman are one item.

citations.text: William Bascom, *Sixteen Cowries: Yoruba Divination from Africa to the New World* (1980).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Ethiopian Protective Healing Scroll
work: African & Diaspora Divination, Sign-Systems & Power Objects
creator: Anonymous (Ethiopian dabtara)
summary:
An Ethiopian protective/healing scroll, a strip of parchment inscribed with prayers, talismanic designs, and figures.

## Iconography
The long vertical scroll combines blocks of Geʿez text with painted talismanic images — geometric "net" patterns, interlace, and frontal faces or angels with large staring eyes, devices meant to bind and repel demons.

## Significance
Such scrolls are produced by the *dabtara*, the unordained learned clerics of the Ethiopian Orthodox tradition who specialise in protective and curative magic. Cut to the height of the person they protect and worn or hung at home, the scroll fights illness and the demon *buda* through holy names, prayers, and the apotropaic power of the eye-motifs. Jacques Mercier's studies established the scrolls as a distinctive Christian-talismanic art bridging liturgy and folk healing.

## For artists & game designers
A scroll cut to the owner's exact body-length is a wonderfully literal "personal ward" item — protection scaled to the character.

citations.text: Jacques Mercier, *Ethiopian Magic Scrolls* (1979).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Equestrian Figure Goldweight (Akan)
work: African & Diaspora Divination, Sign-Systems & Power Objects
creator: Anonymous (Akan)
rights: CC BY 3.0 (Brooklyn Museum). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
An Akan goldweight in the form of a horse and rider, in the Brooklyn Museum.

## Iconography
The lost-wax brass casting depicts a mounted figure — an equestrian, a prestige image in the West African savanna and forest alike, signalling a chief, warrior, or person of rank.

## Significance
Figuratively cast weights like this one belong to the same proverb-bearing tradition as geometric weights but make the message pictorial: the horseman evokes status, authority, and the cavalry powers to the north. As with all [[motif:akan goldweight|goldweights]], the object's first job was metrological — to balance a measure of gold dust — while its image carried a proverb or social ideal. The equestrian type is one of the most prized among collectors and museums.

## For artists & game designers
A mounted-figure token reads instantly as "rank" or "cavalry" — efficient visual shorthand for status in a tabletop or strategy economy.

citations.text: Timothy F. Garrard, *Akan Weights and the Gold Trade* (1980).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Gye Nyame (Adinkra Symbol)
work: African & Diaspora Divination, Sign-Systems & Power Objects
creator: Vector rendering (Yellowfiver)
date: Modern rendering of a traditional Akan symbol
summary:
*Gye Nyame*, "except for God," the best-known of the Akan Adinkra symbols and an emblem of the supremacy of God.

## Iconography
The sign is a pair of mirrored, interlocking spiral hooks forming a balanced, near-symmetrical knot. Its abstract curves carry no pictorial subject; the meaning is wholly conventional.

## Significance
*Gye Nyame* expresses the Akan conviction that nothing was done or will be done "except by God" (*Onyame/Nyame*) — an affirmation of divine omnipotence often paraphrased "None but God." It is among the most widely reproduced [[motif:adinkra|Adinkra]] devices, stamped on funeral cloth and now ubiquitous in Ghanaian and Pan-African design as a statement of faith. Like all Adinkra it belongs to a codified vocabulary of proverb-symbols rather than to figurative art.

## For artists & game designers
A single glyph that stands for an entire theological proposition — useful as a faction crest or a one-symbol "motto" badge.

citations.text: Kwame Anthony Appiah, in *The Adinkra Dictionary* / Akan symbol scholarship.
Wikimedia Commons

title: Ifá Divination Board (LACMA)
work: African & Diaspora Divination, Sign-Systems & Power Objects
creator: Anonymous (Yoruba)
summary:
A divination board for an Ifá priest, in the collection of the Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA).

## Iconography
The rectangular *opon Ifá* is bordered with figural and geometric relief carving framing the working surface. As on most boards the design privileges the top register, where the watchful face of Eshu presides over the act of divination.

## Significance
The board is the central instrument of Ifá practice: powder is strewn on its face and the *babalawo* presses palm-nut counts into it, drawing the eight strokes that fix an *odu*. Boards were heirloom objects, their carved imagery — kneeling devotees, birds, kola, mudfish — encoding the values and *orisha* of the household. The richness of surviving Yoruba boards has made them a touchstone for the study of African divination art (Henry Drewal).

## For artists & game designers
A bordered ritual surface whose carved margin tells a story while its blank centre is the live play-field — a clean separation of lore frame and interactive zone.

citations.text: Henry John Drewal, John Pemberton III & Rowland Abiodun, *Yoruba: Nine Centuries of African Art and Thought* (1989).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Iroke Ifá (Divination Tapper)
work: African & Diaspora Divination, Sign-Systems & Power Objects
creator: Anonymous (Yoruba, Owo)
rights: CC0 (Brooklyn Museum, photo Daderot). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
An ivory *iroke Ifá*, the tapper a Yoruba diviner uses to summon Orunmila at the start of a consultation, in the Brooklyn Museum.

## Iconography
The tapered ivory shaft is surmounted by a finely carved figure — here a kneeling female devotee, a recurrent emblem of piety and offering in Yoruba art. The pointed lower end is struck rhythmically against the *opon Ifá*.

## Significance
Before casting, the *babalawo* taps the tray to wake and greet Orunmila, *orisha* of wisdom. Carved from prestige ivory and often depicting a kneeling woman with breasts cupped in supplication, the *iroke* materialises the proper attitude of the supplicant. Its 18th-century date and Owo provenance place it among the older surviving examples of this regional carving school.

## For artists & game designers
A tool whose use begins with a summoning gesture — the act of "knocking" to wake the oracle — is a tactile ritual-input idea for a divination interface.

citations.text: William Bascom, *Sixteen Cowries: Yoruba Divination from Africa to the New World* (1980).

title: Kuduo (Akan Lidded Brass Vessel)
work: African & Diaspora Divination, Sign-Systems & Power Objects
creator: Anonymous (Akan / Asante)
rights: CC0 (Metropolitan Museum of Art). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A *kuduo*, a lidded cast-brass ritual vessel of the Akan, in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

## Iconography
The lost-wax container is densely worked, often with a figural scene on the lid and bands of geometric and proverbial ornament around the body. Imported brass basins and Islamic metalwork influenced the form.

## Significance
The *kuduo* held gold dust, beads, and offerings and was central to the *kra dware* ("soul-washing") rites that honoured a person's *kra* or life-soul; chiefs' *kuduo* accompanied them in burial. Its surface, like that of the goldweights and Adinkra cloth, participates in the Akan culture of proverb-bearing ornament. It thus belongs to the same web of [[motif:akan goldweight|Akan ritual sign-objects]] as the weights and stamped cloth.

## For artists & game designers
A "soul vessel" that physically stores a character's life-essence and offerings is a vivid object to build a save-the-soul or relic mechanic around.

citations.text: Doran H. Ross, *Gold of the Akan from the Glassell Collection* (2002).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Legba Statue (Vodun, Allada)
work: African & Diaspora Divination, Sign-Systems & Power Objects
creator: Anonymous (Fon), photograph by Netho639
summary:
A Vodun figure of Legba at the Awouto sacred lake near Allada in Benin.

## Iconography
Legba is typically rendered as a rough, earth- and offering-coated mound or figure, often emphatically phallic, set at thresholds, crossroads, and the entrances of compounds and shrines.

## Significance
Legba is the Fon *vodun* of the threshold and the messenger who opens (and closes) the way between humans and the other deities — the cognate of Yoruba Eshu and of Haitian Papa Legba, invoked first in any rite. As gatekeeper he is bound up with [[motif:vodun|Vodun]] divination (Fa): no message reaches the spirits unless Legba carries it. His placement at crossroads and doorways makes him the literal interface of the ritual system, which is why his image guards shrines like this lakeside one.

## For artists & game designers
A "you must greet the gatekeeper first" NPC at every threshold is a clean way to gate access to a divination or spirit-world system.

citations.text: Suzanne Preston Blier, *African Vodun: Art, Psychology, and Power* (1995).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Lukasa (Luba Memory Board)
work: African & Diaspora Divination, Sign-Systems & Power Objects
creator: Anonymous (Luba)
rights: CC0 (Robert C. Williams Paper Museum, photo Daderot). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A Luba *lukasa*, a hand-held wooden memory board used in the initiation of the Mbudye society, in the Robert C. Williams Paper Museum.

## Iconography
The flat, hourglass-shaped board carries a coded surface of beads and pins of varied colour and size set into the wood, sometimes combined with incised or carved relief. The arrangement is not pictorial but mnemonic.

## Significance
The *lukasa* is a mnemonic device of the Mbudye, the Luba royal historians and ritual specialists. Reading the configuration of beads and lines, an initiate could recite migration histories, king-lists, the topography of sacred sites, and the protocols of kingship — "a long hand," the board, guiding a performance of memory. Mary Nooter Roberts and Allen F. Roberts brought the *lukasa* to wide attention as a non-textual information technology of African statecraft.

## For artists & game designers
A bead-board that stores a whole oral archive is a striking model for a diegetic save-file or memory artifact — data as tactile configuration.

citations.text: Mary Nooter Roberts & Allen F. Roberts, *Memory: Luba Art and the Making of History* (1996).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Mangaaka Power Figure (Nkisi Nkondi)
work: African & Diaspora Divination, Sign-Systems & Power Objects
creator: Anonymous (Kongo, Yombe)
rights: CC BY-SA 2.5 (Metropolitan Museum, WLA photo "niborean"). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
The celebrated *Mangaaka* power figure of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, a large Kongo *nkisi nkondi*.

## Iconography
The monumental figure stands with hands on hips (akimbo) and an open, challenging mouth, the body covered in driven iron. *Mangaaka* figures share this commanding stance and an upward, confrontational gaze.

## Significance
*Mangaaka* was a particular force of jurisdiction and supra-village authority invoked in the lower Congo in the period of intensifying European trade and conflict. A cohort of closely related *Mangaaka* figures, dispersed to several museums, has been studied as the output of a regional workshop responding to the disruptions of the late 19th century. Each nail enacted a public oath or judgment. The Met's example is among the best-known [[motif:nkisi|minkisi]] in any collection.

## For artists & game designers
The hands-on-hips, open-mouthed stance is a textbook "authority/challenge" pose — directly usable for an enforcer or judge character silhouette.

citations.text: Alisa LaGamma, *Kongo: Power and Majesty* (2015).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Nkisi Nkondi (Kongo Power Figure)
work: African & Diaspora Divination, Sign-Systems & Power Objects
creator: Anonymous (Kongo)
rights: CC BY 3.0 (Brooklyn Museum). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A Kongo *nkisi nkondi* — a wooden power-figure studded with iron — in the Brooklyn Museum.

## Iconography
The standing figure bristles with driven nails, blades, and pegs. A reflective glass or resin-sealed cavity (often on the belly) holds the *bilongo*, the medicinal/spirit-charging matter; the eyes are frequently mirrored.

## Significance
An *nkisi* (pl. *minkisi*) is a container that localises a spirit; the *nkondi* ("hunter") sub-type pursues wrongdoers and seals oaths. Each nail or blade was hammered in by a ritual specialist (*nganga*) to activate the figure — to ratify a treaty, swear an agreement, or send the spirit against a thief or witch. Wyatt MacGaffey's work reframed these as instruments of justice and contract, not mere "fetishes," correcting a long-distorted colonial reading.

## For artists & game designers
Every nail records a sworn contract or grievance — the object is a tactile ledger of oaths, accreting visible history with use.

citations.text: Wyatt MacGaffey, *Astonishment and Power: Kongo Minkisi* (1993).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Male Figure (Nkisi Nkondi), Vili
work: African & Diaspora Divination, Sign-Systems & Power Objects
creator: Anonymous (Vili)
rights: CC0 (Art Institute of Chicago). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A standing male *nkisi nkondi* attributed to a Vili artist of the Loango coast, in the Art Institute of Chicago.

## Iconography
The full-length figure stands in an assertive pose, its torso and limbs pierced with iron nails and blades accumulated over a working life. The carving's confident frontal stance is typical of Vili/Kongo statuary.

## Significance
The Vili are a Kongo-related people of the Loango coast among whom *minkisi* flourished. As an *nkondi*, this figure "hunted" — it was deployed to enforce agreements and punish offenders, each driven nail marking an act of empowerment by the *nganga*. The empty or once-sealed cavity would have held the *bilongo* that bound a spirit to the wood. Pieces like this in the Art Institute have been central to re-evaluating [[motif:nkisi|Kongo power figures]] as juridical and curative instruments.

## For artists & game designers
Two near-identical hunter-figures from neighbouring peoples show how regional carving "styles" can re-skin one mechanic — good reference for faction visual variants.

citations.text: Wyatt MacGaffey, *Kongo Political Culture* (2000).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Ọpẹlẹ (Ifá Divining Chain)
work: African & Diaspora Divination, Sign-Systems & Power Objects
creator: Anonymous (Yoruba)
summary:
The *ọpẹlẹ*, the divining chain used for rapid everyday Ifá consultation among the Yoruba.

## Iconography
Eight half-seed shells (from the *opele* tree or worked metal/coconut) are strung four to a side along a chain. Each piece can fall concave or convex, so a single throw of the chain instantly displays one of the 256 *odu* as a pattern of eight up/down marks.

## Significance
The chain is the *babalawo*'s quick oracle, reserved for routine questions where the slower palm-nut method on the tray is not needed; major undertakings still use the *ikin* nuts. The eight-element cast makes Ifá an explicitly binary system — a point long noted in comparisons with [[motif:geomancy|geomancy]] and even with Leibniz's binary arithmetic. In the diaspora the chain travelled to Cuba (*okuele*) and Brazil.

## For artists & game designers
Flip eight coins in one motion: the *opele* is the most economical physical random-number generator imaginable for an in-game oracle.

citations.text: William Bascom, *Ifa Divination: Communication Between Gods and Men in West Africa* (1969).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Opon Ifá (Yoruba Divination Tray)
work: African & Diaspora Divination, Sign-Systems & Power Objects
creator: Anonymous (Yoruba)
rights: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Stephanie cheks). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A carved wooden *opon Ifá*, the round or rectangular tray on which a Yoruba diviner reads the oracle of Ifá.

## Iconography
The tray's raised rim is carved in low relief, traditionally crowned at the top edge by the face of Eshu (Èṣù), the trickster messenger who carries communications between humans and the *orisha*. The flat central field is dusted with pale *iyerosun* (camwood/termite) powder, in which the diviner inscribes marks.

## Significance
Ifá is the Yoruba system of wisdom-divination personified by the *orisha* Orunmila. Working the tray, the *babalawo* ("father of secrets") generates one of the 256 *odu* — binary figures of single and double marks — each tied to a vast oral corpus of verses (*ese Ifá*) that the client's case is read against. UNESCO proclaimed the [[motif:ifa divination|Ifá divination system]] a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity in 2005. The form parallels the binary logic of Arabic geomancy (*ʿilm al-raml*).

## For artists & game designers
The 256 *odu* are literally an 8-bit oracle table — a ready-made deterministic lookup keyed to two four-mark casts.

citations.text: William Bascom, *Ifa Divination: Communication Between Gods and Men in West Africa* (1969).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Shaman at Work (Game Pass Shelter Rock Art)
work: African & Diaspora Divination, Sign-Systems & Power Objects
creator: Anonymous (San / Bushman)
place: Game Pass Shelter, Drakensberg, South Africa
summary:
A San (Bushman) rock-painting panel at Game Pass Shelter in the Drakensberg, South Africa — the famous "rosetta" scene of a dying eland and trancing figures.

## Iconography
A large eland sinks with crossed legs and lowered head while human (and part-human, *therianthrope*) figures bend behind it, some with hoofed legs, in the posture of trance. The eland's collapse and the dancers' bowed bodies are rendered in fine polychrome.

## Significance
David Lewis-Williams used this panel to argue that San rock art records the visions and "potency" (*!gi:*) of the trance dance, in which a healer/shaman enters an altered state, "dies" like the dying eland, and travels the spirit world to heal and to make rain. The eland, the most potent animal, fuses with the dancer. This reading reframed Southern African rock art as a ritual record of altered-consciousness experience rather than mere narrative — among the oldest ritual sign-systems in this collection.

## For artists & game designers
The "dying eland" trance scene is a canonical visual of the shaman-dies-to-heal arc — a template for a spirit-journey or downed-and-revived mechanic.

citations.text: J. D. Lewis-Williams, *The Mind in the Cave* (2002).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Sankofa (Adinkra Bird Symbol)
work: African & Diaspora Divination, Sign-Systems & Power Objects
creator: Vector rendering (LunaEclipse)
date: Modern rendering of a traditional Akan symbol
rights: Public domain (SVG rasterized). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
*Sankofa*, the Akan Adinkra symbol of learning from the past, here in its bird form (rasterized from a public-domain SVG).

## Iconography
A stylised bird stands with its body facing forward but its head turned fully back, reaching to take an egg from its own back. A second common form is an abstract heart-like spiral.

## Significance
*Sankofa* derives from the Twi maxim *se wo were fi na wosankɔfa a yenkyi* — "it is not wrong (or taboo) to go back and fetch what you forgot." The backward-looking bird teaches that progress requires reclaiming the wisdom of the past. It has become a central emblem of the African diaspora's recovery of heritage and is among the most-reproduced [[motif:adinkra|Adinkra]] signs in Black Atlantic culture.

## For artists & game designers
The "look back to move forward" bird is a perfect icon for a flashback, recall, or rewind mechanic.

citations.text: R. S. Rattray, *Religion and Art in Ashanti* (1927).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Sikidy (Malagasy Seed Geomancy)
work: African & Diaspora Divination, Sign-Systems & Power Objects
creator: Anonymous (engraving / ethnographic plate)
summary:
A historic plate titled *La Divination par les graines chez les Hova* depicting *sikidy*, the seed-geomancy of Madagascar.

## Iconography
The image shows the *sikidy* tableau: seeds (often fano or tamarind) arranged in a grid of columns and rows, from which the diviner (*ombiasy*) reads paired and odd configurations. The scene records the laying-out of the figures by hand.

## Significance
*Sikidy* is a fully developed geomantic system: starting columns of randomly grasped seeds are reduced to single/double marks and recombined by rule into a tableau of sixteen figures, each with a name and meaning. It is historically connected to Arabic *ʿilm al-raml* ("the science of the sand") carried down the Swahili coast, making it a direct African cousin of Western geomancy and an analogue to the binary logic of [[motif:ifa divination|Ifá]]. Its algorithmic, rule-bound computation has drawn the attention of ethnomathematicians (Marcia Ascher).

## For artists & game designers
*Sikidy* is essentially a deterministic algorithm run on random seed-columns — almost directly codeable as a divination subroutine.

citations.text: Marcia Ascher, "Malagasy Sikidy: A Case in Ethnomathematics," *Historia Mathematica* (1997).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Lusona (Chokwe Sand-Drawing)
work: African & Diaspora Divination, Sign-Systems & Power Objects
creator: Anonymous (Chokwe, diagram after ethnographic record)
summary:
A *lusona* (plural *sona*), one of the geometric sand-drawings of the Chokwe people of Central Africa.

## Iconography
The design begins as a regular grid of dots in the sand around which a single continuous looping line is drawn, weaving over and under itself to form a symmetrical figure that often represents an animal, object, or proverb.

## Significance
The *sona* are drawn by men in the sand to illustrate stories, proverbs, and cosmological ideas; the most skilled (*akwa kuta sona*) execute complex figures in one unbroken stroke. Beyond their narrative use they encode a sophisticated implicit geometry — symmetry, monolinearity, and what mathematicians recognise as graph- and lattice-theoretic structure — studied at length by Paulus Gerdes as a tradition of "sand mathematics." As mnemonic and ritual diagrams they sit alongside the *lukasa* among Central African knowledge-systems.

## For artists & game designers
A single-stroke loop around a dot lattice is a generative drawing algorithm — procedural ornament with a built-in "draw without lifting the pen" puzzle.

citations.text: Paulus Gerdes, *Sona Geometry from Angola: Mathematics of an African Tradition* (2006).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Vodun Shrine (Benin)
work: African & Diaspora Divination, Sign-Systems & Power Objects
creator: Photograph by Kulttuurinavigaattori
summary:
A Vodun shrine in Benin, the West African homeland of the Vodun religion that gave rise to Haitian Vodou and New Orleans Voodoo.

## Iconography
The shrine massed with mounded earthen forms, libation-stained surfaces, cloth, and assembled offerings — the accreted material of repeated sacrifice rather than a single sculpted image.

## Significance
Vodun ("spirit") is the religion of the Fon and Ewe of Benin and Togo, centred on a pantheon of *vodun* deities (Legba, Mawu-Lisa, Dan the serpent, Gu) approached through offering, possession, and divination — notably Fa, the Benin counterpart of Yoruba [[motif:ifa divination|Ifá]]. Carried across the Atlantic in the slave trade, it underlies Haitian Vodou and its *vèvè* ground-drawings and *lwa*. A living shrine like this one documents the tradition at its source, against the long history of its sensational misrepresentation in the West.

## For artists & game designers
An altar built up by use — every offering leaves a trace — is a model for an environment object that visibly records the player's ritual actions over time.

citations.text: Suzanne Preston Blier, *African Vodun: Art, Psychology, and Power* (1995).
Wikimedia Commons

title: *De Re Metallica* — modern Ukrainian edition cover (Books VII–XII)
creator: after Georgius Agricola (modern Ukrainian translation; cover designer unknown)
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: per source — modern Ukrainian edition (Про гірничу справу); Wikimedia scan]
rights: Public domain (cover reproduces public-domain motifs; image via Wikimedia).
summary:
The companion volume cover of the modern Ukrainian Agricola — *Георгій Агрікола, Про гірничу справу XII книг (Книги VII–XII)* ('On Mining, in twelve books — Books VII–XII'). Recorded honestly as a modern book cover rather than a period plate.

## Iconography
The design mirrors its companion: a richly coloured architectural frame with flanking putti (one shouldering a pick), scrolled volutes and a winged crest, enclosing an oval vignette of a craggy landscape under a radiant sun with miners at work, and a figured interior panel below. The Cyrillic title sits across the oval.

## Significance
The two-volume set divides Agricola's twelve books between Books I–VI (prospecting, surveying, machines) and Books VII–XII (assaying, smelting, refining, salts and the subterranean creatures). The cover again demonstrates the continuing [[motif:reception|reception]] of *De Re Metallica* as a living technical classic well into the present.

## For artists & game designers

## Iconography
In the upper cut the assayer leans toward a tall round furnace, its glowing muffle visible; a low wall and a wooded slope close the background. In the lower cut he sits on a stool at a rectangular furnace, holding tongs to the fire. The two designs document alternative furnace forms for the same delicate operation.

## Significance
Assaying — the small-scale [[motif:fire-test|fire test]] that determines how much gold or silver an ore truly holds — is the subject of Agricola's seventh book and the quantitative heart of the metal trades. [[motif:cupellation|Cupellation]] in the muffle, weighing the bead of precious metal against a known charge, gave the assayer an authority the alchemist envied: a true measure won by fire.

Roman and italic type announce the twelve books on mining and metallurgy and the appended *De Animantibus Subterraneis* ('On Subterranean Creatures'). The Froben caduceus marks one of the great scholarly presses of the Renaissance — the house of Erasmus's printer — and lends Agricola's metallurgy the authority of humanist Basel. The book appeared in 1556, the year after the author's death, and became the standard treatise on [[motif:mining|mining]] for two centuries.

Across a broken landscape several figures are at work — one striding with a long forked stick (the divining-rod or *virgula furcata* used to dowse for veins), others crouched at the water's edge sorting and washing heaps of ore, a gentleman observer at left. The search for the vein opens the practical programme of *De Re Metallica*. Agricola describes — and, sceptically, debates — the use of the forked twig to find ore, the lie of the land and the signs of metal in springs and soil. The plate belongs to the foundational work of [[motif:mining|Renaissance mining]] literature, the book that displaced lore with method and that Herbert Hoover and his wife famously translated in 1912.

A lettered key names every part — the iron bands and straps, the iron axle, the wooden rollers, the small iron keys and the large blunt pin — and the same truck is shown upright and turned upside down.

The loaded box-truck sits on its little wheels by a tree at upper right; below, the body is drawn again inverted to expose the rollers and ironwork, with the loose components (axle, pin, keys, rollers) laid out separately and labelled A–G. It is a parts-diagram in the modern sense.

Agricola's exploded mechanical drawings are a landmark in technical illustration: he shows not only the machine in use but its components disassembled and named, so that the reader could build one. The ore-truck running in a wooden guide-track is an ancestor of the railway, and Book VI's catalogue of [[motif:machinery|mine machinery]] remains a key source for the history of engineering.

Smelting is the climactic operation of [[motif:metallurgy|Agricola's metallurgy]] — the reduction of ore to running metal by fire and forced blast. title: Portrait of Cornelius Agrippa (Wellcome L0004889, after Boissard)
creator: Jean-Jacques Boissard (attrib.); engraved unknown
rights: CC BY 4.0. Wellcome Collection. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A Wellcome Collection engraved portrait of Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim (1486–1535), after the tradition of Jean-Jacques Boissard's *Icones* portraits of learned men.

## Iconography
The portrait shows Agrippa in three-quarter or half-length view, wearing academic robes, with the accoutrements of a learned scholar. Such portraits circulated as frontispieces in printed books and as separate engravings, establishing the visual identity of notable humanists for educated European audiences. The Boissard *Icones virorum illustrium* (1597–1599) included Agrippa's portrait as part of its gallery of Renaissance luminaries.

## Significance
Agrippa's visual identity was fixed in the historical imagination partly through engravings like this one. He appears as a respectable scholar rather than a diabolical magician — consistent with his own self-presentation in *De Occulta Philosophia* as a Christian humanist philosopher drawing on legitimate ancient sources. The contrast between this sober portrait and the sensational reputation attributed to him by later legend (including the claim that he was accompanied by a daemon in the form of a black dog) illustrates the gap between the historical Agrippa and the mythological one.

## For artists & game designers
Agrippa's historical portrait type — middle-aged German scholar in academic dress — is the source for the conventional Renaissance magician image: serious, learned, not particularly alarming. The visual dissonance between this and the sensational content of his books is itself a design resource.

title: Portrait of Cornelius Agrippa (British Museum 1879,1213.276)
creator: Unknown engraver
summary:
A portrait engraving of Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim (1486–1535) in the British Museum collection (accession number 1879,1213.276), one of the principal surviving images of the most celebrated occult philosopher of the Northern Renaissance.

## Iconography
The engraving presents Agrippa in half-length, presumably in scholarly dress, with Latin or German inscription identifying him. British Museum portrait prints of this period were typically produced as single-sheet prints for the collector's portrait album market, where images of notable scholars and theologians circulated alongside those of rulers and military commanders.

## Significance
Agrippa's reputation was extraordinary in his own lifetime and immediately after: admired as a prodigy of learning by Erasmus's circle, feared as a dangerous magician by his enemies, repeatedly imprisoned and driven from city to city by powerful opponents. His *De Vanitate Scientiarum* (1530), a devastating satirical critique of all forms of learning including his own *De Occulta Philosophia*, paradoxically increased his fame. The range of portrait prints produced in the years after his death reflects this celebrity. This British Museum print is one of the earlier and more authoritative portraits.

## For artists & game designers
The British Museum portrait is the most historically grounded image of Agrippa available. Using it as a reference for a fictional character based on him provides maximum scholarly credibility.

title: Portrait of Cornelius Agrippa (Wellcome M0002736)
creator: Unknown engraver (Wellcome Collection)
rights: CC BY 4.0. Wellcome Collection. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A Wellcome Collection engraved portrait of Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa (Wellcome no. M0002736), one of multiple portrait prints of the occult philosopher held by the Wellcome Library — which assembled one of the world's largest collections of material relating to the history of medicine and esoteric healing.

## Iconography
The Wellcome M0002736 portrait shows Agrippa in a style typical of 16th–17th-century European scholar portraiture: half-length or three-quarter view, in academic or clerical dress, with name inscription and often date of birth/death. Agrippa's reputation as a physician and medical theorist as well as a magician made his portrait a natural subject for the Wellcome Library's collecting focus on medical history.

## Significance
The Wellcome Collection's multiple portraits of Agrippa (L0004889, L0002995, L0015112, L0015114, M0002736) testify to the sustained 16th–17th-century market for images of learned men whose intellectual lives intersected medicine, natural philosophy, and occult knowledge. Agrippa's *De Occulta Philosophia* Book I includes substantial material on medical magic and natural healing, and his medical doctorate (from Pavia) was a genuine credential in a world that did not sharply distinguish physician from magician. His portrait in the Wellcome collection positions him in a tradition of learned healer rather than popular wizard.

## For artists & game designers
The Wellcome portrait range, with its consistent 'learned physician' framing of Agrippa, provides an alternative to the more dramatic wizard-figure stereotype — useful for fiction that wants to present Renaissance magic as a form of natural philosophy.

title: Woodcut Portrait of Cornelius Agrippa (*Agrippa von Nettesheim*)
creator: Unknown woodcut artist
summary:
A woodcut portrait of Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa von Nettesheim (1486–1535), the most celebrated occult philosopher of the Northern Renaissance, as he was represented in the visual culture of 16th-century Germany.

## Iconography
The woodcut presents Agrippa in three-quarter bust, typically with beard and cap of the German humanist scholar type. Woodcut portraits of this kind were produced as cheap multiple-format images for insertion in books or sale as single sheets, and circulated widely through the German-language print trade. The cut itself has the characteristic rough-hewn quality of 16th-century German woodcut portraiture: bold outlines, hatched shading, and a robust physical presence.

## Significance
Agrippa's reputation in German humanist culture was enormous: he corresponded with Johann Trithemius (abbot of Sponheim and cryptographer), knew Paracelsus at least by reputation, and was known to Erasmus's circle. His career took him from Cologne (where he studied) to Pavia (medical degree), Italy (with Maximilian I's army), Metz (as city advocate), Geneva, Cologne again, Lyon (as archivist), and Antwerp (as imperial historiographer), before ending in poverty. This woodcut portrait fixes him as a German scholar-figure, appropriate to his Cologne formation.

## For artists & game designers
The woodcut portrait type — crude, energetic, immediate — gives Agrippa a popular presence quite different from the refined engraved portraits. The same person can look like an alarming figure in woodcut and a respectable philosopher in copper engraving.
