title: Byzantine Solomonic Manuscript, Full Page — BL Harley MS 5596
work: Ars Notoria & the Angelic Theurgy Tradition
creator: Anonymous (Byzantine Greek scribe)
summary:
Full-page view of British Library Harley MS 5596 — the 15th-century Byzantine Greek *Hygromanteia* (*Magical Treatise of Solomon*), showing the complete manuscript layout of a Solomonic operational text.

## Iconography
The full page reveals the holistic structure of the Byzantine magical manuscript: dense Greek text in a careful minuscule hand, rubrication (red ink for titles and headings), and magical seals or figures embedded in the margins or between sections. The page is a complete unit of the ritual handbook — the text gives the oration, the seal provides the operative image, the rubric identifies the planetary hour or spiritual power being addressed.

## Significance
Viewing the full page of Harley MS 5596 reveals the manuscript as an object rather than merely a text-carrier: a carefully produced, well-preserved working manual of Byzantine Solomonic magic. The *Hygromanteia* was not a fringe text but a widely copied and used handbook; this manuscript's survival in the Harley Collection (assembled by Robert Harley, 1st Earl of Oxford, and donated to the British Museum in 1753) reflects the 18th-century collecting of occult manuscripts as objects of antiquarian interest. It is the most directly accessible Byzantine witness to the Greek-language tradition that shaped the Latin *Ars Notoria* milieu.

## For artists & game designers
The full manuscript aesthetic: Byzantine red-and-black layout, dense handwritten Greek, embedded operational seals — the 'foreign grimoire' or 'eastern magical tradition' visual register.

summary:
A leaf from British Library Harley MS 5596, a 15th-century Byzantine Greek manuscript of the *Hygromanteia* or *Magical Treatise of Solomon* — the Greek-language bridge between late-antique magic and the Western Solomonic grimoire tradition.

## Iconography
The manuscript page shows the characteristic Byzantine magical manuscript format: Greek text interspersed with magical seals (*characteres*), spirit-signs, and ritual instructions for conjuring and binding the angels and spirits of the planetary hours. The dense small-hand calligraphy and the placement of the seals within the text reflect a working manual structure: read the instruction, perform the operation, use the seal depicted on the same page.

## Significance
Harley MS 5596 is one of the principal witnesses to the *Hygromanteia*, the Greek Solomonic handbook that Ioannis Marathakis has edited and translated as *The Magical Treatise of Solomon* (2011). The *Hygromanteia* belongs to a tradition of Byzantine Solomonic magic that predates the Latin *Clavicula* but fed into it, establishing the day-and-hour structure, planetary angel correspondences, and conjuration framework that the Latin tradition adopted. It is the Greek parallel to the same stream that produced the *Ars Notoria*: Solomonic-attributed texts of learned ritual magic aimed at angelic or spirit contact. The *characteres* in this manuscript closely resemble the notae of the *Ars Notoria* tradition — both are graphic instruments of spirit-address.

## For artists & game designers
The Eastern predecessor: the Greek manuscript aesthetics (uncial or minuscule hand, red-and-black ink, embedded spirit-signs) that underlies the Latin tradition, useful for establishing historical depth in a worldbuilding context.

title: First Figure of Grammar (*Ars Notoria*), BnF Latin 9336
work: Ars Notoria & the Angelic Theurgy Tradition
creator: Anonymous (French scribe)
summary:
The first figure of grammar from the *Ars Notoria* — the singular, extraordinary visual instrument of the most widely copied magical learning text of the medieval West — held in BnF Latin 9336, one of the earliest surviving manuscripts of the tradition.

## Iconography
The *nota* is a densely constructed diagram of interlacing bands, concentric rings, and compartments filled with divine names, Hebrew-derived letter-strings, and *verba ignota* — 'unknown words' whose precise pronunciation was believed to carry operative force. This figure corresponds to the art of grammar: correct speech, right understanding, the ground of all literacy. Its visual complexity is not decorative but functional; the practitioner was to gaze upon it for an extended time while reciting the accompanying orations, allowing the discipline to be infused directly into the mind by angelic intermediaries.

## Significance
The *Ars Notoria* (Art of Notes, or Notarial Art) circulated from at least the early 13th century, often attributed to Solomon or Apollonius of Tyana, and claimed to convey the seven liberal arts, memory, eloquence, and divine wisdom through prayer and visual contemplation rather than ordinary study. Thomas Aquinas condemned it as trafficking with demons; John of Salisbury described it in the 12th century; John of Morigny spent years in visionary dialogue reworking it. Its imagery belongs to the tradition of figure-magic: the diagram as channel rather than illustration. BnF Latin 9336 is one of the key witnesses; Julien Véronèse's 2007 critical edition is the standard scholarly treatment.

## For artists & game designers
A 'study figure' the player activates to unlock a skill — knowledge literally written into the mind by an angelic patron, bypassing the ordinary grind of learning.

summary:
The figure of logic (*nota logicae vel dialecticae*) from the *Ars Notoria*, reconstructed from Bodleian MS Bodley 951 — one of the most structurally elaborate of the surviving notae.

## Iconography
The diagram presents the characteristic *nota* structure: a central form — here corresponding to the art of logic or dialectic — composed of interlacing lines, barred bands, and lettered compartments. The compartments carry the divine names and *verba ignota* associated with the angelic powers of reasoned argument and disputational skill. The interlace creates a visual density that is not decorative but mnemonic: the practitioner's gaze is meant to track, hold, and absorb the figure, not merely glance at it.

## Significance
MS Bodley 951 is one of the key English witnesses to the *Ars Notoria*. The Bodleian collection preserves several Ars Notoria manuscripts, reflecting the text's wide 13th–15th century English circulation in clerical and university circles. The scholar Julien Véronèse has catalogued the manuscript witnesses and established that the *notae* underwent significant evolution across transmission: figures were redrawn, simplified, elaborated, and occasionally corrupted. This reconstruction by a modern scholar working from the folio is therefore both a document about the tradition and an act of interpretation within it.

## For artists & game designers
The 'reasoning' skill glyph — unlock debate, persuasion, and deduction mechanics by contemplating this angular, interlaced diagram.

title: Fragment of the *Picatrix* (*Ghāyat al-Ḥakīm*) Manuscript
work: Ars Notoria & the Angelic Theurgy Tradition
creator: Anonymous (attributed to Maslama al-Majriti, 10th–11th c.)
summary:
A fragment of the *Picatrix* (*Ghāyat al-Ḥakīm*, 'Aim of the Sage') — the foundational handbook of astral image-magic, the Islamic parallel to the *Ars Notoria* current and its greatest influence on Renaissance learned magic.

## Iconography
The manuscript leaf presents dense Arabic text — the operational instructions of the *Picatrix*: the manufacture of talismans at elected astrological moments, the carving of planetary and decan images on appropriate metals, the suffumigations and petitions addressed to planetary spirits. The material is technical and precise: times, materials, figures, prayers — a surgical manual for drawing celestial virtue into matter.

## Significance
Compiled in al-Andalus c. 10th–11th century and translated into Castilian and then Latin under Alfonso X of Castile in 1256, the *Picatrix* transmitted Hermetic, Neoplatonic, and Sabian (Harranian) astral magic into European learned culture. Ficino's *De vita coelitus comparanda*, Agrippa's *De occulta philosophia*, and the planetary-talisman chapter of the *Clavicula Salomonis* all descend from the *Picatrix*. David Pingree's edition of both the Arabic (*Ghāyat al-Ḥakīm*) and the Latin (*Picatrix*) texts is the standard reference. Unlike the *Ars Notoria*, the *Picatrix* explicitly describes a mechanical theory — the image carved at the right stellar moment captures the star's influence — rather than the Notoria's relational-angelic model, but both share the project of guaranteed knowledge and power through correct procedure.

## For artists & game designers
The 'craft under the stars' mechanic: talisman creation requiring astrological timing, correct materials, and inscribed planetary figures — the *Picatrix* is the original source.

summary:
A page of *segulot* (protective amulet-diagrams) from the *Sefer Raziel HaMalakh* — the Book of the Angel Raziel, the Hebrew parallel to the Latin *Ars Notoria* tradition in its claim to angelic transmission of universal knowledge.

## Iconography
The page presents rows of circular or square figures inscribed with Hebrew divine names, angelic names, and Psalm verses — the classic *segulot* format. Each figure is keyed to a specific protective or remedial purpose: easing childbirth, warding fire, healing illness, guarding sleep. They were copied onto parchment and worn on the body or hung in the home, the inscribed names themselves acting as the operative force.

## Significance
The *Sefer Raziel*, attributed to the angel Raziel who gave the book to Adam, is a composite work gathering Hekhalot, practical Kabbalah, and medieval learned-magic material. A Latin translation, the *Liber Razielis*, was assembled at the court of Alfonso X of Castile in the 13th century — contemporaneous with the Latin *Ars Notoria* — and circulated widely in learned European circles. Sophie Page's *Magic in the Cloister* documents its presence in English monastic libraries. The parallel traditions — Latin *Ars Notoria* and Hebrew *Sefer Raziel* — drew on overlapping networks of divine-name magic and reflect the shared intellectual world of Jewish and Christian learned magic in medieval Europe.

## For artists & game designers
A page of ready-made portable charms: copy the figure onto parchment, wear it — the magic is in the inscription, not the practitioner.

title: *Shams al-Ma'ārif al-Kubrā* (The Great Sun of Knowledge) — al-Būnī
work: Ars Notoria & the Angelic Theurgy Tradition
creator: Ahmad ibn Ali al-Buni (d. 1225 CE)
rights: CC BY-SA 3.0 igo (Khalili Collections). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A double spread from al-Būnī's *Shams al-Ma'ārif al-Kubrā* (The Great Sun of Knowledge) — the supreme Arabic manual of divine-name magic, letter mysticism, and *wafq* (magic squares), a direct Islamic parallel to the Latin *Ars Notoria*.

## Iconography
The spread shows the characteristic al-Būnī page: dense Arabic calligraphy interleaved with talismanic figures, *wafq* (Arabic numerical magic squares aligned with divine names), geometric diagrams, and rows of inscribed panels. The aesthetic is one of total inscription — no space is dead, every corner carries operative text. The figures combine the visual vocabulary of Islamic geometric ornament with the functional requirements of operative magic.

## Significance
Ahmad ibn Ali al-Būnī (Egypt, d. 1225 CE) wrote the *Shams al-Ma'ārif* contemporaneously with the earliest Latin *Ars Notoria* manuscripts — the two traditions share the moment. Al-Būnī's system centres on *ism al-a'zam* (the greatest name of God), letter combinations (*tarkīb*), and *wafq* magic squares as instruments of divine access and operative power, paralleling the *Ars Notoria*'s divine names and *notae* almost point for point. The *Shams al-Ma'ārif* was the most widely copied Arabic occult text; it circulated across the Islamic world from Morocco to Indonesia and fed into the Ottoman and Persian occult traditions. Liana Saif and Noah Gardiner have written on al-Būnī's work; this Khalili manuscript is a high-quality witness.

## For artists & game designers
The Arabic tradition's master diagram-book: dense, geometric, inscribed — visually distinct from the Latin notae but functionally identical in premise: operate on divine names through correct figures.

title: Sigillum Dei (Giorgio Anselmi / Georgius Parmensis)
work: Ars Notoria & the Angelic Theurgy Tradition
creator: Giorgio Anselmi (Georgius Parmensis), 15th c.
summary:
A version of the *Sigillum Dei* (Seal of God) by Giorgio Anselmi (Georgius Parmensis) — one of the most formidable diagrams of the medieval learned-magic tradition, parent of John Dee's *Sigillum Dei Aemeth*.

## Iconography
The seal is built from nested geometry: an outer ring carrying the names of God and his angels in Latin and pseudo-Hebrew, an inner heptagon or heptagram with angel-names in each vertex, and a pentagram or five-pointed star at the centre. Every zone is packed with divine names, crosses, and characters, each compartment assigned to a specific spiritual power. The overall effect is that of a sealed cosmogram: creation's governance structure rendered in geometry, with no space left unclaimed by divine authority.

## Significance
The *Sigillum Dei* descends from the *Liber Juratus Honorii* (Sworn Book of Honorius, compiled c. 1300) and was the central talisman of the Honorian tradition. Julien Véronèse and Jan R. Veenstra have traced its genealogy and noted its direct dependence on the *Ars Notoria* current — the *Liber Juratus* is, in many respects, an evolved and Christianized redaction of the Notoria. Giorgio Anselmi (fl. 15th c., Parma) was one of the learned Italian practitioners who copied and refined these instruments; his version is notable for its precision and textual richness.

## For artists & game designers
The 'old master' version of the Sigillum — a densely architectural seal suggesting generational accumulation, the protective mandala that has been refined across centuries.

title: Sigillum Dei Aemeth (Seal of God, True)
work: Ars Notoria & the Angelic Theurgy Tradition
creator: John Dee and Edward Kelley (attr.); this rendering anonymous
rights: CC0 (public domain dedication). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
The *Sigillum Dei Aemeth* — 'Seal of the True God' — the master protective and summoning diagram of John Dee's Enochian angelic system, descending directly from the *Liber Juratus* (Sworn Book of Honorius, 13th–14th c.).

## Iconography
The seal is a complex concentric diagram: outer rings carry the divine names and the names of angels governing the seven planets; an inner heptagram and heptagon are inscribed with further angel-names and divine attributes; a central pentagram or five-pointed figure lies at the heart. The whole is a cosmogram encoding the governance of creation through angelic hierarchies — to possess and correctly employ the seal is to operate within the exact structure of celestial order.

## Significance
The *Sigillum Dei* descends from the *Liber Juratus*, where it is presented as the seal by which God governs angels and devils — the master instrument of the Honorian tradition, which is itself the direct heir of the *Ars Notoria* current. John Dee received this version of the seal in 1582 through Edward Kelley, who perceived it during a crystal-gazing session; Dee then had seven copies made in beeswax, placed beneath the legs of his scrying table and his chair. The British Museum preserves Dee's original wax seals. The seal became the central instrument of the Enochian sessions, linking the *Ars Notoria* → *Liber Juratus* → Dee lineage directly.

## For artists & game designers
The master ward of the Western magical tradition: place beneath a workspace to establish a protected ritual environment; nine-fold ring structure makes it visually unmistakable as a 'high tier' seal.

A circular or ringed figure, inscribed with names and characters, designed as a complete operative talisman. The 'Fourth Seal' designation locates it within the systematic enumeration of seals across the book — each seal corresponds to a specific operation or day. The visual vocabulary is consistent with the broader Solomonic seal tradition but rendered in the simplified style of the folk-magic print market.

## Significance
The individual seals of the *Sixth and Seventh Books of Moses* are functionally direct descendants of the *Clavicula Salomonis* pentacles and, through them, of the overall Solomonic-Honorian tradition. The simplification from elaborately inscribed manuscript pentacles to printed single-purpose seals reflects the democratization of learned magic across the 18th and 19th centuries: the same operative logic (divine names in prescribed geometric form), stripped of its Latin scholarly apparatus and made reproducible by ordinary people. In African and African-diaspora contexts, these seals were often further reinterpreted and syncretized with local spiritual practices.

## For artists & game designers
A clean individual seal tile — assign one effect per seal, let the player collect them as a set; the '4th' designation implies a progression or rotation system.

title: *Sixth and Seventh Books of Moses* — Mosaic Magic Symbols Plate (Fig. 104, 1880)
work: Ars Notoria & the Angelic Theurgy Tradition
creator: Anonymous (ed. 1880, after older tradition)
key_concepts: Sixth and Seventh Books of Moses
summary:
A plate of magical symbols from *The Sixth and Seventh Books of Moses* (1880 edition) — the operative seals and figures of the Mosaic magical tradition as it was presented to 19th-century readers.

## Iconography
The figure presents a collection of talismanic signs and symbols described as originating with Moses: geometric shapes, star forms, ringed characters, and name-combinations. The style is simpler and more schematic than the medieval Solomonic pentacles or the *Ars Notoria* notae, reflecting the folk-magic context — these are meant to be copied by ordinary users without specialist training.

## Significance
The seals and symbols of the *Sixth and Seventh Books of Moses* represent the 19th-century popular end of the Solomonic-Mosaic magical tradition — vastly simplified from the learned Latin MS culture of the *Ars Notoria* cycle, but continuous with it in the key claim: that certain diagrams inscribed with divine names carry operative force when correctly reproduced. The book's rapid spread through Afro-Atlantic communities (particularly in Ghana, Nigeria, Jamaica, and southern United States) created one of the most geographically distributed folk-magic traditions of the modern era. George Eaton Simpson and Emmanuel Akyeampong have documented its reception in West Africa.

## For artists & game designers
Folk-level magical symbols: simpler and more accessible than learned seals, but drawing on the same tradition — the 'common person's grimoire' aesthetic.

title: *The Sixth and Seventh Books of Moses* — Frontispiece (1880 edition)
work: Ars Notoria & the Angelic Theurgy Tradition
creator: Anonymous (attributed to Moses; this ed. 1880)
motifs: sixth and seventh books of moses

summary:
The frontispiece of *The Sixth and Seventh Books of Moses* in its 1880 edition — one of the most widely distributed folk-magic grimoires of the German and German-American tradition, placing itself in direct succession to the biblical Moses.

## Iconography
The frontispiece shows the title, the attribution to Moses, and emblematic imagery establishing the work's claimed Mosaic-Solomonic authority. The design is characteristic of 19th-century occult popular publishing: authoritative title, Mosaic or mystical emblem, and a dateline suggesting antiquity.

## Significance
*The Sixth and Seventh Books of Moses* is an 18th–19th century German compilation presenting itself as the secret books that Moses used to perform the plagues and miracles, now supplemented with Solomonic seals and protective charms. It circulated widely among German-speaking immigrant communities in North America (where it fed directly into Pennsylvania Dutch *Pow-wow* folk magic) and in West Africa (where German missionaries and traders introduced it, and it was absorbed into various African and African-diaspora magical traditions, including in Jamaica and Nigeria). The attribution to Moses parallels the Solomonic attribution of the *Ars Notoria* cycle: both invoke biblical authority to legitimate extra-ecclesiastical magical practice.

## For artists & game designers
The immigrant's grimoire: a folk-magic book carried across the Atlantic, absorbed into new cultures, and adapted for new needs — a prop with a genuinely complex historical journey.

title: John Dee's Angelic Operations Notebook (Sloane MS 3188)
work: Ars Notoria & the Angelic Theurgy Tradition
creator: John Dee
summary:
A page from John Dee's own record of his angelic scrying operations, British Library Sloane MS 3188 — the primary document of the Enochian system and the culmination of the *Ars Notoria* → *Liber Juratus* lineage.

## Iconography
The manuscript page shows Dee's meticulous record of an angelic session: arrangements of the instruments (the showstone, the Table of Practice, the Sigillum Dei Aemeth), notation of the spirit communications received through Edward Kelley's visions in the crystal, and the careful logging of angelic names and utterances. The shaky minuscule hand is Dee's own; the record exists as a real-time transcript of an event he believed was literally occurring.

## Significance
Sloane MS 3188 is, alongside the Sloane 3189 and British Library Cotton MSS, the foundational primary source for Dee's Enochian system. Dee understood his sessions as a direct continuation of the Solomonic-Honorian tradition of angelic communication: the *Sigillum Dei Aemeth* beneath his scrying table was the Honorian instrument; the *Liber Juratus* was in his library; the *Ars Notoria* framework of angelic knowledge transmission is the template his system inhabits. Deborah Harkness's *John Dee's Conversations with Angels* and György Szönyi's *John Dee's Occultism* are the standard modern studies.

## For artists & game designers
The working mage's notebook: handwritten session logs, crossed-out errors, careful diagrams — knowledge hard-won in real time from an unreliable supernatural channel.

title: Magical Circles and Seals of Solomon — 19th Century Grimoire Plate
work: Ars Notoria & the Angelic Theurgy Tradition
creator: Anonymous (occultist)
rights: CC BY 4.0 (Wellcome Collection). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
Four diagrams of magical circles and Solomonic seals from a 19th-century grimoire manuscript, held in the Wellcome Collection — the working instruments of Solomonic conjuration as they circulated in the occult revival.

## Iconography
The plate shows four separate figures: a protective circle of Solomon inscribed with divine names in Hebrew and Latin, a Triangle of Solomon into which the summoned spirit is compelled to appear, smaller Solomonic seals, and a vessel or container form. Each is laid out as a practical working diagram — the kind drawn on the floor in chalk, inscribed on parchment, or engraved on wax at the planetary hour.

## Significance
The Wellcome Collection holds an extraordinary archive of occult manuscripts and printed books reflecting European ritual magic from the medieval period through the 19th century. This 19th-century plate documents the continued use and copying of Solomonic conjuration diagrams well into the era of the occult revival, bridging manuscript culture and the printed editions of Mathers and Waite. The protective circle descends directly from the *Heptameron*, the *Clavicula Salomonis*, and ultimately from the spatial-purification principles of the *Ars Notoria* tradition, where the practitioner's space is separated from the ordinary world before angelic contact is attempted.

## For artists & game designers
A complete set of ritual-space blueprints: protective circle, summoning triangle, seals — the three-component system of Solomonic operations depicted together on one plate.

title: Solomon Receives the *Ars Notoria* from the Angel Pamphilius
work: Ars Notoria & the Angelic Theurgy Tradition
creator: Anonymous (French or Italian scribe)
summary:
Solomon receives the *Ars Notoria* from the angel Pamphilius in the Temple — the founding scene of the tradition, in which divine learning passes directly from the angelic realm into human hands.

## Iconography
The image shows a crowned Solomon figure in dialogue with a winged angel, the exchange framed within a temple or palace setting. The angel carries or presents the book — the *Ars Notoria* itself — to the king, establishing its claim to revealed rather than merely human authorship. The hieratic composition deliberately mirrors scenes of scriptural revelation: the gesture and setting echo images of Moses receiving the Law, grounding magical authority in the same vocabulary as sacred tradition.

## Significance
The Solomonic attribution was the standard medieval legitimating device for ritual magic: by claiming derivation from Solomon's own angelic instruction, a text placed itself in the lineage of God's most favoured operative. The angel Pamphilius is unique to the *Ars Notoria* tradition and appears in the prologues of several manuscripts as the celestial transmitter of the figures and orations. This image from BnF Latin 7153 (15th–16th c.) is one of the most evocative surviving frontispieces of the tradition. The *Ars Notoria* was not condemned as diabolical but as problematically circumventing human effort — the scandal was that it worked by divine infusion, not demonic pact.

## For artists & game designers
The definitive 'forbidden gift' scene: a patron-angel privately delivering a system of power, outside the ordinary channels of study, church, or guild.

title: A Theurgist Performing Rituals to Exercise Divine Powers — Wellcome Collection
work: Ars Notoria & the Angelic Theurgy Tradition
creator: Anonymous (coloured aquatint, early 19th c.)
rights: CC BY 4.0 (Wellcome Collection). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A coloured aquatint depicting a theurgist in the midst of a ritual to exercise divine powers — a rare early 19th-century image of the magical practitioner at work, held in the Wellcome Collection.

## Iconography
The image shows a robed figure operating within or around a ritual space — likely a magic circle, with implements of the art (candles, wand, book, diagram). The 'theurgist' label is significant: theurgy, literally 'god-working', was the specific term for ritual magic aimed at divine contact as opposed to lower-order sorcery or demon-conjuration. The coloured aquatint format suggests this is an illustration from an occult or antiquarian publication of the period rather than a working diagram.

## Significance
The Wellcome Collection holds the largest archive of the history of medicine and occult practice in the UK, and images like this one document the visual culture of magical practice in the early 19th century — the period of the occult revival that bridges the Enlightenment dismissal of magic and the Romantic recuperation of it. The theurgist image belongs to the same cultural moment as Barrett's *Magus* (1801) and prefigures the Golden Dawn systematization of 'high magic' as theurgy. The term itself, revived from Iamblichus and Proclus, was used deliberately to distinguish ritual magic aimed at divine/angelic ascent — like the *Ars Notoria* — from mere sorcery.

## For artists & game designers
A rare practitioner scene rather than diagram — shows the human operator in action: robed, centred, working the space. Useful for NPC or player-character magical-practice aesthetics.

title: Adhai-dvipa Paṭa (Two-and-a-Half Continents of the Middle World)
creator: Anonymous (Jain, India)
summary:
An *Adhai-dvipa paṭa*, a Jain cloth cosmogram mapping the *adhai dvipa* — the 'two and a half continents' that make up the only inhabitable region of the middle world.

## Iconography
The map is rigorously concentric: at the centre sits the rose-form continent of *Jambudvipa* with Mount Meru at its hub, ringed by alternating annular oceans and continents (Lavana ocean, Dhatakikhanda, Kaloda ocean, the inner half of Pushkaravara). A circular mountain wall closes off the inhabited zone, beyond which humans cannot be born.

## Significance
This is the cartography of *manushyaloka*, the human world, a tiny disc within the vast Jain universe. The geometric severity is doctrinal: distances and proportions are scriptural facts, and the diagram functions as both devotional object and mnemonic of the cosmos's measured order. Such *paṭa* were hung for instruction and contemplation.

## For artists & game designers
Concentric ring-oceans and ring-continents make an elegant radial world map — distance from the centre is a clean progression axis.

title: The Golden Cosmic Egg (Hiranyagarbha) by Manaku
creator: Manaku of Guler
summary:
A Pahari painting by the master *Manaku of Guler* of the *Hiraṇyagarbha*, the golden cosmic egg or 'golden womb' from which the universe is born.

## Iconography
A luminous golden egg floats on the dark primordial waters, often shown with the creator (Brahma, or Vishnu reclining) within or beside it, the unmanifest cosmos held in a single radiant ovoid before it splits to form heaven and earth.

## Significance
The *Brahmāṇḍa* — literally 'egg of Brahma' — is one of the oldest Indic cosmogonic images, reaching back to the *Ṛgveda*'s hymn of the [[motif:cosmic egg|golden germ]]. Manaku's series for the *Bhagavata Purana* and related texts rendered these metaphysical first-moments with extraordinary economy: the whole of creation as one floating egg. The motif parallels cosmic-egg myths across Eurasia.

## For artists & game designers
A single glowing ovoid on a void of water — a near-perfect 'genesis' splash image or world-seed icon.

title: Burmese Cosmology Manuscript — the Himavanta Forest
creator: Anonymous (Burmese, Buddhist)
summary:
A panel from a Burmese cosmology manuscript showing the *Himavanta* (Himalayan) forest, the legendary highland where Buddhas and ascetics meditate within the larger Mount Meru universe.

## Iconography
The folding-book panel paints a dense forested landscape of lakes, trees, and mythical animals — the great Anotatta lake from which the cosmic rivers flow, the herds and birds of the enchanted wood — set in the foothills of the world-mountain where holy beings retreat from the world of desire.

## Significance
Burmese *kammavaca* and cosmology *parabaik* translated the abstract Meru schema into richly painted scenes, and the Himavanta forest is a favourite station: a paradisal wilderness midway up the cosmic ladder. Such manuscripts were teaching and merit-making objects, mapping the [[motif:cosmography|cosmography]] of rebirth in vivid, narrative form.

## For artists & game designers
A paradisal mythic-forest biome — sacred lakes, exotic beasts — as a contemplative zone perched between the human world and the heavens.

title: The Fourteen Ratna of the Chakravartin (Jain Manuscript Folio)
creator: Anonymous (Jain, India)
summary:
A Jain manuscript folio depicting the fourteen *ratna* ('jewels' or treasures) of the *Chakravartin*, the universal world-emperor who rules the whole human continent.

## Iconography
The folio sets out, in tidy registers, the fourteen possessions that define a *Chakravartin* — among them the spinning discus-wheel (*chakra*), the umbrella, the gem, the queen, the elephant, the horse, the general, the householder — each a token of sovereignty over Jambudvipa.

## Significance
The Chakravartin is the political mirror of the cosmographic order: just as the *Tirthankara* perfects the spiritual cosmos, the world-emperor unifies the inhabited continent, his discus rolling unopposed to its mountain walls. The fourteen jewels are a canonical list, and depicting them is itself a way of mapping the extent and structure of the human world. The motif crosses into Buddhist *cakravartin* imagery as well.

## For artists & game designers
A ready relic-set: fourteen named 'jewels of empire' as collectible artefacts that together unlock world-rulership.

title: Jain Cosmological Map of the Universe — Jambudvipa
creator: Anonymous (Jain, India)
summary:
A large, finely painted Jain map of *Jambudvipa*, the central 'rose-apple continent' at the heart of the cosmos, with the world-mountain Meru at its hub.

## Iconography
Jambudvipa is rendered as a great disc divided by mountain ranges and rivers into the realms of the middle world, with Mount Meru — the cosmic axis — at the exact centre, encircled by rings of ocean and concentric continents. The composition is symmetrical to the point of mandala-like regularity, every river and range placed to scripture.

## Significance
For Jains the universe is uncreated and exactly measured, and Jambudvipa is the navel of that order. Such maps are at once cosmography and meditation aids: tracing the rings is a contemplative descent from the human realm outward into the structure of [[motif:cosmography|cosmography]] itself. The world-mountain motif is shared across South and Inner Asia, a common axis joining Jain, Hindu, and Buddher maps.

## For artists & game designers
The highest-resolution map in this cabinet: a mandala-grade radial continent you can zoom into for districts, rivers, and ranges as discrete regions.

title: Samudra Manthan with Kurma Supporting the Cosmos (1801 Sketch)
creator: Anonymous (South Indian draughtsman)
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: record of the Meenakshi temple, Madurai]
summary:
An 1801 line sketch recording a Madurai temple depiction of *Kurma*, Vishnu's tortoise avatar, bearing Mount Mandara on his back as the axis of the churning cosmos.

## Iconography
The tortoise squats at the base supporting the world-mountain used as a churning-pole, the serpent Vasuki coiled around it. Drawn as a clean documentary outline rather than a coloured painting, it isolates the structural idea: the cosmos resting on the back of the tortoise-god.

## Significance
The [[motif:kurma avatar|Kurma]] episode supplies one of the most widespread of all cosmic-support images — the world borne on a tortoise — and its early-colonial line-record here shows how such temple iconography was catalogued. As a draughtsman's outline it complements the painted *Samudramanthan*, foregrounding the architecture of the myth over its colour.

## For artists & game designers
A crisp line-art reference for the 'world on a tortoise' trope — useful as an austere diagram or tattoo-style emblem.

title: Loka Purusha (the Cosmic Man / Universe as a Giant)
creator: Anonymous (Jain, India)
summary:
The *Loka Purusha*, the Jain image of the entire universe shaped as a colossal standing man (or, in some accounts, a figure standing with arms akimbo), within whose body the worlds are stacked.

## Iconography
The cosmos is drawn as a human figure: the narrow lower legs and feet are the hells (*adhololoka*); the slim waist is the middle world (*madhyaloka*) of humans, marked by the central continents; the broad chest and head are the heavens (*urdhvaloka*), crowned by the *siddhashila*, the crescent abode of the liberated souls at the very top of the skull.

## Significance
Jain cosmology rejects a creator and instead measures an eternal, uncreated universe of fixed proportions. Casting it as a [[motif:cosmic man|cosmic man]] makes the [[motif:macrocosm|macrocosm]] legible at a glance and turns cosmography into an aid to meditation on rebirth and release. The figure is a teaching diagram: to ascend the body is to climb out of *saṃsāra* toward the liberated soul at the crown.

## For artists & game designers
A vertical world literally shaped like a person — hell at the feet, paradise in the skull — is a ready-made tower map where the level layout is also a character.

title: Cosmological Mandala with Mount Meru
creator: Anonymous (Yuan-dynasty China / Tibetan Buddhist tradition)
repository: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
summary:
A celebrated silk *Cosmological Mandala with Mount Meru*, a Yuan-dynasty painting that diagrams the Buddhist universe as a geometric mandala.

## Iconography
At the centre stands Mount Meru, drawn as a stepped hourglass column. Around it concentric squares and circles map the ring-mountains and ring-oceans, with the four island-continents at the cardinal points and the sun and moon as discs to either side. The palette is restrained — gold, red, and ink — and the whole is laid out with diagrammatic precision rather than landscape illusion.

## Significance
The painting marries the [[motif:cosmography|cosmography]] of Mount Meru with the mandala's square-in-circle geometry, turning the universe-map into an object of contemplation and ritual offering. Its survival in the Met makes it one of the most reproduced Asian cosmograms in the West, a touchstone for how Buddhist cosmology is visualised.

## For artists & game designers
A museum-grade square-in-circle world plan — perfect reference for a tarot-flat, diagrammatic map screen.

title: Uma-Maheshvara on Mount Kailash (Pahari-Punjab Mural)
creator: Kangra/Jalandhar muralists (one named Sarfuddin)
summary:
A Punjab-hills mural of *Uma-Maheshvara* — Shiva and Parvati enthroned together on Mount Kailash, the sacred world-axis at the centre of the Hindu and Tibetan cosmos.

## Iconography
Shiva (Maheshvara) sits with his consort Uma (Parvati) upon the snow-peak of Kailash, attended by his bull Nandi and the family of gods. The mountain is rendered as the serene seat of the divine couple, paradise atop the world.

## Significance
Mount Kailash is the most potent of Asia's holy mountains, revered as the home of Shiva by Hindus, as Meru's earthly counterpart, and as a sacred pilgrimage peak by Buddhists, Jains, and Bön alike. The [[motif:world-axis|world-axis]] here is not a diagram but a dwelling: the cosmic mountain humanised as a household of gods. Such Pahari-tradition murals carried this imagery into village shrines.

## For artists & game designers
The 'summit throne of the gods' — a snow-peak sanctuary as the literal top of the world-map, reward for the longest climb.

citations.text: Diana L. Eck, *India: A Sacred Geography* (2012).

title: Illustration of the Mount Sumeru-Centred Universe
creator: A. D. Prakasa (modern rendering of a traditional schema)
summary:
A clear diagram of the Buddhist *Sumeru* (Meru) universe — the world-mountain at the axis of the cosmos, ringed by oceans, mountain walls, and four island-continents.

## Iconography
Mount Sumeru rises at the centre as a great squared mountain, broader at the top than the base, its sides the colours of four jewels. Concentric ranges and seas surround it, and at the cardinal points float the four continents — the southern *Jambudvipa* being the human world. Sun and moon circle the mountain's flanks; the heavens of the gods tier upward above its peak.

## Significance
This is the master-schema of [[motif:buddhist cosmology|Buddhist cosmology]] inherited from the Abhidharma, and the template behind the Tibetan, Nepali, Burmese, and Thai cosmic maps. The vertical stack — hells below, human continents at the waterline, god-realms above — encodes the whole ladder of rebirth on a single mountain. The same axis underlies the mandala offering, in which the cosmos is given to the Buddhas.

## For artists & game designers
The canonical 'world-mountain': a single central megastructure with tiered god-realms above and hells below — the cleanest possible cosmology in one silhouette.

citations.text: Akira Sadakata, *Buddhist Cosmology: Philosophy and Origins* (1997).

title: Nataraja (Shiva as Lord of the Cosmic Dance)
creator: Anonymous (South India), photo by Akhilan
rights: CC BY-SA 4.0 (photo: Akhilan). Object public domain. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
An 18th-century South Indian bronze of *Nataraja*, Shiva as Lord of the Dance, whose *ananda tandava* enacts the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the entire cosmos.

## Iconography
Four-armed Shiva dances within a flaming aureole (*prabhamandala*): one hand holds the drum (*damaru*) that beats out creation, another the fire (*agni*) of destruction; a third gestures 'fear not' (*abhaya*), the fourth points to the raised foot of release. He treads upon the dwarf *Apasmara*, the demon of ignorance, his hair flying out with the river Ganga and a crescent moon.

## Significance
The [[motif:nataraja|Nataraja]] is a cosmogram in bronze: every attribute encodes a cosmic function, the ring of fire is the wheel of *saṃsāra* and the bounds of the universe, and the dance is time itself. Ananda Coomaraswamy's essay 'The Dance of Shiva' made the image a touchstone of how art can compress a whole cosmology into a single pose.

## For artists & game designers
A figure whose every limb is a verb (create / preserve / destroy / release) inside a literal ring of fire — an iconic, readable 'cosmic boss' silhouette.

citations.text: Ananda K. Coomaraswamy, *The Dance of Śiva* (1918).

title: Samavasarana (the Divine Preaching-Hall of a Tirthankara)
creator: Anonymous (Jain) — photograph by Atishay
date: modern model (Kundalpur), of an ancient cosmographic form
rights: CC BY-SA 3.0 (photo: Atishay). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A three-dimensional model of the *Samavasarana*, the miraculous circular preaching-hall the gods raise around a *Tirthankara* the moment he attains omniscience.

## Iconography
The structure rises in concentric tiers — gold, silver, and jewelled ramparts ringed by moats and gateways — with the enlightened teacher seated at the summit, preaching simultaneously to all directions. Steps and terraces lead the assembled beings (humans, gods, animals) up through the rings toward the centre.

## Significance
The Samavasarana is a cosmogram in built form: a perfectly concentric, axially centred world generated by enlightenment itself. Like Mount Meru and the *adhai-dvipa* map, it expresses the Jain conviction that supreme reality is exactly ordered and ascending. The plan echoes the [[motif:mandala-plan|mandala-plan]] shared with the wider Indic world-mountain tradition.

## For artists & game designers
A tiered concentric arena with gates and moats — a literal boss-arena cosmogram you can ascend ring by ring.

title: Samudra Manthan (Churning of the Ocean of Milk)
creator: Anonymous (Indian)
summary:
A painting of the *Samudra Manthan*, the churning of the cosmic ocean of milk by which the gods and demons together wrest the elixir of immortality from the deep.

## Iconography
Mount Mandara is used as a churning-staff, set on the back of Vishnu's tortoise avatar *Kurma*, with the great serpent *Vasuki* wound round it as a rope. The *devas* pull at one end and the *asuras* at the other, and from the foaming ocean rise the treasures of the world — the goddess Lakshmi, the moon, the wish-cow, the physician Dhanvantari with the pot of *amrita*.

## Significance
The churning is a cosmogonic myth of the ordering of the world out of primal flux, a tug-of-war between opposing powers that yields both poison and nectar. It is one of the most depicted scenes in Hindu art (and on the walls of Angkor), a [[motif:cosmogony|cosmogony]] enacted as cooperative violence around the world-axis of Mount Mandara.

## For artists & game designers
A dynamic 'two factions turning the world-engine' set-piece — a cooperative-yet-competitive mechanic with rare loot rising from the churn.

title: Siddhachakra (Jain Yantra of the Perfected Ones)
creator: Vinayavijaya and Yaśovijaya (attrib.)
summary:
A *Siddhachakra* (or *Navpad*), the most important Jain devotional yantra — a nine-fold lotus diagram of the supreme beings and qualities of the path.

## Iconography
At the centre is the *Arihanta* (enlightened teacher), surrounded on the petals of a lotus by the other four of the Five Supreme Beings — *Siddha*, *Acharya*, *Upadhyaya*, *Sadhu* — interleaved with the four qualities of right faith, knowledge, conduct, and austerity. Sacred syllables and script fill the field, making the diagram a map of perfection rather than a picture of place.

## Significance
Where the *paṭa* map outer space, the [[motif:siddhachakra|siddhachakra]] maps the spiritual cosmos — the hierarchy of liberated and liberating beings toward whom the soul ascends. It is venerated especially during the Ayambil Oli festival, recited and worshipped as a condensed cosmogram of the Jain goal.

## For artists & game designers
A nine-cell radial 'tech tree' of virtues and ranks — a clean template for a skill or devotion wheel.

citations.text: John E. Cort, *Jains in the World* (2001).

title: Medicinal Flora and Fauna (Blue Beryl Medical Painting)
creator: Workshop of Sangye Gyatso (Desi Sangye Gyamtso)
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: after the Lhasa Blue Beryl set]
summary:
A leaf from the great Tibetan medical-painting set commissioned under the regent *Desi Sangye Gyatso* to illustrate the *Blue Beryl* commentary on the *Four Tantras*, here cataloguing the medicinal flora and fauna of the Medicine Buddha's healing realm.

## Iconography
The painting arrays plants, minerals, and animals in tidy diagrammatic rows, each a source of remedy gathered around the celestial city of *Bhaiṣajyaguru*, the Medicine Buddha, whose paradise of healing herbs frames the *materia medica*. The format is encyclopaedic — picture as chart — rather than narrative.

## Significance
Tibetan medicine fused cosmology, embryology, and pharmacology into a single visual system; the *Blue Beryl* set (and the related anatomical and embryological thangkas) maps the body and its cures as part of the same ordered cosmos governed by the [[motif:vajrayana|Vajrayana]] Medicine Buddha. These paintings are among the most systematic 'science illustrations' of pre-modern Asia.

## For artists & game designers
An in-world herbarium / bestiary screen — alchemical ingredients laid out as a gridded, paintable catalogue.

title: Traibhumi (Three Worlds) — Thai Cosmological Imagery
creator: Anonymous (Thai, Buddhist)
date: object photographed at the Bangkok National Museum (traditional schema, 18th–19th c. type)
summary:
A Thai depiction of the *Traibhumi* ('Three Worlds') cosmology, the Theravāda map of the realms of desire, form, and formlessness that structures Siamese Buddhist cosmography.

## Iconography
The Three Worlds are shown as a tiered universe rising around Mount Meru: the lower world of desire with its hells, animals, hungry ghosts, humans and lower gods; the middle world of pure form inhabited by the Brahma gods; and the topmost formless realms. Registers of figures and architecture mark each station of rebirth.

## Significance
The *Traibhumikatha* ('Sermon on the Three Worlds'), traditionally ascribed to King Lithai of Sukhothai (14th c.), is the founding text of Thai [[motif:buddhist cosmology|Buddhist cosmology]], and its imagery furnished temple murals and folding-book manuscripts for centuries. The vertical hierarchy of realms is simultaneously a map of the cosmos and a chart of karma — where a being is reborn depends on its deeds.

## For artists & game designers
A stacked 'three worlds' vertical map (desire / form / formless) is a tidy progression of zones from dense matter to pure mind.

citations.text: Frank E. Reynolds & Mani B. Reynolds (trans.), *Three Worlds According to King Ruang* (1982).

title: Vishnu Vishvarupa (the Universal Form)
creator: Anonymous (North Indian)
summary:
A painting of the *Vishvarupa*, the 'Universal Form' of Vishnu (revealed by Krishna to Arjuna in the *Bhagavad Gita*), in which the entire cosmos is seen contained within a single divine body.

## Iconography
The god is shown with innumerable heads, arms, and eyes, his body filled with tier upon tier of worlds, gods, sages, and creatures — the whole of existence packed into the deity's frame. Mouths blaze with fire that devours the warriors of time; the figure is at once awe-inspiring and terrifying, exactly as Arjuna beholds it.

## Significance
The [[motif:vishvarupa|Vishvarupa]] is the supreme Hindu image of the cosmos-as-body: where the Jain Loka Purusha is the universe shaped *like* a man, the Vishvarupa is the universe *as* God, theophany and cosmogram together. The eleventh chapter of the Gita, in which it appears, is among the most quoted passages of world religious literature.

## For artists & game designers
A single colossal figure whose body contains a teeming world of smaller scenes — superb reference for a 'god-of-everything' boss or loading illustration.

citations.text: Diana L. Eck, *Darśan: Seeing the Divine Image in India* (1998).

title: The Planet Jupiter and His Children (De zeven planeten series)
work: The Figural System of Astrology: Decans, Mansions & Planet-Children
creator: Netherlandish printmaker (after the Children of the Planets tradition)
rights: Public domain (CC0). Rijksmuseum, via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
**Jupiter** presiding over his children from a printed Seven Planets series in the Rijksmuseum, part of the Children of the Planets tradition.

## Iconography
The benign greater fortune rides his **chariot** above, his rulership signs (Sagittarius and Pisces) at hand. Below, his children pursue the dignified, prosperous occupations Jupiter governs — judges, scholars, clergy, hunters, and men of law and government — the well-born and fortunate.

## Significance
In the [[motif:children of the planets|Children of the Planets]] doctrine, Jupiter is the **greater benefic**: he confers honour, piety, justice, and worldly success, and rules the sanguine temperament. Where Saturn's children labour and suffer, Jupiter's prosper. The contrast between the two planets structures the moral geography of the whole series.

## For artists & game designers
Jupiter's register of judges, priests and nobles is a ready 'faction of the fortunate' — the lawful, prosperous counterpart to Saturn's underclass.

title: Constellation woodcuts, Hyginus, Poeticon Astronomicon

summary:
A page of constellation woodcuts from an early printed edition of the *Poeticon Astronomicon* attributed to **Hyginus**, the standard classical handbook of the star-myths.

## Iconography
The **constellations** are drawn as classical **personifications** — mythological figures with the stars of each constellation marked upon their bodies. The *Poeticon Astronomicon* gathered the Greek catasterism legends, explaining how heroes and beasts were set among the stars.

## Significance
The text ascribed to Hyginus (Augustan era) was, with Aratus, the great ancient source for the figures of the sky; its richly woodcut Venetian editions (Ratdolt, 1482, and successors) became the visual canon of the constellations for the Renaissance. These figures are also the raw material of the [[motif:paranatellonta|paranatellonta]] — the constellations that rise alongside the zodiac and underlie the decan imagery.

## For artists & game designers
Classical constellation-personifications with stars pricked onto them are a beautiful template for a 'living sky' or star-summoned creature bestiary.

title: Rhetorica (E23), so-called Tarocchi of Mantegna (E-series)
work: The Figural System of Astrology: Decans, Mansions & Planet-Children
creator: Anonymous North Italian engraver ('Master of the E-Series')
summary:
**Rhetorica** (card E23), one of the fifty engravings of the so-called *Tarocchi of Mantegna* (the E-series), a North Italian cosmological print cycle of c. 1465 — not in fact tarot cards nor by Mantegna.

## Iconography
The sheet personifies **Rhetoric** as an allegorical woman with her attributes, one of the seven Liberal Arts in the cycle. The full series ascends a Neoplatonic ladder from the conditions of men, through Apollo and the Muses, the Liberal Arts and Virtues, the seven **planets**, and the spheres up to the *Prima Causa*.

## Significance
The E-series is a complete diagram of the hierarchical cosmos: its planet-cards (Luna to Saturn, then the Eighth Sphere and Prime Mover) place the [[motif:planetary deities|planetary rulers]] within a graded chain of being. It is a key Renaissance synthesis of astrology, the arts, and Neoplatonic cosmology, hugely influential on later print culture (Dürer copied from it).

## For artists & game designers
A fifty-card ladder from common men to the Prime Mover is a ready 'rank / cosmic tier' system — each step a clean allegorical figure.

citations.text: Mark J. Zucker, *The Illustrated Bartsch 24: Early Italian Masters* (the 'Tarocchi').
Jay A. Levenson et al., *Early Italian Engravings from the National Gallery of Art* (1973).

title: Saturn (Francesco Albani planet series), Rijksmuseum
work: The Figural System of Astrology: Decans, Mansions & Planet-Children
creator: Engraver after Francesco Albani
rights: Public domain (CC0). Rijksmuseum, via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
**Saturn** as a planetary deity, an engraving after a painted series by Francesco Albani, in the Rijksmuseum — a Baroque reception of the planet-rulers.

## Iconography
The aged god is shown with the attributes of [[motif:saturn|Saturn]] — the **scythe** of harvest and time, the brooding aspect of age. As Chronos / Saturn he embodies devouring Time, the cold and dry, and the melancholic temperament.

## Significance
The identification of Saturn with melancholy, age, agriculture, and Time runs from antiquity through the medieval Children-of-the-Planets cycles into Renaissance and Baroque art (the great study is Klibansky, Panofsky & Saxl, *Saturn and Melancholy*). Albani's elegant mythological series shows the planetary king surviving as a living artistic type well past the Middle Ages.

## For artists & game designers
The scythe-bearing elder is the definitive 'lord of time and decay' figure — directly usable for a saturnine boss, deity, or melancholic patron.

citations.text: R. Klibansky, E. Panofsky & F. Saxl, *Saturn and Melancholy* (1964).

summary:
**Apollo as Sol**, the Sun, paired with his zodiacal house **Leo**, from a Netherlandish Seven Planets and Constellations engraving series in the Rijksmuseum.

## Iconography
The radiant solar deity is shown with the attributes of [[motif:sol|Sol]] — the blazing face, the sun-disc — set beside the **lion** of Leo, the sign of the Sun's domicile. The print belongs to a series joining each planet to its constellation and its 'children'.

## Significance
The Sun rules royalty, gold, magnanimity, vitality, and the choleric-sanguine in astrological doctrine; Leo is its sole domicile. As Apollo, Sol carries the mythic dignity of the planet-deity into the [[motif:children of the planets|Planetenkinder]] tradition, where the Sun's children are kings, athletes, and men of honour.

## For artists & game designers
A single sheet binding a deity, its sign, and its solar attributes is a tidy 'planet card' template for a celestial-faction or zodiac system.

title: Astrological hall of the Salone, Palazzo della Ragione, Padua
work: The Figural System of Astrology: Decans, Mansions & Planet-Children
creator: After Giotto's lost cycle; repainted by Nicolò Miretto and Stefano da Ferrara
summary:
The vast hall of the **Palazzo della Ragione** in Padua, whose walls carry one of the largest medieval-Renaissance astrological fresco cycles in existence.

## Iconography
The enormous **Salone** is frescoed in registers running the length of the hall: the **zodiac signs**, the planets, the months and their labours, the apostles, and the **decan**-related figures of an astrological calendar, organising the year and the heavens around the room.

## Significance
The Paduan cycle derives from a lost programme designed under the influence of **Pietro d'Abano**, the city's great astrologer-physician (d. c. 1316), and originally painted by Giotto's workshop; it was repainted in the fifteenth century after a fire by Nicolò Miretto and Stefano da Ferrara. With the Schifanoia *Salone dei Mesi*, it is a principal monument of the Italian astrological hall, binding [[motif:decans|decan]] and calendar imagery into a single civic cosmos.

## For artists & game designers
An entire room as a walk-through calendar-cosmos is an architectural model for an astrological 'world map' space the player physically moves through.

citations.text: Eva Frojmovič, 'Giotto's Allegories of Justice and the Commune,' *JWCI* (1996).
Dieter Blume, *Regenten des Himmels* (2000).

title: Allegory of April (Triumph of Venus, Taurus), Salone dei Mesi, Palazzo Schifanoia
work: The Figural System of Astrology: Decans, Mansions & Planet-Children
creator: Francesco del Cossa
summary:
The **April** wall — the **Triumph of Venus** over the sign **Taurus** — from Francesco del Cossa's frescoes in the *Salone dei Mesi*, Palazzo Schifanoia, Ferrara.

## Iconography
The three-band scheme is fully legible here: Venus rides in triumph above in a garden of lovers (Mars kneeling in her chains), the bull of [[motif:taurus|Taurus]] and its three **decan** figures occupy the middle band, and the Este court takes its pleasures below. The triumphs follow the planet that rules each sign — Venus for Taurus.

## Significance
The April panel is the best-preserved and most studied of the whole cycle, the keystone of Aby Warburg's reconstruction of how Egyptian-Indian [[motif:decans|decan]] figures, transmitted through Arabic and medieval Latin astrology, surfaced in Quattrocento Ferrara. It is the single most important monument of Renaissance astrological iconography.

## For artists & game designers
A full month-wall — ruling deity above, sign-and-decans in the middle, courtly life below — is a complete 'celestial governs the world' tableau in one frame.

citations.text: Aby Warburg, 'Italian Art and International Astrology in the Palazzo Schifanoia' (1912).
Kristen Lippincott, 'The Frescoes of the Salone dei Mesi,' (PhD thesis, 1987).

title: Allegory of July (detail, washerwomen), Salone dei Mesi, Palazzo Schifanoia
work: The Figural System of Astrology: Decans, Mansions & Planet-Children
creator: Ferrarese workshop (Salone dei Mesi)
summary:
A detail of washerwomen (*lavandaie*) from the lower band of the **July** wall in the *Salone dei Mesi*, Palazzo Schifanoia, Ferrara.

## Iconography
This detail comes from the lowest of the three registers — the band of Este court and civic life that runs beneath the [[motif:decans|decan]] figures and the triumph of each month. Here women launder at a basin, a vignette of everyday labour set under the rule of the month's sign.

## Significance
The lower band grounds the astrological cosmos of the *Salone* in the lived world of Ferrara: the heavens above (deity-triumph and sign-with-decans) govern the human activity below. The cycle thus joins the abstract [[motif:decans|decan]] system to a vivid panorama of fifteenth-century life, a structure Warburg read as the meeting of high astrology and local court culture.

## For artists & game designers
The genre-detail register shows how to anchor a cosmic scheme in ordinary life — celestial rule made concrete in small scenes of work and play.

citations.text: Aby Warburg, 'Italian Art and International Astrology in the Palazzo Schifanoia' (1912).

title: Allegory of March (Aries), Salone dei Mesi, Palazzo Schifanoia, Ferrara
work: The Figural System of Astrology: Decans, Mansions & Planet-Children
creator: Francesco del Cossa
summary:
A section of the **March** fresco, with the sign **Aries** and its decans, from Francesco del Cossa's contribution to the *Salone dei Mesi* at the Palazzo Schifanoia, Ferrara — the supreme surviving cycle of astrological decan imagery.

## Iconography
Each month's wall is built in three horizontal bands: a triumph of a pagan deity above, the **zodiac sign** with its three **decan** figures in the middle, and scenes of Este court life below. Here March carries [[motif:aries|Aries]] the ram and the strange, unexplained decan-figures of its three ten-degree faces.

## Significance
The Schifanoia decans descend, through Pietro d'Abano's *Astrolabium* and the *Liber Astrologiae* of Georgius Zothorus (Abu Maʿshar's tradition), from the Egyptian and Indian **paranatellonta** — the figures rising with each ten degrees of the zodiac. Aby Warburg's famous 1912 lecture decoded the middle band as this migrated, half-forgotten decan iconography, founding the modern study of astrological image-transmission.

## For artists & game designers
The three-decan band gives 36 enigmatic 'sub-sign' figures — a ready bestiary of celestial minor powers beneath the twelve signs.

citations.text: Aby Warburg, 'Italian Art and International Astrology in the Palazzo Schifanoia' (1912).
Kristen Lippincott, 'The Frescoes of the Salone dei Mesi,' (PhD thesis, 1987).

title: Allegory of December (Triumph of Vesta), Salone dei Mesi, Palazzo Schifanoia
work: The Figural System of Astrology: Decans, Mansions & Planet-Children
creator: Ferrarese workshop (Salone dei Mesi)
summary:
The **December** wall, with its **Triumph of Vesta**, from the *Salone dei Mesi* at the Palazzo Schifanoia, Ferrara. (The Commons filename's '01 dicembre' fixes this as the December, not September, panel.)

## Iconography
The upper band carries the triumph of the deity who rules December's sign — here **Vesta** — above the zodiacal band that would hold [[motif:capricorn|Capricorn]] and its three **decan** figures, with the Este court below. This wall is among the more damaged of the cycle.

## Significance
The *Salone dei Mesi* assigns each month a presiding pagan deity drawn from Manilius's scheme of the tutelary gods of the signs, set over the [[motif:decans|decan]] figures that descend from the Egyptian-Arabic [[motif:paranatellonta|paranatellonta]]. The December panel completes the year's round of triumphs in the great programme Aby Warburg made the founding case-study of astrological iconology.

## For artists & game designers
A triumph-of-a-deity upper register is a clean 'patron god of the month' device for a calendar or seasonal-festival system.

citations.text: Aby Warburg, 'Italian Art and International Astrology in the Palazzo Schifanoia' (1912).
Marco Bertozzi, *La tirannia degli astri: Aby Warburg e l'astrologia di Palazzo Schifanoia* (1985).

title: Bloodletting scene, Codex germanicus monacensis 340
work: Astrological & Occult Medicine: The Body Governed by the Stars
creator: Anonymous
rights: Public domain. Via Wikimedia Commons (Bayerische Staatsbibliothek).
summary:
A bloodletting illustration from Codex germanicus monacensis 340 in the Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, depicting the practice of *Aderlass* rather than the schematic vein-man.

## Iconography
The scene shows the act of phlebotomy itself — a practitioner opening a vein on a seated or standing patient, the blood collected in a bowl. The image belongs to the practical apparatus of the German medical manuscript, complementing the schematic [[motif:aderlassmann|Aderlassmann]] figures with a picture of the procedure.

## Significance
Where the vein-man is a diagram, this folio records the lived reality of [[motif:phlebotomy|letting blood]], the routine therapy of humoral medicine that the astrological calendars sought to time. Such scenes connect the abstract sign-and-planet apparatus to the barber-surgeon's daily work in the German lands.

## For artists & game designers
A depiction of the procedure (not just the chart) gives the 'cutscene' to pair with the diagram — useful for grounding an arcane medical system in visceral practice.

citations.text: Gundolf Keil & Peter Assion (eds.), *Fachprosaforschung* (1974).

title: Aderlassmann (Bloodletting Man), 1491
work: Astrological & Occult Medicine: The Body Governed by the Stars
creator: Anonymous (German woodcut)
summary:
A 1491 German woodcut *Aderlassmann* — the Bloodletting Man — labelling the veins to be opened and the signs that govern the timing.

## Iconography
The nude male figure stands with arms slightly raised; numerous veins are marked along the arms, legs, neck and head, each labelled or keyed to the part of the body and the ailment it serves. The surrounding apparatus ties the bleeding-points to the [[motif:zodiac man|zodiacal]] rulership of the limbs.

## Significance
The *Aderlassmann* is the German vernacular form of the bleeding-figure, central to the *Aderlasskalender* (bloodletting calendars) printed in great numbers after Gutenberg. These cheap broadsheets and almanacs told barber-surgeons and laypeople alike which days the heavens deemed safe for [[motif:phlebotomy|letting blood]] from which vein — among the earliest mass-market applications of astrology to daily life.

## For artists & game designers
The labelled-vein figure makes a perfect 'anatomy unlock screen': tapping each marked vein could reveal its associated humour, ailment and auspicious sign.

citations.text: Peter Murray Jones, *Medieval Medicine in Illuminated Manuscripts* (1998).

title: Aderlassmann (Bloodletting Man), c. 1500
work: Astrological & Occult Medicine: The Body Governed by the Stars
creator: Anonymous (German woodcut)
summary:
A turn-of-the-century German *Aderlassmann*, a more elaborate woodcut of the Bloodletting Man with its full apparatus of marked veins and labels.

## Iconography
The figure is shown frontally, the body's surface crowded with named bleeding-points; banners or labels gloss each vein and its therapeutic use. The richer cutting and denser annotation mark the maturing of the German almanac woodcut around 1500.

## Significance
This exemplar shows how quickly the [[motif:aderlassmann|Aderlassmann]] standardised once it entered print. Sold in the *Aderlasskalender* and the broadsheet almanacs, the figure carried the doctrine of astrologically timed [[motif:phlebotomy|bloodletting]] into ordinary households, where the laity used it without a physician. Such prints are key evidence for the popular reach of medical astrology in the Holy Roman Empire.

## For artists & game designers
Compare with the 1491 cut as an 'era progression' asset — same schematic, more ornament — useful for showing a tradition hardening into convention.

citations.text: Charles Talbot, 'Astrology and Medicine', in *Medicine in Medieval England* (1967).

title: Aderlassmann, Codex Palatinus germanicus 644
work: Astrological & Occult Medicine: The Body Governed by the Stars
creator: Anonymous
rights: Public domain. Via Wikimedia Commons (Bibliotheca Palatina).
summary:
A manuscript Bloodletting Man from Codex Palatinus germanicus 644, one of the Heidelberg Bibliotheca Palatina medical codices.

## Iconography
The figure stands with arms extended; the veins of head, neck, arms, hands, legs and feet are picked out and labelled in German, identifying which vein to open for which complaint. The hand-drawn, coloured form precedes the standardised printed *Aderlassmann*.

## Significance
The Heidelberg *Cpg* medical manuscripts preserve the manuscript ancestry of the printed bleeding-figure. As a witness from the [[motif:aderlassmann|Aderlassmann]] tradition in its handwritten stage, this folio shows the vernacular German vein-map that the early presses would later fix and multiply, linking [[motif:phlebotomy|phlebotomy]] to the wider scheme of astrological timing.

## For artists & game designers
The rougher manuscript hand gives a 'field-notebook' texture distinct from the crisp woodcut — good for a found-document or lore-page aesthetic.

citations.text: Gundolf Keil, 'Aderlass und Aderlassregeln', in *Verfasserlexikon* (1978).

title: Nude figure of the Astrological Man (14th century)
work: Astrological & Occult Medicine: The Body Governed by the Stars
creator: Anonymous
rights: CC BY 4.0. Via Wikimedia Commons (Wellcome Collection).
summary:
A fourteenth-century manuscript miniature of the Astrological Man, a nude figure across which the zodiacal rulership of the body is mapped.

## Iconography
The naked body stands frontally, the twelve signs disposed along it from the ram at the brow to the fishes at the feet. Lines or labels connect each sign to the [[motif:melothesia|member]] it governs. The early date gives the figure the stiff, hieratic posture of Gothic manuscript art rather than the modelled nudes of the later woodcut tradition.

## Significance
Among the earlier surviving witnesses to the [[motif:homo signorum|Homo signorum]], this figure shows the doctrine already fully formed in the fourteenth century, well before its mass diffusion through print. Such miniatures accompanied the prognostic and phlebotomy texts that guided a physician's calendar of safe and dangerous days for intervention on each part of the body.

## For artists & game designers
A spare Gothic line-figure reads as an 'arcane medical schematic' more convincingly than a polished anatomical plate — good reference for a hand-drawn diegetic medicine screen.

citations.text: Roger French, 'Astrology in Medical Practice', in *Practical Medicine from Salerno to the Black Death* (1994).

title: Bloodletting Man showing the influence of zodiac and planets
work: Astrological & Occult Medicine: The Body Governed by the Stars
creator: Anonymous
rights: CC BY 4.0. Via Wikimedia Commons (Wellcome Collection).
summary:
A manuscript Bloodletting Man marking the points of phlebotomy on the body together with the zodiacal signs and planets that govern them.

## Iconography
A standing figure is ringed by the twelve signs in their head-to-foot order; lines run from the signs and from planetary roundels to the precise spots on the body at which a vein may be opened. The figure unites two schemes — the [[motif:zodiac man|Homo signorum]] of sign-rulership and the practical map of bleeding-points used by the surgeon.

## Significance
Bloodletting was the central therapy of humoral medicine, and its timing was governed by the heavens: a vein should be opened when the Moon and the governing planets stood favourably and not while the Moon transited the sign ruling the affected member. Figures like this one served as bedside reference, fusing astrological prognosis with the [[motif:phlebotomy|phlebotomy]] of the practising physician.

## For artists & game designers
The convergence of zodiac roundels, planetary glyphs and anatomical bleeding-points on one figure is an exemplary 'occult procedure diagram' — busy, labelled, and unmistakably operative.

citations.text: Linda Voigts, 'The Golden Table of Pythagoras', in *Popular and Practical Science of Medieval England* (1994).

title: Fasciculus medicinae, illustrated leaf (BSB)
work: Astrological & Occult Medicine: The Body Governed by the Stars
creator: Johannes de Ketham
rights: Public domain. Via Wikimedia Commons (Bayerische Staatsbibliothek).
summary:
An illustrated leaf from a Bayerische Staatsbibliothek copy of Ketham's *Fasciculus medicinae*, one of the work's full-page diagrammatic figures.

## Iconography
The page presents one of the book's schematic bodies or instructional scenes within its woodcut border and Latin text — the *Fasciculus*'s house format, in which a single emblematic figure is wrapped in explanatory letterpress.

## Significance
The survival of multiple early printings in libraries such as the BSB lets scholars trace the *Fasciculus*'s evolving illustration across editions. Each leaf belongs to the integrated programme — [[motif:zodiac man|zodiac]], [[motif:bloodletting man|bleeding]], wound, urine — by which the volume taught the whole of practical medicine through pictures, and by which medical astrology reached its widest early-modern audience.

## For artists & game designers
The text-wrapped full-page figure is a ready 'codex page' layout — central diagram framed by dense letterpress, ideal for an in-game tome spread.

citations.text: Johannes de Ketham, *Fasciculus medicinae* (Venice, 1491–1500).

title: Uroscopy (Harnschau), Gart der Gesundheit
work: Astrological & Occult Medicine: The Body Governed by the Stars
creator: Anonymous (German woodcut)
summary:
A *Harnschau* (urine-inspection) woodcut from the German herbal-medical tradition of the *Gart der Gesundheit*, the physician reading the flask.

## Iconography
A physician holds the urine-flask aloft for inspection, the woodcut rendering the *Harnschau* — the German term for uroscopy — as a discrete diagnostic act. The bold early-printed line is typical of the Mainz medical incunabula.

## Significance
The *Gart der Gesundheit* (Mainz, 1485) was among the most influential printed herbals and household-medicine books of the German Renaissance, and its [[motif:uroscopy|Harnschau]] image carried urine-diagnosis to a broad vernacular readership. The picture shows the practice as a fixed ritual of the German physician, alongside the [[motif:bloodletting man|bloodletting]] and zodiac apparatus of the same medical culture.

## For artists & game designers
The lone physician-with-flask in crisp woodcut line is a clean icon asset — high contrast, instantly readable as 'diagnosis'.

citations.text: *Gart der Gesundheit* (Mainz: Peter Schöffer, 1485).

title: Ketham, Fasciculus medicinae (title figure)
work: Astrological & Occult Medicine: The Body Governed by the Stars
creator: Johannes de Ketham
summary:
A woodcut from the *Fasciculus medicinae* of Johannes de Ketham, the first printed medical book to contain anatomical illustrations.

## Iconography
The plate shows one of the *Fasciculus*'s signature schematic figures or scenes — physicians, the lecturing master, or one of the diagrammatic bodies — rendered in the bold early-Venetian woodcut line of the de Gregori brothers' workshop.

## Significance
First printed at Venice in 1491 and famously expanded in 1493–95, the *Fasciculus medicinae* gathered the standard apparatus of late-medieval medicine — the [[motif:zodiac man|Zodiac Man]], the [[motif:bloodletting man|Bloodletting Man]], the [[motif:wound man|Wound Man]], the Disease Woman, the [[motif:uroscopy|uroscopy]] charts and the dissection scene — into one illustrated volume. It became the most widely diffused medical picture-book of the age and fixed the canonical form of these figures for European print.

## For artists & game designers
The *Fasciculus* is the single best source-book for a Renaissance medical aesthetic: one volume supplies the zodiac body, the vein-man, the wound-man and the urine-wheel in a coherent house style.

citations.text: Johannes de Ketham, *Fasciculus medicinae* (Venice, 1491/1495).
Karl Sudhoff & Charles Singer, *The Fasciculo di Medicina, Venice 1493* (1925).

title: The planets and signs of the zodiac send down their influence
work: Astrological & Occult Medicine: The Body Governed by the Stars
creator: Anonymous
rights: CC BY 4.0. Via Wikimedia Commons (Wellcome Collection).
summary:
A figure showing the planets and zodiac signs casting their influence down upon the human body, the doctrine of celestial 'influence' made literal.

## Iconography
From the heavens above, the seven planets and the twelve signs direct lines or rays of influence onto the parts of a human figure below, each celestial body linked to the organ or member it governs. The image visualises *influentia* — the in-flowing virtue by which the stars were thought to act on the sublunary body.

## Significance
The picture renders the central premise of medical astrology: that the planets and signs continuously shape the [[motif:melothesia|microcosmic body]], so that health and sickness, temperament and crisis all answer to the sky. This is the macrocosm–microcosm doctrine that underwrites the [[motif:zodiac man|Zodiac Man]] and the whole apparatus of astrological prognosis.

## For artists & game designers
Rays of planetary 'influence' descending onto a body is a clean status-effect metaphor — each planet a buff/debuff source streaming down onto the player's anatomy.

citations.text: S. K. Heninger, *The Cosmographical Glass* (1977).

title: Constantine the African examining urine (uroscopy)
work: Astrological & Occult Medicine: The Body Governed by the Stars
creator: Anonymous
summary:
A manuscript miniature of Constantine the African examining a flask of urine, the archetypal image of medieval uroscopy.

## Iconography
The physician holds a *matula* — the round-bottomed urine flask — up to the light, scrutinising its colour, clarity and contents to reach a diagnosis. The patient or an attendant stands by. The single uplifted flask became the universal emblem of the doctor.

## Significance
Constantine the African (d. c. 1099), the Monte Cassino translator who carried Arabic medicine into Latin Europe, stands here for the science of [[motif:uroscopy|uroscopy]] — diagnosis by the inspection of urine. For centuries the urine-flask defined the physician in art, and the reading of the *matula* was woven together with astrological timing and humoral theory into a complete diagnostic and prognostic system.

## For artists & game designers
The doctor-with-flask is the instantly legible icon of the medieval healer — a single prop that signals 'physician' the way a staff signals 'mage'.

citations.text: Michael McVaugh, 'Constantine the African', in *Dictionary of Scientific Biography*.
Wikimedia Commons

title: Illustration of uroscopy, 15th century
work: Astrological & Occult Medicine: The Body Governed by the Stars
creator: Anonymous
rights: CC BY 4.0. Via Wikimedia Commons (Wellcome Collection).
summary:
A fifteenth-century illustration of uroscopy in practice, the physician judging a flask brought by or for the patient.

## Iconography
The scene shows the consultation around the urine-flask: the doctor examines the *matula* while the patient or a messenger looks on, the social ritual by which diagnosis was performed and a prognosis pronounced.

## Significance
Uroscopy was not only a technique but a public performance of medical authority: patients sent their urine to the physician, who could (it was claimed) diagnose at a distance from the flask alone. The practice, fused with astrological and humoral reasoning, defined the late-medieval consultation — and drew satire when over-claimed. Here it is shown straight, as the central diagnostic act of [[motif:uroscopy|uroscopic]] medicine.

## For artists & game designers
The flask-consultation is a compact 'diagnosis encounter' tableau — two figures and a prop carry an entire medical interaction.

citations.text: Laurence Moulinier-Brogi, *L'Uroscopie au Moyen Âge* (2012).

title: Western Uroscopy Chart
work: Astrological & Occult Medicine: The Body Governed by the Stars
creator: Anonymous
rights: CC BY 4.0. Via Wikimedia Commons (Wellcome Collection).
summary:
A Western uroscopy chart — the wheel of urine flasks ringed by their diagnostic colours, the physician's reference for reading the *matula*.

## Iconography
A circular arrangement of urine flasks, each tinted a different shade from pale to dark and keyed to a humoral condition, disease or prognosis. The colour, sediment and clarity of the urine were correlated through the wheel to the patient's state.

## Significance
The [[motif:uroscopy|uroscopy]] wheel (the *Harnschau* chart) systematised diagnosis by urine into a colour-coded instrument. Twenty or more named shades, from *albus* to *niger*, indexed the balance of the humours and the course of an illness; combined with astrological prognosis, the wheel let the physician judge both disease and its critical days. The motif became so emblematic that the flask-wheel stands for medieval medicine itself.

## For artists & game designers
The radial colour-coded flask-wheel is a perfect diegetic UI: a literal diagnostic dial the player rotates to match a sample's hue to a condition.
