The *Hortus sanitatis* (Garden of Health, Mainz 1491) was a sprawling natural-medical encyclopaedia whose woodcuts shaped how the early-modern reader imagined plants, animals and the practice of medicine. MS 784 belongs to the substantial body of [[motif:uroscopy|uroscopic]] manuscripts that circulated as practical reference for physicians and apothecaries. The figure bears the full repertory of wounds — bladed weapons embedded in head, chest, arms and legs, arrows, animal bites and surface lesions — each linked to the surrounding text on diagnosis and cure. The painted manuscript form gives the body colour and modelling absent from the printed cuts.

This [[motif:wound man|Wound Man]] shows the figure circulating in manuscript anatomies attributed to Galen, the great authority whose corpus underwrote medieval medicine. As one of the finest surviving manuscript exemplars, it documents the genre before and alongside its diffusion through Ketham's *Fasciculus*, and its place within the broader teaching of [[motif:anatomy|anatomy]] and surgery.

The man is shown beset by the standard catalogue of wounds — embedded blades, arrows, a spear, animal bites and lesions — with German captions naming each injury and pointing to its treatment in the surrounding surgical text.

The German-legended [[motif:wound man|Wundenmann]] belongs to the vernacular surgical handbooks of the German lands, where works like Gersdorff's *Feldtbuch der Wundartzney* carried the figure to barber-surgeons working in the field. title: Wound Man, Gersdorff Feldtbuch der Wundartzney (1517)

The Wound Man from Hans von Gersdorff's *Feldtbuch der Wundartzney* (Field Book of Wound Surgery, Strasbourg 1517), one of the most celebrated of all Wound Man woodcuts.

## Iconography
A bearded man stands transfixed by a dense array of weapons — sword, dagger, spear, arrows, a thrown club, a flail — and afflicted by animal bites and lesions. Gersdorff's cut, attributed to the Strasbourg workshop of Hans Wechtlin, is unusually crowded and energetic, the body bristling with implements.

## Significance
Gersdorff was a battlefield surgeon, and his *Feldtbuch* distilled decades of practical [[motif:wound man|wound]] and amputation surgery into the most influential German surgical manual of the early sixteenth century. Its Wound Man became the canonical image of the genre, reproduced and adapted for generations. The book joined the same shelf as the astrological-medical figures, surgery and the stars sharing one body-schematic logic.

## For artists & game designers
Gersdorff's exuberantly over-armed figure is the definitive 'maximum damage' diagram — the reference to reach for when an injury screen needs to feel overwhelmed.

The *Wundenmann* (Wound Man) woodcut from the 1491 Venice *Fasciculus medicinae* of Johannes de Ketham, the figure pierced by every weapon and affliction the surgeon must treat.

## Iconography
A standing man is struck simultaneously by a catalogue of injuries: swords and daggers in the torso and limbs, arrows and a spear, a club, thorns, the bites of dog, snake and scorpion, abscesses and skin lesions. Each wound keys to a passage of the surgical text explaining its treatment.

## Significance
The [[motif:wound man|Wound Man]] is a visual index of trauma surgery, gathering on one body every case the practitioner might face. First printed in Ketham's *Fasciculus*, the figure became a fixture of the surgical handbooks of the German and Italian Renaissance. Though not itself astrological, it shares the schematic 'mapped body' logic of the [[motif:zodiac man|Homo signorum]] with which it travelled in the same volumes.

## For artists & game designers
The Wound Man is the original 'damage diagram' — a single figure annotated with every injury type, an ideal template for an injury/affliction codex screen.

title: The Zodiac Man (Homo signorum)
work: Astrological & Occult Medicine: The Body Governed by the Stars
creator: Anonymous
summary:
A diagrammatic Zodiac Man from a medical-astrological manuscript, the human body annotated with the twelve signs and instructions on the importance of astrology to the physician.

## Iconography
A standing figure is overlaid or surrounded by the twelve zodiac signs in the canonical head-to-foot order of [[motif:melothesia|melothesia]]: **Aries** ruling the head, **Taurus** the neck, **Gemini** the shoulders and arms, **Cancer** the chest, **Leo** the heart, **Virgo** the belly, **Libra** the kidneys and loins, **Scorpio** the genitals, **Sagittarius** the thighs, **Capricorn** the knees, **Aquarius** the shins, and **Pisces** the feet. Surrounding text explains the medical use of the scheme.

## Significance
The *Homo signorum* expressed the doctrine that each part of the microcosmic body answered to a sign of the macrocosm. A physician consulting the figure judged whether the Moon stood in a sign governing the affected limb before bleeding, purging, or operating — one should not, the rule ran, 'touch with iron' a member whose sign the Moon then occupied. The scheme descends from Manilius and the *Tetrabiblos* tradition and saturated the calendars and almanacs of the later Middle Ages.

## For artists & game designers
The head-to-foot zodiacal body is a ready-made 'status overlay' — a paper-doll whose twelve regions light up with their ruling sign, perfect for an astrology-driven medicine or affliction system.

citations.text: Charles Clark, 'The Zodiac Man in Medieval Medical Astrology', *Journal of the Rocky Mountain Medieval and Renaissance Association* (1982).

title: The Planet Mars and His Children
creator: after the Planetenkinder tradition
summary:
An engraving from the **'Children of the Planets'** (*Planetenkinder*) tradition — **Mars**, the red planet of war, riding his chariot above the human types he governs.

## Iconography
The planetary deity rides a zodiac-marked chariot (Mars draws Aries and Scorpio); below, his 'children' act out his nature — soldiers, butchers, surgeons, brawlers, burning towns — pairing macrocosm (god in his sphere) with microcosm (lives he rules).

## Significance
The Children of the Planets series — spread by the 15th-c. *Hausbuch* and blockbooks — is the most popular Renaissance image of **astrological determinism**: the seven planets each shape a class of humanity (Iconclass 24C21). It is the everyday face of the cosmology underlying alchemy and magic.

## For artists & game designers
A complete 'planet-as-archetype' design — deity, chariot, zodiac, ruled world. Ideal for a planetary-magic system.

title: Melencolia I (Albrecht Dürer)
creator: Albrecht Dürer
rights: Public domain. Google Art Project / Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
Dürer's 1514 engraving — perhaps the most analysed print in Western art, and a dense compendium of Renaissance occult thought.

## Iconography
A winged genius sits in brooding inaction amid the tools of geometry — compass, scales, hourglass, a truncated polyhedron, a magic square, a sleeping hound, a bat-winged banner reading MELENCOLIA I. A comet and lunar rainbow burn over the sea.

## Significance
The image fuses the doctrine of the four humours (melancholy, ruled by [[tradition:astrology|Saturn]]) with Ficino's Neoplatonic idea that the melancholic temperament is the seat of genius. The 4×4 **magic square** (a Jupiter *kamea*, encoding the date 1514) is a talisman against Saturn's gloom. Klibansky/Panofsky/Saxl's *Saturn and Melancholy* made it the locus classicus of esoteric iconology.

## For artists & game designers
The archetype of the blocked, brilliant adept amid arcane instruments — perfect for a wizard's study or an occult-geometry puzzle.

title: Volvelle from Apianus's *Astronomicum Caesareum*
creator: Petrus Apianus (Peter Apian)
summary:
A **volvelle** (rotating paper instrument) from Petrus Apianus's sumptuous *Astronomicum Caesareum* (Ingolstadt, 1540).

## Iconography
Concentric **rotating discs**, hand-coloured and threaded with silk **pointers**, are layered on the page to form a working calculator. Bands of the **zodiac**, planetary glyphs, and degree-scales are printed on the moving wheels so the user can read off a planet's position by turning the dials.

## Significance
Apianus's book is the masterpiece of the **volvelle** form — dozens of movable paper computers that let a reader compute planetary longitudes, eclipses, and the data an [[motif:astrology|astrologer]] needed to cast a horoscope, without tables or an astrolabe. Made for the Emperor Charles V, it stands at the luxurious height of Renaissance astronomical-astrological print.

## For artists & game designers
The layered, thread-and-disc 'analogue computer' is irresistible UI inspiration for a craftable star-calculating gadget.

title: Cancer, Leo, and Gemini — Bartsch's *Planisphaerium*
creator: Jacob Bartsch
summary:
A constellation plate by **Jacob Bartsch** (Kepler's son-in-law) showing the zodiac figures of **Cancer**, **Leo**, and **Gemini**.

## Iconography
Three **zodiac signs** share the sheet: the crab of **Cancer**, the lion of **Leo**, and the twins of **Gemini**, each drawn as its living figure with the brighter stars marked. Neighbouring constellations and the band of the Milky Way thread between them along the **ecliptic**.

## Significance
Bartsch's *Planisphaerium stellatum* and *Usus astronomicus* (1624) continued the tradition of figured star-maps and introduced several new constellations. As Johannes Kepler's son-in-law and editor, he stood at the meeting point of the new astronomy and an older [[motif:zodiac|astral]] iconography that astrology still relied on.

## For artists & game designers
Three zodiac emblems on one sheet — convenient reference art for a signs-of-summer set or a multi-sign UI.

The constellation **Andromeda** as figured in Bayer's *Uranometria* (1603), the 'chained woman' of Greek myth set among her stars.

Andromeda is drawn as a woman with her arms bound by **chains**, the brightest stars marking her head, girdle, and feet; the star at her head, **Alpheratz** (Sirrah), is shared with Pegasus. Andromeda belongs to the great Perseus cycle of catasterised myths — Cepheus, Cassiopeia, Perseus, Cetus — that fill the northern autumn sky. Bayer's elegant plate carried these ancient [[motif:zodiac|star-myths]] into a precise, lettered atlas usable by astronomer and astrologer alike.

**Cetus**, the sea-monster, on folio 34v of Johann Bayer's *Uranometria* (Augsburg, 1603).

## Iconography
A scaly **sea monster** with gaping jaws and coiling body fills the plate, its stars marking snout, body, and tail. The figure lies over a ruled **coordinate grid**, with magnitudes shown by symbol size and **Bayer designations** lettering the principal stars.

## Significance
Cetus is the beast sent to devour Andromeda in the Perseus myth, and its great sprawl of faint stars dominates the watery quarter of the autumn sky. Bayer's engraving (cut by Alexander Mair) is a characteristic page of the first whole-sky atlas, carrying a classical [[motif:zodiac|catasterism]] into a precisely lettered chart.

summary:
The constellation **Orion** as engraved for Johann Bayer's *Uranometria* (Augsburg, 1603), the first true star atlas to cover the whole celestial sphere.

## Iconography
The **hunter** strides across the plate, club raised and a **lion skin** over his outstretched arm, his belt and sword marked by the bright stars. A fine **coordinate grid** is laid behind the figure, and each star is sized by **magnitude** and lettered with Bayer's Greek-letter **designations**.

Bayer's *Uranometria* fused beautiful figure-drawing with the new rigour of Tycho Brahe's star positions, and introduced the **Bayer designations** (α, β, γ…) still used today. Its constellation figures, derived from the classical [[motif:zodiac|catasterisms]], carried the mythological sky into the age of precise observation.

creator: Johann Bayer (plates engraved by Alexander Mair)
summary:
**Scorpius**, the Scorpion, one of the twelve zodiacal constellations, as engraved for Bayer's *Uranometria* (1603).

## Iconography
The **scorpion** sprawls across the plate, claws spread and tail curling to its sting; the red heart-star **Antares** glows at its body. The figure straddles the **ecliptic**, the stars graded by **magnitude** and lettered with Bayer's Greek **designations**.

As a **zodiac sign**, Scorpius is one of the twelve through which the Sun, Moon, and planets pass; in astrology it governs a swathe of correspondences and was held a fixed water sign. Bayer's plate shows the working machinery of the [[motif:zodiac|zodiac]] in atlas form — a sign that is also a precisely mapped patch of sky.

title: *Coeli Stellati Christiani Haemisphaerium Prius* — the Christianised sky
creator: Andreas Cellarius
summary:
Cellarius's hemisphere of the **Christianised heavens**, in which the pagan constellations are replaced by biblical and saintly figures.

## Iconography
The familiar mythological constellations give way to scriptural ones: apostles, biblical ships, and sacred objects mapped onto the same stars. The plate follows the radical scheme of Julius Schiller's *Coelum Stellatum Christianum* (Augsburg, 1627), here drawn as a full engraved **hemisphere**.

## Significance
Schiller's project — and Cellarius's homage to it — sought to baptise the sky, expelling the heroes and beasts of the [[motif:zodiac|zodiac]] in favour of a Christian iconography. It is a vivid episode in the **reception** of classical astral imagery and the Counter-Reformation impulse to sanctify even the constellations; the experiment never displaced the traditional names.

## For artists & game designers
A 'reskinned night sky' concept made literal — useful for a faction that has rewritten the heavens in its own image.

title: *Planisphaerium Copernicanum* — the Copernican system
creator: Andreas Cellarius
summary:
Cellarius's *Planisphaerium Copernicanum*, the plate of the *Harmonia Macrocosmica* depicting the Sun-centred cosmos of Copernicus.

## Iconography
The **Sun** sits at the centre of a system of concentric **planetary orbits** — Mercury, Venus, Earth with its Moon, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn — each carrying its planetary glyph and, for Earth, the band of the seasons. The whole is encircled by a **zodiac ring** of the twelve signs and watched over by **putti** bearing astronomical instruments.

## Significance
Nearly 120 years after *De revolutionibus* (1543), Cellarius gave the [[motif:heliocentric system|heliocentric model]] a place of honour beside the Ptolemaic and Tychonic plates — a visual register of a cosmos in dispute. The retained zodiac ring shows how astrological geometry survived the move of the Earth from the centre.

## For artists & game designers
Clean nested-orbit diagram with a glowing centre — ideal for an orrery mechanic or a 'systems of the world' selector.

title: Northern stellar hemisphere, *Harmonia Macrocosmica*
creator: Andreas Cellarius (engraved Schenk, Valck, Van Loon)
summary:
A plate from Andreas Cellarius's *Harmonia Macrocosmica* (first published Amsterdam, 1660), the most lavish celestial atlas of the Baroque age.

## Iconography
A circular **planisphere** projects the heavens onto the plane, its grid of meridians and the slanting band of the **ecliptic** crossing a field crowded with classical **constellation figures** — bears, serpents, heroes, and the twelve zodiac beasts drawn as living bodies. The disc is framed by an ornamental cartouche with **putti**, instruments, and a Latin title-banner.

## Significance
Cellarius gathered the cosmology of his century into 29 hand-coloured copperplates. Though presented as astronomy, the atlas preserves the figured sky on which judicial [[motif:astrology|astrology]] still depended: the constellations and the zodiac that gave the planets their dignities. Re-issued by Schenk and Valck, it became the defining image of the early-modern heavens.

## For artists & game designers
The figure-packed disc inside a heavy cartouche is a perfect template for a star-map UI or a 'sky atlas' inventory screen.

citations.text: Robert H. van Gent, *Andreas Cellarius: Harmonia Macrocosmica of 1660* (Taschen, 2006).

title: *Scenographia systematis mundani Ptolemaici*
creator: Andreas Cellarius
summary:
The *Scenographia systematis mundani Ptolemaici*, Cellarius's perspectival 'stage-set' rendering of the Earth-centred Ptolemaic cosmos.

## Iconography
Unlike the flat planispheres, this plate tilts the universe into **perspective**: nested transparent **celestial spheres** carry the planets in order — Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn — around a central **Earth**, the outermost sphere bearing the **zodiac** and fixed stars. Robed **astronomers** observe from the foreground.

## Significance
The **Ptolemaic** geocentric cosmos was the frame within which classical and medieval [[motif:astrology|astrology]] had always operated: the spheres of the seven planets and the eighth of the fixed stars. Cellarius's *scenographia* presents this ancient world-picture as a grand theatrical machine, even as rival systems pressed upon it.

## For artists & game designers
The see-through nested spheres in dramatic perspective are a ready model for a 'celestial machine' set-piece or boss arena.

citations.text: Robert H. van Gent, *Andreas Cellarius: Harmonia Macrocosmica of 1660* (Taschen, 2006).

title: *Planisphaerium Braheum* — the Tychonic system
creator: Andreas Cellarius
summary:
Cellarius's *Planisphaerium Braheum*, the plate setting out the compromise cosmos of **Tycho Brahe**.

## Iconography
The **Earth** holds the centre, circled by the Moon and Sun; the five planets are shown orbiting the **Sun** as it in turn travels around the Earth — the hybrid **geo-heliocentric** arrangement. A **zodiac ring** bounds the diagram and **putti** with instruments fill the corners.

## Significance
Tycho's system (proposed 1588) kept a motionless Earth, as scripture and physics then seemed to require, while granting the elegance of Sun-centred planetary motion. Cellarius's plate enshrines it as a serious third option in the seventeenth-century debate, and its preserved [[motif:zodiac|zodiac]] frame shows astronomy and astrology still sharing one map of the sky.

## For artists & game designers
A visibly 'in-between' cosmology — useful when you want a world-model that is neither fully old nor fully new.

citations.text: Robert H. van Gent, *Andreas Cellarius: Harmonia Macrocosmica of 1660* (Taschen, 2006).

title: Zodiac hemisphere map, *Harmonia Macrocosmica*
creator: Andreas Cellarius
summary:
A Cellarius hemisphere centred on the band of the **zodiac**, isolating the twelve signs from the wider star-atlas.

## Iconography
The disc is organised around the **ecliptic**, the Sun's annual path, along which the twelve **signs of the zodiac** are drawn as their living figures — Aries the ram, Taurus the bull, Gemini the twins, and so on around the circle — with celestial latitude lines fanning out from the ecliptic poles.

## Significance
The zodiac was the working instrument of astrology: the twelvefold division of the ecliptic that located planets, assigned dignities, and framed the houses of a horoscope. By giving it a dedicated hemisphere, Cellarius made explicit the [[motif:zodiac|zodiacal]] backbone shared by astronomy and astrology alike.

## For artists & game designers
A clean, ready-made wheel of the twelve signs around an ecliptic — drop-in art for a calendar, sign-selector, or destiny mechanic.

citations.text: Robert H. van Gent, *Andreas Cellarius: Harmonia Macrocosmica of 1660* (Taschen, 2006).

title: *Imagines coeli septentrionales* — Dürer's northern star map
creator: Albrecht Dürer
summary:
Albrecht Dürer's *Imagines coeli septentrionales* (Nuremberg, 1515), the northern sheet of the first printed European star charts.

## Iconography
A circular map of the **northern hemisphere** is filled with classical **constellation figures** and the twelve **zodiac** signs ringing the ecliptic, drawn in Dürer's confident woodcut line. Four famous **astronomers** of antiquity — including Ptolemy and Aratus — occupy the corners as authorities for the sky depicted.

## Significance
Planned with the astronomers Johannes Stabius and Conrad Heinfogel, Dürer's pair of charts (north and south) translated Ptolemy's catalogue into a beautiful, reproducible image and set the visual standard for two centuries of [[motif:zodiac|figured star maps]] from Bayer to Hevelius. It marks the start of printed celestial cartography.

## For artists & game designers
The foundational 'old star chart' look — corner sages and a figure-packed disc — endlessly reusable as a lore map.

citations.text: Deborah J. Warner, *The Sky Explored: Celestial Cartography 1500–1800* (1979).

title: Scutum (Sobieski's Shield), from Hevelius
creator: Johannes Hevelius
summary:
**Scutum**, the Shield, one of the new constellations introduced by **Johannes Hevelius** in his *Firmamentum Sobiescianum* (Danzig, 1687).

## Iconography
A heraldic **shield** bearing a cross is set among a sparse field of stars — the arms of King Jan III Sobieski of Poland, Hevelius's patron, raised into the heavens. The figure is drawn in the firm engraved line characteristic of Hevelius's atlas.

## Significance
Hevelius mapped the sky with naked-eye instruments to the end of the telescopic age, and invented several constellations that survive — Scutum, Lynx, Sextans, Vulpecula. Naming the **Shield** for Sobieski (victor of Vienna, 1683) shows how seventeenth-century patronage literally rewrote the constellations, a late chapter in the figured-sky tradition that fed [[motif:astrology|astrology]].

## For artists & game designers
A coat-of-arms set in the stars — a neat model for a faction sigil written into the night sky.

title: Southern hemisphere, Hevelius's *Firmamentum Sobiescianum*
creator: Johannes Hevelius
summary:
The southern celestial hemisphere (*Emisfero Australe*) from **Johannes Hevelius**'s *Firmamentum Sobiescianum, sive Uranographia* (Danzig, 1687).

## Iconography
A full **planisphere** shows the constellation figures of the southern sky drawn, in Hevelius's manner, as if seen from *outside* the celestial sphere — so the figures face away from the viewer. Beasts, ships, and mythic forms crowd the disc along the band of the **zodiac** and the southern circles.

## Significance
Hevelius's posthumous atlas (edited by his widow Elisabetha) was among the last great hand-figured star maps and the last major one drawn from naked-eye observation. Its 'external' convention links it to the celestial-globe tradition, and its mythic figures preserve the [[motif:zodiac|astral iconography]] on which astrology depended.

## For artists & game designers
An 'inside-out' sky seen from the outside of the sphere — a fresh perspective for a celestial map or a god's-eye view.

title: Atalanta Fugiens — Frontispiece: The Race of Atalanta and Hippomenes
summary:
The engraved title page to Michael Maier's *Atalanta Fugiens* (Oppenheim, 1617; engraving by Matthäus Merian the Elder) gathers four scenes built around golden apples: the Garden of the Hesperides with its guardian dragon, Hercules reaching for the fruit, Aphrodite handing the apples to Hippomenes, and — at center — the foot-race in which the swift virgin Atalanta stoops to gather a dropped apple and so loses.

## Alchemical meaning
Maier reads the myth as a parable of the Work. Atalanta is the volatile principle (mercury, the fugitive spirit); Hippomenes the fixing principle (sulphur); the three golden apples are the interventions of art that slow the flight of the volatile so that fixation can occur. The book's title — 'Atalanta Fleeing' — names this chase between the volatile and the fixed that the fifty emblems elaborate.

## For artists & game designers
A dense classical tableau: a running maiden, a pursuing youth, a goddess, a hero, an orchard guarded by a serpent-dragon, scattered apples. Excellent reference for a mythic title-card, a foot-race set-piece, or a Hesperides garden environment.

title: Atalanta Fugiens — Emblem I: Portavit eum ventus in ventre suo (The Wind Carried Him in Its Belly)
summary:
Motto: *Portavit eum ventus in ventre suo* — 'The wind carried him in its belly.' The engraving shows Boreas, the north wind, his belly swollen with the embryonic child of the philosophers, set against a wide landscape; the infant is being carried on the air.

## Alchemical meaning
The line is drawn from the *Tabula Smaragdina* (the Emerald Tablet): 'the wind carried it in its belly.' Maier glosses it as the volatile, airy phase in which the nascent stone is borne by 'wind' — that is, by vapour and spirit — before it can be born onto the earth (the subject of Emblem II). It opens the sequence on the principle that the matter must first be sublimed and spiritualised.

## For artists & game designers
A personified wind-god with a gravid belly over open country — useful for an air-elemental, a weather deity, or a 'spirit carried on the wind' motif.

## Reading
Maier continues the the me of Emblem I, now emphasizing that the earth is specifically the nurse, not the mother, of the philosophical substance. He distinguishes between generation (which occurs through the volatile principle, the wind) and nourishment (which requires the fixed, earthy body). The discourse argues that just as human food must be converted into the substance of the body it feeds, so the alchemical earth must be assimilated into the growing Stone. Maier draws a careful analogy between the stages of infant feeding — blood in utero, milk after birth, solid food later — and the progressive fixation of the volatile philosophical substance.

title: Atalanta Fugiens — Emblem III: Go to the woman who washes the sheets

## Reading
Maier argues that the alchemical purification process mirrors the everyday work of washing dirty linen: just as earth-stains on fabric are removed by water and then dried by sun and wind, so the impurities of the philosophical substance must be cleansed through repeated washing and exposure to the elements. The discourse develops the principle that what comes from earth is cleaned by the next element in the sequence — water purifies earth, air dries what water has cleaned. Maier presents the was her woman as a figure for the alchemist who must patiently repeat the cycle of dissolution and drying, an operation the tradition calls the albedo or whitening stage.

Alchemical phase: **Albedo**. Maier's acknowledged sources here include Pseudo Aristotle, Rosarium, Turba.

title: Atalanta Fugiens — Emblem IV: Coniunge fratrem cum sorore (Join the Brother with the Sister)
summary:

This is the *coniunctio*, the chymical wedding of the solar (sulphur, masculine, fixed) and lunar (mercury, feminine, volatile) principles — the central operation of the Work, inherited from the *Rosarium Philosophorum*. The 'incestuous' union of brother and sister signals that the two must spring from one common root (the prima materia) for the marriage to be fertile.

title: Atalanta Fugiens — Emblem V: Appone mulieri super mammas bufonem (Set a Toad to the Woman's Breast)
summary:
Motto: *Appone mulieri super mammas bufonem, ut ablactet eum* — 'Set a toad upon the woman's breasts that she may suckle it; let it grow fat on her milk and let the woman die.' A reclining woman gives suck to a cold, swollen toad.

## Alchemical meaning
The toad is the earthy, cold, poisonous body of the matter — heavy and chthonic; the woman's milk is the nourishing volatile or 'philosophical' moisture. As the toad fattens, the woman (the active volatile) is exhausted and 'dies': the volatile is fixed into the body. The image is a memorable figure for putrefaction and the transfer of life from spirit to body.

## For artists & game designers
A striking, slightly grotesque image — a giant toad nursing at a human breast. Strong reference for a witch's familiar, a poison/earth motif, or body-horror alchemy.

title: Atalanta Fugiens — Emblem VI: Sow your gold in the white foliated earth
motifs: sky + tree + window + building house + flower + hearth
tower chimney + castle + castle building temple + tower chimney

## Reading
Maier develops an extended agricultural analogy: just as the farmer must sow grain in prepared soil to reap a harvest, the alchemist must 'sow' philosophical gold in 'white foliated earth' — a specially prepared mercurial substrate — to produce the Stone. Drawing on Plato's division of the civic body into physicians and farmers, Maier argues that the alchemist combines both roles, healing metals while cultivating them. The discourse establishes a key principle: the seed (gold) must be of the same species as what it produces, and the earth (mercury) must be receptive and properly tempered. The white, foliated quality of the earth indicates the albedo stage, where the purified substrate is ready to receive the active seed.

## In the Work
Alchemical phase: **Albedo**. Maier's acknowledged sources here include Jodocus Greverus, Lullius, Pseudo Aristotle, Rosarium, Senior.

title: Atalanta Fugiens — Emblem VII: The Eaglet Falls Back into the Nest
summary:
Motto (paraphrased from Maier): a young eaglet beats its wings to leave the nest but tires and falls back into it. The plate shows a fledgling eagle and the nest from which it cannot yet escape.

## Alchemical meaning
The eagle is the volatile spirit attempting sublimation — the ascent of the purified substance. Its repeated failure and fall back into the nest figures the cycle of *solve et coagula*: the matter is raised by heat and falls again as it cools, the rising and re-descending repeated many times ('reiteration') until the spirit is fixed enough to fly free. The eagle is one of alchemy's most common ciphers for volatile mercury.

## For artists & game designers

The 'philosophical egg' is the sealed vessel — and, by extension, the chaos of the prima materia containing all elements in potential, like the four parts of an egg (shell, membrane, white, yolk). The fiery sword is the penetrating, dividing action of fire that opens the egg and separates the elements so the Work can proceed. It is a classic emblem of *separatio*.

Maier argues that the old man represents the fixed, aged substance of the philosophical body that must be rejuvenated through exposure to celestial dew — the volatile, purifying spirit descending from above. ## Reading
Maier commands two simultaneous actions: whiten Latona and tear up the books. He develops Latona as a figure for the imperfect philosophical body — an alloy of Sol and Luna stained with black impurities — that must be purified through the albedo. De Jong traces the name Latona to 'laton,' meaning electrum or yellow silver, connecting the mythological goddess to the metallurgical process of whitening a dark alloy. The instruction to destroy books signals Maier's insistence that neither theory alone nor book-learning can substitute for practical laboratory work — the alchemist must act on matter directly, not merely read about it. The discourse argues that both intellect and manual labor are necessary, but that practice takes precedence.

Maier continues the argument of Emblem XI, now emphasizing the bewildering variety and obscurity of alchemical writings as the reason books must be abandoned. The discourse develops the Latona allegory further: she is an impure body of mixed Sol and Luna that must be found in a humble place, immersed in dung where she becomes white lead, from which red lead originates. Maier draws on the biblical story of Naaman the leper, healed by washing seven times in the Jordan, as an allegory for the purification of the philosophical ore. He argues that the 'dropsical' stone — swollen with impurities — must undergo repeated washing to be cleansed, just as Naaman's leprosy was cured only through sevenfold immersion. The discourse connects this to the albedo purification and to the sacramental symbolism of baptism as a prefiguration of alchemical cleansing. Maier cites the Clangor Buccinae as the source of the dropsical ore metaphor, linking it explicitly to the Latona-whitening sequence of the preceding emblems.

title: Atalanta Fugiens — Emblem XIV: Hic est Draco caudam suam devorans (The Dragon Devouring Its Tail)
summary:
Motto: *Hic est Draco caudam suam devorans* — 'Here is the dragon devouring its own tail.' Maier's engraving (Merian) shows the winged dragon curled into a ring, its jaws closed on the tip of its own tail — the **ouroboros**, the most ancient of alchemical signs, whose earliest surviving form appears in the *Chrysopoeia of Kleopatra*.

## Alchemical meaning
The self-devouring dragon figures the closed, self-sustaining circulation of the Work: the matter feeds upon itself, dies, and is reborn from its own substance ('one is all, and by it all, and to it all, and if it does not contain all, it is nothing'). It encodes both the unity of the prima materia and the endless turning of *solve et coagula*. Maier's epigram: 'The hungry dragon, feeding on his tail, his fainting soul relieves... eat and devour, kill and revive anew.'

## For artists & game designers
The canonical ouroboros — a ready-made emblem for cycles, eternity, infinity loops, time magic, or a serpent-ring sigil. One of the single most reusable images in the whole corpus.

Maier argues that the alchemical work requires not one fire but four distinct types, each governing a different phase of the operation. He identifies these as the fire of the lamp (external heat), the fire of the ash-bath (gentle, sustained warmth), the fire of the substance it self (intrinsic reactive heat), and the fire of the water-bath (moist, temperate heat). The discourse develops the principle that fire transforms by making things fiery — communicating its own nature — but can not make gold directly, only prepare the conditions for gold's emergence. Maier cites this fourfold fire as the master key to the practical art, without which even correct materials will fail.

title: Atalanta Fugiens — Emblem XXI: The Squared Circle of the Philosophers' Stone
summary:
One of the most famous images in all of alchemy. A philosopher-geometer, giant compasses in hand, inscribes on a wall the figure of a man and woman standing inside a small circle, enclosed by a square, enclosed by a triangle, enclosed in turn by the great outer circle.

## Alchemical meaning
The motto encodes the recipe as geometry: 'Make of the man and woman a circle, then a square, out of the square a triangle, make again a circle, and you shall have the Stone of the Philosophers.' The nested figures map the reduction of the matter through the four elements (square), the three principles — sulphur, mercury, salt (triangle), the body-soul-spirit, and back to unity (the final circle). John Michell and Allan Brown noted that the design also encodes a near-perfect squaring of the circle (equal areas), tying the alchemical to the geometric quest.

## For artists & game designers
The definitive 'sacred geometry' diagram — circle/square/triangle nesting with a compass-bearing sage. Perfect for a ritual circle, a puzzle glyph, a crafting-recipe UI, or an arcane blueprint.

He develops cooking as the central metaphor for the post-albedo operations, arguing that the white substance must be slowly heated and matured, just as food is transformed by cooking from raw to nourishing. The discourse emphasizes patience and temperature control: the philosophical substance must simmer, not boil. Maier draws on the herms — three-forked road markers — as guides that show the way to straying travelers, an allegory for the textual guideposts left by earlier alchemists.

title: Atalanta Fugiens — Emblem XXIV: The Wolf Devours the King, and Fire Restores Him
summary:
Motto: *Regem lupus voravit, et vita sibi reddidit* — 'A wolf devoured the king, and being burnt restored him to life again.' The plate shows a grey wolf consuming a crowned king, with a fire nearby in which the wolf is to be burned.

## Alchemical meaning
The 'grey wolf' is *lupus metallorum* — stibnite/antimony, used to purify gold (the King). The wolf devours the king (antimony dissolves and carries off impure gold); the wolf is then burnt away, leaving the king reborn purer than before. It is a vivid figure for purification by an aggressive solvent and the death-and-rebirth of the noble metal.

## For artists & game designers
A crowned king being devoured by a wolf beside a fire — potent imagery for a downfall-and-return arc, a beast-king confrontation, or an antimony/poison crafting motif.

title: Atalanta Fugiens — Emblem XLIV: Typhon Dismembers Osiris; Isis Gathers Him
summary:

Death and reintegration are the rhythm of the magistery.

title: Atalanta Fugiens — Emblem XLVII: Emblem XLVII

summary:
Motto: *The wolf coming from the East, and the Dog coming from the West, have bitten each other.*

## Reading
Maier parallels the eagle meeting of Emblem XLVI with a more violent version: the wolf from the East and the dog from the West bite each other in mutual destruction. He argues that while the eagles' conjunction was aerial and spiritual, the wolf-and-dog encounter is terrestrial and material — the same union of opposites enacted at a lower, more physical register. The discourse develops the wolf as the more aggressive, dissolving agent (philosophical mercury in its corrosive aspect) and the dog as the resistant, fixed body that must be broken down. Their mutual biting — each wounding the other — represents the reciprocal action of dissolution, where both substances are transformed by their encounter.

## In the Work
Alchemical phase: **Nigredo**. Maier's acknowledged sources here include Lambsprinck, Pseudo Aristotle, Senior.

motifs: cup + altar + person man old man + woman + hearth + sword axe + hourglass + globe + person + castle building house + cup + sword axe torch + star + crown + window + door window + window

Motto: *The king, fallen ill from drinking, is restored to health by a physician.*

## Reading
Maier develops the Merlini allegory of King Duenech in its final phase: the king, fallen ill from drinking foul waters, is restored to health by physicians who administer the correct elixir. He draws on Xerxes drinking muddy water in the desert as an analogy for the philosophical substance contaminated by impurities. The discourse describes the king's cure through successive stages — first Egyptian, then Alexandrian physicians — corresponding to different alchemical traditions' approaches to purification. Bernard of Treves's allegory describes the restored king dressed in a black cuirass, white tunic, and purple-red cloak — the three colors of the opus (nigredo, albedo, rubedo) worn simultaneously, signaling the completion of the work.

## In the Work
Alchemical phase: **Rubedo**. Maier's acknowledged sources here include Lullius, Merlini.

title: Atalanta Fugiens — Emblem XLIX: Emblem XLIX
motifs: crown + cauldron anvil + person + man old man + woman + person + man old man + scepter + person + woman
summary:
Motto: *The Philosophical Child acknowledges three fathers, just as Orion.*

## Reading
Maier argues that the philosopher's stone, like the mythological Orion, acknowledges three fathers — three distinct sources or principles that contribute to its generation. He develops this as an allegory for the tria prima: the stone is born from salt (the bodily principle), sulphur (the soul principle), and mercury (the spirit principle), each 'fat he ring' a different aspect of the complete substance. The discourse draws on the Orion myth — conceived from the combined seed of Zeus, Poseidon, and Hermes — to argue that no single source suffices for the generation of the philosophical child. Maier presents this as one of the final teachings: the stone's triple origin explains why it can not be produced from any single starting material.

## In the Work
Alchemical phase: **Citrinitas**. Maier's acknowledged sources here include Lullius, Ovid, Robertus Vallensis.

title: Atalanta Fugiens — Emblem L: The Dragon and the Woman Slay Each Other and Bathe in Blood
summary:
Motto (the fiftieth and final emblem): 'The dragon slays the woman and she him, and together they are drenched in blood.' The closing plate shows the mutual slaying of the winged dragon and the woman.

## Alchemical meaning
The last emblem seals the sequence with a final, reciprocal *coniunctio*: the volatile (dragon) and the fixed/feminine (woman) destroy one another and are dissolved together in the 'blood' — the red tincture. Their mutual death is the death that produces the Stone; the bath of blood signals the *rubedo*, the reddening that crowns the Work. After fifty emblems of chase, the fleeing Atalanta is at last caught.

## For artists & game designers
A climactic dragon-versus-woman duel ending in a bath of blood — a natural finale image: a final-boss tableau, a blood-magic rite, or the red 'completion' card of a set.

summary:
A miniature from the Aurora Consurgens cycle, the luminous early-15th-century watercolour treatise once ascribed to Thomas Aquinas.

## Iconography
One of the codex's emblematic watercolour scenes, painted in the loose, fast wash that gives the Zurich Aurora its dreamlike, unfinished quality. The exact subject is not specified in the source filename and is described here in general terms to avoid invention.

## Significance
The Aurora Consurgens ('Rising Dawn') is among the earliest fully illustrated Latin alchemical texts, a florilegium of biblical, Hermetic and sapiential citations welded into a hymn of the dawning Work. Its strange, vivid pictures - dragons, eclipses, winged figures, kings and queens - form the deepest medieval root of the printed emblem tradition and were a touchstone for C. G. Jung's late alchemical studies.

## For artists & game designers

The conjoined or double figure prefigures the [[motif:rebis|rebis]] - the hermaphroditic product of the *coniunctio*, in which the united King and Queen are reborn as a single androgynous body. The Aurora Consurgens, a strange and lyrical treatise once fathered on Thomas Aquinas, is among the first to give this idea sustained pictorial treatment, and it deeply influenced later alchemical iconography and Jung's reading of it.

The fused dual-gendered body is the archetypal 'two characters become one entity' design - a vivid base for a merge or fusion result screen.

A monkey or ape, painted in the codex's watercolour on the opening folio (1r).

## Significance
The proverb *ars simia naturae* casts the alchemist's art as an imitator of nature - at best a faithful collaborator, at worst a foolish mimic producing false gold. Placing the ape near the very start of the cycle frames the whole Work with this self-aware tension between true transmutation and mere imitation. The motif had wide currency in medieval and Renaissance thought about art and craft.

## For artists & game designers
An ape can be a sly antagonist or trickster signalling 'counterfeit / imitation' - e.g. a fake-craft or forgery mechanic.

A standing figure swings one arm to scatter grain from a fold of his garment across furrowed ground. The miniature is painted in the loose, vivid watercolour wash that distinguishes the Zurich codex from later, harder alchemical engraving.

## Significance
The Aurora Consurgens reads scripture alchemically: the Gospel parable of the sower becomes the dictum that the *semina* - the seeds of the metals - must be buried, rot, and germinate before the tincture can grow. The sower belongs to the agricultural metaphor that runs through the [[motif:semina|seed]] language of medieval alchemy, where putrefaction is sowing and the multiplied Stone is the harvest. The text is a florilegium of biblical and Hermetic citations once ascribed to Thomas Aquinas.

## For artists & game designers
A clean visual for a 'plant the seed, wait for the transformation' mechanic - the cost paid now that pays out only after a death-and-rot interval.

creator: Anonymous (pseudo-Thomas Aquinas)

Two crowned lovers - the solar King and lunar Queen - meet in the embrace that medieval alchemy called the *coniunctio*, the marriage of opposites.

## Iconography
A male and a female figure, each crowned, stand close in a gesture of union, painted in the codex's quick watercolour hand. Solar and lunar attributes mark them as Sol and Luna, the red and white principles.

## Significance
The coniunctio is the pivot of the whole opus: the wedding of [[motif:sol and luna|Sol and Luna]], sulphur and mercury, fixed and volatile, whose union and 'death' in the vessel precede the birth of the Stone. The Aurora is the earliest fully illustrated Latin treatise to give this nuptial allegory pictorial form, anticipating the famous woodcut sequence of the *Rosarium Philosophorum* by more than a century. C. G. Jung drew on the Aurora's imagery in his late work on the *coniunctio*.

## For artists & game designers
The royal-couple embrace is the canonical 'fusion of two elements into a third' icon - useful wherever a crafting or relationship system rewards combining opposed inputs.

'Everything by weight, number and measure' (Wisdom 11:21) is a favourite alchemical maxim: the opus succeeds only if the proportions of the ingredients and the degrees of fire are precisely balanced. The scales also carry the moral and cosmic sense of justice and equilibrium. The Aurora, steeped in the sapiential books of scripture, naturally reaches for the balance as a sign of right measure.

title: Aurora Consurgens - The Nursing Figure (f. 13v)
creator: Anonymous (pseudo-Thomas Aquinas)
rights: Public domain. Zentralbibliothek Zurich, Ms. Rh. 172 (e-codices).
summary:
A figure giving suck - the Aurora's image of the *lac virginis*, the 'virgin's milk' that nourishes the infant Stone.

## Iconography
A seated female figure nurses a child at the breast, painted in the manuscript's loose watercolour. Milk and feeding are the visual subject.

## Significance
Medieval alchemy speaks of the *lac virginis*, the milky, mercurial water that feeds and 'raises' the philosophical child after its birth from the coniunctio. The nursing image translates the chemical idea of repeated gentle feeding (imbibition) into a maternal allegory. The Aurora's text steeps the picture in Marian and Song-of-Songs language, fusing devotion and chemistry in a way characteristic of the work.

## For artists & game designers
A tender counter-image to all the dragons and decapitations - useful for a 'nurture / grow the creature you made' phase after a violent crafting step.

title: Aurora Consurgens - The Medicine (f. 14v)
creator: Anonymous (pseudo-Thomas Aquinas)
rights: Public domain. Zentralbibliothek Zurich, Ms. Rh. 172 (e-codices).
summary:
A medicinal scene - the Aurora's image of the Stone as *medicina*, the elixir that heals metals and bodies alike.

## Iconography
A figure preparing, administering or holding a remedy, painted in the codex's watercolour on folio 14v.

## Significance
For the Aurora the Philosophers' Stone is above all a medicine: the *elixir* and *panacea* that perfects imperfect metals to gold and, by extension, cures the diseased body. This medical register links alchemy to the later iatrochemistry of Paracelsus. The Aurora's blending of healing, scripture and chemistry is exactly the devotional-medical voice that made it so influential and so strange.

## For artists & game designers
A clean 'the thing you make is also a cure' beat - ties a crafting payoff to a healing item.

title: Aurora Consurgens - The Peacock (f. 16v)
creator: Anonymous (pseudo-Thomas Aquinas)
rights: Public domain. Zentralbibliothek Zurich, Ms. Rh. 172 (e-codices).
summary:
A peacock - the *cauda pavonis*, 'peacock's tail' - the shimmer of many colours that signals the turning point of the alchemical work.

## Iconography
A peacock displays its eyed, iridescent plumage, rendered in washes of green, blue and gold typical of the Zurich miniatures.

## Significance
The *cauda pavonis* names the moment in the opus when the blackened *nigredo* breaks into a play of fugitive colours before resolving into the white and then the red. To the Aurora's author this iridescence is a sign of life returning to the dead matter in the flask. The peacock became one of the most enduring alchemical emblems, recurring in the Splendor Solis and the Ripley Scrolls. The surrounding text weaves the Song of Songs into a hymn of the rising dawn (*aurora consurgens*).

## For artists & game designers
Perfect shorthand for a 'phase-shift / something is about to change' visual beat - a burst of rainbow colour as a system passes a threshold.

title: Aurora Consurgens - The Boiling Pot (f. 17v)
creator: Anonymous (pseudo-Thomas Aquinas)
rights: Public domain. Zentralbibliothek Zurich, Ms. Rh. 172 (e-codices).
summary:
A pot set boiling - the Aurora's plain emblem of *coction*, the slow cooking in which the matter is digested toward the Stone.

## Iconography
A cooking vessel or pot over heat, contents seething, painted in the codex's watercolour on folio 17v.

## Significance
Coction - patient, regulated boiling - is the engine of the alchemical opus: the matter is 'cooked' in the sealed vessel until it changes colour and nature. The cooking-pot image keeps the work close to the kitchen and the hearth, a homely register the Aurora shares with much practical alchemy. Repeated decoction drives the cycle of colours toward the red.

## For artists & game designers
A literal cook-pot - drop-in art for any brewing, smelting, or crafting station with a heat/time gauge.

title: Aurora Consurgens - The Bed (f. 18r)
creator: Anonymous (pseudo-Thomas Aquinas)
rights: Public domain. Zentralbibliothek Zurich, Ms. Rh. 172 (e-codices).
summary:
A figure laid on a bed - the Aurora's image of the death and putrefaction in which the wedded principles 'die' before they are reborn.

## Iconography
A reclining figure on a bed or bier, painted in the loose watercolour of the Zurich codex.

## Significance
After the coniunctio the united King and Queen must die together in the vessel: the bed is at once nuptial couch and grave, the *nigredo* in which matter blackens and rots. This death-as-marriage is one of alchemy's central paradoxes - corruption is the necessary gate to regeneration. The motif recurs across the tradition, from the Aurora to the entombment scenes of the Rosarium.

## For artists & game designers
The bed-that-is-a-grave is a strong ambiguous-space design: a place of rest that is also a death/transformation trigger.

title: Aurora Consurgens - The Viscera (f. 19v)
creator: Anonymous (pseudo-Thomas Aquinas)
rights: Public domain. Zentralbibliothek Zurich, Ms. Rh. 172 (e-codices).
summary:
A visceral image - the Aurora's confronting picture of the inner matter laid open, the *interiora* of body and earth.

## Iconography
A figure or body shown with its viscera / inner parts exposed, painted in the manuscript's loose watercolour on folio 19v.

## Significance
Alchemy repeatedly opens the body - of king, dragon or man - to reach the hidden seed within: dismemberment and the exposure of the *interiora* are stages on the way to the cleansed essence. The image rhymes with the digger's *interiora terrae*: one must go inside, whether earth or flesh, to recover the buried perfection. The Aurora's frankness here is part of its raw, dreamlike power.

## For artists & game designers
A grisly 'open it up to get what's inside' visual - fits a harvesting or extraction mechanic with a transgressive edge.

title: Aurora Consurgens - The Birds (f. 20r)
creator: Anonymous (pseudo-Thomas Aquinas)
rights: Public domain. Zentralbibliothek Zurich, Ms. Rh. 172 (e-codices).
summary:
Birds - hens or fowl - from the Aurora's bestiary of 'birds of Hermes', the alchemical sign of volatilisation and the spirit that rises and falls in the flask.

## Iconography
Two or more birds painted in the codex's quick watercolour on folio 20r.

## Significance
Throughout alchemy birds figure the volatile principle: the rising bird is sublimation and the spirit ascending, the falling bird is its condensation and return. The repeated ascent and descent of the 'birds of Hermes' is the circulatory distillation that purifies the matter. The Aurora's flocks belong to the same avian symbolism that later produced the black crow, white swan, and red phoenix of the printed treatises.

## For artists & game designers
Rising/falling birds are an elegant loop motif - ideal for a process that must repeat (distil, condense, distil) before it completes.

title: Aurora Consurgens - The Dragon Ring / Ouroboros (f. 20v)
creator: Anonymous (pseudo-Thomas Aquinas)
rights: Public domain. Zentralbibliothek Zurich, Ms. Rh. 172 (e-codices).
summary:
A dragon curled into a ring - the Aurora's ouroboros, the self-devouring serpent that signs the unity and endless circulation of the Work.

## Iconography
A dragon bent into a closed circle, tail toward mouth, painted in the codex's watercolour on folio 20v.

## Significance
The [[motif:ouroboros|ouroboros]] - *hen to pan*, 'the all is one' - is the oldest alchemical sign, the serpent eating its tail to figure a process with no beginning or end, in which the matter continually feeds and renews itself. The Aurora's ring-dragon places this ancient emblem inside the medieval opus, where it stands for the circular distillations and the final unity of the perfected substance.

## For artists & game designers
A dragon biting its own tail is the definitive 'closed loop / eternal cycle' emblem - perfect for a circular UI, an infinite-resource sigil, or a time-loop motif.

title: Aurora Consurgens - The Dragon in the Pot (f. 21v)
creator: Anonymous (pseudo-Thomas Aquinas)
rights: Public domain. Zentralbibliothek Zurich, Ms. Rh. 172 (e-codices).
summary:
A dragon confined in a pot - the Aurora's image of the dangerous matter sealed and tamed within the alchemical vessel.

## Iconography
A dragon set within or rising from a cooking-pot or flask, painted in the codex's watercolour on folio 21v.

## Significance
Sealing the dragon in the vessel dramatises the central laboratory act: the volatile, poisonous spirit must be enclosed in the hermetically stopped flask so it can be cooked, killed and fixed without escaping. The dragon is both venom and the source of the medicine - the poison that, mastered, becomes the cure. The Aurora's pot-dragons are among the earliest examples of this enduring image.

## For artists & game designers
A monster sealed in a container under heat is a complete 'contain and transform the dangerous resource' mechanic in one picture.

title: Aurora Consurgens - The Sky-Swimmers (f. 22v)
creator: Anonymous (pseudo-Thomas Aquinas)
rights: Public domain. Zentralbibliothek Zurich, Ms. Rh. 172 (e-codices).
summary:
Figures that seem to swim through the air - the Aurora's dreamlike image of the spirit ascending, matter made volatile and rising.

## Iconography
Human figures suspended or 'swimming' in an open sky or upper space, painted in the codex's loose watercolour on folio 22v.

## Significance
The ascent of figures into the heavens pictures sublimation and volatilisation - the freeing of the subtle spirit from the gross body so it can rise, be purified, and descend again refined. The Aurora's surreal, weightless compositions are among the reasons modern viewers (and Jung) found the manuscript so suggestive of the dreaming, unconscious mind.

## For artists & game designers
Floating, swimming-in-air figures give an instant 'ascension / out-of-body / spirit-realm' register for a transition or vision sequence.

title: Aurora Consurgens - The Firebird / Phoenix (f. 23v)
creator: Anonymous (pseudo-Thomas Aquinas)
rights: Public domain. Zentralbibliothek Zurich, Ms. Rh. 172 (e-codices).
summary:
A bird in flames - the phoenix or firebird, the Aurora's emblem of the resurrection that crowns the Work in red.

## Iconography
A bird amid fire, painted in the codex's watercolour on folio 23v.

## Significance
The phoenix that burns and is reborn from its own ashes is alchemy's supreme image of the *rubedo*, the reddening in which the dead matter rises perfected as the Stone. It answers the black crow of the *nigredo* and the white swan of the *albedo*. The Aurora places this fiery rebirth near the climax of its cycle, scripture and chemistry fused in the language of the rising dawn the work is named for.

## For artists & game designers
The classic burn-and-rise-again icon - a respawn, revive, or final-evolution visual.

title: Aurora Consurgens - The Digger (f. 24v)
creator: Anonymous (pseudo-Thomas Aquinas)
rights: Public domain. Zentralbibliothek Zurich, Ms. Rh. 172 (e-codices).
summary:
A labourer digging - the Aurora's image of the descent into the earth to find the hidden stone, the *interiora terrae* of the alchemical motto.

## Iconography
A figure works the ground with a spade, painted in the manuscript's loose watercolour on folio 24v.

## Significance
Digging dramatises the famous injunction *Visita Interiora Terrae Rectificando Invenies Occultum Lapidem* - 'visit the interior of the earth; by rectifying you will find the hidden stone.' The buried gold is both literal ore and the latent perfection to be coaxed from base matter. The Aurora frames this labour in scriptural terms of seeking treasure hid in a field.

## For artists & game designers
Pure 'dig here for the hidden thing' iconography - a natural fit for an excavation or buried-loot mechanic.

rights: Public domain. Zentralbibliothek Zurich, Ms. Rh. 172 (e-codices).

Craftsmen at work - the Aurora's image of the *artifex*, the human artisans whose patient labour cooperates with nature to make the Stone.

## Iconography
Two or more workers handling tools or materials, painted in the codex's watercolour on folio 25v.

## Significance
Alchemy styled itself the perfecting of nature by art: the *artifex* does not create the Stone but helps nature finish what she began. Picturing ordinary craftsmen grounds the lofty allegory in real labour - hammering, tending fire, watching the vessel. The Aurora's mixture of high scriptural rhetoric and humble workshop scenes is one of its distinctive notes.

## For artists & game designers
A workshop crew is direct reference for a crafting-station scene or an NPC artisan guild.

title: Aurora Consurgens - The City (f. 27r)
creator: Anonymous (pseudo-Thomas Aquinas)
rights: Public domain. Zentralbibliothek Zurich, Ms. Rh. 172 (e-codices).
summary:
A walled city - the Aurora's image of the goal: the heavenly city, the perfected end toward which the whole Work builds.

## Iconography
A towered, walled city, painted in the codex's watercolour on folio 27r near the close of the cycle.

## Significance
The city, often read as the heavenly Jerusalem, gives the opus an architectural telos: the scattered, purified matter is gathered into a single perfected structure, just as the soul is gathered into the city of God. The Aurora's saturation in scripture makes this overlay of spiritual and chemical fulfilment especially explicit. Building imagery recurs across alchemy as a figure for the assembled, completed Stone.

## For artists & game designers
A shining walled city is the universal 'you have reached the goal' image - an endgame location or victory screen.

title: Aurora Consurgens - Mercurius (f. 27v)
creator: Anonymous (pseudo-Thomas Aquinas)
rights: Public domain. Zentralbibliothek Zurich, Ms. Rh. 172 (e-codices).
summary:
An image of Mercurius - the slippery, dual-natured spirit that medieval alchemy made the soul and solvent of the whole Work.

## Iconography
A figure or emblem of mercury / Mercurius painted in the codex's watercolour wash on folio 27v, in the closing run of the Zurich cycle.

## Significance
Mercurius is the *spiritus* of alchemy: at once the common quicksilver, the philosophical mercury that dissolves and conjoins the metals, and a trickster god-figure who is both poison and medicine. The Aurora treats this volatile principle as the agent that must be fixed and 'killed' to make the Stone. Jung devoted a famous essay ('The Spirit Mercurius') to exactly this ambivalent figure, of which the Aurora is an early witness.

## For artists & game designers
The shapeshifting, can't-be-pinned-down spirit is a ready-made trickster NPC or a volatile resource that escapes unless 'fixed'.

title: Aurora Consurgens - The Dark Angel (f. 29v)
creator: Anonymous (pseudo-Thomas Aquinas)
rights: Public domain. Zentralbibliothek Zurich, Ms. Rh. 172 (e-codices).
summary:
A dark winged figure near the close of the Zurich cycle - a 'dark angel' presiding over the shadowed phase of the Work.

## Iconography
A darkened angelic figure with wings, painted in the codex's watercolour on folio 29v.

## Significance
The Aurora's winged spirits embody the volatile, animating principle of the opus; a darkened angel reads as the spirit of the *nigredo*, the black, dissolving phase that precedes purification. These strange, brooding figures are central to the manuscript's dreamlike atmosphere and to the modern psychological readings (notably Jung's) that the Aurora invited.

## For artists & game designers
A brooding dark angel is strong art for a guardian, harbinger, or boss tied to a story's lowest, darkest turn.

title: Aurora Consurgens - The Chimera in the Vessel (f. 34r)
creator: Anonymous (pseudo-Thomas Aquinas)
rights: Public domain. Zentralbibliothek Zurich, Ms. Rh. 172 (e-codices).
summary:
A composite beast in a vessel - the Aurora's image of the mingled, monstrous matter contained within the alchemical flask.

## Iconography
A chimerical, many-natured creature set within or above a pot, painted in the manuscript's watercolour on folio 34r.

## Significance
The composite monster figures *mixtio*: the unstable union of contrary natures sealed in the vessel, neither one thing nor another until the Work resolves it. Such hybrid creatures populate alchemical imagery to show matter caught mid-transformation. The Aurora's containment of the beast in a pot ties the monstrous mixture to the literal apparatus of the laboratory.

## For artists & game designers
A monster trapped in a jar is a vivid 'unstable creation' visual - useful for a containment, summoning, or failed-craft beat.

title: Aurora Consurgens - The Earthbound Dragon (f. 36r)
creator: Anonymous (pseudo-Thomas Aquinas)
rights: Public domain. Zentralbibliothek Zurich, Ms. Rh. 172 (e-codices).
summary:
A dragon on the ground - the Aurora's earthbound, wingless dragon, sign of the fixed, base matter at the dark start of the Work.

## Iconography
A dragon crouched low on the earth, painted in the codex's loose watercolour on folio 36r in the closing run of the cycle.

## Significance
Alchemy distinguishes the winged (volatile) from the wingless (fixed) dragon. The earthbound dragon is the heavy, fixed body - the [[motif:prima materia|prima materia]] in its dark, poisonous state, the *nigredo* that must be tamed. The Aurora's dragons are among the most striking in medieval alchemical art and helped fix the dragon as the tradition's emblem of raw, dangerous first matter.

## For artists & game designers
A grounded, heavy dragon reads instantly as 'base / fixed / not yet refined' - the before state to a later winged or crowned form.

title: Aaron's Rod Becomes a Serpent before Pharaoh
work: Magic & the Supernatural in the Bible
creator: Anonymous (The Bible Panorama, 1891)
rights: No restrictions. Via Wikimedia Commons (Internet Archive Book Images).
summary:
A late-Victorian book illustration of the rod-to-serpent miracle, from *The Bible Panorama* (1891).

## Iconography
Moses and Aaron stand before the enthroned Pharaoh; Aaron's cast-down rod has become a serpent on the palace floor while the court magicians prepare their answer. The engraving renders the Exodus contest in the crisp narrative style of nineteenth-century scripture-illustration.

## Significance
The scene visualizes Exodus 7, the opening move of the plague cycle, in which the [[motif:miracle contest|sign-contest]] between Moses and Pharaoh's wise men begins. Mass-produced devotional and educational picture-Bibles like this one carried the iconography of biblical magic into Victorian households, fixing how generations imagined the showdown at the Egyptian court.

## For artists & game designers
The popular-print clarity here — single serpent, reacting court — is useful reference for staging a magic duel readably, without Baroque clutter.

title: Balaam and the Ass
work: Magic & the Supernatural in the Bible
creator: Rembrandt van Rijn
rights: Public domain. Via Wikimedia Commons (Musée Cognacq-Jay).
summary:
Rembrandt's early *Balaam and the Ass* (Musée Cognacq-Jay, Paris), the seer beating his donkey before the unseen angel.

## Iconography
The pagan diviner Balaam raises a staff to strike his stalled donkey, which turns its head to speak; above, an angel with a drawn sword — visible to the beast but not the man — bars the road. Rembrandt heightens the comedy and terror of the moment.

## Significance
Numbers 22 tells of Balaam, a Mesopotamian [[motif:seer|seer]] hired by Moab to curse Israel, whose [[motif:talking ass|donkey]] perceives the blocking angel that the professional diviner cannot. Forced instead to bless Israel, Balaam became the ambiguous figure of the prophet-for-hire whose occult sight is humbled by a beast's. The talking ass is one of scripture's strangest supernatural moments.

## For artists & game designers
The creature that sees the hidden threat its master cannot is a fine "animal companion senses the unseen" device — perception inverted between human and beast.

citations.text: Wikimedia Commons

title: Belshazzar's Feast
work: Magic & the Supernatural in the Bible
creator: Rembrandt van Rijn
rights: Public domain. Via Wikimedia Commons (National Gallery, London).
summary:
Rembrandt's *Belshazzar's Feast* (National Gallery, London), the moment a disembodied hand writes the doom of Babylon on the wall.

## Iconography
The Babylonian king Belshazzar lurches back from the table, eyes wide and goblet spilling, as a glowing hand inscribes Hebrew/Aramaic letters in mid-air; courtiers and a startled woman recoil. The famous inscription is set vertically, reflecting a rabbinic explanation for why the king's own sages could not read it.

## Significance
Daniel 5 recounts the *mene mene tekel upharsin* — the spectral [[motif:writing on the wall|writing on the wall]] at Belshazzar's sacrilegious banquet, which only Daniel can interpret as the kingdom's imminent fall. Rembrandt drew the inscription's unusual arrangement from his neighbour, the scholar Menasseh ben Israel. The scene is the supreme biblical image of a supernatural omen.

## For artists & game designers
The glowing, free-floating hand writing a cryptic doom is an iconic "prophetic omen" effect — a single supernatural intrusion that reframes an entire scene.

citations.text: *Daniel* 5:1–31.

title: Moses and the Brazen Serpent
work: Magic & the Supernatural in the Bible
creator: Sébastien Bourdon
summary:
Sébastien Bourdon's classicizing *Moses and the Brazen Serpent*, a measured French treatment of the healing miracle.

## Iconography
Amid a landscape strewn with serpent-bitten Israelites, Moses directs the afflicted toward the bronze serpent on its standard; the figures are arranged in Poussin-like friezes of grief and supplication. The palette is cool and the staging legible.

## Significance
Bourdon, a founder of the French Académie, treats Numbers 21 with the restraint of seventeenth-century classicism, subordinating Baroque turbulence to clear narrative order. The [[motif:brazen serpent|raised serpent]] remains the contested object — at once divinely commanded cure and the future idol *Nehushtan* — here presented as a lesson in obedient faith.

## For artists & game designers
Compare with Rubens's version: Bourdon shows how the same magical-healing episode can be staged for calm legibility rather than visceral chaos.

citations.text: *Numbers* 21:4–9.
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Brazen Serpent (Sistine Chapel pendentive)
work: Magic & the Supernatural in the Bible
creator: Michelangelo Buonarroti
summary:
Michelangelo's pendentive fresco of the Brazen Serpent in the Sistine Chapel, a roiling mass of bodies bitten and healed.

## Iconography
On the right, Israelites writhe and die under an attack of fiery serpents; on the left, those who turn to gaze upon the bronze serpent raised on a pole by Moses are saved. The two halves split the composition between agony and deliverance.

## Significance
Numbers 21 recounts that God sent venomous snakes against the murmuring Israelites, then bade Moses raise a [[motif:brazen serpent|bronze serpent]] (the *Nehushtan*) whose mere sight cured the bitten — a healing image so potent it was later worshipped as an idol and destroyed (2 Kings 18). The Gospel of John reads it as a type of the Crucifixion. The episode hovers between sanctioned talisman and forbidden idol.

## For artists & game designers
The split-field design — death on one side, salvation on the other, hinged on a single raised object — is a powerful layout for any "look upon the relic to be cured" set-piece.

citations.text: *Numbers* 21:4–9; *2 Kings* 18:4; *John* 3:14.

title: Moses and the Brazen Serpent
work: Magic & the Supernatural in the Bible
creator: Peter Paul Rubens
summary:
Rubens's Baroque *Moses and the Brazen Serpent* (National Gallery, London), a dramatic crowd of the stricken turning toward the raised bronze sign.

## Iconography
Moses gestures toward the serpent coiled on its pole; below, muscular figures entwined with snakes twist in pain, while others lift their faces toward the healing image. Rubens floods the scene with diagonal energy and chiaroscuro.

## Significance
The painting renders Numbers 21, in which gazing on the [[motif:brazen serpent|bronze serpent]] cures snakebite — an image medieval and Reformation theologians treated as a type of Christ "lifted up." Rubens, the great Counter-Reformation narrator, emphasizes the bodily drama of plague and rescue, making the talismanic sign the visual hinge of life and death.

## For artists & game designers
Rubens's tangle of serpent-wrapped bodies is prime reference for a poison/curse outbreak crowd, with a single elevated object as the salvation focal point.

citations.text: *Numbers* 21:4–9.
Wikimedia Commons

title: Daniel Interpreting Nebuchadnezzar's Dream
work: Magic & the Supernatural in the Bible
creator: W. A. Spicer (illustration)
summary:
A book illustration of Daniel revealing and interpreting King Nebuchadnezzar's dream of the great statue.

## Iconography
Daniel stands before the Babylonian king, gesturing as he expounds the dream the king's own magicians could not recover; behind or above looms the colossal image with its head of gold and feet of clay. The picture stages prophecy triumphing over court divination.

## Significance
Daniel 2 sets the Hebrew seer against the Chaldean "magicians, enchanters, sorcerers, and astrologers" who fail to tell the king his forgotten dream. Daniel succeeds not by [[motif:divination|divinatory art]] but by revelation, interpreting the statue as a succession of empires. The chapter became a key biblical statement that true foreknowledge comes from God, not occult technique.

## For artists & game designers
The "interpreter who reads the vision the court experts cannot" is a strong NPC beat — knowledge as the decisive power in a throne-room scene.

citations.text: *Daniel* 2:1–49.
