title: Elymas the Sorcerer Struck Blind
work: Magic & the Supernatural in the Bible
creator: after Raphael (Rijksmuseum print)
summary:
An engraving after Raphael's tapestry cartoon *The Blinding of Elymas*, depicting the sorcerer struck blind by St Paul at Paphos.

## Iconography
Elymas (Bar-Jesus) stands at center, arms outstretched and eyes darkened, groping in sudden blindness while the seated proconsul Sergius Paulus and his court react. Paul, at left, pronounces the judgment. The print transmits Raphael's monumental design from the Sistine tapestry series.

## Significance
In Acts 13 the magus Bar-Jesus, attached to the Roman proconsul, opposes Paul and is struck with temporary blindness — a sign that converts the official. The scene is a touchstone for the Renaissance theme of the [[motif:false prophet|false prophet]] overthrown; Raphael's cartoons (now V&A) and the tapestries woven from them in Brussels were among the most influential images of the era.

## For artists & game designers
Elymas's groping, light-deprived stance is a textbook "blinded" status pose — outstretched, off-balance, hands searching the air.

citations.text: *Acts of the Apostles* 13:6–12.
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Shade of Samuel Invoked by Saul (Witch of Endor)
work: Magic & the Supernatural in the Bible
creator: Salvator Rosa
summary:
Salvator Rosa's *The Shade of Samuel Invoked by Saul at the Cave of Endor* (Louvre), one of the most famous necromancy paintings of the Baroque.

## Iconography
The medium of Endor recoils as the shrouded ghost of the prophet Samuel rises in pale light; King Saul prostrates himself in terror on the cave floor while attendants shrink back. Rosa's signature gloom and ragged figures heighten the dread.

## Significance
In 1 Samuel 28 the doomed Saul, having banned mediums, secretly consults the woman of Endor to raise Samuel, who foretells his death in battle. The episode is the Bible's central [[motif:necromancy|necromancy]] text and was endlessly debated — was it the true Samuel, a demon, or fraud? Rosa, himself drawn to witchcraft subjects, made it a meditation on forbidden knowledge and fate.

## For artists & game designers
The rising shroud-wrapped revenant against a cowering king is a master template for a summoned-prophecy beat: the conjuror gets an answer, but it is a sentence of doom.

citations.text: Wikimedia Commons

title: The Adoration of the Golden Calf
work: Magic & the Supernatural in the Bible
creator: Nicolas Poussin
summary:
Nicolas Poussin's *The Adoration of the Golden Calf* (National Gallery, London), the Israelites' ecstatic idol-dance below Sinai.

## Iconography
A circle of figures dances around the gilded calf raised on a pedestal while Aaron, in white, presides; in the far distance Moses descends the mountain and hurls down the tablets. Poussin choreographs the apostasy as a frenzied bacchic round.

## Significance
Exodus 32 narrates how, in Moses's absence, the people compel Aaron to cast a [[motif:golden calf|golden calf]] and worship it with revelry — the archetypal act of biblical idolatry, conflated in later art with pagan rite and magical fertility-cult. Poussin draws explicitly on antique bacchanal imagery, making the scene a study of false worship as intoxicated misrule.

## For artists & game designers
The ring-dance around a raised idol is the definitive "cult ritual in progress" composition — circular motion, central effigy, a presiding officiant.

citations.text: Wikimedia Commons

title: Jacob's Dream (The Ladder of Jacob)
work: Magic & the Supernatural in the Bible
creator: after Jusepe de Ribera (Rijksmuseum photo-reproduction)
rights: CC0. Via Wikimedia Commons (Rijksmuseum reproduction of the Prado painting).
summary:
A reproduction of Jusepe de Ribera's *Jacob's Dream* (Prado), the patriarch asleep beneath a vision of angels.

## Iconography
Jacob lies sleeping against a bank, head on a stone, while a soft burst of light and the dim forms of ascending angels open above him. Ribera, unusually, downplays the architectural ladder in favour of a luminous, almost mystical haze.

## Significance
Genesis 28 recounts Jacob's dream at Bethel of a [[motif:jacobs ladder|ladder]] set between earth and heaven with angels ascending and descending, and the Lord above promising the land — a [[motif:theophany|theophany]] that made the site "the gate of heaven." The ladder became a central symbol in mystical and Kabbalistic thought of graded ascent between worlds. Ribera renders the revelation as inward, contemplative experience.

## For artists & game designers
The sleeping figure beneath a vertical shaft of light and rising figures is a model for a "dream-portal" vision scene — the threshold between realms shown as luminance, not machinery.

citations.text: Wikimedia Commons

title: The Journey of the Magi
work: Magic & the Supernatural in the Bible
creator: Sassetta (Stefano di Giovanni)
rights: CC0. Via Wikimedia Commons (Metropolitan Museum of Art).
summary:
Sassetta's *The Journey of the Magi* (Metropolitan Museum), the wise men following the star toward Bethlehem.

## Iconography
The Magi and their retinue wind down a hillside; above, the star of Bethlehem streaks across a gold sky, sometimes rendered as a comet. The richly dressed travellers gaze upward, guided by the celestial sign.

## Significance
Matthew 2 calls them *magoi* — the term for Persian-Zoroastrian priest-[[motif:astrologers|astrologers]] — who read a new [[motif:star of bethlehem|star]] as the sign of a king's birth. The episode is the Bible's most positive image of astral divination, and Christian tradition long debated whether it sanctioned astrology or merely used it as a vehicle of revelation. Their star inspired Giotto's comet and centuries of cometary iconography.

## For artists & game designers
The star-led caravan is a clean "follow the sign" travel motif: an unmistakable celestial waypoint drawing a procession across the landscape.

citations.text: *Gospel of Matthew* 2:1–12.
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Rods of Moses and the Magicians Turned into Serpents
work: Magic & the Supernatural in the Bible
creator: Gerard Hoet
summary:
Gerard Hoet's engraving of the contest before Pharaoh, where Aaron's rod becomes a serpent that devours those of the Egyptian sorcerers.

## Iconography
In Pharaoh's court, rods cast to the ground writhe into serpents; Aaron's snake swallows those conjured by the magicians Jannes and Jambres, while Moses and Aaron stand before the enthroned king. The Dutch print transmits the scene as a stately courtroom confrontation.

## Significance
Exodus 7 stages the plagues as a [[motif:miracle contest|magic contest]]: Pharaoh's wise men replicate the rod-to-serpent wonder "by their secret arts," yet Aaron's serpent consumes theirs. Later tradition named the magicians Jannes and Jambres (cited in 2 Timothy 3:8 and a lost apocryphon). The episode was the classic proof-text for distinguishing divine miracle from demonic imitation.

## For artists & game designers
The duel of transmuted staffs — one snake eating the others — is an elegant "my summon beats your summon" mechanic rendered as pure spectacle.

citations.text: *Exodus* 7:8–13; cf. *2 Timothy* 3:8.
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Queen of Sheba Meets Solomon
work: Magic & the Supernatural in the Bible
creator: Piero della Francesca
summary:
Piero della Francesca's fresco of the Queen of Sheba meeting Solomon, from the *Legend of the True Cross* cycle at Arezzo.

## Iconography
The scene splits into two: the queen's procession kneels before the wood of a future cross, then she meets the enthroned Solomon amid attendant courtiers. Piero's grave, geometric figures and clear light render the encounter as solemn ceremony.

## Significance
1 Kings 10 tells how the Queen of Sheba comes to test Solomon with "hard questions" — riddles and enigmas — and is awed by his God-given [[motif:wisdom|wisdom]]. In later legend (and the *True Cross* tradition Piero illustrates) she becomes a prophetess who venerates the sacred wood. Sheba accrued associations with arcane knowledge, riddle-lore, and, in some traditions, occult power.

## For artists & game designers
The "contest of riddles before the wise king" is a ready quest frame: a powerful visitor arrives to test the hero's knowledge rather than fight.

citations.text: *1 Kings* 10:1–13; Jacobus de Voragine, *Golden Legend* (True Cross).

title: The Fall of Simon Magus (and the Conversion of St Paul)
work: Magic & the Supernatural in the Bible
creator: Jan Rombouts (attributed)
rights: CC0. Via Wikimedia Commons (Museum M, Leuven).
summary:
A Southern-Netherlandish panel attributed to Jan Rombouts pairing the Fall of Simon Magus with the Conversion of St Paul.

## Iconography
Simon, the sorcerer of Samaria, is shown crashing earthward as the demons who bore him aloft scatter; below, the apostles Peter and Paul kneel in prayer, their intercession breaking the magician's flight. The composition stages the contest as a vertical plunge from the sky.

## Significance
The story, told in Acts 8 (where Simon offers money for the apostles' power — the origin of "simony") and elaborated in the apocryphal *Acts of Peter*, became the archetypal image of false [[motif:sorcery|sorcery]] overthrown by true miracle. Simon's flight before Nero, sustained by demons until Peter's prayer fells him, was read for centuries as the defeat of magic by apostolic grace.

## For artists & game designers
The falling levitator with his demon-bearers dispersing is a compact visual for a "power source severed" defeat — the magician is undone not by force but by the withdrawal of his unholy support.

citations.text: *Acts of the Apostles* 8:9–24; apocryphal *Acts of Peter*.
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Transfiguration
work: Magic & the Supernatural in the Bible
creator: Raphael (Raffaello Sanzio)
rights: Public domain. Via Wikimedia Commons (Vatican Museums).
summary:
Raphael's final masterpiece *The Transfiguration* (Vatican Museums), uniting Christ's radiant ascent with the failed exorcism below.

## Iconography
In the upper register Christ hovers in dazzling light between Moses and Elijah while the apostles fall back blinded; in the lower, a convulsing possessed boy is brought to the helpless disciples, who point upward for aid. The two halves contrast divine glory and earthly affliction.

## Significance
The painting fuses two adjacent Gospel episodes (Matthew 17): the [[motif:transfiguration|Transfiguration]], where Christ's nature shines forth amid the appearance of the dead prophets, and the [[motif:exorcism|exorcism]] of the demoniac boy the apostles could not cure. Together they juxtapose the supreme theophany with a demonic affliction healed only by the descending power — a meditation on the spectrum of the supernatural.

## For artists & game designers
The two-tier composition — luminous power above, a crisis demanding it below — is a superb template for staging the relationship between a source of power and the need that calls it down.

citations.text: *Gospel of Matthew* 17:1–18.
Wikimedia Commons

title: Saul and the Witch of Endor (van Oostsanen)
creator: Jacob Cornelisz. van Oostsanen
summary:
**Jacob Cornelisz. van Oostsanen's** 1526 panel — one of the earliest and richest paintings of the **Witch of Endor** (1 Samuel 28), the Bible's great scene of necromancy.

## Iconography
King Saul kneels before the witch, who works inside a magic **circle** strewn with bones and inscribed with names; the ghost of the prophet **Samuel** rises in a shroud to foretell the king's doom. Van Oostsanen crowds the background with a full [[tradition:witchcraft|witches' sabbath]] — flights, demons, cauldrons.

## Significance
The Endor episode (Iconclass 71H31) was *the* scriptural warrant for debating the reality of magic: did the witch truly raise Samuel, or did a demon counterfeit him? Painted across the whole history of art (van Oostsanen, Rosa, West, Blake), it is the keystone of **biblical-magic iconography**.

## For artists & game designers
A complete necromancy tableau — circle, bones, rising ghost, terrified king.

citations.text: 1 Samuel 28:3–25.
Charles Zika, *Exorcising Our Demons* (Brill, 2003).

title: *De la Pirotechnia* — still-life of mining tools and gear
creator: Vannoccio Biringuccio (woodcuts: anonymous Venetian block-cutters)
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: per source — Internet Archive scan of the 1558 Venice edition (Giolito / Gioseffo)]
summary:
A woodcut still-life of the miner's equipment: picks, shovels, hammers and wedges scattered across the ground, woven baskets (*corbe* and *cestini*), a two-wheeled cart and bundled hides. From the discussion of the gear needed to work and clear a mine.

## Iconography
The tools are arranged for display rather than in use — an inventory rendered in the block. Iron implements lie crossed in the foreground, baskets and a cart fill the middle ground, sacks of raw hide sit at centre. The composition reads like an illustrated equipment-list.

## Significance
The surrounding text enumerates what the mine requires — baskets, hide sacks, iron-shod carts with wheels and without — and adds that one must have oily fuels (olive oil, nut and linseed oil, fats) to keep a light burning underground, for without light no work can be done. The cut is a practical inventory of the extractive trade.

## For artists & game designers
A clean tool-and-equipment reference sheet — directly usable for inventory icons, crafting components or a mine-supply cache.

title: *De la Pirotechnia* — *De luoghi delle minere*: miners at the mine and forge
creator: Vannoccio Biringuccio (woodcuts: anonymous Venetian block-cutters)
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: per source — Internet Archive scan of the 1558 Venice edition (Giolito / Gioseffo)]
summary:
A woodcut heading the chapter *De luoghi delle minere* ("On the places of mines") in Biringuccio's *Pirotechnia*. Under a timber-framed shed, miners work at a small forge or fire while a mountainside opens behind them with a mine adit and a labourer trundling a barrow of ore.

## Iconography
The composition gathers the whole cycle of extraction into one frame: the headframe and shed of the pit-head at left, the smith's fire at centre, the terraced mountain and tunnel mouth at right, and a barrow-man at lower right. Figures are stocky and active in the workmanlike Venetian idiom.

## Significance
The surrounding text counsels the prospector to begin the dig with a prayer to the Trinity or a patron saint — a reminder that, for all Biringuccio's empiricism, mining remained a perilous trade ringed with devotion. The plate is among the earliest printed depictions of practical mining, predating Agricola's *De re metallica* (1556) and feeding the same north-Italian and German technical tradition.

## For artists & game designers
A ready-made mine-site establishing shot: pit-head shed, tunnel adit, ore barrow and a working fire — a complete extraction-economy vignette in one block.

title: *De la Pirotechnia* — *Dell'argento vivo*: spread of mercury-recovery apparatus
creator: Vannoccio Biringuccio (woodcuts: anonymous Venetian block-cutters)
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: per source — Internet Archive scan of the 1558 Venice edition (Giolito / Gioseffo)]
summary:
A two-page opening of Book I, *Dell'argento vivo* ("On quicksilver"), photographed as a spread. The verso repeats the long mercury-distillation furnace with its domed condenser; the recto carries two further woodcuts — a worker at a great washing-vat with a domed earthen vessel, and the pegged cupellation frame with its round cinder-pots.

## Iconography
Three apparatus blocks share the opening, dense with the gear of mercury work: the firing furnace and condenser, the wooden washing-tub, the lidded earthen pots and the slotted recovery frame. The labourers are shown mid-operation, the text flowing tightly around each cut.

## Significance
The spread shows how thickly Biringuccio illustrated this dangerous chapter — vapour caught and condensed, ash washed for its trapped droplets, vessels sealed mouth-to-mouth. Few earlier printed books had pictured chemical apparatus so insistently or so practically.

## For artists & game designers
A full apparatus spread — furnace, condenser, washing-vat and recovery frame on one opening — a ready palette for an entire mercury-works.

title: *De la Pirotechnia* — Book III: refining silver on the cupel (*Il modo d'affinare l'argento*)
creator: Vannoccio Biringuccio (woodcuts: anonymous Venetian block-cutters)
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: per source — Internet Archive scan of the 1558 Venice edition (Giolito / Gioseffo)]
summary:
A woodcut opening Book III, chapter 6 of the *Pirotechnia*, captioned *Il modo d'affinare l'argento con la coppella* ("the way of refining silver with the cupel"). The cut shows the refining hearth with its bellows and channelled fire; a historiated initial begins the chapter below.

## Iconography
The refining furnace is given in working section — the bellows-pipe entering the fire-box, the cupel-bed where lead carries off the base metal and leaves the silver behind, vessels and a workman near the hearth. The accompanying initial carries its own small figure in the Venetian manner.

## Significance
Cupellation — oxidising lead away to leave refined silver or gold — is the master-operation of the precious-metal trades, and Biringuccio sets it out as plainly as any modern manual. He frames the chapter as honest instruction against the frauds of those who would cheat on the fineness of metal.

## For artists & game designers
A cross-section of a refining hearth with bellows — excellent reference for a furnace mechanic or a metallurgy crafting interface.

title: *De la Pirotechnia* — the domed assay-house: interior with assayers at work (Proemio, Book III)
creator: Vannoccio Biringuccio (woodcuts: anonymous Venetian block-cutters)
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: per source — Internet Archive scan of the 1558 Venice edition (Giolito / Gioseffo)]
summary:
A striking woodcut prefacing the third book, *Del saggiare et disporre la minera de metalli alle fusioni*. The cut cuts away a beehive-vaulted assay-house: within the great dome, assayers sit at benches around a central fire, and a small figure stands at the doorway. A historiated initial opens the text below.

## Iconography
The building is drawn as if sliced open so the viewer sees inside the masonry dome — a convention that turns architecture into apparatus. Seated workers attend their tests at flanking benches; the fire and its vessels occupy the centre; the whole is read in steep, slightly naive perspective.

## Significance
This is one of the *Pirotechnia*'s most memorable plates: an early-modern image of a dedicated laboratory — a purpose-built house of fire and assay. It belongs to the same imaginative lineage as Libavius's later "ideal chemical house," picturing the orderly disposition of the chymical workplace. Biringuccio's proem argues that the eye alone cannot judge an ore — only the assay, weighed and tested, gives true knowledge.

## For artists & game designers
A cutaway laboratory dome full of working alchemists — an outstanding establishing interior for an assay-house, guild laboratory or alchemy hub.

title: *De la Pirotechnia* — *Del ferro*: the great water-driven bellows (book on iron)
creator: Vannoccio Biringuccio (woodcuts: anonymous Venetian block-cutters)
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: per source — Internet Archive scan of the 1558 Venice edition (Giolito / Gioseffo)]
summary:
A woodcut on p.17 for the chapter *Del ferro* ("On iron"): a great pair of bellows, set against a brick furnace wall, drives a forced blast into the fire that gusts flame at the right. Shown in working section.

## Iconography
The twin bellows fill the frame "in the manner of a great pair of wings," their boards and nozzle drawn in plain mechanical detail; the masonry furnace stands beside them, flames rising from its stack. The block is wholly given over to apparatus.

## Significance
The text explains that such bellows — six to eight *braccia* tall — are worked by a sound water-wheel to make the powerful, sustained blast that iron-smelting demands. This is the water-powered blast at the threshold of the blast-furnace age, recorded with an engineer's precision a generation before Agricola.

## For artists & game designers
A mechanical study of water-powered blast bellows and furnace — excellent for an ironworks, a powered-machine asset or a steampunk-adjacent forge.

title: *De la Pirotechnia* — workman with cupellation frame and cinder-pots (book I, on quicksilver)
creator: Vannoccio Biringuccio (woodcuts: anonymous Venetian block-cutters)
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: per source — Internet Archive scan of the 1558 Venice edition (Giolito / Gioseffo)]
summary:
A text-set woodcut from Biringuccio's *Pirotechnia*, the book that for the first time set the practice of the foundry and the assay-house into print. A workman kneels to lift the lid of a large rectangular timber frame pierced with two oval wells — a recovery box for cinders and ash — while two great round earthenware pots stand at his side.

## Iconography
The scene is rendered in the plain, legible manner of the Venetian shop block-cutter: a tiled floor read in steep perspective, a single labourer in working dress, and the apparatus given pride of place. The slotted wooden frame, joined with visible pegs, holds two oval cavities; beside it sit the rounded *pignatte* or cinder-pots in which the volatile metal was caught and washed out of the ash.

## Significance
The image belongs to Book I, on quicksilver (*argento vivo*), where Biringuccio describes catching the metal as it condenses and recovering it by washing the ash. It is documentary rather than allegorical — Biringuccio's avowed programme was to record what he had "seen and done" in the shops of Italy and Germany, displacing the secrecy of the alchemists with plain instruction.

## For artists & game designers
A clean reference for a Renaissance metalworker's bench: pegged timber apparatus, bulbous earthen pots, a kneeling artisan — ideal source for a crafting-station or foundry asset.

The letterpress title sits within an elaborate woodcut frame teeming with the instruments of the art.

The ornamental border is itself a catalogue of pyrotechnic apparatus: furnaces, crucibles, bellows, flasks, tongs and tools crowd the margins, with personified figures above and a lion-and-cartouche device below bearing a motto. The whole announces the book's subject before a word is read.

## Significance
Biringuccio's title proclaims a work that treats "not only the diversity of ores, but also all that pertains to the art of fusion or the casting of metals." The decorated frame, a stock Venetian device, frames the first systematic printed treatise on metallurgy and the foundry arts — the book Galileo and the casters of cannon would read.

The furnace is shown in working profile — the fire-mouth where the labourer feeds it, the channelled body, the bell-domed condenser where the metal vapour is caught. Earthen pots (*pignatte*) and a rack of vessels complete the set. A single artisan kneels at his task on the tiled floor.

Mercury — *argento vivo*, the living silver — was won by roasting cinnabar and condensing the volatile metal. Biringuccio describes joining the mouths of vessels so that the quicksilver rises from one and gathers in another, recovered in droplets. The plate documents one of the period's genuinely dangerous chymical operations.

Three or four hooded furnaces stand in a row, fire pouring from their openings; tilted crucibles sit ready below, and at the right edge a large overshot wheel turns the blast-bellows. The block is purely instructional — apparatus shown for its working parts.

## Significance
The passage debates the merits of natural draught against forced blast — furnaces that draw their own air versus those blown by water-powered bellows — a genuinely technical comparison rare in print at this date. title: *Albion Rose* (Glad Day)
creator: William Blake
date: c.1793–1796 (colour-printed etching, from *A Large Book of Designs*)
summary:
*Albion Rose*, also called *Glad Day*, depicts the youth Albion springing up in a radiant burst of light with arms flung wide.

## Iconography
A naked young man stands on a rocky height in a cruciform pose, arms spread and one foot lifted as if dancing, surrounded by a brilliant rainbow nimbus of light. At his feet a moth and a worm-like creature emerge. His face is rapt and joyful.

## Significance
Albion is Blake's personification of England and of universal humanity; his rising is an emblem of spiritual awakening and liberation from materialist bondage. An inscription on one impression reads that Albion 'rose from where he labour'd at the Mill with Slaves, / Giving himself for the Nations he danc'd the dance of Eternal Death,' fusing [[motif:imagination as the divine body|self-sacrifice]] with resurrection. The pose echoes the Vitruvian man, reclaiming Renaissance proportion for visionary ends.

## For artists & game designers
The ultimate 'awakening / ascension' pose: a figure exploding into radiance, arms wide, the instant the spirit breaks free.

title: The Ancient of Days (frontispiece to *Europe a Prophecy*)
creator: William Blake
date: 1794 (this copy K, relief etching with watercolour)
summary:
*The Ancient of Days*, Blake's frontispiece to *Europe a Prophecy* (1794), shows the god-figure Urizen crouching within a blazing sun-disc and reaching down with a golden compass to circumscribe the dark deep below.

## Iconography
A muscular, white-bearded old man kneels inside a solar orb, his hair and beard streaming sideways in a cosmic wind. He leans out of the disc and lowers his left hand, the two splayed fingers forming a pair of compasses that cast rays of dividing light into the formless dark. The composition is severely symmetrical and architectonic.

## Significance
The figure is [[motif:urizen the measurer|Urizen]], Blake's embodiment of bounding reason and law, performing the act described in Proverbs 8:27, 'when he set a compass upon the face of the depth.' For Blake this is not pure creation but a fall into limitation — the imposition of measure, number, and weight upon the infinite. The image fuses the Demiurge of Gnostic thought with the geometer-God of Newtonian deism; it is the visual antithesis of [[motif:imagination as the divine body|imaginative liberty]]. Blake reportedly saw the design hovering at the top of his staircase.

## For artists & game designers
The definitive icon of the cosmic architect / world-bounding demiurge — a god who creates by measuring rather than loving.

title: Behemoth and Leviathan (Book of Job, plate 15)
creator: William Blake
summary:
From Blake's Book of Job illustrations, this design shows God displaying to Job the two primeval monsters Behemoth and Leviathan in a circular vision of earth and sea.

## Iconography
God and angels appear above in an arc of cloud, gesturing downward to a roundel that frames Behemoth, a vast land-beast, above Leviathan, a coiling sea-serpent. Job and his companions watch from below. The encircling composition divides the cosmos into heaven, land, and the watery deep.

## Significance
The scene illustrates God's answer from the whirlwind in Job 40–41, in which the Almighty points to Behemoth and Leviathan as proof of a power beyond human comprehension. Blake reads the two beasts as embodiments of war and tyranny — the brute forces of the fallen world — contained within God's encompassing vision. The watercolour belongs to the Butts set that Blake later engraved as the celebrated *Illustrations of the Book of Job* (1826), studied by Joseph Wicksteed.

## For artists & game designers
A cosmic 'menagerie of monsters' framing device: land-beast over sea-beast, both displayed within a divine circle.

title: *The First Book of Urizen*, Plate 22
creator: William Blake
summary:
A full-page design from *The First Book of Urizen* (1794), Blake's parody of Genesis recounting the self-isolation and fall of the god Urizen.

## Iconography
A figure is shown amid Blake's characteristic flowing, organic forms — bowed bodies, enveloping nets or webs, and the dark, cavernous spaces of Urizen's self-created world. The hand-tinted plate sets a sculptural human form against swirling colour.

## Significance
*The First Book of Urizen* is Blake's mock-Bible, narrating how [[motif:urizen the measurer|Urizen]] — 'the primeval Priest' — withdraws from the Eternals, writes his iron book of laws, and falls into the divided, mortal cosmos, dragging humanity after him into the 'Net of Religion.' It is among Blake's darkest prophecies, the negative counterpart to the liberatory *Marriage of Heaven and Hell*. The relief-etched plates were printed in very few copies, each uniquely coloured; the book is central to study of Blake's private mythology.

## For artists & game designers
A ready-made fallen-creator mythology: a god who legislates the universe into existence and ensnares his creatures in nets of law.

title: The Circle of the Traitors: Dante's Foot Striking Bocca degli Abati
creator: William Blake (engraving; photograph by Daderot)
summary:
An engraving from Blake's Dante series showing the frozen circle of traitors, where Dante's foot strikes the head of the betrayer Bocca degli Abati.

## Iconography
Dante and Virgil move across the icy plain of Cocytus, where traitors are frozen to the neck. Dante's foot collides with the head of one damned soul — Bocca degli Abati — who is locked in the ice. The composition is stark, the figures sharply outlined in Blake's late linear engraving style.

## Significance
The scene illustrates *Inferno* XXXII, set in the ninth and lowest circle, where betrayers are entombed in the ice of Cocytus. Blake undertook the Dante engravings for John Linnell in the last years of his life, completing only seven of an intended large series before his death in 1827. They represent the culmination of his career as an [[motif:prophetic illuminated book|engraver]], translating his watercolour designs into severe, expressive line.

## For artists & game designers
A frozen-hell tableau: betrayers locked neck-deep in ice, the protagonist literally stumbling over the damned.

title: *Elohim Creating Adam*
creator: William Blake
date: 1795/c.1805 (colour print finished in ink and watercolour)
summary:
*Elohim Creating Adam*, a 1795 colour print, shows the creator-god Elohim forming Adam from the earth as a serpent already coils about the man's leg.

## Iconography
A stern, winged Elohim hovers horizontally above the prostrate Adam, pressing him into being with weary, almost grieving effort. Adam lies pinned to the soil, a serpent winding around his thigh. Both figures share an expression of suffering rather than triumph; sun and water lie at the horizon.

## Significance
For Blake the creation of the natural, mortal body was itself a kind of fall — Adam is bound to earth and already entangled with the serpent of mortality at the very moment of his making. Elohim labours under the burden of creating fallen matter, an idea coloured by Blake's reading of Gnostic and Behmenist sources. The work belongs to the same 1795 set as [[motif:fallen reason|Newton]] and *Nebuchadnezzar*.

## For artists & game designers
A creation scene reframed as tragedy: the maker exhausted, the made already doomed and serpent-bound.

citations.text: Anthony Blunt, *The Art of William Blake* (1959).

title: *The Ghost of a Flea*
creator: William Blake
date: c.1819–1820 (tempera and gold on mahogany panel)
summary:
*The Ghost of a Flea* is a small visionary tempera depicting the soul of a flea as a muscular, reptilian humanoid striding between curtains, holding a bowl to catch blood.

## Iconography
A bald, scaly, heavily muscled creature moves across a small stage between drawn curtains spangled with stars. It carries a thorn or dagger in one hand and a cupped acorn-bowl for drinking blood in the other; its tongue darts hungrily from its mouth. The figure is bathed in an eerie spotlight.

## Significance
The image arose from Blake's 'visionary heads,' drawn for the astrologer John Varley during late-night séance-like sessions. Blake claimed the spirit told him that fleas were inhabited by the souls of bloodthirsty men, confined to such tiny bodies lest they lay waste to humankind — a grim joke on [[motif:contrary states of the soul|metempsychosis]]. Varley recorded the encounter; the panel is glittered with gold to suggest its supernatural light.

## For artists & game designers
The perfect 'tiny evil made monstrous' design — a microscopic predator's soul rendered as a stage-lit blood-drinking demon.

citations.text: John Varley, *A Treatise on Zodiacal Physiognomy* (1828).
Wikimedia Commons

title: God Judging Adam
creator: William Blake
date: 1795 (colour print finished in ink and watercolour)
summary:
*God Judging Adam*, a 1795 colour print, shows an enthroned, flame-wreathed god pronouncing judgement on a grey, aged Adam who mirrors him.

## Iconography
A bearded god sits in a chariot ringed by flames, holding a scroll and extending his hand toward Adam, who stands before him bowed and old. The two figures strikingly resemble each other, both white-bearded; horses of fire rear behind the throne. The palette is hot and oppressive.

## Significance
Long mistitled 'God Creating Adam,' the print actually shows the giving of the law and the sentence of mortality. The near-identity of judge and judged expresses Blake's conviction that the punitive law-giving god — [[motif:urizen the measurer|Urizen]] — is a projection of fallen man, not a transcendent other. The fiery chariot recalls Ezekiel's vision turned tyrannical. It belongs to the famous 1795 colour-print group studied by Butlin and Bindman.

## For artists & game designers
Judge and condemned rendered as mirror images — the oppressor revealed as the self.

citations.text: David Bindman, *Blake as an Artist* (1977).
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Great Red Dragon and the Woman Clothed with the Sun
creator: William Blake
summary:
From Blake's series illustrating the Book of Revelation, this watercolour depicts the Great Red Dragon of chapter 12 looming over the Woman Clothed with the Sun.

## Iconography
A monstrous winged dragon, seen from behind, rears up with vast bat-like wings spread across the whole sheet and a serpentine tail coiling. Far below, the radiant Woman lies with the crescent moon beneath her feet, her arms flung out as the dragon prepares to devour her child. The dragon's muscular, almost heroic back dominates the design.

## Significance
The scene illustrates Revelation 12, where the dragon — identified as Satan — waits to consume the child of the sun-crowned woman. Blake renders cosmic evil as overwhelming physical power and beauty, a tension central to his vision of the [[motif:contrary states of the soul|contraries]]. The series was commissioned by Thomas Butts. The image gained pop-cultural notoriety through Thomas Harris's *Red Dragon*; art-historically it is studied via Martin Butlin's catalogue raisonné.

## For artists & game designers
A masterclass in depicting a monster from behind, so the viewer shares its menacing vantage over a helpless victim below.

citations.text: Martin Butlin, *The Paintings and Drawings of William Blake* (1981).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Hecate, or *The Night of Enitharmon's Joy*
creator: William Blake
date: c.1795 (colour print finished in ink and watercolour)
summary:
This 1795 colour print depicts a triple female figure — the witch-goddess Hecate, or Blake's own Enitharmon — presiding over a nocturnal world of dark creatures with her hand on an open book.

## Iconography
A seated woman rests her hand on a large open book, while two further figures press against her back, forming the triple form of Hecate. Around them lurk creatures of the night: an owl, a bat-winged reptile, a braying ass, a thistle, and a serpent. The scene is steeped in lunar gloom.

## Significance
The classical Hecate, goddess of witchcraft, crossroads, and the moon, is here fused with [[motif:female dominion|Enitharmon]], a figure of Blake's mythology whose 'night of joy' is the eighteen-hundred-year reign of female-dominated, restrictive religion. The open book signals occult or doctrinal authority; the surrounding beasts embody fear and superstition. Scholars including Kathleen Raine read the work through Blake's ambivalence toward the feminine and toward organised religion.

## For artists & game designers
The definitive triple-goddess / night-witch tableau: one figure, three aspects, ringed by familiars and a book of dark lore.

citations.text: Kathleen Raine, *Blake and Tradition* (1968).
Wikimedia Commons

title: *Jerusalem, The Emanation of the Giant Albion*, Plate 51
creator: William Blake
summary: Plate 51 of *Jerusalem*, Blake's longest and most ambitious illuminated prophecy, showing three seated figures sunk in despair beneath thrones of error.

citations.text: Morton D. Paley, *The Continuing City: William Blake's Jerusalem* (1983).
Wikimedia Commons

title: *The Marriage of Heaven and Hell* (title plate)
creator: William Blake
date: c.1790–1793 (copy G; relief etching with watercolour)
summary:
The title plate of *The Marriage of Heaven and Hell*, Blake's prose-poem of visionary inversion, with figures embracing across the divide of cloud and flame.

## Iconography
The title lettering arches over a scene split between an upper region of trees and clouds and a lower region of fire. Tiny couples embrace and figures stride through the flames; flowering branches and birds animate the margins. The hand-coloured plate glows in ochres, blues and reds.

## Significance
*The Marriage of Heaven and Hell* (c.1790–93) is Blake's most quoted prophetic book, home to the 'Proverbs of Hell' and the doctrine that 'Without Contraries is no progression.' It inverts conventional morality: energy is 'Eternal Delight,' and the [[motif:contrary states of the soul|contraries]] of reason and desire must wed rather than war. The book exemplifies Blake's relief-etched 'illuminated printing,' in which text and image are etched together from a single copperplate. It was produced amid the ferment of the French Revolution.

## For artists & game designers
The foundational text of moral inversion — a world where 'hell' is creative energy and the two opposed realms must be married, not conquered.

citations.text: Joseph Viscomi, *Blake and the Idea of the Book* (1993).
Wikimedia Commons

title: *Milton: A Poem in Two Books*, Plate 4 (copy C)
creator: William Blake
summary:
A plate from *Milton: A Poem*, in which the spirit of the dead poet John Milton descends to earth and into Blake himself to correct his own errors.

## Iconography
The relief-etched plate combines Blake's illuminated text with marginal and interlinear figures — striding, falling, or reaching forms wreathed in flame and vine — set into the body of the verse so that words and bodies share the page.

## Significance
*Milton* (c.1804–1811) tells how the poet Milton, troubled in eternity, undertakes a journey of [[motif:imagination as the divine body|self-annihilation]] back into the world, entering Blake through the foot to redeem his Puritan misconceptions of God and gender. The book's preface contains the lyric 'And did those feet in ancient time' (later set as the hymn *Jerusalem*) with its 'dark Satanic Mills.' It is a meditation on poetic inspiration and the correction of error, exemplifying Blake's fusion of literary criticism and prophecy.

## For artists & game designers
A model for the 'mentor-spirit possesses the hero' device — a dead master returning through the living artist to undo his own mistakes.

citations.text: Susan Fox, *Poetic Form in Blake's Milton* (1976).
Wikimedia Commons

title: When the Morning Stars Sang Together (Book of Job, plate 14)
creator: William Blake
summary:
A central plate of Blake's *Illustrations of the Book of Job*, depicting the moment in God's whirlwind speech when 'the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy.'

## Iconography
God stretches out his arms at the centre, flanked by a row of jubilant angels with raised arms — the singing morning stars. Below, in horizontal registers, the sun-god drives his four horses, the moon-goddess rides her serpent-drawn car, and Job's family looks up. The whole forms a tiered cosmic theatre.

## Significance
The plate illustrates Job 38:7 and stands at the spiritual climax of Blake's Job cycle, the turning from suffering to renewed vision. The 'sons of God' become a choir of angels; the personified sun and moon set the rejoicing within a fully animated, imaginative cosmos rather than a mechanical one — Blake's answer to [[motif:fallen reason|Newtonian]] astronomy. Engraved in 1826, the *Illustrations of the Book of Job* are regarded as the summit of his printmaking.

## For artists & game designers
A layered cosmic-rejoicing composition: a choir of angels above, personified sun and moon driving their chariots below.

citations.text: Joseph Wicksteed, *Blake's Vision of the Book of Job* (1910).
Wikimedia Commons

key_concepts: Illustrations of the Book of Job (1826)

title: *Nebuchadnezzar*
creator: William Blake
date: 1795/c.1805 (colour print finished in ink and watercolour)
summary:
*Nebuchadnezzar*, one of the 1795 large colour prints, shows the Babylonian king reduced to a beast crawling on all fours after God's judgement.

## Iconography
A naked, heavily muscled king crawls on hands and knees, his eyes wide with terror and madness, his hair and beard grown long and matted, his fingernails curled into talons. He stares out from a dark cavern of vegetation, more animal than man.

## Significance
The subject is from Daniel 4: the proud king Nebuchadnezzar is driven from men 'and did eat grass as oxen' until he acknowledged heaven's rule. For Blake the image dramatises the degradation of the rational, tyrannical mind — the same fallen-reason theme as [[motif:urizen the measurer|Urizen]] and Newton — into pure bestiality. The terrified animal stare is among the most psychologically intense faces in British art. The print descends from a small design in *The Marriage of Heaven and Hell*.

## For artists & game designers
The template for the proud ruler broken into a feral, grass-eating beast — sanity stripped to instinct.

citations.text: David Bindman, *Blake as an Artist* (1977).
Wikimedia Commons

title: *Newton*
creator: William Blake
date: 1795/c.1805 (colour print finished in ink and watercolour)
summary:
*Newton* is one of Blake's twelve 'large colour prints' of 1795, showing the natural philosopher Isaac Newton as a nude figure bent double on the floor of the sea, drawing a diagram with a compass.

## Iconography
A powerful young nude crouches on a dark, encrusted rock at the bottom of the ocean. Oblivious to the living, jewel-like coral around him, he bends his whole body toward a white scroll and inscribes a geometric figure with a pair of compasses. His eye is fixed on the abstract diagram alone.

## Significance
Newton here is the personification of what Blake called 'single vision and Newton's sleep' — reason and measurement divorced from imagination. The compass links him directly to [[motif:urizen the measurer|Urizen]] in *The Ancient of Days*; both reduce the living cosmos to mechanical geometry. That Newton sits at the bottom of the sea of materialism, blind to the organic splendour behind him, is Blake's critique of Enlightenment rationalism and Lockean empiricism. The work was a touchstone for later readings of Blake by S. Foster Damon and Northrop Frye.

## For artists & game designers
The archetype of the brilliant-but-blinkered rationalist: genius turned inward on abstraction while the living world glows ignored behind him.

citations.text: Northrop Frye, *Fearful Symmetry: A Study of William Blake* (1947).
Wikimedia Commons

title: *Pity*
creator: William Blake
date: c.1795 (colour print finished in ink and watercolour)
summary: *Pity* is a 1795 colour print that literally visualises a simile from Shakespeare's *Macbeth*, in which pity is 'like a naked new-born babe, striding the blast.'

citations.text: S. Foster Damon, *A Blake Dictionary* (1965).
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Great Red Dragon and the Woman Clothed with the Sun (Brooklyn variant)
creator: William Blake
rights: Public domain ('No restrictions'). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A second of Blake's Revelation watercolours on the Great Red Dragon theme, here showing the dragon frontally with the woman below.

## Iconography
The seven-headed, ten-horned dragon faces the viewer with arms raised and wings outspread, crowned with diadems, hovering above the prostrate Woman Clothed with the Sun who clutches her gown amid streaming light. The frontal, cruciform pose makes the dragon a dark parody of a blessing or crucified figure.

## Significance
Blake painted several treatments of Revelation 12 for Thomas Butts; this frontal composition contrasts with the better-known rear view. The dragon's diademed heads literalise Revelation's 'seven heads and ten horns, and upon his heads seven crowns,' presenting Satanic tyranny as a counterfeit sovereignty. The image belongs to Blake's late biblical watercolour project, his most sustained engagement with [[motif:fourfold vision|apocalyptic prophecy]].

## For artists & game designers
The frontal, arms-raised monster reads as blasphemous icon — evil posed in the body-language of worship.

citations.text: Martin Butlin, *The Paintings and Drawings of William Blake* (1981).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Satan Arousing the Rebel Angels
creator: William Blake
summary:
From Blake's watercolour series illustrating Milton's *Paradise Lost*, this design (the Butts set) shows Satan rallying his fallen angels.

## Iconography
A radiant, youthful Satan stands at the centre with arms outstretched, a starburst of light behind his head, holding spear and shield. Around and below him the rebel host rouses from the burning lake, their bodies surging upward in answer to his call. Satan is still beautiful, his fall not yet legible in his form.

## Significance
Blake illustrated *Paradise Lost* for Thomas Butts in 1808. His Satan is deliberately glorious — consistent with Blake's famous remark in [[motif:contrary states of the soul|The Marriage of Heaven and Hell]] that Milton 'was of the Devil's party without knowing it.' The radiant rebel embodies energy and revolt, qualities Blake prized even as he traced their tragic limits. The series is catalogued by Martin Butlin.

## For artists & game designers
The charismatic fallen leader at the moment of rallying his army — beauty and defiance before ruin sets in.

citations.text: Martin Butlin, *The Paintings and Drawings of William Blake* (1981).
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Sick Rose (*Songs of Experience*)
creator: William Blake
summary:
The plate of 'The Sick Rose,' a brief, dark lyric of *Songs of Experience* about an invisible worm destroying a rose's life.

## Iconography
A thorny rose-stem curves across the page; the bloom droops downward and a small human figure or worm sinks into its heart, while caterpillars and a despairing female form cling to the bending stem and thorns. The verse sits within and beside the foliage.

## Significance
The poem — 'O Rose thou art sick. / The invisible worm... / Has found out thy bed / Of crimson joy' — compresses Blake's vision of corrupted, secretive [[motif:contrary states of the soul|love in the fallen world of Experience]] into eight lines. The 'invisible worm' has been read as jealousy, disease, concealment, and the deformation of desire by repressive morality. The integration of the figures into the literal plant is a model instance of Blake's fusion of word and design. It pairs with the open joy of *Innocence*.

## For artists & game designers
A compact emblem of hidden corruption: beauty visibly drooping while the rot works unseen at its core.

citations.text: S. Foster Damon, *A Blake Dictionary* (1965).
Wikimedia Commons

title: *Songs of Innocence and of Experience* (combined title page)
creator: William Blake
summary:
The combined title page of *Songs of Innocence and of Experience*, Blake's paired lyric cycle 'Shewing the Two Contrary States of the Human Soul.'

## Iconography
The decorative title is interwoven with flame-like lettering and figures; this combined title page shows Adam and Eve, cowering beneath the flames of expulsion, set amid Blake's characteristic foliate scrolls and small human and animal forms climbing through the letters.

## Significance
The *Songs* (Innocence 1789; combined with Experience 1794) present matched poems — 'The Lamb' against 'The Tyger,' the two 'Chimney Sweeper' and 'Nurse's Song' pairs — to dramatise the [[motif:contrary states of the soul|two contrary states]] through which the soul must pass. Innocence is not naivety to be discarded but a vision to be regained on the far side of Experience. Produced by Blake's relief-etched illuminated printing and hand-coloured, the book is his most widely loved work; mystical plates such as 'The Divine Image' make the human form itself divine.

## For artists & game designers
The paired-states structure is a design pattern in itself: every motif rendered twice, once in innocence and once in experience.

citations.text: Robert N. Essick, *William Blake, Printmaker* (1980).
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Tyger (*Songs of Experience*)
creator: William Blake
summary:
The illuminated plate of 'The Tyger,' Blake's most famous lyric, in which the poet asks what immortal hand could frame the tiger's 'fearful symmetry.'

## Iconography
The text of the poem fills the plate beneath a slender tree, at the foot of which stands a small, oddly mild tiger — its meekness in pointed tension with the ferocity of the verse. Foliage and a star-touched sky frame the hand-coloured page.

## Significance
'The Tyger' is the dark counterpart, in *Songs of Experience*, to 'The Lamb' of *Innocence*: 'Did he who made the Lamb make thee?' The poem poses the problem of evil and creative energy — the same maker forging both gentleness and terror — and is the lyric heart of Blake's doctrine of [[motif:contrary states of the soul|contraries]]. The almost tame depicted tiger has long provoked comment, as if the image deliberately withholds the terror the words invoke. The plate is a touchstone of English Romantic art and poetry alike.

## For artists & game designers
The productive gap between fearsome text and meek image is itself a technique — let the words carry the dread the picture refuses.

citations.text: Hazard Adams, *William Blake: A Reading of the Shorter Poems* (1963).
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Whirlwind of Lovers (Dante, *Inferno* Canto V)
creator: William Blake
summary:
From Blake's unfinished illustrations to Dante's *Divine Comedy*, this design shows the whirlwind of carnal sinners in the second circle of Hell, with Paolo and Francesca.

## Iconography
A great spiralling vortex of naked lovers sweeps across the upper sheet, swept on the eternal storm of the lustful. Below, Dante has swooned to the ground while Virgil supports or gestures over him; a radiant flame-bordered sun-disc enclosing the embracing Paolo and Francesca floats to one side.

## Significance
The scene illustrates *Inferno* V, where Dante hears the tale of Paolo and Francesca and faints with pity. Blake, commissioned by John Linnell in his final years, both honoured and quietly criticised Dante's hell; the luminous disc enfolding the lovers hints at Blake's own more forgiving view of [[motif:contrary states of the soul|desire]] against Dante's damnation. The watercolours, left unfinished at Blake's death in 1827, are among his last and most freely coloured works.

## For artists & game designers
The definitive 'storm of souls' vortex — bodies spiralling on an eternal wind, witnessed by a fainting traveller below.

citations.text: Albert S. Roe, *Blake's Illustrations to the Divine Comedy* (1953).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Death and the Miser
work: Bosch, Bruegel & the Demonic Fantastic of the Low Countries
creator: Hieronymus Bosch
summary:
Hieronymus Bosch's *Death and the Miser* (National Gallery of Art, Washington), a vertical panel from a dismembered triptych staging the *ars moriendi*.

## Iconography
A dying miser sits up in a tall canopied bed as skeletal [[motif:death|Death]] slips through the door with an arrow. A guardian angel steadies him and points to a crucifix in the window, but a small demon offers a bag of gold from beneath the bed-curtain, while other imps swarm the chest and money below. The man hesitates, his hand reaching between salvation and the proffered purse.

## Significance
The panel is a direct visualization of the late-medieval handbook on *the art of dying well*, in which angels and devils contend for the soul at the last moment. Bosch localizes the cosmic struggle in a single bedroom, the imps as familiar household vermin. The work is a touchstone in studies of the deathbed contest (Silver, Marrow) and of Bosch's restrained, almost monochrome demonology.

## For artists & game designers
A model for a 'final choice' encounter: angel and demon as opposing prompts at a character's death, the outcome hinging on one reaching hand.

citations.text: Larry Silver, *Hieronymus Bosch* (2006).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Christ's Descent into Hell (Harrowing of Hell)
work: Bosch, Bruegel & the Demonic Fantastic of the Low Countries
creator: Follower of Hieronymus Bosch
rights: Public domain (CC0). Via Wikimedia Commons. Metropolitan Museum of Art.
summary:
*Christ's Descent into Hell* (Metropolitan Museum of Art), a Boschian panel of the Harrowing of Hell by a follower of Hieronymus Bosch.

## Iconography
A fiery cavern teems with grotesque [[motif:hybrid monster|hybrid devils]] — beaked, horned, finned and clawed — who guard and torment crowds of naked souls amid burning ruins. Christ, a small luminous figure, descends to lead the righteous of the Old Testament out of Limbo, breaking the gates of hell as monstrous fiends recoil. Toads, reptiles and broken-bodied creatures crawl through the gloom.

## Significance
The Harrowing — Christ's descent between Crucifixion and Resurrection to free the souls of the patriarchs — gave painters license for an entire panel of hell. The picture shows how Bosch's idiom was carried by anonymous followers into the mid-16th century, the master's monster-vocabulary becoming a shared Netherlandish style for the infernal. Catalogued by the Met as a work after Bosch.

## For artists & game designers
A 'breach the underworld' scene: a single bright protagonist storming a cavern packed with diverse guardian demons.

citations.text: Metropolitan Museum of Art, object record (Follower of Hieronymus Bosch).
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Haywain Triptych
work: Bosch, Bruegel & the Demonic Fantastic of the Low Countries
creator: Hieronymus Bosch or workshop
summary:
Hieronymus Bosch's *Haywain* triptych (Museo del Prado), an allegory of worldly greed dragged toward hell.

## Iconography
In the central panel a giant wagon of hay rolls forward while people of every estate — peasants, clerics, even the emperor and pope on horseback — claw, trample and murder one another to seize a handful. Atop the load, lovers flirt while an angel prays and a blue demon pipes. Fish-bodied and rat-snouted [[motif:demon|devils]] haul the wain toward the right panel, where they build a tower in a burning hell-landscape.

## Significance
The picture turns a Flemish proverb — 'the world is a haystack and each man plucks what he can' — into a moving image of universal avarice. As Larry Silver and Walter Bosing note, the relentless procession from Eden (left) through greed (center) to hell (right) makes the triptych a compressed sermon on the wages of cupidity, with demons as the literal teamsters of damnation.

## For artists & game designers
The 'doomed procession' set-piece: a slow-moving objective everyone fights over, escorted by monsters toward an inevitable infernal end.

citations.text: Walter Bosing, *Hieronymus Bosch* (1973).
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Last Judgement (Bosch)
work: Bosch, Bruegel & the Demonic Fantastic of the Low Countries
creator: Hieronymus Bosch
summary:
Hieronymus Bosch's *Last Judgement* triptych (Akademie der bildenden Künste, Vienna), among the most densely populated of his infernal visions.

## Iconography
After a narrow band of heaven and the Fall in the upper register, almost the entire surface is given over to a world that has become hell. Naked sinners are roasted on spits, pressed in mills, knifed, drowned and devoured by hybrid devils. Demons combining human, animal, insect and mechanical parts torment the damned in punishments tailored to their sins, amid burning towers and pools of fire.

## Significance
Bosch collapses the traditional separation of judgement and damnation: the verdict has already fallen and the canvas is one vast penal landscape. The work is central to the literature on Bosch's eschatology (Bosing, Silver) and shows how the late-medieval theology of the *contrapasso* — sins punished by their own image — generated an inexhaustible bestiary of torture-demons.

## For artists & game designers
A reference sheet for a 'punishment hell' biome: each torment is a discrete, legible vignette pairing a specific sin with a bespoke demon.

citations.text: Larry Silver, *Hieronymus Bosch* (2006).
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Ship of Fools
work: Bosch, Bruegel & the Demonic Fantastic of the Low Countries
creator: Hieronymus Bosch
rights: Public domain. Via Wikimedia Commons. Musée du Louvre.
summary:
Hieronymus Bosch's *The Ship of Fools* (*La Nef des fous*, Musée du Louvre), a satirical panel of humanity adrift in folly.

## Iconography
A crowded little boat carries a cargo of fools — a monk and a nun singing over a lute, revellers gorging and drinking, one vomiting overboard, another climbing the mast for a roast fowl tied aloft. The mast is a living tree topped by a fool's banner and a death's-head; a jester perches apart on a branch. The vessel drifts with no helmsman toward nowhere.

## Significance
The panel belongs to the late-medieval satire of folly that culminated in Sebastian Brant's *Das Narrenschiff* (1494). It is a fragment of a larger dismembered work, its companion (the *Allegory of Gluttony and Lust*) now at Yale. Bosch turns ecclesiastical and worldly appetite into a rudderless ship of the damned — folly as a moral and spiritual shipwreck (Bosing, Silver).

## For artists & game designers
A self-contained 'vessel of vice' tableau: a single small craft packed with distinct sinning archetypes, drifting toward doom.

citations.text: Walter Bosing, *Hieronymus Bosch* (1973).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Fall of the Damned into Hell (Visions of the Hereafter)
work: Bosch, Bruegel & the Demonic Fantastic of the Low Countries
creator: Hieronymus Bosch
summary:
*Fall of the Damned into Hell*, one of four panels of Hieronymus Bosch's *Visions of the Hereafter* (Palazzo Grimani / Gallerie dell'Accademia, Venice).

## Iconography
In a near-black void, naked souls tumble downward, seized and dragged by winged [[motif:demon|demons]] toward a smoking pit of fire at the bottom of the panel. Flames and embers rake the darkness; the damned writhe in the grip of their captors. Its companion panel, the *Ascent of the Blessed*, shows souls rising instead through a luminous tunnel of light toward heaven.

## Significance
The four Venice panels are among Bosch's most abstract and atmospheric works, reducing the afterlife to elemental contrasts of light and dark, ascent and fall. The luminous tunnel of the *Ascent* has often been linked in popular writing to near-death 'tunnel of light' accounts. As a pair, the panels distill the medieval topography of the hereafter into pure vertical drama, as discussed by Silver and Bosing.

## For artists & game designers
A pure 'descent' visual: bodies and embers falling through darkness toward a fire-lit pit, minimal architecture, maximal atmosphere.

citations.text: Walter Bosing, *Hieronymus Bosch* (1973).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Avaritia (Greed), from The Seven Deadly Sins
work: Bosch, Bruegel & the Demonic Fantastic of the Low Countries
creator: Pieter Bruegel the Elder (engraved by Pieter van der Heyden)
rights: Public domain (CC0). Via Wikimedia Commons. Rijksmuseum.
summary:
*Avaritia* (Greed / *Gierigheid*), from the *Seven Deadly Sins* engravings after Pieter Bruegel the Elder, engraved by Pieter van der Heyden for Hieronymus Cock (1558).

## Iconography
The personification of Avarice counts and hoards coins while all around her people scrape, dig and cheat for money. Demons and [[motif:hybrid monster|hybrid creatures]] embody the obsession — money-disgorging beasts, treasure-guarding monsters — and absurd Boschian structures fill the background. The vice is named in the lower margin.

## Significance
Avarice, the 'root of all evil' in Pauline and medieval moral theology, is here dramatized as a whole society deformed by the pursuit of coin — a resonant theme in mercantile Antwerp. The print belongs to Bruegel's hugely influential *Seven Deadly Sins*, the series that made Bosch's demonic style a renewable commodity of the Netherlandish print market (Sellink, Silver).

## For artists & game designers
A 'greed dungeon' palette: treasure-guardian monsters and coin-disgorging beasts arrayed around a single hoarder figure.

citations.text: Larry Silver, *Pieter Bruegel* (2011).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Desidia (Sloth), from The Seven Deadly Sins
work: Bosch, Bruegel & the Demonic Fantastic of the Low Countries
creator: Pieter Bruegel the Elder (engraved by Pieter van der Heyden)
rights: Public domain (CC0). Via Wikimedia Commons. Rijksmuseum.
summary:
*Desidia* (Sloth / *Luiheid*), from the *Seven Deadly Sins* engravings after Pieter Bruegel the Elder, engraved by Pieter van der Heyden for Hieronymus Cock (1558).

## Iconography
The personification of Sloth sleeps slumped against a snail or a great resting beast while torpid figures doze, dawdle and rot around her. Boschian [[motif:hybrid monster|hybrid creatures]] embody inertia — a giant clock-like form, a sluggish monster bearing the sleeper, dreamlike half-built structures — with the vice named in the lower margin.

## Significance
*Desidia* / *Acedia* (sloth) was the monk's besetting sin in medieval theology, the spiritual listlessness that opens the soul to the devil. Bruegel renders it as a whole landscape sunk into stupor. The sheet completes the demon-filled set of the *Seven Deadly Sins*, the series through which Bosch's fantastic was transmitted to all of Europe via Antwerp printmaking (Sellink, Orenstein).

## For artists & game designers
A 'torpor zone' reference: a sleeping environment where even the architecture sags, useful for an enchantment-of-sleep level.

citations.text: Nadine Orenstein (ed.), *Pieter Bruegel the Elder: Drawings and Prints* (2001).

title: Dulle Griet (Mad Meg)
work: Bosch, Bruegel & the Demonic Fantastic of the Low Countries
creator: Pieter Bruegel the Elder
summary:
Pieter Bruegel the Elder's *Dulle Griet* ('Mad Meg', Museum Mayer van den Bergh, Antwerp), a fiery virago striding before the mouth of hell.

## Iconography
A gaunt woman in helmet and breastplate, sword in one hand and arms full of plundered goods, marches toward the left across a burning, Boschian wasteland. Behind her a literal [[motif:mouth of hell|hell-mouth]] gapes — a vast monstrous face spewing fire — while a horde of soldier-women storm a demon-held bridge and grotesque [[motif:hybrid monster|hybrids]] crawl through the ruined land.

## Significance
Mad Meg embodies the Flemish proverb of the woman who 'could plunder in front of hell and return unscathed', a figure of avarice and shrewish fury. Bruegel fuses social satire with Bosch's infernal vocabulary, painting one of the great images of the world turned upside-down. The work is central to studies of Bruegel's proverb-pictures and his debt to Bosch (Gibson, Silver).

## For artists & game designers
The 'lone raider at the gates of hell': a single armored protagonist looting across an apocalyptic battlefield with a monstrous hell-mouth as backdrop.

citations.text: Walter S. Gibson, *Bruegel* (1977).

title: Gula (Gluttony), from The Seven Deadly Sins
work: Bosch, Bruegel & the Demonic Fantastic of the Low Countries
creator: Pieter Bruegel the Elder (engraved by Pieter van der Heyden)
rights: Public domain (CC0). Via Wikimedia Commons. Rijksmuseum.
summary:
*Gula* (Gluttony / *Gulzigheid*), from the *Seven Deadly Sins* engravings after Pieter Bruegel the Elder, engraved by Pieter van der Heyden for Hieronymus Cock (1558).

## Iconography
The personification of Gluttony tips a jug to drink as figures around her gorge and swill. A giant tippling head, monstrous mouths and [[motif:hybrid monster|hybrid devils]] turn the whole landscape into an organism of consumption — buildings shaped like flagons, beasts vomiting and devouring — with the vice named below.

## Significance
Gluttony, traditionally paired with drunkenness in Netherlandish moral imagery, here swells into an entire ingesting world. The sheet is part of Bruegel's *Seven Deadly Sins*, designed for Hieronymus Cock's press, which carried Bosch's monster-vocabulary into mass circulation and shaped European demonological imagery for generations (Orenstein, Sellink).

## For artists & game designers
The 'devouring environment' idea: architecture and monsters built from mouths, jugs and bellies — consumption as level theme.

citations.text: Manfred Sellink, *Bruegel: The Complete Paintings, Drawings and Prints* (2007).

title: Ira (Wrath), from The Seven Deadly Sins
work: Bosch, Bruegel & the Demonic Fantastic of the Low Countries
creator: Pieter Bruegel the Elder (engraved by Pieter van der Heyden)
rights: Public domain (CC0). Via Wikimedia Commons. Rijksmuseum.
summary:
*Ira* (Wrath / *Toorn*), from the *Seven Deadly Sins* engravings after Pieter Bruegel the Elder, engraved by Pieter van der Heyden for Hieronymus Cock (1558).

## Iconography
Wrath is personified amid a field of mutual slaughter: figures hack, stab and brawl with knives and improvised weapons while a giant knife and a vast cauldron-tent loom over the scene. Boschian [[motif:hybrid monster|hybrid monsters]] join the carnage, and a winged demon presides over the violence. A motto identifies the vice along the lower border.

## Significance
The sheet visualizes wrath as a landscape that has dissolved into general warfare — an apt image for the strife-torn Low Countries on the eve of the Dutch Revolt. With the rest of the series it transmitted Bosch's monster-idiom across Europe in reproducible form and cemented Bruegel's standing as a print designer (Orenstein, Sellink).

## For artists & game designers
A 'riot biome' reference: a whole environment in which every figure is locked in localized combat, oversized weapons as set dressing.

citations.text: Nadine Orenstein (ed.), *Pieter Bruegel the Elder: Drawings and Prints* (2001).

title: Luxuria (Lust), from The Seven Deadly Sins
work: Bosch, Bruegel & the Demonic Fantastic of the Low Countries
creator: Pieter Bruegel the Elder (engraved by Pieter van der Heyden)
rights: Public domain (CC0). Via Wikimedia Commons. Rijksmuseum.
summary:
*Luxuria* (Lust / *Wellust*), from the *Seven Deadly Sins* engravings after Pieter Bruegel the Elder, engraved by Pieter van der Heyden for Hieronymus Cock (1558).

## Iconography
The personification of Lust sits caressed by a demon within a pink shell-like pavilion, while around her the landscape erupts in [[motif:hybrid monster|monstrous]] obscenity: embracing couples sheltered by lewd contraptions, beaked and finned devils, and absurd hybrid architecture, all glossing carnal sin in the Boschian manner. A Latin-Flemish motto names the vice below.

## Significance
Like the rest of the series, *Luxuria* revived Bosch's demonic fantastic for the Antwerp print trade four decades after Bosch's death, marrying moral allegory to virtuoso monster-invention. The *Seven Deadly Sins* and the companion *Seven Virtues* established Bruegel's reputation as the 'second Bosch' and are foundational to the study of his graphic work (Orenstein, Sellink).

## For artists & game designers
Use the central shell-pavilion as a 'sin shrine' motif: a tempting interior framed by escalating grotesque detail.

citations.text: Manfred Sellink, *Bruegel: The Complete Paintings, Drawings and Prints* (2007).

title: The Fall of the Rebel Angels (Bruegel)
work: Bosch, Bruegel & the Demonic Fantastic of the Low Countries
creator: Pieter Bruegel the Elder
summary:
Pieter Bruegel the Elder's *The Fall of the Rebel Angels* (Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium, Brussels), painted 1562 in unmistakably Boschian idiom.

## Iconography
At the top, the golden archangel Michael in gleaming armor and his bright-robed angels drive the rebel host downward with sword and trumpet. As they fall, the rebels metamorphose mid-air into grotesque [[motif:hybrid monster|hybrids]] — fish, frogs, insects, fruit and fungus fused into writhing devils — tumbling toward the dark bottom of the panel. The composition is a vertical cascade of transformation from light into the monstrous.

## Significance
The subject — the primal revolt of Lucifer's angels cast out of heaven (Revelation 12) — let Bruegel rival Bosch directly, and the picture was long attributed to Bosch before its 1562 monogram and date were recognized. It exemplifies how the war-in-heaven theme generated demon-imagery and stands among the masterpieces of Netherlandish fantastic painting (Gibson, Silver).

## For artists & game designers
A 'corruption-in-motion' reference: enemies that visibly mutate from angelic to monstrous as they fall, a single readable downward composition.

citations.text: Walter S. Gibson, *Bruegel* (1977).

title: Superbia (Pride), from The Seven Deadly Sins
work: Bosch, Bruegel & the Demonic Fantastic of the Low Countries
creator: Pieter Bruegel the Elder (engraved by Pieter van der Heyden)
rights: Public domain (CC0). Via Wikimedia Commons. Rijksmuseum.
summary:
*Superbia* (Pride), one of the *Seven Deadly Sins* (*De zeven hoofdzonden*) engravings after Pieter Bruegel the Elder, engraved by Pieter van der Heyden and published by Hieronymus Cock (1558).

## Iconography
A crowned female personification of Pride admires herself in a mirror held by a demon, a [[motif:peacock|peacock]] beside her. Around this central allegory swarms a Bosch-inspired world of [[motif:hybrid monster|hybrid monsters]]: building-headed beasts, walking pots, beaked and finned devils, and absurd architecture, each detail glossing the sin of vanity. A Flemish-Latin inscription names the vice along the lower margin.

## Significance
Bruegel's *Seven Deadly Sins* series, designed for the print publisher Hieronymus Cock, deliberately revived Bosch's monstrous fantastic for the booming Antwerp print market a generation after Bosch's death. The engravings spread the Boschian idiom across Europe in reproducible form and are foundational to studies of Bruegel as a designer of prints (Orenstein, Sellink).

## For artists & game designers
A dense 'sin-world' page: one clear allegorical figure surrounded by dozens of kitbashed micro-monsters illustrating a single theme.

citations.text: Nadine Orenstein (ed.), *Pieter Bruegel the Elder: Drawings and Prints* (2001).

title: The Triumph of Death
work: Bosch, Bruegel & the Demonic Fantastic of the Low Countries
creator: Pieter Bruegel the Elder
summary:
Pieter Bruegel the Elder's *The Triumph of Death* (Museo del Prado), a panoramic apocalypse of skeleton armies harvesting the living.

## Iconography
Across a scorched, smoke-blackened landscape, legions of [[motif:skeleton army|skeletons]] drive humanity toward a great coffin-lidded trap. The dead toll bells, drag carts of skulls, slit throats and ferry souls; kings, cardinals, lovers and peasants are seized without distinction. A skeletal rider on a pale horse mows through a crowd with a scythe while fires burn on the horizon and ships sink at sea.

## Significance
Bruegel universalizes the *danse macabre* into a single battlefield where Death triumphs over every estate, echoing the Italian *Trionfo della Morte* tradition (Palermo, Pisa) seen through Netherlandish eyes. The painting is read as a response to war, plague and the religious violence of the 16th-century Low Countries, and remains the canonical image of death as the great leveller (Gibson, Silver).

## For artists & game designers
The definitive 'undead horde overruns the world' tableau: an entire society processed by an army of skeletons across a burning plain.

citations.text: Larry Silver, *Pieter Bruegel* (2011).

title: The Tree-Man (Garden of Earthly Delights, Hell panel detail)
work: Bosch, Bruegel & the Demonic Fantastic of the Low Countries
creator: Hieronymus Bosch
summary:
A detail of the so-called *Tree-Man*, the central monster of the Hell panel of Hieronymus Bosch's *Garden of Earthly Delights* (Museo del Prado).

## Iconography
The figure has a pale, egg-shaped, broken torso hollowed into a tavern where small naked figures sit and drink. Its limbs are two dead tree-trunks ending in boats that float on a dark lake; its face turns back over its shoulder with a sidelong, melancholy stare. On the flat disk-shaped hat balanced on its head, demons and damned souls parade around a large [[motif:hat with bagpipe|bagpipe]], the instrument long read as an emblem of lust and folly.

## Significance
The Tree-Man is the most famous single invention of Bosch's infernal imagination and is widely thought to be a veiled self-portrait, since a related drawing survives in the Albertina. It crystallizes Bosch's method of building monsters from hybrid, hollow and broken bodies. As discussed by scholars such as Walter Bosing and Hans Belting, the Hell panel turns the instruments of pleasure into instruments of torment.

## For artists & game designers
A template for the 'environment-creature': a monster whose hollow body is itself a haunted interior space the player can enter.

citations.text: Hans Belting, *Hieronymus Bosch: Garden of Earthly Delights* (2002).

title: The Garden of Earthly Delights (full triptych)
work: Bosch, Bruegel & the Demonic Fantastic of the Low Countries
creator: Hieronymus Bosch
summary:
Hieronymus Bosch's *The Garden of Earthly Delights* (Museo del Prado), the supreme triptych of the visionary fantastic, here in the full open three-panel view.

## Iconography
The left wing shows Eden, where God joins Adam and Eve amid strange beasts and a pink fountain of life. The vast central panel teems with nude figures cavorting with giant birds, fruit and crystalline structures in a lake-dotted garden of sensual fantasy. The right wing is a frozen, fire-lit [[motif:hell|hell]]: the [[motif:tree-man|Tree-Man]], a bird-headed devil devouring sinners, instruments of music turned to torture, and a swarm of [[motif:hybrid monster|hybrid demons]] punishing the damned.

## Significance
The triptych's meaning remains contested — moral warning against lust, heterodox paradise, or alchemical-astrological allegory — and that very ambiguity has made it the most analyzed of all Bosch's works (Fraenger, Bosing, Belting, Silver). As a whole it maps the Christian arc from creation through sin to damnation while inventing a wholly original repertoire of the monstrous.

## For artists & game designers
The ultimate three-act world map: paradise, pleasure and punishment as adjacent, traversable biomes, each with its own creature logic.

citations.text: Hans Belting, *Hieronymus Bosch: Garden of Earthly Delights* (2002).

title: The Temptation of Saint Anthony (Pieter Huys)
work: Bosch, Bruegel & the Demonic Fantastic of the Low Countries
creator: Pieter Huys
rights: Public domain (CC0). Via Wikimedia Commons. Metropolitan Museum of Art.
summary:
Pieter Huys's *The Temptation of Saint Anthony* (Metropolitan Museum of Art), a Boschian assault on the desert hermit.

## Iconography
The aged Saint Anthony kneels at his book amid a riot of [[motif:hybrid monster|hybrid demons]] — fish-bodied, beaked, multi-limbed creatures that crawl, fly and grimace around him. A richly dressed temptress (a demon in disguise) offers worldly enticement, while monstrous heads, burning ruins and absurd vessels fill the surrounding landscape. Imps pluck at the saint and brandish grotesque instruments.

## Significance
Huys (c. 1519–1584) was among the Antwerp specialists who kept Bosch's *Temptation of St Anthony* type commercially alive through the mid-16th century. The subject — drawn from Athanasius's *Life of St Anthony* — let painters combine spiritual exemplum with virtuoso monster-invention. Huys's signed and dated versions are key documents of the Boschian revival catalogued in studies of Netherlandish demonology in art (Silver, *Peasant Scenes and Landscapes*; Met records).

## For artists & game designers
The classic 'besieged saint' setup: a still, praying figure at the calm center of a 360-degree swirl of distinct tormentor-demons.

citations.text: Metropolitan Museum of Art, object record (Pieter Huys, 1547).

title: The Temptation of Saint Anthony (Workshop of Jan Mandijn)
work: Bosch, Bruegel & the Demonic Fantastic of the Low Countries
creator: Workshop of Jan Mandijn
summary:
*The Temptation of Saint Anthony* from the workshop of Jan Mandijn, a Boschian panel of the hermit beset by monsters.

## Iconography
Saint Anthony endures a teeming landscape of [[motif:hybrid monster|hybrid devils]]: creatures fused from man, beast, bird and machine flock around him while fires burn in the distance and grotesque processions wind through the wasteland. Demons fly, scuttle and float on absurd contraptions, the whole forming a panoramic catalogue of the monstrous in the manner of Bosch.

## Significance
Jan Mandijn (c. 1500–1560), active in Antwerp, was one of the most important transmitters of Bosch's demonic style in the generation between Bosch and Bruegel; Karel van Mander praised his 'droll' and uncanny manner. Workshop versions like this one show how the *Temptation of St Anthony* became a near-industrial Antwerp product, each painter recombining a stock of Boschian monster-motifs. Such pictures anchor the art-historical account of Bosch's reception (Unverfehrt, Silver).

## For artists & game designers
A 'monster-catalogue landscape': a wide scene whose density of distinct fantastical creatures is itself the spectacle.

citations.text: Gerd Unverfehrt, *Hieronymus Bosch: die Rezeption seiner Kunst* (1980).
