title: Morgan le Fay
work: The Reception of Ancient Magic in Later Art
creator: Frederick Sandys
summary:
Frederick Sandys's *Morgan le Fay* (1864), the Arthurian enchantress caught in the frenzy of casting a destructive spell.

## Iconography
**Morgan le Fay** twists in mid-incantation, throwing on the enchanted, flame-coloured **robe** she has woven on the **loom** behind her to destroy King Arthur. Talismanic objects, a leopard-skin, and runic decoration crowd the chamber; her contorted pose and glaring eyes convey the violence of the working **spell**.

## Significance
Though medieval and Arthurian rather than antique, Morgan belongs to the same 19th-century re-imagining of the powerful magical woman as Sandys's [[motif:medea-the-sorceress|Medea]] and Waterhouse's [[motif:circe-the-enchantress|Circe]] — the *enchantress* descended ultimately from Circe and Medea. Sandys renders her with the same jewelled, claustrophobic intensity, making her a Pre-Raphaelite icon of female sorcery.

## For artists & game designers
Spell-casting as physical performance: a witch shown mid-gesture donning her enchanted garment, the magic dramatized through the body rather than through effects.

title: The Tabula Cebetis (Table of Cebes) — allegorical print
work: The Reception of Ancient Magic in Later Art
creator: Anonymous; Rijksmuseum print
rights: Public domain (CC0). Rijksmuseum, via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A detail from an engraved *Tabula Cebetis* (Table of Cebes), the allegorical map of human life derived from a Greek text ascribed to the Pythagorean Cebes.

## Iconography
The print lays out the **allegory of human life** as a series of **concentric enclosures**: souls enter the gate of life past **Fortune** and Deceit, pass through the precincts of false and **true education**, and ascend toward the citadel of Happiness. Each personified figure is labelled, making the whole a walkable moral diagram.

## Significance
The *Tabula Cebetis* (*pinax*), a dialogue of the 1st century CE attributed to a follower of [[motif:pythagoras|Pythagoras]], describes a votive panel in a temple of Kronos that maps the soul's pilgrimage. Rediscovered and printed throughout the Renaissance, it became a favourite subject for emblematic engravings uniting Platonic-Pythagorean philosophy with [[motif:hermetic|Hermetic]] and Stoic moral teaching.

## For artists & game designers
Literally a level-map of life: nested rings of trials and false paths leading to a final citadel — an allegory that is already a game board.

title: Circe Offering the Cup to Ulysses
work: The Reception of Ancient Magic in Later Art
creator: John William Waterhouse
summary:
Waterhouse's monumental Circe, the archetypal Pre-Raphaelite image of the antique enchantress, painted in 1891.

## Iconography
**Circe** sits enthroned and frontal, raising in one hand the drugged **cup** and in the other the **wand** with which she turns men to beasts. At her feet a transformed companion lies as a **swine**; behind her a **mirror** reflects the tiny approaching figure of **Ulysses**. Lions and a pool of spilled enchantment complete the composition.

## Significance
The scene is from *Odyssey* X, where the goddess-witch of Aiaia drugs Odysseus's crew. Waterhouse makes her the calm, commanding [[motif:circe-the-enchantress|sorceress]] who became the Victorian type of the dangerous magical woman, descended from Homer through Ovid. The mirror device — showing the hero she cannot yet see — is the painter's own theatrical addition.

## For artists & game designers
A seated boss-enchantress, cup-and-wand in hand, with a victim already transformed at her feet: a complete 'beast-maker' encounter in one frame.

citations.text: P. Trippi, *J. W. Waterhouse* (2002).
Homer, *Odyssey* X.

title: Circe Invidiosa
work: The Reception of Ancient Magic in Later Art
creator: John William Waterhouse
summary:
Waterhouse's 1892 *Circe Invidiosa* ('jealous Circe'), the enchantress poisoning the sea-pool of her rival Scylla.

## Iconography
**Circe** stands tall in an iridescent green-blue gown, pouring a stream of **poison** from a shallow bowl into the water below, where the half-glimpsed form of **Scylla** begins her monstrous **metamorphosis**. A grotesque sea-creature rises beneath her feet; the whole canvas is bathed in venomous green.

## Significance
The subject is from Ovid's *Metamorphoses* XIV: spurned by Glaucus, who loves Scylla, Circe out of [[motif:circe-the-enchantress|jealousy]] poisons the nymph's bathing-place and transforms her into a monster. Waterhouse condenses the Ovidian tale into a single vertical icon of cold, deliberate sorcery — magic as envy made visible.

## For artists & game designers
A vertical poisoning ritual rendered almost monochrome green — a study in how a single colour can encode toxicity and malice.

title: Saul and the Witch of Endor (etching, Rijksmuseum)
work: The Reception of Ancient Magic in Later Art
creator: Anonymous; Rijksmuseum print
rights: Public domain (CC0). Rijksmuseum, via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A second Rijksmuseum print of Saul and the Witch of Endor, showing a different compositional treatment of the conjuring of Samuel.

## Iconography
The **Witch of Endor** stands or kneels at her conjuring as the prophet **Samuel** appears; the disguised **King Saul** and his companions recoil. The print emphasizes the moment of the **apparition** and the king's dismay at hearing his coming defeat foretold.

## Significance
The story of En-dor (1 Samuel 28) generated a long print tradition across the Low Countries and beyond, since it offered the rare spectacle of a sanctioned biblical [[motif:necromancy|necromancy]]. Such engravings carried the imagery of the [[motif:witch-of-endor|raising of Samuel]] into Bibles and emblem books, fixing the visual formula of witch, rising shade, and stricken king.

## For artists & game designers
Variant blocking of the same beat — useful for studying how the 'summoner / apparition / horrified witness' triangle can be re-staged.

title: The Complete Cycle of 22 Demonological Woodcuts — Compendium Maleficarum (Guazzo, 1608)
work: Compendium Maleficarum — Guazzo's Demonological Woodcut Cycle (1608/1626)
creator: Anonymous woodcut engraver; text by Francesco Maria Guazzo O.F.M.
rights: Public Domain. Francesco Maria Guazzo, Compendium Maleficarum (1608). Photographs via Internet Archive.
repository: Internet Archive (source: compendium-maleficarum-engraving-122-panorama, IA 2023 composite photograph of the 1608 woodcut suite)
summary:
A composite photograph showing all 22 woodcut engravings from Francesco Maria Guazzo's *Compendium Maleficarum* (Milan, 1608), the most comprehensive visual typology of witchcraft practices produced in the early modern period. The 22 scenes are arranged in a grid, each depicting a distinct category of diabolical act as classified by Guazzo's three-book demonological treatise.

## Iconography

The 22 woodcuts form a systematic visual encyclopaedia of the pact-sabbath-maleficium triad that structured early modern witchcraft belief. Scene 1: the Pact — a witch kneels before the Devil (depicted in hybrid human-bestial form) and signs the diabolical contract with blood or pen; the Devil places his hand on the witch's shoulder. Scene 2: Renunciation of Baptism — the witch formally abjures Christian faith. Scene 3: the Devil's Mark — a demon or Devil applies the infamous *stigma diabolicum* to the witch's body, often the back, shoulder, or hidden areas; later magistrates would probe for this insensible mark during trials. Scene 4: the Devil's Kiss (*osculum infame*) — the witch kisses the Devil's posterior in a ceremony of diabolical submission. Scene 5–8: Witches' Sabbath preparations — robing in animal skins, receiving unguents from the Devil, smearing broomstick or pitchfork with flying ointment. Scenes 9–12: the Flight — witches fly through the night air on broomsticks, shovels, pitchforks, and on the backs of animals (goat, ram). Scenes 13–15: the Sabbath assembly — witches dancing back-to-back in a ring with the Devil presiding, feasting at the sabbath table, sexual intercourse with incubi/succubi. Scenes 16–18: Weather magic — witches boiling a cauldron to raise storms, striking cattle dead with cursed wands. Scenes 19–22: Maleficium — witches poisoning individuals and animals, digging up corpses for body-part ingredients, causing impotence and disease through magical objects buried at thresholds.

## Significance

Guazzo's woodcut cycle is the pivotal visual document in the history of the sabbath concept. By 1608 the major components of the accumulated sabbath image — the night flight, the assembly, the pact with the Devil, the inverted Christian rites — had been codified through a century of demonological writing (Institoris and Sprenger's *Malleus Maleficarum* 1486, Bodin's *De la Démonomanie* 1580, del Río's *Disquisitionum Magicarum* 1599–1600), but Guazzo was the first to give these concepts a comprehensive, numbered visual form. Charles Zika's fundamental study (*The Appearance of Witchcraft*, 2007) demonstrates how Guazzo's woodcuts built on and systematized the previous century of witch imagery in German and Flemish prints — particularly Baldung Grien's *Witches' Sabbath* (1510), Dürer's *Witch Riding Backwards* (c.1500), and the Flemish sabbath compositions. Stuart Clark (*Thinking with Demons*, 1997) places the Guazzo imagery within the epistemological framework of inversion and the *mundus inversus* that structured demonological thought: each Guazzo woodcut visualizes a deliberate parody or inversion of a Christian sacrament (pact = baptism inverted; sabbath feast = Eucharist inverted; osculum infame = reverence inverted). Lyndal Roper (*Witch Craze*, 2004) and Brian Levack (*The Witch-Hunt in Early Modern Europe*, 2016) situate the Guazzo imagery within the social and psychological context of early modern confessions obtained under torture, which projected fantasies of sexual disorder, cannibalism, and social inversion onto accused witches — fantasies that Guazzo's woodcuts reified and circulated. The composite photograph used for this entry was made from the original 1608 copper plates photographed through photogrammetric reconstruction, providing unusually sharp detail of all 22 scenes simultaneously.

## For artists & game designers

Guazzo's 22 scenes constitute the definitive visual toolkit for early modern witchcraft iconography: every major category of sabbath activity, maleficium, and diabolical pact is here, precisely labelled by the demonological tradition. The flight scenes (broomstick, pitchfork, goat, ram) are the primary historical source for the witch-flight image that entered popular culture. The pact scene is the model for almost all subsequent diabolical-contract imagery in Western art. The witch's mark scene is essential for understanding historical trial procedures and their visual representation in broadsheets.

title: Conjuration Circle, *Astrologer of the Nineteenth Century* (1825)
creator: Anonymous engraver (published by Robert Cross Smith 'Raphael')
repository: Published: *The Astrologer of the Nineteenth Century* (London, 1825)
rights: Public domain (no known restrictions). Via Internet Archive / Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A plate showing a conjuration circle diagram from *The Astrologer of the Nineteenth Century* (London, 1825), the popular occult compendium published by Robert Cross Smith ('Raphael').

## Iconography
The plate presents the circle itself as an object of study — a diagram of the operator's working space with its concentric rings, divine name inscriptions, cross-guards at the quarters, and the spatial arrangement of the ritual equipment. Unlike the scene-plates showing the magician at work, this is an instructional diagram: a template to be reproduced and worked within.

## Significance
The instructional circles of *The Astrologer of the Nineteenth Century* were among the most widely circulated conjuration diagrams in early Victorian England, appearing in a book that was affordable, widely distributed, and aimed at a curious lay readership. They represent the moment at which Solomonic circles passed from manuscript transmission (copied hand to hand among practitioners) into print culture — available to anyone who could afford a popular occult compendium. This democratisation of the grimoire is a key moment in the history of Western magic.

## For artists & game designers
A printed instructional circle — cleaner and more regularised than manuscript working copies, but retaining the divine name inscriptions that signal authentic Solomonic material.

title: The Magician Raising a Spirit, *Astrologer of the Nineteenth Century* (1825)
creator: Anonymous engraver (published by Robert Cross Smith 'Raphael')
repository: Published: *The Astrologer of the Nineteenth Century* (London, 1825)
rights: Public domain (no known restrictions). Via Internet Archive / Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A plate from *The Astrologer of the Nineteenth Century* (London, 1825), one of the key popular occult compendiums of the early Victorian period, showing a magician raising a spirit within his protective circle.

## Iconography
The robed magician stands within a double circle inscribed with divine names, holding his wand aloft as a luminous spirit materialises in response to his conjuration. Around him are the standard props of Solomonic ceremonial magic: the ritual sword, the lamp, the inscribed parchments. The spirit appears not in a separate triangle but rising directly before the conjurer — a more dramatic theatrical arrangement than the strict triangle-of-art prescription.

## Significance
*The Astrologer of the Nineteenth Century*, published by Robert Cross Smith ('Raphael'), packaged Solomonic and grimoire material for a Georgian popular audience hungry for occult knowledge in an accessible form. Its engravings — of robed conjurers, rising spirits, and smoking censers — were enormously influential on popular imagination and helped fix the romantic image of the ceremonial magician in the English-speaking world. The book is a direct ancestor of the Victorian occult revival that would culminate in the Golden Dawn.

## For artists & game designers
A complete 'summoning scene' reference from the popular imagination: robed figure, inscribed circle, materialising spirit. The composition is so archetypal it has become the baseline template for fantasy magic illustration.

title: Circle of Solomon and Triangle of Solomon, *Lesser Key of Solomon*
creator: Samuel Liddell MacGregor Mathers and Aleister Crowley
summary:
The Circle of Solomon and Triangle of Solomon as rendered in the standard diagram from the Mathers–Crowley *Goetia* (1904) — shown together on a single plate, demonstrating their relational geometry.

## Iconography
The plate shows both ritual instruments to scale. The Circle of Solomon is the operator's domain: triple rings bearing divine names, a central pentagram, and four cross-guards at the quarters. The Triangle of Solomon sits adjacent — an equilateral figure with 'Anaphaxeton', 'Primeumaton', and 'Tetragrammaton' inscribed on its three sides, and the name 'Michael' written within. The spirit is commanded into the triangle; the operator works from within the circle.

## Significance
Together these two geometrical spaces constitute the entire spatial grammar of Goetic evocation: inside the circle is safety and divine authority; inside the triangle is compelled appearance. The arrangement encodes a theology of names — the Hebrew divine names function as legal instruments to enforce the spirit's attendance and prevent its causing harm. The *Lemegeton* specifies that the triangle should be placed nine feet north-east of the circle.

## For artists & game designers
This two-object diagram is the master template for summoning-system design: a safe zone for the caster and a contained zone for the entity. The inscriptions can be swapped for any in-world language system while preserving the structural logic.

title: Pentacle Diagram, *Clavicula Salomonis* (BL Oriental MS 14759)
creator: Anonymous (Hebrew scribe)
summary:
A pentacle diagram from a Hebrew manuscript of the *Clavicula Salomonis* held in the British Library (Oriental MS 14759, f. 35a).

## Iconography
The diagram presents a circular magical figure inscribed with Hebrew script — divine names, angel names, or phrases from the Psalms — arrayed within a geometric frame of nested rings or a star pattern. The Hebrew character gives this version of the circle a markedly different aesthetic from the Latin manuscripts: the script flows with calligraphic fluency, and the diagram breathes with a different visual grammar than its European counterparts.

## Significance
The Hebrew tradition of Solomonic magic is distinct from — and predates — the European Latin manuscripts. The *Clavicula* circulated in Hebrew and Judeo-Arabic versions long before it was absorbed into European grimoire culture; this British Library manuscript is a rare witness to that Eastern strand. The divine names inscribed belong to the same system as those in the Latin texts — Tetragrammaton, the seventy-two names, angelic designations — but are rendered with the authority of the original scriptural language.

## For artists & game designers
A reference for a 'Hebraic' aesthetic in magic circle design — the Hebrew script creates a very different visual texture from Gothic or Roman lettering, useful for distinguishing traditions.

creator: Anonymous (French scribe)
rights: CC BY 4.0. Via Wellcome Collection / Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A page from *La Clavicure de Salomon Roy des Hebreux*, an 18th-century French manuscript of the *Key of Solomon* tradition held in the Wellcome Collection.

## Iconography
The manuscript page shows the characteristic French presentation of Solomonic material: elegant penmanship, decorative borders, and a circular magical figure inscribed with divine names in Latin and pseudo-Hebrew characters. French manuscript grimoires of this period often show a polished, almost luxury-item quality compared to rougher English working copies — these were prestige objects as much as practical manuals.

## Significance
France was a major conduit for the *Clavicula Salomonis* tradition in the 17th and 18th centuries, and the Wellcome Collection holds several important French Solomonic manuscripts. The French title — *La Clavicure de Salomon Roy des Hebreux* — underscores the claim of Hebraic antiquity that legitimated the whole grimoire tradition. The Wellcome bequest (Sir Henry Wellcome, 1936) brought a remarkable assemblage of magical manuscripts into public accessibility.

## For artists & game designers
French 18th-century manuscript grimoires have a polished Rococo quality absent from their English and German counterparts — use this aesthetic for a 'noble's grimoire' prop distinct from rougher working copies.

title: The Holy Table, Enochian System (John Dee)
creator: John Dee (designed); digital reconstruction
summary:
The *Holy Table* (Tabula Sancta), John Dee's ritual working table for the Enochian operations — a diagram of the surface on which the scrying stone was placed during the angelic séances of 1582–1589.

## Iconography
The Table is a square divided into a nine-cell grid, each cell bearing a divine or angelic name derived from the Enochian communications. The *Sigillum Dei Aemeth* wax disc was placed at the centre and at the four legs; the crystal ball rested on the central sigil. The overall design was dictated to Dee by the angel Uriel through Kelley's visions and constitutes a complete spatial apparatus for establishing contact with the angelic hierarchy.

## Significance
Unlike the Solomonic circles designed to constrain spirits, Dee's *Holy Table* is an invitational instrument — a sanctified platform for angelic communication rather than a prison. It represents the translation of the medieval magic circle into a piece of furniture, part of a complete Enochian cosmological system that includes the *Sigillum*, the Watchtowers, and the Enochian language itself. The British Museum holds both the original *Sigillum* wax disc and Dee's Enochian diaries.

## For artists & game designers
The Holy Table is the magic circle's domestic cousin — a ritual surface rather than a floor diagram. Useful for a 'scholar's study' magic system where the working space is a piece of furniture rather than a chalked floor.

title: Sigillum Dei Aemeth (John Dee's Wax Disc, British Museum)
creator: John Dee (designed); craftsman (executed)
shelfmark: British Museum, Department of Britain, Europe and Prehistory
rights: CC0. Photo: Vassil. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
John Dee's *Sigillum Dei Aemeth* — the Seal of God's Truth — the central instrument of his Enochian operations with Edward Kelley (1582–1589), photographed in the British Museum.

## Iconography
The wax disc (approximately 22 cm across) carries a bewilderingly complex diagram: seven concentric rings of Hebrew letters alternating with a heptagrammic star, forty-nine angelic names arranged in a precise geometric code, and the names of the seven archangels radiating from the centre. The disc was placed beneath Dee's 'shewstone' (crystal ball) and at the legs of the *Holy Table* during the seances at which Kelley received the Enochian revelations.

## Significance
The *Sigillum Dei Aemeth* is the culmination of the medieval circle tradition translated into an Elizabethan cosmological instrument. Dee based his design on the *Sigillum Dei* of the *Sworn Book of Honorius* (13th c.) — one of the most ambitious of medieval magic circles — and elaborated it through his angelic communications. Where Solomonic circles use divine names to compel spirits, Dee's *Sigillum* encodes an entire cosmology of angelic hierarchy. This British Museum object is one of the few surviving physical ritual instruments from a named magician's working practice.

## For artists & game designers
The *Sigillum Dei Aemeth* is the most complex single circle in the Western tradition — a full cosmological map compressed into a disc. Study it for a 'master-tier' ritual object whose reading requires specialist knowledge.

title: First Pentacle of the Moon, *Clavicula Salomonis* (Sloane MS 3091)
creator: Anonymous (English scribe); digital reconstruction by Fuzzypeg
summary:
The First Pentacle of the Moon from Sloane MS 3091, a 17th-century English manuscript of the *Clavicula Salomonis* held in the British Library.

## Iconography
The pentacle is a circular diagram inscribed with a pair of angel names flanking a central figure — a stylised eye or sigil — enclosed by a ring of Hebrew text taken from Psalm 107 ('They that go down to the sea in ships'). The *Key of Solomon* prescribes this pentacle to serve at night and to discover hidden and secret things.

## Significance
Sloane MS 3091 is one of the most important English manuscripts of the *Clavicula Salomonis*, part of the extraordinary collection of magical and scientific manuscripts assembled by Sir Hans Sloane (1660–1753) and now forming part of the founding collection of the British Library. The lunar pentacles of the *Key of Solomon* are a suite of seven diagrams, each governing a different aspect of lunar magic: discovery of secrets, protection against night dangers, spirit evocation, and so forth. They represent the most 'scholastic' layer of Solomonic magic — celestial forces systematically harnessed through inscribed symbols.

## For artists & game designers
The moon pentacles have a distinctive compositional vocabulary — eye or crescent at the centre, angelic names at the compass points, Psalm verse in the outer ring — that makes them easily distinguishable from the planetary pentacles. Clean reference for a lunar magic tier in a multilevel system.

title: The Goetic Circle, *Lesser Key of Solomon* (Mathers–Crowley edition)
creator: Samuel Liddell MacGregor Mathers and Aleister Crowley
summary:
The Goetic Circle as printed in Mathers and Crowley's landmark 1904 edition of *The Goetia* (Book I of the *Lemegeton Clavicula Salomonis*).

## Iconography
The double ring is densely packed with divine and angelic names arranged at the cardinal and intercardinal points, the whole girded by a third outer ring. A pentagram is inscribed in the centre and an equilateral triangle extends outside the circle at the south — the Triangle of Art into which the spirit is commanded to appear visible. Cross-marks divide the annular bands. The operator stands inside; the spirit is confined to the triangle.

## Significance
This is the canonical conjuration apparatus of the Goetic tradition. The *Lemegeton* compiles and systematises earlier English Solomonic manuscripts into a definitive instrument of spirit-working, and this circle is the operator's sanctified ground for all seventy-two operations it describes. The divine names inscribed — drawn from Hebrew scripture, the Psalms, and angelic nomenclature — theoretically compel any spirit to come, appear, and speak truthfully within the triangle. Mathers and Crowley's 1904 edition standardised the diagrammatic conventions that all subsequent ceremonial magic inherits.

## For artists & game designers
The Circle-plus-Triangle layout is the archetypal 'summoning circle' design: two concentric rings for the operator, a geometric extrusion for the entity. Copy this structure directly for any game summoning mechanic and it reads instantly as authentic.

title: Grand Pentacle of Solomon, 1547 French *Heptameron*
creator: Anonymous (attributed to Peter de Abano)
summary:
The *Grand Pentacle de Salomon* from the 1547 French edition of the *Heptameron*, the supreme protective talisman of the whole Solomonic system.

## Iconography
The Grand Pentacle is a six-pointed star (hexagram, the Star of David, called the *Seal of Solomon* in this context) inscribed within a circle, with divine names positioned at the points and within the interlocking triangles. The outer ring bears further names of God in Hebrew and Latin. Unlike the working circles used during conjuration, the Grand Pentacle is a concentrated talisman — an object or diagram to be carried or displayed as universal protection.

## Significance
The *Grand Pentacle* (sometimes called the *Hexagram of Solomon*) stands at the head of the *Clavicula* and *Heptameron* traditions as the master symbol whose presence compels the obedience of all spirits. It is simultaneously a seal, a circle, and a cosmogram — the divine names inscribed within it encode Solomon's authority over the whole spirit world. The 1547 French *Heptameron* is a landmark early printed edition that fixed many of the visual conventions inherited by later grimoires.

## For artists & game designers
The Grand Pentacle is the 'master key' of the Solomonic system — a hexagram-in-circle that outranks all other symbols. Use it as a universal access token or override command in any sigil-based game system.

title: Grimoire du Pape Honorius (allegedly 1760)
creator: Anonymous
summary:
The title page (or a key page) of the *Grimoire du Pape Honorius*, allegedly printed in Rome in 1760 — one of the most notorious and controversial works in the history of occult literature.

## Iconography
The page shows the characteristic layout of an 18th-century French popular grimoire: dense typeset text combined with printed magical diagrams — circles, sigils, or characters meant to be reproduced during the ritual operations. The title claims papal authority, a claim that simultaneously shocked Christian readers and inflated the text's perceived power.

## Significance
The *Grimoire du Pape Honorius* (not to be confused with the medieval *Sworn Book of Honorius*, though the confusion is deliberate) is a Catholic-inflected diabolical grimoire that combines standard Solomonic conjuration with elements of Black Mass iconography. Its claim to derive from Pope Honorius III gave it enormous notoriety; it circulated widely in France and Italy and was repeatedly condemned. The text exemplifies the 18th-century strand of anti-clerical black magic grimoires that parody Catholic ritual as a vehicle for diabolical operation. Owen Davies describes it as one of the most scandalous grimoires ever printed.

## For artists & game designers
The *Grimoire du Pape Honorius* is the archetype of the 'forbidden book' — a text whose title promises (false) religious authority for black magic. A reference for a corrupt-cleric antagonist or a forbidden library prop.

title: Magic Circle of the Hours, *Heptameron*
creator: Peter de Abano (attrib.)
summary:
The signature magic circle of the *Heptameron*, the influential treatise of angel magic attributed to Peter de Abano (1250–1316), first printed in 1496.

## Iconography
The circle is remarkable for its layered complexity: the innermost ring bears the operator's space, the second ring names the angels of the day and hour, the third inscribes the name of the current season and its ruling angel, and the outermost ring cycles through the names of the winds and cardinal directions. Unlike the Goetic circle, which focuses on constraining dangerous spirits, the *Heptameron* circle is oriented toward angelic beneficence — it is an invitation to divine attendants, not a prison for demons.

## Significance
The *Heptameron* (so called for its seven-day structure) bridged medieval learned astral magic and the emerging Solomonic grimoire tradition. Its approach — invoking angels through their proper hours, days, and seasons — is rooted in the Arabic-derived *picatrix* tradition and influenced Agrippa's *De occulta philosophia*. The circle's architecture of concentric annuli encoding celestial time became a template for many subsequent conjuration circles.

## For artists & game designers
The *Heptameron* circle encodes a cosmological clock — concentric rings as nested temporal systems. A rich template for any game calendar or astral-time mechanic expressed visually.

title: Magic Circle, *Heptameron* (Variant Manuscript)
creator: Pseudo-Peter de Abano
summary:
A variant manuscript circle from the *Heptameron* tradition, showing the variability of the working diagram across manuscript copies.

## Iconography
The circle follows the general *Heptameron* structure — concentric rings bearing divine names and angelic designations — but shows the inevitable variations of manuscript transmission: different proportions, slightly different name placement, and the individual hand of the scribe. No two manuscript copies of a conjuration circle are exactly alike, and these variations are themselves a record of how magical knowledge circulated and mutated as it passed between hands.

## Significance
The *Heptameron* circle exists in dozens of manuscript variants, each a faithful-in-intent but variable-in-detail copy of the tradition. This variant illustrates the 'living manuscript' quality of magical texts: unlike printed books, each manuscript is an active intervention, with copyists correcting, updating, or elaborating the diagrams they transmit. The differences between variants are data about how the tradition was understood and modified at different times and places.

## For artists & game designers
Manuscript variants give a 'hand-copied' magic circle a plausible authenticity — slight imperfections, unusual proportions, marginal annotations all signal that this is a real working copy rather than a printed template.

title: Edward Kelly Raising a Ghost
creator: Robert Cross Smith 'Raphael' (publisher)
repository: Published: Robert Cross Smith, *The Astrologer of the Nineteenth Century* (London, 1825)
summary:
A 19th-century engraving of Edward Kelly raising a ghost, published in Robert Cross Smith's *Astrologer of the Nineteenth Century* (1825) — a lighter, more theatrical variant of the Sibly necromancy scene.

## Iconography
Kelley stands in a magic circle holding his wand toward a luminous apparition — a ghost or shade rising at his command. The scene is set at night in a churchyard, the standard setting for necromantic operations in the English popular imagination. The circle glows with a contained, protective light.

## Significance
This image from Smith's compendium recycles and perpetuates the Sibly tradition of the necromancer Kelley, fixing the scene as a stock image of English magical practice. Edward Kelley (1555–1597), John Dee's scryer, became the iconic necromancer in English popular memory — partly because of Sibly's influential engraving, partly because of the genuine strangeness of his relationship with Dee and the Enochian angel communications. Both Sibly's and Smith's versions of the Kelly necromancy scene were reproduced and adapted throughout the 19th century.

## For artists & game designers
A companion to the Sibly engraving — simpler composition, same iconic elements. The Kelly necromancy images are the primary source for the visual grammar of 'Western necromancer plus magic circle'.

title: Magic Circle from an Early *Key of Solomon* Manuscript
creator: Anonymous (English or Italian scribe)
summary:
A conjuration circle from one of the earliest manuscript witnesses to the *Key of Solomon*, the foundational text of the Western grimoire tradition.

## Iconography
The circle is a compact schematic: concentric rings bearing divine names in Latin, a central pentagram or hexagram, and radial divisions marking the quarters. The lettering is a mixture of Latin and Hebraic-style script, reflecting the text's claims to Hebraic antiquity. The diagram is characteristic of the working-copy tradition — meant to be reproduced on the floor or on parchment, not to be admired as art.

## Significance
The *Clavicula Salomonis* ('Little Key of Solomon') exists in hundreds of manuscript copies across Europe, each slightly different, each claiming to transmit the authentic circles and pentacles by which Solomon commanded spirits. This example captures the circle in its raw manuscript state, before the regularising influence of the print tradition. The divine names inscribed — drawn from Hebrew scripture, angelology, and the *Shem ha-Mephorash* — constitute its operative force: they compel the spirit's attendance and guarantee the operator's protection.

## For artists & game designers
A rawer, more hand-drawn aesthetic than the printed Goetia diagrams — useful when a grimoire prop needs to look like a working copy rather than a typeset edition.

title: Page from *Les Clavicules de R. Salomon* (Wellcome Collection, Vol. II)
creator: Anonymous (French scribe)
rights: CC BY 4.0. Via Wellcome Collection / Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A manuscript page from Volume II of *Les Clavicules de R. Salomon* (Wellcome Collection, MS L0073043) — a French 18th-century copy of the *Key of Solomon* tradition.

## Iconography
The folio shows the text of the *Clavicules* in elegant French handwriting, interspersed with diagrams or figures — magical characters, circles, or pentacle schematics woven into the instruction text. The French manuscript tradition of the *Clavicula* tends toward legible penmanship and decorated layouts, producing working books that are also objects of prestige.

## Significance
The Wellcome Collection's two-volume French *Clavicules de Salomon* represents the mainstream of 18th-century French occultism: the Solomonic tradition preserved in costly hand-copied manuscripts for aristocratic and bourgeois collectors as much as working magicians. Sir Henry Wellcome's collecting of such manuscripts — now accessible digitally through the Wellcome Library — has made this stratum of European occult culture newly visible to scholars. The *Clavicules* tradition in France produced some of the most elaborate and beautiful manuscript grimoires of the early modern period.

## For artists & game designers
A reference for the interior pages of a luxury grimoire — dense text and interspersed diagrams, in a calligraphic hand that signals education and refinement. The visual grammar of 'expensive forbidden knowledge'.

title: Magic Seals, Harley MS 5596 (c. 1450)
creator: Anonymous (English or continental scribe)
summary:
A folio of magic seals from Harley MS 5596, a 15th-century British Library manuscript remarkable for its striking visual similarity to later Icelandic magical staves (*galdrastafir*).

## Iconography
The page shows a series of linear, angular symbols — branching, intersecting lines without accompanying circles — that resemble the runic-derived stave patterns documented in 17th-century Icelandic magical manuscripts. Unlike the circular pentacles of the Solomonic tradition, these are linear marks, drawn on a page rather than inscribed in a ritual circle.

## Significance
Harley MS 5596 is a minor but important witness to the breadth of medieval English magical diagram traditions. The visual similarity to Icelandic galdrastafir suggests either a shared origin in a common European magical stave tradition or a parallel development of linear seal-forms independently of the circular Solomonic system. The Harley Collection, formed by Robert Harley (d. 1724) and his son Edward, contains numerous magical manuscripts that remain understudied relative to the more glamorous Sloane and Lansdowne collections.

## For artists & game designers
Linear stave-forms are visually distinct from circular pentacles — they look like runes or structural schematics rather than celestial diagrams. Useful for a 'northern' or 'runic' magic tradition within a world that also contains Solomonic circles.

title: Pentacle from the *Heptameron*, 1565 Edition
creator: Anonymous (attributed to Peter de Abano)
summary:
A pentacle diagram from the 1565 printed edition of the *Heptameron*, showing the characteristic woodcut style of early modern grimoire illustration.

## Iconography
The pentacle is a compact circular diagram with concentric rings and internal divisions — a geometric figure inscribed with names of God, angels, and sacred words in a mixture of Latin and pseudo-Hebrew. The woodcut medium imposes a crisp, high-contrast aesthetic: bold outlines, crosshatched shading, and the slight roughness of the relief-printed line. This was the visual vocabulary that readers of popular magical books in the 16th century would have recognised as authoritative.

## Significance
The 1565 edition of the *Heptameron* (printed alongside Agrippa's *Occult Philosophy* in many cases) reached an enormous audience and fixed the visual vocabulary of the magical circle for subsequent generations. The woodcut pentacle, cheap to reproduce and widely circulated, became the template for countless manuscript copies made by readers who traced or reinterpreted the printed designs. This is the printed grimoire circle at the moment of its greatest cultural dissemination.

## For artists & game designers
Woodcut grimoire diagrams have a distinctive aesthetic — bold, graphic, high-contrast — that reads differently from the fluid lines of manuscript circles. Useful for printed spellbook props or a 'popular magic' visual register.

title: Pentacles of Saturn (Plate II), *The Key of Solomon* (Mathers, 1888)
creator: Samuel Liddell MacGregor Mathers (ed.); source manuscripts 17th c.
repository: Published edition (Mathers, *The Key of Solomon the King*, 1888)
summary:
The Saturnian pentacles from Plate II of S. L. MacGregor Mathers's landmark 1888 edition of *The Key of Solomon the King*, the first scholarly English translation of the *Clavicula*.

## Iconography
The plate presents two or three Saturnian pentacles — circular diagrams bearing planetary symbols, Hebrew divine names, angelic signatures, and scriptural verses related to Saturn's domain of time, death, darkness, and binding. The Saturn pentacles of the *Key* are among the most severe in the collection: they govern the restraint of enemies, the prevention of access, and the compulsion of spirits associated with the underworld.

## Significance
Mathers's 1888 edition of the *Key of Solomon* was a watershed event for the English-speaking occult revival: for the first time, the Solomonic pentacles were available in a scholarly printed edition based on the British Library manuscripts. The book fed the Golden Dawn's ritual system directly — Mathers was a founding member — and through them influenced every subsequent Western ceremonial magic revival. The Saturnian pentacles carry the grimoire's most severe operations: binding, constraining, and compelling.

## For artists & game designers
Saturn pentacles encode themes of time, death, binding, and the underworld. In a tiered magic system, Saturnian imagery signals high-risk, binding-oriented operations distinct from the more beneficent planetary tiers.

title: Faust in His Study (Rembrandt, c. 1652)
creator: Rembrandt van Rijn
summary:
Rembrandt's famous etching (*c.* 1652) of a scholar in his study — traditionally called 'Doctor Faustus' or 'The Alchemist' — confronting a luminous magical disk inscribed with letters.

## Iconography
The scholar stands at his study window in the early morning, gazing at a glowing circular apparition that has materialised in the room. The disk bears a central monogram (INRI or AGLA) surrounded by a ring of Hebrew or Latin letters — a conjured emblem that appears to be the result of the figure's magical operations. His hands are raised in astonishment or invocation. The interplay of light — the dawn outside, the supernatural glow of the disk — is among Rembrandt's most refined chiaroscuro passages.

## Significance
The identification as 'Faust' is traditional but uncertain — the figure may be the alchemist or magus as generic type rather than the specific legend. What is certain is that Rembrandt has depicted the moment of magical appearance: the circle not as protective device but as apparition, materialising as a luminous, letter-inscribed disk in the practitioner's own space. The etching engages directly with the Paracelsian and Faustian imagery of the learned magician who summons and converses with spirits through inscribed symbols.

## For artists & game designers
Rembrandt's 'Faust' gives the magic circle its most sophisticated artistic treatment: not a floor diagram but an apparition, the circle itself as the spirit's body. A model for depicting conjuration as a scholarly encounter rather than a dramatic set-piece.

title: La Danse du Sabbat (The Sabbath Dance Circle)
creator: Emile Bayard (attrib.)
summary:
*La Danse du Sabbat* — the Sabbath Dance — a 19th-century French illustration of witches dancing in a ring around a demonic figure, representing the folk-demonological tradition of the magic circle as collective ritual space.

## Iconography
Witches of both sexes dance in a circle around a central diabolical figure — a demonic animal or horned being — with their backs turned toward the centre in the characteristic posture described in early modern demonology. The scene is set at night outdoors, lit by the uncanny light of the sabbath fire or the demon's presence. The circle here is not inscribed on the ground but constituted by the dancers' bodies — the ring as living geometry.

## Significance
The witches' sabbath circle is the demonic inversion of the Solomonic protective circle: where the conjurer's circle excluded dangerous spirits, the sabbath circle enclosed them. The tradition of a circular dance at the sabbath derives from early modern demonological treatises — the *Malleus Maleficarum*, Jean Bodin's *De la démonomanie* — which described the sabbath in terms adapted from popular festive customs and then demonised. 19th-century French illustrators like Bayard gave this tradition a romantic-macabre aesthetic that fed the occult revival's imagery of witchcraft.

## For artists & game designers
The sabbath circle is the folk-magic alternative to the grimoire circle: not inscribed and geometric but constituted by bodies in motion. A visual counterpart to the scholarly Solomonic system — useful for a coven-based or populist magic tradition.

title: Edward Kelly Invoking the Spirit of a Deceased Person (Ebenezer Sibly)
creator: Engraved by Ames of Bristol (after Ebenezer Sibly)
repository: Published: Ebenezer Sibly, *A New and Complete Illustration of the Occult Sciences* (c. 1790)
summary:
Ebenezer Sibly's famous engraving of Edward Kelly (Kelley) invoking the spirit of a deceased person, from *A New and Complete Illustration of the Occult Sciences* (c. 1790) — the most influential visual representation of necromancy in British popular culture.

## Iconography
Kelley and a companion (traditionally identified as John Dee) stand within a glowing magic circle in a churchyard at night, holding wands and lanterns, as a swathed spirit rises from the ground before them. A corpse is visible in the background, and the scene is lit with a lurid supernal light. The circle is inscribed and appears luminous — a zone of safety amid the dangerous contact with the dead.

## Significance
Ebenezer Sibly (1751–1800) was an English physician and occultist who published his enormous encyclopaedic *Illustration of the Occult Sciences* (1787–1793) at the height of popular interest in magic and astrology. His engraving of Kelley's graveyard necromancy is the source image for virtually every subsequent popular depiction of the British necromancer: circle on the ground, wand in hand, corpse nearby, spirit rising. The image fused the respectable Dee-and-Kelley Elizabethan occult legacy with the lurid graveyard necromancy tradition to create an enduring national myth.

## For artists & game designers
The definitive 'necromancy scene' in the British tradition: circle, wand, corpse, ghost, night. Every element that makes necromancy visually legible is present and correctly staged.

title: The Antikythera mechanism (main fragment)
work: Cosmic Machines: Astronomical Clocks & Planetary Mechanisms
creator: Anonymous (Hellenistic Greek); photograph by Joyofmuseums
place: National Archaeological Museum, Athens (found off Antikythera)
rights: CC BY-SA 4.0 (photo: Joyofmuseums). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
The largest surviving fragment ('Fragment A') of the Antikythera mechanism, a Hellenistic geared device recovered in 1901 from a shipwreck off the island of Antikythera and now in the National Archaeological Museum, Athens.

## Iconography
What survives is a mass of corroded **bronze gear-wheels** fused into a lump, with the teeth of one large wheel clearly visible. X-ray and CT imaging have revealed at least thirty interlocking gears and inscriptions. Reconstructions show it as a hand-cranked box whose dials displayed the **lunisolar calendar**, the phase and position of the Moon, the dates of **eclipses** (via the Saros and Exeligmos cycles), the Metonic cycle, and probably the motions of the planets and the timing of the Panhellenic games.

## Significance
The Antikythera mechanism is the oldest known analogue computer and the direct ancestor of the medieval astronomical clock: proof that the Greeks could embody astronomical *theory* in gearwork. Its sophistication was so unexpected that it reshaped the history of ancient technology (work by Derek de Solla Price, and the modern Antikythera Mechanism Research Project).

## For artists & game designers
A corroded green lump that turns out to be a precision computer is the perfect 'ancient impossible artefact' — its mundane ruin is exactly what makes the reveal land.

citations.text: D. de Solla Price, *Gears from the Greeks* (1974).
T. Freeth et al., 'Decoding the Antikythera Mechanism', *Nature* (2006).

title: Brass astronomical compendium / pocket instrument
work: Cosmic Machines: Astronomical Clocks & Planetary Mechanisms
creator: Anonymous instrument-maker; photograph by Rosie Summers
summary:
A small engraved brass instrument of the kind carried as a portable **astronomical compendium** — a pocket case combining several instruments on hinged leaves.

## Iconography
The piece is built around a finely **engraved brass dial** with a graduated rim and a magnetic compass for orientation. Compendia of this type typically fold open to reveal, on successive leaves, a portable **sundial** (often with a string gnomon), a list of city latitudes, a lunar volvelle for converting Sun-time to Moon-time at night, a wind-rose, and a table of the zodiac — the whole sky-reckoning kit of a Renaissance traveller in one brass box.

## Significance
The astronomical compendium is the personal, portable cousin of the great fixed clocks: where the cathedral clock modelled the heavens for a whole city, the compendium let one well-off owner reckon time, latitude and the [[motif:zodiac-signs|zodiac]] anywhere. Such objects (Augsburg and Nuremberg were the great centres) blur instrument, status-symbol and curio.

## For artists & game designers
A brass box that unfolds into five different instruments is a compact 'multi-tool' object — each leaf a different mini-mechanic the player can flip to.

citations.text: G. L'E. Turner, *Elizabethan Instrument Makers* (2000).

title: Volvelle from Apian's Astronomicum Caesareum (1540)
work: Cosmic Machines: Astronomical Clocks & Planetary Mechanisms
creator: Petrus Apianus (Peter Apian)
rights: Public domain. Via Wikimedia Commons (Houghton Library).
summary:
A leaf (f. 2r) of Petrus Apianus's *Astronomicum Caesareum*, printed at Ingolstadt in 1540 — one of the most lavish scientific books ever produced, here in the Houghton Library copy.

## Iconography
The page is dominated by a **volvelle**: layered, hand-coloured paper discs pinned at the center and fitted with silk threads and tiny seed-pearl markers, which the reader rotates to read off astronomical quantities. Apian's volvelles function as **paper equatoria** and computers — set the discs for a date and they give the geocentric longitude of a planet, the phase of the Moon, the time of an eclipse, or the position of the lunar dragon's head and tail.

## Significance
The *Astronomicum Caesareum*, dedicated to the Emperor Charles V (hence 'Caesarean'), is the high-water mark of the printed astronomical instrument: it puts a working planetary calculator into the hands of a reader who owns no brass. It belongs to the same impulse as the great clocks — to make the [[motif:planetary-motion|motions of the planets]] mechanically obtainable — but achieves it in paper and thread.

## For artists & game designers
A book whose pages are working machines (spin the disc, read the fate) is a tactile model for an in-game grimoire that is also a tool, not just lore text.

citations.text: O. Gingerich, 'Apianus's Astronomicum Caesareum', *Journal for the History of Astronomy* (1971).

title: Dials of the Besançon astronomical clock
work: Cosmic Machines: Astronomical Clocks & Planetary Mechanisms
creator: Auguste-Lucien Vérité (1858–60); photograph by PCouton
rights: CC BY-SA 4.0 (photo: PCouton). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
An array of dials on the astronomical clock of Besançon Cathedral, built 1858–60 by Auguste-Lucien Vérité.

## Iconography
The clock is a cabinet of some **70 dials and indicators** distributed over a tall neo-Gothic case. They report not only the hour but the **tides** at major French ports, the rising and setting of Sun and Moon, the lengths of day and night, the movements of the **planets**, eclipses, leap years and a perpetual calendar. Small **automata** representing the Resurrection and the days of the week animate at intervals.

## Significance
Besançon (Vérité also built the comparable Beauvais clock) is the 19th-century culmination of the cathedral-clock idea: an industrial-age machine that gathers astronomy, tide-tables and the liturgical calendar into one devotional instrument. It belongs to a moment when precision clockwork could finally *compute* the heavens it had long only symbolised.

## For artists & game designers
Seventy dials on one cabinet is a design lesson in information density — a single object that rewards close reading because every face tells a different truth.

title: The mechanism of the Eise Eisinga Planetarium, Franeker
work: Cosmic Machines: Astronomical Clocks & Planetary Mechanisms
creator: Eise Eisinga (1774–1781); photograph by Vera de Kok
rights: CC BY-SA 3.0 (photo: Vera de Kok). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
The driving mechanism, mounted in the attic above the living-room ceiling, of the Eise Eisinga Planetarium in Franeker — the oldest working planetarium in the world, built by the wool-comber Eise Eisinga between 1774 and 1781.

## Iconography
The photograph shows the **wooden gear-train** of hand-cut oak wheels, driving-weights and a pendulum clock that powers the display. On the ceiling of the room below, gilded discs representing the **planets** ride in grooved tracks across a painted sky, moving in real time to scale; pointers give the date, the phase of the Moon, the signs of the zodiac and the hour.

## Significance
Eisinga built his **heliocentric** orrery partly to calm neighbours panicked by a 1774 pamphlet predicting that a planetary conjunction would destroy the Earth — a machine made to answer astrological dread with Newtonian order. It is the supreme survival of the domestic planetarium and a monument to Enlightenment self-education: a labourer's living room rebuilt as a model of the solar system.

## For artists & game designers
A secret machine-room above a humble parlour, full of slowly turning wooden gears that move the painted heavens below, is an irresistible set-piece for a hidden-mechanism reveal.

citations.text: A. van der Werf, *Eise Eisinga's Planetarium* (1981).

title: Model of the Lund Cathedral astronomical clock (Horologium mirabile)
work: Cosmic Machines: Astronomical Clocks & Planetary Mechanisms
creator: Model after the medieval clock; built under Theodor Wåhlin, c. 1913
rights: CC0 (public domain dedication). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A model (made c. 1913, in connection with the restoration overseen by Theodor Wåhlin) of the *Horologium mirabile Lundense*, the astronomical clock of Lund Cathedral, originally built around 1424.

## Iconography
The clock has two faces. The upper **astronomical dial** is an astrolabe showing the hours, the [[motif:zodiac-signs|zodiac]], and the positions of Sun and Moon over a fixed Earth; mechanical **knights** clash above it. The lower **calendar dial** is a vast computus disc for finding the dates of Easter and the feasts. At noon and 3 p.m. the **Magi** process before the Virgin and Child while the organ pipes play *In dulci jubilo*.

## Significance
Lund's medieval clock — rediscovered and reconstructed in the early 20th century — is the great Scandinavian survivor of the type. The byname *Horologium mirabile* ('the wonderful clock') captures the medieval reception of these machines as marvels at the edge of the miraculous.

## For artists & game designers
The paired dials — one for the sky, one for the calendar — are a clean two-screen UI metaphor: 'where the stars are' versus 'what day it is'.

citations.text: A. Ungerer, *Les Horloges astronomiques et monumentales* (1931).
Wikimedia Commons

title: The astronomical clock of Lyon Cathedral
work: Cosmic Machines: Astronomical Clocks & Planetary Mechanisms
creator: Medieval, much rebuilt (14th–17th c.); photograph by Zairon
rights: CC BY-SA 4.0 (photo: Zairon). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
The astronomical clock in the north transept of the Primatiale Saint-Jean-Baptiste in Lyon, one of the oldest in Europe, its origins medieval and the present case largely 17th-century.

## Iconography
Within a tall painted Gothic case an **astrolabe dial** shows the positions of Sun, Moon and stars over Lyon and an ecclesiastical calendar good for movable feasts to the 2nd millennium's end. On the hour an **Annunciation** plays out above — God the Father, doves and angels move, a **rooster** at the summit beats its wings and crows three times.

## Significance
Lyon's clock is among the earliest astronomical clocks of France, repeatedly rebuilt (notably after damage in the Wars of Religion). Like its peers it married the *computus* — the church's calculation of Easter — to an astrolabe model of the sky, turning the cathedral transept into an observatory of sacred time.

## For artists & game designers
The crowing automaton rooster is a recurring motif across these clocks; as a sound-cue it makes a memorable, diegetic 'the hour has turned' signal.

citations.text: A. Ungerer, *Les Horloges astronomiques et monumentales* (1931).

title: The astronomical clock of Münster Cathedral
work: Cosmic Machines: Astronomical Clocks & Planetary Mechanisms
creator: Dietrich Tzwyvel & Nikolaus Windemaker (1540–43); photograph by Dietmar Rabich
rights: CC BY-SA 4.0 (photo: Dietmar Rabich). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
The astronomical clock in the ambulatory of St Paul's Cathedral, Münster, built 1540–43 after the destruction of an earlier clock in the 1534 Anabaptist rising.

## Iconography
The richly painted face turns **anticlockwise**. A large central dial maps the positions of the **planets** in the zodiac on a geocentric scheme, surrounded by painted panels of the [[motif:zodiac-signs|signs]], the planetary gods and a learned border of astronomical figures. Below runs a perpetual calendar reaching to 2071. On the hour the **Three Magi** and a servant bow before the Virgin and Child while a carillon plays.

## Significance
Münster's clock is a Renaissance encyclopaedia of the sky painted in brilliant colour: a teaching machine that shows where every planet stands among the stars on any day. Its anticlockwise motion follows the apparent westward drift of the heavens — a learned choice that turns the whole face into a slow image of the turning firmament.

## For artists & game designers
An anticlockwise clock is a small uncanny detail that signals 'this place keeps time by older, stranger rules' without a word of exposition.

citations.text: E. Zinner, *Deutsche und niederländische astronomische Instrumente* (1956).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Nocturnal by Erasmus Habermel, Prague c. 1600
work: Cosmic Machines: Astronomical Clocks & Planetary Mechanisms
creator: Erasmus Habermel; photograph by Daderot
summary:
A brass **nocturnal** made by the master instrument-maker Erasmus Habermel in Prague around 1600, now in the Mathematisch-Physikalischer Salon, Dresden.

## Iconography
The nocturnal is a hand-held disc with a central **sighting hole** and a long rotating arm. To use it one sights **Polaris** through the hole, sets an outer ring to the date, then swings the arm onto the **pointer stars of the Big Dipper** (or Little Dipper); the arm's position against the hour-scale gives the time. Habermel's piece is finely engraved and pierced in the Mannerist court style of Rudolf II's Prague.

## Significance
The nocturnal turns the slow rotation of the [[motif:celestial-mechanism|circumpolar sky]] into a clock you carry: the heavens themselves are the moving part, the instrument merely reads them. Made for Rudolf II's celebrated court of astronomers and alchemists, it links the world of practical star-time to the same milieu that produced the Prague Orloj and the imperial astrological enterprise.

## For artists & game designers
A pocket device that requires you to find a real star before it works ties an in-game tool to the actual night sky — a satisfying loop of look-up-then-read.

citations.text: R.J.W. Evans, *Rudolf II and His World* (1973).
Wikimedia Commons

title: The astronomical clock of Olomouc (historical postcard)
work: Cosmic Machines: Astronomical Clocks & Planetary Mechanisms
creator: Anonymous (postcard); medieval clock, much altered
date: clock 15th c., rebuilt; postcard early 20th c.
summary:
A historical postcard of the astronomical clock set into the tower of the Town Hall of Olomouc in Moravia, showing the clock as it appeared before its 20th-century remodelling.

## Iconography
The tall niche holds an **astrolabe-type dial** of the heavens above a **calendar dial**, framed by Gothic tracery and ranks of painted and sculpted figures — saints, allegories and craftsmen. The postcard preserves a religious, late-medieval iconography that the present clock (rebuilt in a Socialist-Realist style in 1955, with mosaic workers replacing the saints) no longer shows.

## Significance
Olomouc belongs to the Central European family of civic astronomical clocks alongside Prague, displaying the same marriage of [[motif:astrolabe-dial|astrolabe]] and calendar on a town-hall façade. The image is valuable precisely as a record of a lost state: a reminder that these 'eternal' machines are repeatedly remade in the image of the regimes that own them.

## For artists & game designers
A before/after pair (sacred clock vs. its ideological rebuild) is a ready-made environmental-storytelling device about who controls public time.

citations.text: A. Ungerer, *Les Horloges astronomiques et monumentales* (1931).
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Salone of the Palazzo della Ragione, Padua
work: Cosmic Machines: Astronomical Clocks & Planetary Mechanisms
creator: Astrological fresco cycle after Pietro d'Abano (14th c.; repainted by Niccolò Miretto, 15th c.); photograph by Armin Kleiner
rights: CC BY-SA 4.0 (photo: Armin Kleiner). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
The interior of the *Salone*, the immense first-floor hall of the Palazzo della Ragione in Padua, whose walls carry one of the largest astrological fresco cycles of the Middle Ages.

## Iconography
Under a vast keel-shaped wooden vault the walls are divided into hundreds of panels arranged as a great **astrological calendar**: the twelve [[motif:zodiac-signs|signs]] of the zodiac, their associated **decans** and planetary rulers, the **labours of the months**, apostles and saints, all keyed to a now-lost program devised by the physician-astrologer **Pietro d'Abano**. The cycle was repainted by Niccolò Miretto and assistants after a fire of 1420.

## Significance
The Salone is a building turned into a cosmic machine: a civic court of justice roofed over with the whole working astrology of the year, so that human law sat literally beneath the rule of the stars. With the Hall of the Months at Schifanoia (Ferrara), it is the supreme monumental survival of medieval astrological iconography, much studied since Aby Warburg.

## For artists & game designers
A single room whose walls *are* the calendar — every panel a date and its ruling power — is a model for a 'hub' space that doubles as the game's almanac.

citations.text: A. Warburg, 'Italian Art and International Astrology' (1912).
Wikimedia Commons

title: The calendar dial of the Prague Orloj
work: Cosmic Machines: Astronomical Clocks & Planetary Mechanisms
creator: Calendar plate after Josef Mánes (1865); photograph by George Groutas
rights: CC BY 2.0 (photo: George Groutas). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
The lower, calendar dial of the Prague Orloj, set beneath the astronomical face. The painted disc rotates once a year.

## Iconography
A great circular plate carries, in concentric rings, the 365 days of the year with their **saints' names**, the twelve [[motif:zodiac-signs|signs of the zodiac]], and twelve medallions of the **Labours of the Months** — agricultural and seasonal scenes (the present paintings are a 19th-century medallion cycle after the Czech painter Josef Mánes, the original now in a museum). At the very center are the arms of Prague's Old Town. Gilded figures of a chronicler, an angel, an astronomer and a philosopher flank the dial.

## Significance
Where the upper dial maps the *sky*, the calendar dial maps the *year* as lived on Earth: the liturgical round of feast days bound to the turning of the zodiac and the rhythm of the fields. Together the two faces present the medieval cosmos as one geared whole, sacred time and star-time on a single wall.

## For artists & game designers
The Labours-of-the-Months ring is a compact visual calendar of seasonal activity — useful shorthand for a farming or festival cycle in a game year.

citations.text: Z. Horský, *The Prague Astronomical Clock* (1988).
Wikimedia Commons

title: The astronomical dial of the Prague Orloj
work: Cosmic Machines: Astronomical Clocks & Planetary Mechanisms
creator: Mikuláš of Kadaň & Jan Šindel (1410); later restorers; photograph by Godot13
rights: CC BY-SA 4.0 (photo: Godot13). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
The astronomical dial of the Prague Orloj, the oldest astronomical clock still in operation, mounted on the south wall of the Old Town Hall and first installed in 1410.

## Iconography
The dial is a working **astrolabe** projected onto the clock face. A fixed background shows the Earth at the center, the blue sky, and the orange band of night; a rotating golden [[motif:zodiac-ring|zodiac ring]] carries the ecliptic. Three hands track the **Sun**, the **Moon** (a sphere that turns to show its phase), and the stars. Concentric scales give the time in several systems at once — Central European, Old Bohemian (counted from sunset), Babylonian (unequal day-hours), and sidereal star-time.

## Significance
The Orloj is the supreme survival of the medieval conviction that the cosmos is a [[motif:celestial-mechanism|machine]] and that machine can be re-built in brass. Its design is credited to the astronomer Jan Šindel with the clockmaker Mikuláš of Kadaň; the figures of Death and the procession of the Apostles were added later. It fuses astronomy, astrology and memento-mori theatre on a single face.

## For artists & game designers
A single dial that reports four different time-systems at once is a beautiful model for an in-world clock that means different things to different cultures sharing one city.

citations.text: Z. Horský, *The Prague Astronomical Clock* (1988).

title: Detail of the Strasbourg Cathedral astronomical clock
work: Cosmic Machines: Astronomical Clocks & Planetary Mechanisms
creator: Jean-Baptiste Schwilgué (1842 mechanism); photograph by Tangopaso
summary:
Detail of the celebrated astronomical clock in the south transept of Strasbourg Cathedral — the third clock on the site, the mechanism rebuilt by Jean-Baptiste Schwilgué and completed in 1842.

## Iconography
The towering painted Renaissance case (its decoration from the 1571–74 clock) frames a stack of indicators: a perpetual ecclesiastical **calendar** computing the movable feasts, dials for the **planets** in their geocentric order, a globe of the Moon's phases, and a small orrery. Carved and gilded **automata** perform — the Ages of Man pass before Death who strikes the hours, a cock crows, and at noon the Apostles process before Christ.

## Significance
Strasbourg's clock is the grand baroque heir to the cathedral-clock tradition: a single machine made to compute the date of Easter forever, to model the heavens, and to preach the brevity of life. Schwilgué's 1842 *comput ecclésiastique* is a famous early mechanical calculator. The clock fascinated visitors as proof that the universe could be wound up and made to run.

## For artists & game designers
A machine whose whole purpose is to compute one shifting date (Easter) forever is a wonderful quest object — a device that answers a question no human can hold in their head.

citations.text: H. Bach & J.-P. Rieb, *Les Trois Horloges Astronomiques de la Cathédrale de Strasbourg* (1992).

title: The torquetum of Regiomontanus (engraving)
work: Cosmic Machines: Astronomical Clocks & Planetary Mechanisms
creator: After Johannes Regiomontanus / Petrus Apianus tradition; engraving reproduced via DPLA
summary:
An engraving of the **torquetum**, a medieval and Renaissance observing instrument here associated with the astronomer Regiomontanus.

## Iconography
The torquetum is built as a stack of **inclined graduated discs**, each plane representing one of the great coordinate systems of the sky — the **horizon**, the **celestial equator**, and the **ecliptic** — hinged so that an observer can pass a measured position from one system to another by mechanical reading rather than calculation. A plumb-line and sighting alidades complete it. The engraving labels the parts in the manner of a Renaissance instrument-book.

## Significance
The torquetum is a three-dimensional model of the heavens' geometry: it physically embodies the transformations between ecliptic, equatorial and horizon coordinates that astronomers otherwise did by spherical trigonometry. Described by Bernard of Verdun and Peter Apian's *Astronomicum Caesareum*, it stands between the [[motif:astrolabe-dial|astrolabe]] and the great clocks as a tool that *computes the sky's geometry* by turning brass.

## For artists & game designers
An instrument whose nested tilted rings literally are the planes of the sky is gorgeous, legible machinery — ideal for an astronomer-character's desk or a puzzle of 'align the rings'.

citations.text: E. Zinner, *Regiomontanus: His Life and Work* (trans. 1990).

title: Zodiac and dial of the Torre dell'Orologio, Venice
work: Cosmic Machines: Astronomical Clocks & Planetary Mechanisms
creator: Gian Paolo & Gian Carlo Rainieri (1493–99); photograph by Zairon
rights: CC BY-SA 4.0 (photo: Zairon). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
The great enamelled clock face of the Torre dell'Orologio above the entrance to the Merceria on the Piazza San Marco, built 1493–99 by Gian Paolo and Gian Carlo Rainieri.

## Iconography
A disc of deep **blue and gold** carries an outer ring of 24 Roman hour-numerals, an inner ring of the twelve [[motif:zodiac-signs|zodiac signs]], and at the center the **Earth** with the **Sun** riding a golden pointer around it. The phase of the **Moon** is shown by a revolving half-gilt sphere. Above the dial stand a winged Lion of St Mark and, on the terrace, the two bronze **Moors** who strike the bell.

## Significance
The Venetian clock fused civic pride, navigation and astrology: a merchant republic announcing that it kept time by the same stars its ships sailed under. The zodiacal dial let any passer-by read the Sun's place in the ecliptic — astrology as public utility. The bronze Mori striking the hours became one of Venice's signature spectacles.

## For artists & game designers
The blue-and-gold celestial dial is an instantly readable shorthand for 'a city that measures itself against the heavens' — strong establishing-shot iconography.

citations.text: G. Brusa, *L'Orologio della Torre di San Marco* (1999).

title: The astronomical clock of Wells Cathedral
work: Cosmic Machines: Astronomical Clocks & Planetary Mechanisms
creator: Medieval (c. 1390, dial); photograph by Tilman2007
rights: CC BY-SA 4.0 (photo: Tilman2007). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
The astronomical clock of Wells Cathedral, one of the oldest surviving clock faces in the world, the dial dating to around 1390.

## Iconography
The great painted dial presents an explicitly **geocentric** universe. The Earth sits at the center; the Sun-hand and a separate ball showing the **phases of the Moon** travel around a 24-hour ring numbered twice (I–XII, I–XII). An inner dial counts the **minutes**, and another shows the age of the Moon in days. Above the dial, on the quarters, jousting knights spin in a tournament while a figure called **Jack Blandifers** kicks bells with his heels.

## Significance
Wells embodies the late-medieval clock as a working model of the [[motif:ptolemaic-universe|Ptolemaic cosmos]] — the heavens turning about a fixed Earth, made visible and audible to a congregation. The original mechanism survives (now in the Science Museum, London) and is among the earliest geared clocks anywhere; the dial here is a faithful replacement of the medieval face.

## For artists & game designers
The combat automaton — knights endlessly jousting on the hour — is a tidy idea: a clock whose moving parts are a frozen story replayed forever.

citations.text: C.F.C. Beeson, *English Church Clocks 1280–1850* (1971).

title: The Hampton Court astronomical (zodiac) clock
work: Cosmic Machines: Astronomical Clocks & Planetary Mechanisms
creator: Nicholas Oursian (1540, for Henry VIII); photograph by Mike Cattell
rights: CC BY 2.0 (photo: Mike Cattell). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
The astronomical clock in the Anne Boleyn Gateway of Hampton Court Palace, made in 1540 by Nicholas Oursian for Henry VIII.

## Iconography
The great **blue-and-gold dial** shows, on a fixed Earth at the center, the **Sun** travelling through the twelve [[motif:zodiac-signs|zodiac signs]] and the 365 days of the year, the **phase and age of the Moon**, and — uniquely useful to a riverside court — the time of **high water at London Bridge**, which governed when one could travel to the city by barge. Its scheme is frankly **pre-Copernican**, the Sun circling the Earth.

## Significance
The Hampton Court clock is a rare survival of a Tudor astronomical dial in situ, a court instrument that read at a glance both the heavens and the tides. As a practical-astrology object it shows the genre at its most worldly: the cosmos consulted not for prophecy but for catching the next boat.

## For artists & game designers
A celestial clock whose killer feature is a tide-table is a lovely reminder that 'cosmic' instruments earned their keep with mundane utility — good texture for a grounded fantasy court.

citations.text: C.F.C. Beeson, *English Church Clocks 1280–1850* (1971).

title: Geocentric Universe of the Spheres, Apian's *Cosmographia*
creator: Petrus Apianus (Peter Apian)
summary:
A diagram of the geocentric cosmos from Peter Apian's *Cosmographia*, the immensely popular Renaissance handbook of astronomy and geography.

## Iconography
The earth, with its concentric shells of water, air, and fire, sits at the centre. Around it run the spheres of the seven planets (Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn), then the sphere of the fixed stars marked with the zodiac, the crystalline heavens, the *primum mobile*, and the outermost **Empyrean** of God and the elect.

## Significance
Apian's *Cosmographia* (first ed. 1524), later revised by Gemma Frisius, codified the Ptolemaic [[motif:celestial spheres|sphere model]] for generations of students and was famous for its movable paper *volvelles*. The nested-spheres image is the standard Renaissance picture of the universe just before the Copernican turn — a finite, ordered, God-crowned cosmos.

## For artists & game designers
The canonical 'orrery of nested spheres' — a clean template for a star-map UI or a layered cosmology screen.

citations.text: Peter Apian, *Cosmographia* (1524; rev. Gemma Frisius).
S. K. Heninger, *The Cosmographical Glass: Renaissance Diagrams of the Universe* (1977).

title: Cover and volvelle apparatus, Apian's *Cosmographia* (Cosmograph.)
creator: Petrus Apianus & Gemma Frisius
summary:
A page from an edition of Apian's *Cosmographia* (here in the Latin *Cosmograph.*, with Gemma Frisius), the cosmographic handbook celebrated for its working paper instruments.

## Iconography
The leaf presents the cosmographic apparatus of the book — its framed title and the rotating-disc *volvelles* by which the reader computes positions of sun, moon, and stars, finds latitudes, and tells time. The printed circles are designed to be cut and pinned so the diagram becomes a literal calculating machine.

## Significance
The [[motif:volvelle|volvelle]] — a paper instrument of nested rotating discs — was a Renaissance speciality, and Apian's *Cosmographia* is its most famous showcase. These movable diagrams turn cosmology into computation, embodying the period's conviction that the heavens are governed by a knowable, calculable order. Gemma Frisius's revisions made the work a European standard for decades.

## For artists & game designers
A paper-machine aesthetic: pinned rotating dials that turn a static diagram into an interactive astronomical computer.

citations.text: Peter Apian, *Cosmographia*, rev. Gemma Frisius (16th c.).
Suzanne Karr Schmidt, *Interactive and Sculptural Printmaking in the Renaissance* (2017).

title: Byrhtferth's Diagram (the harmony of the months, elements, and seasons)
creator: Byrhtferth of Ramsey
summary:
A version of Byrhtferth's diagram, the great computistic schema correlating the four elements, four cardinal directions, four seasons, solstices and equinoxes, ages of man, and the letters of Adam's name.

## Iconography
The page is organized as nested lozenges and circles. At the centre stand the four elements — fire, air, water, earth — each tied to its qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) and to a cardinal point, a season, a solstice or equinox, and a humour. The outer frame carries the twelve signs and the two solstice/equinox axes, binding the year and the world into one balanced tetradic figure.

## Significance
Byrhtferth of Ramsey (fl. c. 986–1016) composed his *Enchiridion* as a teaching manual for computus, the reckoning of time. The diagram is the visual heart of that work: an argument that the same fourfold harmony — the doctrine of [[motif:four elements|the four elements]] and their qualities — governs the cosmos, the year, and the human body. It is among the earliest and most influential English microcosm–macrocosm figures.

## For artists & game designers
A self-contained elemental-correspondence wheel: four elements × qualities × seasons × directions, ideal for an alchemy or affinity system.

citations.text: Byrhtferth, *Enchiridion*, ed. Peter S. Baker & Michael Lapidge (EETS, 1995).
Faith Wallis, 'Byrhtferth's Diagram,' in *Medieval Manuscripts and the Order of Knowledge*.

title: The Ptolemaic System, Cellarius *Harmonia Macrocosmica*
creator: Andreas Cellarius (engr. Jan van Loon)
summary:
The plate of the Ptolemaic (geocentric) system from Andreas Cellarius's *Harmonia Macrocosmica* (1660), the most lavish celestial atlas of the baroque age.

## Iconography
A central earth is encircled by the spheres of the Moon, the planets, and the Sun, ringed by the band of the **zodiac** and the firmament, all rendered in vivid colour and hung about with putti, astronomers, and decorative cartouches. The scheme is the classical Ptolemaic order of nested heavens, presented as a single harmonious machine.

## Significance
Cellarius's atlas displays the competing world-systems of the seventeenth century — Ptolemaic, Copernican, and Tychonic — as grand allegorical plates. The geocentric plate preserves the ancient picture of [[motif:celestial spheres|concentric heavens]] even as the Copernican revolution was overtaking it; the very title, *Harmonia Macrocosmica*, asserts the old conviction that the macrocosm is an ordered harmony. Engraved by Jan van Loon, published by Johannes Janssonius.

## For artists & game designers
A richly ornamented cosmology poster — the gold standard for a 'baroque star atlas' visual treatment.

citations.text: Andreas Cellarius, *Harmonia Macrocosmica* (Amsterdam, 1660–61).
Robert van Gent, *The Celestial Atlas of Andreas Cellarius* (2006).
