title: *Anima Mundi* / Integrae Naturae, Robert Fludd's macrocosm
creator: Robert Fludd
summary:
The famous *Integrae Naturae Speculum* / *Anima Mundi* engraving from Robert Fludd's *Utriusque Cosmi Historia* (1617), depicting the whole macrocosm as a chained order under God.

## Iconography
A naked female figure — **Natura**, the world-soul — stands upon the elemental and mineral earth, her head among the stars; one hand is chained to the cloud-borne hand of God above, the other holds a chain leading down to an ape (*ars*, art/the human) seated upon the globe. Concentric bands rise from minerals, plants, and animals through the planetary spheres and the angelic hierarchies to the divine name at the summit.

## Significance
Fludd (1574–1637), the great English Paracelsian and Rosicrucian apologist, makes this the frontispiece-statement of his system: nature is God's intermediary, art is the 'ape of nature,' and the cosmos is a single chained continuum from matter to deity — a Hermetic fusion of the [[motif:great chain of being|Great Chain]] with the [[motif:anima mundi|world-soul]]. It is among the most reproduced of all esoteric cosmological images.

## For artists & game designers
A vertical 'world-soul' axis linking God, Nature, and human Art by literal chains — a striking cosmology splash or progression spine.

citations.text: Robert Fludd, *Utriusque Cosmi … Historia* (Oppenheim, 1617–21).
Joscelyn Godwin, *Robert Fludd: Hermetic Philosopher and Surveyor of Two Worlds* (1979).

title: The Great Chain of Being (*scala naturae*), Diego Valadés
creator: Diego Valadés (Didacus Valades)
summary:
A *scala naturae* or Great Chain of Being from Diego Valadés's *Rhetorica Christiana* (1579), arranging all creation as a graded ladder.

## Iconography
A vertical ladder or chain ascends from inanimate matter at the foot — minerals and the elements — upward through plants, animals, and humankind, then through the angelic orders, to God at the summit. Each rung is a degree of being and perfection; the whole is a single continuous hierarchy from the basest body to the divine.

## Significance
The Great Chain of Being is one of the most durable structures of Western cosmology: the idea, traced by A. O. Lovejoy, that the universe is a full, continuous, and graded hierarchy of forms. Rooted in Plato and Aristotle and elaborated by Neoplatonism and scholasticism, it dominated medieval and Renaissance thought about [[motif:hierarchy|cosmic order]]. Valadés, a Franciscan of mixed Spanish-Indigenous descent, printed this influential version to teach the order of creation.

## For artists & game designers
A literal vertical hierarchy of being — usable as a progression ladder, a moral alignment axis, or a cosmology of tiers.

citations.text: Arthur O. Lovejoy, *The Great Chain of Being* (1936).
Diego Valadés, *Rhetorica Christiana* (Perugia, 1579).

title: The Cosmic Man, Hildegard of Bingen, *Liber Divinorum Operum*
creator: Hildegard of Bingen (school of)
summary:
The cosmic-man vision opening Hildegard of Bingen's *Liber Divinorum Operum* (Book of Divine Works), in which a human figure is set at the centre of the wheeling universe.

## Iconography
A standing human figure stands with arms outstretched at the centre of a series of concentric rings — bands of fire, ether, air, and water studded with stars, planets, and the heads of the winds blowing from the cosmic circumference. Above and behind, a vast red figure (Caritas, divine Love) embraces the whole wheel. The body of the inner man is dimensioned to the cosmos: its limbs reach to the elemental zones.

## Significance
The image is the classic medieval statement of [[motif:microcosm-macrocosm|microcosm and macrocosm]] — that the human being is a 'little world' whose proportions answer to the structure of the great one. Hildegard (1098–1179) frames it theologically: the cosmos and the body are bound together in God's love. The composition descends from late-antique and Carolingian cosmic diagrams and looks forward to the Renaissance Vitruvian and Fluddian cosmic men.

## For artists & game designers
A ready cosmology screen: concentric elemental rings with a player-figure at the hub, wind-heads marking the cardinal directions.

citations.text: Barbara Newman, *Sister of Wisdom: St. Hildegard's Theology of the Feminine* (1987).
Hildegard of Bingen, *Liber Divinorum Operum*, ed. A. Derolez & P. Dronke (CCCM 92, 1996).

title: Philosophy and the Seven Liberal Arts, *Hortus Deliciarum*
creator: Herrad of Landsberg
summary:
The wheel of Philosophy and the Seven Liberal Arts from the *Hortus Deliciarum* (Garden of Delights), compiled by Herrad of Landsberg for the nuns of Hohenburg.

## Iconography
A crowned **Philosophia** is enthroned at the centre of a great circle, with the springs of wisdom issuing from her. Around her, in seven arched compartments, sit the personified liberal arts — Grammar, Rhetoric, Dialectic, Music, Arithmetic, Geometry, Astronomy — each with her tools. Socrates and Plato write below; poets and magicians, inspired by 'unclean spirits,' are cast outside the holy circle.

## Significance
The diagram makes knowledge itself a *cosmos*: a concentric, hierarchical wheel descending from divine Wisdom through the ordered disciplines. Herrad (d. 1195) and her community built the *Hortus Deliciarum* as an encyclopaedic teaching manuscript; the twelfth-century original burned in 1870, but careful tracings preserve its imagery. It is a key witness to the medieval ordering of the [[motif:seven liberal arts|liberal arts]] as a structured whole.

## For artists & game designers
A radial skill-tree archetype: a central authority figure ringed by seven discipline 'classes,' each with iconographic kit.

citations.text: Rosalie Green et al., *Herrad of Hohenbourg: Hortus Deliciarum* (1979).
Fiona Griffiths, *The Garden of Delights: Reform and Renaissance for Women in the Twelfth Century* (2007).

title: Diagrammatic T-O World Map (after Isidore of Seville)
creator: after Isidore of Seville
summary:
A twelfth-century *T-O* world map of the type devised by Isidore of Seville, schematizing the inhabited earth as a wheel divided by a T into three continents.

## Iconography
A circle (the *O*, the encircling Ocean) is split by a *T* of water: the horizontal bar is the Don–Nile axis, the vertical stroke the Mediterranean. The three resulting fields are labelled **Asia** (the top half), **Europe**, and **Africa**, traditionally assigned to the three sons of Noah — Shem, Japheth, and Ham. East (Asia, the site of Paradise) is placed at the top.

## Significance
Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636) set out this diagram in his *Etymologiae* and *De natura rerum*; copied for a millennium, the [[motif:t-o map|T-O scheme]] is less a geography than a cosmological *rota* — a wheel-figure asserting that the world's structure is rational, tripartite, and divinely ordered. It belongs to the same diagrammatic family as the elemental and seasonal *rotae*.

## For artists & game designers
The minimal, instantly legible 'three-realm wheel' makes an excellent stylized world map or faction emblem.

citations.text: Isidore of Seville, *Etymologiae*, Book XIV; *De natura rerum*.
Evelyn Edson, *Mapping Time and Space: How Medieval Mapmakers Viewed Their World* (1997).

title: Cosmological folio from Lambert's *Liber Floridus*
creator: Lambert of Saint-Omer
summary:
A folio from the *Liber Floridus* (Book of Flowers), the encyclopaedic compilation assembled by Lambert, canon of Saint-Omer, around 1120.

## Iconography
The page shows the author-scribe at work amid the diagrammatic apparatus of his book — the circular figures, spheres, and *rotae* through which the *Liber Floridus* organizes the heavens, the elements, the winds, and the ages of the world. The manuscript is famous for its wheel-diagrams of the cosmos and its planetary and zodiacal schemes.

## Significance
Lambert's *Liber Floridus* is one of the great medieval visual encyclopaedias, gathering Isidore, Bede, and apocalyptic and computistic lore into an interlocking set of diagrams. Its cosmological *rotae* — concentric rings of spheres, elements, and winds — transmit the [[motif:microcosm-macrocosm|microcosm–macrocosm]] worldview to the high Middle Ages and influenced later encyclopaedic illumination. The autograph survives at Ghent University Library.

## For artists & game designers
A model 'wizard's compendium' page: a scribe surrounded by the spinning diagrams of his own cosmology.

citations.text: Albert Derolez, *The Autograph Manuscript of the Liber Floridus* (1998).
Lambert of Saint-Omer, *Liber Floridus* (Ghent UB MS 92).

title: *Arbor Scientiae* (Tree of Knowledge), Ramon Llull
creator: after Ramon Llull
summary:
The *Arbor Scientiae* (Tree of Knowledge / Tree of Science), Ramon Llull's vast botanical diagram of all the sciences, in an early-printed form.

## Iconography
A single tree carries the whole of knowledge: its roots are labelled with the nine 'divine dignities' and Llullian principles (goodness, greatness, eternity, power, wisdom…); its successive trunks and branches grow into the trees of the elements, the vegetal, the sensual, the imaginal, the human, the moral, the celestial, the angelic, the eternal, and the divine. Each level bears its leaves, flowers, and fruits of sub-topics.

## Significance
Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316) devised the *Arbor Scientiae* (1295–96) as a more accessible presentation of his *Ars* — a combinatorial, encyclopaedic system meant to derive all truths from a few divine attributes. The tree is at once a cosmology and an epistemology: the ladder of being (elemental → angelic → divine) doubles as the ladder of the sciences. Llull's diagrams shaped later Renaissance combinatorics and the art of memory.

## For artists & game designers
A literal tech/knowledge tree, rooted in 'principles' and branching into tiers of being — directly mappable to a skill or research system.

citations.text: Ramon Llull, *Arbor Scientiae* (1295–96).
Anthony Bonner, *The Art and Logic of Ramon Llull: A User's Guide* (2007).

title: Llullian Combinatorial Wheel (figure of the *Ars Magna*)
creator: modern recreation after Ramon Llull
summary:
A clean modern recreation of one of the rotating combinatorial figures of Ramon Llull's *Ars Magna* (Great Art), the volvelle-wheel that generates combinations of fundamental principles.

## Iconography
Concentric lettered circles (the letters B–K standing for the divine dignities and relational principles) can be rotated against one another so that every term is paired with every other. The diagram is a working device: by turning the inner wheel one reads off all the binary (and higher) combinations of Llull's basic concepts.

## Significance
Llull's *Ars* (from c. 1274; the *Ars Magna* / *Ars Generalis Ultima*, 1305–08) sought a universal method for demonstrating truths by mechanically combining a small alphabet of principles. Its [[motif:volvelle|rotating wheels]] are ancestors of the art of memory, of Bruno's and Kircher's combinatorial schemes, and — by a celebrated line through Leibniz — of formal logic and computation. This image is a present-day redrawing (CC BY-SA), not a historical manuscript.

## For artists & game designers
A functioning crafting/spell-combination dial: rotate lettered rings to enumerate every pairing of base 'principles.'

citations.text: Ramon Llull, *Ars Generalis Ultima* (1305–08).
Frances A. Yates, *The Art of Memory* (1966), ch. on Lull.

title: Schematic of the Ptolemaic Geocentric System
creator: Anonymous (modern schematic)
summary:
A simplified labelled schematic of the Ptolemaic geocentric system, showing the canonical order of the planetary spheres around a central earth.

## Iconography
Concentric rings radiate from the central earth outward through the spheres of the Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, to the sphere of the fixed stars (the zodiac) and the *primum mobile*. The diagram strips the cosmos to its bare geometric structure — the nested-spheres order codified in Ptolemy's *Almagest*.

## Significance
The geocentric model of [[motif:celestial spheres|concentric heavens]] set out by Claudius Ptolemy (2nd c. CE) governed Western and Islamic astronomy for some 1,400 years and underlay all medieval and Renaissance cosmological diagrams in this collection. This clean modern redrawing makes the planetary ordering — the backbone of astrological correspondence — immediately legible; it is a present-day schematic, not a historical print.

## For artists & game designers
The minimal reference diagram of planetary order — handy as a base layer for any astrological or cosmological UI.

citations.text: Claudius Ptolemy, *Almagest* (2nd c. CE).
Olaf Pedersen, *A Survey of the Almagest* (1974).

title: Integrae Naturae Speculum Artisque Imago (Fludd's Great Chain)
creator: Robert Fludd (engr. Matthäus Merian)
summary:
The most celebrated single image in [[creator:robert-fludd]]'s *Utriusque Cosmi … Historia* (Oppenheim, 1617; engraved by Matthäus Merian, who also cut [[work:atalanta_fugiens]]). Its title — *Integrae Naturae Speculum Artisque Imago* — means "The Mirror of the Whole of Nature and the Image of Art."

## Iconography
At the top right, the **hand of God** emerges from cloud and the Tetragrammaton, holding a chain. The chain descends to a nude woman — **Natura**, the *anima mundi* or World-Soul — who stands upon the elemental earth, one foot in water, a sun on her breast and a moon on her belly. From *her* left hand a second chain runs down to an **ape** seated on the globe: *Ars*, Art (human craft, including alchemy), which imitates Nature as Nature imitates God. Around them are arrayed, in concentric rings, the realms of creation: the elements, the mineral, vegetable, and animal kingdoms, the mechanical arts, the liberal arts, the planetary spheres, and the angelic hierarchies.

## Significance
The plate is the definitive visualisation of the **Great Chain of Being** and the Hermetic axiom *as above, so below*: divine power is transmitted, link by link, from God through the World-Soul to nature and finally to human art. It encapsulates Fludd's entire programme — a cosmos legible as a hierarchy of correspondences ([[tradition:hermetic]]) rather than as Kepler's mathematics, a disagreement that became one of the defining methodological quarrels of the seventeenth century.

## For artists & game designers
A complete cosmological map in one frame — divine hand, chained World-Soul, ape of Art, nested spheres of elements, planets, and angels. Unmatched reference for a tech/magic tree, a cosmology screen, a "chain of being" progression, or an arcane wall-mural.

citations.text: Robert Fludd, *Utriusque Cosmi … Historia*, vol. I (Oppenheim: de Bry, 1617), frontispiece.
J. Godwin, *Robert Fludd: Hermetic Philosopher and Surveyor of Two Worlds* (Thames & Hudson, 1979).

title: The Divine Monochord (Robert Fludd)
creator: Robert Fludd
summary:
**Robert Fludd's** 'Divine Monochord' (*Monochordum mundi*), from the *Utriusque Cosmi Historia* (1617) — the universe drawn as a single tuned string.

## Iconography
A monochord stretches from earth at the base to the empyrean at the top, its bridge tuned by the **hand of God** from a cloud. Along the string the elements, planets, and angelic spheres are marked off as musical intervals (diapason, diapente, diatessaron), so the whole cosmos sounds as one octave.

The purest statement of the **music of the spheres** — the cosmos ordered by harmonic proportion, the macrocosm a chord. It belongs to Fludd's quarrel with Kepler over whether the universe is read by [[tradition:hermetic|symbolic harmony]] or mathematics, and pairs with Fludd's [[work:cosmology|Great Chain]] already in this archive.

Cosmos-as-instrument — a vivid metaphor for a music-magic system or a harmony-of-the-spheres UI.

creator: Daniel Cramer
summary:
Plate from Daniel Cramer's *Emblemata Sacra*: a circular emblem of the human heart watered by a hand from the clouds, the recurring devotional-alchemical image at the centre of the book.

## Iconography
A round emblematic medallion frames a single great heart watered by a hand from the clouds, set in a small landscape and ringed by a Latin motto; the page is one half of an opening that pairs the engraving with a Latin and German verse and a scriptural citation. The specific motto and biblical text of this individual plate are not identified here, so only the shared visual programme of the series is described, to avoid invention.

## Significance
Cramer's *Emblemata Sacra* (Frankfurt, 1624) is a cycle of devotional heart-emblems in which a single heart is subjected, plate by plate, to a sequence of operations - wounded, burned, watered, washed, hammered, weighed, winged and finally crowned. The imagery deliberately borrows the language of the alchemical laboratory: the heart is treated like *prima materia* purified in the furnace, so that the believer's inner transformation mirrors the refining of metals. Here this plate shows the heart irrigated by heavenly dew or rain, made fruitful by grace from above. The flaming, operated heart made Cramer's emblems enormously popular and they were widely reused across 17th-century devotional and esoteric print, carrying a Rosicrucian resonance into Protestant piety. The motto-image-verse-citation structure is the classic tripartite emblem form codified by Andrea Alciato.

## For artists & game designers
The 'one heart, many operations' series is a ready template for a transformation track: a single object (heart, gem, core) shown wounded -> fired -> washed -> winged -> crowned across stages, each stage a discrete upgrade icon.

title: Ars moriendi (block-book woodcut)
work: Memento Mori: The Art of Death, the Danse Macabre & the Triumph of Death
creator: Anonymous (printed by Conrad Kachelofen)
summary:
A woodcut from the *Ars moriendi* ("The Art of Dying"), the immensely popular fifteenth-century manual on the good death, here in an edition printed by Conrad Kachelofen.

## Iconography
A dying man lies on his bed surrounded by the unseen combatants for his soul: demons crowd in with temptations — to despair, impatience, pride, avarice and loss of faith — while angels, saints and Christ offer consolation. The deathbed becomes the stage of a final spiritual contest.

## Significance
The *Ars moriendi*, circulating both as a blockbook and in typeset editions from the 1450s onward, taught the laity to die well by resisting the five temptations and embracing their consoling counter-images. It is a cornerstone of late-medieval death culture, complementing the danse macabre's communal *memento mori* with a private, dramatised psychomachia at the bedside, as studied by Mary Catharine O'Connor and others.

## For artists & game designers
Staging an invisible tug-of-war of demons and angels around a single vulnerable figure is a clean template for a "contest for the soul" encounter.

title: The Triumph of Death (Pieter Bruegel the Elder)
work: Memento Mori: The Art of Death, the Danse Macabre & the Triumph of Death
creator: Pieter Bruegel the Elder
summary:
Pieter Bruegel the Elder's panoramic panel *The Triumph of Death* (c. 1562, Museo del Prado), a vast apocalyptic landscape in which armies of skeletons overwhelm the living.

## Iconography
Legions of the dead drive humanity toward a great coffin-trap; a skeleton on a pale horse mows the crowd with a scythe, bells toll, a king's treasure is plundered, lovers play on oblivious. Every social rank — cardinal, soldier, peasant, gambler — is engulfed in a blasted, fire-lit world.

## Significance
Bruegel fuses the medieval *Triumph of Death* and *danse macabre* into a single eschatological panorama, drawing on the Italian frescoes and on Netherlandish print culture. The work reads both as universal *memento mori* and, many scholars argue, as a coded response to the religious violence of the sixteenth-century Low Countries. It is the most ambitious painted version of the theme.

## For artists & game designers
Massing identical skeletons as a relentless army — rather than a single reaper — converts a moral emblem into a horror set-piece of overwhelming scale.

title: The Triumph of Death (Camposanto, Pisa — fragment)
work: Memento Mori: The Art of Death, the Danse Macabre & the Triumph of Death
creator: Buonamico Buffalmacco (attributed)
rights: Public domain (CC0, Rijksmuseum reproduction). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A fragment of the great *Trionfo della Morte* fresco in the Camposanto Monumentale at Pisa, generally attributed to Buonamico Buffalmacco and dated to around 1336–1341 — before the Black Death — and badly damaged by fire in 1944.

## Iconography
The cycle combines several mortuary themes: an elegant hunting party recoils before three open coffins of decaying corpses (the [[motif:three living and three dead|Three Living and the Three Dead]]); a scythe-bearing Death swoops over heaps of the dead; and beggars vainly implore Death to take them. This reproduction preserves a portion of the composition.

## Significance
The Pisan *Triumph of Death* is one of the earliest and most ambitious survivals of the theme and a touchstone for its iconography, influencing later treatments down to Bruegel. Its early date shows that the meditation on universal mortality predates the plague, though the epidemic intensified it. Scholars such as Millard Meiss read such frescoes as expressions of a penitential, death-haunted Tuscan piety.

## For artists & game designers
Stacking three death-motifs in one scene — the corpse-confrontation, the reaping figure, the unanswered plea — builds a single image that rewards close reading.

summary:
A page from *La grande danse macabre des hommes et des femmes*, a long-lived French popular-print version of the Dance of Death (this copy an 1862 reissue) that extends the procession to the female estates.

## Iconography
Woodcut figures of Death lead women of differing ranks — queen, abbess, bourgeoise, bride, nurse — alongside the men, each accompanied by verses. The *danse macabre des femmes* gives the genre its full social and gendered range.

## Significance
The Dance of Death of women, developed in the later fifteenth century (notably in editions following Marchant), added the estates of women to a tradition that had begun with men only. These cheap, repeatedly reprinted *bibliothèque bleue*-style chapbooks kept the medieval *memento mori* alive into the nineteenth century, long after elite art had moved on, as historians of popular print have shown.

## For artists & game designers
Extending an archetype-procession to a parallel cast (here, women's estates) is a low-cost way to double a roster while keeping one coherent visual system.

title: Death and the Maiden (Hans Baldung Grien)
work: Memento Mori: The Art of Death, the Danse Macabre & the Triumph of Death
creator: Hans Baldung Grien
summary:
Hans Baldung Grien's panel *Death and the Maiden* (c. 1518–1520), one of several treatments by the artist of a young woman seized by a putrefying corpse.

## Iconography
A beautiful nude young woman, often with mirror or flowing hair, is grasped from behind by a decaying cadaver who pulls her toward the grave; she recoils in dread. Youth, sensuality and vanity are confronted directly by physical corruption.

## Significance
*Death and the Maiden* is a German Renaissance offshoot of the *danse macabre*, narrowing the universal dance to a single, erotically charged pairing of *Eros* and *Thanatos*. Baldung, a pupil of Dürer, made the theme his own, using the contrast of flawless flesh and rotting body to preach the transience of beauty — a gendered intensification of the *memento mori* that scholars such as Joseph Koerner have analysed at length.

## For artists & game designers
The beauty-and-corpse embrace compresses an entire mortality sermon into a single two-figure tableau charged with dread and desire.

title: The Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse (Dürer)
work: Memento Mori: The Art of Death, the Danse Macabre & the Triumph of Death
creator: Albrecht Dürer
summary:
Albrecht Dürer's woodcut *The Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse* from his *Apocalypse* series (c. 1498), the defining image of the riders of Revelation, with Death on the pale horse at the front.

## Iconography
Four riders — Conquest, War, Famine and, lowest and gauntest, Death astride a pale horse and brandishing nothing but a pitchfork — trample humanity, from emperor to commoner, beneath their hooves; the maw of Hell opens to swallow the fallen. The riders surge diagonally with terrifying momentum.

## Significance
Dürer's *Apocalypse*, published in 1498 amid pre-millennial anxiety, gave Revelation 6 its most powerful visual form and made the [[motif:death on a pale horse|pale-horse rider]] a permanent fixture of Western death-imagery. The series fused the eschatological horseman with the leveller of the *Triumph of Death*: emperors and peasants perish together. Its technical brilliance also marked the woodcut's arrival as a vehicle for ambitious art.

## For artists & game designers
Giving the most lethal rider the meanest weapon — a farm pitchfork, not a sword — makes Death's inevitability feel casual and therefore more chilling.

An allegorical engraved title-page (1732) for an edition of Samuel von Pufendorf's *Introduction à l'histoire générale et politique de l'univers*, in which Death appears as a skeleton with scythe beside the muse of history, Clio.

## Iconography
A skeletal figure of Death wields the great scythe, the agricultural reaping-tool that became its standard attribute, set in an allegorical assembly with the personified muse who records the deeds and falls of nations. Time and mortality frame the writing of history.

## Significance
The skeleton with the scythe — and often an hourglass — is the fully crystallised early-modern personification of Death, the "Grim Reaper," descended from the reaping Death of the *Triumph* and the *danse macabre*. Its appearance on a history book's frontispiece shows how thoroughly the *memento mori* had entered the visual grammar of learned culture, reminding readers that empires too are mown down.

## For artists & game designers
The scythe reads instantly as "Death" even in silhouette — the single most recognisable attribute for personifying mortality.

title: Knight, Death and the Devil (Dürer)
work: Memento Mori: The Art of Death, the Danse Macabre & the Triumph of Death
creator: Albrecht Dürer
rights: Public domain (CC0, Metropolitan Museum). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
Albrecht Dürer's master engraving *Ritter, Tod und Teufel* (Knight, Death and the Devil, 1513), one of his three *Meisterstiche*, in which a mounted knight rides resolutely past Death and a swinish devil.

## Iconography
A Christian knight in full armour advances through a gloomy ravine. Death, a crowned, snake-wreathed corpse on a pale nag, raises an hourglass to remind him his time is short; a horned, hog-snouted devil shambles behind. The knight neither flinches nor looks aside, fixed on the distant fortress.

## Significance
Usually read in light of Erasmus's *Enchiridion militis Christiani* (the "Handbook of the Christian Soldier"), the print shows steadfast faith riding unmoved through the terrors of death and temptation. The hourglass-bearing corpse is a quintessential *memento mori*, but here the lesson is turned to courage rather than despair. Panofsky's reading of the engraving remains classic.

## For artists & game designers
Death as a heckler holding up an hourglass — present but powerless against a resolute hero — flips the usual dynamic and characterises the protagonist through what he ignores.

title: The Bishop and the Squire (Danse Macabre, Marchant tradition)
work: Memento Mori: The Art of Death, the Danse Macabre & the Triumph of Death
creator: after Guyot Marchant (anonymous woodcutter)
summary:
A *Danse Macabre* woodcut in the tradition of Guyot Marchant's Parisian editions (first printed 1485), reproducing the pairing of the Bishop and the Squire; this plate appears in Johan Huizinga's *The Waning of the Middle Ages*.

## Iconography
Two cavorting corpses lead a mitred bishop and a young squire into the dance. Each living figure is partnered by a lively skeleton, and a verse exchange (in the original) has Death address the victim and the victim lament his fate.

## Significance
Marchant's 1485 *Danse Macabre*, drawn from the lost mural painted around 1424–25 in the cemetery of the Saints-Innocents in Paris, was the first printed edition of the theme and spread it across Europe. The procession descends the social ladder, insisting that office and youth alike are powerless before death — the central lesson Huizinga made famous in his account of late-medieval mortuary culture.

## For artists & game designers
Pairing each victim with an animated, almost gleeful corpse turns a grim subject into a darkly comic dance — tone as much as theme.

title: The Expulsion from Paradise (Holbein, Dance of Death series)
work: Memento Mori: The Art of Death, the Danse Macabre & the Triumph of Death
creator: Hans Holbein the Younger (designer); Hans Lützelburger (cutter)
summary:
An opening woodcut from Hans Holbein the Younger's *Les simulachres & historiees faces de la mort* (the "Dance of Death"), designed in Basel around 1526 and first published at Lyon in 1538, here showing the Expulsion from Paradise that brings death into the world.

## Iconography
An angel drives Adam and Eve from Eden while a skeletal figure of Death, already accompanying them, plays a stringed instrument — situating the entire series as the consequence of the Fall. The German caption *Vßtribung Ade Eue* names the scene.

## Significance
Holbein's miniature woodcuts, cut by Hans Lützelburger, transformed the older mural *Danse Macabre* into a portable book in which Death seizes each estate — pope, emperor, merchant, ploughman — at its daily business. The series became the most influential treatment of the theme; scholars from Werner Gundersheimer to the editors of the Dover facsimile trace its diffusion across confessional Europe. Beginning with the Fall frames death as universal punishment rather than mere chance.

## For artists & game designers
Opening a death-themed sequence with origin-of-death imagery, rather than a generic skeleton, gives the whole set a narrative spine.

title: Death and the Knight (Holbein, Dance of Death)
work: Memento Mori: The Art of Death, the Danse Macabre & the Triumph of Death
creator: after Hans Holbein the Younger
summary:
A plate from Holbein's *Dance of Death* in which Death overcomes an armoured knight, one of the social estates seized in turn throughout the series.

## Iconography
A skeleton attacks a fully armoured nobleman, running him through despite his plate and weapons; the soldier's martial strength is shown to be useless against the universal leveller. The composition continues the book's procession through every rank of society.

## Significance
The *Danse Macabre* asserts that death erases the hierarchy of estates — emperor, bishop, knight, peasant fall alike. The knight's plate, the ultimate sign of worldly power and protection, is pierced as easily as a beggar's rags, dramatising the medieval commonplace [[motif:memento mori|*memento mori*]]. Holbein's individualised, action-filled scenes broke from the static earlier mural tradition and fixed the leveller motif in the European imagination.

## For artists & game designers
Defeating the most heavily armoured archetype with the cheapest enemy is a compact way to signal that ordinary rules no longer apply.

citations.text: Hans Holbein the Younger, *The Dance of Death* (Lyon, 1538).
James M. Clark, *The Dance of Death in the Middle Ages and the Renaissance* (1950).

title: The Lübeck Totentanz (Marienkirche Dance of Death)
work: Memento Mori: The Art of Death, the Danse Macabre & the Triumph of Death
creator: after Bernt Notke (1701 copy by Anton Wortmann)
summary:
A panoramic record of the *Totentanz* (Dance of Death) once in the Marienkirche at Lübeck, originally painted by Bernt Notke in 1463 and known through a 1701 repainting by Anton Wortmann; the medieval original was destroyed in 1942.

## Iconography
A long frieze shows skeletal figures of Death leading an alternating chain of the living — pope, emperor, cardinal, king, down to the peasant and the infant — each clasped by a corpse in a grim dance. Verse dialogues once accompanied each pairing.

## Significance
The Lübeck mural was among the most celebrated north-German *Totentänze* and a key witness to the genre that flourished after the Black Death. Its alternation of the powerful and the humble embodies death as the great leveller; the dancing dead are not the deceased themselves but Death personified, summoning each estate. The loss of Notke's original in the wartime bombing makes such copies the principal evidence, as art historians of the *Totentanz* tradition emphasise.

## For artists & game designers
A horizontal procession alternating finely dressed figures with identical corpses reads instantly as "everyone, no exceptions."

citations.text: Hartmut Freytag (ed.), *Der Totentanz der Marienkirche in Lübeck* (1993).
James M. Clark, *The Dance of Death in the Middle Ages and the Renaissance* (1950).

title: Doctor Schnabel von Rom (the Plague Doctor)
work: Memento Mori: The Art of Death, the Danse Macabre & the Triumph of Death
creator: Paul Fürst (publisher); after 'I. Columbina'
summary:
*Der Doctor Schnabel von Rom* ("Doctor Beak of Rome"), an engraving published by Paul Fürst of Nuremberg around 1656, the most famous image of the beaked plague doctor.

## Iconography
A gowned physician is encased head to foot in a waxed leather costume with a long bird-like beak (packed with aromatics against miasma), gloves, hat and a pointing wand. A mocking macaronic verse surrounds him, deriding doctors who profit from the dead while doing little for the living.

## Significance
The costume responded to the miasma theory of contagion during the great seventeenth-century plagues, the beak filled with herbs to filter "corrupt air." The print is at once documentary and satirical, a grim joke on the impotence of medicine before pestilence — a recurring partner of the *memento mori*, since the plague was the great quickener of death-imagery from the danse macabre onward. Astrological and divine causes of pestilence were debated alongside such remedies.

## For artists & game designers
The beaked silhouette is one of the most instantly evocative period costumes in existence — pure mood with a built-in story of fear and quackery.

citations.text: Christine M. Boeckl, *Images of Plague and Pestilence* (2000).
Paul Fürst, *Der Doctor Schnabel von Rom* (Nuremberg, c. 1656).

title: The Plague of Florence in 1348 (after Boccaccio)
work: Memento Mori: The Art of Death, the Danse Macabre & the Triumph of Death
creator: Anonymous (Wellcome Collection impression)
rights: CC BY 4.0, Wellcome Collection. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
An etching depicting *The Plague of Florence in 1348* as described in the introduction to Boccaccio's *Decameron*, from the Wellcome Collection.

## Iconography
The streets and interiors of Florence are strewn with the dead and dying; the living flee, mourn or carry off corpses while the social order collapses under the Black Death. The scene visualises Boccaccio's harrowing account of the epidemic that frames his hundred tales.

## Significance
The Black Death of 1347–1351 killed perhaps a third of Europe and is the historical engine behind the whole macabre tradition — the danse macabre, the *Triumph of Death* and the transi tomb all intensify in its wake. Boccaccio's eyewitness preface became the canonical literary description, repeatedly illustrated. Contemporaries sought causes in divine wrath, corrupt air and adverse planetary conjunctions, binding pestilence to the astrology of disaster.

## For artists & game designers
A city scene of collapsing social order — not just individual death — conveys catastrophe at a scale that a single skeleton cannot.

citations.text: Giovanni Boccaccio, *Decameron* (c. 1353), Introduction.
Christine M. Boeckl, *Images of Plague and Pestilence* (2000).

title: The Three Living and the Three Dead (Master of the Dresden Prayer Book)
work: Memento Mori: The Art of Death, the Danse Macabre & the Triumph of Death
creator: Master of the Dresden Prayer Book (or workshop)
summary:
A Flemish manuscript illumination of *The Three Living and the Three Dead*, attributed to the Master of the Dresden Prayer Book or his workshop (active c. 1480–1515).

## Iconography
Three richly dressed young noblemen, often out hunting, come face to face with three corpses in varying stages of decay, who warn them: *"As you are, so once were we; as we are, so shall you be."* The living recoil at the mirror of their own future.

## Significance
This *exemplum*, current in Europe from the thirteenth century in poetry and wall-painting, is a direct ancestor of the danse macabre: it confronts youth, rank and vitality with their inevitable corruption. The encounter-of-three structure, frequently placed in Books of Hours beside the Office of the Dead, drives home the personal *memento mori*. The motif is documented across French, English and Italian art by scholars of medieval death imagery.

## For artists & game designers
The mirror-encounter — confronting the player-character with rotting versions of themselves — is a stark, economical way to deliver a mortality theme without exposition.

citations.text: Ashby Kinch, *Imago Mortis: Mediating Images of Death in Late Medieval Culture* (2013).
Paul Binski, *Medieval Death: Ritual and Representation* (1996).

title: Le Transi de René de Chalon (Ligier Richier)
work: Memento Mori: The Art of Death, the Danse Macabre & the Triumph of Death
creator: Ligier Richier
summary:
Ligier Richier's *transi* (cadaver effigy) of René de Chalon, Prince of Orange, carved around 1545–1547 for the church of Saint-Étienne at Bar-le-Duc — one of the supreme *memento mori* sculptures.

## Iconography
In place of a serene recumbent effigy, the prince is shown as a partly decomposed, flayed standing corpse, skin hanging in tatters, who raises his left hand to offer his own withered heart heavenward. The figure is upright and almost defiant, gazing toward God.

## Significance
The *transi* or cadaver tomb, which flourished from the late fourteenth century, depicts the deceased not in idealised repose but in graphic decay, fusing aristocratic commemoration with the universal lesson of bodily corruption. Richier's masterpiece pushes the type to a sculptural extreme; Erwin Panofsky and Kathleen Cohen treat such monuments as the funerary counterpart of the danse macabre. The offered heart converts horror into an act of devotion.

## For artists & game designers
A standing, active corpse that performs a gesture of devotion is far more unsettling — and characterful — than a passive skeleton lying down.

citations.text: Kathleen Cohen, *Metamorphosis of a Death Symbol: The Transi Tomb in the Late Middle Ages and the Renaissance* (1973).
Erwin Panofsky, *Tomb Sculpture* (1964).
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Triumph of Death (Palazzo Sclafani / Palazzo Abatellis, Palermo)
work: Memento Mori: The Art of Death, the Danse Macabre & the Triumph of Death
creator: Anonymous (Maestro del Trionfo della Morte)
summary:
A large detached fresco of *Il Trionfo della Morte* (the Triumph of Death), painted around 1446 for the courtyard of the Palazzo Sclafani in Palermo and now in the Galleria Regionale di Palazzo Abatellis.

## Iconography
A skeletal Death rides a gaunt, ghostly horse, loosing arrows into a company of the rich, young and powerful — courtiers, lovers, a pope and emperor — while the poor and infirm at the left, who beg for death, are pointedly spared. The composition is among the most powerful realisations of the theme.

## Significance
The *Triumph of Death*, a theme spread by Petrarch's *Trionfi* and the trauma of the Black Death, shows Death conquering all earthly estates at once rather than in sequence. The Palermo fresco's mounted archer became iconic; its modern fame was amplified when Picasso is said to have studied it. It belongs to the same fifteenth-century mortuary culture as the danse macabre and the transi tomb.

## For artists & game designers
A mounted skeletal archer who spares the suffering and strikes the fortunate inverts the usual logic of mercy — an unsettling, memorable rule.

citations.text: Alberto Tenenti, *Il senso della morte e l'amore della vita nel Rinascimento* (1957).
Joël Saugnieux, *Les danses macabres de France et d'Espagne* (1972).

title: Vanitas Still Life with Skull, Hourglass and Globe (Gijsbrechts)
work: Memento Mori: The Art of Death, the Danse Macabre & the Triumph of Death
creator: Cornelis Norbertus Gijsbrechts
summary:
A *vanitas* still life by the Flemish painter Cornelis Norbertus Gijsbrechts, assembling a skull, hourglass, guttering candle, violin, globe, sheet music and playing cards on a draped table.

## Iconography
Each object is an emblem of transience: the skull and extinguished candle for death, the hourglass for fleeting time, the bubble-like instruments, music and cards for fragile worldly pleasure and chance. Together they preach the vanity of earthly things — *vanitas vanitatum*.

## Significance
The Dutch and Flemish *vanitas* of the seventeenth century translated the medieval *memento mori* into the language of the bourgeois still life, where the skull beside the hourglass distils centuries of death-imagery into a single contemplative arrangement. The genre is rooted in Ecclesiastes' "all is vanity" and studied as a meditation on mortality and the futility of accumulation. Gijsbrechts was a noted specialist of the type and of *trompe-l'œil*.

## For artists & game designers
The skull-plus-hourglass pairing is the most compact, universally legible death symbol in Western art — instant shorthand for "time is running out."

citations.text: Alberto Veca, *Vanitas: il simbolismo del tempo* (1981).
Ingvar Bergström, *Dutch Still-Life Painting in the Seventeenth Century* (1956).
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Wheel of Fortune (Carmina Burana manuscript)
work: Memento Mori: The Art of Death, the Danse Macabre & the Triumph of Death
creator: Anonymous (Carmina Burana illuminator)
summary:
The celebrated *Rota Fortunae* (Wheel of Fortune) illumination from the *Carmina Burana* manuscript (c. 1230), illustrating the goddess Fortuna turning her wheel.

## Iconography
Four figures ride the rim, each labelled: *regnabo* ("I shall reign"), *regno* ("I reign"), *regnavi* ("I have reigned") and *sum sine regno* ("I am without a kingdom"). A crowned king rides the summit while another tumbles headlong, as blind Fortune spins all from glory to ruin.

## Significance
The Wheel of Fortune, given its enduring form by Boethius's *Consolation of Philosophy*, became the medieval emblem of worldly mutability and a close kin of the *memento mori*: like Death, Fortune levels the proud and reminds the mighty of their fall. The *Carmina Burana* image is the genre's most reproduced witness, opening a manuscript whose verses lament fate's caprice — the same fatalism that underlies the danse macabre.

## For artists & game designers
A rotating wheel whose four stations spell rise, rule, fall and ruin is a ready-made visual loop for systems about fortune, status, or impermanence.

citations.text: Boethius, *De consolatione philosophiae* (c. 524).
Howard R. Patch, *The Goddess Fortuna in Mediaeval Literature* (1927).

title: Abraxas
work: Demonology, the Goetia & the Iconography of Devils
creator: After J. Collin de Plancy
summary:
*Abraxas* as engraved for the *Dictionnaire Infernal* — the cock-headed, serpent-legged power of late-antique Gnosticism re-presented among the demons.

## Iconography
Abraxas is the classic *anguipede*: a warrior with the head of a rooster, a cuirassed human torso, and two serpents for legs, bearing a shield and a whip or flail. The form is copied from ancient [[motif:abraxas|magical gems]] (the so-called Abraxas stones).

## Significance
In the system of the Gnostic teacher Basilides (2nd c. Alexandria), *Abraxas* was the supreme Archon whose name totals 365 by Greek isopsephy — one for each of the 365 heavens. Engraved on amulets as a protective deity, he was later absorbed into demonological and occult literature, and C. G. Jung invoked him in the *Seven Sermons to the Dead* as a god uniting opposites. Collin de Plancy lists him among the infernal powers.

## For artists & game designers
The rooster-headed, snake-legged soldier is one of the oldest composite-deity designs in Western magic — instantly evocative for amulet or boss art.

citations.text: J. Collin de Plancy, *Dictionnaire Infernal* (1863 ed.).
Irenaeus on Basilides; C. G. Jung, *Septem Sermones ad Mortuos* (1916).

title: Adramelech
work: Demonology, the Goetia & the Iconography of Devils
creator: Louis Le Breton
summary:
Le Breton's *Adramelech*, grand chancellor of Hell, shown with a mule's body and peacock tail in the 1863 *Dictionnaire Infernal*.

## Iconography
Adramelech appears with a man's torso, a crowned bestial head, the lower body of a mule (or sometimes a peacock's fanned tail). The regalia mark his office as chancellor and president of the High Council of devils.

## Significance
Adramelech (Adrammelech) is named in 2 Kings 17 as a god of Sepharvaim to whom colonists 'burned their children in fire.' Demonologists such as those compiled by Collin de Plancy made him chancellor of the infernal order and superintendent of Satan's wardrobe. His association with [[motif:child sacrifice|child sacrifice]] links him to Moloch in the biblical roster of condemned deities.

## For artists & game designers
The crowned man-mule-peacock hybrid is an ornate courtly demon — cast him as a scheming infernal bureaucrat rather than a frontline fighter.

citations.text: J. Collin de Plancy, *Dictionnaire Infernal* (1863 ed., ill. Louis Le Breton).
2 Kings 17:31.

title: Amon (Aamon)
work: Demonology, the Goetia & the Iconography of Devils
creator: Louis Le Breton
summary:
Le Breton's *Amon*, a marquis of Hell who reconciles disputes, in the 1863 *Dictionnaire Infernal*.

## Iconography
Amon is depicted as a wolf-headed figure with a serpent's tail, sometimes vomiting flame. The composite follows the Goetia, which describes him appearing as a wolf with a serpent's tail breathing fire, or as a man with the teeth of a dog.

## Significance
Amon (Aamon), likely echoing the Egyptian *Amun* or the Carthaginian *Baal-hammon*, is the seventh spirit of the *Ars Goetia*, a Great Marquis commanding forty legions. He discerns past and future and [[motif:reconciler|procures love and reconciliation]] between friends and foes — one of the demons valued for social rather than martial powers.

## For artists & game designers
The wolf-head/serpent-tail combination is a clean two-animal hybrid; the 'reconciler' role suits a non-combat NPC who brokers truces.

citations.text: J. Collin de Plancy, *Dictionnaire Infernal* (1863 ed., ill. Louis Le Breton).
*The Lesser Key of Solomon: Ars Goetia*, spirit 7.

title: Andras
work: Demonology, the Goetia & the Iconography of Devils
creator: Louis Le Breton
summary:
Le Breton's *Andras*, the owl-headed demon of discord, from the 1863 *Dictionnaire Infernal*.

## Iconography
Andras is shown with the head of an owl (or raven) on a winged angelic body, brandishing a sharp sword and riding upon a strong black wolf. The image follows the Goetia exactly, including the wolf mount and drawn blade.

## Significance
Andras is the sixty-third spirit of the *Ars Goetia*, a Great Marquis commanding thirty legions, who sows [[motif:discord|discord and slaughter]]. The grimoire issues a stark warning: he comes to kill the careless conjurer and his companions, making him one of the most dangerous spirits in the catalogue — a demon to be bound with great caution.

## For artists & game designers
The owl-headed swordsman on a black wolf is a sleek, aggressive design — ideal for a high-threat assassin demon with a 'kills the unwary' gimmick.

citations.text: J. Collin de Plancy, *Dictionnaire Infernal* (1863 ed., ill. Louis Le Breton).
*The Lesser Key of Solomon: Ars Goetia*, spirit 63.
Wikimedia Commons

title: Asmodeus
work: Demonology, the Goetia & the Iconography of Devils
creator: Louis Le Breton
summary:
Louis Le Breton's *Asmodeus*, the three-headed king of demons, from the 1863 *Dictionnaire Infernal*.

## Iconography
Asmodeus is depicted with three heads — a bull, a man, and a ram — webbed feet, a serpent's tail, and a lance, riding upon an infernal dragon. The composite heads correspond to the description in the *Ars Goetia*, where he breathes fire and rides a dragon while bearing a lance and banner.

## Significance
Asmodeus (Aeshma-daeva) enters Jewish tradition through the deuterocanonical *Book of Tobit*, where he slays Sarah's bridegrooms before being driven off by Tobias and the angel Raphael. In the *Testament of Solomon* he is bound to manufacture the Temple. He became the demon of [[motif:lust|lust]] and discord, and one of the seventy-two spirits ruling thirty-six legions. Le Breton synthesized these textual cues into a single iconic portrait.

## For artists & game designers
The tri-headed, lance-bearing dragon-rider is a maximalist demon-king design — combine bestial heads to signal his rank without text.

citations.text: J. Collin de Plancy, *Dictionnaire Infernal* (1863 ed., ill. Louis Le Breton).
*Book of Tobit*; *Testament of Solomon*.

title: Astaroth
work: Demonology, the Goetia & the Iconography of Devils
creator: Louis Le Breton
summary:
Louis Le Breton's engraving of *Astaroth*, the Great Duke of Hell, for the 1863 edition of Collin de Plancy's *Dictionnaire Infernal*.

## Iconography
Astaroth is shown as a nude, ugly figure riding an infernal dragon or wyvern, gripping a viper in his left hand. The image follows the literary description in which he appears mounted, holding a serpent, with a fetid breath the conjurer must guard against by holding a magical ring to the face.

## Significance
Astaroth derives from the ancient Near-Eastern goddess Astarte, demoted in Christian demonology to a male duke of the infernal hierarchy. He appears among the [[motif:infernal hierarchy|seventy-two spirits]] of the *Ars Goetia* and in the *Pseudomonarchia Daemonum* of Johann Weyer, where he answers questions on the past, present, and future and discourses on the fall of the rebel angels. Le Breton's plates fixed the modern visual vocabulary of named demons.

## For artists & game designers
The dragon-mounted duke is a ready boss archetype: a humanoid commander riding a serpentine beast, paired with a poison/breath hazard mechanic.

citations.text: J. Collin de Plancy, *Dictionnaire Infernal* (1863 ed., ill. Louis Le Breton).
Johann Weyer, *Pseudomonarchia Daemonum* (1577).

title: Bael (Baal)
work: Demonology, the Goetia & the Iconography of Devils
creator: Louis Le Breton
summary:
Le Breton's *Bael*, the first king of the *Ars Goetia*, rendered as a tripartite monster in the 1863 *Dictionnaire Infernal*.

## Iconography
Bael appears with three heads — a toad, a man, and a cat — set upon a body supported by spider-like legs. This precisely follows the Goetic description of a king who appears 'with three heads, the first like a toad, the second like a man, the third like a cat,' speaking with a hoarse voice.

## Significance
Bael descends from the Canaanite storm-god *Baal* (Ba'al, 'lord'), the great rival of Yahweh in the Hebrew Bible, demonised in Christian tradition. In the *Ars Goetia* he is the first of the seventy-two spirits, commanding sixty-six legions and granting [[motif:invisibility|invisibility]]. Le Breton's spider-legged composite became the canonical modern image of the demon.

## For artists & game designers
The toad-man-cat triad on spider legs is a striking 'wrongness' silhouette — assemble mismatched animal heads to make an unsettling first-tier boss.

citations.text: J. Collin de Plancy, *Dictionnaire Infernal* (1863 ed., ill. Louis Le Breton).
*The Lesser Key of Solomon: Ars Goetia*.
Wikimedia Commons

title: Beelzebub
work: Demonology, the Goetia & the Iconography of Devils
creator: Louis Le Breton
summary:
Le Breton's *Beelzebub*, the 'Lord of the Flies' and a supreme chief of the infernal empire, from the 1863 *Dictionnaire Infernal*.

## Iconography
The demon is rendered as a colossal winged fly, an explicit visual pun on the name *Baal-zebub*, 'lord of the flies.' The insect form distils the demonological tradition that Beelzebub presided over swarms of plague-bearing flies.

## Significance
Beelzebub originates as *Baal-Zebul* ('Baal the prince'), the Philistine god of Ekron in 2 Kings, deliberately mangled into *Baal-Zebub* by Hebrew scribes. In the Gospels he is named 'prince of the demons,' and later demonologists ranked him second only to Satan, even identifying him as the supreme ruler of Hell. He is one of the chief tempters in the [[motif:infernal hierarchy|classification of demons]] by sin.

## For artists & game designers
The giant-fly form is a vivid, instantly legible monster — pair with a swarm/plague mechanic that fragments into lesser flies.

citations.text: J. Collin de Plancy, *Dictionnaire Infernal* (1863 ed., ill. Louis Le Breton).
2 Kings 1; Matthew 12:24.

title: Behemoth
work: Demonology, the Goetia & the Iconography of Devils
creator: Louis Le Breton
summary:
Le Breton's *Behemoth*, the gluttonous demon-beast, from the 1863 *Dictionnaire Infernal*.

## Iconography
Behemoth is shown as an enormous elephant-headed demon with a swollen belly, standing upright on stout legs. The grotesque potbelly and beast-head encode his role as the demon of [[motif:gluttony|gluttony]] and brute appetite.

## Significance
Behemoth derives from the primordial land-monster of the Book of Job (40:15–24), counterpart to the sea-beast Leviathan. Christian demonology recast him as the demon presiding over gluttony and the pleasures of the belly, master of Hell's feasts and revels. He stands among the great mythic monsters that demonologists folded into the infernal court.

## For artists & game designers
A hulking, slow elephant-demon is an ideal heavy 'tank' enemy whose gluttony theme can drive a swallow/devour attack.

citations.text: J. Collin de Plancy, *Dictionnaire Infernal* (1863 ed., ill. Louis Le Breton).
Book of Job 40:15–24.

title: Belphegor
work: Demonology, the Goetia & the Iconography of Devils
creator: Louis Le Breton
summary:
Le Breton's grotesque *Belphegor*, the demon of sloth and ingenious discoveries, enthroned on a privy in the 1863 *Dictionnaire Infernal*.

## Iconography
The horned, bearded, claw-handed demon sits upon an open latrine — a deliberately scatological throne. The image visualises the medieval etymology connecting Belphegor with the Moabite *Baal-Peor*, a god whose rites were imagined to involve excrement.

## Significance
Belphegor (from Baal-Peor of Numbers 25) was reinterpreted in Christian demonology as the demon who tempts mankind with ingenious inventions and the promise of effortless wealth, and was paired with the deadly sin of [[motif:sloth|sloth]]. The legend that he was sent up from Hell to test whether married happiness existed on earth was popularised by Machiavelli's tale and later by Milton among the fallen powers.

## For artists & game designers
A comic-grotesque demon: rank, lazy, and bound to a filthy throne — perfect for a sin-themed bestiary slot that reads as repulsive rather than fearsome.

citations.text: J. Collin de Plancy, *Dictionnaire Infernal* (1863 ed., ill. Louis Le Breton).
Numbers 25 (Baal-Peor); N. Machiavelli, *Belfagor arcidiavolo*.

title: Berith (Beal)
work: Demonology, the Goetia & the Iconography of Devils
creator: Louis Le Breton
summary:
Le Breton's *Berith*, the soldier-duke who rides a red horse, from the 1863 *Dictionnaire Infernal*.

## Iconography
Berith is depicted as a soldier in red armour wearing a golden crown, mounted on a red horse. The martial dress and crimson colouring follow the Goetic description of a 'great and terrible duke' appearing as a red-clad soldier riding a red horse.

## Significance
Berith is the twenty-eighth spirit of the *Ars Goetia*, a Great Duke commanding twenty-six legions. He answers truly of past, present, and future, can [[motif:alchemy|turn all metals into gold]], and gives dignities — yet the grimoire warns he is a notorious liar who must not be trusted. His name echoes the Canaanite *Baal-Berith* of Judges 8–9.

## For artists & game designers
A crowned red knight on a red steed is a clean, heraldic boss; the alchemical gold-making power supplies a tempting but treacherous reward hook.

citations.text: J. Collin de Plancy, *Dictionnaire Infernal* (1863 ed., ill. Louis Le Breton).
*The Lesser Key of Solomon: Ars Goetia*, spirit 28; Judges 8:33.
Wikimedia Commons

title: Buer
work: Demonology, the Goetia & the Iconography of Devils
creator: Louis Le Breton
summary:
Le Breton's celebrated *Buer*, the wheel-shaped Goetic president, from the 1863 *Dictionnaire Infernal* — one of the most recognisable demon images ever printed.

## Iconography
Buer is shown as a lion-faced head ringed by five radiating goat-like legs arranged like the spokes of a wheel, allowing him to roll in any direction. The bizarre rotational anatomy follows the Goetic note that he appears 'when the Sun is in Sagittarius.'

## Significance
Buer is the tenth spirit of the *Ars Goetia*, a Great President who teaches natural and moral philosophy, logic, and the virtues of herbs and plants, and who [[motif:healing|heals all distempers]] of man. He commands fifty legions. Le Breton's wheel-of-legs design has become an icon of demonological illustration, widely reproduced and parodied.

## For artists & game designers
The radially symmetric, rolling 'wheel beast' is a memorable enemy whose locomotion can drive unusual movement AI.

citations.text: J. Collin de Plancy, *Dictionnaire Infernal* (1863 ed., ill. Louis Le Breton).
*The Lesser Key of Solomon: Ars Goetia*, spirit 10.

title: The Devil (Le Diable), Tarot Trump XV
work: Demonology, the Goetia & the Iconography of Devils
creator: Tarot World Project (after the Marseille pattern)
rights: CC0 / Public domain. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A detail of *Le Diable* (The Devil), trump XV of the Tarot de Marseille, holding the infernal torch.

## Iconography
The [[motif:devil|Devil]] of the Marseille pattern stands frontal with bat-wings, stag or goat horns, a torch in one hand, and clawed feet on a pedestal to which two small horned, tailed figures are chained by the neck. The downward torch and the willing captives encode bondage to material desire.

## Significance
In the standard Tarot de Marseille (codified in 18th-century France from earlier Italian *trionfi*), trump XV follows Temptation/Death and Tower in the sequence of the soul's trials. Esoteric tarotists from Éliéphas Lévi onward read the card as Baphomet, matter, and the bondage of the appetites; in divination it signals attachment, addiction, or the shadow. It is the tarot's principal demonic image.

## For artists & game designers
A compact, symbol-dense devil — wings, torch, horns, chained captives — that reads as 'bondage/temptation' at a glance for card or tile art.

citations.text: Éliphas Lévi, *Dogme et rituel de la haute magie* (1856).
M. Dummett, *The Game of Tarot* (1980).

title: Abigor (Eligos)
work: Demonology, the Goetia & the Iconography of Devils
creator: Louis Le Breton
summary:
Le Breton's mounted knight-demon, the war-counsellor of the *Ars Goetia*, from the 1863 *Dictionnaire Infernal* (the Commons file is titled *Abigor*; the figure embodies the warrior-duke type also borne by Eligos).

## Iconography
The demon appears as an armoured knight bearing a lance, banner, or sceptre and riding a war-horse — in some printings a skeletal or monstrous steed. The chivalric panoply marks a duke who commands the arts of war.

## Significance
The warrior-dukes of the Goetia (Eligos, spirit 15, and Abigor/Eligor in variant lists) foresee the outcome of wars, reveal hidden things, and [[motif:favour of lords|procure the favour of lords]] and the loyalty of soldiers. They typify the grimoire's military spirits, consulted for strategy and command — a reminder that Renaissance and early-modern magic served princely as well as scholarly ambitions.

## For artists & game designers
A lance-bearing demon knight on a war-horse is the quintessential cavalry boss; tie his powers to morale and recruitment mechanics.

citations.text: J. Collin de Plancy, *Dictionnaire Infernal* (1863 ed., ill. Louis Le Breton).
*The Lesser Key of Solomon: Ars Goetia*, spirit 15.
Wikimedia Commons

title: Seal of Botis (Goetic Sigil)
work: Demonology, the Goetia & the Iconography of Devils
creator: Anonymous (after the Lemegeton)
summary:
The *Seal of Botis*, one of the seventy-two demon sigils of the *Ars Goetia*, the abstract glyph by which a spirit is summoned and bound.

## Iconography
The seal is a compact emblem of intersecting lines, loops, small crosses, and points enclosed within or beside a circle. Each Goetic sigil is unique, a non-figurative 'signature' or [[motif:demon seal|character]] of its spirit, meant to be engraved (ideally on the proper metal) and worn or displayed during the operation.

## Significance
The *Ars Goetia*, first book of the *Lemegeton* (Lesser Key of Solomon, 17th c.), assigns to each of its seventy-two spirits a name, rank, legions, office, and such a seal. Botis is the seventeenth spirit, a president and earl who appears first as a viper, then as a horned man with a sword, reconciling friends and foes. S. L. MacGregor Mathers and Aleister Crowley's 1904 edition standardised the seals for the modern occult revival.

## For artists & game designers
These sigils are a ready alphabet of summoning glyphs — assign one per creature for instantly readable 'binding circle' UI.

citations.text: S. L. MacGregor Mathers & A. Crowley (eds.), *The Goetia: The Lesser Key of Solomon the King* (1904).
*Lemegeton Clavicula Salomonis* (17th c.).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Witches' Sabbath (The Great He-Goat)
work: Demonology, the Goetia & the Iconography of Devils
creator: Francisco Goya
summary:
Francisco Goya's *Witches' Sabbath* (*El aquelarre* / *The Great He-Goat*), one of the Black Paintings from the Quinta del Sordo, c. 1821–23.

## Iconography
A monstrous silhouetted [[motif:black goat|he-goat]] — the Devil presiding as goat — looms at the left before a huddled, grimacing crowd of witches gathered in the dark. The frieze-like mass of frightened, deformed faces conveys collective hysteria rather than orgiastic revelry.

## Significance
Goya returned repeatedly to the sabbath theme (an earlier 1798 *Aquelarre* and the *Caprichos*), drawing on Spanish witch-lore and the inquisitorial trials of Logroño. Painted directly on his villa walls and never meant for public view, the Black Painting transforms the folkloric sabbath into a bleak meditation on superstition, fanaticism, and the herd. It is the most famous post-Enlightenment image of the goat-devil and his coven.

## For artists & game designers
A study in mood over monster: the Devil is mostly shadow, the horror carried by the crowd's faces — useful for atmospheric cult scenes.

citations.text: Francisco Goya, *El aquelarre / The Great He-Goat* (Black Paintings, c. 1821–23), Museo del Prado.
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Pact with the Devil (Compendium Maleficarum)
work: Demonology, the Goetia & the Iconography of Devils
creator: Francesco Maria Guazzo
summary:
A woodcut from Francesco Maria Guazzo's *Compendium Maleficarum* (1608) depicting a stage in the witch's pact with the Devil.

## Iconography
The scene shows the demon and the initiate enacting the formal compact — the new witch renouncing the faith, being inscribed in the [[motif:book of death|devil's book]], or receiving the diabolical mark. The crude, forceful woodcut style suits the inquisitorial subject.

## Significance
Guazzo, an Ambrosian friar, compiled the *Compendium Maleficarum* as a practical handbook for witch-hunters, illustrated with a famous series of woodcuts cataloguing the eleven stages of the pact: the renunciation of baptism, the *osculum infame*, the new name, the surrender of a piece of clothing, the oath within the circle, enrolment in the book of death, and more. These images crystallised the early-modern theology of the demonic pact that underwrote the witch trials.

## For artists & game designers
A primary source for ritual-pact imagery — use the staged 'contract' beats as a cutscene template for a soul-bargain quest.

citations.text: Francesco Maria Guazzo, *Compendium Maleficarum* (1608).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Satan Cast into Hell (Hell-mouth)
work: Demonology, the Goetia & the Iconography of Devils
creator: Anonymous
rights: CC BY 4.0. Wellcome Collection. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A print of *Satan thrown into Hell* at the Last Judgement, deploying the medieval [[motif:hellmouth|Hell-mouth]] motif (Wellcome Collection).

## Iconography
Hell is figured as the gaping, fanged maw of a vast beast — the jaws of Leviathan — into which Satan and the damned are hurled amid flames and tormenting demons. The animal mouth swallows sinners whole, its teeth framing the fiery interior.

## Significance
The Hell-mouth, derived from the Leviathan of Job and Isaiah's image of Sheol opening its jaws, became one of the most enduring inventions of medieval Christian art — from Anglo-Saxon manuscripts to the *Hortus Deliciarum*, doom paintings, and mystery-play stage machinery that belched smoke and sinners. It localised damnation as ingestion by a monster, a vivid pedagogical terror linked to the Last Judgement and the fall of the rebel angels.

## For artists & game designers
The ur-design for a 'gate to Hell' — a literal monstrous mouth as portal, ideal for a dungeon entrance or boss arena.

citations.text: Gary D. Schmidt, *The Iconography of the Mouth of Hell* (1995).
Wellcome Collection (CC BY 4.0).
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Nightmare (Der Alp)
work: Demonology, the Goetia & the Iconography of Devils
creator: Henry Fuseli (Johann Heinrich Füssli)
summary:
Henry Fuseli's *Nightmare* (here the 1810 variant, *Der Alp leaves the bed of two sleeping women*), the iconic Romantic image of the incubus demon.

## Iconography
A squat, ape-like [[motif:incubus|incubus]] crouches on the breast of a sleeping woman flung backward in abandon, while a blind-eyed spectral horse — the 'night-mare' — thrusts its head through the curtains. The demon's weight on the chest visualises the crushing oppression of sleep paralysis.

## Significance
Fuseli's first *Nightmare* (1781) was a sensation; he repeated the theme in several versions. The painting fuses folklore — the *Mahr*/*Alp* night-demon that sits on sleepers and the incubus that assaults women in their sleep — with a charged erotic and psychological subtext later prized by Freud (a print of it hung in his study). It remains the defining modern depiction of demonic nocturnal oppression.

## For artists & game designers
The template for a sleep/paralysis horror beat — a heavy demon perched on a victim's chest, paired with an uncanny animal omen.

citations.text: Henry Fuseli, *The Nightmare* (1781 and later versions).
N. Powell, *Fuseli: The Nightmare* (1973).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Léonard, Grand Master of the Sabbath
work: Demonology, the Goetia & the Iconography of Devils
creator: Louis Le Breton
summary:
Le Breton's *Léonard*, the great black goat who presides over the witches' sabbath, in the 1863 *Dictionnaire Infernal*.

## Iconography
Léonard appears as a three-horned goat with a fox-like or human face, standing upright. The three horns — one burning between the others — and the goat's body crystallise the inquisitorial stereotype of the devil worshipped at the [[motif:witches sabbath|sabbath]].

## Significance
In French witch-trial demonology Léonard (the 'Grand Master Léonard') was the inspector-general of black magic and demon of the sabbath, before whom witches performed the *osculum infame*, the obscene kiss. He embodies the early-modern construction of the goat-devil presiding over the nocturnal assembly, a figure elaborated by demonologists such as Pierre de Lancre. Le Breton fixed the visual type later echoed by Goya and Baphomet imagery.

## For artists & game designers
The upright black goat is the archetypal cult-leader devil — use for a sabbath-boss whose ritual buffs lesser witch enemies.

citations.text: J. Collin de Plancy, *Dictionnaire Infernal* (1863 ed., ill. Louis Le Breton).
Pierre de Lancre, *Tableau de l'inconstance des mauvais anges* (1612).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Lucifer
work: Demonology, the Goetia & the Iconography of Devils
creator: Louis Le Breton
summary:
Le Breton's *Lucifer*, the fallen light-bringer and emperor of Hell, in the 1863 *Dictionnaire Infernal*.

## Iconography
Lucifer is rendered as a winged, horned demon, his angelic origin still legible in his form even as bat-wings and bestial features mark his fall. The image presents him as a ruler rather than a tormentor.

## Significance
Lucifer ('light-bearer') translates the Hebrew *Helel ben Shahar*, the 'morning star' of Isaiah 14 cast down for [[motif:pride|pride]]. Conflated with Satan by patristic writers and immortalised as the tragic rebel of Milton's *Paradise Lost*, he heads many demonological hierarchies as emperor of Hell, distinct in some schemes from Satan and Beelzebub. The Le Breton plate gave the literary archfiend a definite Victorian-era face.

## For artists & game designers
The ruined-angel design — beautiful proportions corrupted by bat-wings and horns — is the template for a sympathetic final antagonist.

citations.text: J. Collin de Plancy, *Dictionnaire Infernal* (1863 ed., ill. Louis Le Breton).
Isaiah 14:12; J. Milton, *Paradise Lost*.
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Devil of the Codex Gigas
work: Demonology, the Goetia & the Iconography of Devils
creator: Herman the Recluse (attrib.)
rights: CC0 / Public domain. National Library of Sweden. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
The famous full-page portrait of the Devil in the *Codex Gigas* ('Giant Book' / Devil's Bible), the largest surviving medieval manuscript.

## Iconography
The [[motif:devil|Devil]] squats frontally, crowned with two great horns, a green face with red eyes, a forked red tongue, clawed hands and feet, and an ermine loincloth. The crouching, symmetrical pose and bald cranium give him a uniquely heraldic, almost frog-like menace, set against an empty arched frame.

## Significance
Produced in a Bohemian Benedictine monastery in the early 13th century, the *Codex Gigas* contains the entire Vulgate plus Josephus, Isidore, exorcism formulae, and a medical compendium. Legend held that a monk facing death walled-up sold his soul to finish it in a single night, hence the devil portrait facing a page on confession and exorcism. It is the most reproduced of all medieval manuscript devils.

## For artists & game designers
A rare full-figure medieval devil with a distinctive ermine-and-horns costume — an authentic alternative to the generic red demon.

citations.text: *Codex Gigas* (early 13th c.), National Library of Sweden, MS A 148.
Wikimedia Commons

title: Moloch
work: Demonology, the Goetia & the Iconography of Devils
creator: Louis Le Breton
summary:
Le Breton's crowned and horned *Moloch*, the demon-prince associated with child sacrifice, in the 1863 *Dictionnaire Infernal*.

## Iconography
Moloch is shown as a crowned, regal demon with horns, an aged bearded face, and clawed hands. The crown and bearing signal his rank as a great prince of Hell; the iconography draws on the Bible's account of a deity to whom children were 'passed through the fire.'

## Significance
Moloch (Molech) appears in Leviticus and Kings as an Ammonite god condemned for the sacrifice of children in the valley of Hinnom (Gehenna). Milton ranks him first among the fallen angels in *Paradise Lost*, 'horrid king besmeared with blood / Of human sacrifice.' In modern usage he became a byword for systems that devour the young, a reading amplified by [[motif:child sacrifice|the brazen-idol legend]].

## For artists & game designers
A somber, regal antagonist tied to a sacrificial-altar mechanic — Moloch works as a cult deity rather than a brawler.

citations.text: J. Collin de Plancy, *Dictionnaire Infernal* (1863 ed., ill. Louis Le Breton).
Leviticus 18:21; J. Milton, *Paradise Lost*, Book I.
Wikimedia Commons

title: A Scholar in His Study ('Faust')
work: Demonology, the Goetia & the Iconography of Devils
creator: Rembrandt van Rijn
rights: CC0 / Public domain. The Metropolitan Museum of Art. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
Rembrandt's enigmatic etching long known as *Faust*, the supreme image of the scholar-magician confronted by a conjured vision.

## Iconography
A scholar in his cluttered study turns from his desk toward a window where a radiant disc has appeared, inscribed with a cabbalistic anagram (INRI / mystical letters) and pierced by a hand pointing to a mirror. The luminous apparition stands for the [[motif:magic apparition|spirit or revelation]] summoned by the magus.

## Significance
Though Rembrandt gave it no title, the print was associated with the Faust legend by the 18th century and chosen by Goethe to illustrate the first edition of his *Faust*. Scholars (e.g. H. van de Waal) read the glowing monogram as a meditation on divine versus diabolical knowledge — the very ambiguity at the heart of the pact narrative, where forbidden learning is bought at the price of the soul.

## For artists & game designers
A masterclass in depicting a summoning by light alone — the unseen spirit is implied by a glowing sigil-disc, not a monster.

citations.text: H. van de Waal, studies on Rembrandt's 'Faust' etching.
The Metropolitan Museum of Art (CC0).
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Temptation of St Anthony
work: Demonology, the Goetia & the Iconography of Devils
creator: Martin Schongauer
summary:
Martin Schongauer's celebrated engraving of *The Temptation of St Anthony*, in which a swarm of demons lifts and torments the desert hermit in mid-air.

## Iconography
St Anthony is borne aloft, clutching his book, while a ring of grotesque [[motif:hybrid monsters|hybrid demons]] — feathered, scaled, beaked, horned, and clawed — beat, bite, and drag at him. Each fiend is a virtuoso assemblage of animal parts, the whole forming a churning wheel of torment.

## Significance
The scene illustrates the Life of St Anthony by Athanasius, the foundational text of Christian eremitic struggle against demonic assault. Schongauer's print (c. 1470s) was so admired that the young Michelangelo copied it in paint. It became the template for centuries of demon-swarm imagery, from Grünewald's Isenheim Altarpiece to Callot, and exemplifies the late-medieval imagination of the devil as a multiplicity of monstrous forms.

## For artists & game designers
The definitive reference for designing a 'demon swarm' encounter — every monster is a unique kitbash of beast parts.

citations.text: Athanasius, *Life of St Anthony*.
Martin Schongauer, *The Temptation of St Anthony* (engraving, c. 1470–75).

title: Stolas
work: Demonology, the Goetia & the Iconography of Devils
creator: Louis Le Breton
summary:
Le Breton's *Stolas*, the crowned-owl prince of the *Ars Goetia*, from the 1863 *Dictionnaire Infernal*.

## Iconography
Stolas is shown as a great horned owl or long-legged crowned night-raven. The owl form follows the Goetic description of a powerful prince who first appears 'in the form of a night raven' before taking human shape.

## Significance
Stolas (Stolos) is the thirty-sixth spirit of the *Ars Goetia*, a Great Prince commanding twenty-six legions, who teaches [[motif:astronomy|astronomy]] and the properties of herbs and precious stones. He belongs to the class of demons prized as tutors of natural science rather than as warriors, reflecting the grimoire tradition's fascination with hidden knowledge.

## For artists & game designers
A dignified owl-demon makes an excellent scholarly familiar or quest-giver who trades arcane lore for a price.

citations.text: J. Collin de Plancy, *Dictionnaire Infernal* (1863 ed., ill. Louis Le Breton).
*The Lesser Key of Solomon: Ars Goetia*, spirit 36.
