title: The Cage of the Sacred Chickens (Auspices)
creator: Anonymous (after a Roman model)
summary:
An engraving of the *cage of the sacred chickens* used by Roman augurs to take the auspices, the *auspicia ex tripudiis*.

## Iconography
The plate shows the portable coop in which the sacred poultry were kept. In practice the *pullarius* (chicken-keeper) released the birds and scattered grain: how eagerly they ate, and whether food fell from their beaks to strike the ground (the *tripudium solistimum*), determined whether the gods approved an undertaking.

## Significance
Roman [[motif:augury|augury]] was a state discipline: no major public action — battle, election, assembly — proceeded without favourable auspices read from the flight, cries, or feeding of birds. The chicken-omen was the form most used on campaign for its portability. The famous anecdote of the consul Publius Claudius Pulcher, who threw the unwilling chickens overboard before his defeat at Drepana (249 BCE), shows how seriously the omens were taken.

## For artists & game designers
A low-tech, high-stakes oracle: feed the birds, read the result — a clean binary omen mechanic with rich flavour.

citations.text: Cicero, *De Divinatione*; Livy, *Ab Urbe Condita*.
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Fortune Teller (Caravaggio)
creator: Caravaggio (Michelangelo Merisi)
summary:
Caravaggio's *The Fortune Teller* (*La Buona Ventura*, c. 1595), in which a young gallant has his palm read — and his ring quietly stolen — by a smiling Romani woman.

## Iconography
A finely dressed youth offers his hand to a [[motif:palmistry|palm-reader]] who gazes into his eyes as she traces his palm; her other hand slips the ring from his finger. The exchange of glances and the hidden theft make the deception the true subject. The half-length, dramatically lit figures are a hallmark of Caravaggio's early naturalism.

## Significance
The picture launched a hugely influential genre of fortune-teller and cardsharp scenes across Baroque Europe (Vouet, Valentin, La Tour, the Le Nain). It reflects the early-modern stereotype of the wandering Romani diviner as a charming swindler, and the moralising theme of youth gulled by sensual distraction. Caravaggio painted at least two versions (Capitoline, Rome; Louvre, Paris).

## For artists & game designers
The canonical 'con artist diviner' beat — fortune-telling as misdirection while the real theft happens in plain sight.

citations.text: Caravaggio, *The Fortune Teller* (c. 1595), Pinacoteca Capitolina, Rome.
Wikimedia Commons

title: Crystal Gazing (fortune-telling poster)
creator: Anonymous (advertising lithograph)
summary:
A turn-of-the-century advertising poster for a 'crystal gazing' fortune-telling act ('Chandra Yogi'), illustrating the popular stage-magic afterlife of crystallomancy.

## Iconography
A performer in 'oriental' costume gazes into a crystal ball, the standard prop of [[motif:crystal gazing|crystallomancy]]. The exoticising imagery — turban, robes, an air of Eastern mystery — is typical of the commercial seer and mind-reading acts that toured theatres and fairs.

## Significance
While crystal-gazing descends from learned Renaissance scrying (Dee's shew-stones) and folk practice, by the nineteenth century it had become a fixture of spiritualist parlours, fairground fortune-tellers, and vaudeville mentalism. Posters like this document the popularisation and theatrical commodification of divination — the crystal ball cemented as the universal shorthand for telling the future. The 'Oriental' branding reflects the era's orientalist marketing of occult wonder.

## For artists & game designers
The definitive 'fortune-teller booth' visual language — crystal ball, robes, exotic signage — for a carnival-seer scene.

citations.text: On stage scrying and mentalism, see histories of spiritualism and the magic theatre.
Wikimedia Commons

title: John Dee's Obsidian Mirror (case)
creator: Aztec; later owned by John Dee
rights: CC0 / Public domain. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
The obsidian mirror associated with the Elizabethan magus John Dee, an Aztec ritual object later used for scrying (British Museum; the photograph shows the mirror in its case).

## Iconography
The object is a disc of polished black volcanic glass with a small pierced handle-tab. Its mirror-dark surface is the classic [[motif:scrying|scrying]] speculum — a 'shew-stone' into which the seer gazes to summon visions. Such mirrors were also kept in fitted cases, as here.

## Significance
The mirror is a *tezcatlipoca* device — Aztec obsidian mirrors were sacred to the 'Smoking Mirror' god — brought to Europe after the conquest of Mexico. It entered the collection of John Dee, who with his scryer Edward Kelley conducted the 'angelic conversations' that produced the Enochian system. Long held in the British Museum and once owned by Horace Walpole, it is the most famous physical instrument of Renaissance crystallomancy and a striking case of New-World ritual objects absorbed into European occult practice.

## For artists & game designers
A real, dateable scrying artefact — a black glass disc as a 'vision portal' prop with a genuine cross-cultural backstory.

citations.text: British Museum, obsidian mirror (Dee); on Dee & Kelley, D. Harkness, *John Dee's Conversations with Angels* (1999).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Human and Animal Physiognomies (della Porta)
creator: After Giambattista della Porta
rights: CC BY 4.0. Wellcome Collection. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A plate after Giambattista della Porta's *De humana physiognomonia* (1586), juxtaposing human profiles with animal heads to argue a correspondence of form and character (Wellcome Collection).

## Iconography
Human faces are set beside the heads of beasts — a man paired with a ram, an ox, a lion, an owl — so that shared contours (a heavy brow, a snub nose, a jutting jaw) suggest a shared temperament. The comparison is the signature device of [[motif:physiognomy|zoomorphic physiognomy]].

## Significance
della Porta revived the ancient pseudo-Aristotelian *Physiognomonica*, systematising the reading of character from outward form and especially the human-animal analogy. His plates fixed a visual method that ran on through Charles Le Brun's lectures to Lavater's *Essays on Physiognomy* and, much later, into the discredited racial 'sciences' of the nineteenth century. As divination, physiognomy claimed to read fate and disposition written in the face.

## For artists & game designers
The original 'beast-aspect' character chart: pair each face with an animal to telegraph temperament at a glance.

citations.text: G. della Porta, *De humana physiognomonia* (1586).
Wellcome Collection (CC BY 4.0).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Sikidy Geomantic Divination
creator: Anonymous (Malagasy)
summary:
A photograph (c. 1900) of *sikidy*, the Malagasy geomantic divination in which a diviner generates a tableau of binary figures from arranged seeds.

## Iconography
The diviner lays out rows of seeds or beans, reducing each pile to a one-or-two remainder to build columns of [[motif:geomancy|geomantic figures]] — the same odd/even dot-patterns used across the Old World geomantic family. The resulting grid (the *toetry*) is then read for the questioner's fate.

## Significance
Sikidy is the East African and Malagasy branch of the geomantic tradition that runs from Arabic *'ilm al-raml* ('the science of the sand') through medieval Latin *geomantia* (Hugh of Santalla, Pietro d'Abano) to European fortune-telling. All share the sixteen tetragram figures generated by tallying marks into odd or even. The example shows the living, non-European face of a divinatory system Europe imported and Latinised, and underlines how widely the binary geomantic method travelled.

## For artists & game designers
A pure binary oracle — random marks collapse to sixteen named figures; trivial to implement and historically deep.

citations.text: M. Bloch, on Malagasy sikidy; S. Skinner, *Geomancy in Theory and Practice*.
Wikimedia Commons

title: Haruspices Interpreting Caesar's Dream
creator: Anonymous (manuscript illumination)
rights: CC0 / Public domain. British Library. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A manuscript miniature (British Library, Royal 16 G VIII) showing diviners interpreting an omen or dream for Julius Caesar.

## Iconography
Caesar is depicted attended by [[motif:haruspicy|haruspices]] or soothsayers who read the signs and deliver their counsel. The medieval illuminator dresses the antique diviners in contemporary costume, transposing the Roman art of reading entrails and dreams into a chivalric setting.

## Significance
The scene belongs to a tradition of vernacular histories of Caesar (the *Faits des Romains* and related texts) much copied in the later Middle Ages, in which classical divination is retold for a courtly audience. It illustrates the long medieval afterlife of Roman *haruspicy* and *oneiromancy*, and recalls the warnings — the soothsayer's 'Beware the Ides of March,' Calpurnia's dream — that Caesar famously disregarded.

## For artists & game designers
A template for the 'court diviner' scene: a ruler flanked by seers delivering a portent he may heed or ignore.

citations.text: London, British Library, Royal MS 16 G VIII, f. 39.
Suetonius, *Divus Iulius*; Plutarch, *Life of Caesar*.
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Fortune Teller (Georges de La Tour)
creator: Georges de La Tour
rights: Public domain. The Metropolitan Museum of Art. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
Georges de La Tour's *The Fortune Teller* (c. 1630s, Metropolitan Museum of Art), a richly costumed scene of a young man robbed while his fortune is told.

## Iconography
An old [[motif:fortune-telling|fortune-teller]] takes the youth's coin to 'cross his palm with silver' while, on either side, her young accomplices pick his pocket and cut a medal from its chain. The youth's distracted gaze and the converging hands of the thieves stage a slow, theatrical robbery in brilliant brocades and frozen glances.

## Significance
La Tour reworks the Caravaggesque fortune-teller theme that had spread north from Rome, turning it into a tableau of multiple deception and worldly warning. The painting carries a partly hidden inscription naming the artist and Lunéville. It exemplifies the moralised genre of the duped innocent and remains one of the most celebrated treatments of the diviner-as-trickster — an image of fortune-telling as social danger rather than true prophecy.

## For artists & game designers
A masterclass in staging a coordinated theft inside a divination scene — every accomplice's hand has a job.

citations.text: Georges de La Tour, *The Fortune Teller* (c. 1630s), The Metropolitan Museum of Art.
Wikimedia Commons

title: Lavater, Essays on Physiognomy (design plate)
creator: After Johann Caspar Lavater
rights: CC BY 4.0. Wellcome Collection. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A design plate from an English edition of Johann Caspar Lavater's *Essays on Physiognomy*, the work that made face-reading a fashionable late-Enlightenment science (Wellcome Collection).

## Iconography
The plate presents a row of profile heads and silhouettes for comparative analysis — the slope of a forehead, the line of a nose, the set of a mouth read as indices of intellect and morality. Lavater favoured the cut-paper [[motif:silhouette|silhouette]] as the purest record of a profile's contour.

## Significance
Lavater's *Physiognomische Fragmente* (1775–78), translated and lavishly engraved across Europe, claimed that inner character is legibly written in outward form, especially the face in profile. Hugely popular, it drew sharp criticism from Lichtenberg and others, yet seeded both the silhouette portrait craze and the later quasi-sciences of phrenology and criminal anthropology. As a divinatory art it promised to read a person's soul and destiny from their features.

## For artists & game designers
Silhouette-as-character: a profile cut-out carrying moral meaning is a strong stylised portrait device for a 'judge the stranger' mechanic.

citations.text: J. C. Lavater, *Essays on Physiognomy* (Eng. ed., 1789–98).
Wellcome Collection (CC BY 4.0).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Petit Lenormand Fortune-Telling Cards
creator: After Marie Anne Lenormand (tradition)
summary:
A card from the *Petit Lenormand*, the 36-card cartomantic deck named for the celebrated French fortune-teller Marie Anne Lenormand.

## Iconography
Each Lenormand card bears a single emblematic symbol — the Ship, the Tree, the Scythe, the Tower, the Stars, the Clover — often with a small inset playing card. The symbols are read in combination, neighbouring cards modifying one another, rather than through the elaborate single-card symbolism of tarot.

## Significance
Marie Anne Lenormand (1772–1843) was the most famous fortune-teller of Napoleonic France, reputed to have read for Joséphine and Robespierre. The decks published after her death under her name codified a distinct system of [[motif:cartomancy|cartomancy]] — simpler, more concrete, and grid-read (the *Grand Tableau*) — that remains popular across Europe alongside tarot. It represents the nineteenth-century commercialisation of card divination for a mass public.

## For artists & game designers
A compact symbol-set (36 plain emblems) ideal for a readable, modular divination minigame distinct from tarot's heavier iconography.

title: Misero (The Beggar) — Mantegna Tarocchi
creator: Master of the E-Series Tarocchi (so-called 'Mantegna')
rights: CC0 / Public domain. Rijksmuseum. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
*Misero* (the Beggar), the lowest of the fifty cards of the so-called *Mantegna Tarocchi*, an engraved didactic series of c. 1465 (Rijksmuseum impression).

## Iconography
A ragged beggar leans on a staff, accompanied by two dogs — the bottom rung of the 'Conditions of Man.' He opens the first decade (E1) of the series, beneath the Servant, Artisan, Merchant, and so up to the Emperor and Pope. The image is plain, labelled, and emblematic.

## Significance
The *Mantegna Tarocchi* is not a true playing tarot but an encyclopaedic engraved set of fifty cards in five decades — the [[motif:estates of man|estates of man]], the Muses and Apollo, the Liberal Arts, the cosmic principles, and the planets and spheres. Wrongly attributed to Mantegna, it is a North-Italian humanist teaching device of the Ferrarese circle, and an essential witness to how the early image-systems behind tarot encoded a hierarchical, divinatory map of the cosmos. *Misero* fixes the bottom of that ladder of fortune.

## For artists & game designers
A clean labelled 'rank card' from the very dawn of tarot imagery — useful as a historic, pre-Waite alternative to modern decks.

citations.text: M. Dummett, *The Game of Tarot* (1980).

title: XIII (Death / l'Arcane sans nom) — Tarot de Marseille
creator: Nicolas Conver (after); Tarot World Project (photo)
rights: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Tarot World Project, after the 1760 Conver deck). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
Trump XIII of the Tarot de Marseille — the skeletal reaper traditionally called Death, the 'arcane sans nom,' in the Nicolas Conver pattern of 1760.

## Iconography
A black-boned skeleton wields a scythe, mowing a field strewn with severed heads, hands, and feet that sprout afresh from the dark soil. In the Marseille tradition the card is famously left *unnamed* on many decks (hence *l'arcane sans nom*), reinforcing its taboo. The sprouting limbs hint at regeneration as much as ending.

## Significance
Trump XIII belongs to the tarot's central sequence of trials and transformations and descends from the medieval *Danse Macabre* and *memento mori* tradition. Esoteric tarotists from Court de Gébelin and Éliphas Lévi onward read it not as literal death but as [[motif:transformation|transformation]], the clearing-away that precedes renewal. It is the most iconic and most superstitiously regarded card of the deck.

## For artists & game designers
The scythe-skeleton over a sprouting field is the classic 'death = change' symbol — useful where literal mortality should read as transition.

title: La Lune (The Moon) — Tarot de Marseille XVIII
creator: Nicolas Conver (after); Tarot World Project (photo)
rights: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Tarot World Project, after the 1760 Conver deck). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
*La Lune* (The Moon), trump XVIII of the Tarot de Marseille, in the Nicolas Conver pattern of 1760.

## Iconography
A great face-in-the-moon sheds drops of light over a landscape where two dogs (or a dog and a wolf) bay upward, two towers flank the horizon, and a crayfish or crustacean crawls from a pool below. The composition reads as a nocturnal world of instinct, water, and threshold.

## Significance
The Moon, second of the celestial triad, traditionally signifies [[motif:illusion|illusion]], the unconscious, dreams, and the deceptive light that obscures as much as it reveals. The baying dogs and the creature emerging from the deep were read by esoteric tarotists as the animal soul and the path through dark waters. In divination it warns of confusion, hidden enemies, and the uncertain path that must nonetheless be travelled.

## For artists & game designers
The baying-dogs-and-crayfish moonscape is a ready 'uncanny night / illusion' tableau for a dream or threshold scene.

citations.text: É. Lévi, *Dogme et rituel de la haute magie* (1856).

title: L'Étoile (The Star) — Tarot de Marseille XVII
creator: Nicolas Conver (after); Tarot World Project (photo)
rights: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Tarot World Project, after the 1760 Conver deck). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
*L'Étoile* (The Star), trump XVII of the Tarot de Marseille, in the Nicolas Conver pattern of 1760.

## Iconography
A nude woman kneels by a stream, pouring water from two ewers — one onto the land, one back into the water — beneath a great central star surrounded by seven lesser stars, with a bird perched in a tree. The endless pouring evokes renewal, flow, and replenishment.

## Significance
The Star comes after the Tower in the sequence, beginning the celestial triad of [[motif:hope|Star, Moon, and Sun]] that follows catastrophe with hope and guidance. Esoteric tarotists associated her with the goddess pouring the waters of life, with hope and inspiration, and with astral influence descending to earth. The eight-star arrangement was variously read as the planets, the Pleiades, or the waters above and below.

## For artists & game designers
The water-pouring star-maiden is the tarot's 'hope/renewal' card — a serene counterpoint to the Tower's disaster.

citations.text: É. Lévi, *Dogme et rituel de la haute magie* (1856).

title: La Maison-Dieu (The Tower) — Tarot de Marseille
creator: Anonymous (Tarot de Marseille pattern, drawing)
rights: Public domain. Bibliothèque nationale de France. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
*La Maison-Dieu* (The Tower), trump XVI of the Tarot de Marseille, here a drawing after the standard pattern (Bibliothèque nationale de France).

## Iconography
A tall tower is struck at its crown by a bolt from the heavens; the crenellated top flies off and two figures tumble headlong amid a shower of coloured discs or flames. The French name *La Maison-Dieu* ('the House of God') is an old crux — possibly a corruption referring to a hospice, an almshouse, or the fallen Tower of Babel.

## Significance
Trump XVI follows the Devil in the sequence and signals sudden [[motif:catastrophe|catastrophe]] — the violent overthrow of pride, false structures, or illusion by a stroke from above. Esoteric readers linked it to Babel, to the lightning of divine judgement, and to the necessary shattering that precedes spiritual renewal (the Star, Moon, and Sun follow). It is the tarot's image of crisis and abrupt revelation.

## For artists & game designers
The lightning-struck tower with falling figures is the universal 'sudden disaster' icon — drop it on any moment of structural collapse.

citations.text: M. Dummett, *The Game of Tarot* (1980).

title: La Roue de Fortune — Tarot de Marseille X
creator: Nicolas Conver (after); Tarot World Project (photo)
rights: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Tarot World Project, after the 1760 Conver deck). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
*La Roue de Fortune*, trump X of the Tarot de Marseille, in the pattern of Nicolas Conver's 1760 Marseille deck.

## Iconography
A great wheel turns, its rim ridden by hybrid creatures: one ascends, one descends head-down, and a crowned beast (often sphinx-like) is poised at the top with a sword. The image fuses the [[motif:wheel of fortune|Wheel of Fortune]] of medieval *Rota Fortunae* iconography with the tarot trump's animal riders.

## Significance
The Tarot de Marseille is the standardised woodcut pattern that crystallised in 17th–18th-century France and became the basis of all Western occult tarot. Trump X transmits the ancient and medieval image of Fortune's wheel — the blind goddess raising and casting down kings (Boethius, *De consolatione*) — into the tarot's allegorical sequence, where it signals cycles, chance, and reversal of fate. The Conver deck of 1760 is the most influential single edition of the Marseille pattern.

## For artists & game designers
The purest 'turn of fortune' card: a wheel with rising/falling figures, instantly legible as a luck or random-event icon.

citations.text: Boethius, *De consolatione philosophiae*.
M. Dummett, *The Game of Tarot* (1980).

title: Metoposcopia (Forehead-Line Divination)
creator: Samuel Fuchs
rights: CC BY 4.0. Wellcome Collection. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A face diagram from Samuel Fuchs's *Metoposcopia* (1615), in which the lines of the forehead are read as planetary signs of character and fate (Wellcome Collection).

## Iconography
A human face is overlaid with horizontal [[motif:forehead lines|forehead lines]], each assigned to one of the seven planets — Saturn highest, then Jupiter, Mars, Sun, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon lowest near the brows. The depth, breaks, and crossings of these lines are interpreted as the heavens' imprint on the individual.

## Significance
Metoposcopy — a specialised offshoot of physiognomy — was given its classic form by Girolamo Cardano, whose posthumous *Metoposcopia* (1658) supplied hundreds of forehead diagrams with prognostications. Fuchs's earlier treatise belongs to the same tradition that mapped the seven planetary lines across the brow. It exemplifies the early-modern conviction that astral influence is inscribed on the body and can be read like a horoscope from the skin itself.

## For artists & game designers
A seven-line 'planetary forehead' overlay is a compact, exotic divination graphic for a fortune-teller NPC.

G. Cardano, *Metoposcopia* (1658).

title: Chiromancy Hand (De Occulta Philosophia)
creator: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa
summary:
A chiromantic hand diagram associated with Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa's *De Occulta Philosophia*, mapping the lines and mounts of the palm to the planets.

## Iconography
The open palm is overlaid with named [[motif:chiromancy|lines]] (life, head, heart, the Girdle of Venus) and the fleshy *mounts* at the base of each finger and the thumb, each mount assigned to a planet — Jupiter, Saturn, Apollo/Sun, Mercury, Venus, the Moon, and the Mars regions. The diagram turns the hand into an astrological microcosm.

## Significance
Chiromancy (palmistry) treated the hand as a legible text written by the heavens at birth. Agrippa's three-book *De Occulta Philosophia* (1533) systematised Renaissance magic and gave the palmistry-astrology correspondence its standard learned form, building on earlier authors such as Bartolommeo della Rocca (Cocles). The planetary mounts remain the backbone of palmistry to this day.

## For artists & game designers
The canonical palm-map — labelled mounts and lines tied to planets — works directly as a diegetic divination chart or character-sheet overlay.

citations.text: H. C. Agrippa, *De Occulta Philosophia libri tres* (1533).

title: The Liver of Piacenza
creator: Etruscan (anonymous)
rights: CC0 / Public domain. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
The *Fegato di Piacenza*, a life-size Etruscan bronze model of a sheep's liver inscribed as a diviner's reference chart, c. 100 BCE.

## Iconography
The convex bronze is divided into regions by incised lines, each cell bearing the abbreviated name of an Etruscan deity. The outer rim carries sixteen divisions corresponding to the sixteen houses of the Etruscan sky; the central lobes (the *processus pyramidalis* and gall-bladder) are also labelled. It is, in effect, a map of the cosmos projected onto an organ.

## Significance
The object is the key surviving artefact of Etruscan [[motif:haruspicy|hepatoscopy]] — divination by reading the liver of a sacrificed animal, the discipline the Romans inherited as the *haruspices*' art. Its sixteenfold division of the heavens parallels the cosmological scheme described by Martianus Capella and Pliny, and it links Etruscan practice to the older Mesopotamian liver-omen tradition. It remains the primary teaching model for understanding how ancient diviners correlated celestial regions with portions of the entrails.

## For artists & game designers
A ready-made 'divination interface': a labelled organ-map whose zones map to gods and sky-houses — perfect for an augury minigame UI.

citations.text: L. B. van der Meer, *The Bronze Liver of Piacenza* (1987).

title: Thalia — Mantegna Tarocchi (Muse)
creator: Master of the E-Series Tarocchi (so-called 'Mantegna')
rights: CC0 / Public domain. Cleveland Museum of Art. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
*Thalia*, muse of comedy and pastoral poetry, from the second decade (Apollo and the Muses) of the *Mantegna Tarocchi*, c. 1465 (Cleveland Museum of Art).

## Iconography
Thalia stands as a graceful classical figure, her attribute marking her as the [[motif:muse|muse]] of comedy and bucolic verse. She belongs to the 'D' decade (E11–E20) that ranges Apollo and the nine Muses, the second tier of the fifty-card system above the estates of man.

## Significance
The Muse decade displays the Ferrarese humanists' revival of classical learning within an ordered, ascending scheme — from the conditions of mortal life up through the arts, the cosmos, and the heavens. The fine engraving, once credited to Mantegna himself, transmits the antique iconography of the Muses to Renaissance Europe and shows tarot's early imagery as a curriculum of knowledge rather than a mere game. Albrecht Dürer is known to have copied figures from the series.

## For artists & game designers
An authentic 15th-century Muse figure — period reference for allegorical 'patron of an art' cards.

citations.text: J. A. Levenson et al., *Early Italian Engravings from the National Gallery of Art* (1973).

title: Cary-Yale Visconti Tarot card
creator: Bonifacio Bembo (attrib.)
summary:
A card from the Cary-Yale (Visconti di Modrone) tarot, c. 1440s, among the earliest surviving hand-painted tarot decks, attributed to Bonifacio Bembo for the Milanese court.

## Iconography
The card is hand-painted on a tooled [[motif:gold ground|gold ground]], in the luxurious International Gothic manner of the Visconti-Sforza workshop. The Cary-Yale deck is unusually expanded, including extra court figures (a Female Knight and Page alongside the male) and theological-virtue trumps not found in the standard later pattern.

## Significance
The Visconti and Visconti-Sforza decks are the foundational monuments of tarot: bespoke *trionfi* (triumph) cards made for the rulers of Milan in the mid-fifteenth century, long before any documented use for fortune-telling. They preserve the original trump iconography — the Wheel, Death, the Tower, the World — that the printed Tarot de Marseille would later standardise and that occultists would, from the 18th century, reinterpret as a divinatory book of wisdom.

## For artists & game designers
The gold-ground, courtly origin of tarot — a reference for 'luxury commissioned deck' art distinct from cheap printed cards.

citations.text: M. Dummett, *The Visconti-Sforza Tarot Cards* (1986).

title: Bagua Mirror Talismans (Eight Trigrams)
work: Eastern Esoterica: Magic & Inner Alchemy of Asia
creator: Anonymous (Chinese; photo Physicist1204)
rights: CC0 / Public domain. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
Three *bagua* mirror talismans, octagonal protective charms displaying the Eight Trigrams arranged around a central mirror.

## Iconography
Each charm is an octagon bearing the eight three-line [[motif:eight trigrams|trigrams]] (☰ Qian, ☷ Kun, ☵ Kan, ☲ Li, and the rest) around its rim, usually framing a *Taijitu* and a small convex, flat, or concave mirror at the centre. The arrangement shown is typically the 'Later Heaven' (King Wen) sequence used in feng shui.

## Significance
The *bagua* — eight trigrams formed from broken and unbroken lines — is the combinatorial heart of the *I Ching* and of Chinese correlative cosmology, each trigram keyed to a direction, element, season, family member, and bodily organ. Mounted with a mirror above a doorway, the bagua becomes an [[motif:apotropaic|apotropaic]] device that deflects malign *sha* energy in feng-shui practice. The object thus fuses divinatory cosmology with everyday domestic magic.

## For artists & game designers
An eight-fold directional key (trigram = element + compass point) usable as a ward icon or an attunement wheel.

citations.text: Richard J. Smith, *Fathoming the Cosmos and Ordering the World: The Yijing* (2008).

title: Fifty-Eight Wrathful Deities of the Bardo Thodol
work: Eastern Esoterica: Magic & Inner Alchemy of Asia
creator: Anonymous (Tibetan; rendering by Djampa)
summary:
A diagram of the fifty-eight wrathful deities encountered in the intermediate state (*bardo*) according to the *Bardo Thodol*, the so-called Tibetan Book of the Dead.

## Iconography
Ranks of flame-wreathed [[motif:wrathful deity|wrathful deities]] — *herukas* in union with consorts, animal-headed goddesses, and gatekeepers — are arrayed in their fixed iconographic order. With the forty-two peaceful deities they form the 'hundred peaceful and wrathful' that arise to the consciousness of the dying and dead.

## Significance
The *Bardo Thodol* ('Liberation Through Hearing in the Intermediate State') is a treasure-text (*terma*) of the Nyingma tradition, read aloud to guide the deceased through the visionary states between death and rebirth. The peaceful and wrathful deities are taught to be projections of the person's own mind; recognising them as such brings liberation, while reacting with fear drives one toward another rebirth. The text became globally famous through W. Y. Evans-Wentz's 1927 edition and shaped Western reception of Tibetan thought, including C. G. Jung's commentary.

## For artists & game designers
A fixed roster of 58 ordered apparitions — a ready 'judgement of the dead' gauntlet with named, designed forms.

citations.text: W. Y. Evans-Wentz (ed.), *The Tibetan Book of the Dead* (1927).

title: Bhavachakra (Wheel of Life), Tawang Monastery
work: Eastern Esoterica: Magic & Inner Alchemy of Asia
creator: Anonymous (Tibetan; photo Kingshuk Mondal)
rights: CC BY-SA 4.0 (photo Kingshuk Mondal). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A *Bhavachakra*, the Buddhist 'Wheel of Life,' painted at the entrance of Tawang Monastery — a diagram of cyclic existence held in the jaws of the lord of death.

## Iconography
The great wheel is clutched by [[motif:yama|Yama]], lord of death. At its hub spin the three poisons (cock, snake, pig: greed, hatred, delusion); the next ring shows beings rising and falling by karma; the broad band is divided into the [[motif:six realms|six realms]] of rebirth (gods, demigods, humans, animals, hungry ghosts, hells); the outer rim runs the twelve links of dependent origination (*nidanas*). Outside, a Buddha points to the moon of liberation.

## Significance
The *Bhavachakra* is Buddhism's master-diagram of *samsara* — the round of birth, death, and rebirth driven by craving and ignorance — and a teaching device traditionally painted at monastery gates. It compresses the doctrines of karma, the realms of rebirth, and the twelve-fold chain of causation into a single legible image, with the Buddha's gesture marking the only exit. It is among the most widely reproduced of all Buddhist instructional paintings.

## For artists & game designers
A nested wheel of realms and causes — a full reincarnation/karma system rendered as one diagram.

citations.text: Robert Beer, *The Encyclopedia of Tibetan Symbols and Motifs* (1999).

title: Yogin in Meditation with Chakras and Kundalini
work: Eastern Esoterica: Magic & Inner Alchemy of Asia
creator: Anonymous (Indian)
summary:
An Indian painting of a yogin in meditation, his body marked with the *chakras* and the rising *kundalini* serpent of the subtle anatomy.

## Iconography
The seated figure is overlaid with a vertical column of lotus-[[motif:chakras|chakras]] strung along the central channel, from the root at the perineum to the thousand-petalled lotus at the crown. The coiled [[motif:kundalini|kundalini]] serpent, the dormant 'serpent power,' rises through them, and the side channels (*ida* and *pingala*) twine around the central *sushumna*.

## Significance
This is the classic visual scheme of *kundalini yoga* and tantric physiology: a [[motif:subtle body|subtle body]] of channels (*nadis*) and energy-centres (*chakras*) superimposed on the physical form. Through breath, posture, and visualisation the practitioner awakens the kundalini at the base and draws it upward to union at the crown, attaining liberation. Systematised in texts like the *Sat-Chakra-Nirupana* (and popularised in the West by Arthur Avalon's *The Serpent Power*, 1919), this map of the inner body parallels the Daoist neidan charts as Asia's other great science of energetic self-cultivation.

## For artists & game designers
A vertical 'energy ladder' of named centres with a rising-power mechanic — a ready progression/charge system overlaid on a body.

citations.text: Arthur Avalon (John Woodroffe), *The Serpent Power* (1919).

title: Diamond World Mandala (Kongōkai), Mandala of the Two Worlds
work: Eastern Esoterica: Magic & Inner Alchemy of Asia
creator: Anonymous (Japanese; Chester Beatty Library copy)
date: later copy of the esoteric (Shingon) type
summary:
The *Kongōkai* (Diamond World) mandala, one half of the paired Mandala of the Two Worlds central to Japanese Shingon esoteric Buddhism (Chester Beatty Library copy).

## Iconography
The Diamond World is laid out as a three-by-three grid of nine 'assemblies,' each a sub-[[motif:mandala|mandala]] of Buddhas and bodhisattvas centred on the cosmic Buddha [[motif:vairocana|Vairocana]] (Dainichi). The rigid lattice expresses the adamantine, indestructible wisdom aspect of reality.

## Significance
With its partner the *Taizōkai* (Womb World), the *Kongōkai* forms the *ryōkai* mandala that Kūkai brought from China in 806 to found the Shingon school. The Diamond World represents the unchanging wisdom of Vairocana; the Womb World the dynamic compassion that pervades phenomena. Hung facing each other in the ritual hall, the pair maps the entire esoteric cosmos and structures Shingon initiation and visualisation. The nine-assembly grid is one of East Asian Buddhism's most influential diagrammatic schemes.

## For artists & game designers
A 3×3 grid of self-contained sub-worlds, each centred on the same lord — a fractal, modular map structure.

citations.text: Adrian Snodgrass, *The Matrix and Diamond World Mandalas in Shingon Buddhism* (1988).

title: Vishnu Riding Garuda (Nepalese schist)
work: Eastern Esoterica: Magic & Inner Alchemy of Asia
creator: Anonymous (Nepalese)
rights: CC0 / Public domain. Art Institute of Chicago. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A Nepalese schist sculpture (16th–17th c.) of the god Vishnu riding his mount *Garuda*, the eagle-being who is a potent protective and serpent-quelling deity (Art Institute of Chicago).

## Iconography
Vishnu sits enthroned upon [[motif:garuda|Garuda]], the great bird-man with wings, beak or eagle features, and human torso, carved in dark stone. Garuda is shown bearing his divine rider aloft, the canonical *vahana* (vehicle) pose.

## Significance
Garuda, sworn enemy of the *nagas* (serpents), is invoked across Hindu and Buddhist Asia as a protector against snakebite, poison, and malign serpent-spirits; Garuda *mantras* and amulets are a staple of protective magic from India and Nepal to Tibet, Southeast Asia, and beyond. In the Vajrayana he also appears as a wrathful enlightened form. As Vishnu's mount he links the great Hindu pantheon to the everyday apotropaic practice of warding off poison and disease.

## For artists & game designers
A winged bird-rider deity with a clear function (anti-poison, anti-serpent) — a ready protective-summon design.

title: Nine-Deity Mandala of Two-Armed Hevajra
work: Eastern Esoterica: Magic & Inner Alchemy of Asia
creator: Anonymous (Tibetan)
summary:
A painted mandala of the two-armed *Hevajra* in his nine-deity configuration, a Vajrayana meditational diagram (Google Art Project).

## Iconography
At the centre of a square palace within concentric protective rings stands [[motif:hevajra|Hevajra]] in union with his consort Nairatmya, surrounded by eight attendant *yogini* goddesses set in the petals of a lotus — the 'nine deities' of the title. The four-gated [[motif:mandala|mandala]] is enclosed by rings of vajras and flame.

## Significance
Hevajra is the central deity of the *Hevajra Tantra*, a major 'mother tantra' especially important to the Sakya school and historically influential at the Mongol Yuan court. The mandala is not merely a picture but a meditative architecture: the practitioner visualises themselves entering the palace and identifying with the central deity and retinue. The nine-deity scheme — a centre plus eight — is a recurrent tantric pattern echoing the Luoshu's nine cells and the eightfold lotus.

## For artists & game designers
A centre-plus-eight 'party formation' inside a gated palace — a compact mandala template for a hub-and-ring layout.

citations.text: David Snellgrove, *The Hevajra Tantra* (1959).

title: Fuxi Order of the 64 Hexagrams (Grid and Circle)
work: Eastern Esoterica: Magic & Inner Alchemy of Asia
creator: After Shao Yong; engraving in James Legge, *The Yi King* (1882)
summary:
The 'Former Heaven' (Fuxi) arrangement of the sixty-four *I Ching* hexagrams as both a square grid and a surrounding circle, reproduced in James Legge's 1882 translation.

## Iconography
Sixty-four six-line [[motif:hexagrams|hexagrams]] are laid out in a square block and again around a great ring. Read in the Fuxi order they follow a strict doubling pattern, so that the sequence is, in effect, a binary count from 0 to 63 expressed in broken and unbroken lines.

## Significance
This is the diagram, devised by the Song philosopher Shao Yong, that the printed broadsheet of which Joachim Bouvet sent to Leibniz — who recognised in its order his own binary arithmetic. The *I Ching* (*Book of Changes*) is the foundational Chinese divination classic, its hexagrams generated by yarrow stalks or coins and read for guidance. The Fuxi circle-and-grid makes visible the mathematical regularity beneath the oracle and became a key node in the early-modern European reception of Chinese thought.

## For artists & game designers
A 64-state binary lattice — every hexagram an address — ideal for a procedurally ordered oracle or map key.

citations.text: James Legge, *The Yî King* (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 16, 1882).
Richard J. Smith, *The I Ching: A Biography* (2012).

title: Kalachakra Sand Mandala (Namgyal monks)
work: Eastern Esoterica: Magic & Inner Alchemy of Asia
creator: Namgyal Monastery monks (photo Wonderlane)
rights: CC BY 2.0 (photo Wonderlane). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
Tibetan Buddhist monks of the Namgyal Monastery constructing the *Kalachakra* ('Wheel of Time') sand mandala, the most elaborate of the Vajrayana mandalas.

## Iconography
Coloured sand is laid grain by grain into a vast circular [[motif:mandala|mandala]] — a square palace of four gates set within concentric rings of fire, vajra, lotus, and protective deities, all keyed to the Kalachakra deity at the centre. The whole is a two-dimensional ground-plan of a three-dimensional celestial palace.

## Significance
The *Kalachakra* tantra integrates cosmology, the calendar, subtle-body yoga, and the figure of the messianic kingdom of Shambhala. Its mandala is built over days for a major public initiation, then ceremonially swept away and poured into water — a deliberate enactment of [[motif:impermanence|impermanence]]. The Dalai Lamas, whose personal monastery is Namgyal, are especially associated with conferring the Kalachakra empowerment. As ritual technology the sand mandala is a temporary cosmos created to be entered in meditation and then dissolved.

## For artists & game designers
The canonical four-gated palace plan — concentric protective rings around a central deity, a ready map for a sacred-architecture level.

citations.text: Vesna A. Wallace, *The Inner Kalacakratantra* (2001).

title: Leibniz's Diagram of the I Ching Hexagrams (1701)
work: Eastern Esoterica: Magic & Inner Alchemy of Asia
creator: Joachim Bouvet / G. W. Leibniz (annotated)
summary:
The diagram of the *I Ching* hexagrams in the arrangement of Shao Yong, owned and annotated by Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, sent to him in 1701 by the Jesuit Joachim Bouvet.

## Iconography
A circular and square arrangement of the sixty-four [[motif:hexagrams|hexagrams]] of the *Book of Changes*, with Leibniz's marginal numbering correlating each figure to a value in his binary notation — broken lines as 0, unbroken as 1.

## Significance
This sheet is the famous artefact of cross-cultural mathematics: Bouvet, working in Beijing, recognised that the Fuxi order of the hexagrams matched the binary arithmetic Leibniz had developed, and sent him the diagram. Leibniz published the connection in 1703, reading the ancient Chinese oracle as an unwitting expression of dyadic (base-2) numeration — and, in his Christian-philosophical framing, of creation from 0 (nothing) and 1 (God). It is a touchstone of the European Enlightenment's encounter with Chinese cosmology and a landmark in the prehistory of binary computing.

## For artists & game designers
The historical moment binary met divination — a prop for any 'ancient code = modern machine' narrative.

citations.text: G. W. Leibniz, 'Explication de l'arithmétique binaire' (1703).

title: Feng-Shui Compass (Luopan)
work: Eastern Esoterica: Magic & Inner Alchemy of Asia
creator: Anonymous (Chinese)
rights: CC0 / Public domain. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A Chinese *luopan*, the geomancer's compass used in *feng shui* to determine the auspicious siting and orientation of buildings and graves (lacquer on wood and brass, 20th c.).

## Iconography
A magnetic needle sits at the centre of a disc ringed by many concentric bands, each inscribed with a layer of cosmological data — the eight [[motif:eight trigrams|trigrams]], the twenty-four directions, the sixty *jiazi* cycle, the lunar mansions, the five phases — read outward from the needle to correlate a site with the heavens.

## Significance
The *luopan* is the working instrument of *kanyu* (feng shui), the Chinese geomantic art of harmonising human structures with the flow of *qi* across the landscape. Its many rings compress the whole apparatus of correlative cosmology into a single hand-held device, and its central magnetised needle reflects China's early mastery of the lodestone compass — first developed, in fact, for divination and siting before navigation. Each school of feng shui favours its own ring configuration.

## For artists & game designers
A dense concentric dial encoding direction, element, and cycle — a perfect diegetic 'cosmic instrument' UI.

citations.text: Stephen Skinner, *Guide to the Feng Shui Compass* (2008).

title: Luoshu (Magic Square of Order Three)
work: Eastern Esoterica: Magic & Inner Alchemy of Asia
creator: Anonymous (Chinese; diagram)
summary:
A diagram of the *Luoshu* ('Writing of the Luo River'), the 3×3 magic square in which every row, column, and diagonal sums to fifteen, foundational to Chinese numerological cosmology.

## Iconography
The nine digits 1–9 are arranged so that the central cell is 5 and each line sums to 15; in traditional form the numbers appear as clusters of dark (yin, even) and light (yang, odd) dots, said to have been seen on the shell of a sacred turtle emerging from the Luo River.

## Significance
The [[motif:luoshu|Luoshu]], paired with the *Hetu* ('River Chart'), is one of the two primal diagrams of Chinese cosmology. Its nine cells became the 'Nine Palaces' mapped onto the compass directions, the trigrams, the five phases, and the calendar, and it underlies *feng shui*, divination, and ritual orientation. As the earliest documented magic square, it also occupies a place in the global history of recreational and esoteric mathematics, mirrored later in Islamic and European magic squares.

## For artists & game designers
A 3×3 numeric grid where every line balances — a built-in puzzle lattice and a directional cosmology in nine cells.

citations.text: Frank J. Swetz, *Legacy of the Luoshu* (2002).

title: Mongolian Shaman's Instruments
work: Eastern Esoterica: Magic & Inner Alchemy of Asia
creator: Anonymous (Mongolian; photo Gary Todd)
rights: CC0 / Public domain. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A display of Mongolian shaman's instruments — the drum, costume, and ritual implements used to enter trance and engage the spirit world.

## Iconography
The objects include the broad single-headed frame [[motif:ritual drum|drum]] (the shaman's 'mount' to the other world), a fringed and tasselled spirit-costume hung with metal pendants, bells, and bronze mirrors (*toli*), and assorted ritual gear. Their materials and ornament identify the wearer's helping spirits.

## Significance
Mongolian shamanism, rooted in *Tengrism* (the cult of the sky-father Tengri and the spirits of land and ancestors), centres on the shaman (*böö*) who drums into ecstatic trance to journey among spirits, heal, divine, and mediate with the dead. The drum carries the shaman in flight; the mirror deflects harmful forces and 'sees' spirits; the costume's pendants give voice to the helpers. Surviving alongside and beneath Tibetan Buddhism, Mongolian shamanism is a key living branch of the North-Asian shamanic complex studied by Mircea Eliade and others.

## For artists & game designers
A complete shaman kit — drum as travel-portal, mirror as spirit-sight, costume as spirit-roster — a ready toolkit of ritual items.

citations.text: Mircea Eliade, *Shamanism: Archaic Techniques of Ecstasy* (1951).

title: Neijing Tu (Chart of the Inner Landscape)
work: Eastern Esoterica: Magic & Inner Alchemy of Asia
creator: Anonymous (Chinese, Daoist)
date: 19th c. (after a Qing stele in the White Cloud Monastery, Beijing)
summary:
The *Neijing Tu* ('Chart of the Inner Landscape / Inner Warp'), a Daoist diagram of the human body imagined as a mountain landscape through which the vital breath circulates in the practice of internal alchemy.

## Iconography
The seated body is shown in profile as a vertical world: the head a peaked mountain with sun and moon (the eyes), the spine a river or watercourse, the lower belly a terraced field where an ox ploughs and a child treads a water-wheel to raise the energy. Pagodas, weaving maidens, and a herd-boy mark the three *dantian* (cinnabar fields) and the gates along the spinal pathway.

## Significance
The chart visualises [[motif:neidan|neidan]], Daoist 'internal alchemy,' in which the adept refines *jing*, *qi*, and *shen* by circulating breath up the spine and down the front in the 'microcosmic orbit.' The body is read as a sealed cosmos — a [[motif:microcosm|microcosm]] mirroring the heavens — so that the alchemical Work performed by outer adepts on cinnabar and mercury is here turned inward. The best-known version derives from a stone stele preserved at the Baiyun Guan (White Cloud Monastery) in Beijing.

## For artists & game designers
A complete 'body-as-landscape' map: organs become locations and qi a resource to route — a ready inner-world level design.

citations.text: Catherine Despeux, *Taoïsme et corps humain: le Xiuzhen tu* (1994).

title: Ofuda Paper Talisman (Yanagidani Kannon)
work: Eastern Esoterica: Magic & Inner Alchemy of Asia
creator: Anonymous (Japanese; Yanagidani Kannon temple)
summary:
An *ofuda*, a Japanese paper (or wooden) household talisman, issued by the Yanagidani Kannon temple.

## Iconography
The tall strip bears the name or seal of the enshrined deity or Buddha — here associated with [[motif:kannon|Kannon]], the bodhisattva of compassion — in bold calligraphy, often with a temple stamp. It is meant to be enshrined in the home, typically on a *kamidana* or *butsudan*, or pasted by the door.

## Significance
The [[motif:ofuda|ofuda]] carries the presence and protective power of the deity into the household, warding misfortune, fire, and illness over the year before being returned and renewed. Issued by both Shinto shrines and Buddhist temples, ofuda exemplify Japanese 'practical religion,' in which sacred names and seals function as portable, renewable instruments of blessing and protection — the everyday end of the same talismanic logic seen in Daoist fú and Buddhist *dharani* slips.

## For artists & game designers
A renewable, place-based blessing token — a clean 'shrine buff' item with an annual expiry mechanic.

citations.text: Ian Reader & George J. Tanabe, *Practically Religious* (1998).

title: Omamori Amulet (Tachiki Kannon)
work: Eastern Esoterica: Magic & Inner Alchemy of Asia
creator: Anonymous (Japanese; Tachiki Kannon temple)
summary:
An *omamori*, a Japanese portable amulet in a small brocade pouch, issued by the Tachiki Kannon temple.

## Iconography
The charm is a little drawstring bag of patterned silk brocade, printed or embroidered with the temple's name and purpose. Sealed inside is a slip of paper or wood (a miniature *ofuda*) bearing the sacred name; the pouch is never meant to be opened.

## Significance
The [[motif:omamori|omamori]] is the portable counterpart of the household ofuda — carried on the person, hung from a bag or phone, or kept in a car for a specific blessing: traffic safety, success in study, easy childbirth, love, or general protection. Like the ofuda it embodies the deity's protective power and is renewed yearly. Omamori are among the most visible everyday objects of Japanese religious life and a vivid example of talismanic practice thriving in a modern, commercial setting.

## For artists & game designers
A wearable single-purpose charm in a sealed pouch — a tidy equippable buff item with thematic variants.

citations.text: Ian Reader & George J. Tanabe, *Practically Religious* (1998).

title: Wrathful Deities of the Guhyagarbha Tantra (chart)
work: Eastern Esoterica: Magic & Inner Alchemy of Asia
creator: Anonymous (Tibetan; via Himalayan Art Resources)
summary:
An iconographic chart of the wrathful deities of the *Guhyagarbha Tantra*, the root tantra of the Nyingma 'Mahayoga' that underlies the peaceful-and-wrathful deity scheme.

## Iconography
The deities are laid out as a labelled key — the central *herukas* and their retinues, gatekeepers, and goddesses set in ordered registers, in the manner of a reference sheet rather than a devotional thangka. This is the deity assembly from which the [[motif:bardo thodol|Bardo Thodol]] visions are drawn.

## Significance
The *Guhyagarbha Tantra* ('Secret Essence') is the foundational scripture for the mandala of the hundred peaceful and wrathful deities in the Nyingma tradition; the *Bardo Thodol* and the *zhitro* ('peaceful-wrathful') practices elaborate its assembly. A systematic chart like this serves practitioners as an iconographic and liturgical map — fixing the names, attributes, and positions of each deity in the mandala. It exemplifies the precise, encoded visual taxonomy of Tibetan tantra.

## For artists & game designers
A labelled deity-roster sheet — exactly the kind of reference key for building a coherent pantheon with fixed attributes.

citations.text: Gyurme Dorje (trans.), *The Guhyagarbha Tantra* and commentaries.

title: Yant Paed Tidt (Eight-Direction Thai Yantra)
work: Eastern Esoterica: Magic & Inner Alchemy of Asia
creator: Anonymous (Thai)
summary:
*Yant Paed Tidt* ('Yantra of the Eight Directions'), a classic Thai *sak yant* design used as a protective tattoo or cloth/paper amulet.

## Iconography
The geometric [[motif:sak yant|yantra]] radiates protection toward the eight compass directions, its cells filled with sacred *Khom* (Khmer) script syllables and topped by spiralling *unalome* and rows of mantra-letters. Each direction and syllable carries a specific guarding power.

## Significance
*Sak yant* is the Thai (and broader Southeast Asian) tradition of sacred yantra tattooing, practised by Buddhist monks and lay masters (*ajarn*), fusing Theravada Buddhist devotion with older animist and Brahmanic magic. The designs confer protection, charisma, invulnerability, or luck, activated by the master's recited *kata* (mantra). The *Yant Paed Tidt* in particular shields the bearer from danger arriving from any of the eight directions. The same yantras appear on cloth (*pha yant*) and rolled-metal *takrut* amulets.

## For artists & game designers
A directional ward (protection from eight headings) rendered as inscribed geometry — a strong tattoo/sigil asset.

citations.text: On sak yant, see studies of Thai protective tattooing and Buddhist magic.

title: Abe no Seimei (Onmyōji with the Seiman Pentagram)
work: Eastern Esoterica: Magic & Inner Alchemy of Asia
creator: Suzuki Masanao (Japan, 1815–1890)
rights: Public domain. LACMA. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A nineteenth-century Japanese print of *Abe no Seimei*, the legendary Heian-era *onmyōji* (diviner-magician) whose emblem is the five-pointed *Seiman* star (Suzuki Masanao; LACMA).

## Iconography
The sage is shown in courtly robes amid the apparatus of his art. His signature device, the [[motif:seiman pentagram|Seiman]], is a unicursal five-pointed star whose five points stand for the five phases — wood, fire, earth, metal, water — and their cycles of generation and conquest, used as a protective seal.

## Significance
Abe no Seimei (921–1005) is the most famous practitioner of *onmyōdō* ('the way of yin and yang'), the Japanese court discipline blending Chinese five-phase cosmology, calendrical science, divination, and apotropaic ritual. Around him gathered legends of commanding *shikigami* (spirit-servants) and defeating curses. The Seiman pentagram and the grid-like *Dōman* remain his emblems, still sold as protective talismans at the Seimei Shrine in Kyoto. He embodies the East Asian counterpart to the learned ritual magus.

## For artists & game designers
A court-sorcerer archetype with a ready sigil (five-element pentagram) and spirit-servant mechanic.

citations.text: Shigeta Shin'ichi, on onmyōdō and Abe no Seimei.

title: Sri Yantra (Engraved Copper Plate)
work: Eastern Esoterica: Magic & Inner Alchemy of Asia
creator: Anonymous (Indian)
summary:
A *Sri Yantra* (Shri Chakra) engraved on a copper plate, the supreme diagram of the Hindu Shakta tantric tradition.

## Iconography
Nine interlocking [[motif:interlocking triangles|triangles]] — five pointing down (the goddess) and four up (the god) — interpenetrate to generate forty-three smaller triangles around a central point (*bindu*), the whole enclosed by lotus petals and a square 'earth-citadel' with four gates. The intricate symmetry radiates from, and resolves into, the central dot.

## Significance
The [[motif:sri yantra|Sri Yantra]] is the geometric body of the goddess Lalita Tripura Sundari and the central icon of the Shri Vidya school of tantra. It is read as a cosmogram — the unfolding of the manifest universe from the undifferentiated *bindu* and its reabsorption — and serves as a support for worship and meditation, the adept ascending its nine enclosures (*chakras*) inward toward the centre. Its mathematically demanding construction has fascinated geometers as well as devotees.

## For artists & game designers
A recursive nested-triangle cosmogram converging on a single point — a striking sacred-geometry asset and meditation-target motif.

citations.text: Madhu Khanna, *Yantra: The Tantric Symbol of Cosmic Unity* (1979).

title: Taijitu (Yin-Yang Diagram) with Laozi
work: Eastern Esoterica: Magic & Inner Alchemy of Asia
creator: Anonymous (Chinese)
summary:
The *Taijitu* ('Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate'), the familiar yin-yang symbol of interlocked light and dark, here paired with an image of Laozi.

## Iconography
A circle is divided by an S-curve into a dark ([[motif:yin yang|yin]]) and a light (yang) field, each carrying a seed-dot of its opposite. The rotational symmetry expresses ceaseless interchange: each pole at its fullest already contains the germ of the other.

## Significance
The *Taiji* ('Supreme Ultimate') is the undivided whole from which yin and yang, and then the 'ten thousand things,' unfold — a cosmogonic principle systematised by the Song Neo-Confucian Zhou Dunyi in his *Taijitu Shuo*. As the master-symbol of Daoist correlative cosmology it underlies the *I Ching*, internal alchemy, medicine, and feng shui. The associated figure of Laozi marks the diagram's place within the Daoist tradition that took the *Daodejing* as scripture.

## For artists & game designers
The ultimate 'balance/duality' icon — instantly legible as paired opposing forces with embedded reversal.

citations.text: Zhou Dunyi, *Taijitu Shuo* ('Explanation of the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate').

title: Chinese Fú Talisman (Han-dynasty bamboo strip)
work: Eastern Esoterica: Magic & Inner Alchemy of Asia
creator: Anonymous (Chinese)
summary:
A Chinese *fú* (符) talisman written on an excavated Han-dynasty bamboo slip, an early example of the Daoist charm-script tradition.

## Iconography
The slip bears columns of contorted, quasi-calligraphic graphs — the 'cloud-script' or 'celestial writing' of [[motif:fulu|fú-lù]] talismans — in which characters are deliberately distorted, doubled, or fused into sigils legible to spirits rather than ordinary readers. Such marks command, summon, or repel unseen powers.

## Significance
The *fú* (often paired with *lù*, registers) is the core instrument of Daoist ritual magic: a written contract or command issued in the name of celestial bureaucrats, used to heal, exorcise, protect a household, or empower an adept. Believed to descend from heavenly archetypes, fú talismans were burned, ingested in water, or pasted at thresholds. This excavated example shows the practice already current in the Han, anchoring a tradition that runs unbroken into living Daoist and folk use.

## For artists & game designers
A real ancient 'spell scroll' — distorted glyphs as a commandable script system for an in-world magic language.

citations.text: Gil Raz, *The Emergence of Daoism* (2012).

title: Four Mandalas of the Vajravali Series (Ngor Monastery)
work: Eastern Esoterica: Magic & Inner Alchemy of Asia
creator: Anonymous (Tibetan, Tsang; Ngor Monastery, Sakya order)
summary:
A thangka from the *Vajravali* series of the Ngor Monastery (Sakya order), showing four mandalas arranged in a grid on a single painting.

## Iconography
Four complete [[motif:mandala|mandalas]] are set in a two-by-two arrangement, each a four-gated palace within rings of flame and vajra, populated by the deities of a particular tantric cycle. The geometric precision and rich mineral pigments are characteristic of the Ngor workshop's mandala sets.

## Significance
The *Vajravali* ('Garland of Vajras') is a compendium of tantric mandalas compiled by the Indian master Abhayakaragupta, and the Ngor Monastery — a major Sakya seat founded in 1429 — produced celebrated painted sets illustrating its cycles. Multi-mandala thangkas like this functioned as visual indexes to whole liturgical systems, each diagram a palace the initiate could enter in visualisation. They are prime documents of the systematised, encyclopedic side of Tibetan tantra.

## For artists & game designers
Four palace-plans on one sheet — a tileset of mandala variations to mix and recombine.

citations.text: Martin Brauen, *The Mandala: Sacred Circle in Tibetan Buddhism* (1997).

title: Vajrayogini Thangka
work: Eastern Esoterica: Magic & Inner Alchemy of Asia
creator: Anonymous (Tibetan, commissioned in Dharamsala)
summary:
A thangka of *Vajrayogini*, the red tantric goddess (*dakini*) central to many Vajrayana meditation practices.

## Iconography
The deity is a vivid red, naked but for bone ornaments, dancing in a ring of flame. She holds a curved flaying-knife (*kartika*) and a skull-cup (*kapala*) brimming with blood, a tantric staff (*khatvanga*) at her shoulder, and treads on prone figures — the standard form of the [[motif:dakini|dakini]] who embodies blissful wisdom.

## Significance
[[motif:vajrayogini|Vajrayogini]] is a 'highest yoga tantra' deity whose practice transmutes desire and the energies of the subtle body into the realisation of emptiness and bliss. As the archetypal *dakini* — a female embodiment of awakened energy — she is a principal meditational deity (*yidam*) in the Sakya, Kagyu, and Gelug traditions. Her fierce, sensual iconography encodes the tantric principle that the passions themselves, skilfully handled, become the path to liberation.

## For artists & game designers
A flame-haloed dancing figure with knife and skull-cup — a complete character design for a fierce-wisdom archetype.

citations.text: Elizabeth English, *Vajrayogini: Her Visualizations, Rituals, and Forms* (2002).

title: Womb World Mandala (Taizōkai), Buddha-in-Lotus detail
work: Eastern Esoterica: Magic & Inner Alchemy of Asia
creator: Anonymous (Japanese; Kyōōgokoku-ji / Tō-ji)
summary:
A detail of the central lotus from the *Taizōkai* (Womb World) mandala, the ninth-century Mandala of the Two Realms preserved at Kyōōgokoku-ji (Tō-ji), Kyoto.

## Iconography
The detail shows the heart of the Womb World: the Buddha [[motif:vairocana|Vairocana]] (Dainichi) seated at the centre of an eight-petalled red lotus, each petal bearing a Buddha or bodhisattva. From this 'Central Dais of Eight Petals' the compassion of the cosmic Buddha radiates outward through the mandala's enclosing courts.

## Significance
The *Taizōkai* ('Womb-Store World') is the matrix-half of the Shingon two-world [[motif:mandala|mandala]], representing the principle (*ri*) and compassionate unfolding of reality, complementary to the Diamond World's wisdom. The eight-petalled lotus at its core is among the most reproduced of all Buddhist diagrams, a model of how a single centre generates an ordered cosmos. This Tō-ji set is one of the oldest surviving versions, descending from Kūkai's transmission of esoteric Buddhism to Japan.

## For artists & game designers
The eight-petal lotus with a central lord and eight aspects — a clean radial hub for a skill wheel or pantheon ring.

citations.text: Adrian Snodgrass, *The Matrix and Diamond World Mandalas in Shingon Buddhism* (1988).

title: Diverse Forms of Mahakala and Other Protectors
work: Eastern Esoterica: Magic & Inner Alchemy of Asia
creator: Anonymous (Tibetan)
summary:
A Tibetan thangka depicting diverse forms of *Mahakala* and other *dharmapala* (protector) deities, the wrathful guardians of the Buddhist teaching.

## Iconography
Dark-bodied [[motif:wrathful deity|wrathful figures]] crowd the painting: Mahakala in his several forms — multi-armed, fanged, wreathed in flame, crowned with skulls, trampling enemies and brandishing chopper and skull-cup — surrounded by lesser protectors. The terrifying aspect, far from demonic, expresses the ferocity of compassion against ignorance.

## Significance
*Dharmapalas* such as [[motif:mahakala|Mahakala]] guard the Dharma and its practitioners; Mahakala (a Buddhist transformation of the Hindu Shiva-Mahakala) is among the most important protectors across Tibetan, Mongolian, and East Asian Vajrayana, and a special guardian of particular lineages and the Mongol and Manchu courts. The wrathful iconography is read as the enlightened mind's power to destroy obstacles, not as malevolence — a key principle of tantric symbolism.

## For artists & game designers
A full bestiary sheet of flame-wreathed guardian forms — directly usable as boss/protector design reference.

citations.text: Robert Beer, *The Encyclopedia of Tibetan Symbols and Motifs* (1999).

title: Xiuzhen Tu (Chart for the Cultivation of Perfection)
work: Eastern Esoterica: Magic & Inner Alchemy of Asia
creator: Anonymous (Chinese, Daoist)
summary:
The *Xiuzhen Tu* ('Chart for the Cultivation of Perfection'), a Daoist anatomical-alchemical diagram detailing the inner organs, channels, and energetic centres used in self-cultivation.

## Iconography
A tall frontal chart of the trunk shows the viscera rendered as palaces and deities, the spinal passage with its named gates, columns of explanatory text, and the circulating routes of breath. Where the *Neijing Tu* is a landscape, the *Xiuzhen Tu* is closer to a labelled medical-mystical anatomy.

## Significance
The chart codifies the inner geography of [[motif:neidan|internal alchemy]], naming the bodily 'palaces' inhabited by tutelary spirits and the pathways along which *qi* is refined toward the embryonic 'immortal' body. It belongs to the same lineage as the *Neijing Tu* and was studied by Catherine Despeux in the foundational scholarly treatment of these body-cosmos diagrams. Such charts united Daoist physiology, ritual, and the quest for transcendence in a single image.

## For artists & game designers
A labelled 'skill-tree of the body' — viscera as upgradeable palaces, each with a resident spirit and a stat.

citations.text: Catherine Despeux, *Taoïsme et corps humain: le Xiuzhen tu* (1994).

title: Weighing of the Heart, Papyrus of Ani
work: Ancient Egyptian Magic, Amulets & Funerary Protection
creator: Anonymous (Egyptian scribes and painters)
summary:
The judgement scene from the *Papyrus of Ani*, the most celebrated copy of the Egyptian Book of the Dead, now in the British Museum.

## Iconography
Jackal-headed Anubis weighs the scribe Ani's heart against the feather of Maat on a great balance. Ibis-headed Thoth records the verdict, while the composite monster Ammit — part crocodile, lion and hippopotamus — waits to devour the heart of the unjust. Ani and his wife look on at the left.

## Significance
The *psychostasia* enacts spell 125 of the Book of the Dead, in which the deceased recites the "negative confession" before forty-two assessor gods. The scene is the visual heart of Egyptian funerary belief: the heart (*ib*), seat of conscience, must balance against cosmic order ([[motif:maat feather|Maat]]) for the dead to be reborn. Edited and translated by E. A. Wallis Budge (1895), the Ani papyrus shaped the modern Western image of Egyptian afterlife.

## For artists & game designers
The balance-scale judgement is a ready morality mechanic: weigh a character's deeds against a single feather, with a devourer waiting for failure.

citations.text: E. A. Wallis Budge, *The Book of the Dead: The Papyrus of Ani* (1895).

title: Apotropaic Wand ("Birth Tusk") Fragment (MET 55475)
work: Ancient Egyptian Magic, Amulets & Funerary Protection
creator: Anonymous (Egypt)
summary:
A fragment of an Egyptian apotropaic wand, or "birth tusk," of carved hippopotamus ivory, in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

## Iconography
A curved, flat blade of ivory (following the shape of a hippopotamus canine) incised with a procession of protective beings: Taweret, Bes, lions, snakes, knife-wielding genii and composite demons who ward off danger.

## Significance
These Middle Kingdom "magic knives" were used to draw a protective circle around a mother and newborn — traces of wear at the tips suggest they were dragged across the ground or a bed. The parade of fierce guardians, several gripping knives, formed a frontier no hostile spirit could cross. They are the principal evidence for [[motif:apotropaic magic|domestic protective magic]] around childbirth, studied in detail by Hartwig Altenmüller and Geraldine Pinch.

## For artists & game designers
A wand whose engraved monsters are the spell — a portable bestiary that doubles as a ward — is an evocative magic-item concept.

citations.text: Geraldine Pinch, *Magic in Ancient Egypt* (1994).

title: Faience Amulet of the God Bes (Museo Egizio C 615)
work: Ancient Egyptian Magic, Amulets & Funerary Protection
creator: Anonymous (Egypt)
summary:
A glazed faience amulet of the dwarf-god Bes in the Museo Egizio, Turin.

## Iconography
A squat, frontal dwarf deity with bandy legs, a lion-like bearded face, protruding tongue and a feathered crown. The deliberately grotesque face — meant to frighten away evil — is Bes's signature.

## Significance
Bes was a benevolent household protector, guarding sleepers, women in childbirth and young children against snakes, scorpions and malevolent spirits. Unlike most Egyptian gods he is shown full-face, confronting the viewer (and the threat) directly. His image proliferated on amulets, beds, headrests and mirror handles from the Middle Kingdom onward and survived into Greco-Roman [[motif:apotropaic magic|apotropaic magic]], underpinning the composite Bes-Pantheos figures.

## For artists & game designers
Bes is the archetype of the friendly-grotesque guardian: ugliness as a feature, protection through intimidation.

citations.text: Geraldine Pinch, *Magic in Ancient Egypt* (1994).

title: Djed Pillar Amulet (Metropolitan Museum)
work: Ancient Egyptian Magic, Amulets & Funerary Protection
creator: Anonymous (Egypt)
summary:
A *djed*-pillar amulet in the Metropolitan Museum of Art, one of the core funerary amulets prescribed by the Book of the Dead.

## Iconography
A columnar form crowned by four stacked horizontal bars or capitals. Variously interpreted as a stylised tree-trunk, a bundle of stalks, or — most enduringly — the backbone of Osiris.

## Significance
The [[motif:djed pillar|djed]] hieroglyph means "stability/endurance," and as the spine of Osiris it promised the deceased a stable, re-membered body and resurrection. Book of the Dead spell 155 calls for a gold djed at the throat of the mummy so "you raise up your backbone, O weary-hearted one." The "raising of the djed" was also a major royal festival affirming cosmic order. It is, with the wedjat and the tyet, one of the most frequently buried amulets.

## For artists & game designers
A spine-as-pillar glyph signifying "stability" is a strong icon for a fortification, anchor, or resurrection mechanic.

citations.text: Carol Andrews, *Amulets of Ancient Egypt* (1994).

title: Vignettes from the Greenfield Papyrus (Sheet 12)
work: Ancient Egyptian Magic, Amulets & Funerary Protection
creator: Anonymous (Egyptian scribes and painters)
summary:
A strip of vignettes from the *Greenfield Papyrus*, the Book of the Dead of the priestess Nestanebetisheru, in the British Museum.

## Iconography
A register of small painted scenes (vignettes) illustrating the spells of the Book of the Dead — deities, the deceased in adoration, and ritual episodes — running above or beside columns of hieratic text.

## Significance
At over 37 metres, the Greenfield Papyrus is the longest known Book of the Dead. Made for a high-ranking woman of the Theban priestly elite around 950 BCE, it is a key witness to the 21st-Dynasty recension of funerary [[motif:book of the dead|spells]], when such papyri were produced for an aristocratic clientele. Its vignettes are an invaluable corpus of Egyptian afterlife iconography, named for Edith Mary Greenfield, who donated it in 1910.

## For artists & game designers
A scrolling band of captioned vignettes is a natural template for an in-world illuminated codex or a side-scrolling ritual sequence.

citations.text: E. A. Wallis Budge, *The Greenfield Papyrus in the British Museum* (1912).

title: Heart Scarab in Egyptian Blue (Museo Egizio C 6016)
work: Ancient Egyptian Magic, Amulets & Funerary Protection
creator: Anonymous (Egypt)
summary:
A large heart scarab of Egyptian blue in the Museo Egizio, Turin, the type of funerary amulet placed over the mummy's heart.

## Iconography
A carved beetle (a dung-beetle, *Scarabaeus sacer*) with detailed wing-cases and legs; the flat underside of such scarabs was inscribed with a magical spell. Heart scarabs are notably larger than ordinary scarab seals.

## Significance
The heart scarab carried spell 30B of the Book of the Dead, addressing the heart: "do not stand as a witness against me" at the weighing of the heart. By magically silencing the heart's potential self-incrimination, the amulet insured the deceased against failing the judgement. The scarab form itself evoked Khepri, the self-renewing morning sun, making the object a double charm for [[motif:rebirth|rebirth]]. Carol Andrews's catalogue treats it as the funerary amulet par excellence.

## For artists & game designers
An object that literally bribes a character's own conscience to stay silent at judgement is a wonderfully ambiguous talisman.

citations.text: Carol Andrews, *Amulets of Ancient Egypt* (1994).

title: Heart Scarab of Bak-en-Djehuti (Walters 42380)
work: Ancient Egyptian Magic, Amulets & Funerary Protection
creator: Anonymous (Egypt)
summary:
The inscribed heart scarab of a man named Bak-en-Djehuti, in the Walters Art Museum, Baltimore.

## Iconography
A carved scarab beetle whose flat base bears a hieroglyphic inscription naming the owner and giving the heart-spell. The naming personalises the otherwise standardised amulet for a specific deceased individual.

## Significance
This scarab carries the version of Book of the Dead spell 30B that begins "O my heart which I had from my mother...," pleading with the heart not to betray its owner before the divine tribunal. Named heart scarabs let Egyptologists tie magical objects to particular biographies and to the spread of the spell across the New Kingdom. The Walters example is a clear teaching specimen of how text and amulet fused into a single funerary safeguard.

## For artists & game designers
Inscribing the owner's name turns a generic protective item into a bespoke relic — a small detail that makes loot feel personal.

citations.text: John H. Taylor (ed.), *Journey through the Afterlife* (2010).

title: Cippus with Pataikos on the Crocodiles (MET 30.8.87)
work: Ancient Egyptian Magic, Amulets & Funerary Protection
creator: Anonymous (Egypt)
summary:
A magical stela (cippus) in the Metropolitan Museum on which the dwarf-god Pataikos replaces the usual Horus-child standing on the crocodiles, flanked by Isis and Nephthys.

## Iconography
A frontal apotropaic figure stands on two crocodiles, grasping serpents and noxious animals; here the body is the squat form of Pataikos rather than the youthful Horus. The protective goddesses Isis and Nephthys stand to either side, with magical inscriptions covering the field.

## Significance
The substitution of Pataikos shows how flexible the [[motif:horus on the crocodiles|Horus-on-the-crocodiles]] formula was: the protective power lay in the composition — mastery over dangerous creatures — more than in any single deity. Such cippi, poured over with water to heal snakebite, are catalogued among Egyptian healing magic and demonstrate the syncretic crowding of protective gods (Bes, Pataikos, Horus) into one apotropaic image.

## For artists & game designers
A single "slot" in a protective composition that different guardian figures can fill is a neat modular design pattern for ward objects.

citations.text: Heike Sternberg-el Hotabi, *Untersuchungen zur Überlieferungsgeschichte der Horusstelen* (1999).

title: Child Horus Standing on Crocodiles (Healing Stela)
work: Ancient Egyptian Magic, Amulets & Funerary Protection
creator: Anonymous (Egypt)
summary:
A photograph (Tupper / Boston Public Library) of a Horus-cippus showing the child god triumphant over crocodiles and venomous creatures.

## Iconography
The naked Horus-child, with the side-lock of youth, stands frontally upon two crocodiles. In his outstretched hands he grips serpents, scorpions and other dangerous animals, demonstrating total mastery over the agents of poison.

## Significance
The "Horus on the crocodiles" type (*Horus cippi* or *Horus stelae*) was the standard Egyptian device against snakebite and scorpion sting. Its logic is sympathetic: because the infant Horus survived every venomous threat under Isis's protection, water charged by the inscribed stela could transfer that immunity to a patient. Thousands survive, from monumental stelae to pocket amulets, making it one of the most widespread forms of practical [[motif:healing magic|Egyptian magic]].

## For artists & game designers
The child-who-grips-snakes-and-survives is a compact emblem of immunity — useful for an antidote item or a poison-resistant character sigil.

citations.text: Geraldine Pinch, *Magic in Ancient Egypt* (1994).

title: Judgement Scene from the Papyrus of Hunefer
work: Ancient Egyptian Magic, Amulets & Funerary Protection
creator: Anonymous (Egyptian scribes and painters)
summary:
The weighing-of-the-heart vignette from the *Papyrus of Hunefer*, a royal scribe of Seti I, held in the British Museum.

## Iconography
Anubis leads Hunefer to the scales and adjusts the balance; the heart is checked against Maat's feather while Thoth notes the result and Ammit crouches beneath. At right, falcon-headed Horus presents the vindicated Hunefer to enthroned Osiris, flanked by Isis and Nephthys.

## Significance
The Hunefer scene is the textbook illustration of [[motif:funerary judgement|Egyptian judgement of the dead]], reproduced in nearly every survey of Egyptian art. It compresses spell 125 of the Book of the Dead into a continuous narrative: trial, verdict and presentation to Osiris, lord of the underworld. The crisp Ramesside draughtsmanship makes it the standard comparandum to the Ani papyrus.

## For artists & game designers
The left-to-right "trial then presentation to the throne" sequence is a clean storyboard for an afterlife judgement cutscene.

citations.text: John H. Taylor (ed.), *Journey through the Afterlife: Ancient Egyptian Book of the Dead* (2010).
