title: The Metternich Stela (Cippus of Horus)
work: Ancient Egyptian Magic, Amulets & Funerary Protection
creator: Anonymous (Egypt); commissioned by the priest Esatum
date: c. 360–343 BCE (30th Dynasty, reign of Nectanebo II)
rights: CC BY-SA 3.0 (photo Eb.hoop). Object public domain. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
The *Metternich Stela*, the largest and finest of the Horus-cippi, now in the Metropolitan Museum of Art (Fletcher Fund, 1950).

## Iconography
The young god Horus-the-child stands frontally on two crocodiles, grasping serpents, scorpions, a lion and an oryx in his fists, surmounted by the grotesque mask of Bes. The whole surface is densely covered with hieroglyphic spells against the bites of snakes, scorpions and other dangerous creatures.

## Significance
Cippi of Horus were healing devices: water poured over the carved spells absorbed their power and was drunk or applied to neutralise venom. The Metternich Stela preserves a long magical narrative in which Isis heals the poisoned infant Horus, the mythic precedent guaranteeing the cure. Studied by C. E. Sander-Hansen and central to Egyptian medical-magical practice, it shows [[motif:healing magic|magic and medicine]] as one continuous craft.

## For artists & game designers
A carved stone whose inscriptions "charge" poured water is a vivid, tactile healing-item mechanic.

citations.text: C. E. Sander-Hansen, *Die Texte der Metternichstele* (1956).

title: Scarab Engravings, *The Sacred Beetle* (1902)
work: Ancient Egyptian Magic, Amulets & Funerary Protection
creator: John Ward (author/illustrator of the treatise)
rights: Public domain (No restrictions). Via Wikimedia Commons / Internet Archive.
summary:
An illustration from John Ward's *The Sacred Beetle: A Popular Treatise on Egyptian Scarabs in Art and History* (1902), documenting types of scarab.

## Iconography
A printed antiquarian plate showing rows of scarabs in profile and underside view, recording the variety of forms, inscriptions and designs of these beetle amulets.

## Significance
Ward's treatise was part of the turn-of-the-century antiquarian enthusiasm that turned the scarab into the emblem of ancient Egypt for Western collectors. Such typological plates both popularised the [[motif:scarab|scarab]] and fed the Egyptian-revival and reception interest that later flowed into occult and Theosophical circles. The image is thus a useful witness to how Egyptian magical objects were catalogued, reproduced and re-enchanted in the modern era.

## For artists & game designers
A period engraved "catalogue plate" of magical objects is a handy in-world artefact: a collector's reference sheet the player can consult.

citations.text: John Ward, *The Sacred Beetle* (1902).

title: Scarab Seal of Imeni (Walters 42.21)
work: Ancient Egyptian Magic, Amulets & Funerary Protection
creator: Anonymous (Egypt)
summary:
A steatite scarab seal naming a man called Imeni, in the Walters Art Museum, Baltimore.

## Iconography
A small beetle carved in the round on top, its flat underside engraved with a name and decorative design for use as a stamp seal. Pierced lengthwise, it could be strung as a ring or pendant.

## Significance
The scarab was simultaneously seal, amulet and sign: its dung-beetle form embodied Khepri, the self-generating sun, so even a humble administrative seal carried connotations of [[motif:rebirth|rebirth]] and good fortune. Middle Kingdom name- and title-scarabs like Imeni's document the merging of bureaucratic identity with protective magic. Scarab seals are among the most abundant Egyptian artifacts and a backbone of dating and prosopography for Egyptologists.

## For artists & game designers
An object that is at once an ID badge, a lucky charm and a signature stamp compresses identity, magic and authority into one tiny prop.

citations.text: Carol Andrews, *Amulets of Ancient Egypt* (1994).

title: Taweret Figure Vase with Human Head (MET)
work: Ancient Egyptian Magic, Amulets & Funerary Protection
creator: Anonymous (Egypt)
summary:
A figure-vase in the form of the goddess Taweret (here with a human head) in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

## Iconography
Taweret combines the body of a pregnant hippopotamus standing upright, the limbs and paws of a lion, the back and tail of a crocodile, and pendulous breasts and belly; this vessel substitutes a human head for the usual hippo head. She often rests a paw on the *sa* hieroglyph of protection.

## Significance
[[motif:taweret|Taweret]] ("the Great One") was, with Bes, the chief protector of women in pregnancy and childbirth and of infants. Her fearsome hybrid form channelled the danger of the hippopotamus into a guardian against the demons that threatened mother and child. Figure vases like this likely held milk or protective liquids used in birth ritual, fusing object and deity into a single magical implement.

## For artists & game designers
Taweret models the "dangerous animal turned protector" archetype: terrifying anatomy repurposed to guard the vulnerable.

citations.text: Geraldine Pinch, *Magic in Ancient Egypt* (1994).

title: Red Jasper Tyet Amulet (Knot of Isis, MET)
work: Ancient Egyptian Magic, Amulets & Funerary Protection
creator: Anonymous (Egypt)
summary:
A red jasper *tyet* amulet — the "Knot of Isis" or "Blood of Isis" — in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

## Iconography
A looped knot resembling the ankh but with its two side-arms folded downward, like a sash tied at the waist. The deep red of jasper or carnelian was the prescribed material.

## Significance
The [[motif:tyet|tyet]] is closely paired with the djed: where the djed gives Osirian stability, the tyet invokes the protective power of Isis. Book of the Dead spell 156 requires a tyet of red jasper at the mummy's throat so that "the power of Isis is the protection of this great one." Its red colour was read as the blood of Isis, a potent safeguarding fluid. The tyet, djed and wedjat together form the standard amuletic triad of Egyptian burial.

## For artists & game designers
Material-specified magic (it only works in *red* stone) is a clean crafting constraint: the colour is part of the spell.

citations.text: Carol Andrews, *Amulets of Ancient Egypt* (1994).

title: Faience Overseer Ushabti (Metropolitan Museum)
work: Ancient Egyptian Magic, Amulets & Funerary Protection
creator: Anonymous (Egypt)
summary:
A glazed faience "overseer" *ushabti* in the Metropolitan Museum of Art — a magical servant figure for the afterlife.

## Iconography
A small mummiform (or, as an overseer, kilted and whip-bearing) figurine of bright faience, inscribed with a spell. Overseer ushabtis are shown in the dress of the living to command the gangs of worker ushabtis.

## Significance
Ushabtis ("answerers") were animated by spell 6 of the Book of the Dead: when the deceased was called to labour in the [[motif:field of reeds|Field of Reeds]], the figurine would answer "Here I am!" and do the work in their stead. Wealthy burials held hundreds — ideally 365 workers plus 36 overseers. They are the clearest case of Egyptian magic as labour-saving technology, substituting an enchanted proxy for the owner's own toil.

## For artists & game designers
A figurine that answers a summons and works on your behalf is a ready-made minion or familiar mechanic, complete with overseer hierarchy.

citations.text: Harry M. Stewart, *Egyptian Shabtis* (1995).

title: Faience Wedjat-Eye Amulet (Museo Egizio C 1108)
work: Ancient Egyptian Magic, Amulets & Funerary Protection
creator: Anonymous (Egypt)
summary:
A glazed faience *wedjat*-eye amulet — the Eye of Horus — in the Museo Egizio, Turin.

## Iconography
The stylised falcon's eye combines a human eyebrow and lid with the markings of a lanner falcon: the curling "teardrop" and the spiral below the eye. It is among the most instantly recognisable of all Egyptian symbols.

## Significance
The [[motif:wedjat|wedjat]] ("the whole / sound one") embodies the eye Horus lost in battle with Seth and had restored by Thoth — hence it signifies healing, wholeness and protection. Worn by the living and laid on mummies (often over the embalming incision), it was the commonest of all Egyptian amulets. Its six geometric parts were later read as fractions in scribal arithmetic, linking magic to measure.

## For artists & game designers
The wedjat is a near-universal "protection" glyph; its restored-from-injury backstory makes it a natural icon for a healing or shield power-up.

citations.text: Carol Andrews, *Amulets of Ancient Egypt* (1994).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Pectoral with Winged Scarab (Museo Egizio C 6850)
work: Ancient Egyptian Magic, Amulets & Funerary Protection
creator: Anonymous (Egypt)
summary:
A pectoral in the form of a winged scarab, in the Museo Egizio, Turin, of the type sewn onto the mummy's chest wrappings.

## Iconography
A central scarab beetle spreads broad outstretched wings to either side, often pushing or framing a solar disk. The winged scarab is a single composite emblem of the reborn sun.

## Significance
The scarab pushing the sun across the sky personified Khepri, "he who comes into being," the morning aspect of the sun-god and a guarantee of daily renewal. Placed as a winged pectoral over the heart, it transferred that promise of [[motif:rebirth|solar rebirth]] to the deceased. Winged scarab pectorals are among the most spectacular pieces of Egyptian funerary jewellery, fusing precious craft with potent resurrection symbolism.

## For artists & game designers
The winged-scarab-and-sun is a clean heraldic device for a faction of rebirth or dawn; it reads instantly even at small scale.

citations.text: Carol Andrews, *Amulets of Ancient Egypt* (1994).

title: Emblem 'Potentissimus affectus amor' (Alciato, 1531)
work: The Emblem Tradition & the Theory of the Hidden Image
creator: Andrea Alciato; woodcut by Hans Schäufelin after Jörg Breu the Elder
summary:
A page from the first edition of Andrea Alciato's *Emblematum liber* (Augsburg, 1531), the book that founded the entire emblem genre.

## Iconography
The leaf carries the canonical three-part emblem structure: a Latin **motto** (*Potentissimus affectus amor*, 'love, the most powerful passion'), a **woodcut** picture, and an explanatory verse **epigram**. The image shows winged **Cupid** mastering wild beasts, the visual proof that love subdues even the strongest creatures.

## Significance
Alciato's collection assembled short Latin epigrams to which the Augsburg printer Heinrich Steyner attached woodcuts, accidentally inventing the [[motif:emblem-motto-picture-epigram|emblem]] as a fixed form of *motto + picture + poem*. The book ran to hundreds of editions across Europe and made the encoding of a moral or abstract idea in a decodable picture a central Renaissance art. Every later emblem book — sacred, amorous, Hermetic — descends from it.

## For artists & game designers
The three-slot template (title / image / caption) is a ready-made card layout: a single icon that 'means' a virtue, vice, or power, with motto and flavour text built in.

citations.text: A. Alciato, *Emblematum liber* (Augsburg, 1531).
P. M. Daly, *Literature in the Light of the Emblem* (1998).

title: Alciati Emblemata cum commentariis (Padua, 1621) — illustrated page
work: The Emblem Tradition & the Theory of the Hidden Image
creator: Andrea Alciato, with commentary by Claude Mignault and Lorenzo Pignoria
summary:
A page from the great annotated *Alciati Emblemata cum commentariis*, the heavily glossed Paduan edition that turned Alciato's slim emblem book into a vast scholarly encyclopedia.

## Iconography
An engraved **emblem** picture sits within dense columns of humanist **commentary** by Claude Mignault (Minois) and Lorenzo Pignoria, surrounded by sources, parallels and moral exposition. The image proper has shrunk to a small framed scene embedded in a sea of learned text.

## Significance
By the early 17th century the [[motif:emblem-motto-picture-epigram|Alciato]] corpus had accreted layer upon layer of commentary, treating each emblem as a riddle whose hidden meaning required scholarly decoding — the very [[motif:hieroglyph-and-hidden-meaning|theory of the hidden image]] in action. This edition shows the emblem as object of erudite interpretation, midway between poetry and the Hermetic 'hieroglyphics' of Valeriano.

## For artists & game designers
A model for layered lore: a small symbolic image surrounded by expanding tiers of annotation, where the picture is the key and the text is the unlockable codex entry.

citations.text: A. Alciato, *Emblemata cum commentariis Claudii Minois* (Padua, 1621).
D. Russell, *Emblematic Structures in Renaissance French Culture* (1995).

title: Symbolicarum Quaestionum libri quinque (Bocchi, 1574) — engraved symbol
work: The Emblem Tradition & the Theory of the Hidden Image
creator: Achille Bocchi; engravings by Giulio Bonasone (after Prospero Fontana)
summary:
An engraved 'symbol' from Achille Bocchi's *Symbolicarum Quaestionum libri quinque*, one of the most intellectually ambitious and Hermetic of all Renaissance emblem books.

## Iconography
A finely engraved allegorical scene by **Giulio Bonasone** is paired with a Latin **symbolum** and verse, the whole posed as a *quaestio* — a learned 'question' whose meaning the reader must resolve. The figures and attributes are arranged as a deliberate visual puzzle of Neoplatonic and moral ideas.

## Significance
Bocchi, founder of a Bolognese academy, conceived his 150 'symbolic questions' as serious philosophical play (*quas serio ludebat*), steeped in [[motif:hieroglyph-and-hidden-meaning|hieroglyphic]] and Hermetic thought of the kind associated with the Egyptian wisdom of Hermes Trismegistus. The Bonasone plates are among the finest emblem engravings of the century and place Bocchi at the esoteric, Neoplatonic end of the [[motif:emblem-motto-picture-epigram|emblem]] tradition.

## For artists & game designers
A gold standard for 'cryptic device' art: tightly composed allegorical engravings that present as solvable riddles rather than illustrations.

citations.text: A. Bocchi, *Symbolicarum Quaestionum... libri quinque* (Bologna, 1555/1574).
E. See & others on Bocchi's academy; cf. M. Watson, *Achille Bocchi and the Emblem Book as Symbolic Form* (1993).

title: Frontispiece to Robert Fludd's Utriusque Cosmi Historia (1617)
work: The Emblem Tradition & the Theory of the Hidden Image
creator: Robert Fludd; engraved frontispiece (Theodore de Bry workshop, Oppenheim)
summary:
The engraved title page of Robert Fludd's *Utriusque Cosmi... Historia* (1617–19), the encyclopedic Hermetic work on the 'two worlds', macrocosm and microcosm.

## Iconography
The **allegorical frontispiece** frames the title in an architectural portal flanked by personified figures and emblematic devices that announce the book's theme: the correspondence of the great world (**macrocosm**) and the little world of man (**microcosm**), bound by cosmic harmony.

## Significance
Fludd, English physician and Rosicrucian apologist, produced through the De Bry press at Oppenheim a series of the most spectacular [[motif:allegorical-frontispiece|occult title pages]] of the age. The frontispiece is itself a Hermetic emblem writ large: the whole argument of the book compressed into one decodable image, exemplifying the [[motif:hieroglyph-and-hidden-meaning|theory of the hidden image]] applied to the title page of a printed book.

## For artists & game designers
The architectural title-portal: an ornate frame whose personifications and symbols pre-load the entire 'world' the reader is about to enter — a splash-screen that is also a thesis.

citations.text: R. Fludd, *Utriusque Cosmi... Historia* (Oppenheim, 1617–19).
J. Godwin, *Robert Fludd: Hermetic Philosopher and Surveyor of Two Worlds* (1979).

title: Hadrianus Junius, Emblemata (1565) — illustrated emblem
work: The Emblem Tradition & the Theory of the Hidden Image
creator: Hadrianus Junius (Adriaen de Jonghe); printed by Christopher Plantin
summary:
An emblem from the *Emblemata* of Hadrianus Junius (Antwerp, 1565), a learned humanist contribution to the genre printed by the great Plantin press.

## Iconography
A neatly engraved **device** is set beneath a Latin **motto** and above a Neo-Latin **epigram**, in the classic Alciatan arrangement. Junius's images are compact allegorical conceits, each unfolding a moral or philosophical commonplace.

## Significance
Junius, a Dutch physician and polymath, was among the humanist authors who, in the generation after [[motif:emblem-motto-picture-epigram|Alciato]], expanded the emblem into an instrument of erudite display. Issued by **Christopher Plantin**, his *Emblemata* belongs to the dense Netherlandish production of the 1560s (alongside Sambucus) that made Antwerp the European capital of the printed emblem and refined the picture-as-hidden-meaning into a polished scholarly art.

## For artists & game designers
A clean, repeatable emblem template from the genre's classic period — useful as a reference for period-accurate device design and layout.

citations.text: H. Junius, *Emblemata* (Antwerp: Plantin, 1565).
C. Heesakkers, in *The Emblem in Renaissance and Baroque Europe* (1993).

title: Plate from Khunrath's Amphitheatrum Sapientiae Aeternae (1595/1609)
work: The Emblem Tradition & the Theory of the Hidden Image
creator: Heinrich Khunrath
summary:
An engraved plate from Heinrich Khunrath's *Amphitheatrum Sapientiae Aeternae* ('Amphitheatre of Eternal Wisdom'), among the most celebrated theosophical-alchemical emblem plates of the era.

## Iconography
The large circular composition stages an emblematic 'amphitheatre' of divine **wisdom**: figures, inscriptions, and ritual or laboratory apparatus arranged so that the whole functions as a meditative diagram uniting prayer and alchemical work (*ora et labora*).

## Significance
Khunrath's plates — most famously the 'oratory-laboratory' — fuse Christian piety, Paracelsian [[motif:alchemy|alchemy]] and proto-Rosicrucian [[motif:rosicrucian|theosophy]] into single image-arguments. They are emblems on a monumental scale, where each inscription and figure is a station in a contemplative ascent toward eternal wisdom, exemplifying how the [[motif:allegorical-frontispiece|allegorical plate]] could serve as a tool of esoteric meditation.

## For artists & game designers
A full circular 'temple of knowledge' tableau: a single ornate scene that doubles as a map of stations to be visited in order.

citations.text: H. Khunrath, *Amphitheatrum Sapientiae Aeternae* (Hanau, 1609).
U. Szulakowska, *The Alchemy of Light* (2000).

title: Frontispiece of Athanasius Kircher's Oedipus Aegyptiacus (1652)
work: The Emblem Tradition & the Theory of the Hidden Image
creator: Athanasius Kircher; engraved frontispiece
summary:
The allegorical frontispiece of Athanasius Kircher's *Oedipus Aegyptiacus* (Rome, 1652–54), his vast attempt to 'decipher' Egyptian hieroglyphs as a hidden Hermetic theology.

## Iconography
The **frontispiece** marshals Egyptianizing emblems — obelisks, sphinxes, personified figures and hieroglyphic devices — around the title, casting Kircher as the new **Oedipus** who will solve the riddle of Egyptian wisdom just as the original solved the Sphinx's.

## Significance
Kircher believed the **hieroglyphs** encoded a secret philosophy descending from [[motif:hermetic|Hermes Trismegistus]], and his work is the grand Baroque monument to the Renaissance [[motif:hieroglyph-and-hidden-meaning|theory of the hidden image]] — the conviction that pictures could carry esoteric truths legible only to initiates. His decipherments were almost wholly wrong, but the frontispiece perfectly embodies the dream of the readable sacred symbol.

## For artists & game designers
The 'cipher-puzzle world' announced visually: obelisks and sphinxes as promise of a script to be cracked — the title page as the game's central riddle in miniature.

citations.text: A. Kircher, *Oedipus Aegyptiacus* (Rome, 1652–54).
D. Stolzenberg, *Egyptian Oedipus: Athanasius Kircher and the Secrets of Antiquity* (2013).

title: Frontispiece to Burton's Anatomy of Melancholy (1638)
work: The Emblem Tradition & the Theory of the Hidden Image
creator: Robert Burton; engraved frontispiece by Christian Le Blon (Christof Le Blon)
summary:
The famous emblematic frontispiece to Robert Burton's *The Anatomy of Melancholy* (1638 edition), a title page that is itself a chart of the melancholic temperament.

## Iconography
The **frontispiece** is divided into compartments, each an emblem of a melancholic type — Jealousy, Solitude, the Lover, the Hypochondriac, the superstitious and the maniac — flanked by the planet **Saturn** above and the figures of Democritus and the author below, with explanatory verses ('The Argument of the Frontispiece').

## Significance
Burton's title page is a model of the [[motif:allegorical-frontispiece|emblematic frontispiece]]: a grid of personified states that diagrams the whole book's subject before a word of text. It ties **melancholy** to its astral governor [[motif:saturn|Saturn]] in the tradition analysed by Klibansky, Panofsky and Saxl, presenting a 'hidden image' of the diseased soul that the reader decodes compartment by compartment.

## For artists & game designers
A gridded character-select screen avant la lettre: each panel a distinct 'type' with its own emblem, framed by the governing planet and presiding sages.

citations.text: R. Burton, *The Anatomy of Melancholy* (Oxford, 1638).
R. Klibansky, E. Panofsky & F. Saxl, *Saturn and Melancholy* (1964).

title: Quarles, Emblems Divine and Moral (1736 ed.) — engraved emblem
work: The Emblem Tradition & the Theory of the Hidden Image
creator: Francis Quarles (after William Marshall / Boetius à Bolswert designs)
summary:
An engraved emblem from Francis Quarles's *Emblems, Divine and Moral* (here the 1736 edition; first published 1635), the most popular English emblem book.

## Iconography
A religious **emblem** pairs an engraved scene — often the soul (*Anima*) and Divine Love (the child Christ) acting out a spiritual conceit — with a scriptural motto and a meditative verse. The picture renders an inward, devotional truth as an outward, decodable image.

## Significance
Quarles adapted his designs from Continental Jesuit emblem books (the *Pia Desideria* of Hugo and the *Typus Mundi*), Protestantizing them for an English audience. *Emblems* became a household devotional classic, carrying the [[motif:emblem-motto-picture-epigram|emblem]] tradition deep into English religious culture and demonstrating the form's power to make the soul's hidden states visible. The full title's 'hieroglyphicks of the life of man' explicitly invokes the [[motif:hieroglyph-and-hidden-meaning|hidden-image]] theory.

## For artists & game designers
The soul as a recurring little protagonist: an inner spiritual journey externalized as a sequence of symbolic vignettes.

citations.text: F. Quarles, *Emblems, Divine and Moral* (London, 1635; 1736 ed.).
K. J. Höltgen, *Francis Quarles 1592–1644* (1978).

title: Personification of 'Academy' (Ripa tradition, Wellcome plate)
work: The Emblem Tradition & the Theory of the Hidden Image
creator: Anonymous (after Cesare Ripa's Iconologia)
rights: CC BY 4.0. Wellcome Collection, via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
An engraved plate (Wellcome Collection) personifying **Academy** in the manner of Ripa's *Iconologia*, illustrating the allegory of organized learning.

## Iconography
A female **personification** of Academy is shown with attributes signifying study, the liberal arts and disciplined enquiry — books, instruments, and emblematic devices that mark her as the embodiment of an institution of learning rather than a single abstract virtue.

## Significance
The figure belongs to the long afterlife of Cesare Ripa's [[motif:personification-of-abstractions|Iconologia]], whose method of clothing abstractions in fixed attributes was copied and extended in countless later engraved series. 'Academy' personified shows how the system reached beyond classical virtues to embody the very institutions of Renaissance and early-modern intellectual life, including those (academies, *studia*) that nurtured Hermetic and natural-philosophical pursuits.

## For artists & game designers
Proof that the Ripa kit scales to institutions, not just virtues: a guild, college, or order can be given a single allegorical avatar with its own attribute set.

citations.text: C. Ripa, *Iconologia* (and later illustrated derivatives).
Wellcome Collection, catalogue record L0035392.

title: Ripa's Iconologia (1603) — illustrated page of personifications
work: The Emblem Tradition & the Theory of the Hidden Image
creator: Cesare Ripa
summary:
A page from the 1603 illustrated *Iconologia* of Cesare Ripa, the standard handbook for personifying abstract ideas in Western art.

## Iconography
A woodcut **personification** stands with its diagnostic **attributes** — the objects, animals, postures and colours by which an abstraction (a virtue, art, passion, or place) is to be recognized — beneath a heading and an explanatory description of why each attribute is chosen.

## Significance
Ripa's *Iconologia* (text 1593, illustrated 1603) codified the visual vocabulary of [[motif:personification-of-abstractions|allegory]]: for two centuries painters, sculptors and designers of frontispieces consulted it to give bodily form to Wisdom, Melancholy, Alchemy, the Elements, the Liberal Arts and countless other concepts. It is the indispensable key to reading the personified figures that crowd Baroque ceilings, title pages and occult emblems.

## For artists & game designers
The definitive 'attribute kit' for allegory: look up an abstraction and get the exact props and colours that will make it legible at a glance.

citations.text: C. Ripa, *Iconologia* (Rome, 1603).
E. Mandowsky, *Ricerche intorno all'Iconologia di Cesare Ripa* (1939).

title: Personification of Africa (Ripa's Iconologia, 1603)
work: The Emblem Tradition & the Theory of the Hidden Image
creator: Cesare Ripa
summary:
The personification of **Africa** from Cesare Ripa's *Iconologia* (1603), a characteristic example of how Ripa embodies an abstraction through fixed attributes.

## Iconography
Africa appears as a woman wearing the famous **elephant-head** headdress and accompanied by attributes such as a scorpion, a lion or serpent, and a cornucopia — the signs by which Ripa's reader was to identify the continent and its supposed qualities of heat and wildness.

## Significance
The four continents were among the most-copied of Ripa's [[motif:personification-of-abstractions|personifications]], and his Africa-with-elephant-headdress became the canonical formula, repeated on fountains, ceilings and title pages across Baroque Europe (most famously by Tiepolo). The figure shows the *Iconologia*'s method exactly: an abstract idea (a continent) made into a readable body through a checklist of emblematic attributes.

## For artists & game designers
A textbook 'faction personified' design: one figure whose headdress and companions instantly encode a whole region's identity.

citations.text: C. Ripa, *Iconologia* (Rome, 1603), 's.v. Africa'.

title: Emblem 'Non dolo sed virtute' (Sambucus, Emblemata)
work: The Emblem Tradition & the Theory of the Hidden Image
creator: Joannes Sambucus (János Zsámboky)
motifs: not by guile but by virtue
summary:
The emblem *Non dolo sed virtute* ('not by guile but by virtue') from the *Emblemata* of Joannes Sambucus, a leading humanist emblematist of the 1560s.

## Iconography
The **device** illustrates the motto *Non dolo sed virtute* — a scene contrasting honest valour with trickery — accompanied by an epigram drawing the moral that worthy ends should be won by virtue and not by deceit.

## Significance
Sambucus, a Hungarian humanist working in the orbit of the Plantin press, produced one of the most reprinted [[motif:emblem-motto-picture-epigram|emblem books]] of the century, valued for its classical learning and elegant Latin. Emblems such as this typify the genre's ethical core: a memorable picture fixing a moral maxim in the mind, the *hidden* lesson made legible through image and motto.

## For artists & game designers
A clean maxim-emblem: a single contrast-scene that locks an aphorism to an image — the model for a 'proverb card' system.

title: Tabula Cebetis (Carta Vitae) — allegorical print (detail)
work: The Emblem Tradition & the Theory of the Hidden Image
creator: Anonymous; Rijksmuseum print
rights: Public domain (CC0). Rijksmuseum, via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A detail (upper right corner) of an engraved *Tabula Cebetis* (*Carta Vitae*, 'map of life'), the allegorical picture-diagram of human existence (Rijksmuseum).

## Iconography
The print lays out the **allegory of life** as nested **enclosures**: souls enter the gate of life past **Fortune** and Deceit, traverse the regions of false and **true education**, and climb toward the citadel of Happiness, each personification labelled so the whole reads as a walkable moral map.

## Significance
The *Tabula Cebetis*, a Greek dialogue of the 1st century CE ascribed to a follower of [[motif:pythagoras|Pythagoras]], describes a votive panel mapping the soul's pilgrimage. Rediscovered and endlessly printed in the Renaissance, it became a favourite emblematic subject uniting Pythagorean-Platonic ethics with [[motif:hermetic|Hermetic]] and Stoic teaching — the supreme example of the picture that is also a readable map of the inner life.

## For artists & game designers
Literally a level map of life: nested rings of trials and false paths leading to a final citadel — an allegory that already is a game board.

citations.text: *Tabula Cebetis* (Pseudo-Cebes), ed. J. T. Fitzgerald & L. M. White (1983).
R. Schleier, *Tabula Cebetis* (1973).

title: 'Ghewensten Strijdt / Combat Heureux' (Vaenius, Amorum Emblemata, 1608)
work: The Emblem Tradition & the Theory of the Hidden Image
creator: Otto van Veen (Vaenius)
summary:
An emblem from Otto van Veen's *Amorum Emblemata* (Antwerp, 1608), the influential picture-book of secular love-emblems.

## Iconography
The engraving shows winged **Cupid** (Amor) acting out a conceit of love — here a 'happy combat' (*Ghewensten Strijdt / Combat Heureux*) — beneath mottoes given in several languages, with verses expanding the amorous lesson.

## Significance
Vaenius, Rubens's teacher, produced in his *Amorum Emblemata* the model secular [[motif:emblem-motto-picture-epigram|emblem book]] of love, in which Cupid enacts the paradoxes of desire across a hundred plates. The work was hugely popular and helped spread the emblem form into vernacular and amorous registers across Europe; it stands beside his moral *Emblemata Horatiana* as the secular wing of the tradition that Alciato founded.

## For artists & game designers
A cohesive 'recurring mascot' device: a single character (Cupid) re-posed across dozens of plates to dramatize an abstract theme, with multilingual captioning.

citations.text: O. van Veen, *Amorum Emblemata* (Antwerp, 1608).

title: Moral emblem 'Socrates and Xanthippe' (Vaenius tradition)
work: The Emblem Tradition & the Theory of the Hidden Image
creator: Otto van Veen (Vaenius)
summary:
A moral emblem of **Socrates and Xanthippe** by Otto van Veen, illustrating a philosophical lesson in patience drawn from the Neo-Stoic emblem tradition.

## Iconography
The philosopher **Socrates** endures the rage of his wife **Xanthippe**, who in the familiar anecdote drenches him with water; Socrates remains calm. The scene serves as the picture of an emblem teaching forbearance — that after thunder (scolding) comes the downpour, met with equanimity.

## Significance
Vaenius's moral emblem books, above all the *Emblemata Horatiana*, translated the ethics of Horace and the Stoics into [[motif:emblem-motto-picture-epigram|picture-mottoes]] for a wide readership. The Socrates-and-Xanthippe exemplum was a stock image of the wise man's imperturbability, showing how the [[motif:emblem-motto-picture-epigram|emblem]] form carried not only love and Hermetic mystery but practical ethical instruction by visual anecdote.

## For artists & game designers
A compact 'virtue lesson' scene: a single famous anecdote staged so its moral (patience) reads instantly — useful as illustrative loading-screen wisdom.

citations.text: O. van Veen, *Emblemata Horatiana* (Antwerp, 1607).
M. Praz, *Studies in Seventeenth-Century Imagery* (2nd ed., 1964).

title: Valeriano's Hieroglyphica (1556) — illustrated page
work: The Emblem Tradition & the Theory of the Hidden Image
creator: Pierio Valeriano (Giovanni Pierio Valeriano Bolzani)
summary:
A page from Pierio Valeriano's *Hieroglyphica, sive De sacris Aegyptiorum literis commentarii* (1556), the great Renaissance encyclopedia of symbolic meaning.

## Iconography
A woodcut **symbolic image** (typically an animal, object, or natural sign) accompanies commentary explaining its hidden significations, drawn from ancient authors and from the supposed 'sacred letters' (*sacrae literae*) of the Egyptians. Each entry treats a thing as a sign with layered meanings.

## Significance
Valeriano systematized the Renaissance belief, founded on the recovery of [[motif:hieroglyph-and-hidden-meaning|Horapollo]], that the world is a book of symbols and that the Egyptian **hieroglyph** was a perfect picture-language of ideas. His vast *Hieroglyphica* supplied artists, emblematists and Hermetic philosophers with a reference work of decodable images, and stands directly behind the theory that an abstract concept can be carried by a sacred picture.

## For artists & game designers
A ready-made symbol dictionary: each creature or object keyed to a meaning, ideal for a consistent iconographic language across a project.

citations.text: P. Valeriano, *Hieroglyphica* (Basel, 1556).
K. Giehlow, *The Humanist Interpretation of Hieroglyphs in the Allegorical Studies of the Renaissance* (Eng. trans. 2015).

title: The Monas Hieroglyphica (John Dee)
creator: John Dee
summary:
The **Monas Hieroglyphica** — the single composite glyph **John Dee** unveiled in his cryptic 1564 treatise, claiming it encoded the unity of the cosmos.

## Iconography
A built-up sigil: the **crescent moon** over the **circle-and-point of the sun**, set on a **cross** (the four elements), with the horned sign of **Aries** (fire) at the base. Dee derives it across 24 'theorems' as the root from which every planetary and alchemical sign can be drawn.

## Significance
The Monas fuses [[tradition:hermetic|Hermetic]], alchemical, astrological, and [[tradition:kabbalah|Kabbalistic]] symbolism into one mark — a claim that all the cosmos springs from a single hieroglyph. It is the intellectual seed of Dee's later angelic ('Enochian') work.

## For artists & game designers
A self-contained 'master sigil' — clean line-art that reads as the ultimate arcane rune.

citations.text: John Dee, *Monas Hieroglyphica* (Antwerp, 1564); trans. C. H. Josten, *Ambix* 12 (1964).
György Szőnyi, *John Dee's Occultism* (SUNY, 2004).

title: Portrait of John Dee (Ashmolean Museum)
work: John Dee, Edward Kelley & the Enochian / Angelic Magic System
creator: Unidentified painter (English school)
summary:
Oil portrait of the English mathematician, astrologer and magus John Dee (1527–1608/9), held by the Ashmolean Museum, Oxford, and long regarded as the standard likeness of the man who attempted to converse with angels.

## Iconography
Dee is shown in old age, half-length, against a dark ground: a gaunt face with a long white beard, a black scholar's skullcap and a plain white ruff over dark robes. The image radiates sober gravity rather than occult drama — the costume is that of a learned Tudor gentleman and natural philosopher. A later tradition holds that a ring of skulls once surrounded the figure and was painted out, a [[motif:memento mori|memento mori]] consistent with the sitter's reputation.

## Significance
Dee was the most learned Englishman of his generation — adviser to Elizabeth I, author of the *Monas Hieroglyphica*, owner of the greatest private library in England — yet from 1582 he devoted himself to the "angelic conversations" recorded with Edward Kelley, the seed of the Enochian system. This portrait fixes the public memory of the [[motif:renaissance magus|renaissance magus]] who bridged mathematics, navigation and ceremonial magic. Modern scholarship (Deborah Harkness, *John Dee's Conversations with Angels*, 1999) reads the angelic project as natural philosophy by other means.

## For artists & game designers
The definitive "wise old magus" reference: skullcap, white beard, ruff, austere palette — instantly legible as a Renaissance scholar-mage without a single occult prop.

citations.text: Deborah E. Harkness, *John Dee's Conversations with Angels* (Cambridge UP, 1999).

title: John Dee (line engraving by Francis Cleyn, 1658)
work: John Dee, Edward Kelley & the Enochian / Angelic Magic System
creator: Francis Cleyn (Franz Klein)
rights: CC BY 4.0. Wellcome Collection. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A line engraving of John Dee by Francis Cleyn, dated 1658 — produced half a century after Dee's death, in the decade that saw his angelic diaries finally reach print.

## Iconography
The bust portrait, often set within an oval, repeats the established Dee type: aged scholar, long beard, skullcap and ruff, rendered now in the crisp parallel hatching of mid-seventeenth-century engraving. As a print it was designed for reproduction and circulation in books rather than for a wall.

## Significance
The date is telling: in 1659 Meric Casaubon published *A True & Faithful Relation of What Passed for Many Years Between Dr John Dee... and Some Spirits*, the first printing of the angelic conversations, intended to discredit Dee as a deluded enthusiast. Engraved likenesses such as Cleyn's belong to this moment of renewed, sceptical public interest, when Dee became a cautionary figure in the debate over [[motif:angelic conversation|spirit communication]] and credulity. The portrait thus marks the transition of Dee from living philosopher to printed legend.

## For artists & game designers
A period-accurate "engraved frontispiece" asset — ideal for a discovered book or grimoire whose author's face stares out from the title page in hatched black line.

citations.text: Meric Casaubon (ed.), *A True & Faithful Relation...* (London, 1659).

title: John Dee's gold disc (Sigillum Aemeth fitting), British Museum
work: John Dee, Edward Kelley & the Enochian / Angelic Magic System
creator: Anonymous goldsmith (for John Dee)
rights: CC0. Photograph by Vassil, British Museum. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A small engraved gold disc associated with John Dee's angelic practice, now in the British Museum — distinct from the large wax *Sigillum Dei Aemeth* discs, and engraved with a vision Kelley reported in the crystal.

## Iconography
The thin gold roundel is incised with a schematic scene: a central cross or arrangement of figures within a circle, recording one of the visions "shown" to Edward Kelley in the [[motif:scrying crystal|shew-stone]] — traditionally identified with the four watchtowers or castles seen during the angelic sessions. The metalwork is fine and the engraving deliberately diagrammatic rather than pictorial.

## Significance
Dee's surviving ritual apparatus in the British Museum — the obsidian mirror, the crystal, the wax seals and this gold disc — constitutes the rare case of a Renaissance magical practice preserved as physical objects. The disc materialises the principle that the angels did not merely speak but *displayed* structured images to be copied down, the visual logic that produced the Enochian tablets. It connects the abstract diagrams to a tangible, precious instrument fit for a [[motif:seal of god|seal of God]].

## For artists & game designers
A luxe quest-object: an engraved gold talisman whose incised diagram is itself a clue — the picture on the disc is a map of somewhere the player must go.

citations.text: British Museum, *John Dee's gold seal/disc* (collection object).

title: Letter in the hand of John Dee, 1588
work: John Dee, Edward Kelley & the Enochian / Angelic Magic System
creator: John Dee
summary:
An autograph letter written by John Dee in 1588, during or just after the years of his continental travels with Edward Kelley among the courts of the Holy Roman Empire and Poland.

## Iconography
A single leaf of laid paper covered in Dee's tight Elizabethan secretary hand, closing with his signature. The document is a piece of working correspondence rather than a magical text, but it presents the magus through the most intimate evidence of all — his own handwriting.

## Significance
1588 was a pivotal year: the famous "cross-matching" episode, in which the angels reportedly instructed Dee and Kelley to share their wives, had strained the partnership, and Dee was preparing his return to an England transformed by the Armada. Surviving autographs anchor the angelic diaries (the *Libri Mysteriorum*, today Sloane MSS in the British Library) to a real, datable hand, and let palaeographers test which manuscripts are genuinely Dee's. The letter is a reminder that the [[motif:renaissance magus|magus]] was also a courtier, diplomat and tireless writer of business.

## For artists & game designers
A convincing "handwritten document" prop: dense secretary hand and a flourished signature read instantly as an authentic period letter discovered among a scholar's papers.

citations.text: Glyn Parry, *The Arch-Conjuror of England: John Dee* (Yale UP, 2011).

title: Portrait of John Dee (Wellcome Collection)
work: John Dee, Edward Kelley & the Enochian / Angelic Magic System
creator: Unidentified artist (after the Ashmolean type)
rights: CC BY 4.0. Wellcome Collection. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A portrait of John Dee preserved in the Wellcome Collection, London, one of several derivatives of the canonical Ashmolean likeness that carried Dee's face into the history of medicine and science.

## Iconography
Dee appears half-length and frontal, an old man with a flowing white beard, the black skullcap of a scholar and a white ruff at the throat, set against a plain dark ground. The treatment is restrained and documentary, presenting him as a grave physician–philosopher rather than a conjuror.

## Significance
The Wellcome holds extensive material on Dee because his reputation straddles medicine, astrology and magic; his casting of horoscopes, his work on calendar reform and his angelic experiments were all of a piece in the Elizabethan understanding of natural knowledge. The survival of multiple portrait versions testifies to the long fascination with the man whom later ages cast as the model wizard. On the angelic side his great monument is the *Libri Mysteriorum* — the diaries of his sessions with [[motif:angelic conversation|the angels]].

## For artists & game designers
Use alongside the Ashmolean portrait to show how a single "face of the magus" propagates through copies — handy for a lore item that exists in several slightly different painted versions.

citations.text: Wellcome Collection, *Portrait of John Dee* (M0014535).

title: The Holy Table (*Mensa Sancta*), *A True & Faithful Relation*
work: John Dee, Edward Kelley & the Enochian / Angelic Magic System
creator: John Dee (engraved for Meric Casaubon's edition)
summary:
The design of the Holy Table (*Mensa Sancta*), the consecrated table on which Dee and Kelley performed the angelic actions, as printed in Meric Casaubon's *A True & Faithful Relation* (London, 1659) from Dee's own records of 1582–83.

## Iconography
A large square table-top bordered on all four edges by a continuous band of [[motif:enochian script|Enochian (angelic) letters]]. Within the border are set further characters and, at the centre, a grid or compartmented square; in practice the wax *Sigillum Dei Aemeth* rested at the centre and smaller seals supported the legs. The whole is a working diagram: every glyph had to be reproduced exactly for the table to function.

## Significance
The Holy Table is the physical stage of Enochian magic. Its border script was among the first deliverances of the angels, and the table organised the apparatus — seals, shew-stone, candles — into a single sanctified field. Casaubon printed these diagrams to expose Dee, but in doing so created the source from which the nineteenth-century [[motif:ceremonial magic|Golden Dawn]] reconstructed the system. It is the architectural plan of the angelic experiments.

## For artists & game designers
A ready-made ritual-circle floor: a square bordered in alien script with a seal at its heart — drop props onto the marked positions and the table becomes an interactive summoning device.

citations.text: Meric Casaubon (ed.), *A True & Faithful Relation...* (London, 1659).

title: Edward Kelley (coloured aquatint)
work: John Dee, Edward Kelley & the Enochian / Angelic Magic System
creator: Anonymous (coloured aquatint)
rights: CC BY 4.0. Wellcome Collection. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A coloured aquatint of Edward Kelley in the Wellcome Collection, a richer, tinted counterpart to the line and stipple portraits of Dee's scryer.

## Iconography
Kelley is shown half-length as a robed, bearded figure in a skullcap, the soft aquatint ground washed with colour to give warmth and depth. As with every Kelley likeness the features are conjectural; the colouring serves to make the alchemist vivid and collectible rather than to record a true face.

## Significance
The survival of Kelley in line engraving (Cooper), antiquarian print (Pennant) and coloured aquatint shows how thoroughly the print trade mythologised the pair. Kelley's alchemical fame — the claim that he transmuted metals before the court of [[motif:reception|Rudolf II]] in Prague — kept him in demand among collectors of "famous adepts," independent of the angelic work. The coloured plate is the most decorative phase of that afterlife.

## For artists & game designers
A tinted character portrait ready for a card frame — the colour palette (warm robes, shadowed ground) is a usable reference for an alchemist NPC.

citations.text: Wellcome Collection, *Edward Kelley*, coloured aquatint (V0003199).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Edward Kelley (stipple engraving by R. Cooper)
work: John Dee, Edward Kelley & the Enochian / Angelic Magic System
creator: Richard Cooper (stipple engraving)
rights: CC BY 4.0. Wellcome Collection. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A stipple-engraved portrait of Edward Kelley by Richard Cooper, in the Wellcome Collection — a refined nineteenth-century likeness of Dee's scryer and alchemical partner.

## Iconography
A bust portrait, usually within an oval, shows Kelley as a bearded man in a close skullcap, gazing aside. The soft tonal dots of [[motif:reception|stipple engraving]] lend the face a smooth, almost sentimental finish far removed from any documented Elizabethan source; like all Kelley portraits it is essentially invented, since no life-portrait survives. Tradition held that Kelley's ears had been cropped as punishment for forgery, and some images allude to the skullcap that hid them.

## Significance
Edward Kelley (1555–1597/8) was the medium who actually "saw" in the shew-stone while Dee recorded; without his visions the Enochian system would not exist. His shadowed biography — convicted coiner, alchemist, knighted and then imprisoned by Rudolf II — made him irresistible to print-shops cataloguing famous magi. This portrait belongs to the antiquarian and biographical literature (Thomas Pennant, the alchemical compilers) that kept the [[motif:scryer|scryer]]'s memory alive.

## For artists & game designers
A polished "wanted-poster" likeness for the roguish medium of the pair — pair it with the necromancy print to show the gap between elegant portrait and lurid legend.

citations.text: Wellcome Collection, *Edward Kelley*, stipple engraving by R. Cooper (V0003198).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Edward Kelley Raising the Dead (Sibly engraving)
work: John Dee, Edward Kelley & the Enochian / Angelic Magic System
creator: Ebenezer Sibly (engraving)
summary:
An engraving from Ebenezer Sibly's *A New and Complete Illustration of the Occult Sciences* (London, 1780s–90s) depicting Edward Kelley raising the dead — the image that fixed Kelley's reputation as a necromancer (German captions title it *Totenbeschwörung*).

## Iconography
In a moonlit churchyard two cloaked figures stand within a protective [[motif:magic circle|magic circle]] inscribed with names and characters; one holds a torch or wand and an open book while a shrouded corpse rises stiffly from an opened grave before them. Tombs, a ruined church and night sky complete the gothic setting. The scene is wholly imaginary — an eighteenth-century fantasy projected back onto the Elizabethan scryer.

## Significance
Though Kelley's documented work with Dee was angelic, not funerary, this print made him the archetype of the graveyard necromancer and became one of the most reproduced images of Renaissance magic. It marks the [[motif:reception|reception]] of Dee and Kelley by the Romantic occult revival, which preferred lurid sorcery to the tedious tabulation of angelic names. Sibly's engraving is the visual ancestor of every later "two magicians and a rising corpse" illustration.

## For artists & game designers
The canonical necromancy tableau: circle, torch, book, open grave, rising shroud — a complete spell-scene composition you can restage almost beat for beat.

citations.text: Ebenezer Sibly, *A New and Complete Illustration of the Occult Sciences* (London, c. 1790).

title: Edward Kelly, Prophet or Seer to Dr Dee
work: John Dee, Edward Kelley & the Enochian / Angelic Magic System
creator: After Thomas Pennant
summary:
An antiquarian print labelled "Edward Kelly, Prophet or Seer to Dr Dee," associated with the collections of the Welsh antiquary Thomas Pennant — an image that names Kelley precisely by his function in the partnership.

## Iconography
A bust portrait of a bearded man in a skullcap, captioned with his name and the telling title "prophet or seer to Dr Dee." The plate sits among eighteenth-century antiquarian portraits of notable Britons; its lettering does the interpretive work, fixing Kelley's identity as the [[motif:scryer|seer]] of the pair rather than as an independent magus.

## Significance
The caption captures the division of labour that defined Enochian magic: Dee, the learned director, posed questions and wrote everything down; Kelley, the gifted (and suspect) medium, reported what appeared in the crystal. Calling him "prophet or seer" — with that hedging "or" — also registers the perennial doubt over whether Kelley genuinely scryed or fabricated his visions, a question argued from his own century to ours. The print belongs to the antiquarian [[motif:reception|reception]] that historicised the duo.

## For artists & game designers
A labelled NPC card: the same bearded face, but the caption assigns a role — "Seer" — turning a portrait into a class identity for the party's medium.

summary:
A memorial plaque to John Dee in the church of St Mary the Virgin, Mortlake, where the magus was buried after his death in 1608/9 — the only fixed monument to a man whose grave itself is lost.

## Iconography
An inscribed commemorative plate mounted in the parish church, naming Dee and recording his association with Mortlake. The plaque is modern; Dee's actual tomb and gravestone have not survived, so the memorial stands in for a vanished burial.

## Significance
Mortlake on the Thames was Dee's home and the site of his celebrated library — the largest in Elizabethan England, with thousands of volumes and scientific instruments — to which scholars, courtiers and the queen herself came. It was here that much of the angelic work was conducted and here that, during his absence abroad, his collection was plundered. The plaque marks the geographical anchor of Dee's life and the [[motif:reception|continuing local memory]] of the "Mortlake conjuror."

## For artists & game designers
A quiet "end of the trail" location: a church plaque that confirms a legendary figure was a real, buried person — good for a reflective late-game discovery.

summary:
A house on Mortlake High Street associated with John Dee, marking the riverside site of his home and famous library on the Thames west of London.

## Iconography
A street-level photograph of a building on Mortlake High Street linked by local tradition to Dee. The structure is unremarkable domestic architecture; its significance is entirely commemorative, pinning a legendary household to an actual address.

## Significance
Dee's Mortlake house was an intellectual powerhouse of Elizabethan England: it held his vast library, his alchemical laboratories and his instruments, and it was here, in the early 1580s, that he and Edward Kelley began the [[motif:angelic conversation|angelic conversations]] over the shew-stone. The library was a resource of national importance, consulted on navigation, calendar reform and natural philosophy, and its dispersal during Dee's continental years was a real loss to English learning. The surviving site keeps the [[motif:reception|memory]] of where the Enochian system was first received.

## For artists & game designers
A hub location reference: the unassuming exterior of the magus's house — the contrast between mundane street frontage and the wonders worked inside is a usable narrative beat.

title: The Order of the *Inspirati*, *A True & Faithful Relation*
work: John Dee, Edward Kelley & the Enochian / Angelic Magic System
creator: John Dee (engraved for Meric Casaubon's edition)
summary:
A diagram titled "The Order of the *Inspirati*" from Casaubon's *A True & Faithful Relation* (1659), one of the structured tables by which Dee organised the angelic names and hierarchies received through Edward Kelley.

## Iconography
The plate is a ruled chart: rows and columns of names, letters and titles arranged to display rank and relationship among the angelic and spirit beings of the system. Latin headings frame compartments filled with the transliterated angelic names, the inspired ones (*inspirati*) set in their proper order. It is information design, not pictorial art — a taxonomy of invisible powers.

## Significance
The angelic conversations did not deliver loose oracles but an entire administrative cosmos: governors, kings and ministering angels each with a name, a seal and a sphere of authority. Charts like this one show Dee the mathematician imposing order on revelation, tabulating heaven as he might tabulate a star catalogue. Such tables of [[motif:angelic hierarchy|angelic hierarchy]] became the backbone of later Enochian practice, supplying the names invoked in the calls of the Aethyrs.

## For artists & game designers
A lore codex page: a grid of named entities with ranks and sigils — perfect as a discoverable "bestiary of angels" the player decodes one row at a time.

citations.text: Meric Casaubon (ed.), *A True & Faithful Relation...* (London, 1659).

title: Order of Emperor Rudolf II for the Arrest of Edward Kelley
work: John Dee, Edward Kelley & the Enochian / Angelic Magic System
creator: Imperial chancery of Rudolf II
rights: CC BY 4.0. Wellcome Collection. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A document signed by the Holy Roman Emperor Rudolf II ordering the arrest of Edward Kelley, preserved in the Wellcome Collection — the bureaucratic record of the scryer's spectacular fall in Bohemia.

## Iconography
A leaf of formal chancery script bearing the imperial signature and authority, its weight conveyed by layout and subscription rather than by image. As a state paper it stands in sharp contrast to the fanciful portrait prints: this is the real administrative trace of a magician's life.

## Significance
After Dee returned to England in 1589, Kelley remained on the Continent and won the patronage of Rudolf II of Prague — emperor, melancholic and the greatest collector-patron of [[motif:alchemy|alchemy]] of his age — even being knighted on the strength of his promised transmutations. When the gold failed to materialise, favour turned to imprisonment; Kelley is said to have died after a fall while attempting escape. This order documents the dangerous economy of court alchemy, where a failed adept could be jailed at imperial command. It closes the historical arc of the Dee–Kelley partnership.

## For artists & game designers
A "bounty warrant" prop with real stakes: an imperial arrest order for your alchemist NPC, signed and sealed — a quest hook the moment the player finds it.

title: Angelic Chart from *A True & Faithful Relation*
work: John Dee, Edward Kelley & the Enochian / Angelic Magic System
creator: John Dee (engraved for Meric Casaubon's edition)
summary:
One of the lettered charts reproduced in Casaubon's *A True & Faithful Relation* (1659), recording a grid of characters dictated to Dee and Kelley during the angelic actions.

## Iconography
A squared field subdivided into many small cells, each holding a single letter or character. The reader is meant to extract names and words from the grid by prescribed paths — across rows, down columns, or along marked diagonals. This is the form in which much of the angelic language and the Enochian tablets were delivered: as letter-by-letter dictation into a matrix.

## Significance
The great tables of Enochian magic — the four elemental watchtowers and the unifying Tabula Recensa — are precisely such lettered squares, from which the names of governing angels are read out to compose the "calls." Charts like this preserve the raw deliverance before interpretation, showing how revelation arrived as structured data. The slow, error-prone copying of these grids (and the angels' insistence on exactness) is a recurring drama of the [[motif:angelic conversation|conversations]]. The same combinatorial logic links Dee's project to the [[motif:enochian script|Kabbalistic letter-mysticism]] he knew.

## For artists & game designers
A cipher puzzle in object form: a letter-grid whose hidden words the player must trace along the right path to unlock an angel's name.

citations.text: Meric Casaubon (ed.), *A True & Faithful Relation...* (London, 1659).

title: Portrait of John Dee (the Ashmolean Portrait)
creator: Anonymous (16th-c. English school)
rights: Public domain. Ashmolean Museum, Oxford; via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
The best-known likeness of **[[creator:john-dee]]** (1527–1608/9) — Elizabethan mathematician, astrologer, and angel-summoner — painted late in his life and now in the Ashmolean Museum, Oxford. Dee is shown in the dark gown and skullcap of a scholar, his beard white, an austere and slightly haunted presence.

## Why it matters
Dee is the hinge between Renaissance science and ceremonial magic: author of the *Monas Hieroglyphica*, adviser to Elizabeth I, and (with Edward Kelley) recorder of the **Enochian** angelic system. A portrait of the magus himself anchors the human side of the archive — the faces behind the diagrams.

## For artists & game designers
A textbook "Renaissance magus / court astrologer" reference: black gown, white ruff, skullcap, grave expression. Ideal for an NPC scholar, a wizard advisor, or a portrait-in-a-frame asset.

[PLACEHOLDER: the painting was later trimmed; some versions show a border of skulls — note if you source that state.]

## Significance

Portraits of the Renaissance and early modern adepts -- magicians, alchemists, and astrologers -- constructed the visual identity of the practitioner-scholar at the intersection of natural philosophy, occult practice, and social legitimacy. Frances Yates's foundational work on the Hermetic tradition in the Renaissance situates these portraits within the broader cultural project of rehabilitating magic as a natural science. John Dee's portraits (the Ashmolean and the Wellcome versions) have been analyzed by Deborah Harkness and Benjamin Woolley in relation to Dee's self-presentation as a court mathematician and angelic intermediary rather than a wizard in the folk sense.

## For artists & game designers

Portraits of historical magicians and alchemists provide essential visual references for depicting practitioners within historical settings. The scholarly dress, books, and instruments visible in these portraits define the visual identity of the Renaissance magus as learned natural philosopher, distinct from both the folk image of the sorcerer and the diabolical witch of the demonological tradition.

citations.text: Yates, Frances A. Giordano Bruno and the Hermetic Tradition. London: Routledge, 1964.
Woolley, Benjamin. The Queen's Conjurer: The Science and Magic of Dr. John Dee. New York: Henry Holt, 2001.
Harkness, Deborah E. John Dee's Conversations with Angels: Cabala, Alchemy, and the End of Nature. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1999.

title: Figure I from the *Book of Abraham the Jew*

summary:
A figure reproduced from the legendary *Book of Abraham the Jew* — the gilt-leaved volume Nicolas Flamel claimed to have bought and, after years of study, to have decoded, achieving the Philosophers' Stone.

## Iconography
The plate shows one of the book's enigmatic images — serpents and a rod recalling the [[motif:caduceus|caduceus]] of Mercury, the kind of figure Flamel said filled the manuscript between its pages of crabbed writing. The originals were always described, never securely seen, so the engravings reconstruct the legend's lost source.

## Significance
The [[motif:book of abraham the jew|Book of Abraham the Jew]] is the mythic origin of the whole Flamel story: a Kabbalistic-alchemical codex by a fictitious Jewish sage, intelligible only after pilgrimage and inspired help. As a 'book that cannot be found,' it became one of esotericism's most enduring images of forbidden, half-lost knowledge.

## For artists & game designers
The ultimate MacGuffin tome: a fragmentary picture-book whose plates are themselves the quest, decoded scene by scene.

citations.text: Lawrence M. Principe, *The Secrets of Alchemy* (2013).

title: Figure III from the *Book of Abraham the Jew*
creator: after the legendary *Book of Abraham the Jew*
date: engraving after a legend of c.1400
summary:
A further figure from the legendary *Book of Abraham the Jew*, the cryptic manuscript at the root of the Flamel legend, reproduced in engraved form.

## Iconography
The plate carries another of the book's allegorical scenes — serpents and emblematic bodies — meant to encode a stage of the work without words. Flamel's narrative dwells on his long inability to read such pictures until a learned Jew at Santiago de Compostela helped unlock them.

## Significance
The figures of [[motif:book of abraham the jew|Abraham the Jew]] dramatise the alchemical conviction that the deepest secrets are entrusted to images rather than plain text. The motif of a hidden Hebrew wisdom decoded only through pilgrimage links the Flamel story to the wider Christian fascination with [[motif:lost manuscript|Kabbalah]] and lost ancient learning.

## For artists & game designers
A second codex page that only makes sense once an NPC sage is found and consulted — gating the puzzle behind a journey.

summary:
The fighting dragons of Nicolas Flamel's hieroglyphic figures in Denys Molinier's eighteenth-century engraved version, a companion to the famous title-cut of the two serpents.

## Iconography
Two dragons, one winged and one without wings, twist together in mortal combat at the foot of the charnel arch. Flamel's text names them as the two natures whose battle and union generate the philosophical matter.

## Significance
Within the engraved cycle the [[motif:green and red dragons|dragons]] state the central theme — the strife and reconciliation of the [[motif:fixed and volatile|fixed and the volatile]] — that the rest of the figures elaborate. Molinier's plates standardised the look of these creatures for generations of readers who never saw the lost originals.

## For artists & game designers
A recurring sigil motif: two intertwined serpents that the player meets first as enemies and later as a unified emblem of mastery.

title: The King & the Slaughter of the Innocents (Hieroglyphic Figures)
creator: Denys Molinier (engraving after Flamel)
summary:
The crowned King ordering the slaughter of the innocents, from Nicolas Flamel's hieroglyphic figures engraved by Denys Molinier — the most notorious and bloodiest of the charnel-arch scenes.

## Iconography
A king on his throne commands armed soldiers who put infants to the sword; the children's blood is gathered up. The scene quotes the biblical Massacre of the Innocents under Herod, doubly apt for paintings set at the Cemetery of the Holy Innocents.

## Significance
Flamel's exposition reads the [[motif:massacre of the innocents|spilt blood of the children]] as the [[motif:philosophical mercury|philosophical mercury]] required for the reddening — a deliberately shocking veil over a chemical operation. The image became a stock example of how violently literal alchemical 'decknamen' (cover-names) could be, and of the legend's taste for sacred-profane double meaning.

## For artists & game designers
A morally charged set-piece: an atrocity in the surface story that, decoded, is only a recipe — a puzzle about reading past the literal.

title: Saints Peter & Paul (Figure of the Hieroglyphic Figures)
creator: Denys Molinier (engraving after Flamel)
summary:
Saints Peter and Paul from Nicolas Flamel's hieroglyphic figures, engraved by Denys Molinier — a devotional pair that Flamel's exposition reads as the twin principles of the alchemical work.

## Iconography
The two apostles stand as a balanced pair, Peter with his keys and Paul with his sword, framed in the manner of an altar image. In Flamel's text the saints to whom he professed devotion double as emblems of the two complementary matters that must be joined.

## Significance
Placing the patrons [[motif:saint peter|Peter]] and [[motif:saint paul|Paul]] at the head of the figures let Flamel cloak the work in unimpeachable piety while quietly assigning them the roles of [[motif:sol and luna|sun and moon]], fixed and volatile. It is a model instance of the legend's strategy of hiding chemistry inside orthodox Christian imagery.

## For artists & game designers
A paired-patron UI: two saints whose attributes (key vs. sword) cue two opposed but complementary play styles.

title: The Procession (Figure I of the Hieroglyphic Figures)
creator: Denys Molinier (engraving after Flamel)
summary:
The opening procession of Nicolas Flamel's hieroglyphic figures, engraved by Denys Molinier among the plates of the *Livre des figures hiéroglyphiques* that reproduce the paintings Flamel claimed to set on the fourth arch of the Cemetery of the Holy Innocents.

## Iconography
Robed figures move in solemn file across the panel, the first of the painted scenes Flamel said he placed at the charnel arch. In his printed exposition each grouping is read as a station of the Great Work rather than a literal funeral.

## Significance
Flamel framed the whole charnel-arch programme as a [[motif:hieroglyphic figures|hieroglyphic]] sermon: outwardly a Christian memento mori for the dead of the [[motif:innocents cemetery|Innocents]], inwardly a coded sequence of the alchemical operations. The plates engraved by Molinier are the form in which most readers met these now-lost paintings, fixing the iconography of the legend for centuries.

## For artists & game designers
A processional intro cutscene whose figures each foreshadow a later stage of the player's transformation.

title: The Resurrection of the Dead (Figure of the Hieroglyphic Figures)
creator: Denys Molinier (engraving after Flamel)
summary:
The Resurrection of the Dead from Nicolas Flamel's hieroglyphic figures, engraved by Denys Molinier — naked bodies rising from their graves, read by Flamel as a figure of the final stage of the alchemical work.

## Iconography
The dead climb from the earth at the call of a trumpet, an image drawn from the Christian Last Judgment. In Flamel's exposition the risen bodies stand for the matter brought back to life, perfected and multiplied after passing through dissolution.

## Significance
The [[motif:resurrection of the dead|resurrection]] is the governing emblem of the charnel-arch programme: placed fittingly at a cemetery, it lets Flamel align the Christian hope of bodily rising with the alchemical [[motif:multiplication|multiplication]] and reddening of the Stone. The doubling of sacred and chemical meaning is exactly the 'hieroglyphic' method his book advertises.

## For artists & game designers
A revival mechanic visualised as the dead rising in ranks — a literal respawn shrine that also signals the final upgrade tier.

title: The Charnel House of the Cemetery of the Holy Innocents
creator: Theodor Josef Hubert Hoffbauer
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: after T. J. H. Hoffbauer, *Paris à travers les âges*]
summary:
A reconstruction of the charnel galleries (charniers) of the Cemetery of the Holy Innocents in Paris — the arcaded burial ground on one of whose arches Nicolas Flamel was said to have painted his hieroglyphic figures.

## Iconography
The view shows the long arcaded charnel-house galleries that ringed the cemetery, their attics heaped with bones and their walls bearing painted images. It was on the fourth arch of these arcades, in 1407, that Flamel claimed to have set his enigmatic paintings.

## Significance
The [[motif:innocents cemetery|Innocents]] was the most crowded burial ground in medieval Paris, famous for its painted [[motif:danse macabre|Danse Macabre]] and its overflowing [[motif:ossuary|ossuaries]]. Siting his coded alchemical programme amid this great public theatre of death let Flamel hide the Great Work in plain sight; the cemetery was cleared in 1786 and the arch lost, surviving only through engravings.

## For artists & game designers
A macabre hub-level: a bone-filled arcaded gallery whose painted arches each conceal a puzzle behind a memento-mori surface.

title: The Two Dragons (Green & Red), *Livre des figures hiéroglyphiques*
creator: after Nicolas Flamel (engraving)
summary:
The two fighting dragons — one winged and red, one wingless and dark — the most reproduced of the hieroglyphic figures Nicolas Flamel was said to have painted at the Cemetery of the Holy Innocents, here in the engraved version printed in the *Livre des figures hiéroglyphiques* (1612).

## Iconography
Two serpentine dragons coil and bite at one another in a barren landscape: one bears wings, the other none. Flamel's own commentary (as printed) glosses them as the two principles of the work — the volatile and the fixed — locked in the struggle from which the philosophical matter is born.

## Significance
The [[motif:green and red dragons|two dragons]] became shorthand for the alchemical marriage of opposites: [[motif:sulphur and mercury|sulphur and mercury]], hot and cold, the wingless 'fixed' body and the winged 'volatile' spirit. Transmitted through the 1612 edition attributed to Arnauld de la Chevalerie and the 1624 English *Exposition* of Eirenaeus Orandus, the figure anchored the Flamel legend at the centre of early-modern alchemical iconography.

## For artists & game designers
A clean dual-boss silhouette: one creature winged and fast, one earthbound and heavy, that must be made to fight each other.

citations.text: Nigel Wilkins, *Nicolas Flamel: Des livres et de l'or* (1993).

title: Epitaph of Nicolas Flamel (Musée de Cluny)
creator: Anonymous (Parisian carver)
repository: Musée de Cluny (Musée national du Moyen Âge), Paris
summary:
A high-resolution photograph of Nicolas Flamel's carved epitaph stone, preserved at the Musée de Cluny, recording in gothic script his name, death, and charitable foundations.

## Iconography
The slab combines a dense gothic inscription with small relief figures of holy persons and a corpse, in the standard idiom of an early-fifteenth-century Parisian funerary monument. The text asks prayers for Flamel's soul and details the alms and chapels he endowed.

## Significance
The [[motif:epitaph|epitaph]] is primary evidence for the documented Flamel and the genuine wealth that, redistributed as conspicuous [[motif:pious bequest|charity]], seeded the rumour of made gold. Modern scholarship leans on stones like this to reconstruct a bourgeois benefactor quite distinct from the immortal [[motif:scrivener-alchemist|adept]] of legend.

## For artists & game designers
An epigraphy prop: a weathered inscription whose deciphering rewards the player with the real backstory.

creator: after Nicolas Flamel (composite engraving)
date: early modern engraving (after a legend of c.1400)

A composite plate gathering Nicolas Flamel's hieroglyphic figures together, the way the painted arch of the Cemetery of the Holy Innocents was reconstructed for print.

The sheet assembles the principal scenes — the processions, the rising dead, the dragons and the saintly figures — in the arrangement Flamel said he gave the fourth arch of the charnel ground, so the whole programme can be read at a glance.

## Significance
The composite makes plain that the [[motif:hieroglyphic figures|hieroglyphic figures]] were conceived as a single, legible programme: a public monument that was simultaneously a pious memorial and an encrypted treatise. It is the form in which Flamel's lost arch survives in cultural memory, the painted original having vanished with the demolition of the cemetery.

A single 'level map' panel: one image whose tiled scenes are the stations the player must pass through in order.

creator: Georges-Henri Manesse (drawing)

A drawing of the surviving house Nicolas Flamel built in 1407 at 51 rue de Montmorency, the 'maison du grand pignon' — reputedly the oldest stone house in Paris.

The sheet records the tall gabled facade with its carved frieze of saints, angels, and labourers and its inscription asking each tenant to say a prayer for the dead. Flamel raised it not as a laboratory but as a lodging-house whose poor occupants prayed for his soul.

## Significance
The [[motif:flamel house|house]] is a tangible monument of the historical Flamel's [[motif:almshouse|charity]] — the very generosity later read as proof of alchemical riches. Pilgrims and treasure-hunters long searched it for hidden gold, and it remains a stop on the Parisian map of the [[motif:scrivener-alchemist|Flamel legend]].

A real explorable landmark: a carved medieval facade whose inscriptions are clues, ransacked by past seekers for a hoard that was never there.

The [[motif:tour saint-jacques|Tour Saint-Jacques]] is the most conspicuous surviving link to the [[motif:scrivener-alchemist|Flamel legend]] in modern Paris: a soaring gothic landmark that fixes the alchemist in the city's topography. Carved [[motif:monogram|ciphers]] like this one feed the enduring popular hunt for Flamel's hidden signs in Parisian stone.

## For artists & game designers
A findable glyph on a real monument: a carved cipher the player photographs and decodes as part of an urban-legend trail.

Drawings like this are how the [[motif:flamel monument|Flamel monuments]] survive at all: many of the actual stones and arches were destroyed in later centuries, and the [[motif:antiquarian record|antiquarian record]] becomes the principal witness. The carved tombstone of Nicolas Flamel, a genuine surviving relic of the man behind the legend, today held at the Musée de Cluny in Paris.

## Iconography
The stone bears, above an inscription naming Flamel and recording his pious bequests, small carved figures of Christ flanked by Saints Peter and Paul, with the sun and moon and a recumbent body below. It is a conventional late-medieval funerary slab, its restrained imagery a world away from the lurid charnel-arch figures.

## Significance
The [[motif:tombstone|tombstone]] documents the historical Flamel: a prosperous scrivener whose real charity, not transmutation, paid for his monuments. Its survival — long after the [[motif:scrivener-alchemist|legend]] outgrew the man — lets historians separate the documented Parisian bourgeois from the immortal adept of folklore.

## For artists & game designers
A real artifact to anchor a tall tale: a plain gravestone the player can examine to learn the unglamorous truth behind a legend.

An engraving of the portal of the church of Saint-Jacques-de-la-Boucherie, Flamel's parish church, which he helped to endow and decorate — from Abbé Villain's critical history of Flamel.

## Iconography
The plate records the gothic doorway of the now-demolished church, with carved sculpture and the kind of donor inscriptions Flamel attached to the buildings he funded. Only the great bell-tower, the Tour Saint-Jacques, still stands.

## Significance
Saint-Jacques-de-la-Boucherie was the focus of [[motif:flamel benefaction|Flamel's benefactions]] and, by tradition, a repository of his carved emblems; Abbé Villain's 1761 *Histoire critique* used such records to mount the first sceptical, documentary account of the legend. The portal is thus both a monument of Flamel's real piety and a touchstone of the [[motif:scrivener-alchemist|critical scholarship]] that grew up around him.

## For artists & game designers
A lost-building plate: a richly carved church door, since demolished, that the player explores only through an old engraving.

summary:
The Tour Saint-Jacques, the lone Flamboyant-gothic bell-tower that survives from the church of Saint-Jacques-de-la-Boucherie, long bound up with the legend of Nicolas Flamel.

## Iconography
The slender, richly pinnacled tower (1509–23) rises alone in its square, all that remains after the church was demolished during the Revolution. Its sculpture and gargoyles have invited generations of esoteric 'readings' connecting it to Flamel's alchemy.

## Significance
As the great surviving fragment of Flamel's [[motif:pilgrim church|parish church]] — a starting point of the pilgrimage to Santiago de Compostela, where the legend places Flamel's decisive encounter — the [[motif:tour saint-jacques|tower]] became the chief Parisian shrine of the [[motif:scrivener-alchemist|Flamel myth]], celebrated by nineteenth-century occult revivalists and still pointed out on every esoteric tour of the city.

## For artists & game designers
An iconic vertical landmark for an occult-Paris setting: a solitary carved tower that anchors a whole district's secret-history quests.

A glass instrument with an air-filled head over a liquid column stands graduated against a scale; as the trapped **air** expands and contracts with heat and cold, the liquid moves. The plate ties the apparatus to Fludd's cosmic physics of expansion and contraction.

## Significance
Fludd's thermoscope is one of the most-cited early thermometers. The same prop as the *Mosaicall* weather-glass in an earlier, higher-resolution state — good reference for a richly engraved scientific instrument.

The plate lays out a **mnemonic scheme for numbers**, associating digits and figures with memorable images or places so that calculations and quantities can be held in the mind. It belongs to the same memory-art apparatus as the *Oculus imaginationis* and the theatre.

Fludd extended the classical [[motif:art-of-memory|art of memory]] into arithmetic and music, treating mnemonics as a universal technique for compressing knowledge into images. These plates document the early-modern conviction that the trained imagination could store the encyclopaedia of the arts.
