title: Euclid I.47 (The 47th Problem) — Vatican Manuscript
creator: Euclid (manuscript copyist)
summary:
A manuscript page of Euclid's *Elements*, Book I, Proposition 47 — the Pythagorean theorem — which Freemasonry venerates as the '47th Problem of Euclid' and the badge of the Past Master.

## Iconography
The diagram shows a right-angled triangle with a square erected on each of its three sides, the classic 'windmill' figure that demonstrates the equality of the square on the hypotenuse to the sum of the squares on the other two sides, accompanied by Greek demonstrative text.

## Significance
Masonic tradition, following the legend that Pythagoras cried *Eureka!* on discovering the proof, adopted the [[motif:47th problem of euclid|47th Problem]] as the emblem of the Past Master and a symbol of the love of the arts and sciences. It encapsulates the Craft's reverence for [[motif:geometry|geometry]] as the foundational and divine science 'whereon Masonry is founded.'

## For artists & game designers
A geometry-as-power glyph: the three-square figure can serve as a craftable emblem whose correct construction unlocks a 'master' tier.

citations.text: Euclid, *Elements*, Book I, Proposition 47.

title: Illustration from Duncan's Masonic Ritual and Monitor
creator: Malcolm C. Duncan
summary:
A diagram from Malcolm C. Duncan's *Masonic Ritual and Monitor* (1866), the celebrated printed exposure that illustrated the signs, words, and ceremonies of the degrees.

## Iconography
The figure presents ritual instruction in printed form — a hieroglyphic or word-diagram (here relating to the Royal Arch word) set among explanatory text describing the postures, grips, and passwords of a degree.

## Significance
Duncan's *Monitor* is the best-known of the nineteenth-century printed 'exposures' that, despite the Craft's secrecy, set its rituals and [[motif:ritual monitor|monitorial lectures]] in cheap, widely circulated books. Whatever their accuracy, such works fixed in popular print the gestures, mottoes, and degree-lore of Freemasonry, and remain a primary source for the form of the American ritual.

## For artists & game designers
An 'unlocked secret' document: a diagram of signs and passwords the player can study to bluff their way past gatekeepers.

citations.text: Malcolm C. Duncan, *Duncan's Masonic Ritual and Monitor* (1866).

title: The All-Seeing Eye of Providence (Lodge Decoration)
creator: Anonymous (photographed by Michael Coghlan)
rights: CC BY-SA 2.0 (Michael Coghlan). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A Masonic lodge ornament of the All-Seeing Eye of Providence, the radiant single eye that watches over the assembled brethren.

## Iconography
A single human eye, set within a triangle or burst of golden rays and clouds, gazes outward; the motto bids the visitor welcome under its watch. The eye is surrounded by a 'glory' of beams, the standard emblem of divine effulgence.

## Significance
The [[motif:all-seeing eye|All-Seeing Eye]] represents the ever-watchful providence of the Great Architect, reminding the Mason that thoughts and deeds are observed by the Most High. Though far older than the Craft — rooted in Renaissance and biblical imagery of the divine eye — it was adopted by Freemasonry in the later eighteenth century and, via the Great Seal of the United States, passed into the broadest popular iconography.

## For artists & game designers
A surveillance/conscience motif: a luminous eye that reacts to the player's moral choices, opening wider or clouding over.

citations.text: Albert G. Mackey, *An Encyclopædia of Freemasonry* (1874).

title: Hiram Abiff and the Pillar Boaz
creator: Anonymous
summary:
An illustration of Hiram Abiff, the legendary master builder of Solomon's Temple, shown with one of the great pillars — the central figure of the Third Degree drama.

## Iconography
A robed craftsman stands beside the pillar Boaz, holding or gesturing toward the tools of his office. The composition identifies him as the master of the work, set against the architecture of the Temple he directs.

## Significance
[[motif:hiram abiff|Hiram Abiff]], the 'widow's son' and chief artificer of the Temple, is murdered (in the Masonic legend) for refusing to betray the secrets of a Master Mason; his death, burial, and raising form the allegorical heart of the Craft. Though the elaborated legend is a speculative-era construction built around the biblical Hiram of Tyre, it furnishes Freemasonry with its myth of fidelity, loss, and recovery.

## For artists & game designers
A tragic-mentor archetype: a master craftsman NPC whose death sets the central quest — recovering 'that which was lost' — in motion.

citations.text: Albert G. Mackey, *Encyclopædia of Freemasonry* (1874).

title: The Brazen Pillars Jachin and Boaz
creator: Anonymous (architectural reconstruction)
summary:
A reconstruction of the two brazen pillars, Jachin and Boaz, that stood at the porch of Solomon's Temple and which Freemasonry sets at the entrance of every symbolic lodge.

## Iconography
Two free-standing columns rise side by side, each crowned by a capital decorated with lily-work, pomegranates, and chains of network, surmounted by a terrestrial and a celestial globe. The pillars are figured exactly as described in the Books of Kings and Chronicles.

## Significance
[[motif:jachin|Jachin]] ('He shall establish') and [[motif:boaz|Boaz]] ('In strength') frame the entrance to the lodge as they framed the Temple porch; the Mason passes between establishment and strength to reach the holy place. The crowning globes, terrestrial and celestial, were read as emblems of the universality of Masonry and the comprehensiveness of its science.

## For artists & game designers
A threshold gate: two named pillars the player must pass between, each granting a paired attribute (stability vs. force) that shapes the route ahead.

citations.text: 1 Kings 7:15–22; Albert G. Mackey, *Encyclopædia of Freemasonry* (1874).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Léo Taxil, *La Bible amusante* (Anti-clerical/Anti-Masonic Hoaxer)
creator: Léo Taxil (Gabriel Jogand-Pagès)
summary:
An illustration from a work by Léo Taxil (Gabriel Jogand-Pagès), the French writer notorious for the great anti-Masonic 'Palladism' hoax of the 1890s.

## Iconography
The caricatural plate (from his anticlerical *La Bible amusante*) shows Taxil's mocking satirical manner — the same pen later turned to lurid, invented exposés of Masonic 'devil worship.'

## Significance
[[motif:leo taxil|Léo Taxil]] first attacked the Church, then publicly 'converted' and fabricated an elaborate myth of a satanic Masonic inner order, *Palladism*, complete with a fictitious priestess, [[motif:diana vaughan|Diana Vaughan]]. In 1897 he triumphantly confessed the whole thing was a hoax designed to ridicule credulous anti-Masons and clerics alike. The episode is the classic case of the [[motif:devil worship myth|satanic-Freemasonry myth]], a conspiracy fantasy whose imagery still circulates.

## For artists & game designers
The unreliable-source trope made literal: a propaganda pamphlet whose 'revelations' the player slowly discovers were invented to manipulate them.

citations.text: Eugen Weber, *Satan franc-maçon: la mystification de Léo Taxil* (1964).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Masonic Lodge Interior with Mosaic Pavement
creator: Anonymous (photographed by UpdateNerd)
summary:
The interior of a Masonic lodge room, showing the chequered floor and the arrangement of the symbolic temple in which the degrees are worked.

## Iconography
The room is laid out as a symbolic [[motif:temple of solomon|Temple]]: a black-and-white [[motif:mosaic pavement|mosaic pavement]] underfoot, the Master's chair raised 'in the East,' the Wardens' stations to West and South, and pillars or columns marking the officers' places, the whole bordered with tessellated ornament.

## Significance
Every Craft lodge is furnished as a microcosm of Solomon's Temple and, beyond it, of the ordered cosmos. The [[motif:mosaic pavement|mosaic pavement]] of alternating light and dark squares represents the mingling of good and evil in human life; the orientation toward the East, source of light, governs the placement of officers and the movement of ritual. The room is itself a three-dimensional tracing board.

## For artists & game designers
A ready blueprint for a ritual chamber: a checker-floored hall with cardinal stations the player circumambulates in a fixed ceremonial order.

citations.text: Albert G. Mackey, *Encyclopædia of Freemasonry* (1874).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Masonic Apron of Major William Christy
creator: Anonymous (American lodge regalia)
summary:
The personal Masonic apron of Major William Christy, a painted lambskin regalia apron crowded with the Craft's emblems.

## Iconography
The white apron bears a flap and a square field painted with a dense programme of symbols — the [[motif:square and compasses|square and compasses]], the [[motif:all-seeing eye|All-Seeing Eye]] in its glory, the two pillars, columns, the beehive, and instruments of the work — bordered with rosettes and tassels.

## Significance
The lambskin apron is the first and most enduring badge presented to a Mason, emblem of the innocence and labour proper to the Craft and said to be 'more ancient than the Golden Fleece.' Hand-painted aprons like this one, common in early American lodges, served as portable tracing boards, the wearer carrying the whole symbolic cosmos on his person.

## For artists & game designers
A wearable inventory of insignia — an apron whose painted emblems can be 'earned' and added one by one as the character advances.

citations.text: Aimee E. Newell, *The Badge of a Freemason: Masonic Aprons from the Scottish Rite Masonic Museum* (2015).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Masonic Certificate, Grand United Order of Odd Fellows
creator: Popular Graphic Arts (lithographer)
summary:
An engraved fraternal membership certificate of the Grand United Order of Odd Fellows, bearing the motto *Amicitia, Amor et Veritas* (Friendship, Love and Truth).

## Iconography
The sheet frames a central text panel with allegorical personifications and dense emblematic ornament — clasped hands, hearts, the all-seeing eye, tools and regalia of the order — arranged in a symmetrical border around the motto and the member's name.

## Significance
Fraternal certificates and diplomas were the portable proof of initiation across the nineteenth-century lodge societies — Masonry, Odd Fellowship, and their many affiliates — that shared a common visual vocabulary of clasped hands, mottoes, and moral emblems. The G.U.O.O.F. was a major African-American fraternal order; its handsome engraved certificates show how the [[motif:fraternal certificate|emblematic diploma]] carried the order's ideals of [[motif:friendship love truth|friendship, love, and truth]].

## For artists & game designers
An ornate in-world credential — a printed diploma whose emblem-border can be 'read' for the bearer's affiliations and rank.

citations.text: Mark A. Tabbert, *American Freemasons: Three Centuries of Building Communities* (2005).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Master Mason's Chart (Third Section)
creator: Anonymous
summary:
A Master Mason's chart illustrating the monitorial emblems of the Third Degree's lecture, the moving symbols of mortality and virtue.

## Iconography
The chart sets out the classic Third Degree emblems in sequence: the [[motif:pot of incense|pot of incense]], the beehive, the book of constitutions guarded by the Tyler's sword, the sword pointing to a naked heart, the all-seeing eye, the anchor and ark, the [[motif:hourglass|hourglass]], the scythe, and the three steps — each a 'moving image' of human life and duty.

## Significance
These emblems derive from the monitors of Thomas Smith Webb and Jeremy Cross, who systematised the American 'monitorial' lectures around 1800. The chart compresses the degree's meditation on time, death, and moral watchfulness into a memorable visual catechism — the [[motif:hourglass|hourglass]] and scythe marking the brevity of life, the anchor and ark the hope of a well-spent one.

## For artists & game designers
A panel of status icons each tied to a virtue or mortality theme — a ready-made HUD of moral 'meters' for a contemplative game.

citations.text: Jeremy L. Cross, *The True Masonic Chart, or Hieroglyphic Monitor* (1819).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Emblematic Chart and Masonic History (Ramsey, Millett & Hudson)
creator: Ramsey, Millett & Hudson Steam Lith. Co.
summary:
A large lithographed 'Emblematic Chart and Masonic History of Free and Accepted Masons,' a compendious wall print gathering the Craft's symbols into a single didactic composition.

## Iconography
The chart arrays the working tools, degree emblems, pillars, the all-seeing eye, the ark, the beehive, and scenes of Temple history across a panelled field, each cell captioned, so that the entire symbolic system can be surveyed at a glance.

## Significance
Mass-produced chromolithographs like this one, issued by commercial steam-lithography firms in the Gilded Age, democratised Masonic iconography, hanging the whole [[motif:compendium of symbols|compendium of symbols]] on lodge and parlour walls. They functioned as printed encyclopedias of the Craft, fixing a standard repertoire of emblems in the popular American imagination.

## For artists & game designers
A reference plate for an entire symbol-set: useful as an in-game 'codex' screen where each emblem is a tappable lore entry.

citations.text: Mark A. Tabbert, *American Freemasons* (2005).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Past Master's Jewel (Mount Anthony Lodge No. 13)
creator: Anonymous silversmith
summary:
A Past Master's jewel presented to Judge Charles H. Darling on his retirement as Master of Mount Anthony Lodge No. 13, Bennington, Vermont, in 1899.

## Iconography
The pendant jewel carries the emblem proper to the office of Past Master — a pair of compasses opened on a quadrant (or a representation of the 47th Problem of Euclid) — suspended from a ribbon and engraved with a presentation dedication.

## Significance
Masonic [[motif:officers jewel|jewels]] are the metal badges of lodge office, each office distinguished by its emblem: the square for the Master, the level for the Senior Warden, the plumb for the Junior Warden, and the [[motif:47th problem emblem|compasses-and-quadrant]] or Euclidean figure for the Past Master. Presentation jewels like this commemorated faithful service, blending the symbolic vocabulary of the Craft with the personal honour of an individual brother.

## For artists & game designers
A rank-insignia object: a pendant whose distinct emblem instantly signals an NPC's office and history within the lodge hierarchy.

citations.text: Albert G. Mackey, *Encyclopædia of Freemasonry* (1874).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Masonic Triangle (Bicentennial Plate, 1789–1989)
creator: Jebulon
summary:
A French Masonic plate built around the luminous triangle (the *delta*), commemorating the bicentennial 1789–1989 with the symbols of the Craft.

## Iconography
A radiant triangle — often enclosing an eye or the divine name — sits at the centre, flanked and underlaid by the working tools: square, compasses, level, and plumb. The arrangement is geometric and heraldic, the triangle crowning the assembly of emblems.

## Significance
The [[motif:masonic triangle|luminous delta]] is the Masonic figure of deity and of geometric perfection — three sides for the ternary that recurs throughout the Craft (the three degrees, three lights, three principal officers). In French Freemasonry especially, the radiant triangle over the Master's chair focuses the lodge's contemplation of the Great Architect, and its conjunction here with 1789 ties the fraternity to the Enlightenment and the Revolution.

## For artists & game designers
A glowing triangular emblem suited to a 'sanctum' marker; rotating its tools could encode different rites or factions.

title: *Freemasonry Exposed* (William Morgan), Front Cover
creator: Capt. William Morgan
summary:
The front cover of *Freemasonry Exposed* (often *Illustrations of Masonry*), the 1826 exposure attributed to Captain William Morgan whose suppression ignited the American anti-Masonic movement.

## Iconography
A plain printed title page announces the disclosure of the secrets of the Craft 'by one of the fraternity,' the typographic cover promising to lay bare the hidden signs, grips, and ceremonies of the order.

## Significance
Morgan's threatened publication led to his abduction and presumed murder in western New York in 1826 — the [[motif:morgan affair|Morgan affair]] — which provoked a wave of public outrage, the founding of the [[motif:anti-masonic movement|Anti-Masonic Party]] (America's first third party), and a sharp decline in lodge membership. The book and the scandal around it made Freemasonry, for a generation, the focus of a national controversy over secrecy and republican virtue.

## For artists & game designers
A forbidden book whose mere existence triggers a faction-wide manhunt — a plot device for an exposure-and-pursuit storyline.

citations.text: William Morgan, *Illustrations of Masonry* (Batavia, NY, 1826).
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Square and Compasses
creator: Anonymous (modern rendering)
date: symbol c. 18th c.; this rendering modern
summary:
The Square and Compasses, the single most recognisable emblem of speculative Freemasonry, here in a clean graphic rendering of the interlaced instruments.

## Iconography
A carpenter's square and a pair of compasses are interlocked to form a lozenge, the square opening upward and the compasses straddling it; in many versions the letter **G** sits at the centre. The two working tools — borrowed from operative stonemasonry — are arranged so that the points and arms enclose a shared field.

## Significance
The emblem condenses the Craft's [[motif:moral allegory|moral allegory]]: the square teaches the Mason to act 'on the square' (uprightly), the compasses to circumscribe his passions within due bounds. The central **G** is glossed as both Geometry — the divine science — and God, the Great Architect of the Universe. Adopted across Anglo-American and Continental lodges by the later eighteenth century, it became the badge of the fraternity worldwide.

## For artists & game designers
A faction sigil that reads instantly at any size; the openness of the compass legs can encode rank (the degree is signalled by which limb sits above the square).

citations.text: Albert G. Mackey, *An Encyclopædia of Freemasonry* (1874).
Wikimedia Commons

title: First Degree Tracing Board (Engraving)
creator: Anonymous engraver
summary:
An engraving of a First Degree (Entered Apprentice) Masonic tracing board, the illustrated teaching-chart laid before candidates in the opening degree (c. 1850–1900).

## Iconography
The board crowds the lodge's emblems into one scene: the two pillars at the porchway, a chequered [[motif:mosaic pavement|mosaic pavement]], Jacob's Ladder ascending to a [[motif:blazing star|blazing star]] amid clouds, the three lesser lights, and assorted working tools. A border of indented tessels frames the whole.

## Significance
Tracing boards descend from the chalk designs once drawn on the lodge floor and erased after the meeting; by the nineteenth century they had become painted or engraved panels carrying the symbolic 'furniture' of each degree. The First Degree board maps the moral cosmos the [[motif:entered apprentice|Entered Apprentice]] is taught to read — ladder of virtues, pillars of strength and establishment, the pavement of light and dark.

## For artists & game designers
A single image that doubles as a level legend: every emblem on the board corresponds to a lesson or station the player will later encounter in sequence.

citations.text: Julian Rees, *Tracing Boards of the Three Degrees in Craft Freemasonry Explained* (2009).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Second Degree Tracing Board, Josiah Bowring
creator: Josiah Bowring (1757–1832)
summary:
The Second Degree (Fellowcraft) tracing board painted by Josiah Bowring, whose designs became standard models for the Emulation working (Museum of Freemasonry, London).

## Iconography
A [[motif:winding staircase|winding staircase]] of fifteen steps rises between the two great pillars toward a doorway, a flow of water and an ear of corn set beside it. The stair's divisions allude to the three, five, and seven, and the porch leads to the 'Middle Chamber' where the Fellowcraft receives his wages.

## Significance
The Fellowcraft degree dramatises the pursuit of knowledge: the ascent of the staircase past the orders of architecture and the [[motif:seven liberal arts|seven liberal arts]] toward hidden wisdom. Bowring's boards, produced in the early nineteenth century, fixed the visual canon of the English Craft so thoroughly that later lodges commissioned copies of his compositions for generations.

## For artists & game designers
The winding stair is a ready-made progression mechanic: a numbered ascent (3-5-7) where each landing gates a new skill or revelation.

citations.text: Julian Rees, *Tracing Boards of the Three Degrees in Craft Freemasonry Explained* (2009).

title: Third Degree Tracing Board (Master Mason)
creator: Anonymous
summary:
The Third Degree (Master Mason) tracing board, centred on the grave of Hiram Abiff and the symbols of mortality and raising (Museum of Freemasonry, London).

## Iconography
The panel is dominated by a [[motif:coffin|coffin]] or open grave, often inscribed with emblems of mortality — [[motif:skull and bones|skull and crossbones]] — and marked by a [[motif:sprig of acacia|sprig of acacia]]. Compasses, a setting maul, and other instruments of the Hiramic legend lie about; the whole is rendered in sombre tones against a dark ground.

## Significance
The Master Mason's degree enacts the death and raising of [[motif:hiram abiff|Hiram Abiff]], the architect of Solomon's Temple, as an allegory of fidelity, the inevitability of death, and the hope of a 'raising' to come. The acacia marking the grave signals both discovery of the body and the immortality of the soul. This board is the lodge's *memento mori*, the visual climax of the Craft system.

## For artists & game designers
A death-and-resurrection set piece: a grave scene whose scattered tools are clues to a reconstruction puzzle the player solves to be 'raised'.

citations.text: Julian Rees, *Tracing Boards of the Three Degrees in Craft Freemasonry Explained* (2009).

title: *Summa Perfectionis* (pseudo-Geber) — Letterpress Page
creator: Pseudo-Geber (attributed; ed. Nuremberg, Johann Petreius)
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: per source — Internet Archive copy of the 1542 Nuremberg (Petreius) edition]
summary:
A letterpress leaf of the Nuremberg *Summa Perfectionis* of pseudo-Geber (Johann Petreius, 1542) — a page of the running Latin treatise (or its index / opening matter), not a figured diagram.

## Iconography
Clean humanist roman type, headed by a running book-title (*Primus*, *Secundus*, *Tertius*, *Quartus*, *Investigationis*, *Mineralia*) and chapter rubrics; some leaves open with a woodcut historiated initial, and the front matter includes a blank/stained flyleaf and a printed index, but these pages carry no apparatus illustration. Recorded honestly as text.

## Significance
The *Summa Perfectionis Magisterii* (c. 1300) is the most important medieval Latin alchemical treatise — long ascribed to the Arab Jabir ibn Hayyan ('Geber') but shown by William R. Newman to be the work of the Franciscan **Paul of Taranto**. Its corpuscular matter-theory and its sober, operational account of sublimation, distillation, calcination and the rest made it foundational. These text pages carry that argument; the handful of apparatus woodcuts are catalogued separately.

## For artists & game designers
A sober sixteenth-century printed page — usable as a manuscript-prop texture or a readable codex leaf for set-dressing.

title: Baculus Terreus — The Earthen Stirring-Rod (Apparatus Woodcut)
creator: Pseudo-Geber (attributed; ed. Nuremberg, Johann Petreius)
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: per source — Internet Archive copy of the 1542 Nuremberg (Petreius) edition]
summary:
A small technical woodcut from Book II of the Nuremberg *Summa Perfectionis* of pseudo-Geber (Johann Petreius, 1542) figuring the *baculus terreus* — the 'earthen rod' used in sublimation.

## Iconography
Centred on an otherwise text page, a single slender cylindrical rod is shown in profile, captioned *Baculus* at left and *terreus* at right. The surrounding Latin describes how the well-fired earthen rod, pierced with a small hole near its tip, is introduced into the sublimation vessel to test and stir the charge.

## Significance
Tiny as it is, the figure typifies the *Summa*'s hands-on character: the treatise repeatedly pauses to specify a tool or gesture of the bench. Pseudo-Geber's insistence on **experientia** — that the artist must handle, test, and verify — made the work a touchstone of practical [[motif:alchemy|alchemy]] for centuries. William R. Newman's edition attributes the text to Paul of Taranto and stresses exactly this experimental temper.

## For artists & game designers
A humble but authentic laboratory implement — a fired-clay stirring rod with a vent hole. Good reference for a tool icon or an inventory item in a crafting system.

title: Four Modes of Distillation — Apparatus Woodcut
creator: Pseudo-Geber (attributed; ed. Nuremberg, Johann Petreius)
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: per source — Internet Archive copy of the 1542 Nuremberg (Petreius) edition]
summary:
The principal apparatus woodcut of the Nuremberg *Summa Perfectionis* of pseudo-Geber (Johann Petreius, 1542), illustrating the *primus, secundus, tertius* and *quartus distillationis modus* — four ways of distilling — in Book II.

## Iconography
Four labelled distillation set-ups share the page. Two upper diagrams show a cucurbit fitted with a curved-beak still-head (*alembicus*) discharging into a receiving flask (*ampulla recipiens*); a lower-left diagram sets a vessel over a fire of flames (*ignis*, *receptaculum*); the lower-right shows a flat alembic-and-receiver. Marginal Latin captions name the parts — alembic, lapides (the luted joints), concha, vas recipiens.

## Significance
The *Summa Perfectionis*, the most influential Latin alchemical treatise of the later Middle Ages (c. 1300, long ascribed to the Arab Jabir / 'Geber' but argued by William R. Newman to be the work of the Franciscan **Paul of Taranto**), is famous for its precise, operational descriptions of laboratory practice. This woodcut renders that precision visible: it is among the earliest printed diagrams of [[motif:distillation|distillation]] apparatus, a direct ancestor of the furnace-and-alembic plates of the later alchemical tradition.

## For artists & game designers
A genuine period schematic of stills and a flaming furnace — ready reference for an alchemist's-bench crafting UI or for modelling believable distillation props.

Clean humanist roman type, headed by a running book-title (*Primus*, *Secundus*, *Tertius*, *Quartus*, *Investigationis*, *Mineralia*) and chapter rubrics; some leaves open with a woodcut historiated initial, and the front matter includes a blank/stained flyleaf and a printed index, but these pages carry no apparatus illustration. ## Significance
The *Summa Perfectionis Magisterii* (c. 1300) is the most important medieval Latin alchemical treatise — long ascribed to the Arab Jabir ibn Hayyan ('Geber') but shown by William R. Newman to be the work of the Franciscan **Paul of Taranto**. Its corpuscular matter-theory and its sober, operational account of sublimation, distillation, calcination and the rest made it foundational. These text pages carry that argument; the handful of apparatus woodcuts are catalogued separately.

title: Arab Geomantic Figures: The Sixteen
work: Geomancy, Chiromancy & the Renaissance Divination Arts
creator: Anonymous
summary:
A classification diagram of the sixteen Arabic geomantic figures (*ashkal al-raml*), the core combinatorial vocabulary of *'ilm al-raml*, 'the science of the sand.'

## Iconography
The diagram arrays the sixteen [[motif:geomancy|geomantic figures]] — each a column of four rows, each row carrying one or two dots — in their traditional groupings. The figures are distinguished by the odd/even parity of each row: one dot = odd (active); two dots = even (passive). The sixteen possible combinations of four binary rows generate every figure in the system, from Puer (single dot in each of the first three rows, two in the fourth) to Via (single dots throughout).

## Significance
*'Ilm al-raml* ('the science of the sand') crystallised in the Arabic-speaking world between the 9th and 12th centuries, drawing on older Mesopotamian and possibly sub-Saharan African precedents. The 12th-century translations of Hugo of Santalla and Gerard of Cremona introduced the figures to Latin Europe as *geomantia*, where they were adopted wholesale, their Arabic names Latinised (Rubeus, Albus, Laetitia, Tristitia, etc.) and their interpretive apparatus fused with European astrology. The sixteen figures have an exact formal parallel in the 256 *odu* of Yoruba Ifa divination (pairs of figures), confirming deep structural links across the Old World.

## For artists & game designers
The canonical reference sheet for all sixteen figures: each a combinatorial icon as compact and legible as a heraldic charge, directly usable as a symbol system in a game or illustration.

citations.text: S. Skinner, *Geomancy in Theory and Practice* (1980).
T. Fahd, 'Geomancy,' in *Encyclopaedia of Islam* (2nd ed.).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Berliner Chiromantie: German Palmistry Broadsheet
work: Geomancy, Chiromancy & the Renaissance Divination Arts
creator: Anonymous (German)
summary:
A German chiromantic broadsheet — the *Berliner Chiromantie* — showing a diagrammatic hand with labelled lines and mounts for palmistry reading.

## Iconography
The open palm is mapped with named [[motif:chiromancy|chiromantic lines]] (Lebens-, Kopf-, and Herzlinie; the Girdle of Venus) and the fleshy mounts at the base of each finger and thumb, each assigned to a planet. Text blocks in German gloss the lines' meanings. The broadsheet format suggests popular distribution: chiromancy was the most widely practised of the 'occult sciences' in the German-speaking world.

## Significance
German chiromantic literature was particularly rich in the 15th and 16th centuries, with major works by Johannes Hartlieb (*Buch aller verbotenen Kunst*, 1456) and Johannes ab Indagine (*Introductiones Apotelesmaticae*, 1522) reaching wide audiences. Broadsheets like this one disseminated chiromantic knowledge to non-Latin readers. The planetary system of mounts — each finger base ruled by Jupiter, Saturn, Apollo, or Mercury, and the thumb mount by Venus — was Agrippa's systematisation of an older, more ad hoc tradition. By the 16th century chiromancy had become a vernacular science, taught in universities and practised by physicians.

## For artists & game designers
A vernacular, popular version of the palm-map: simpler and more direct than the learned Latin diagrams, closer to what a village fortune-teller would have owned.

citations.text: J. Hartlieb, *Buch aller verbotenen Kunst* (1456).
J. ab Indagine, *Introductiones Apotelesmaticae* (1522).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Divination Board (Pako Ifa), Brooklyn Museum
work: Geomancy, Chiromancy & the Renaissance Divination Arts
creator: Yoruba (anonymous carver)
rights: CC BY 3.0. Brooklyn Museum (22.237). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A *Pako Ifa* (Ifa divination board with handle/stand), Yoruba, Nigeria, from the Brooklyn Museum collection (22.237).

## Iconography
The board is a variant *Opon Ifa* format with an extended handle or foot, making it portable and free-standing. The carved relief decoration on the border and handle displays [[motif:Ifa|Yoruba iconographic]] motifs — human figures, Eshu faces, geometric patterns — framing the divination surface. Such variation in board form reflects local workshop traditions and individual patron requirements.

## Significance
The Brooklyn Museum's Yoruba collection is one of the most significant in North America. The *Pako Ifa* format demonstrates the range of material culture developed around Ifa divination: the basic wooden tray could be an austere functional tool or an elaborately carved prestige object commissioned by a wealthy *babalawo* (Ifa divination priest). The *babalawo* occupies a position of high status in Yoruba society, comparable in some respects to the medieval Latin geomancer who served courts and nobles. The formal parallel between the *babalawo*'s sixteen primary figures and European geomancy's sixteen is a standing scholarly puzzle.

## For artists & game designers
A handled divination board: the variant format suggests portability, travel, the diviner who moves between clients — a useful prop detail for character design.

citations.text: Brooklyn Museum (22.237), New York.
Wikimedia Commons

title: Divination Tray (Opon Ifa), Brooklyn Museum
work: Geomancy, Chiromancy & the Renaissance Divination Arts
creator: Yoruba (anonymous carver)
rights: CC BY 3.0. Brooklyn Museum (75.147.1). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
An *Opon Ifa* (Ifa divination tray) from the Brooklyn Museum collection (75.147.1), used by a Yoruba Ifa priest (*babalawo*) to generate and record divinatory signs.

## Iconography
The tray presents a flat circular surface bounded by carved relief decoration. In practice it would be lightly dusted with *iyerosun* (the powdered wood of the *Baphia nitida* tree), and the *babalawo* would use his finger or a divining chain to mark [[motif:Ifa|Ifa figures]] in the dust, recording each *odu* as it appears. The marks are then read against the memorised corpus of *Odu Ifa*, the enormous oral literature associated with each figure.

## Significance
The *Opon Ifa* is the material centre of one of the world's most elaborate divination systems. UNESCO has inscribed Ifa divination on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity (2008). The *babalawo* memorises the 256 *odu* and their associated *ese* (poems) — a corpus estimated in the hundreds of thousands of lines — making Ifa one of the largest oral literary traditions ever documented. The formal structure of the sixteen primary figures and their 240 compounds exactly parallels European geomancy's sixteen figures and their shield-chart combinations, one of the most intriguing structural echoes in the history of divination.

## For artists & game designers
The standard form of the Ifa tray: a ritual object that is both tool (the divination surface) and artwork (the carved border). Clean, functional, and numinous.

citations.text: Brooklyn Museum (75.147.1), New York.
W. Abimbola, *Ifa: An Exposition of Ifa Literary Corpus* (1976).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Chiromancy and Veterinary Receipts (Wellcome L0015603)
work: Geomancy, Chiromancy & the Renaissance Divination Arts
creator: Anonymous
rights: CC BY 4.0. Wellcome Collection. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A Wellcome Collection manuscript (L0015603) combining chiromantic hand diagrams with veterinary medical recipes — a typically eclectic practical notebook of the medieval or early modern period.

## Iconography
The manuscript page juxtaposes [[motif:chiromancy|chiromancy]] (palm diagram with labelled lines and mounts) with *veterinary receipts* — recipes for treating livestock. The combination is characteristic of the practical medical-occult notebooks kept by rural practitioners, stewards, and householders who needed both to diagnose disease (human and animal) and to interpret natural signs.

## Significance
The conjunction of palmistry and veterinary medicine in a single notebook reveals the practical, synthetic character of popular occult knowledge in medieval and early modern Europe. The reader was not a theorist but a practitioner who needed usable knowledge from multiple domains in one portable reference. Such compilations — chiromancy + herbal + receipts + almanac material — were among the most common manuscript genres. Chiromancy in this context is not mystical entertainment but a diagnostic tool alongside bloodletting charts and livestock remedies.

## For artists & game designers
A reminder that medieval occultism was practical: the diviner who read your palm might also have a cure for your sick ox. A useful texture for a realistic setting.

citations.text: Wellcome Collection (CC BY 4.0), L0015603.
Wikimedia Commons

title: Gypsy Woman Reading the Hand of a Young Man (Jan Cossiers)
work: Geomancy, Chiromancy & the Renaissance Divination Arts
creator: Jan Cossiers
summary:
A Flemish Baroque genre painting by Jan Cossiers (1600–1671) of a Romani woman reading the palm of a young man — a companion to the de Wael and Caravaggio tradition of the 'gypsy fortune-teller' genre.

## Iconography
A young man extends his right hand toward a woman who leans close to examine the lines of his palm. Other figures may be present in the background — the group of Romani travellers, or companions of the young man watching the encounter. The [[motif:chiromancy|palm-reading encounter]] is framed as a moment of theatre: the man's fate is in the woman's reading, and the viewer is positioned as an additional witness.

## Significance
Jan Cossiers was an Antwerp painter who spent time in Rome and was influenced by Caravaggio's genre scenes. The 'gypsy fortune-teller' was already an established genre by the 1630s, but Cossiers' versions are notable for their atmospheric handling of light and their relatively sympathetic — or at least non-caricatural — rendering of the Romani figure. Like de Wael's treatment, the painting is as much a social document as a depiction of divination: the encounter dramatises the boundary between settled and nomadic, learned and intuitive, credulous youth and knowing woman.

## For artists & game designers
A high-quality Baroque source for the palm-reading encounter scene: close physical proximity, direct gaze, the exchange of knowledge for coin — the fundamental divinatory transaction.

A 19th-century genre painting by Gabriel von Max (1840–1915) showing a woman consulting a fortune-teller — a scene of palm-reading, card-laying, or crystal-gazing.

## Iconography
A young woman is shown in consultation with a fortune-teller, the exchange charged with the mixture of credulity and anxiety that characterises the Romantic genre of [[motif:chiromancy|divinatory encounter]]. Von Max specialised in subjects at the edge of the rational and supernatural — spiritualism, hypnosis, mysticism — and the fortune-teller scene fits naturally into his thematic range.

## Significance
Gabriel von Max (1840–1915), the Czech-German painter, was the pre-eminent painter of the supernatural in the late 19th century, an era fascinated by spiritualism, Theosophy, and the edges of science. His fortune-teller paintings are part of a broader cultural moment when the divinatory arts — discredited by the Enlightenment — were being rehabilitated through the Romantic imagination and later through Spiritualism. The scene of a woman consulting a diviner was gendered in a specific way: women were understood as both more credulous and more receptive to the supernatural, a stereotype that shaped both the practice and the depiction of 19th-century fortune-telling.

A Symbolist/Romantic atmosphere for a divination scene: soft light, anxious client, knowing diviner — the mood of mystery that the 19th century attached to these arts.

title: Magnus Hundt, Antropologium (Wellcome L0032471)
work: Geomancy, Chiromancy & the Renaissance Divination Arts
creator: Magnus Hundt
rights: CC BY 4.0. Wellcome Collection. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A plate from Magnus Hundt's *Antropologium de hominis dignitate, natura et proprietatibus* (Leipzig, 1501), a proto-anthropological and physiognomical treatise (Wellcome Collection, L0032471).

## Iconography
The woodcut plate illustrates human bodily structure and proportion in the style characteristic of early printed physiognomic literature — schematic figures with labelled anatomical features and possibly a body-proportion diagram. Hundt's *Antropologium* sits at the intersection of scholastic philosophy, natural history, and [[motif:physiognomy|physiognomy]].

## Significance
Magnus Hundt (1449–1519) was a Leipzig physician and philosopher whose *Antropologium* (1501) — an early use of the term — attempted a systematic account of human nature drawing on Aristotle, Galen, and Albert the Great. The work includes physiognomical material and body-diagram conventions later developed by della Porta and others. As one of the earliest printed anthropological treatises, it marks the moment when the medieval compendium tradition (body + soul + stars) begins to transform into something approaching Renaissance humanism. The Wellcome Collection's copy preserves the woodcut illustrations that were the book's primary teaching apparatus.

## For artists & game designers
An early Renaissance body-diagram: the human figure systematically labelled as both anatomical specimen and philosophical subject — a template for an in-world occult textbook plate.

A second plate from Magnus Hundt's *Antropologium de hominis dignitate* (Leipzig, 1501), the Wellcome Collection copy (L0032472).

## Iconography
This companion woodcut develops the body-diagram and [[motif:physiognomy|physiognomical]] apparatus of the preceding plate — a further illustration from the same treatise, likely showing different aspects of the human figure: head and face diagrams, limb proportions, or internal organ schemes. Together the two plates reconstruct the visual content of Hundt's contribution to Renaissance body philosophy.

## Significance
The *Antropologium*'s two Wellcome plates together show the range of the early printed body-diagram tradition, from anatomical-proportional schemes to physiognomic reading. Hundt's work predates the anatomical revolution of Vesalius (*De Humani Corporis Fabrica*, 1543) by forty years; its diagrams are still Galenic and philosophical rather than dissection-based, but they show the same impulse to systematise and illustrate the human body as a legible text. The physiognomical content — reading character from bodily features — connects Hundt directly to the divinatory tradition.

title: Kitab al-Bulhan: Devils and Supernatural Beings
work: Geomancy, Chiromancy & the Renaissance Divination Arts
creator: Anonymous (Abdulhasan al-Isfahani, attrib.)
summary:
A miniature from the *Kitab al-Bulhan* ('Book of Wonders,' Bodleian Library, MS Arab. d. 138, late 14th c.) depicting supernatural beings — *jinn*, demons, or devils — associated with astrological and divinatory sections of this Arabic occult encyclopedia.

## Iconography
The [[motif:Islamic occult|miniature]] shows one or more supernatural figures — rendered in the vivid, slightly monstrous style of late medieval Islamic book painting — associated with hours of the day, planets, or divinatory lots. The *Kitab al-Bulhan* is lavishly illustrated with such beings, which are keyed to astrological and prognostic texts.

## Significance
The *Kitab al-Bulhan* (compiled in Baghdad, late 14th century, under the Jalayirid sultans) is one of the most elaborately illustrated Islamic occult encyclopedias to survive. It combines astrology, geomancy (*'ilm al-raml*), lot-books (*zairja*), weather prediction, and demonology in a richly illustrated compendium. The images of supernatural beings index the *decans* (face-rulers) and planetary hours, providing the diviner with a visual catalogue of the spirits governing different times. The manuscript is held by the Bodleian Library, Oxford, and its plates have become widely reproduced in studies of Islamic occultism.

## For artists & game designers
Late medieval Islamic supernatural iconography: vivid demon figures with clearly defined character — each tied to a planet, hour, or omen — a ready-made monster manual from the geomantic tradition.

title: Kitab al-Bulhan: Birds and Serpents (Omen Illustration)
work: Geomancy, Chiromancy & the Renaissance Divination Arts
creator: Anonymous (Abdulhasan al-Isfahani, attrib.)
summary:
A miniature from the *Kitab al-Bulhan* ('Book of Wonders,' Bodleian Library, MS Arab. d. 138, late 14th c.) showing birds swooping on serpents — an [[motif:augury|omen illustration]] from the divinatory sections of this Arabic occult encyclopedia.

## Iconography
Birds are shown attacking or swooping on snakes or serpents below them — a classic omen image. In both Graeco-Roman and Islamic omenology, the sight of birds and serpents in combat was a significant portent, carrying meanings about victory and defeat, the higher principle overcoming the chthonic. The [[motif:Islamic occult|miniature]] is typical of the *Kitab al-Bulhan*'s lavish illustration of its omen and divination texts.

## Significance
The *Kitab al-Bulhan*'s section on ornithomancy (bird omens) and prognostication from natural signs connects the manuscript to the ancient Near Eastern omen tradition (the Babylonian *Enuma Anu Enlil* and related texts) as well as to the Arabic divinatory arts. The image of birds defeating serpents is also cosmologically charged: in Islamic iconography it can figure the victory of spiritual over material, or the triumph of wisdom over earthly dangers. The *Kitab al-Bulhan* weaves these layers of meaning together in a single compendium that a court diviner could consult for omens of every kind.

## For artists & game designers
A medieval Islamic omen image in vivid colour: birds vs. serpents as cosmic drama — directly usable as an omen card or prophetic image in a fantasy setting with Islamic aesthetic influences.

title: Divination Board for Ifa Priest (LACMA)
work: Geomancy, Chiromancy & the Renaissance Divination Arts
creator: Yoruba (anonymous carver)
rights: Public domain. LACMA (AC1993.218.3). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
An *Opon Ifa* (Ifa divination tray) from the Yoruba tradition, Nigeria, held by the Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA, AC1993.218.3).

## Iconography
The circular carved wooden tray is edged with a border of relief-carved figures and decorative motifs — typically including Eshu/Elegba, the divine messenger who must be acknowledged before any Ifa divination can proceed, along with faces, geometric patterns, and animal images. The flat central surface is dusted with powdered wood (*iyerosun*) on which the [[motif:Ifa|divination marks]] (*odu*) are drawn.

## Significance
[[motif:Ifa|Ifa]] divination — the divinatory system of the Yoruba people of southwestern Nigeria — operates through a corpus of 256 *odu* (named sign-complexes, each the union of two of the sixteen primary figures). The structural parallel with Arab-European geomancy's sixteen figures and their combinations is more than coincidental: both systems generate binary figures through a process of random mark-making and odd/even tallying. Whether this represents convergent invention or historical contact (via trans-Saharan or Indian Ocean routes) is debated, but the formal identity is exact. The LACMA board is one of the finest museum examples of the *Opon Ifa*.

## For artists & game designers
A masterwork of divinatory object design: the tray's carved border frames the act of divination as a sacred theatrical event — the marks appear within a cosmologically charged space.

The image shows [[motif:geomancy|marks]] or figures drawn on a flat surface — sand, paper, or cloth — in a pattern suggestive of geomantic casting or astrological charting. The 'mapping fortunes' title connects the image to the broader tradition of divination as a spatial practice: fortune is laid out, mapped, read from a two-dimensional field of signs.

Geomantic and astrological street-divination remains a living practice across South and Southeast Asia, the Middle East, and Africa. The image serves as a reminder that the tradition documented in medieval Latin manuscripts and Islamic treatises has never died: it is still being practiced in contemporary contexts with the same fundamental logic of marks, patterns, and interpreted fate. Connecting the archival record to the living practice is essential for understanding these arts not as historical curiosities but as durable technologies of knowledge.

title: Sikidy Divination Session, Madagascar (c. 1895)
work: Geomancy, Chiromancy & the Renaissance Divination Arts
creator: Anonymous photographer
summary:
A photograph (c. 1895) documenting a *sikidy* divination session in Madagascar, showing a *mpisikidy* (diviner) working with seeds.

## Iconography
The photograph shows one or more figures engaged in a *sikidy* reading — the diviners lay out seeds or beans, counting them down to odd or even remainders to build the [[motif:geomancy|geomantic figures]], then read the resulting tableau. The colonial-era photograph is a rare ethnographic record of the practice in action.

## Significance
Photographic documentation of *sikidy* in the late 19th century catches the tradition at a moment when French colonial rule was consolidating its grip on Madagascar (French conquest was completed in 1895–96). The photograph is part of a broader colonial archive of 'native practices,' though it preserves an invaluable record of a geomantic tradition that remained largely oral and performance-based rather than textual. The *mpisikidy* occupied an important social role in Malagasy society, consulted on questions ranging from health to agriculture to political decisions.

## For artists & game designers
A period image of divination in action: seeds on the ground, a consulting client, a working diviner — a direct source for a living divinatory practice rather than a manuscript diagram.

title: Sikidy: Working Example Diagram (Ascher)
work: Geomancy, Chiromancy & the Renaissance Divination Arts
creator: After Marcia Ascher
summary:
A schematic working example of *sikidy*, the Malagasy geomantic divination system, drawn after the mathematical ethnologist Marcia Ascher's analysis.

## Iconography
The diagram shows a completed *sikidy* tableau: seeds or beans are arranged in columns, reduced by counting to one-or-two remainders in each of four rows, generating a column of four binary [[motif:geomancy|geomantic figures]]. Multiple columns are combined, producing derived figures through a process of addition (odd + odd = even, odd + even = odd), until the full tableau — mothers, daughters, nieces, and witnesses — is complete.

## Significance
*Sikidy* is the oldest continuously documented geomantic tradition outside the Arab world. Its Malagasy vocabulary and cosmological framework are independent of Arabic *'ilm al-raml*, yet the underlying sixteen-figure binary system is structurally identical. Ascher's mathematical analysis demonstrated that *sikidy* constitutes a sophisticated combinatorial system encoding ecological, calendrical, and cosmological knowledge — not a degenerated import but a fully developed indigenous science. Together with Arabic and African geomantic traditions, *sikidy* shows how widely and independently a binary divination logic can develop.

## For artists & game designers
An oracle generation algorithm as clean as a flowchart: reduce random quantities to odd/even, build figures, combine them. Trivially implementable as a game mechanic with deep historical authenticity.

citations.text: M. Ascher, *Ethnomathematics: A Multicultural View of Mathematical Ideas* (1991), ch. 5.

title: Sikidy Lands: The Sixteen Figures in Malagasy Tradition
work: Geomancy, Chiromancy & the Renaissance Divination Arts
creator: After Marcia Ascher
summary:
A diagram mapping the sixteen *sikidy* geomantic figures to their associated cosmological 'lands' (*tany*) in Malagasy divination, after Marcia Ascher.

## Iconography
The diagram lays out the full set of sixteen [[motif:geomancy|geomantic figures]] as used in *sikidy*, each named in Malagasy and associated with a region, direction, season, or quality. The names differ from their Arabic and Latin counterparts (the same figure called Acquisitio in Latin geomancy has a distinct Malagasy name and set of associations), showing how the binary figure system was culturally re-coded.

## Significance
The 'lands' system is one of the most distinctive features of *sikidy*: each figure is not merely a sign but a place in a living cosmological map, with associations to time, space, and human fate. Ascher's reconstruction shows the system's internal coherence. The existence of such a fully developed cosmological lattice in Madagascar — an island settled by Austronesians from Southeast Asia and Bantu-speaking peoples from East Africa — raises intriguing questions about the routes by which geomantic knowledge travelled.

## For artists & game designers
A ready-made exotic world-cosmology: sixteen named 'lands' each tied to a direction, season, and quality — a complete geography of fate for a fantasy setting.

title: Malagasy Diviner with Sikidy at Tamatave (c. 1900)
work: Geomancy, Chiromancy & the Renaissance Divination Arts
creator: Anonymous photographer
summary:
A photograph (c. 1900) of a Malagasy diviner — captioned 'sorcier malgache' in the colonial French style — practicing *sikidy* at Tamatave on Madagascar's east coast.

## Iconography
The diviner is shown with the materials of *sikidy* practice: seeds arranged for counting, the results being read. The port city of Tamatave (now Toamasina) was a major point of cultural exchange between Madagascar, the East African coast, and the wider Indian Ocean world — appropriately, given the Arabic geomantic roots of *sikidy*.

## Significance
The French colonial label 'sorcier' (sorcerer) betrays the colonial frame: a sophisticated mathematical and cosmological divination system is reduced to sorcery for the colonial gaze. The photograph nonetheless records a *mpisikidy* at work in a specific named location and time, making it a rare piece of evidence for the geographic distribution and social status of [[motif:geomancy|geomantic divination]] in late-19th-century Madagascar. The east coast location is significant: Tamatave's Indian Ocean trade connections are the most likely historical channel through which *'ilm al-raml* reached Madagascar.

## For artists & game designers
A period portrait of a working diviner: the contrast between the colonial label and the sophisticated practice it misnames gives the image a layered historical richness.

title: Sikidy Tableau Diagram (Working Calculation)
work: Geomancy, Chiromancy & the Renaissance Divination Arts
creator: After Marcia Ascher
summary:
A linear tableau diagram showing the complete sequence of a *sikidy* reading: mothers, daughters, nieces, and witnesses generated by binary addition of the sixteen figures.

## Iconography
The strip tableau shows four 'mother' figures (generated from seeds), then four 'daughters' (derived by recombining the mothers' rows), then four 'nieces' (derived from mothers and daughters), then two 'witnesses,' and finally the 'judge.' This is the same cascade structure as European Latin [[motif:geomancy|geomancy]] — mothers (*matres*), daughters (*filiae*), nephews (*nepotes*), witnesses (*testes*), judge (*iudex*) — demonstrating the structural identity between the two traditions.

## Significance
The tableau structure is the geomantic method's most characteristic feature, and its preservation in *sikidy* alongside the identical sixteen-figure binary vocabulary is the strongest evidence for the historical connection between Arab *'ilm al-raml* and Malagasy divination. Whether the method arrived via direct Arab trade contact with the East African coast (from which Madagascar was peopled) or through an older route is debated, but the structural match is undeniable. Ascher's diagram makes the cascade logic transparent.

## For artists & game designers
A clean generative algorithm: four random inputs cascade through a defined transformation into a single output 'judgement' — ideal for a procedurally generated oracle system.

title: Gypsies Reading the Hand of a Young Traveler (Cornelis de Wael)
work: Geomancy, Chiromancy & the Renaissance Divination Arts
creator: Cornelis de Wael
summary:
A genre painting by Cornelis de Wael (1592–1667) showing Romani fortune-tellers reading the palm of a young traveler — one of the most common scenes in 17th-century European genre painting.

## Iconography
A young man extends his hand to a woman (or women) who scrutinise it while others in the group look on. The scene is set outdoors or in a marginal social space — a roadside, a fair, the edge of a city. The [[motif:chiromancy|palm-reading encounter]] between a naive young man and cunning Romani women was a standard genre trope, carrying coded messages about social boundaries, deception, and the lure of the forbidden.

## Significance
Cornelis de Wael worked principally in Antwerp and Italy, and the 'gypsy fortune-teller' genre (pioneered in painting by Caravaggio's *Buona Ventura* of c. 1594) was one of the most popular in 17th-century European art. The genre simultaneously mythologises Romani people as possessors of mysterious divinatory knowledge and figures them as thieves and deceivers. The palm-reading encounter is a social drama: the young man's hand is open, his fortune visible to those who can read it — but will they tell the truth? The paintings raise questions about trust, knowledge, and social hierarchy as much as about divination itself.

## For artists & game designers
The classic encounter scene: innocent hand extended to knowing reader — the palm-reading as moment of vulnerability and revelation.

title: Astrology, Chiromancy & Physiognomy (Wellcome MS, plate 1)
work: Geomancy, Chiromancy & the Renaissance Divination Arts
creator: Anonymous
rights: CC BY 4.0. Wellcome Collection. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A manuscript page from the Wellcome Collection (L0018732) combining [[motif:chiromancy|chiromancy]], physiognomy, and astrological diagrams in a single folio.

## Iconography
The page brings together the three great body-reading arts of the medieval and Renaissance period: palm diagrams (chiromancy), face or body illustrations (physiognomy), and astrological figures — the standard triumvirate of a learned diviner's handbook. Such compilations were common: the arts were regarded as complementary, each reading a different surface of the same astrologically-inscribed body.

## Significance
The combination of chiromancy, physiognomy, and astrology on a single page reflects the medieval understanding of the body as a microcosm of the heavens. Every line on the palm, every contour of the face, was held to be the imprint of planetary influence at birth. Manuscripts combining all three arts were practical reference tools: the diviner who could read hand, face, and horoscope had a complete forensic picture of the client. The Wellcome Collection holds an unusually rich array of such practical medical-divinatory manuscripts.

## For artists & game designers
A multi-modal divination reference page: the conjunction of palm map, face diagram, and star chart on one folio is a compact archetype for an in-world 'occultist's notebook.'

title: Astrology, Chiromancy & Physiognomy (Wellcome MS, plate 2)
work: Geomancy, Chiromancy & the Renaissance Divination Arts
creator: Anonymous

A second manuscript plate from the same Wellcome Collection source (L0018733), continuing the combined presentation of chiromancy, physiognomy, and astrology.

## Iconography
This companion folio develops the diagrammatic apparatus further — additional palm maps, body-part assignments, or facial-feature keys. Such manuscripts typically provided multiple hands or faces labelled with different planetary attributions, allowing the reader to compare types. The scribal and visual tradition of these compilations was remarkably stable across Latin Europe.

## Significance
The two Wellcome plates together illustrate the standard contents of a practical diviner's reference book as compiled in medieval and early modern Europe. The Wellcome Collection preserves many such manuscripts, which were typically owned by physicians, barber-surgeons, and educated laypeople with an interest in prognostic medicine. [[motif:chiromancy|Chiromancy]] and astrology were not clearly separated from medicine: the planetary mounts of the hand, for example, were used diagnostically as well as prognostically, and physiognomy (face-reading) overlapped with humoral medicine.

## For artists & game designers
The second plate from the same notebook: read together, the pair reconstruct a complete working diviner's reference — two openings of a small handbook that was consulted in practice.

The second plate from the same notebook: read together, the pair reconstruct a complete working diviner's reference — two openings of a small handbook that was consulted in practice.

title: Hand Covered in Symbols (Wellcome L0068573)
work: Geomancy, Chiromancy & the Renaissance Divination Arts
creator: Anonymous
rights: CC BY 4.0. Wellcome Collection. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A striking Wellcome Collection image (L0068573) of a hand densely covered in occult symbols — an unusually elaborate example of the divinatory hand-diagram tradition.

## Iconography
The palm and fingers are covered with an unusual density of [[motif:chiromancy|symbolic marks]] — possibly including letters, signs, astrological symbols, or other occult inscriptions beyond the standard planetary line-and-mount system. Such over-marked hands were used in talismanic contexts as well as for palmistry, and the hand itself was a privileged surface for occult inscription across traditions.

## Significance
The hand as a site of occult inscription goes beyond chiromancy proper into the broader traditions of talisman-making, medical astrology, and practical magic. Physicians and diviners used the palm as a mnemonic surface — the 'physician's hand,' the 'chiromantic hand,' and the 'magical hand' overlapped in the medieval medical-occult encyclopedia. The Wellcome example is an unusually rich instance of this over-inscription, closer to a talisman than a simple diagnostic diagram.

## For artists & game designers
The hand as maximalist occult canvas: cover every surface with symbols and it becomes something between a diagram and an amulet — a direct model for game art or character design.

title: Men Examining a Palm (Wellcome V0025922, engraving by Joseph Haynes)
work: Geomancy, Chiromancy & the Renaissance Divination Arts
creator: Joseph Haynes (engraver)
rights: Public domain. Wellcome Collection (V0025922). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
An engraving (Wellcome V0025922, attributed to engraver Joseph Haynes) of a group of men seated around a table examining a palm — a scholarly or social palm-reading scene.

## Iconography
Several men in contemporary costume are grouped around a table, one extending his hand while others scrutinise it. The setting suggests a drawing-room or tavern rather than a professional diviner's booth — [[motif:chiromancy|palmistry]] as a social entertainment or serious discussion, not a commercial transaction. The engraving conveys the learned-gentlemanly side of the chiromantic tradition.

## Significance
By the 17th and 18th centuries, palmistry had become a drawing-room accomplishment as well as a professional practice. Works like Richard Saunders' *Palmistry, the Secrets Thereof Disclosed* (1663) circulated in polite society, and the reading of palms was a social performance that could be learned from a book. Joseph Haynes (c. 1654–1701) was an English comedian and engraver associated with theatrical illustration; if this attribution is correct, the scene may have theatrical as well as social resonances. The image captures the genteel, sceptical-yet-curious attitude of Enlightenment-adjacent society towards divinatory arts.

## For artists & game designers
A social scene of palm-reading: not a sinister fortune-teller's booth but a civilised gathering of curious men — the respectable face of the chiromantic tradition.

title: Yoruba Divination Board (Fetish, Twins Theme), Nigeria
work: Geomancy, Chiromancy & the Renaissance Divination Arts
creator: Yoruba (anonymous carver; photograph by Mickey Mystique)
rights: CC BY-SA 4.0. Mickey Mystique / Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A Yoruba divination board (possibly an *Opon Ifa* variant or related divinatory object) from Nigeria, decorated with motifs relating to twins (*Ibeji*) and ancestral figures.

## Iconography
The carved board displays motifs associated with twins (*Ibeji*) and protective figures (*orisa*), alongside standard Yoruba divinatory iconography. Twins hold special significance in Yoruba culture — born at far above the global average rate among the Yoruba, they are considered sacred, and the death of a twin requires the carving of a commemorative figure. The presence of [[motif:Ifa|twin motifs]] on a divination board connects Ifa to the cult of Ibeji and to the broader system of Yoruba religion.

## Significance
The diversity of Yoruba divinatory objects — *Opon Ifa* trays, *opele* (divination chains), *ibo* (casting objects), and associated figures — reflects the complexity and internal differentiation of the Ifa system. Not every Yoruba carving called a 'divination board' functions in exactly the same way: some are specifically *Opon Ifa*, others are associated with particular *orisa* or with protective functions. The twin/Ibeji connection places this board at the intersection of Ifa divination and the cult of sacred twins — one of Yoruba culture's most distinctive features, widely exported across the diaspora to Brazil, Cuba, and the United States.

## For artists & game designers
A divination object dense with symbolic content — the twin motif, the guardian figures, the structured carved surface — a model for a richly characterised magical artefact.

title: Roman Abrasax intaglio — cock-headed anguipede in bloodstone
work: Gnostic Scripture & Cosmology (Codices, Demiurge & Dualist Heresy)
creator: Anonymous (Roman-era gem-cutter)
rights: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Maxime Cambreling). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A Roman magical intaglio in bloodstone (jasper) carved with *Abrasax* the anguipede — a cock-headed god with serpent legs — surrounded by the names of angels.

## Iconography
The figure stands in a cuirass, a cock's (or lion's) head above, two snakes for legs, brandishing a whip in one hand and a round shield in the other; the shield and field carry voces magicae and angelic names. This *alectorocephalic anguipede* is the single most recognisable type among the thousands of surviving 'Gnostic' or 'Abraxas' gems.

## Significance
The name [[motif:abraxas|Abrasax / Abraxas]] sums in Greek isopsephy to 365, the number of heavens and of days, marking the god as ruler of the cosmic year. Though the gems are products of a broad Graeco-Egyptian magical milieu rather than a single sect, Basilides' followers and later writers tied the name to Gnostic speculation, and Bonner's *Studies in Magical Amulets* remains the foundational catalogue.

## For artists & game designers
The quintessential occult-amulet asset: a snake-legged, beast-headed warrior with shield and whip, encircled by barbarous names — a self-contained sigil-item.

citations.text: Campbell Bonner, *Studies in Magical Amulets* (1950).

title: Abraxas gems with human forms, from Macarius's *Abraxas seu Apistopistus*
work: Gnostic Scripture & Cosmology (Codices, Demiurge & Dualist Heresy)
creator: Jacob van Werden (engraver), after Jean Chifflet / Macarius
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: plate from Macarius, Abraxas seu Apistopistus, 1657]
summary:
An engraved plate of Abraxas gems 'with human forms', from Jean l'Heureux's (Macarius's) *Abraxas, seu Apistopistus*, edited by Jean Chifflet (Antwerp, 1657) — the first great printed catalogue of the Gnostic amulet stones.

## Iconography
Rows of numbered gems are reproduced in fine engraving, each showing a deity or hybrid in human form with attendant inscriptions. The plate is an antiquarian inventory: object after object lifted onto the page so the learned reader can compare the magical types.

## Significance
Macarius's *Apistopistus* ('the unbelievable believed') gathered and engraved the [[motif:abraxas|Abraxas]]-stones at a moment when antiquaries were first treating magical gems as evidence rather than mere curiosities. Its plates fixed the visual canon of 'Gnostic gems' for two centuries and stand behind every later corpus down to Bonner and the modern *Campbell Bonner Magical Gems Database*.

## For artists & game designers
A period 'catalogue sheet' device: an array of numbered amulet thumbnails, perfect as an in-game compendium or codex page the player fills in by collecting gems.

citations.text: Jean Chifflet (ed.), *Macarii Abraxas seu Apistopistus* (Antwerp, 1657).

title: *Apocryphon of John* — the Sethian creation myth (text page)
work: Gnostic Scripture & Cosmology (Codices, Demiurge & Dualist Heresy)
creator: Anonymous (Coptic scribe)
date: text 2nd c. CE; Coptic copies 4th c.
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: Nag Hammadi codices, Coptic Museum, Cairo / related witness]
summary:
A page representing the *Apocryphon (Secret Book) of John*, the central Sethian cosmogony preserved in several Coptic copies, including three in the Nag Hammadi codices.

## Iconography
The page is text, not picture: the *Apocryphon* is a revelation-dialogue in which the risen Christ instructs the apostle John. Its 'imagery' is verbal — the unfolding of the invisible Spirit, the Barbelo, and the aeons into a full divine world.

## Significance
The *Apocryphon of John* is the most complete account of the [[motif:sophia and the aeons|Sethian]] system: from the ineffable Monad emanate Barbelo and the aeons; [[motif:sophia and the aeons|Sophia]] acts without her consort and brings forth the misshapen [[motif:ialdabaoth|Ialdabaoth]], who steals power and fashions the lower world and its [[motif:archons|archons]]. It supplies the master-narrative of the demiurge and the entrapment of the divine spark — the spine of Gnostic mythology. Michael Waldstein and Frederik Wisse produced the synoptic edition.

## For artists & game designers
The canonical 'how the false world was made' lore-text: a single dialogue that gives you a creator-god, a flawed demiurge, his archon lieutenants, and a stolen spark to recover.

citations.text: Michael Waldstein & Frederik Wisse, *The Apocryphon of John* (1995).

title: Bosnian Bogomil tombstone (*stećak*), reproduced 1901
work: Gnostic Scripture & Cosmology (Codices, Demiurge & Dualist Heresy)
creator: Hugo Charlemont (drawing), after a medieval stećak
repository: in situ, Bosnia (reproduced in a 1901 publication)
summary:
A 1901 reproduction (after a drawing by Hugo Charlemont) of a medieval Bosnian *stećak* — a monumental carved tombstone traditionally associated with the Bogomils.

## Iconography
A massive recumbent or standing stone block bears carved relief: arcading, rosettes, hunting and dance scenes, and emblematic figures in the distinctive idiom of the *stećci*. The carving is bold and flat, more emblem than portrait.

## Significance
The Bogomils were a tenth-century Balkan [[motif:dualist heresy|dualist]] movement — named for the priest Bogomil — who, like the later [[motif:cathars|Cathars]] they helped inspire, rejected the material creation as the devil's work. Older scholarship tied the spectacular *stećci* to the heretical 'Bosnian Church'; more recent work questions any neat Bogomil attribution, treating the tombs as a broader regional culture. Either way they are the most monumental surviving trace of medieval Balkan dualism, and a key link in the chain from the Paulicians to the Cathars.

## For artists & game designers
A carved-megalith asset for a heretic or 'old faith' graveyard: flat-relief tombstones with cryptic dancers and rosettes.

citations.text: Dmitri Obolensky, *The Bogomils* (1948).

title: Magical Diagram from the *Books of Jeu*
work: Gnostic Scripture & Cosmology (Codices, Demiurge & Dualist Heresy)
creator: Anonymous (Coptic scribe)
date: text 3rd–4th c. CE; codex later copy
summary:
One of the *topos*-diagrams of the aeons from the *Books of Jeu* in the Bruce Codex — a famous early Gnostic ritual diagram.

## Iconography
A boxed emanation-diagram in which a central enclosure is ringed by smaller cells, each inscribed with letters, numerals, and the magical names of the powers it contains. The *Books of Jeu* are densely filled with such schematics, mapping the topography of the heavenly *treasuries* and the figure of Jeu, the 'true God' set as overseer over them.

## Significance
These diagrams are among the oldest surviving worked examples of Gnostic ritual cartography: they fix in ink the invisible architecture of the upper world so the initiate can navigate it. Each enclosed name is a station, each seal a key. Scholars from Carl Schmidt onward have treated them as a bridge between speculative cosmology and operative magic — the cosmos rendered as a diagram you can actually use.

## For artists & game designers
A literal level-map: nested chambers labelled with passwords, ready to drop in as the dungeon schematic of a celestial ascent.

citations.text: Carl Schmidt & Violet MacDermot, *The Books of Jeu and the Untitled Text in the Bruce Codex* (1978).

title: Gnostic Cross from the Bruce Codex (Books of Jeu)
work: Gnostic Scripture & Cosmology (Codices, Demiurge & Dualist Heresy)
creator: Anonymous (Coptic scribe)
date: text 3rd–4th c. CE; codex later copy
summary:
A cruciform ritual diagram copied from the *Bruce Codex*, the papyrus book (Bodleian MS Bruce 96) that preserves the two *Books of Jeu*.

## Iconography
The figure is a stark cross-shaped seal of the kind that punctuates the *Books of Jeu*: geometric arms enclosing letters, numbers, and divine names. Such diagrams were not decorative — they are the working apparatus of the text, the seals and passwords the ascending soul must present at each celestial gate.

## Significance
The *Books of Jeu* are among the earliest Gnostic ritual manuals to survive, describing how the soul rises through the *treasuries of light* by uttering the right name and displaying the right [[motif:seal|seal]] at each archon-guarded threshold. Carl Schmidt's edition established their importance; the diagrams are direct ancestors of the magical seals of the later grimoire tradition.

## For artists & game designers
A gate-key system in miniature: each diagram is a sigil-and-password the player must possess to pass a guardian and climb to the next sphere.

citations.text: Carl Schmidt & Violet MacDermot, *The Books of Jeu and the Untitled Text in the Bruce Codex* (1978).

title: The Cathars expelled from Carcassonne (1209)
work: Gnostic Scripture & Cosmology (Codices, Demiurge & Dualist Heresy)
creator: Workshop of the Master of Boucicaut
summary:
An early-fifteenth-century illuminated miniature, from the workshop of the Master of Boucicaut, showing the Cathars being expelled from Carcassonne in 1209 during the Albigensian Crusade.

## Iconography
A file of stripped, dispossessed townspeople streams out through the gate of a turreted city as armoured figures look on. The miniature compresses the violent suppression of the Languedoc heresy into a single procession of the expelled.

## Significance
The Cathars ('the pure') were a medieval [[motif:dualist heresy|dualist]] movement who held the visible world to be the work of an evil creator and salvation to lie in the spirit's escape from matter — a structure that scholars have long compared to ancient Gnosticism. Their *perfecti* renounced the flesh; their challenge to the Church provoked the Albigensian Crusade (1209–1229) and the Inquisition. Whether Catharism was a true survival of Gnosticism or a fresh dualism is debated (Mark Pegg vs. the older 'great heresy' thesis), but its imagery is the medieval face of the [[motif:demiurge|evil-creator]] idea.

## For artists & game designers
A grim event-illustration: a heretic people driven from a walled city — usable for any 'purge of the dissenters' story beat.

citations.text: Malcolm Lambert, *The Cathars* (1998).

title: Chnoubis intaglio — lion-headed serpent magical gem (BnF)
work: Gnostic Scripture & Cosmology (Codices, Demiurge & Dualist Heresy)
creator: Anonymous (Graeco-Egyptian gem-cutter)
repository: Bibliothèque nationale de France, Paris (Cabinet des Médailles)
summary:
A magical intaglio in the Bibliothèque nationale de France (Cabinet des Médailles) carved with *Chnoubis* — a lion-headed serpent crowned with solar rays.

## Iconography
The gem shows an upright serpent with a radiate lion's head, often accompanied by the triple-bar 'Chnoubis sign' and barbarous names. The type is compact and emblematic, the whole power of the stone concentrated in one hybrid creature.

## Significance
Chnoubis was an *agathodaimon* (good spirit) and solar-stomach guardian: such gems were worn as healing amulets, especially against ailments of the stomach and digestion, drawing on the serpent's chthonic and the lion's solar force. Like the [[motif:abraxas|Abraxas]] stones, Chnoubis gems sit at the crossroads of Graeco-Egyptian magic and the [[motif:demiurge|lion-serpent]] imagery that Gnostic writers read into the figure of the archon. They are catalogued by Bonner and in the Campbell Bonner database.

## For artists & game designers
A tidy talisman-icon: radiant lion-headed snake on a single stone — drop-in art for a healing charm or status-cure item.

citations.text: Campbell Bonner, *Studies in Magical Amulets* (1950).

title: Gnostic gem with scarab (Walters Art Museum)
work: Gnostic Scripture & Cosmology (Codices, Demiurge & Dualist Heresy)
creator: Anonymous (Graeco-Egyptian gem-cutter)
summary:
A so-called 'Gnostic gem' in the Walters Art Museum, carved with a scarab — an Egyptian symbol of rebirth absorbed into the magical-amulet repertoire of late antiquity.

## Iconography
The small engraved stone presents a scarab beetle, the Egyptian *kheper*, set among magical signs. As an amulet it folds the Pharaonic emblem of self-renewal into the Graeco-Roman magical idiom that museums conventionally label 'Gnostic'.

## Significance
The Walters' label 'Gnostic gem' reflects the older catalogue habit of grouping all the engraved Graeco-Egyptian magical stones under that heading; modern scholarship treats them as products of a broad ritual culture rather than of any one Gnostic church. The scarab's presence shows how deeply [[motif:abraxas|these amulets]] drew on Egyptian funerary symbolism of death and [[motif:demiurge|rebirth]], a continuity studied by Bonner, Michel, and the Campbell Bonner database.

## For artists & game designers
A museum-real amulet asset: a carved beetle-stone for a 'rebirth' or 'second chance' charm, with authentic Greco-Egyptian provenance.

citations.text: Simone Michel, *Die magischen Gemmen* (2004).
