title: The Macrobian cosmos (Dream of Scipio world map)
work: The Music of the Spheres & Cosmic Harmony
creator: Anonymous (after Macrobius)
date: Macrobius c. 430 CE; printed map after his scheme
summary:
A map after Macrobius's *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio* (early 5th c.), the text that carried the ancient doctrine of the harmony of the spheres through the Middle Ages.

## Iconography
The earth is divided into the Macrobian **climatic zones** — two frigid caps, two temperate bands and a torrid equatorial belt crossed by an ocean — the scheme Macrobius derived from contemplating the cosmos in Scipio's dream. In the full vision this terrestrial globe sits at the still centre of the revolving **celestial spheres** whose motion sounds the cosmic music.

## Significance
In Cicero's *Somnium Scipionis*, expounded by Macrobius, the elder Scipio shows the dreamer the nine [[motif:music-of-the-spheres|spheres]] whose turning produces a great concord, too constant for mortal ears to notice. Macrobius's commentary made this the standard medieval account of cosmic [[motif:cosmic-harmony|harmony]] and of the soul's descent and return, shaping writers from Boethius to Dante.

## For artists & game designers
The zoned earth at the hub of singing spheres is a ready cosmology: a silent centre ringed by sounding shells.

title: Pythagoras with bells, glasses and monochord (Theorica Musicae)
work: The Music of the Spheres & Cosmic Harmony
creator: Franchino Gaffurio (woodcut)
summary:
The four-panel Pythagoras illustration from Gaffurio's *Theorica Musicae* (1492), isolating the legendary experiments by which the consonances were found.

## Iconography
In successive scenes Pythagoras (and in one panel Philolaus) tests sounding bodies marked with the numbers **4, 6, 8, 9, 12, 16**: hammers at a forge, tuned **bells**, water-filled **glasses**, strings stretched by hanging weights, and graduated **pipes**. The last panel shows a divided string — the [[motif:monochord|monochord]] — the one instrument that genuinely demonstrates that halving a string yields the octave (2:1).

## Significance
The sequence is the visual catechism of Pythagorean harmonics: every consonance proceeds from ratios among the first numbers. Only the monochord experiment is physically sound; the rest are legendary, yet together they enshrine the conviction that number is the hidden cause of beauty and that the same ratios tune the [[motif:music-of-the-spheres|cosmos]].

## For artists & game designers
The numbered sounding objects are a tidy 'lab' of ratio puzzles; the monochord alone is the honest one — useful for a 'find the real law' beat.

citations.text: F. Gaffurio, *Theorica Musicae* (Milan, 1492).

title: The Pythagorean Tetractys
work: The Music of the Spheres & Cosmic Harmony
creator: Anonymous (diagram)
date: modern rendering of an ancient figure
summary:
A diagram of the Pythagorean *tetractys*, the triangular figure of ten points in rows of 1-2-3-4, here paired with the Hebrew Tetragrammaton.

## Iconography
Ten dots are stacked in a perfect equilateral **triangle**: one at the apex, then two, three and four below, summing to the sacred **decad** (10). The four rows correspond to point, line, plane and solid, and to the ratios 1:2, 2:3, 3:4 that generate the octave, fifth and fourth. In the kabbalistic overlay each row bears the letters of the divine Name in expanding combination.

## Significance
The [[motif:tetractys|tetractys]] was so holy to the Pythagoreans that they swore oaths upon it as 'the source and root of ever-flowing nature'. Because its first four numbers contain all the musical consonances, it is the seed of the entire doctrine of cosmic [[motif:musical-ratios|harmony]]: the same little triangle holds the scale, the dimensions of space and, for later Christian-cabalist readers, the structure of the divine Name.

## For artists & game designers
A four-row triangle that encodes both geometry and the musical scale is a perfect minimalist sigil — one shape, total cosmology.

citations.text: Iamblichus, *Life of Pythagoras*.

title: Typus Arithmeticae: Boethius and Pythagoras reckon (Margarita Philosophica)
work: The Music of the Spheres & Cosmic Harmony
creator: Gregor Reisch (woodcut)
summary:
The *Typus Arithmeticae* woodcut from Gregor Reisch's encyclopaedia *Margarita Philosophica* (1503), the famous contest of the new written calculation against the old counting board.

## Iconography
Lady **Arithmetica**, her gown patterned with the doubling and triple proportions (2 4 8 / 3 9 27 that generate the musical intervals), presides between two reckoners. On the left **Boethius** computes with Hindu-Arabic numerals and pen (*algorismus*); on the right **Pythagoras** works counters on an **abacus** (*abacus*). Arithmetica's gaze favours the smiling Boethius.

## Significance
Reisch personifies the foundational art of the [[motif:quadrivium|quadrivium]]: arithmetic, the science of number, parent of music, geometry and astronomy. The numbers woven into her dress are precisely the Platonic *lambda* series whose ratios yield the harmonic intervals, so the image quietly asserts that the same numbers underlie calculation and the [[motif:music-of-the-spheres|harmony of the spheres]]. It also dramatises the historical victory of written arithmetic over the abacus.

## For artists & game designers
The 'two methods, one judge' staging is a vivid template for an in-game contest between an old and a new system of power.

citations.text: G. Reisch, *Margarita Philosophica* (Freiburg, 1503).

title: Oracle-creature from the Heidelberg Book of Fate (fol. 96v)
work: The Heidelberg Book of Fate (Cod. Pal. germ. 832)
creator: Anonymous (German, workshop of Ludwig Henfflin?)
summary:
A single coloured miniature of an oracle-animal heading its column of text, from the *Heidelberger Schicksalsbuch*.

## Iconography
At the top of the page a framed painting of a beast on a green ground introduces the prognostic text below. Animals recur through the *Losbuch* as pointer-figures, each lending its emblematic character to the fate it announces.

## Significance
The bestiary of the German fate-books — lions, stags, birds, fabulous beasts — turns the casting of lots into a procession through a symbolic menagerie, each animal a node in the divinatory path. The blending of zodiacal, bestiary, and prophetic imagery in a single popular oracle-book exemplifies how late-medieval divination drew freely across the esoteric image-stock.

## For artists & game designers
An emblematic oracle-beast with its prophecy — the kind of symbolic creature-card a fate or tarot system is built from.

title: Lot-table from the Heidelberg Book of Fate (fol. 11v)
work: The Heidelberg Book of Fate (Cod. Pal. germ. 832)
creator: Anonymous (German, workshop of Ludwig Henfflin?)
summary:
A lot-table from the *Heidelberger Schicksalsbuch*, the apparatus by which the book of fate was consulted.

## Iconography
A grid of numbers ruled in red and black fills the page in columns. Each entry routes the querent — after casting dice on a question-page — onward through the book's branching structure toward a verse-answer. The whole page is a working divinatory algorithm rendered as a table.

## Significance
The medieval *Losbuch* (book of lots) was a sortilege machine: a reader posed one of a fixed set of questions, threw dice, and followed the resulting number through tables, pointer-figures, and 'judges' to a rhymed oracle. Such books sat at the licit edge of divination, framed as a game yet drawing on the same impulse as astrology and geomancy. This copy is one of the most lavishly illustrated to survive.

## For artists & game designers
A literal pre-modern randomisation table — the original 'roll on the fate chart' mechanic, beautifully laid out.

citations.text: *Heidelberger Schicksalsbuch*, Cod. Pal. germ. 832 (c. 1491).

title: Oracle miniatures from the Heidelberg Book of Fate (fol. 41v)
work: The Heidelberg Book of Fate (Cod. Pal. germ. 832)
creator: Anonymous (German, workshop of Ludwig Henfflin?)
summary:
A page of four coloured oracle-miniatures from the *Heidelberger Schicksalsbuch*.

## Iconography
Four small framed paintings are set into the text in a two-by-two array, each captioned in red and black. The miniatures illustrate the oracle's verse-answers — figures, scenes, and emblems that the querent reaches at the end of a chain of dice-throws.

## Significance
The illustrations are not decoration but signposts in the divinatory machine: the *Losbuch* threads the reader through question-pages, number-tables, and pointer-figures to one of these painted answers. The genre fused entertainment, moral counsel, and genuine fortune-telling, and its picture-cycles are a rich, under-studied seam of late-medieval popular esoterica.

## For artists & game designers
A ready-made 'oracle deck' page — discrete illustrated outcomes, each with its caption, exactly as a fate-table result screen.

title: Oracle-figures from the Heidelberg Book of Fate (fol. 76v)
work: The Heidelberg Book of Fate (Cod. Pal. germ. 832)
creator: Anonymous (German, workshop of Ludwig Henfflin?)
summary:
Four coloured oracle-figures with their verse-answers, from the *Heidelberger Schicksalsbuch*.

## Iconography
Four framed miniatures sit among the red-and-black text. In the *Losbuch* tradition such figures act as the 'masters', 'judges', or pointer-personifications who deliver the fate the dice have selected — each paired with a rhymed German prognostication.

## Significance
The *Schicksalsbuch* organises its divination around a cast of recurring figures (planets, prophets, judges, animals) through whom the answer is voiced. This narrative scaffolding — a question routed through a gallery of speaking figures — is what distinguishes the illustrated German Losbuch from a bare lot-table, and makes it one of the most vivid windows onto everyday late-medieval fortune-telling.

## For artists & game designers
A cast of 'oracle NPCs', each delivering a fixed prophetic line — directly usable as a divination interface.

title: Hell (Circle of Hieronymus Bosch)
work: The Hellmouth: The Jaws of Damnation
creator: Circle of Hieronymus Bosch
summary:
A panel of *Hell* from the circle of Hieronymus Bosch (early sixteenth century), in the unmistakable infernal idiom the master of 's-Hertogenbosch made his own.

## Iconography
The damned are tormented across a fire-lit, nocturnal landscape by a teeming bestiary of hybrid devils — part insect, part machine, part reptile — who impale, devour, ride and dismember the naked sinners. Burning towers and cities glow on the horizon; punishments are often tuned, in true Boschian fashion, to the specific sins of the lost.

## Significance
Bosch transformed the medieval [[motif:hellmouth|hellmouth]] into an entire phantasmagoric world: the single devouring maw gives way to an inexhaustible swarm of monstrous tormentors and absurd infernal contraptions. Hugely influential and endlessly imitated by his circle and followers, this vision shaped the European imagination of Hell more than any other, as Walter Gibson and the recent Bosch Research Project document.

## For artists & game designers
Bosch's principle — invent a unique, sin-specific monster for each torment rather than repeat one demon — is a generative engine for endlessly varied, legible enemy design.

citations.text: Walter S. Gibson, *Hieronymus Bosch* (1973).
Matthijs Ilsink et al., *Hieronymus Bosch, Painter and Draughtsman* (Bosch Research and Conservation Project, 2016).

title: The Last Judgment Tympanum (Bourges Cathedral)
work: The Hellmouth: The Jaws of Damnation
creator: Anonymous (Gothic sculptor)
summary:
The central tympanum of the west façade of Bourges Cathedral (c. 1230–1250), a Gothic Last Judgment whose lower register stages the weighing of souls and their delivery into the cauldron-mouth of Hell.

## Iconography
The dead rise from their tombs; Saint Michael weighs souls in a balance as a devil tries to cheat the scales. The damned are chained and driven toward a great [[motif:cauldron of hell|cauldron]] set in a monstrous mouth, where grinning devils stuff kings, bishops and misers into the boiling pot. The blessed, serene, are led the other way to Abraham's bosom.

## Significance
The Bourges tympanum is among the most vivid Gothic treatments of judgment, its cauldron of the damned a celebrated and unusually dramatic detail. The contrast of the orderly weighing above and the gleeful infernal cookery below distils the Gothic theology of justice and mercy. Its sculpture has been central to studies of the Last Judgment portal by Willibald Sauerländer and others.

## For artists & game designers
A devil's hand tipping the scale during the weighing of souls is a perfect micro-detail: it injects cheating, suspense and dark comedy into an otherwise solemn ritual.

citations.text: Willibald Sauerländer, *Gothic Sculpture in France 1140–1270* (1972).
Émile Mâle, *L'art religieux du XIIIe siècle en France* (1898).

title: The Mouth of Hell (Hours of Catherine of Cleves)
work: The Hellmouth: The Jaws of Damnation
creator: Master of Catherine of Cleves
summary:
The dazzling *Mouth of Hell* from the *Hours of Catherine of Cleves* (c. 1440), the masterpiece of the anonymous Utrecht illuminator known from this very book — perhaps the most inventive hellmouth ever painted.

## Iconography
Hell is conceived as a fortified gate-tower built into the jaws of a vast fanged monster: through the gaping mouth, fitted with a portcullis-like cauldron, devils shove and boil the damned, while smaller beasts and grotesques crawl over the brickwork battlements above. The whole architecture is the head of a beast, its eyes glaring windows.

## Significance
The Cleves Master merges the [[motif:hellmouth|monster-jaws]] tradition with the late-medieval image of hell as a fortress-gatehouse, producing an inventiveness in his borders and grotesques that is unmatched. The Morgan's two-volume facsimile made the book a touchstone of Northern manuscript art; this page is its most reproduced opening. The cauldron set in the throat ties it to the [[motif:cauldron of hell|cauldron]] tradition.

## For artists & game designers
Building a dungeon gatehouse *as* a monster's head — windows for eyes, portcullis for teeth — fuses architecture and creature into one unforgettable threshold.

citations.text: John Plummer, *The Hours of Catherine of Cleves* (1966).
Rob Dückers & Ruud Priem (eds.), *The Hours of Catherine of Cleves: Devotion, Demons and Daily Life* (2009).

title: The Anastasis Fresco (Chora Church, Constantinople)
work: The Hellmouth: The Jaws of Damnation
creator: Anonymous (Byzantine fresco painter)
summary:
The celebrated *Anastasis* fresco in the parekklesion (funerary chapel) of the Chora Church (Kariye Camii) in Constantinople, painted c. 1315–1321 under Theodore Metochites — the most admired of all Byzantine Harrowings.

## Iconography
A white-robed Christ in a star-filled mandorla strides forward with explosive energy, seizing Adam and Eve by the wrists and wrenching them bodily from their sarcophagi; beneath his feet the doors of Hell lie smashed in a cross, and the bound figure of Hades-Satan is fettered in the black pit amid a scatter of broken locks, bolts and keys. The righteous kings and the Baptist look on.

## Significance
The Chora *Anastasis* is the supreme expression of the Eastern harrowing, its dynamism a high point of the Palaiologan renaissance. The shattered gates and chained Hades are the Byzantine answer to the Western [[motif:hellmouth|hellmouth]] — Hell as a broken prison rather than a devouring mouth. Placed in a burial chapel, it promised resurrection to the dead, as Robert Ousterhout and Anna Kartsonis emphasise.

## For artists & game designers
Motion sells the moment: a figure mid-stride, dragging others up out of their graves, conveys rescue far more powerfully than a static, posed tableau.

citations.text: Robert Ousterhout, *The Art of the Kariye Camii* (2002).
Anna D. Kartsonis, *Anastasis: The Making of an Image* (1986).

title: Hell of the Last Judgment Tympanum (Sainte-Foy, Conques)
work: The Hellmouth: The Jaws of Damnation
creator: Anonymous (Romanesque sculptor)
repository: Abbey Church of Sainte-Foy, Conques (in situ)
summary:
The great carved tympanum of the Last Judgment over the west door of the abbey church of Sainte-Foy at Conques (c. 1107–1125), one of the supreme Romanesque sculptures, with its terrifying Hell at the lower right.

## Iconography
Christ in Majesty divides the saved from the damned. On the sinister side a gaping [[motif:hellmouth|monster's mouth]] swallows the condemned, who are tipped headlong into a chaos of devils; an enthroned Satan presides while demons hang, boil and rack the damned by their sins. An inscription warns sinners they will know terror.

## Significance
Conques is the most complete and legible of the Romanesque Last Judgment portals, designed to confront pilgrims on the road to Santiago with the choice between paradise and the hellmouth. Its ordered architecture of Heaven against the writhing disorder of Hell exemplifies the twelfth-century theology of judgment, much studied by Émile Mâle and later by Marcello Angheben.

## For artists & game designers
Placing the maw of hell at the threshold a traveller must literally walk through turns architecture into a moral checkpoint — the doorway itself delivers the warning.

citations.text: Émile Mâle, *L'art religieux du XIIe siècle en France* (1922).
Marcello Angheben, *Les jugements derniers byzantins et l'iconographie du jugement immédiat* (2002, art.).

title: Icon of the Descent into Hell (Anastasis)
work: The Hellmouth: The Jaws of Damnation
creator: Anonymous (Russian icon painter)
summary:
A Russian icon of the *Anastasis* — the Descent into Hell — from the Walters Art Museum, the Orthodox counterpart to the Western Harrowing, in which the risen Christ tramples the gates of Hades to raise the dead.

## Iconography
Christ, in a radiant mandorla, stands on the shattered doors of Hell — crossed over the black pit of Hades, where the bound figure of Satan or Death lies amid broken locks, keys and chains. He grasps Adam and Eve by the wrists and lifts them from their tombs; behind them the kings David and Solomon, John the Baptist and the righteous press forward to be saved.

## Significance
In Byzantine and Russian tradition the *Anastasis* — not the empty tomb — is the standard image of the Resurrection. The dark cavern of Hades functions as the Eastern equivalent of the [[motif:hellmouth|hellmouth]], its gates broken rather than locked. Drawn from the *Gospel of Nicodemus*, the type was codified at Chora and the Mistra churches and is treated authoritatively by Anna Kartsonis.

## For artists & game designers
Standing the hero on the literally shattered doors of the underworld, keys and broken locks scattered beneath, makes "the prison is broken" visible at a glance.

citations.text: Anna D. Kartsonis, *Anastasis: The Making of an Image* (1986).
Walters Art Museum, object 37.1074.

title: Hell (Hortus Deliciarum, after Herrad of Landsberg)
work: The Hellmouth: The Jaws of Damnation
creator: After Herrad of Landsberg (19th-c. tracing by A. de Bastard)
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: original destroyed 1870, Strasbourg; copy after A. de Bastard]
summary:
The Hell-page of the *Hortus Deliciarum* ("Garden of Delights"), the great illustrated encyclopedia compiled c. 1180 by the abbess Herrad of Landsberg for her nuns at Hohenburg; the medieval original burned in 1870 and survives only through tracings such as this.

## Iconography
Hell is laid out as a many-chambered pit. A monstrous, enthroned Satan holds a small damned soul (Antichrist) on his lap; around him devils torment the damned by category of sin — the proud, the avaricious, the lustful — boiling some in cauldrons, hanging others, and goading souls deeper. Tituli label each punishment in the lost original.

## Significance
Herrad's *Hortus* is among the most ambitious works of the twelfth-century cloister and one of the earliest by a named woman. Its Hell systematizes damnation as a graded penal architecture, a precursor to the [[motif:cauldron of hell|cauldron]]-and-category infernos of the later Middle Ages and of Dante. Because the codex was destroyed in the bombardment of Strasbourg, copies like this are the sole witnesses, as Rosalie Green's reconstruction established.

## For artists & game designers
A hell divided into labelled chambers, each punishing one named vice, is a ready blueprint for a level whose rooms each embody a different sin.

citations.text: Rosalie Green et al., *Herrad of Hohenbourg: Hortus Deliciarum* (reconstruction, 1979).
Fiona Griffiths, *The Garden of Delights: Reform and Renaissance for Women in the Twelfth Century* (2007).

title: Hell and the Fall of the Rebel Angels (Junius / Cædmon Manuscript)
work: The Hellmouth: The Jaws of Damnation
creator: Anonymous (Anglo-Saxon illuminator)
summary:
A pen drawing from the *Junius Manuscript* (the so-called Cædmon Manuscript), the illustrated Old English biblical poems made in England around 1000, showing Hell and the bound Satan among the consequences of the angelic fall.

## Iconography
The damned and the rebel angels are crowded into a dark infernal region; in many of its openings Hell appears as a toothed maw or pit, and Satan is shown fettered below, the first prisoner of his own kingdom. The line-drawn style, partly unfinished, is characteristic of Anglo-Saxon "Winchester" draughtsmanship.

## Significance
Junius 11 is one of the earliest and most important witnesses to the [[motif:hellmouth|hellmouth]] in Western art: its illustrations to *Genesis B* and *Christ and Satan* helped fix the image of Hell as a devouring mouth and of Satan as a bound rebel — imagery that fed directly into the Old English imagination and, some argue, into Milton. Schmidt treats these drawings as the fountainhead of the English hellmouth tradition.

## For artists & game designers
The unfinished, raw line-drawing here shows how little is needed to read "hell": a jagged maw and a chained figure already carry the whole idea.

citations.text: Gary D. Schmidt, *The Iconography of the Mouth of Hell* (1995).
George Henderson, *Early Medieval* (1972); and Barbara Raw, *Anglo-Saxon Crucifixion Iconography* (1990).

title: Hell (Hans Memling, wing of the Last Judgment Triptych)
work: The Hellmouth: The Jaws of Damnation
creator: Hans Memling
summary:
The Hell wing of Hans Memling's great *Last Judgment Triptych* (c. 1467–1471), now in Gdańsk — the right-hand panel into which the damned tumble from Saint Michael's scales at the centre.

## Iconography
Naked sinners cascade down a dark, fiery slope, clawed and goaded by leathery, insectile devils into a smoking abyss; their faces are contorted in despair as the flames rise to meet them. There is no architectural [[motif:hellmouth|hellmouth]] here — the whole burning gulf is the maw — and the falling, entangled bodies dramatise the helpless plunge into perdition.

## Significance
Memling's triptych, painted in Bruges for an Italian patron and famously seized by privateers en route to Florence, brought the Netherlandish judgment to a new pitch of psychological realism. Its Hell descends from the [[motif:hellmouth|jaws-of-hell]] tradition but reconceives damnation as a vertiginous fall, anticipating the infernos of Bosch. Dirk De Vos's catalogue treats it as a landmark of early Netherlandish painting.

## For artists & game designers
Replacing a discrete "hell gate" with a continuous downward plunge of bodies turns damnation into pure motion and gravity — the fall itself is the punishment.

citations.text: Dirk De Vos, *Hans Memling: The Complete Works* (1994).
Barbara Lane, *Hans Memling: Master Painter in Fifteenth-Century Bruges* (2009).

title: The Portal of the Last Judgment (Notre-Dame de Paris)
work: The Hellmouth: The Jaws of Damnation
creator: Anonymous (Gothic sculptors; 19th-c. Viollet-le-Duc restoration)
repository: Notre-Dame de Paris (in situ, west façade central portal)
rights: CC BY 2.0 (Jorge Láscar). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
The west front of Notre-Dame de Paris, centred on the Portal of the Last Judgment (c. 1220–1230, heavily restored by Viollet-le-Duc), where Saint Michael weighs souls and devils chain the damned toward hell.

## Iconography
On the central tympanum the dead rise at the trumpet; in the middle register Saint Michael holds the scales while a demon tugs at them, and a file of the naked damned, roped and chained at the neck, is led by grinning devils away from the elect toward the [[motif:hellmouth|jaws of hell]]. Christ the Judge presides above, displaying his wounds.

## Significance
The Paris portal is the model Gothic Last Judgment, copied across northern France and beyond; the chained procession of the damned and the contested weighing became standard. Though much of the present sculpture is nineteenth-century restoration, it preserves the medieval programme that made the cathedral door a daily *memento* of judgment, analysed by Adolf Katzenellenbogen and Willibald Sauerländer.

## For artists & game designers
The roped column of the damned — bodies linked neck-to-neck and dragged by devils — is a compact way to show captivity and loss of agency without a single word.

citations.text: Adolf Katzenellenbogen, *The Sculptural Programs of Chartres Cathedral* (1959).
Willibald Sauerländer, *Gothic Sculpture in France 1140–1270* (1972).

title: The Salisbury Doom (St Thomas's Church)
work: The Hellmouth: The Jaws of Damnation
creator: Anonymous (English parish painter)
repository: Church of St Thomas and St Edmund, Salisbury (in situ)
rights: CC BY-SA 2.0 (Michael Garlick / Geograph). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
The *Salisbury Doom* over the chancel arch of St Thomas's Church, Salisbury — the largest and most complete medieval Last Judgment wall painting surviving in England, executed about 1470–1500 and recovered from whitewash in 1881.

## Iconography
Christ sits enthroned on a rainbow at the apex, displaying his wounds, flanked by the Virgin and apostles. Below, the dead rise from their graves; to the right the damned — including a crowned king, a bishop, a miser with his money-bags, and an alewife — are driven by devils into a fiery [[motif:hellmouth|hellmouth]], while on the left the saved climb toward the heavenly city.

## Significance
The Salisbury Doom is the benchmark survival of the genre that once dominated the English parish church, its inclusion of the dishonest alewife and worldly clergy giving the universal judgment a pointed social satire. Like Wenhaston it escaped destruction only by being limewashed at the Reformation. It is a cornerstone of the study of English medieval Dooms by Rosewell and the late-medieval church surveys.

## For artists & game designers
Naming the damned by trade — the crooked alewife, the hoarding miser — turns an abstract hell into pointed satire the audience recognises from daily life.

citations.text: Roger Rosewell, *Medieval Wall Paintings in English and Welsh Churches* (2008).
Anne Marshall, *Medieval Wall Painting in the English Parish Church* (online corpus).

title: The Last Judgment (Torcello Cathedral, detail)
work: The Hellmouth: The Jaws of Damnation
creator: Anonymous (Veneto-Byzantine mosaicists)
repository: Cathedral of Santa Maria Assunta, Torcello (in situ)
summary:
A detail of the monumental *Last Judgment* mosaic covering the west wall of the Cathedral of Santa Maria Assunta on Torcello in the Venetian Lagoon (twelfth century), one of the grandest Byzantine-influenced Judgments in Italy.

## Iconography
The great mosaic is ordered in registers from Christ's Anastasis at the top to Hell at the bottom. In the infernal zone shown here, a river of fire pours from Christ's throne into a realm where a blue-black Satan enthroned cradles the Antichrist, and the damned are sorted into compartments of torment — skulls, worms, flames and devils — each labelled for a category of the lost.

## Significance
The Torcello Judgment transmits the fully developed Byzantine schema — fiery river, compartmented hell, enthroned Satan with Antichrist — into the medieval West, a sister to the [[motif:hellmouth|hellmouths]] of the Latin tradition. Its register-by-register clarity made it a model image of cosmic justice; Otto Demus's studies of Venetian and Byzantine mosaic treat it as a key monument.

## For artists & game designers
A vertical cascade — heaven at the top, a river of fire pouring down into compartmented torments below — is a clean way to map an entire moral cosmos onto a single wall.

citations.text: Otto Demus, *Byzantine Art and the West* (1970).
Irina Andreescu, *Torcello* studies in *Dumbarton Oaks Papers* (1972–76).

title: Hell (Très Riches Heures du Duc de Berry, f.108r)
work: The Hellmouth: The Jaws of Damnation
creator: Limbourg brothers
summary:
The full-page *Enfer* (Hell) from the *Très Riches Heures du Duc de Berry*, painted by the Limbourg brothers c. 1411–1416 — among the supreme images of the medieval inferno.

## Iconography
A colossal Satan lies stretched on a flaming iron grill, crushing the damned in his fists and devouring others; from his mouth and the maw of Hell a great jet of fire and screaming souls is blasted upward, pumped by devils working enormous bellows at either side. The whole composition is a furnace of which Leviathan-Satan is both fuel and fire.

## Significance
The Limbourgs fuse the [[motif:hellmouth|hellmouth]] with the recumbent giant Satan of Job's Leviathan, drawing too on the visionary *Tundale's Vision* in which Lucifer lies bound on a grate. The bellows-stoked fire turns hell into an industrial torment, anticipating later furnace-imagery. It is the most reproduced single page of the most famous of all Books of Hours, central to Millard Meiss's study of the Limbourgs.

## For artists & game designers
A giant villain who is literally the engine of the place — bellows pumping his fire — collapses boss and environment into one, a striking way to make a level feel alive and hostile.

citations.text: Millard Meiss, *French Painting in the Time of Jean de Berry: The Limbourgs and Their Contemporaries* (1974).
Raymond Cazelles & Johannes Rathofer, *Illuminations of Heaven and Earth: The Glories of the Très Riches Heures* (1988).

title: The Wenhaston Doom (St Peter's Church, Suffolk)
work: The Hellmouth: The Jaws of Damnation
creator: Anonymous (English parish painter)
rights: CC BY-SA 2.0 (Michael Garlick / Geograph). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
The *Wenhaston Doom*, a rare survival of an English parish-church Last Judgment painted on boards around 1500 for the chancel arch of St Peter's, Wenhaston in Suffolk — preserved because whitewash at the Reformation hid, and later peeled to reveal, the image.

## Iconography
Christ sits in judgment on a rainbow above the rood; Saint Michael weighs naked souls in his scales while a devil tries to drag the pan down. The saved process toward Saint Peter at the gate of Heaven; the damned are herded by demons into a [[motif:hellmouth|hellmouth]] — a great toothed maw belching fire at the painting's edge.

## Significance
England's medieval churches were once filled with such Dooms over the chancel arch, confronting every worshipper with judgment; almost all were destroyed at the Reformation, making Wenhaston, Salisbury and a handful of others precious survivals. The blank silhouettes of the rood figures, lost when the cross was removed, are themselves a record of iconoclasm, as E. W. Tristram's surveys of English wall painting record.

## For artists & game designers
A folk-art Doom — flat, bold, almost cartoonish — shows that the hellmouth reads instantly even without sophistication; clarity of silhouette beats refinement.

citations.text: E. W. Tristram, *English Wall Painting of the Fourteenth Century* (1955); and English medieval Doom surveys.
Roger Rosewell, *Medieval Wall Paintings in English and Welsh Churches* (2008).

title: An Angel Locks the Mouth of Hell (Winchester Psalter)
work: The Hellmouth: The Jaws of Damnation
creator: Anonymous (English illuminator)
shelfmark: Cotton MS Nero C IV, fol. 39r
summary:
The most celebrated of all hellmouths: the full-page miniature from the *Winchester Psalter* (or Psalter of Henry of Blois), c. 1150, in which an angel turns a great key in the lock of Hell's jaws to seal the damned within forever.

## Iconography
A double-headed monster's maw, set with fangs, fills the page; within its throat the damned — among them crowned and tonsured figures, kings and clergy — writhe in tangled torment among grinning devils. Across the locked jaws an angel inserts an enormous key, fixing the door of perdition shut. The inscription names the scene as the closing of the gates of the underworld.

## Significance
The [[motif:hellmouth|hellmouth]] gives visual form to the Leviathan of Job 41, whose jaws no man can open, fused with the apocryphal harrowing of hell. The Winchester miniature is the type-image of the genre, frequently reproduced in studies of medieval eschatology; the locking angel insists that damnation is irrevocable — once the key turns, there is no return. Gary Schmidt and Pamela Sheingorn trace the motif from Anglo-Saxon art through this manuscript into the mystery plays.

## For artists & game designers
A single locking gesture across a monster's jaws converts a passive horror into a sealed, final state — the visual grammar of a point of no return.

citations.text: Gary D. Schmidt, *The Iconography of the Mouth of Hell* (1995).
Kristine Edmondson Haney, *The Winchester Psalter: An Iconographic Study* (1986).

title: The Harrowing of Hell (Winchester Psalter, f.39)
work: The Hellmouth: The Jaws of Damnation
creator: Anonymous (English illuminator)
shelfmark: Cotton MS Nero C IV, fol. 39
summary:
A second hellmouth from the *Winchester Psalter* (c. 1150), here showing the Harrowing of Hell: the risen Christ stands at the broken jaws of the underworld to draw the righteous out of its throat.

## Iconography
The great fanged maw gapes open, but now Christ — cross-staff in hand — reaches into the dark gullet to grasp the wrists of Adam, Eve and the patriarchs, hauling them from among the swallowed dead. Devils recoil; the previously locked jaws are forced. The composition pairs directly with the *locked* hellmouth elsewhere in the manuscript.

## Significance
The *Descensus ad inferos*, derived from the apocryphal Gospel of Nicodemus, recasts the [[motif:hellmouth|hellmouth]] as a prison Christ shatters between Crucifixion and Resurrection. Setting the rescue at the same monstrous jaws that elsewhere lock the damned dramatises salvation as the reversal of damnation. The motif is a cornerstone of medieval Easter imagery and of the mystery-play "Harrowing," as studied by Sheingorn and Karl Young.

## For artists & game designers
Reusing the same monster-jaws asset for both "sealed prison" and "breached gate" lets one location carry an entire arc of doom and rescue.

citations.text: Pamela Sheingorn, *The Easter Sepulchre in England* (1987).
Gary D. Schmidt, *The Iconography of the Mouth of Hell* (1995).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Apis, the sacred Egyptian bull (Musgrave engraving)
work: Egyptosophy — The Hermetic & Baroque Reception of Egyptian Wisdom
creator: William Musgrave (antiquarian engraving)
summary:
An antiquarian engraving of Apis, the sacred bull of Memphis, from the work of the English scholar William Musgrave — a specimen of the early-modern study of Egyptian animal-gods.

## Iconography
[[motif:apis bull|Apis]] is shown as a striding bull bearing the solar disc between his horns, the distinctive markings by which the living bull-god was identified by the priests of Memphis.

## Significance
Apis, linked in death to Osiris and later assimilated to the Hellenistic god Serapis, exemplified the Egyptian animal worship that fascinated and puzzled European antiquarians. Renaissance and Baroque scholars folded such cults into their Hermetic reading of Egypt as a land of veiled theological symbols, while classical authors had already debated whether the beast-gods were idolatry or allegory.

## For artists & game designers
A sacred-beast emblem: a marked bull crowned with a sun-disc, ready as a cult-animal icon or temple guardian.

A woodcut of a monumental Egyptianising structure from the *Hypnerotomachia Poliphili* (Venice, Aldus Manutius, 1499), the dream-romance whose hero wanders a landscape of antique marvels.

## Iconography
The image presents a towering ancient monument — part of the book's parade of obelisks, hieroglyph-bearing pylons, and fantastic architecture — drawn in the spare elegant line of the celebrated Aldine woodcuts. [[motif:hieroglyphs|Hieroglyphic]] devices appear as enigmatic captions to be decoded by the dreamer Polifilo.

## Significance
The *Hypnerotomachia* fused humanist antiquarianism with invented hieroglyphs, popularising the idea that Egyptian signs were a silent language of pure image. Its woodcuts — including the famous obelisk borne by an elephant — became a touchstone for Renaissance design and for the obelisk's later career as an esoteric monument, a lineage examined by Anthony Grafton and Liane Lefaivre.

## For artists & game designers
A model for dreamlike ruin-exploration: monumental architecture inscribed with riddles the player must read to progress.

title: Artemis of Ephesus (the 'many-breasted' goddess) — read as Isis-Nature
work: Egyptosophy — The Hermetic & Baroque Reception of Egyptian Wisdom

summary:
A statue of the 'many-breasted' Artemis of Ephesus, the type that Renaissance and Baroque writers fused with Isis to personify veiled Nature.

## Iconography
The goddess stands rigid and frontal, her lower body a tapering sheath of animal registers, her chest covered with the rows of bulbous protuberances (variously read as breasts, eggs, or bull-testes) that gave her the epithet *multimammia*.

## Significance
Humanist mythographers identified this composite Great Mother with [[motif:isis-nature|Isis]] as *Natura* — the nourishing, many-breasted World-Soul whose face is veiled. The image became the standard allegory of Nature on Baroque frontispieces (including Kircher's), embodying the Hermetic conviction, traced by Pierre Hadot in *The Veil of Isis*, that Egyptian Isis personified the hidden order of the cosmos.

## For artists & game designers
A 'Nature incarnate' deity design: a frontal, hieratic mother-goddess sheathed in animals and overflowing with breasts — fecundity made monstrous and sacred.

title: Frontispiece to Kircher's *Mundus Subterraneus* (Theodor Matham)
work: Egyptosophy — The Hermetic & Baroque Reception of Egyptian Wisdom
creator: Theodor Matham (engraver), after Athanasius Kircher
summary:
The engraved frontispiece, by Theodor Matham, to Athanasius Kircher's *Mundus Subterraneus* (Amsterdam, 1665), his cosmography of the hidden world beneath the earth.

## Iconography
An allegorical title page descends from a radiant divine source through the heavens to the fiery interior of the globe, personifying the chain of causes that animates the subterranean realm. Figures of Nature and Providence mediate the influx of [[motif:divine light|divine light]] into matter.

## Significance
Though not strictly an Egyptological book, *Mundus Subterraneus* belongs to the same Hermetic-Jesuit vision: a cosmos bound by hidden correspondences and sympathetic forces, the natural-philosophical counterpart to Kircher's Egyptian theology of secret meanings. It is a key text in the history of geology, volcanology, and Baroque natural magic.

## For artists & game designers
A vertical 'as above, so below' splash image: heaven, earth's surface, and a molten underworld linked by a single shaft of light.

citations.text: Joscelyn Godwin, *Athanasius Kircher's Theatre of the World* (2009).

title: Hieroglyphic obelisk plate from Kircher's *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*
work: Egyptosophy — The Hermetic & Baroque Reception of Egyptian Wisdom
creator: Athanasius Kircher
summary:
An engraved plate from the third volume of Kircher's *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*, presenting an obelisk shaft covered in hieroglyphs alongside his 'reading' of them.

## Iconography
A tall obelisk face is rendered glyph by glyph, each [[motif:hieroglyphs|hieroglyphic]] register paired with Kircher's allegorical Latin gloss. The plate belongs to his project of recovering the *prisca aegyptiorum sapientia* — the 'ancient wisdom of the Egyptians'.

## Significance
Kircher treated each sign as an ideogram encoding a whole theological proposition, producing elaborate sentences from a handful of figures. Champollion's later decipherment showed the hieroglyphs to be a mixed phonetic-logographic script, but Kircher's engravings remain the visual emblem of the Hermetic dream that Egypt held a primordial revelation.

## For artists & game designers
A reusable 'annotated monument' layout: a carved column flanked by a scholar's confident, sprawling translation — instant arcane exposition.

title: Kircher's *Sphinx Mystagoga* (1676)
work: Egyptosophy — The Hermetic & Baroque Reception of Egyptian Wisdom
creator: Athanasius Kircher
summary:
A plate from Athanasius Kircher's late work *Sphinx Mystagoga* (1676), in which the Egyptian Sphinx is cast as the 'leader into the mysteries' (*mystagogos*).

## Iconography
The engraving displays Egyptian funerary material — mummies, sarcophagi, and inscriptions — framed by the title's promise that the [[motif:sphinx|Sphinx]] will conduct the reader into hidden truth. The plate gathers reports of mummies and tombs into Kircher's enduring symbolic-theological scheme.

## Significance
*Sphinx Mystagoga* extended Kircher's Egyptological programme to mummification and the afterlife, treating the riddling Sphinx as guardian of an initiatory wisdom. Though his decipherments were illusory, his framing of Egypt as a land of [[motif:initiation|sacred mysteries]] shaped the esoteric imagination from the Enlightenment through the modern occult revival.

## For artists & game designers
A tomb-crawl frontispiece: a Sphinx-warded chamber of mummies presented as the threshold to secret knowledge.

work: Egyptosophy — The Hermetic & Baroque Reception of Egyptian Wisdom

An eighteenth-century view of the Piazza San Giovanni in Laterano, dominated by the Lateran Obelisk — the tallest standing Egyptian obelisk in the world.

## Iconography
The veduta shows the colossal [[motif:obelisk|obelisk]], originally of Thutmose III/IV from Karnak, towering before the basilica where Domenico Fontana re-erected it for Pope Sixtus V in 1588, surmounted by a cross.

## Significance
Sixtus V's campaign of raising Rome's fallen obelisks topped each with a cross or papal emblem, recasting the pagan solar pillars as trophies of the triumphant Church. The engineering feat of moving them, narrated in Fontana's own treatise, made the obelisk an emblem of both Egyptian antiquity and Counter-Reformation power, as discussed by Erik Iversen.

## For artists & game designers
A cathedral-square landmark: an ancient foreign monolith repurposed and crowned with the conqueror's holy symbol.

title: The Mensa Isiaca (Bembine Tablet of Isis), Museo Egizio, Turin
work: Egyptosophy — The Hermetic & Baroque Reception of Egyptian Wisdom
creator: Anonymous (Roman workshop, Egyptianising style)
summary:
The *Mensa Isiaca* — the celebrated 'Bembine Tablet of Isis', a large bronze altar-table inlaid with silver and niello, the single most influential object in the early-modern misreading of Egypt.

## Iconography
A central shrine frames an enthroned [[motif:isis enthroned|Isis]] surrounded by registers of Egyptian and Egyptianising deities, processions, and bands of pseudo-hieroglyphic signs. Though Roman work of the imperial Isiac cult, its glyphs are largely decorative imitations rather than legible Egyptian script.

## Significance
Named for Cardinal Pietro Bembo, who owned it in the sixteenth century, the tablet was read by Renaissance scholars as a key to Egyptian theology. [[motif:hermes trismegistus|Athanasius Kircher]] devoted much of his *Oedipus Aegyptiacus* to 'translating' its imaginary inscriptions, an enterprise wholly overturned once Champollion deciphered the real hieroglyphs in 1822, exposing it as Roman pastiche.

## For artists & game designers
A master 'mysterious tablet' prop: a metal slab crowded with gods and undecipherable signs that any scholar-NPC will confidently — and wrongly — claim to read.

title: Plate from Kircher's *Obeliscus Pamphilius* (the Pamphilj obelisk)
work: Egyptosophy — The Hermetic & Baroque Reception of Egyptian Wisdom
creator: Athanasius Kircher
summary:
A page (444) from Athanasius Kircher's *Obeliscus Pamphilius* (Rome, 1650), his study of the obelisk Pope Innocent X raised over Bernini's Fountain of the Four Rivers in Piazza Navona.

## Iconography
The plate reproduces the obelisk's [[motif:hieroglyphs|hieroglyphic]] faces with Kircher's interpretive apparatus. The book served as a learned prelude to the still grander *Oedipus Aegyptiacus* two years later.

## Significance
The Pamphilj obelisk is a Roman-made monument in the Egyptian manner; Kircher nonetheless 'translated' its glyphs as a Hermetic-theological message, lending Baroque papal Rome the prestige of Egyptian antiquity. The episode is central to accounts of how the Counter-Reformation papacy appropriated [[motif:obelisk|obelisks]] as Christianised solar monuments.

## For artists & game designers
A case study in monument-as-propaganda: a ruler crowns a public fountain with an ancient pillar and commissions a scholar to declare it prophesies his reign.

citations.text: Brian Curran et al., *Obelisk: A History* (2009).

Gian Lorenzo Bernini's *Fontana dei Quattro Fiumi* (1648–51) in Piazza Navona, crowned by the Pamphilj obelisk that Athanasius Kircher 'deciphered'.

## Iconography
Four river-gods of the personified continents recline around a rocky base from which rises the slender [[motif:obelisk|obelisk]], its faces carved with [[motif:hieroglyphs|hieroglyphs]]. A dove — emblem of the Pamphilj pope Innocent X — alights at the summit, Christianising the ancient solar shaft.

## Significance
The ensemble is the supreme statement of Baroque papal Egyptomania: a Roman-made obelisk re-erected as a monument to universal Christian dominion, its glyphs glossed by Kircher in the *Obeliscus Pamphilius*. The fusion of Egyptian form and papal triumph is a central episode in Brian Curran's history of the obelisk.

A grand civic set-piece: a watery plaza dominated by an ancient pillar that a regime has rebranded as a sign of its own destiny.

title: The Flaminio Obelisk, Piazza del Popolo, Rome
work: Egyptosophy — The Hermetic & Baroque Reception of Egyptian Wisdom
creator: Photograph by Dudva (monument: ancient Egyptian, re-erected 1589)
summary:
The Flaminio Obelisk in the Piazza del Popolo, one of the ancient Egyptian obelisks re-erected in Rome under Pope Sixtus V.

## Iconography
The tall red-granite shaft, carved on all faces with [[motif:hieroglyphs|hieroglyphs]] of Seti I and Ramesses II, rises from a fountain base at the centre of the great oval piazza, a cross at its apex.

## Significance
Brought to Rome by Augustus for the Circus Maximus and raised again in 1589 by Domenico Fontana, the [[motif:obelisk|obelisk]] is part of Sixtus V's urban programme that turned Rome's scattered Egyptian monuments into a network of Christianised landmarks. Such obelisks fed the Hermetic-antiquarian fascination with Egypt that Kircher would systematise.

A city-planning beacon: an ancient inscribed needle set as the focal point of a radiating public square.

title: Frontispiece to Kircher's *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*
work: Egyptosophy — The Hermetic & Baroque Reception of Egyptian Wisdom
creator: Athanasius Kircher (author)
summary:
The frontispiece to Athanasius Kircher's vast *Oedipus Aegyptiacus* (Rome, 1652–54), the Jesuit polymath's attempt to restore the 'lost' wisdom of the hieroglyphs.

## Iconography
The Baroque title page massess Egyptian emblems — sphinxes, obelisks, and ranks of [[motif:hieroglyphs|hieroglyphic signs]] — around the title, casting Kircher as the new Oedipus who will solve the riddle of the Egyptian Sphinx.

## Significance
Kircher believed the hieroglyphs were a symbolic theology concealing Hermetic and Neoplatonic truths handed down from [[motif:hermes trismegistus|Hermes Trismegistus]]. His 'translations' were entirely fanciful, yet the *Oedipus* became the encyclopedic monument of seventeenth-century Egyptomania and a cornerstone of the *prisca theologia* idea later studied by Frances Yates and Erik Iversen.

## For artists & game designers
A definitive 'tome of forbidden Egyptian lore' cover: dense, authoritative, and confidently mistaken — perfect set dressing for a scholar's study.

creator: Hubert Robert

Hubert Robert's painted view of the Pyramid of Cestius in Rome, the Augustan-age tomb-pyramid that kept the Egyptian form alive in the heart of the city.

## Iconography
The steep marble-faced [[motif:pyramid of cestius|pyramid]] rises amid the picturesque ruins and figures characteristic of Robert, nicknamed 'Robert des Ruines'. The Egyptian silhouette stands incongruous and arresting against the Roman setting.

## Significance
Built around 12 BCE as the tomb of Gaius Cestius, the pyramid testified to Rome's own first wave of Egyptomania under Augustus and later became a magnet for Grand Tour antiquarians and the Romantic cult of ruins. Its enduring presence helped sustain the Western fascination with Egypt as the land of death-mysteries and hidden wisdom.

title: The Pyramids and Sphinx of Memphis at Sunset (engraving)
work: Egyptosophy — The Hermetic & Baroque Reception of Egyptian Wisdom
creator: Imprimerie impériale (after the *Description de l'Égypte*)
summary:
A general view of the pyramids of Memphis and the Great Sphinx at sunset, from the great French survey tradition that closed the era of Egyptosophy and opened scientific Egyptology.

## Iconography
The panoramic engraving sets the [[motif:sphinx|Great Sphinx]] and the pyramids of Giza against a low sun, emphasising scale and desolation in the picturesque manner of the *Description de l'Égypte*.

## Significance
Napoleon's 1798 expedition and its monumental *Description de l'Égypte* produced precise surveys that transformed Europe's image of Egypt from a realm of Hermetic riddles into an object of empirical study — even as the Sphinx and pyramids remained potent symbols of secret wisdom for the nineteenth-century occult revival. The shift from Kircher's fantasy to Champollion's decipherment runs straight through this corpus.

## For artists & game designers
A wide establishing shot for an Egyptian setting: monumental, sun-baked, and freighted with the promise of buried secrets.

title: *Tabula Smaragdina* (Emerald Tablet) — Theosophie & Alchemie engraving
work: Egyptosophy — The Hermetic & Baroque Reception of Egyptian Wisdom
creator: Anonymous (early-modern engraving)
summary:
An early-modern emblematic engraving of the *Tabula Smaragdina* — the Emerald Tablet — the terse alchemical axiom-text ascribed to Hermes Trismegistus and imagined as Egyptian-Hermetic revelation (Deutsche Fotothek).

## Iconography
The plate presents the tablet's sentences within an emblematic frame of theosophical and alchemical figures, expounding the maxim that 'that which is above is as that which is below'. The composition treats [[motif:hermes trismegistus|Hermes]]'s words as the foundation of the whole work of transmutation.

## Significance
Though the Emerald Tablet's earliest texts are medieval Arabic, the European tradition received it as the most ancient utterance of Egyptian Hermes, the compressed creed of [[motif:as above so below|correspondence]] between macrocosm and microcosm. Its history was untangled by Julius Ruska, who showed how thoroughly it was woven into the Hermetic myth of Egypt.

## For artists & game designers
A single 'law of the world' artifact-card: a tablet of axioms ringed by emblems, studied to unlock the correspondence mechanics of an alchemy system.

title: Thoth, the ibis-headed god (handbook engraving)
work: Egyptosophy — The Hermetic & Baroque Reception of Egyptian Wisdom
creator: Anonymous (engraving from a 19th-c. handbook of archaeology)
summary:
An engraving of Thoth, the ibis-headed Egyptian god of writing and wisdom, from a nineteenth-century handbook of archaeology — the deity the Greeks equated with Hermes.

## Iconography
[[motif:thoth|Thoth]] appears with the head of an ibis (sometimes a baboon), often bearing a scribe's palette or recording the verdict at the weighing of the heart. The engraving renders him in the conventionalised profile of Egyptian relief.

## Significance
As scribe of the gods and master of sacred letters, Thoth was identified by the Greeks with Hermes, and the compound figure of [[motif:hermes trismegistus|Hermes Trismegistus]] — 'thrice-great' — fused the two into the legendary author of the Hermetica. The whole Egyptosophical tradition, from Ficino to Kircher, traced its 'ancient theology' back to this god of hidden knowledge, as set out by Garth Fowden.

## For artists & game designers
A clean reference for a 'god of knowledge' design: animal-headed scribe with palette and stylus, patron of writing and magic.

title: Pierio Valeriano, *Hieroglyphica* (1556) — page of Egyptian symbols
work: Egyptosophy — The Hermetic & Baroque Reception of Egyptian Wisdom
creator: Giovanni Pierio Valeriano Bolzani
summary:
A page from Pierio Valeriano's *Hieroglyphica, sive De sacris Aegyptiorum literis commentarii* (1556), the great Renaissance dictionary of symbolic meanings 'on the sacred letters of the Egyptians'.

## Iconography
The book pairs woodcut images of animals, plants, and objects with learned commentary on their allegorical sense, treating each as a [[motif:hieroglyphs|hieroglyphic]] sign whose hidden meaning the humanist scholar must unfold.

## Significance
Building on the rediscovered *Hieroglyphica* of Horapollo, Valeriano's vast compendium reconceived Egyptian writing as a universal symbolic language and supplied a quarry of motifs for emblem books, imprese, and Baroque iconography. It is a foundational text of the Renaissance conviction, traced by E. H. Gombrich and Erik Iversen, that hieroglyphs were pictures of timeless ideas.

## For artists & game designers
A ready-made symbol-lexicon: each entry is an icon plus its 'true meaning', ideal for a puzzle system where creatures and objects spell out hidden messages.

title: The Vatican Obelisk before St Peter's Basilica
work: Egyptosophy — The Hermetic & Baroque Reception of Egyptian Wisdom
creator: Anonymous (monument re-erected by Domenico Fontana, 1586)

The Vatican Obelisk standing at the centre of St Peter's Square, the obelisk whose dramatic re-erection in 1586 inaugurated Sixtus V's obelisk campaign.

The smooth red-granite [[motif:obelisk|shaft]] — uniquely among Rome's great obelisks, uninscribed with [[motif:hieroglyphs|hieroglyphs]] — rises from a base of bronze lions and is topped by a cross said to enclose a relic of the True Cross.

Domenico Fontana's feat of transporting and raising the 300-tonne monolith for Pope Sixtus V was celebrated across Europe and recorded in his own illustrated treatise. Placed before the new basilica, the pagan Egyptian pillar was exorcised and consecrated, becoming the prototype for the Christianisation of Rome's obelisks and a spur to Hermetic-Egyptian antiquarianism.

title: Hildegard of Bingen — Scivias, First Illumination (c. 1150)
summary: The first illuminated miniature from Hildegard of Bingen's Liber Scivias Domini (c. 1150), the opening image of the foundational illustrated visionary manuscript. Hildegard composed Scivias (Know the Ways of the Lord) between 1141 and 1151 at the Disibodenberg monastery, dictating her visions to the monk Volmar and her nun Richardis von Stade. The Rupertsberg Codex — for which these illuminations were likely made under Hildegard's personal direction — was evacuated to Dresden during World War II and is now lost; it is known through a 1927 hand-painted facsimile held at Eibingen Abbey.

title: Scivias, Codex Salisburgensis X,16 — Independent Manuscript Witness, c. 1150
summary: A page from the Scivias manuscript preserved in the Codex Salisburgensis (Salzburg Codex X,16), an independent manuscript witness to Hildegard's visions separate from the Rupertsberg Codex. The Salzburg codex provides important evidence for the early reception and transmission of Hildegard's visual program beyond Rupertsberg — showing that the illuminations were copied and circulated in the decades following composition. Held at the Salzburg Museum / Stiftsbibliothek Salzburg.

title: Hildegard of Bingen — Six Days of Creation, Scivias, c. 1152
summary: Illuminated manuscript painting depicting God's six days of creation of the world, from Hildegard of Bingen's Scivias tradition. Shows divine creation of Earth, Heaven, and Adam in characteristic 12th-century Romanesque style, with strong use of azure blues and gold. Hildegard's Genesis visions in Scivias Part I merge cosmogony with theology: the creation of light, the firmament, and the first human are simultaneous with the formation of the moral and spiritual order.

title: Hildegard of Bingen — 'True Trinity in True Unity', Scivias, c. 1165
medium: manuscript illumination (1927 facsimile of lost original)
summary: Illuminated page from the Scivias Codex depicting 'The True Trinity in True Unity' (Die wahre Dreiheit in der wahren Einheit) — a key Trinitarian vision from Scivias II.2. Hildegard depicts the Trinity through a series of concentric rings: a brilliant sapphire-blue center (the Son), a gold ring (the Father), and an enveloping fire (the Holy Spirit). This diagrammatic approach to Trinity theology — using concentric forms rather than figurative representation — is characteristic of her cosmological mode of vision. From the 1927 Eibingen facsimile via the Yorck Project.

title: Hildegard of Bingen — 'Das Weltall' (The Universe), Scivias, c. 1165
medium: manuscript illumination (1927 facsimile of lost original)
summary: The iconic 'Universe' illumination from the Hildegardis-Codex (Scivias), depicting the cosmos as a great egg-shaped form surrounded by flames and encompassing concentric rings of elements, seasons, and winds. This egg-shaped cosmological diagram corresponds to Scivias I.3 and represents one of Hildegard's most distinctive contributions to medieval cosmography — a vision of the universe as a living, structured whole governed by divine harmony. The original Rupertsberg Codex is lost; this reproduces the 1927 hand-painted facsimile (Eibingen Abbey). From the Yorck Project digitization.

title: *Hypnerotomachia Poliphili* (Aldus, 1499) — woodcut (leaf 4)
creator: Francesco Colonna (attrib.); printed by Aldus Manutius
rights: Public domain. 1499 Aldine edition via Internet Archive.
summary:
A woodcut from the *Hypnerotomachia Poliphili*, printed by Aldus Manutius at Venice in 1499 and traditionally attributed to Francesco Colonna, the supreme illustrated incunabulum of the Italian Renaissance. This leaf falls from the opening of Poliphilo's dream, where the lover loses himself in a dark wood and emerges among the first marvels of the visionary landscape.

## Iconography
At this point near the beginning of the dream, the woodcuts of the *Hypnerotomachia* render the visionary's first wanderings: the dark wood and the thirst that drives him on, the wellspring and the wild country, and the dawning architecture of an enchanted land. Hatching is sparing and the line is famously pure, leaving large fields of white incunabular page. (The catalogued plate is identified by its sequence within the 1499 edition rather than by a separately verified scene, so this entry characterises the woodcut type at this point in the narrative.)

## Significance
The opening sequence stages the descent into dream as a Neoplatonic *itinerarium* in which the soul, lost in the [[motif:dark wood|silva]] of the senses, sets out toward beauty. The 1499 cuts, anonymous but long admired, fuse Albertian architectural clarity with the erotic-initiatory frame that Francesco Colonna's text demands.

## For artists & game designers
The 1499 *Hypnerotomachia* woodcut style, pure outline, minimal hatching, antique architecture and ceremonious figures on open white ground, is an ideal reference for a dream-logic, hermetic-Renaissance visual register: temples, triumphs, hieroglyphic friezes and processions rendered as clean, almost diagrammatic line.

citations.text: Francesco Colonna (attrib.), *Hypnerotomachia Poliphili* (Venice: Aldus Manutius, 1499).
Joscelyn Godwin (trans.), *Hypnerotomachia Poliphili: The Strife of Love in a Dream* (Thames & Hudson, 1999).

A woodcut from the *Hypnerotomachia Poliphili*, printed by Aldus Manutius at Venice in 1499 and traditionally attributed to Francesco Colonna, the supreme illustrated incunabulum of the Italian Renaissance. This leaf falls among the great architectural marvels of Poliphilo's journey: the colossal portal, the pyramid-and-obelisk, the ruins and hieroglyphic friezes.

## Iconography
In this stretch the *Hypnerotomachia*'s celebrated architectural woodcuts dominate: a colossal gateway and triumphal portal, the stepped pyramid surmounted by an obelisk and bronze figure, broken classical ruins, inscribed tablets, and friezes of Egyptian-style hieroglyphs. The draughtsman renders entablature, moulding and perspective with the measured precision of a Renaissance architectural treatise. (The catalogued plate is identified by its sequence within the 1499 edition rather than by a separately verified scene, so this entry characterises the woodcut type at this point in the narrative.)

## Significance
These are among the most influential images in the book: their hieroglyphic frieze and antique architecture shaped Renaissance ideas of the [[motif:hieroglyph|hieroglyph]] as a silent, sacred picture-writing, feeding into Pierio Valeriano and later emblem theory. Architecture here is itself allegory, proportion, ruin and inscription read as a hermetic alphabet the dreamer must decipher.

## For artists & game designers
The 1499 *Hypnerotomachia* woodcut style, pure outline, minimal hatching, antique architecture and ceremonious figures on open white ground, is an ideal reference for a dream-logic, hermetic-Renaissance visual register: temples, triumphs, hieroglyphic friezes and processions rendered as clean, almost diagrammatic line.

This leaf falls within the palace and gardens of the dream: the court of Queen Eleuterylida, the allegorical fountains, the marvellous gardens of glass and silk.

## Iconography
The woodcuts of this region show the architecture and ceremony of the dream-court: colonnaded palaces, ornamental gardens (including the famed gardens of glass and of silk), allegorical fountains and statuary, and processions of attendant figures. Ornament is dense and antiquarian, with vases, candelabra, grotesques and inscribed bases. (The catalogued plate is identified by its sequence within the 1499 edition rather than by a separately verified scene, so this entry characterises the woodcut type at this point in the narrative.)

## Significance
The court of Queen Eleuterylida ('free will') and her marvels stage a moral-philosophical pageant in which the dreamer is offered choices and instructed in the meaning of the figures he meets. The passages model the Renaissance ideal of the garden as a designed allegory, and the cuts furnished motifs to generations of garden, festival and emblem designers.

summary:
A woodcut from the *Hypnerotomachia Poliphili*, printed by Aldus Manutius at Venice in 1499 and traditionally attributed to Francesco Colonna, the supreme illustrated incunabulum of the Italian Renaissance. This leaf falls among the Triumphs of Love and the temple rites: the processional triumphal cars, the temple of Venus, the sacrifices and nuptial ceremonies.

## Iconography
In this central sequence appear the *Hypnerotomachia*'s great triumphal woodcuts: processional cars (*trionfi*) drawn in classical pomp, the temple of Venus with its altar and priestess, and the rites of sacrifice and betrothal that unite Poliphilo and Polia. Crowds, garlands, musical instruments and antique trophies fill the friezes. (The catalogued plate is identified by its sequence within the 1499 edition rather than by a separately verified scene, so this entry characterises the woodcut type at this point in the narrative.)

## Significance
Modelled on Petrarch's *Trionfi* and on Roman triumphal imagery, these cars and ceremonies are the iconographic heart of the book and among the most copied of all Renaissance processional designs. The temple rites fuse pagan sacrifice with a Neoplatonic sacrament of love, the lovers consecrated before [[motif:venus|Venus]].

summary:

This leaf falls in Book II, where the nymph Polia narrates the lovers' history and the dream draws to its close.

## Iconography
The closing woodcuts accompany Book II, in which the nymph Polia tells the lovers' story from her side: her vow of chastity to Diana, the plague and its terrors, her conversion to Venus, and the dream's dissolution at dawn. The cuts are sparser here, marking key turns of the recollected tale. (The catalogued plate is identified by its sequence within the 1499 edition rather than by a separately verified scene, so this entry characterises the woodcut type at this point in the narrative.)

## Significance
Book II reframes the whole dream as a love-history told by Polia, supplying the human and devotional ground beneath the allegory, chastity surrendered to love, death and plague answered by Venus's mercy. The waking that ends the book returns the reader from vision to loss, the classic melancholy close of the Renaissance dream-poem.

title: Chapter Section with Letter-Sigil Symbol — Shams al-Ma'arif MS (p. 530)
rights: Public Domain — manuscript c. 1500 CE. Scan: Internet Archive.
summary: Page 530 of the c. 1500 CE Shams al-Ma'arif manuscript, showing a chapter section with a small angular letter-sigil or geometric symbol drawn in red ink. The section is titled 'Fi Huruf al-Saghir' (On the Small Letters) and falls within the chapters discussing the huruf al-khatim (seal letters) and their talismanic applications. Small geometric sigils — angular letter-configurations that represent the compressed essence of divine Names or planetary spirits — appear throughout the Shams al-Ma'arif as practical talisman templates. The red chapter headings visible on this page mark the transition between thematic sections on different aspects of the letter-science.

title: Magic Squares and Diamond-Lattice Geometric Diagram — Shams al-Ma'arif MS (p.200)
rights: Public Domain — manuscript c. 1500 CE. Scan: Internet Archive.
summary: A spectacular page from the Shams al-Ma'arif manuscript (c. 1500 CE) that juxtaposes two distinct diagrammatic modes: the upper and middle zones contain multiple standard magic square grids (awfaq), including a large letter-number grid, while the lower right features a pure geometric diamond-lattice pattern — a mashrabiyya-like grid of crossing diagonal lines forming interlocked diamond cells. The diamond-lattice form appears in al-Buni's system both as a structural variant of the standard square wafq (the 'rotated wafq') and as a purely geometric symbol of the mathematical order underpinning the letter-cosmological system. The coexistence of numerical and geometric modes on one page captures the double nature of Buniyan magic: precise numerical combinatorics in dialogue with the visual beauty of Islamic geometric art.

summary: A chapter-opening page from a manuscript of Ahmad al-Buni's Shams al-Ma'arif al-Kubra (c. 1500 CE), showing the characteristic format of luxury Buniyan manuscripts: Arabic text in black ink surrounded by a bold red rectangular frame, with the chapter title (bab) written in large red thuluth calligraphy inside a ruled red box that breaks the running text. This page illustrates how the Shams al-Ma'arif organizes its occult knowledge into discrete chapters, each a self-contained magical domain. The framed title box is itself a kind of khatim (seal) for the chapter.

title: Cosmological Circle Diagram Divided into Quadrants — Shams al-Ma'arif MS (p.420)
rights: Public Domain — manuscript c. 1500 CE. Scan: Internet Archive.
summary: A cosmological circle diagram from the Shams al-Ma'arif manuscript (c. 1500 CE), drawn in red ink inside a rectangular frame. The large circle is divided into four quadrants by a cross — the cardinal axes — with Arabic text inscribed in each sector, corresponding to the four elements, four humors, four winds, four cardinal directions, or four divine Names depending on the chapter's topic. The quadrant circle is one of al-Buni's most frequently deployed cosmological schemata: it maps the fourfold structure of creation (samawat wa ard, heavens and earth) onto the circular form of divine unity, making cosmological order visually legible. Similar diagrams appear in the parallel Lata'if al-Isharat manuscripts (Berlin Or. 80, BnF Ar. 2657) as the celestial-spheres diagram.

rights: Public Domain — manuscript c. 1500 CE. Scan: Internet Archive.
summary: A large star-khatim talisman diagram from the Shams al-Ma'arif manuscript (c. 1500 CE), drawn in red ink at the center of a full-page framed diagram. This complex letter-cosmological layering — where geometry, angelic hierarchy, elemental theory, and divine Name mysticism converge in a single visual form — is the hallmark of Buniyan lettrism. One of the most visually distinctive pages in the manuscript.

rights: Public Domain — manuscript c. 1500 CE. Scan: Internet Archive.
summary: Page 570 of the c. 1500 CE Shams al-Ma'arif manuscript, showing a numeric awfaq (magic square) table drawn in red ink. Numeric wafq in the Shams al-Ma'arif work by converting letter values (abjad) into numerals, arranging them so that every row, column, and diagonal sums to the same 'magic constant' (al-makhraj). The chapter heading above the table (Bab al-Asma' al-Akbar, 'Chapter on the Greatest Names') places this wafq in the context of the Divine Names and their numerical correspondences.

title: Ea/Enki flanked by fish-cloaked apkallu, basalt basin from Assur (Pergamon Museum)
creator: Anonymous (Neo-Assyrian); photograph by Osama Shukir Muhammed Amin
date: Neo-Assyrian, reign of Sennacherib (7th c. BCE)
rights: CC BY-SA 4.0 (photo: Osama Shukir Muhammed Amin). Pergamon Museum, via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A basalt water-basin from Assur carved with the god Ea/Enki flanked by fish-cloaked apkallu sages — the aquatic, purifying form of Mesopotamia's protective genii.

## Iconography
The central figure is **Ea (Sumerian Enki)**, god of the sweet waters and of wisdom and magic, identified by the streams flowing from his shoulders. He is flanked by **apkallu** wearing the whole skin of a great **fish** as a cloak, the fish-head rising above their own — the *purādu*-fish sages associated with the primordial sage Adapa/Oannes.

## Significance
The **fish-cloaked apkallu** are the bringers of civilization and the masters of purification and exorcism, who served Ea, the divine patron of incantation. Figurines of these beings were buried under floors to ward off evil, exactly as the [[motif:incantation-bowl|incantation bowls]] would later be. The basin, used in temple purification rites, ties the apotropaic sages to the cleansing power of water that runs through Mesopotamian magic. See Wiggermann (1992) and the *Bīt Rimki* ritual.

## For artists & game designers
The fish-cloak priest is a striking, under-used 'water-magic exorcist' design — half-man, half-fish, attendant on a god of the deep.

S. Parpola, 'The Assyrian Tree of Life,' *JNES* 52 (1993).

title: Assyrian winged genie, Palace of Ashurnasirpal II at Nimrud
creator: Anonymous (Neo-Assyrian); photograph by Gary Todd
rights: Public domain (CC0, photo: Gary Todd). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A Neo-Assyrian relief of a winged 'genie' (apkallu) from the Northwest Palace of Ashurnasirpal II at Nimrud, performing a rite of purification and protection.

## Iconography
The bearded, **winged** figure stands in profile holding a **cone** (a date-palm spathe) in one hand and a **bucket** (*banduddû*) in the other, the implements of a purifying, fertilizing aspersion. He wears a horned cap marking divine or semi-divine status. These are the **apkallu** — protective sages or genii.

## Significance
The **apkallu** were the antediluvian sages of Mesopotamian lore, guardians of secret wisdom who carried out apotropaic and purificatory rites. Lined along palace walls and buried as figurines under thresholds, they protected the king and the building from demons and disease. They embody the *benign* pole of the same protective magic whose hostile targets are the demons trapped in the [[motif:incantation-bowl|incantation bowls]]. Wiggermann's *Mesopotamian Protective Spirits* (1992) is the key study.

## For artists & game designers
The quintessential 'guardian sage' figure — winged, ritually equipped, lining the walls as a permanent protective garrison.

citations.text: F. A. M. Wiggermann, *Mesopotamian Protective Spirits: The Ritual Texts* (1992).
J. E. Reade, *Assyrian Sculpture* (1983).

title: Incantation bowl with pseudo-Aramaic inscription (Metropolitan Museum)
creator: Anonymous (Sasanian Mesopotamia)
rights: Public domain (CC0). The Metropolitan Museum of Art, via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A terracotta incantation bowl in the Metropolitan Museum whose interior is filled with a spiral of pseudo-Aramaic writing, a clay 'demon-trap' buried beneath the floor of a Mesopotamian home.

## Iconography
The shallow earthenware bowl is inscribed on its concave inner surface with lines of script running in a **spiral** from rim to centre. Here the characters imitate Aramaic without forming a fully legible text — a *pseudo-inscription* produced by or for an illiterate client, showing that the bowl's form and the act of spiralling words were themselves felt to be efficacious.

## Significance
Mesopotamian incantation bowls (5th–7th c. CE) were inverted and set into the corners and thresholds of houses to **bind and trap** demons, the [[motif:evil-eye|evil eye]], curses, and the night-hag Lilith. The spell typically names the client, invokes divine and angelic authority, and 'seals' the demon — a domestic descendant of the older Akkadian exorcistic tradition. The standard corpus is J. A. Montgomery's *Aramaic Incantation Texts from Nippur* (1913), with later editions by Shaked, Ford and Bhayro.

## For artists & game designers
A buried bowl whose written spell only 'works' as a spiral is a perfect environmental trap object — the magic is in the geometry as much as the words.

citations.text: J. A. Montgomery, *Aramaic Incantation Texts from Nippur* (1913).
S. Shaked, J. N. Ford & S. Bhayro, *Aramaic Bowl Spells* (2013).

title: The Burney Relief / Queen of the Night (British Museum)
creator: Anonymous (Old Babylonian); photograph by Osama Shukir Muhammed Amin
rights: CC BY-SA 4.0 (photo: Osama Shukir Muhammed Amin). The British Museum, via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
The Burney Relief, also called the 'Queen of the Night' — an Old Babylonian terracotta plaque of a winged, bird-taloned goddess long debated as Ishtar, Ereshkigal, or a Lilith-figure.

## Iconography
A nude **winged** female stands frontally on the backs of two **lions**, flanked by **owls**, her feet ending in bird **talons**. She holds the **rod-and-ring** symbols of divine authority and wears the horned crown of a deity. The talons and owls give her a nocturnal, chthonic character.

## Significance
The identity of the figure is contested: she has been read as **Ishtar/Inanna**, as her underworld sister **Ereshkigal**, or — in older and popular literature — as a *lilītu* (Lilith-type) night-demon, a reading now largely doubted by specialists. Whatever her name, the relief stands at the source of the imagery of dangerous winged female night-powers that flows down to the **Lilith** of the later [[motif:incantation-bowl|incantation bowls]]. I keep the identification open, following the British Museum and Frankfort's classic discussion.

## For artists & game designers
The definitive 'winged night-goddess' silhouette — talons, owls, lions — endlessly reusable for an ambiguous deity who is neither wholly good nor wholly demonic.

citations.text: H. Frankfort, 'The Burney Relief,' *Archiv für Orientforschung* 12 (1937–39).
D. Collon, *The Queen of the Night* (British Museum Objects in Focus, 2005).

title: Cylinder seal with archer and winged lion-demon (Walters Art Museum)
creator: Anonymous (Mesopotamia)
rights: Public domain. The Walters Art Museum, via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A Mesopotamian cylinder seal engraved with an archer confronting a winged lion-demon — a contest scene that doubled as a protective device.

## Iconography
The rolled-out design shows an **archer** drawing his bow against a **winged lion** or composite demon, a version of the ancient Near Eastern 'contest' or 'hero-vs-beast' scene. Cut into hardstone, the seal both authenticated and protected, the engraved combat charging the little cylinder with warding force.

## Significance
**Cylinder seals** were Mesopotamia's signature personal objects, worn on a cord and used to sign documents, but they were also amulets: the choice of imagery — gods, protective genii, the defeat of demons — gave them apotropaic value. Scenes of a hero or god overpowering a demonic beast assert order over chaos, the same victory dramatized in the [[motif:lamashtu|Lamashtu]] plaques and later sealed into the [[motif:incantation-bowl|incantation bowls]]. Standard reference: D. Collon, *First Impressions* (1987).

## For artists & game designers
A tiny rollable object whose imprinted scene is a frozen boss-fight — identity, signature, and protective talisman in one.

title: Incantation bowl with a bound demon drawn at the centre (Metropolitan Museum)
creator: Anonymous (Sasanian Mesopotamia); photograph by Marie-Lan Nguyen
rights: Public domain (photo: Marie-Lan Nguyen). The Metropolitan Museum of Art, via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
An Aramaic incantation bowl with a crude figure of a fettered demon drawn in the centre, encircled by the binding spell — the classic 'devil-trap' bowl.

## Iconography
A schematic **demon** is sketched at the bowl's base: a frontal figure with wild hair, sometimes shown with bound hands and feet or chained at the neck. Around it the spell winds in a **spiral** of Aramaic letters. The image is not decorative but operative — the demon is depicted *already captured*, its likeness imprisoned by the surrounding text.

## Significance
The drawn-demon bowls make the magic visible: the threatening power (Lilith, a *lilith*, a curse-demon, or the personified [[motif:evil-eye|evil eye]]) is named, depicted, and shackled, so that representation enacts capture. Such bowls were prepared by Jewish, Mandaean, Christian and pagan practitioners alike across Sasanian Babylonia, drawing on a shared repertoire of angelic names, Solomonic authority, and the formula of the *get* (writ of divorce) served on the demon.

## For artists & game designers
The 'bind the monster by drawing it in chains' mechanic in one object — depiction *is* containment.

D. Levene, *A Corpus of Magic Bowls* (2003).
