title: Mask of the demon Humbaba (Louvre, SB 6567)
creator: Anonymous (Old Babylonian); photograph by Shonagon
date: Old Babylonian period (c. early 2nd millennium BCE)
rights: Public domain (CC0, photo: Shonagon). Musée du Louvre, via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A clay mask of Humbaba (Huwawa), the monstrous guardian of the Cedar Forest slain by Gilgamesh, whose face was rendered as a single coiling line.

## Iconography
The grimacing **Humbaba** face is formed from one continuous **coiled line**, a labyrinthine pattern that ancient sources explicitly compared to the convolutions of animal **entrails**. The result is a frontal, apotropaic grotesque — a face that menaces whoever meets its gaze.

## Significance
**Humbaba/Huwawa** is the terrible guardian-demon of the *Epic of Gilgamesh*, but his single-line face had a second life in **extispicy** (divination by entrails): omen texts state that when the coils of a sheep's intestines formed 'the face of Humbaba,' it portended revolution or a usurper. The mask thus links epic myth, [[motif:apotropaic|apotropaic]] art, and Babylonian divination. Discussed by Wiggermann and by the Gilgamesh scholarship of A. R. George.

## For artists & game designers
A monster whose entire face is one unbroken maze-line — a brilliant, instantly recognizable motif for a labyrinth-guardian or omen-sign.

citations.text: A. R. George, *The Babylonian Gilgamesh Epic* (2003).
F. A. M. Wiggermann, *Mesopotamian Protective Spirits* (1992).

title: Mandaic magical bowl from Mesopotamia (Wellcome Collection)
creator: Anonymous (Mandaean, Mesopotamia)
rights: CC BY 4.0 (Wellcome Collection). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A magical bowl inscribed in Mandaic from the Wellcome Collection, another witness to the demon-binding bowls of late-antique Mesopotamia.

## Iconography
The bowl's interior carries a **spiral** of Mandaic letters. As in the wider genre, the text would name the client, summon protective powers, and pronounce a binding or expulsion against demons and the [[motif:evil-eye|evil eye]] threatening the household.

## Significance
Held in a medical-history collection, this bowl underlines that the spells were practical health-and-home magic: protection against miscarriage, disease, and malign spirits. Mandaic, Jewish Aramaic, and Syriac bowls share formulae and angelic names, evidence of a common Babylonian magical koine crossing religious lines. The corpus is edited by Yamauchi, Müller-Kessler, and the Shaked–Ford–Bhayro project.

## For artists & game designers
A museum-quality reference for a 'health charm' object whose protective intent is domestic and bodily rather than martial.

citations.text: E. M. Yamauchi, *Mandaic Incantation Texts* (1967).
S. Shaked, J. N. Ford & S. Bhayro, *Aramaic Bowl Spells* (2013).

title: Plaque of protection against Lamashtu
creator: Anonymous (Mesopotamia)
summary:
An apotropaic plaque directed against Lamashtu, the lion-headed female demon who menaced pregnant women and infants in Mesopotamian belief.

## Iconography
**Lamashtu** is shown with a lion's or bird's head, ass's teeth and ears, taloned bird feet, and pendulous breasts at which a piglet and a puppy suckle; she clutches **serpents** and often stands on a donkey crossing the underworld river. The plaque, hung in the home or worn, presents her image precisely in order to repel her.

## Significance
Lamashtu (Akkadian *Lamaštu*) was the archetypal **child-snatching, fever-bringing demon**, blamed for miscarriage, crib-death, and puerperal disease. She was countered by incantation series and by amuletic plaques, frequently paired with [[motif:pazuzu|Pazuzu]], the only power thought able to drive her back. This Mesopotamian therapeutic-magical complex is a direct ancestor of the later Aramaic bowls' war on Lilith. F. A. M. Wiggermann and W. Farber have produced the standard studies.

## For artists & game designers
A fully realized 'plague-bringing hag' design — lion head, animal teeth, suckling beasts, serpents — terrifying and instantly legible.

citations.text: W. Farber, *Lamaštu: An Edition of the Canonical Series* (2014).
F. A. M. Wiggermann, 'Lamaštu, Daughter of Anu,' in M. Stol, *Birth in Babylonia* (2000).

title: Lamashtu amulet (British Museum)
creator: Anonymous (Mesopotamia)
rights: Public domain. The British Museum, via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A Lamashtu amulet in the British Museum, a portable version of the protective plaque carried to ward the child-snatching demon from mother and infant.

## Iconography
The amulet depicts **Lamashtu** in her canonical form — leonine head, bared teeth, taloned feet, snakes in her raised hands, often suckling a piglet and pup and kneeling on her **donkey**. A perforation or loop allowed it to be worn or hung at the bedside of the vulnerable.

## Significance
Worn amulets extended the protection of the larger plaques to the body itself, especially around childbirth — the moment Lamashtu was most feared. Bearing the demon's own image turned her power against her, the same apotropaic logic that governs [[motif:pazuzu|Pazuzu]] heads and, centuries later, the drawn demons of the Aramaic [[motif:incantation-bowl|incantation bowls]]. Wiggermann and Farber remain the authorities.

## For artists & game designers
A wearable charm bearing the very monster it repels — the 'fight fire with fire' amulet, scaled down to jewelry.

citations.text: F. A. M. Wiggermann, 'Lamaštu, Daughter of Anu' (2000).
W. Farber, *Lamaštu* (2014).

title: Plaque of conjuration against Lamashtu (Louvre, AO 22205)
creator: Anonymous (Mesopotamia); photograph by Tangopaso
rights: Public domain. Musée du Louvre, via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A Louvre 'Lamashtu plaque' (AO 22205), one of the celebrated multi-register exorcism plaques showing the demon driven down to the underworld river. (The annotated overlay labels the figures.)

## Iconography
The plaque is divided into horizontal **registers**: above, ranks of protective deities and astral symbols; in the centre, ritual acts at a sickbed; below, **Lamashtu** kneeling on her donkey as it is ferried across the river of the netherworld, surrounded by her serpents, comb, and spindle. A looming head — that of [[motif:pazuzu|Pazuzu]] — often peers over the top edge, expelling her.

## Significance
These 'Hell plaques' or *plaques de conjuration* are among the most complex apotropaic objects of the ancient Near East, compressing a whole exorcistic ritual into a single carved scene. They visually narrate the demon's defeat and banishment, functioning as a permanent, self-renewing spell. Wiggermann's studies of the *bīt mēseri* protective rites illuminate their logic.

## For artists & game designers
A single object that storyboards an entire exorcism in stacked registers — a model for environmental art that tells a ritual narrative top-to-bottom.

citations.text: F. A. M. Wiggermann, *Mesopotamian Protective Spirits* (1992).
W. Farber, *Lamaštu* (2014).

title: Mandaic incantation bowl for Buktuya and household (Royal Ontario Museum)
creator: Anonymous (Mandaean, Southern Mesopotamia); photograph by Daderot
rights: Public domain (CC0). Royal Ontario Museum, via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A Mandaic-language incantation bowl inscribed for a named client, Buktuya, and his household — a window onto the Mandaean branch of the Mesopotamian magic-bowl tradition.

## Iconography
The bowl carries a dense **spiral** of cursive **Mandaic** script, the sacred script of the Mandaeans of southern Iraq. The text names the beneficiary (Buktuya) and his household and invokes protection over them, sealing out the demonic forces that threaten the home.

## Significance
Mandaic bowls form one of the three main scriptural streams of the genre, alongside Jewish Babylonian Aramaic and Syriac. The Mandaeans — a surviving Gnostic baptismal community — produced bowls drawing on their own cosmology of light and darkness. Naming the client personalizes the charm, a feature exploited by scholars to reconstruct Sasanian-era onomastics and social history. Key editions are by E. M. Yamauchi (*Mandaic Incantation Texts*, 1967) and C. Müller-Kessler.

## For artists & game designers
A protective charm keyed to a *named* owner and their dependents — a model for binding magic that is personal, not generic.

title: Aramaic incantation bowl from Nippur (Oriental Institute, Chicago)
creator: Anonymous (Sasanian Babylonia); photograph by Daderot
rights: Public domain (CC0). Oriental Institute Museum, University of Chicago, via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
An Aramaic incantation bowl excavated at Nippur, the site whose finds founded the modern study of the entire genre.

## Iconography
The earthenware bowl bears the characteristic concentric **spiral** of square Aramaic letters, the binding spell coiling inward. Bowls of this type were recovered *in situ* at Nippur, often inverted and placed at the corners of rooms or beneath floors and doorways.

## Significance
Nippur is the type-site: the University of Pennsylvania excavations of the 1880s–90s yielded the bowls that John A. Montgomery published in *Aramaic Incantation Texts from Nippur* (1913), the foundational corpus. The Sasanian date (240–641 CE) anchors the genre firmly in late antiquity, in a Babylonia shared by Jews, Mandaeans, Christians and Zoroastrians whose magical practices visibly intermingle on the bowls.

## For artists & game designers
An archaeologically grounded artifact — the buried, inverted spell-bowl as found, useful reference for an excavation or dungeon-floor discovery.

title: Pazuzu amulet
creator: Anonymous (Mesopotamia); photograph by Zunkir
rights: CC BY-SA 4.0 (photo: Zunkir). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A small Pazuzu amulet, the wearable form of the wind-demon that placed his protective ferocity directly on the body of the bearer.

## Iconography
The amulet reproduces **Pazuzu** in miniature — canine snout, four **wings**, talons, and **scorpion tail** — frequently as just the head, pierced for suspension. Pazuzu heads were hung at thresholds, on furniture, and worn at the neck, often by or for pregnant women.

## Significance
The proliferation of cheap Pazuzu amulets shows how thoroughly his apotropaic role saturated daily life. Worn against [[motif:lamashtu|Lamashtu]] and against the diseases borne on the wind, the amulet works by the same principle as the [[motif:incantation-bowl|incantation bowls]]: confronting a demonic threat with a more terrible, allied power. Heeßel catalogues the typology of statuettes, heads, and plaques.

## For artists & game designers
A compact 'equip the lesser evil' talisman — proof that the scariest silhouette can read as a ward, not a threat.

citations.text: N. P. Heeßel, *Pazuzu* (2002).
F. A. M. Wiggermann, *Mesopotamian Protective Spirits* (1992).

title: Cylinder seal with the head of Pazuzu (Louvre, AO 21111)
creator: Anonymous (Mesopotamia); photograph by Zunkir
rights: CC BY-SA 4.0 (photo: Zunkir). Musée du Louvre, via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A Louvre cylinder seal carved with the head of Pazuzu (AO 21111), combining the apotropaic demon with the administrative-magical technology of the seal.

## Iconography
The **head of Pazuzu** — snarling canine muzzle, deep brow, bulging eyes — is engraved on the body of a **cylinder seal**, an object normally rolled across clay to authenticate documents. Here the demon's face turns the seal into a protective device as much as a signature.

## Significance
The disembodied **Pazuzu head** was itself a potent apotropaion, believed to embody the whole demon; seals and amulets bearing it carried his warding power. The crossover of seal and amulet shows how Mesopotamian magic permeated even bureaucratic objects, and prefigures the later use of seals and signs to bind demons in the [[motif:incantation-bowl|bowl spells]] and grimoire tradition.

## For artists & game designers
A stamp/seal whose impression *is* a protective demon — a neat fusion of identity-marking and warding magic.

citations.text: N. P. Heeßel, *Pazuzu* (2002).
D. Collon, *First Impressions: Cylinder Seals in the Ancient Near East* (1987).

title: Bronze statuette of the demon Pazuzu (Louvre)
creator: Anonymous (Mesopotamia); photograph by Vassil
rights: Public domain (CC0). Musée du Louvre, via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A bronze statuette of Pazuzu, king of the wind-demons, shown in profile — the apotropaic demon enlisted to fight other demons.

## Iconography
**Pazuzu** has a snarling **canine or leonine face**, bulging eyes, two pairs of bird **wings**, the **talons** of a bird of prey, a **scorpion tail**, and an erect serpent-headed phallus. One hand is raised, the other lowered — the gesture of his standard formula, 'I ascended and descended.' His grotesque ferocity is precisely what makes him protective.

## Significance
Though himself a malevolent bringer of the destructive west wind and fevers, **Pazuzu** was harnessed *against* worse evils — above all [[motif:lamashtu|Lamashtu]], whom he alone could drive back to the underworld. His image guarded homes, pregnant women, and (via small heads) was worn as an amulet. Pazuzu's modern fame owes much to *The Exorcist* (1973); the scholarly study is N. Heeßel's *Pazuzu* (2002).

## For artists & game designers
The definitive 'monstrous protector' — assembled from dog, eagle, scorpion and snake, terrifying yet on the player's side.

title: Protective bowl with inscription and a demon (Louvre)
creator: Anonymous (Sasanian Mesopotamia)
summary:
A *bol de protection* — a protective incantation bowl combining a spiral spell with a drawn demon, exemplifying the union of word and image that defines the genre.

## Iconography
The spell spirals across the bowl's interior while a **demon** is figured within it. Text and image work together: the [[motif:bound-demon|demon]] is named in the writing and depicted in the drawing, doubly fixing it. The inward-turning spiral mimics the act of enclosing and confining the hostile power at the bowl's centre.

## Significance
Protective bowls addressed the everyday terrors of Sasanian domestic life — sickness, miscarriage, the [[motif:evil-eye|evil eye]], and night-demons such as Lilith and the *lilin*. Many invoke the same angelic and divine names found in contemporary Jewish, Christian and Mandaean magic, and some deploy the legal fiction of issuing the demon a writ of divorce. The interpenetration of traditions makes the bowls a prime source for the religious history of late-antique Babylonia.

## For artists & game designers
The coiling text + caged figure is a ready-made 'sealing circle' visual: a spell whose very shape is a prison.

citations.text: D. Levene, *A Corpus of Magic Bowls* (2003).
S. Shaked, J. N. Ford & S. Bhayro, *Aramaic Bowl Spells* (2013).

title: The Alchemist's Dream: Folly and Hope in the Laboratory
work: Islamic and Persian Alchemy: The Jabirian Tradition and Eastern Science (9th–17th centuries)
creator: Popular Graphic Arts (attributed)
place: Europe (likely USA, Library of Congress holdings)
summary:
An engraving titled **The Alchemist's Dream**—a popular print that encodes the moral ambiguity surrounding alchemy: the alchemist is either a patient seeker after truth or a deluded fool, depending on one's reading.

## Iconography
The central figure of the alchemist, bent over his work, is surrounded by dream-visions or smoke: golden images, phantasms, symbolic scenes. The composition suggests that what the alchemist sees—the promise of transmutation, the revelation of secrets—may be dream or delusion rather than reality.

## Significance
This print exemplifies a long European tradition of satirizing alchemy—the *Alchemy-Satire* that reaches back to the 15th century and forward through the 18th. Critics charged that alchemists were duped by their own hopes, mistaking chemical color-changes for true transmutation, or falling victim to con artists promising the Philosopher's Stone. Yet the print's ambiguity is telling: the dream-visions could also represent genuine insight, the revelation of hidden order. This tension—between alchemy as delusion and alchemy as legitimate science—haunted the tradition until chemistry itself emerged as the heir to alchemical practice. The print circulated in America (hence its Library of Congress provenance), where it served both as a warning against fraud and as a nostalgic evocation of a more mystical scientific past.

## For artists & game designers
Useful for depicting the moment when a character questions whether their magical pursuit is wisdom or folly—or for suggesting that the line between them is thinner than it appears.

citations.text: Tara Nummedal, *Alchemy and Authority in the Holy Roman Empire* (2007).
Lauren Kassell, *Medicine and Magic in the Early Modern World* (2005).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Amoretti in an Alchemist's Workshop: Love and Science
work: Islamic and Persian Alchemy: The Jabirian Tradition and Eastern Science (9th–17th centuries)
creator: David Teniers the Younger
summary:
A painting by **David Teniers the Younger** (1610–1690)—**Amoretti in an Alchemist's Workshop**—depicting playful cupids (Amoretti) engaged in the work of alchemy. The painting is both humorous and profound: love and [[motif:philosophical egg|the Great Work]] as parallel pursuits.

## Iconography
Cupids, nude or lightly draped, work at alchemical apparatus—stirring crucibles, tending furnaces, reading books. The juxtaposition of erotic play and solemn alchemy suggests that both are forms of transformation, binding, and the quest for a perfect union.

## Significance
Teniers was the master of the alchemist-workshop genre, and this painting is among his most elaborate. The introduction of Amoretti—playful love-spirits—is a characteristically Flemish Mannerist device, turning the alchemical workshop into a site of allegory and wit. The painting works on multiple levels: as satire (the alchemist's pursuit is foolish like cupid's games), as alchemy (the [[motif:conjunctio|union of opposites]]—the marriage of substances—mirrors the union of lovers), and as a celebration of creative work in all its forms. The painting demonstrates how thoroughly alchemical apparatus and philosophy had been absorbed into European visual culture by the 17th century. Teniers's versions of the laboratory scene, repeated in many variations, became canonical—more people saw alchemy through Teniers's paintings than through actual texts or laboratories.

## For artists & game designers
The aestheticization and humanization of alchemy—useful for depicting laboratories as lively, cultured spaces rather than grim dungeons.

citations.text: Lawrence M. Principe & Lloyd DeWitt, *Transmutations: Alchemy in Art* (2002).
Michael Levey, *Painting in Eighteenth-Century Venice* (1998).

title: The Alchemical Properties of Metal: Mercury, Vulcan, and the Alchemist
work: Islamic and Persian Alchemy: The Jabirian Tradition and Eastern Science (9th–17th centuries)
creator: Domenico Beccafumi
summary:
Domenico Beccafumi's engraving **The Alchemical Properties of Metal, Mercury, Vulcan, and the Alchemist in the Cave**—a Renaissance meditation on alchemy that synthesizes classical mythology, Islamic apparatus-knowledge, and Christian esoteric philosophy.

## Iconography
A figure (the Alchemist) in a cave or underground chamber tends a furnace. Hovering above or nearby are personifications of Mercury (the quicksilver god, also the key reagent in transmutation) and Vulcan (the god of fire and metalwork, patron of the forge). The composition suggests that alchemy is the human participation in divine creative power—the alchemist as a mortal who has learned the secrets of cosmic transformation.

## Significance
Beccafumi was trained in the Sienese tradition and created this engraving at a moment when Renaissance artists and scholars were recovering both classical (Hermetic) and Islamic alchemical texts. The layering of mythology onto apparatus-knowledge is deliberate: the Alchemist becomes a hero-figure undertaking a quasi-divine work. The cave setting evokes both Plato's cave (the place where illusion gives way to truth) and the alchemist's laboratory. By invoking Mercury and Vulcan, Beccafumi claims that alchemy is not a new or heretical practice but a recovery of ancient wisdom, sanctioned by the gods themselves. This rhetorical strategy—alchemy as ancient science—became standard in Renaissance texts, feeding directly from Islamic scholars' own claims about the Jabirian tradition and Hermetic wisdom.

## For artists & game designers
The alchemist as a hero-sage in communion with cosmic forces—useful for high-magic settings where alchemy is treated as humanity's greatest aspiration.

citations.text: Lawrence M. Principe & Lloyd DeWitt, *Transmutations: Alchemy in Art* (2002).
Eugenio Battisti & Giuliano Briganti, *Domenico Beccafumi* (1971).

title: Greek Alchemical Text: The Transmission of Hellenistic Knowledge
work: Islamic and Persian Alchemy: The Jabirian Tradition and Eastern Science (9th–17th centuries)
creator: Byzantine or Islamic copyist
place: Byzantine territories or Islamic scholarly center
summary:
A folio from **Marcianus gr. 299**—a Byzantine manuscript preserving texts from the Greek alchemical tradition (especially the works of Zosimos and the Alexandrian corpus).

## Iconography
Greek text on vellum, preserving the technical vocabulary and philosophical framework of Hellenistic alchemy. The page is a window onto the textual tradition that Islamic scholars inherited and transformed.

## Significance
When Islamic scholars encountered the Greek alchemical corpus (through the Syriac and Arabic translations that circulated in the 8th–9th centuries), they inherited a tradition stretching back to Zosimos of Panopolis (3rd century CE) and the Alexandrian craftsmen. Greek alchemy was pragmatic—focused on gold-making, color changes, and [[motif:distillation tower|distillation]]—but also suffused with mystical philosophy (Neoplatonism, Hermeticism). The Islamic alchemists did not simply copy this tradition but restructured it: they imposed systematic organization (Jābir's corpus), mathematical rigor (al-Khāzinī), and philosophical grounding (al-Kindī). The Byzantine preservation of the original Greek texts (as seen in the Marciana manuscript) allowed this dialogue to continue—Islamic and Byzantine scholars maintained contact through trade, diplomacy, and scholarship, enabling mutual influence.

## For artists & game designers
A bridge text—useful for depicting how knowledge passed between civilizations and how each culture reshaped inherited wisdom to fit its own philosophical and practical needs.

summary:
**Abū Yūsuf Yaʿqūb ibn Isḥāq al-Kindī** (c. 801–873 CE)—the 9th-century Baghdad philosopher whose treatises on occult properties and the nature of substances grounded Islamic alchemy in Aristotelian natural philosophy.

## Iconography
A small portrait in the Islamic scholarly tradition, marked by the spare elegance typical of later manuscript reproduction.

## Significance
Al-Kindī's *Risālat al-Kindī fī al-ʿilal al-ṣināʿiyyah* (On the Causes of Artificial Substances) was a foundational text for understanding chymical transmutation as a philosophical problem. Unlike mystical approaches, al-Kindī argued that color-change and apparent transmutation could occur without the essential form changing—a crucial distinction that preserved Aristotelian metaphysics while explaining apparent transformations. His work on [[motif:distillation tower|distillation]] and [[motif:furnace and bellows|furnace operation]] was practical and precise. Though he opposed the claim that metals could be transmuted into gold, his rational framework for understanding chymical operations was canonical.

## For artists & game designers
A figure bridging skeptical rationalism and occult inquiry—useful for dialogue between scientists and alchemists, or for a character whose authority rests on philosophical argument rather than magical authority.

The manuscript tradition preserved these texts with remarkable fidelity, ensuring that European translators (Robert of Chester, Gerard of Cremona) could transmit the full apparatus of Islamic chymistry to the Latin world.

A schematic diagram of the **Athanor** (also called the *Digesting Oven*)—the legendary self-regulating furnace capable of maintaining perfect, unwavering heat for months or years, essential to the [[motif:philosophical egg|Great Work]].

## Iconography
A round, brick furnace with carefully designed ventilation and heat-regulation mechanisms. The diagram shows how medieval alchemists attempted to engineer a furnace that required minimal supervision while maintaining precise thermal conditions.

## Significance
The Athanor is partly historical (actual designs exist), partly legendary. Islamic and European alchemists pursued the design as a holy grail of apparatus engineering—a furnace that would free them from the constant tending required by ordinary furnaces. The Athanor represents the dream of automation in alchemy: the idea that once the operation was set in motion, natural law (carefully engineered) would bring it to completion. Later European alchemists, especially the [[motif:distillation tower|Paracelsians]], made the Athanor symbolic of patience, faith, and the belief that the philosopher need only create the right conditions and let nature work. The modern reconstruction shown here preserves medieval ingenuity in thermal management.

## For artists & game designers
A symbol of patient, self-sustaining magical operation—useful for depicting long-term ritual magic or for suggesting that the alchemist's role is to set things in motion, not to force outcomes.

**Abū ʿAlī al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAbdallāh Ibn Sīnā** (980–1037), known in the West as **Avicenna**—the Persian polymathwho unified medicine, metaphysics, and the alchemical arts in his vast philosophical corpus.

Avicenna's *Kitāb al-Shifāʾ* (The Healing) and *Al-Qānūn fī al-ṭibb* (The Canon of Medicine) dominated medical theory from the 12th century onward. His contributions to alchemical theory include sophisticated treatments of the [[motif:philosophical egg|philosophical egg]], the stages of distillation, and the relationship between mineral and animal substances. His philosophy of the soul and the intellect also shaped later Hermetic thought. Though not primarily an alchemist, Avicenna's intellectual authority made alchemy a branch of legitimate philosophical inquiry in both the Islamic and Christian worlds.

The universal scholar—a figure of Renaissance admiration whose authority spans medicine, ethics, metaphysics, and the hidden sciences. Useful for worldbuilding that posits unified knowledge systems.

The metallurgical techniques of Islamic craftsmen—known through textual sources and occasionally through archaeological finds like this one—influenced European metalworkers. The organized packing of these strips suggests a professional, systematic approach to material—not casual but intentional. This artifact is a tangible link between textual alchemical theory and material practice.

A detailed technical diagram showing the furnace, the sealed vessels, the condensing apparatus, and the flow of vapor and liquid. Each component serves a precise function in the separation and purification of the volatile substance.

## Significance
Sulfur [[motif:distillation tower|distillation]] was a cornerstone of Islamic alchemy. The apparatus shown here—with its efficiency in capturing vapors and condensing them back to liquid—represents centuries of refinement in the Islamic laboratory tradition. Such systems allowed the preparation of the highly reactive, purified sulfur used in [[motif:philosophical egg|philosophical egg]] operations and in the later European pursuit of the Philosopher's Stone. Louis Figuier's 19th-century *L'Alchimie et les alchimistes* popularized these diagrams, making the actual historical apparatus of the medieval alchemist visible to modern readers.

title: The Book of Alchemy by Tao Zhi: East-West Convergence

summary:
A page from the annotated **Book of Alchemy by Tao Zhi**—a Chinese alchemical text that, while independent of Islamic tradition, pursued strikingly parallel goals: the creation of an [[motif:distillation tower|elixir]] of immortality through careful manipulation of substances.

## Iconography
Chinese text and annotation, documenting recipes and philosophical commentary on the transformation of matter and spirit.

## Significance
Chinese alchemy (dating back to the 4th century BCE) developed independently of Islamic tradition but arrived at similar practical concerns and theoretical frameworks. Both traditions pursued immortality (Islamic alchemists sought the [[motif:philosophical egg|Philosopher's Stone]], Chinese adepts sought the elixir), both relied on [[motif:distillation tower|distillation]] and heating, both synthesized practical [[motif:furnace and bellows|laboratory]] work with philosophical Taoism/Sufism. By the medieval period, transmission routes between Islamic and Chinese alchemy may have existed through Silk Road trade and scholarship. This convergence suggests that alchemy addresses universal human concerns (material transformation, immortality, hidden knowledge) that different civilizations discovered independently. The inclusion of Tao Zhi's text in the Islamic alchemy collection serves as a reminder that the tradition was global, not merely Mediterranean or Islamic, even if the Western record focuses on Islamic-to-European transmission.

## For artists & game designers
Useful for depicting alchemy as a universal human endeavor, not tied to one culture or religious framework.

summary:
A Persian manuscript copy of the **Tabula Smaragdina** (Emerald Tablet)—the foundational text of Hermetic alchemy, attributed to Hermes Trismegistus and circulated in Arabic and Persian translations throughout the Islamic world.

## Iconography
Persian calligraphy presenting the cryptic aphorisms of the Tablet: maxims on the unity of heaven and earth, the doctrine of correspondence ("as above, so below"), and the secret of the Great Work compressed into dense, riddling language.

## Significance
The Emerald Tablet's origins are murky—likely a late-antique or early Islamic synthesis of Hermetic philosophy, Neoplatonism, and alchemy, attributed retroactively to the legendary Hermes. It entered the Islamic tradition early (Arabic versions exist from the 9th century onward) and was embraced as the crown jewel of Hermetic wisdom. The Tablet's central claim—that the macrocosm and microcosm obey the same laws, that human and cosmic transformation are homologous—became the operating principle of Islamic alchemy. Its influence on Jābir, al-Rāzī, and later European alchemists (including Roger Bacon and Ramon Llull) cannot be overstated. The Persian copy shown here attests to the text's canonical status in Safavid intellectual culture.

## For artists & game designers
A magical constitution—invoke the Emerald Tablet for instant philosophical weight and the claim that all knowledge is unified and interconnected.

This painting—probably 17th century, though the apparatus is timeless—shows the alchemist's workshop as it would have functioned from the Islamic period onward. The [[motif:distillation tower|apparatus for distillation]], the management of heat in the furnace, the collection of vapors and liquids—all derive from Islamic chymical innovation. The painting captures the temporal dimension of alchemy: the long, patient operation requiring constant attention. This is not mystical rapture but disciplined, unglamorous craft.

A full-page portrait engraving of **Geber** (*Jābir ibn Ḥayyān*)—the legendary figure of Islamic alchemy, here rendered in the Romantic-era European style as the bearded sage-alchemist surrounded by symbols of the craft.

## Iconography
The figure is robed, bearded, mature—a visual shorthand for the wise master. The surrounding motifs—furnaces, vessels, instruments—situate him in his laboratory as the mind directing the work. This is the alchemist as both theorist and operator.

## Significance
Geber's legend grew with each translation and commentary. By the time European alchemists took up his work in the 12th and 13th centuries (through Latin renderings by Robert of Chester), he had become the patron saint of experimental alchemy. Whether or not all the texts attributed to him were authored by him—modern scholarship remains divided—his name carried immense authority. Later alchemists invoked "Geber" as shorthand for the entire tradition of disciplined, apparatus-based chymical work. This portrait, romantic as it is, captures how Geber had transcended his historical moment to become a symbol of alchemy itself.

## For artists & game designers
The archetypal Master Alchemist across European and Islamic traditions—invoke this name for instant gravitas and connection to an imagined historical alchemy.

An opening from a luxurious Safavid manuscript of Firdausi's **Shahnameh** (The Book of Kings)—a Persian epic whose narrative of kingship, transformation, and cosmic order parallels alchemical philosophy.

Gold-leaf illuminations and vibrant lapis lazuli blues frame the Persian calligraphy. The page is almost pictorial in its ornamentation—the text exists within a jeweled casket of decoration, suggesting that the words themselves are treasured, precious.

## Significance
The Shahnameh is not primarily an alchemical text, but its themes—the transformation of kingdoms, the testing of heroes, the cycles of rise and fall—mirror the philosophical preoccupations of Islamic alchemy. The Safavid period (16th–17th centuries) saw a remarkable synthesis of court culture, philosophical learning, and esoteric knowledge. Shah Isma'il II (r. 1576–1577) was known as a patron of learning and a practitioner of esoteric disciplines. Manuscripts like this one were status symbols but also spiritual tools: the act of commissioning and reading such texts was itself a form of philosophical participation. The alchemist's laboratory and the royal court converge in Safavid Persia as spaces of transformation and hidden knowledge.

Hunayn's *Kitāb al-Masāʾil fī al-ṭibb* (Book of Medical Questions) and his ophthalmological treatise *Dix traités d'ophtalmologie* dominated medical education. Though not primarily an alchemist, his systematic treatment of substances, their properties, and their transformations in the human body bridged medicine and alchemy. His work on pharmacology—the preparation of medicines through distillation, infusion, and precipitation—exemplified the chymical method applied to healing. His authority on the [[motif:philosophical egg|philosophical egg]] and [[motif:distillation tower|distillation]] is evident in later references by alchemical authors seeking to ground their claims in medical legitimacy.

The legendary **Jābir ibn Ḥayyān** (c. 721–815 CE, called *Geber* in Latin texts)—transmuted into symbolic portraiture as the founder of systematic Islamic alchemy.

## Iconography
The bearded, turbaned figure embodies the 8th-century Iraqi scholar whose reputation for empirical method and prolific writing made him the patriarch of Jabirian alchemy. The Wellcome version is a later romantic reconstruction; no authentic period portrait survives.

## Significance
Jābir authored or inspired the vast *Jabirian corpus*—over 70 major treatises attributed to him or his school—covering distillation theory, metal transmutation, color changes, and the preparation of [[motif:philosophical egg|philosophical eggs]]. He systematized the concept of *mizan* (balance/proportion), arguing that transmutation rested on precise ratios of ingredients and heat. His theories dominated Islamic and Western alchemical thought through the Renaissance and beyond. Modern scholarship (Holmyard, Kraus) has disentangled the historical Jābir from legendary accretions, yet his role as the systematic architect of chymical theory is secure.

## For artists & game designers
The archetypal master alchemist: systematic thinker, vast library, precision and patience. Perfect for a mentor figure in quest narratives or a founding sage in magical histories.

title: Paracelsus (Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim): The Alchemist-Physician
work: Islamic and Persian Alchemy: The Jabirian Tradition and Eastern Science (9th–17th centuries)
creator: Richard Cooper (engraver)

summary:
An engraving of **Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim**, called **Paracelsus** (1493–1541)—the Swiss physician-alchemist who revolutionized medicine by grounding it explicitly in alchemy and mystical philosophy, and who claimed to build his entire system on the [[motif:distillation tower|distillation]] and [[motif:furnace and bellows|laboratory]] innovations of Islamic alchemy.

## Iconography
The bearded, intense figure represents the archetype of the Renaissance individual genius—a man at odds with established orthodoxy, possessed of hidden knowledge.

## Significance
Paracelsus openly acknowledged the Islamic alchemical tradition as the foundation of his own work. He praised al-Rāzī and claimed that the true physician must be an alchemist, capable of preparing medicines through [[motif:distillation tower|distillation]] and other chymical processes. His insistence on [[motif:furnace and bellows|laboratory experiment]] and pharmaceutical alchemy (rather than purely theoretical transmutation) gave the Islamic apparatus-tradition new legitimacy and vigor in 16th-century Europe. Paracelsus's students and followers carried his methods into the 17th century, when alchemy was increasingly applied to practical medicine and mining. By the 18th century, the pharmaceutical branch of alchemy had transformed into modern chemistry. Paracelsus stands as a bridge figure: he was the last great alchemist-physician to command wide authority, and also a precursor to the chemical medicine that would displace alchemy. His success in synthesizing Islamic practical alchemy with Neoplatonic mysticism ensured that even as alchemy's mystical pretensions faded, its practical legacy (distillation, reaction, apparatus-design) persisted in chemistry.

## For artists & game designers
The revolutionary alchemist who claims to overturn the old order while actually building on hidden precedent—useful for characters attempting synthesis or radical reform.

Al-Khāzinī's *Mīzān al-Ḥikma* (c. 1121 CE) was revolutionary for its insistence on precise measurement and [[motif:mizan (balance/proportion)|mathematical balance]] as the key to understanding change and transformation. summary:
The title page of Conrad Gessner's **New Jewell of Health** (1576)—a prominent medical-alchemical treatise featuring detailed woodcuts of apparatus for the [[motif:distillation tower|extraction of quintessence]] from plants and minerals.

## Iconography
An ornate title page incorporating apparatus diagrams: [[motif:alembic and retort|retorts and alembics]], [[motif:furnace and bellows|furnaces with bellows]], distillation towers, and crucibles. The page announces that this is a practical manual—the beauty of the print conveys the value of the knowledge within.

## Significance
Gessner (1516–1565) was a Swiss naturalist and physician who synthesized Islamic medical knowledge (transmitted through Avicenna and others) with contemporary pharmaceutical alchemy. His *Treasurie of Euonymus* (1559) and *New Jewell of Health* pioneered the printing and illustration of alchemical apparatus, making the technical details of [[motif:distillation tower|distillation]] and extraction visible to a vernacular audience. The apparatus shown is based on centuries of Islamic innovation: the [[motif:alembic and retort|alembic and retort]], the controlled heating, the separation of components. By publishing these illustrations, Gessner democratized alchemy—no longer an exclusive secret transmitted by masters to initiates, but a learnable craft documented in printed books.

## For artists & game designers
The transition point from medieval craft-secrecy to early-modern scientific transparency—useful for depicting the moment when alchemy began to shed its mystique and become empirical pharmacy.

work: Islamic and Persian Alchemy: The Jabirian Tradition and Eastern Science (9th–17th centuries)
creator: Unknown (later period portrait)
summary:
A portrait of **Abū Bakr Muḥammad ibn Zakarīyā al-Rāzī** (Rhazes, AD 865–925), the Persian physician and alchemist whose experimental writings on distillation and chemical substances defined the early chymical tradition.

## Iconography
The figure is shown as a mature scholar, bearded, in scholarly dress—iconic of the Islamic polymaths whose learning synthesized medicine, philosophy, and the practice of alchemy. The Wellcome Collection preserves this portrait as a witness to the transmission of Islamic science.

## Significance
Al-Rāzī was one of the great experimental chemists of his era, known for *Kitāb al-Asrār* (The Secret of Secrets) and *De Alchemia*, which documented laboratory apparatus, mercury distillation, and the theory of substances. Scholars including William R. Newman argue that al-Rāzī's quantitative approach to reaction and sublimation laid the conceptual groundwork for later European chymistry. His work on vitriol, sal ammoniac, and the preparation of distilled waters was canonical until the 17th century.

## For artists & game designers
The alchemist-physician is a recognizable archetype combining scholarly authority (the scholar's robes, the mature bearing) with practical experiment—useful for any character bridging theory and empirical craft.

title: The Sabians: The Hidden Philosophers of Islamic Alchemy
work: Islamic and Persian Alchemy: The Jabirian Tradition and Eastern Science (9th–17th centuries)
creator: Maghribi calligrapher
summary:
A fragment of Qur'anic text in Maghribi script invoking the **Ṣābʾa** (Sabians)—the mysterious "people of the Book" whom Islamic theology recognised as possessors of revealed wisdom, and whom medieval Islamic alchemists claimed as intellectual ancestors.

## Iconography
The Qur'ānic text in elegant Maghribi hand preserves the names and references by which the Sabians were known in Islamic tradition. The script itself—the distinctive angular Maghribi style—marks this as a North African or Andalusian production.

## Significance
The Sabians were a real historical group—probably the remnants of a pre-Islamic astral-religion from Mesopotamia, later identified with the followers of Hermes Trismegistus and the Hermetic corpus. Islamic theologians and philosophers granted them the honorific status of a "People of the Book," alongside Jews and Christians. This theological tolerance allowed Sabian and Hermetic texts to circulate in Islamic scholarly circles without accusation of un-Islamic heresy. The Sabian connection was thus crucial to the transmission of Hermetic alchemy and magic into the Islamic tradition, and thence into the Christian West. The *Picatrix* and other grimoric texts carried a fictional "Sabian" pedigree for this reason.

## For artists & game designers
The Sabians are a legendary scholarly tradition that can be invoked to justify magical learning within a religiously-strict world—a textual workaround that allowed medieval scholars to pursue occult philosophy.

citations.text: Jan Gemert, 'The Sabians of Islam', in *Encyclopaedia of Islam*, 2nd ed. (1995).

title: Sal Ammoniac (Sal Armoniac): The Volatile Salt of Alchemy
work: Islamic and Persian Alchemy: The Jabirian Tradition and Eastern Science (9th–17th centuries)
creator: Unknown
summary:
A diagram or recipe notation for **Sal Ammoniac** (ammonium chloride)—one of the most sought-after substances in medieval and Renaissance alchemy, prized for its volatility and role in transmutation operations.

## Iconography
A text-based diagram or recipe, possibly from the papers of Sir Kenelm Digby (1603–1665), the English scholar who was among the last educated alchemists and compiled vast collections of [[motif:distillation tower|alchemical recipes]].

## Significance
Sal ammoniac is mentioned repeatedly in Islamic alchemical texts (Jābir, al-Rāzī, and others describe its preparation from [[motif:distillation tower|distillation]] of camel urine or ammonia-containing substances). Its sharp, biting volatility made it symbolically important—it was one of the few substances that readily transformed between solid and gaseous states, embodying the alchemist's dream of matter's fluidity. Medieval and Renaissance alchemists pursued sal ammoniac as an ingredient in the [[motif:philosophical egg|Great Work]], especially in operations aimed at preparing the [[motif:mercury amalgam|mercury amalgam]] or the [[motif:philosophical egg|philosophical egg]]. Digby's collection—visible here in fragmentary form—represents the last generation of learned amateurs trying to work out the old recipes before alchemy was eclipsed by chemistry proper.

## For artists & game designers
A magical ingredient with a real historical pedigree—one of the few substances alchemists pursued that modern chemistry confirms has remarkable properties.

title: Zosimos of Panopolis: The First Western Alchemist
work: Islamic and Persian Alchemy: The Jabirian Tradition and Eastern Science (9th–17th centuries)
creator: Byzantine copyist (preserving Zosimos original)
summary:
A page from **Paris, Grec 2327**—a Byzantine manuscript preserving texts of **Zosimos of Panopolis** (fl. c. 300 CE), the legendary figure regarded as the founder of Western alchemy.

## Iconography
Greek text, possibly showing mystical diagrams or apparatus descriptions from Zosimos's lost works. The manuscript itself is a palimpsest of tradition: Zosimos writing in Greek Egypt, Byzantine scholars copying and preserving his words, Islamic scholars translating and building upon them, and finally Western scholars discovering the Greek originals through Byzantine manuscripts.

## Significance
Zosimos is the earliest figure we can confidently identify as practicing and writing about alchemy in the Western tradition. He worked in Panopolis (Akhmim) in Upper Egypt in the 3rd century CE, a time when Egypt was under Roman rule and Greek remained the language of educated thought. Zosimos synthesized Greek natural philosophy (the four elements, transformations of matter) with Egyptian and possibly Jewish mystical traditions. His writings describe actual chemical operations (distillation, sublimation, color-changes) alongside visionary experiences and mystical philosophy. Islamic scholars inherited Zosimos through Syriac translations, incorporated him into their own frameworks (Jābir and later alchemists all engaged with Zosimos), and eventually transmitted him back to Europe through Latin translations. The lineage is direct: Zosimos → Islamic alchemy → European Renaissance alchemy.

## For artists & game designers
The ancestral voice—invoke Zosimos when claiming that alchemy is an ancient science with continuous practice from classical antiquity onward.

citations.text: Marcelin Berthelot & Eugène Ruelle, *Collection des anciens alchimistes grecs* (1888).

title: Talismanic Prayer Scroll (ACM-03625)
summary: A talismanic prayer scroll from an Islamic collection, written on a long strip of paper or vellum and folded to be worn on the body or hung in the home. title: Francis Barrett’s Magic Squares Plate from *The Magus* (1801)
summary: The first plate of magic squares (planetary kamea) from Francis Barrett's *The Magus* (London, 1801), reproducing Agrippa's planetary magic-square system: Saturn 3x3, Jupiter 4x4, Mars 5x5, Sol 6x6, Venus 7x7, Mercury 8x8, Luna 9x9. Barrett's *Magus* was a key conduit for Cornelius Agrippa's Renaissance occult philosophy into the 19th-century occult revival.

title: Talismanic Brass Bowl with Serpent and Zodiac
summary: A talismanic brass bowl decorated with a knotted serpent and zodiacal medallions. Such bowls were used for healing: water poured into the bowl was believed to absorb the protective power of the inscriptions and could be drunk by the patient. The serpent motif recalls the Solomonic seal tradition and the healing properties attributed to the planet Mercury.

title: Buduh Magic Square (al-Qazwini, 13th c.)
summary: The Buduh magic square from al-Qazwini's *Aja'ib al-Makhluqat* (Wonders of Creation, c. 1280). Buduh (b-d-w-h) is a four-letter divine name whose letters, assigned numerical values, yield the classic 3x3 magic square. This is the foundational wafq of the Islamic talismanic tradition, discussed by al-Buni and applied to amulets, garments, and magical operations across the Islamic world.

title: The Budūḥ Magic Square
creator: Anonymous (lettrist tradition)
summary:
The famous **budūḥ** square — the 3×3 magic square whose corner letters spell the talismanic word *budūḥ*.

## Iconography
A simple **3×3 grid** holds the numbers 2-9-4 / 7-5-3 / 6-1-8 (every row, column and diagonal summing to fifteen). Read by their *abjad* letter-values, the four corner cells (b–d–w–ḥ) form the magic name **BUDŪḤ**, which was itself written as a charm in place of the full square.

## Significance
The budūḥ square is the best-known device of Islamic lettrist magic (*ʿilm al-ḥurūf*), invoked for protection, safe childbirth and the safe arrival of letters and goods. Its reduction from a numerical [[motif:magic square|wafq]] to a single pronounceable name shows how operative magic compressed a whole diagram into one potent word.

## For artists & game designers
A glyph with a self-contained internal logic (equal sums) and a 'true name' hidden in its corners — an elegant model for a rune whose power has an in-world rationale.

citations.text: Emilie Savage-Smith (ed.), *Magic and Divination in Early Islam* (2004).

title: Demons (Devils), Kitāb al-Bulhān
creator: Workshop of ʿAbd al-Ḥasan al-Iṣfāhānī (attrib.), with later additions
summary:
A page of **devils** (*shayāṭīn*) from the *Kitāb al-Bulhān* (Book of Wonders), the illustrated compendium of astrology, divination and the spirit-world made in Jalayirid Baghdad.

## Iconography
Clustered dark **demons** with horns, fangs, clawed limbs and flame-coloured or smoke-grey bodies crowd the leaf. Each belongs to the manuscript's gallery of [[motif:jinn|jinn]] and devil-chiefs, marked off from humans by bestial heads and unnatural skin so that the practitioner could recognise — and ritually master — them.

## Significance
The *Kitāb al-Bulhān* (Bodleian MS Or. 133) gathers the divinatory lore of Abū Maʿshar and others; its Ottoman recensions ordered the spirit-rulers into a scheme of days, planets and colours. Such demon-galleries lie at the root of the talismanic tradition that, through the *Picatrix*, fed European astral magic.

## For artists & game designers
A ready-made roster of named demon-chiefs with built-in planetary and chromatic correspondences — a summoning bestiary in one frame.

citations.text: Stefano Carboni, *The Wonders of Creation and the Singularities of Painting* (2015).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Spirit-King Folio (fol. 32a), Book of Wonders (Kitāb al-Bulhān)
creator: Anonymous (Arabic collectaneous manuscript)
summary:
Folio 32a of a fifteenth-century *Kitāb al-Bulhān* (Book of Wonders), showing one of the manuscript's enthroned **spirit-kings**.

## Iconography
A commanding **jinn-king** is set centrally with smaller attendant demons, in the manuscript's recurring 'ruler-and-retinue' format. Horn-shape, body-colour and regalia mark his rank within the hierarchy of day- and planet-rulers.

## Significance
The *Kitāb al-Bulhān* is the single richest illustrated source for the Islamicate doctrine of governable [[motif:jinn|spirit-rulers]]. Each king's image is effectively a talismanic portrait, intended to make the spirit recognisable so that incantation and timing could bind him. The leaf belongs to Bodleian MS Or. 133.

## For artists & game designers
The 'enthroned chief with demon retinue' composition is a clean boss-and-minions template lifted straight from a medieval magical handbook.

citations.text: Stefano Carboni, *Il Kitāb al-Bulhān di Oxford* (1988).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Devils Talking (Conversing Demons), Kitāb al-Bulhān
creator: Workshop of ʿAbd al-Ḥasan al-Iṣfāhānī (attrib.), with later additions
summary:
A scene of **conversing devils** from the *Kitāb al-Bulhān*, showing demons in close exchange rather than menace.

## Iconography
Two or more horned, party-coloured **jinn** lean together as if in council or conversation. The grouping belongs to the manuscript's demonological cycle, where the spirits are individuated by colour, horn-shape and posture so the reader can tell one ruler from another.

## Significance
The *Kitāb al-Bulhān* treats the [[motif:jinn|jinn]] not as a faceless horde but as a hierarchy of named, planet-bound chiefs who could be addressed and bound. Depicting them in social converse underlines the Islamicate premise that the spirit-world was an ordered society, governable by the talismanic sciences.

## For artists & game designers
A 'demons in parley' tableau is a useful counter-image to the usual snarling monster — spirits shown scheming or negotiating among themselves.

citations.text: Stefano Carboni, *Il Kitāb al-Bulhān di Oxford* (1988).
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Jinn King of Tuesday (al-Aḥmar), Kitāb al-Bulhān
creator: Workshop of ʿAbd al-Ḥasan al-Iṣfāhānī (attrib.), with later additions
figures: al-Aḥmar (the Red King, jinn-king of Tuesday)
summary:
The **Jinn King of Tuesday** from the *Kitāb al-Bulhān*, one of the seven day-ruling spirit-kings of the manuscript's demonological scheme.

## Iconography
A large enthroned or striding **demon-king** dominates the leaf, attended by lesser spirits. As ruler of Tuesday he is tied to **Mars** and to the colour red — *al-Aḥmar*, 'the Red' — the planet of war and iron, his form coloured and armed to match.

## Significance
The *Kitāb al-Bulhān* assigns each weekday a presiding [[motif:jinn|jinn]]-king with a planet, a colour and an angelic overseer, so a magician could time and address a conjuration to the right ruler. This seven-king scheme, systematised in the Ottoman recensions, is one of the clearest surviving visual codifications of Islamicate planetary spirit-magic.

## For artists & game designers
Seven planet-coded spirit-kings, one per weekday, give a complete calendrical summoning system — pick the day, get the king, the planet and the colour.

citations.text: Stefano Carboni, *The Wonders of Creation and the Singularities of Painting* (2015).

title: Page of al-Būnī's Shams al-Maʿārif (the Sun of Knowledge)
creator: Aḥmad ibn ʿAlī al-Būnī (text); printed edition
summary:
A page from al-Būnī's *Shams al-Maʿārif* (The Sun of Knowledge), the foundational handbook of Islamic lettrist magic (*ʿilm al-ḥurūf*).

## Iconography
The page sets **gridded letter- and number-squares** among lines of Arabic text. The squares deploy the Arabic letters and their numerical (*abjad*) values, together with the [[motif:divine names|Beautiful Names of God]], to concentrate celestial and divine power into a usable talismanic device.

## Significance
Attributed to Aḥmad al-Būnī (d. c. 1225), the *Shams al-Maʿārif* systematised the science of letters: the idea that the twenty-eight Arabic letters carry the powers by which God created the world, so arranging them in squares and names channels those powers. It became the single most influential — and most feared — grimoire of the Islamicate world.

## For artists & game designers
The living-letter premise — every glyph a unit of creative power — turns an alphabet itself into a magic system, with squares as spells you literally assemble from letters.

citations.text: Noah Gardiner, 'Esotericism in a Manuscript Culture: Aḥmad al-Būnī and His Readers' (PhD diss., 2014).
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Fallen Angels Hārūt and Mārūt
creator: Anonymous (Persianate workshop)
summary:
A painting of the **fallen angels Hārūt and Mārūt**, the two angels who, in Islamic tradition, taught humankind magic at Babylon.

## Iconography
The two **angels** are shown suspended head-downward in the pit at Babel — the punishment for teaching forbidden sorcery — winged and haloed yet inverted, set against a rocky well. The composition pictures the moment that magic entered the world.

## Significance
Qurʾan 2:102 names **Hārūt and Mārūt** as the source from which men learned magic that 'could separate a man from his wife'. The pair became the mythic origin-point of the whole talismanic and astral science: angels who held the forbidden knowledge and were punished for dispensing it. Their image frames Islamicate magic as a dangerous, heaven-derived gift.

## For artists & game designers
The inverted-angels-in-a-pit motif is a striking origin-myth image for a magic system — power that came from above but at a cost, its teachers eternally punished.

citations.text: G. Vajda, 'Hārūt wa-Mārūt,' *Encyclopaedia of Islam* (2nd ed.).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Diagram of the Levels of Heaven (Islamic Cosmology)
creator: Modern diagram (SPQR10) after Islamic Neoplatonic cosmology
summary:
A modern diagram of the **concentric heavens** of Islamic Neoplatonic cosmology — the model of nested spheres behind Ibn ʿArabī's and the Sufi cosmologists' circle-diagrams.

## Iconography
**Concentric circles** rise from the earthly centre through the planetary heavens to the outermost spheres, each ring labelled. The form is the classic Ptolemaic-Islamic cosmos: a graded ladder of being mapped as nested rings.

## Significance
The descent-of-being and the ranked heavens were core to the cosmologies of [[motif:emanation|Islamic Neoplatonism]], al-Ghazālī and Ibn ʿArabī, whose *Futūḥāt* circle-diagrams chart the divine names, the spheres and the 'Breath of the Merciful' radiating the cosmos into existence. This reconstruction renders that nested-spheres model clearly; it is a modern educational diagram rather than a historical manuscript leaf.

## For artists & game designers
Nested concentric heavens give a ready vertical-world map — ascend ring by ring toward the source, each sphere a level with its own ruler.

citations.text: William C. Chittick, *The Sufi Path of Knowledge: Ibn al-ʿArabī's Metaphysics of Imagination* (1989).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Celestial Map: Zodiac and Lunar Mansions
creator: Seyyid Lokman (workshop)
summary:
An Ottoman **celestial map** combining the signs of the zodiac with the twenty-eight **lunar mansions** (*manāzil al-qamar*).

## Iconography
A concentric circular diagram sets the twelve zodiac signs in an outer band and the twenty-eight **lunar mansions** — the moon's nightly stations along the ecliptic — in an inner ring, each compartment labelled and ornamented. The whole reads as a working wheel of the sky.

## Significance
The lunar mansions were central to Islamicate astral magic: each of the twenty-eight stations had its own influence, image and use, and the *Picatrix* drew on them for timing talismans. This map, associated with the workshop of the Ottoman court historian Seyyid Lokman, shows the mansion-system as a precise calendrical-astrological instrument.

## For artists & game designers
A twenty-eight-station lunar wheel gives a fine-grained timing mechanic — each night-station with its own image and effect, layered over the twelve-sign year.

citations.text: Emilie Savage-Smith (ed.), *Magic and Divination in Early Islam* (2004).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Mandaean Scroll of Abathur (Diwan Abatur)
creator: Anonymous (Mandaean priestly scribe)
rights: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Ethan Doyle White). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A **Mandaean ritual scroll** illustrating the *Diwan Abatur*, the realm of the weigher-of-souls **Abathur** and the purgatories the soul passes after death.

## Iconography
The long scroll runs as a sequence of simple linear **drawings** of the *maṭarata* — the watch-houses or purgatories — and the throne of **Abathur**, who weighs souls on his scales. The schematic, register-by-register figures map the soul's astral ascent through stations of judgement.

## Significance
The Mandaeans of southern Iraq and Iran preserve a Gnostic religion with strong astral and stellar elements, long linked by outsiders to the 'Sabians' of the Qurʾan. Their cosmographic scrolls chart the soul's post-mortem journey through planetary watch-houses — a distinctive Near Eastern astral-eschatological tradition standing at the fringe of the Islamicate occult world.

## For artists & game designers
A register-by-register 'scroll of the afterlife journey' — a linear sequence of watch-houses and a soul-weighing gate — is a ready level-progression map drawn from a living tradition.

citations.text: E. S. Drower, *The Mandaeans of Iraq and Iran* (1937).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Astrological Figure from a Book of Nativities (after Abū Maʿshar)
creator: after Abū Maʿshar al-Balkhī
summary:
An illustrated leaf associated with the astrology of **Abū Maʿshar al-Balkhī** (Albumasar), the master of the *Kitāb al-Mawālīd* (Book of Nativities).

## Iconography
A robed figure — the astrologer or a personified planet — is set among the apparatus of **judicial astrology**: the casting of a birth-chart and the reading of planetary positions at the moment of nativity. The image stands for the science of computing a life from the heavens.

## Significance
Abū Maʿshar (787–886) was the most authoritative astrologer of the Islamic world; his works on nativities and great conjunctions, translated into Latin, made him the chief astrological authority of the medieval West. The *Kitāb al-Mawālīd* set out how the natal horoscope determines character and fate — the core practice of [[motif:horoscopy|judicial astrology]].

## For artists & game designers
The natal-chart astrologer is a perfect 'fate-reader' NPC: present a birth moment, receive a destiny — a built-in character-generation oracle.

citations.text: Charles Burnett & Keiji Yamamoto, *Abū Maʿšar on Historical Astrology* (2000).

title: Engraved Brass Astrolabe
creator: Anonymous instrument-maker
repository: Musée national de la Marine, Paris
rights: CC BY-SA 4.0 (photo Rama). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
An engraved **brass astrolabe**, the master instrument of Islamicate astronomy and astrology, photographed against white.

## Iconography
The disc shows a pierced **rete** — an openwork star-map with curved pointers to named bright stars and a ring for the ecliptic — turning over engraved latitude plates, with degree- and hour-scales around the rim. Every line is calculation made visible: time, star positions, and the casting of horoscopes.

## Significance
Perfected by Islamic makers from the ninth century, the astrolabe let an astrologer find the **ascendant** and the planets' places for any instant — the indispensable first move in casting a [[motif:horoscopy|nativity]]. A portable model of the heavens, it fused exact science with astral divination and passed directly into the medieval Latin West. This example is in the Musée national de la Marine, Paris.

## For artists & game designers
The rotating rete is a real analog-computer UI — a turnable star-dial that can drive a time-and-fate mechanic with genuine historical pedigree.

citations.text: David A. King, *In Synchrony with the Heavens* (2004–05).

title: The Magical Circle of Solomon (Hockley)
creator: Frederick Hockley and Henry Dawson Lea
rights: Public domain (Wellcome Collection). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A nineteenth-century English **Magical Circle of Solomon**, drawn in the Solomonic grimoire tradition that descends — through the *Picatrix* and the *Key of Solomon* — from the Near Eastern lore of Solomon as master of spirits.

## Iconography
A carefully ruled **protective circle** is inscribed with divine and angelic **names**, crosses and characters, the operator's standing-ground for conjuration. The design belongs to the Western Solomonic books, here in a clean draughtsman's copy by the occultist Frederick Hockley.

## Significance
The figure of **Solomon** as commander of *jinn* and demons is shared across Islamicate and European magic; the [[motif:seal of solomon|Seal of Solomon]] (the hexagram *khātam Sulaymān*) and the conjuring-circle pass between the traditions. This English drawing represents the late reception of that current — a Solomonic image whose roots lie in the Near Eastern science of binding spirits.

## For artists & game designers
The inscribed conjuring-circle is the canonical 'safe zone' of summoning magic — a ringed ground of names that protects the caster while the spirit is bound outside it.

citations.text: Owen Davies, *Grimoires: A History of Magic Books* (2009).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Orion (al-Jabbār), al-Ṣūfī's Book of Fixed Stars
creator: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Ṣūfī
summary:
The constellation **Orion** — *al-Jabbār*, 'the Giant' — from a 1125 Baghdad copy of al-Ṣūfī's *Kitāb ṣuwar al-kawākib al-thābita* (Book of the Fixed Stars).

## Iconography
A standing, robed **giant** holds a staff and a hide or sleeve, his catalogued **stars** marked on the body with their magnitudes. Following al-Ṣūfī's method, the figure embodies the constellation while serving as a labelled, usable star-map.

## Significance
Completed in 964 CE, al-Ṣūfī's treatise reconciled Ptolemy's catalogue with indigenous Arab star-lore and became the canonical source of constellation imagery across the Islamic world and Renaissance Europe. This early copy (Museum of Islamic Art, Doha, MS 2.1998) is among the finest surviving witnesses to his Orion. The fixed stars it maps were the raw material of both astronomy and astral magic.

## For artists & game designers
The 'giant whose body is a star-chart' is a vivid way to render a sky-figure that is at once a character and a navigational diagram.

citations.text: Emmy Wellesz, *An Islamic Book of Constellations* (1965).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Talismanic Scroll (Met DP119750)
creator: Anonymous
repository: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
rights: Public domain (CC0, Metropolitan Museum of Art). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A long **talismanic scroll** densely inscribed with Qurʾanic text, divine names and magic squares, made to be rolled into an amulet and carried.

## Iconography
The narrow strip is filled top to bottom with minute **calligraphy** — Qurʾanic verses, the [[motif:names of god|Beautiful Names of God]], prayers and gridded **magic squares** (*wafq*) — arranged in panels, roundels and ruled bands. The whole surface is charged text, the format echoing block-printed amulet scrolls.

## Significance
Talismanic scrolls applied the lettrist principle of *ʿilm al-ḥurūf* in portable form: rolled tight and worn or hung, they carried the protective virtue of sacred words against illness, the evil eye and danger in war. Many were block-printed from the medieval period, anticipating mass-produced amulets. This example is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

## For artists & game designers
A wearable 'scroll of protection' literally built from inscribed words — unrolling it reveals stacked sigils and squares, a satisfying physical artefact.

citations.text: Yasmine Al-Saleh, 'Amulets and Talismans from the Islamic World,' *Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History*, Met Museum (2010).

title: Arabic Diagram of Geomantic Figures Classification (15th c., from Madagascar)
place: Madagascar (Arabic geomantic tradition in the Indian Ocean world)
rights: Public domain. Sourced from OpenEdition Journals (L'Homme).
summary: A 15th-century Arabic diagram from Madagascar showing a classification of the geomantic figures (al-ashkal), demonstrating the remarkable geographical reach of Islamic raml. Geomancy arrived in Madagascar with Arab and Swahili traders and became the sikidy, a local divination system that adapted the 16 Islamic geomantic figures to a bamboo-stalk binary reading system. This diagram shows the figures in their classification scheme — probably grouped by element (fire, air, water, earth) and associated characteristics (entering/exiting, fortunate/unfortunate). The document evidences the transmission of Islamic occult science across the Indian Ocean trade networks, where it merged with indigenous divination traditions throughout coastal East Africa and the islands.

title: Geomantic Instrument — Detail 1: Rotating Disk (British Museum, 1241/42 CE)

summary: Detail view of the rotating inner disk of the 1241/42 CE Islamic geomantic instrument (British Museum OA+.2730, made by Muhammad ibn Khutlukh al-Mawsuli). The disk surface is engraved with the 16 geomantic figures (al-ashkal) arranged in their traditional sequence, each figure shown as a pattern of single and double dots that encodes a binary sequence — the same binary structure found in the Chinese I Ching hexagrams (transmitted through a parallel but independent system). The engravings show the figures labeled with their Arabic names (like Layla/Nusrat, Tariq, Jamaa, etc.), planetary correspondences, and elemental natures. The craftsmanship demonstrates that geomantic instruments were luxury objects as well as functional divination tools.

title: Geomantic Instrument — Detail 2: Outer Ring with Houses (British Museum, 1241/42 CE)

summary: Detail view of the fixed outer ring of the 1241/42 CE Islamic geomantic instrument (British Museum OA+.2730), showing the 12 astrological house divisions engraved in Arabic. Each house position names the domain it governs: the first house (life, body), the second (wealth), the third (siblings), and so on through the twelve houses of the astrological chart. The outer ring is the fixed 'sky' against which the rotating inner disk ('earth') is read — the instrument thus mechanizes the process of casting a geomantic chart and placing the derived figures into astrological houses. This integration of raml divination with judicial astrology (astrological house interpretation) is characteristic of the mature Islamic geomantic tradition, which reached Europe as 'geomancy' via the 12th-century Latin translations.

title: Geomantic Instrument — Egypt or Syria, 1241/42 CE (Full View)

creator: Muhammad ibn Khutlukh al-Mawsuli
rights: Public domain. Photographed at the British Museum by User:PHGCOM, 2009.
summary: The earliest precisely dated Islamic geomantic instrument (zairaja/darb al-raml), made by Muhammad ibn Khutlukh al-Mawsuli in Egypt or Syria in 629–630 AH (1241–42 CE). Now in the British Museum (OA+.2730). Made of engraved and inlaid brass, the instrument consists of a rotating inner disk (called the 'mother') mounted inside a fixed outer ring (the 'father'), both engraved with the 16 geomantic figures (al-ashkal), their Arabic letter correspondences, planetary associations, and the 12 astrological houses. To consult it, the querent makes binary marks in sand or paper, derives the four 'mothers', and rotates the disk to read the chart. The instrument synthesizes the combinatory logic of raml with astrological house interpretation in a single mechanical device. The signed and dated inscription makes this a key benchmark object for Islamic occult instrument-making. The full view shows both the rotating inner disk and the fixed outer ring with all 16 figure positions.

title: Arabic Geomantic Signs, Wheel of Life and Death, and Zodiac — Wellcome Collection
commons_file: File:Arabic geomantic signs, wheel of life and death, the zodiac Wellcome V0025818ER.jpg
summary: A European engraving depicting Arabic geomantic signs alongside a wheel of life and death and zodiac symbols, from the Wellcome Collection's iconographic collections. The engraving places the 16 geomantic figures in tabular form alongside circular diagrams — a zodiac wheel and a life/death wheel — demonstrating how Islamic geomancy was understood and represented in European occult literature. By the 17th–18th century, raml had entered European geomancy texts (including those by Robert Fludd and Christopher Cattan) as 'geomantia', where the Arabic figures were transliterated with Latin names (Albus, Puer, Cauda Draconis, etc.). This image documents the transmission of Islamic divinatory science into European esoteric tradition.

title: Geomantic Figures Detail — Wellcome Library MS Arabic 823
commons_file: File:Detail of Wellcome Library MS Arabic 823 showing geomantic figures.png
summary: A detail from Wellcome Library MS Arabic 823 showing individual geomantic figures (al-ashkal) in their characteristic notation: each figure is represented as a column of four rows, where each row contains either one dot (odd) or two dots (even). The 16 geomantic figures encode 16 distinct binary patterns — combinations of odd/even across 4 positions — making them the Islamic equivalent of the 64 I Ching hexagrams (each uses 6 binary positions). This detail captures the core notational convention that makes geomancy a binary calculus: the entire art rests on correctly reading and combining these simple dot-patterns. The figures shown here include some of the most commonly encountered forms.

summary: Page 19 from an anonymous Arabic treatise on geomancy (Wellcome Library MS Arabic 823), a 62-page manuscript of uncertain date (probably 17th–18th century). The page shows the characteristic format of Islamic geomancy MSS: Arabic prose with technical terminology, organized by question-type (the standard 12 astrological houses). Wellcome MS Arabic 823 is a practical manual for raml divination — it systematically explains how to derive geomantic figures from sand-marks, assign them to houses, and interpret the resulting shield chart. The Wellcome Library acquired it as part of its collection of manuscripts related to the history of medicine and scientific practice; geomancy was practiced by physicians as well as professional diviners in the Islamic world. title: Sagittarius (zodiac centaur), Kitāb al-Bulhān
creator: ʿAbd al-Ḥasan al-Iṣfāhānī (attrib.)
summary:
The sign **Sagittarius** rendered as the archer-centaur in the *Kitāb al-Bulhān*.

## Iconography
A **centaur** twists to draw a bow, the classical *qaws* (archer) of the zodiac. In the manuscript's scheme he is bound to **Jupiter**, lord of the sign, and set among the figures that personify the celestial houses.

## Significance
The archer-centaur descends from Hellenistic constellation imagery transmitted through Arabic astronomy and re-coloured in the Persianate idiom of Jalayirid Baghdad. The *Kitāb al-Bulhān*'s zodiac cycle is among the most influential medieval Islamic visualisations of the signs, mediating the iconography that later reached Europe.

## For artists & game designers
The self-aiming centaur archer is an archetype that reads instantly as a ranged-attacker class keyed to the fire element and Jupiter.

creator: Workshop of ʿAbd al-Ḥasan al-Iṣfāhānī (attrib.)
date: late 14th c. (Jalayirid Baghdad), with later additions
summary:
A folio from the *Kitāb al-Bulhān* (Book of Wonders), an illustrated compendium of astrology, divination and the spirit-world produced in Jalayirid Baghdad.

## Iconography
A central robed figure is flanked by dark, horned and clawed **devils** (shayāṭīn) with bestial heads and flaming or smoke-like bodies. The grouping belongs to the manuscript's gallery of [[motif:jinn|jinn]] and demon-kings, each ruler associated with a day, a planet and a colour, depicted to be recognised and ritually controlled.

## Significance
The *Kitāb al-Bulhān* (Oxford, Bodleian MS Or. 133) compiles the astrological-divinatory lore of Abū Maʿshar and others; its later Ottoman recensions systematised the demon-kings into a ruler-of-the-week scheme. Such images sit at the root of the talismanic tradition that fed, through the Picatrix, into European astral magic.

## For artists & game designers
A ready bestiary of named, colour- and planet-coded demon lords — a complete summoning roster with built-in correspondences.

title: Leo, Kitāb al-Bulhān
creator: ʿAbd al-Ḥasan al-Iṣfāhānī
summary:
The zodiac sign **Leo** as personified in the *Kitāb al-Bulhān*, where each sign is shown with its planetary lord and astrological dignities.

## Iconography
A striding **lion** is paired with a solar disc or enthroned figure, marking Leo as the domicile of the **Sun**. The painting follows the manuscript's habit of fusing the constellation-beast with the planet that rules it, so the image encodes both sign and rulership at a glance.

## Significance
The sign-and-planet pairings of the *Kitāb al-Bulhān* visualise the doctrine of [[motif:domicile|planetary domiciles]] central to Arabic and, in turn, Latin judicial astrology. The leaf is attributed to the painter ʿAbd al-Ḥasan al-Iṣfāhānī and survives in Bodleian MS Or. 133.

## For artists & game designers
A clean template for a 'sign + ruling planet' card set where each zodiac beast carries its governing power as a visible attribute.

title: Celestial Globe (silvered brass), Mughal India
creator: Anonymous instrument-maker
summary:
A silvered-brass **celestial globe** of the Mughal period, modelling the sphere of the fixed stars.

## Iconography
The globe's surface is engraved with the **constellation figures** and inlaid star-points, ringed by the great circles of the celestial sphere — equator, ecliptic and colures. The figures follow the al-Ṣūfī tradition, here rendered in metal to be turned in the hand.

## Significance
Islamicate celestial globes, often cast in a single seamless piece by the famed instrument-makers of Lahore, gave astronomers and astrologers a three-dimensional sky to model star risings and the framework of the horoscope. They are the sculptural counterpart of the star catalogue, and among the most refined scientific objects of the Mughal world.

## For artists & game designers
A hand-held star sphere is an evocative artifact — a turnable model of the whole heavens that an astrologer-character can consult.

citations.text: Emilie Savage-Smith, *Islamicate Celestial Globes* (1985).
