title: The Seven Sleepers of Ephesus, Folio from a Falnāma (Book of Omens)
creator: Anonymous (Safavid or Ottoman court workshop)
rights: Public domain (CC0, Metropolitan Museum of Art). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A large-format divinatory painting from a *Falnāma* (Book of Omens), showing the **Seven Sleepers of Ephesus** (Aṣḥāb al-Kahf) and their dog discovered in the cave.

## Iconography
The sleepers and the dog **Qiṭmīr** lie in a rocky cave while a royal party (here named for Alexander) arrives; the scene fills a monumental folio meant to face a page of omen-text. The brilliant palette and dramatic framing are typical of *Falnāma* divinatory paintings.

## Significance
The *Falnāma* was used for **bibliomancy**: a seeker opened the book at random, and the priest read the image and its facing prognostication as an omen of the querent's fortune. The genre flourished in the Safavid and Ottoman courts of the 16th–17th centuries. This folio is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

## For artists & game designers
A fully realised 'draw-a-card-of-fate' mechanic: one striking image paired to a fortune text, designed to be opened at random.

citations.text: Massumeh Farhad & Serpil Bağcı, *Falnama: The Book of Omens* (2009).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Geomantic Instrument of Muḥammad ibn Khutlukh al-Mawṣilī
creator: Muḥammad ibn Khutlukh al-Mawṣilī
summary:
The earliest known **geomantic instrument**, a brass device inlaid with silver and gold for mechanically generating the figures of *ʿilm al-raml* (the science of the sand).

## Iconography
The rectangular brass plate carries rows of rotating **dials** and sliders; turning them produces the sixteen four-line **geomantic figures** that would otherwise be made by marking dots in sand. Bands of inscription name the figures and their meanings around the apparatus.

## Significance
Geomancy (*ʿilm al-raml*) generated a chart of sixteen figures, read for divinatory answers much as a horoscope is read; it was among the most popular Islamic divinatory arts and passed to Europe as *geomantia*. Signed by Muḥammad ibn Khutlukh al-Mawṣilī and dated 639 AH (1241–42), this device (now British Museum) mechanised the casting of figures into a single elegant machine.

## For artists & game designers
A genuine 'fortune-telling machine' — turnable dials that output a fixed set of sixteen symbolic results, a ready divination minigame.

citations.text: Emilie Savage-Smith & Marion B. Smith, *Islamic Geomancy and a Thirteenth-Century Divinatory Device* (1980).

title: Alchemical Folio from a Miscellany of Magical and Alchemical Recipes
creator: Anonymous (Jābirian tradition)
summary:
An **alchemical** page from an Arabic recipe miscellany standing in the tradition of Jābir ibn Ḥayyān (Latin *Geber*).

## Iconography
Columns of Arabic procedural text set out an **alchemical** operation — proportions, substances and stages of the work — in the terse imperative of a laboratory recipe. Such pages rarely illustrate apparatus; the diagram is the procedure itself.

## Significance
The Jābirian corpus founded Arabic alchemy on the **sulphur–mercury** theory of metals and the doctrine of the *mīzān* (balance), aiming at the elixir that perfects base matter. Translated into Latin, this body of work became the bedrock of European alchemy. Working miscellanies like this one carried the operative tradition through the centuries.

## For artists & game designers
Procedural alchemical text is ideal flavour for a transmutation crafting system — terse, imperative, and convincingly technical.

citations.text: Syed Nomanul Haq, *Names, Natures and Things: The Alchemist Jābir ibn Ḥayyān* (1994).

title: Magic Bowl (magische schaal)
creator: Anonymous
rights: CC BY-SA 3.0 (Tropenmuseum / Nationaal Museum van Wereldculturen). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A **magic-medicinal bowl** of the Islamic type, inscribed inside and out to charge water with healing power.

## Iconography
The metal bowl is engraved with **inscriptions** — Qurʾanic verses, names, and often **magic squares** and figural or astrological signs — covering its interior. Water poured in and drunk was believed to absorb the virtue of the words and cure poisoning, fever, fright or the bite of a mad dog.

## Significance
The so-called **poison cup** or healing bowl is one of the most widespread instruments of Islamicate practical magic, made from the medieval period onward across Syria, Egypt, Iran and India. It applies the same lettrist principle as the talismanic shirt and the magic square: sacred and numerically potent text transfers power to the body, here through ingested water.

## For artists & game designers
An inscribed healing vessel — water charged by reading the bowl's words — is a tidy in-world potion mechanic with a clear ritual logic.

citations.text: H. Henry Spoer, 'Arabic Magic Medicinal Bowls,' *Journal of the American Oriental Society* (1935).

title: Shiʿi Stamped Amulet with Magic Square
creator: Anonymous
summary:
A stamped (block-printed) **amulet** carrying a **magic square** and pious inscriptions, of the kind produced for personal protection in the Shiʿi world.

## Iconography
The sheet bears a gridded numerical or lettered **magic square** (*wafq*) framed by lines of devotional text and the names of holy figures. The square's rows, columns and diagonals each sum to the same value — the property held to bind its protective force.

## Significance
The science of the *wafq* (magic squares) and the famous **budūḥ** square belong to *ʿilm al-ḥurūf*, the lettrist occult science systematised by al-Būnī. Squares were inscribed on paper, metal and cloth to heal, protect in childbirth, or guard against evil. Mass-stamped amulets like this democratised what had been an elite talismanic art.

## For artists & game designers
The magic square is a self-contained 'rune of power' glyph whose internal logic (equal sums) gives an in-world rationale for why it works.

citations.text: Emilie Savage-Smith (ed.), *Magic and Divination in Early Islam* (2004).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Persian Astrolabe (brass)
creator: Anonymous instrument-maker
rights: Public domain (CC0, Huntington Museum of Art). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A brass **astrolabe** from Iran, the master instrument of Islamicate astronomy and astrology.

## Iconography
The disc carries a pierced **rete** — a star-map with curved **pointers** to named bright stars and a ring for the ecliptic — rotating over engraved latitude plates. Scales of degrees and hours ring the rim. Every line serves computation: time, star positions, and the casting of horoscopes.

## Significance
The astrolabe, perfected by Islamic makers from the 9th century, let an astrologer find the **ascendant** and the positions of the planets for any moment — the indispensable first step of casting a nativity. As a portable model of the heavens it embodied the union of exact science and astral divination, and its design passed directly into medieval Europe.

## For artists & game designers
The rotating rete is a beautiful real-world 'analog computer' UI — a turnable star-dial that can drive a time-and-fate mechanic.

citations.text: Emilie Savage-Smith & others; David A. King, *In Synchrony with the Heavens* (2004–05).

title: Winged Angels (and Winged Feline and Cow), al-Qazwīnī's ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt
creator: after Zakariyyāʾ al-Qazwīnī
summary:
A folio from a manuscript of al-Qazwīnī's *ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt* (Wonders of Creation), showing two winged **angels** beside winged hybrid beasts.

## Iconography
Two robed, haloed **angels** (*malāʾika*) with broad feathered wings stand in a register above (or beside) a winged feline and a winged cow. The pairing places the angelic order of creation next to the marvellous beasts, both classes of the *ʿajāʾib* — the wonders God set in the cosmos.

## Significance
al-Qazwīnī's thirteenth-century cosmography organises the universe from the celestial spheres and their angels down through the elements, plants, animals and monstrous races. Its angelic hierarchy — angels governing the planets and the throne — supplied later Islamic and even European magical lore with a populated heaven. This leaf is LACMA M.88.213.8.

## For artists & game designers
The register layout 'angelic rank above, beast rank below' is a compact way to show a cosmic hierarchy in a single illustrated frame.

citations.text: Persis Berlekamp, *Wonder, Image, and Cosmos in Medieval Islam* (2011).

title: Cepheus and Corona Borealis (Wonders of Creation)
creator: Muḥammad ibn Muḥammad Shākir Ruzmah-ʾi Nāthānī, after al-Qazwīnī
summary:
A constellation page from an Ottoman copy of al-Qazwīnī's *ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt*, illustrating **Cepheus** and the **Corona Borealis** (Northern Crown).

## Iconography
A standing, robed figure personifies the constellation **Cepheus**, his body studded with marked stars; a jewelled crown-arc renders the **Corona Borealis**. The stars are placed on the figure to double as a usable star map and a mythic portrait.

## Significance
Islamic constellation imagery descends from al-Ṣūfī's *Book of Fixed Stars*, which reconciled Ptolemy's catalogue with indigenous Arab star-lore. Copyists such as Ruzmah-ʾi Nāthānī (this leaf dated 1717, Walters W.659) kept the tradition alive into the Ottoman period, preserving the figures that astrologers used to read celestial influence.

## For artists & game designers
The 'human body as constellation map' device — stars fixed to anatomy — is a striking way to render a sky chart that is also a character.

citations.text: Emmy Wellesz, *An Islamic Book of Constellations* (1965).
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Singer Ibrāhīm and the Jinn
creator: Anonymous (Persianate workshop)
summary:
A narrative miniature from the *ʿajāʾib* tradition depicting the singer Ibrāhīm's encounter with a **jinn**.

## Iconography
A seated musician meets a horned, fanged **jinnī** with a coloured, semi-bestial body. The composition follows the convention for human–spirit encounters: the supernatural being is marked off by horns, flame-like hair and unnatural skin tone, yet engages the human in a recognisable social scene.

## Significance
The jinn are intelligent, fiery beings of the *ʿajāʾib* and Qurʾanic cosmology, capable of music, mischief and bargains. Tales of musicians taught or tormented by jinn dramatise the porousness between the human and spirit worlds that the occult sciences sought to manage through talismans and incantations.

## For artists & game designers
A model for the 'mortal makes a deal with a spirit' set-piece — note how only a few visual cues (horns, hue, flame) flip an otherwise human figure into a jinn.

citations.text: Amira El-Zein, *Islam, Arabs, and the Intelligent World of the Jinn* (2009).

title: Ursa Major, al-Ṣūfī's Book of Fixed Stars
creator: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Ṣūfī
date: manuscript copy of a 964 CE text
summary:
The constellation **Ursa Major** (the Great Bear) from a copy of al-Ṣūfī's *Kitāb ṣuwar al-kawākib al-thābita* (Book of the Fixed Stars).

## Iconography
A naturalistic **bear** is drawn with its catalogued stars marked on the body, each labelled with magnitude. al-Ṣūfī characteristically shows each figure twice — as seen in the sky and as mirror-reversed on a celestial globe — fusing observation with the inherited Ptolemaic image.

## Significance
Completed in 964 CE, al-Ṣūfī's treatise corrected and updated Ptolemy's *Almagest* with fresh observations and Arab star-names, and became the canonical source for constellation imagery across the Islamic world and, eventually, Renaissance Europe. This copy is Bodleian MS Marsh 144. Its figures underlie almost all later Islamic celestial globes and star maps.

## For artists & game designers
The 'observed vs. mirrored' double-image is an elegant way to show the difference between the sky as seen and the sky as modelled on a globe.

citations.text: Emmy Wellesz, *An Islamic Book of Constellations* (1965).

title: Sagittarius, al-Ṣūfī's Book of Fixed Stars
creator: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Ṣūfī
date: manuscript copy of a 964 CE text
summary:
The constellation **Sagittarius** as figured in al-Ṣūfī's *Book of the Fixed Stars*.

## Iconography
The archer-**centaur** draws his bow, his catalogued **stars** marked along body and weapon. As elsewhere in al-Ṣūfī, the figure follows the Ptolemaic constellation while bearing the magnitudes and Arab star-names of his updated catalogue.

## Significance
al-Ṣūfī's constellation figures, fixed in the late tenth century, became the visual standard for the zodiac and the fixed stars throughout Islamic astronomy and astrology, and passed into European celestial cartography. Sagittarius, lord-house of Jupiter, was among the most-copied of his images.

## For artists & game designers
A reference-grade archer-centaur with stars mapped onto anatomy — a sky-figure that doubles as a labelled diagram.

title: Talismanic Shirt (jāmah)
creator: Anonymous
rights: Public domain (CC0, Metropolitan Museum of Art). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A **talismanic shirt** (jāmah / *kamīṣ*) covered in protective inscriptions, worn under armour for supernatural defence.

## Iconography
The whole surface is gridded with minute **calligraphy** — Qurʾanic verses, the ninety-nine Beautiful Names of God, prayers and **magic squares** (*wafq*) — arranged in roundels, cartouches and borders. Every field is a charged word; the garment is text made wearable.

## Significance
Such shirts were produced across the Islamic world from the 15th century onward, especially for soldiers, who believed the divine words would turn blades and arrows. They embody the central premise of Islamicate talismanic science: that the [[motif:names of god|names of God]] and numerically potent squares channel celestial and divine power onto the body. This example is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art.

## For artists & game designers
A literal 'armour of words' — a wearable that grants protection through inscribed text, ideal for an enchanted-garment item.

citations.text: Maryam Ekhtiar et al., *Masterpieces from the Department of Islamic Art* (2011).

title: Ilyās (Elijah) Given a Horse to Ascend (Chester Beatty T 414)
creator: Anonymous (Ottoman workshop)
summary:
An Ottoman manuscript painting (Chester Beatty MS T 414) showing the prophet **Ilyās** (Elijah) given a horse for his heavenly ascent, attended by **angels**.

## Iconography
The robed prophet receives a mount as winged, flame-haloed **angels** hover in a gold sky. The angelic figures follow the Persianate-Ottoman convention — multicoloured wings, scarf-like sashes — that renders the celestial hierarchy mediating between heaven and earth.

## Significance
Angels (*malāʾika*) populate Islamic cosmology as governors of the spheres, bearers of revelation and conductors of souls; the seven planetary heavens each have their presiding angel. Scenes of prophetic ascent visualise the ladder of heavens that astral and visionary lore mapped onto the cosmos. The leaf belongs to a 16th–17th-century Ottoman codex in the Chester Beatty Library.

## For artists & game designers
The 'mount granted for an ascent through the heavens' motif gives a clean visual grammar for a level-by-level vertical journey guarded by angelic figures.

title: Diagram of the Names of God (Kircher)
creator: Athanasius Kircher
summary:
Athanasius Kircher's circular diagram of the divine names, radiating the Hebrew names and epithets of God outward from the Tetragrammaton.

## Iconography
A radiant centre holds the [[motif:tetragrammaton|Tetragrammaton]] (YHWH); around it concentric bands and spokes distribute the many Hebrew names and attributes of God, arranged so that the seventy-two-fold and other name-systems fan out from the single ineffable Name like rays from a sun.

## Significance
Kircher (1602–1680), the Jesuit polymath, devoted parts of his *Oedipus Aegyptiacus* (1652–54) to Kabbalah, reading the divine names as a key linking Hebrew wisdom to a supposed universal Egyptian theology. His name-diagrams transmitted the Kabbalistic doctrine of the *Shem ha-Mephorash* — the explicit seventy-two-letter Name — to a wide learned audience as a centerpiece of Christian Kabbalah.

## For artists & game designers
A solar 'name-wheel' UI: a single sacred word at the hub spawning rays of lesser names, each a selectable invocation.

title: Ezekiel's Vision (William Blake)
creator: William Blake
summary:
William Blake's watercolour of Ezekiel's vision (ca. 1803–05, Museum of Fine Arts, Boston), a Romantic-visionary reading of the *Merkabah* chariot.

## Iconography
Blake renders the prophet beneath a great cloud of fire from which the four-faced [[motif:tetramorph|living creatures]] and the eyed wheels emerge, the human figures swept up in his characteristic flowing, energetic line. The composition fuses the biblical throne-vision with Blake's own mythology of imaginative apocalypse.

## Significance
Blake (1757–1827) read the prophets as fellow visionaries and made Ezekiel's chariot a touchstone of his art and poetry; for him the Merkabah was an emblem of the imagination's power to behold the eternal. The piece exemplifies the Romantic and later esoteric reception of Jewish throne-mysticism into Western visionary art. Kathleen Raine traced Blake's debts to the esoteric tradition.

## For artists & game designers
A reference for the 'ecstatic vision' register — chaotic fire, multiple faces, and swirling motion to depict a mind overwhelmed by the divine.

citations.text: Kathleen Raine, *Blake and Tradition* (1968).

title: Sefirot diagram from *Kabbala Denudata*
creator: Christian Knorr von Rosenroth
summary:
A sefirot diagram from Knorr von Rosenroth's *Kabbala Denudata*, presenting the ten emanations as a vertical Tree of divine attributes.

## Iconography
The ten [[motif:sefirot|sefirot]] descend in the familiar three-column arrangement — the pillars of mercy, severity, and the middle balance — each sphere labelled with its Hebrew name and joined to its neighbours by the twenty-two connective paths. The whole reads as a single articulated body of the divine emanations.

## Significance
This plainer Tree-diagram from the *Kabbala Denudata* shows the schematic form in which Lurianic and Zoharic teaching reached Christian Europe. The three-pillar layout it transmits became the standard template for the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn and virtually all later Western occult Kabbalah. Gershom Scholem traces the historical Kabbalah behind such schemata.

## For artists & game designers
The textbook three-pillar Tree — left/right/centre columns map neatly onto a balance of opposed forces with a reconciling middle path.

citations.text: Christian Knorr von Rosenroth, *Kabbala Denudata* (1677–84).
Gershom Scholem, *Kabbalah* (1974).

title: The Sefirot (Robert Fludd)
creator: Robert Fludd
summary:
Robert Fludd's engraved diagram of the sefirot, integrating the Kabbalistic Tree into his vast Christian-Hermetic cosmology of the two worlds.

## Iconography
The ten [[motif:sefirot|sefirot]] are arranged with their Hebrew names as a descending order of emanation from *Ein Sof* (the Infinite), often drawn as a flaming or radiant source above, down through the named powers to the material world. Fludd surrounds the scheme with Latin glosses tying each emanation to cosmological and theological correspondences.

## Significance
Fludd (1574–1637), the English Paracelsian physician and defender of the Rosicrucians, folded Kabbalah into the macrocosm-microcosm system of his *Utriusque Cosmi Historia* (1617–21). His sefirotic diagrams exemplify how 17th-century Christian Kabbalah read the Tree as a universal cosmogony rather than a specifically Jewish theology. Frances Yates and Joscelyn Godwin survey Fludd's project.

## For artists & game designers
A richly engraved 'cosmic ladder' — pair the ten emanations with descending planes or realms for a vertical world-map.

citations.text: Robert Fludd, *Utriusque Cosmi … Historia* (Oppenheim, 1617–21).
Joscelyn Godwin, *Robert Fludd* (1979).

title: The Golem of Prague (reproduction)
creator: Anonymous (after the Prague legend)
date: Modern reproduction of a legendary subject
summary:
A reproduction depicting the Golem of Prague, the clay man animated by holy letters in the most famous legend of practical Kabbalah.

## Iconography
The Golem is shown as a hulking humanoid of clay; in the legend it is brought to life by inscribing the word *emet* ('truth') on its forehead (or placing a name-inscribed *shem* in its mouth), and deactivated by erasing the *aleph* to leave *met* ('dead'). The [[motif:hebrew letters|letters]] themselves are the source of its life.

## Significance
The creation of a golem is rooted in the *Sefer Yetzirah*'s doctrine that letters can shape matter; medieval Ashkenazi pietists describe such rituals, and the legend later attached to Rabbi Judah Loew ben Bezalel (the Maharal) of 16th-century Prague, who supposedly made a golem to defend the Jewish community. Scholem's essay 'The Idea of the Golem' is the classic treatment; the tale became foundational for modern stories of artificial life.

## For artists & game designers
The original 'craftable construct': a servant golem activated and deactivated by inscribing or erasing a single word.

citations.text: Gershom Scholem, 'The Idea of the Golem,' in *On the Kabbalah and Its Symbolism* (1965).

title: Facsimile of Aaron's Breastplate (the *Hoshen*)
creator: Anonymous (facsimile)
date: Modern facsimile of an antique design
summary:
A facsimile of the *Hoshen*, the jewelled breastplate of the Israelite High Priest — Scripture's own oracular and protective object.

## Iconography
The breastplate is a square panel set with twelve gemstones in four rows, each engraved with the name of one of the [[motif:twelve tribes|twelve tribes]] of Israel. Folded within it lay the *Urim and Thummim*, the lots by which the divine will was inquired; the whole was worn over the heart of the High Priest when he entered the sanctuary.

## Significance
Described in Exodus 28, the *Hoshen mishpat* ('breastplate of judgement') was the Bible's licit oracle, and later Jewish and esoteric tradition treated its stones and the *Shem ha-Mephorash* hidden in it as a deeply magical object — the priest's stones flashing to give God's answer. It became a key reference for esoteric correspondences of stones, tribes, and the zodiac. (Stone identifications vary across sources; this is a reconstructed facsimile.)

## For artists & game designers
A wearable 'oracle item': twelve named gems whose lighting pattern answers yes/no questions — a built-in divination mechanic.

citations.text: Exodus 28:15–30 (the *Hoshen* and *Urim and Thummim*).

title: Plate from *Kabbala Denudata* (Knorr von Rosenroth)
creator: Christian Knorr von Rosenroth
rights: CC BY 4.0 (Wellcome Collection). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
An engraved plate from the *Kabbala Denudata* (Kabbalah Unveiled, 1677–84), Christian Knorr von Rosenroth's monumental Latin anthology of Kabbalistic — especially Lurianic — texts.

## Iconography
The plate diagrams the structure of the divine worlds: the [[motif:sefirot|sefirot]] and their groupings into the *partzufim* (configured 'faces' or personae of the godhead), labelled in Hebrew and Latin, mapping the Lurianic account of how the broken vessels are repaired and the divine countenance reconstituted.

## Significance
Knorr von Rosenroth (1636–1689) compiled the *Kabbala Denudata* at Sulzbach with the help of Francis Mercury van Helmont, translating the *Zohar* and Lurianic treatises of Isaac Luria and Hayyim Vital for a Christian readership. It was the single most influential channel of Jewish Kabbalah into early-modern Europe and, via 19th-century occultists, into the modern Western tradition. Allison Coudert's studies are standard.

## For artists & game designers
The 'advanced tech-tree' version of the Tree: nested faces and worlds, ideal for a layered cosmology where each tier reveals a deeper structure.

citations.text: Christian Knorr von Rosenroth, *Kabbala Denudata* (Sulzbach/Frankfurt, 1677–84).

title: Lilith (John Collier, 1892)
creator: John Collier
summary:
John Collier's 1892 painting *Lilith*, the Pre-Raphaelite image of the demonic first woman entwined with a serpent.

## Iconography
A nude woman stands embraced by a great serpent coiling about her body, her eyes closed in sensual reverie. Collier renders [[motif:lilith|Lilith]] as the archetypal *femme fatale* — beautiful, dangerous, and intimate with the serpent, conflating her with the temptation of Eden.

## Significance
In Jewish tradition — crystallized in the medieval *Alphabet of Ben Sira* — Lilith is Adam's rebellious first wife, who flees Eden and becomes a night-demon and slayer of infants, against whom childbirth amulets invoke the angels Senoy, Sansenoy, and Semangelof. The *Zohar* develops her as a queen of the demonic 'other side' (*sitra achra*). The 19th-century Romantic and esoteric revival, seen here, recast her as a symbol of dangerous female autonomy. Raphael Patai's *The Hebrew Goddess* surveys the Lilith myth.

## For artists & game designers
A ready archetype for a seductive demon-queen antagonist — beauty, serpent, and lethal allure in one figure.

citations.text: Raphael Patai, *The Hebrew Goddess* (1967), ch. on Lilith.
*Alphabet of Ben Sira* (medieval), on Lilith as Adam's first wife.

title: The Golem and Rabbi Loew (Mikoláš Aleš, 1899)
creator: Mikoláš Aleš
summary:
Mikoláš Aleš's 1899 illustration of the Golem with Rabbi Loew, made for a collection of Prague legends.

## Iconography
The Czech artist depicts the towering [[motif:golem|Golem]] beside or commanded by the figure of Rabbi Judah Loew (the Maharal), staging the moment of the creature's animation or service. The drawing belongs to the romantic-folkloric visual tradition that crystallized the Prague Golem as a national and literary legend.

## Significance
Mikoláš Aleš (1852–1913), a central figure of the Czech national revival, illustrated the Golem for the *Věnec pražských pověstí* ('Garland of Prague Legends'). Such turn-of-the-century images — alongside Hugo Steiner-Prag's and the 1915–20 Golem films — cemented the Maharal's golem in modern culture, ancestor of every fictional artificial being from the robot to the digital homunculus. The legend's Kabbalistic root remains the letter-animation of the *Sefer Yetzirah*.

## For artists & game designers
A period-accurate 'master and construct' composition for a summoner archetype — the small maker beside the giant he commands.

citations.text: *Věnec pražských pověstí* (Garland of Prague Legends, 1908), illustr. Mikoláš Aleš.

title: Ezekiel's Vision of the Merkabah (Merian)
creator: Matthäus Merian the Elder
summary:
Matthäus Merian's engraving of Ezekiel's vision of the *Merkabah* — the divine chariot-throne that founds the oldest current of Jewish mysticism.

## Iconography
The prophet beholds the four living creatures (the [[motif:tetramorph|tetramorph]] of man, lion, ox, and eagle), the gleaming 'wheels within wheels' (*ophanim*) studded with eyes, and above them the crystalline firmament bearing the sapphire throne and the radiant likeness of a human form — the *kavod*, the Glory of God.

## Significance
Ezekiel 1 and 10 supplied the foundational imagery of *Ma'aseh Merkabah*, the 'work of the chariot,' the visionary throne-mysticism of the Hekhalot literature in which adepts ascend through heavenly palaces to behold the enthroned Glory. Scholem treated Merkabah mysticism as the wellspring of the whole Kabbalistic tradition. Merian's engraving, from a Bible-illustration cycle, gave the vision its enduring early-modern visual form.

## For artists & game designers
A blueprint for a divine 'boss-encounter': spinning eyed wheels, a four-faced guardian, and an unapproachable throne of light.

citations.text: Gershom Scholem, *Jewish Gnosticism, Merkabah Mysticism, and Talmudic Tradition* (1960).

title: Mizrah papercut (Israel Dov Rosenbaum)
creator: Israel Dov Rosenbaum
summary:
An elaborate *Mizrah* papercut by Israel Dov Rosenbaum, marking the eastern wall toward which Jews turn in prayer.

## Iconography
The symmetrical cut-paper panel centres the word *Mizrah* ('east') amid a dense field of [[motif:hebrew letters|Hebrew]] verses, divine names, columns, crowns, and flanking lions or birds, frequently incorporating a [[motif:menorah|menorah]] and protective formulae. The intricate openwork doubles as both orientation marker and blessing for the home.

## Significance
The *Mizrah*, like the related *Shiviti*, situates the worshipper toward Jerusalem and gathers protective verses and holy names into a devotional object hung on the eastern wall. The papercut (*reyzele*) tradition flourished in 18th–19th-century Eastern European Jewish folk art, blending kabbalistic name-magic with decorative craft. Such works are studied in the scholarship on Jewish folk and ritual art.

## For artists & game designers
A decorative 'directional ward' — an intricate wall-piece that both signals orientation and confers a passive blessing on its room.

citations.text: Studies in Jewish papercut and folk art (e.g. Joseph & Yehudit Shadur, *Traditional Jewish Papercuts*, 2002).

title: Frontispiece of *Portae Lucis* (Gates of Light)
creator: Joseph Gikatilla; Latin trans. Paulus Ricius; woodcut after Leonhard Beck
summary:
The woodcut frontispiece of *Portae Lucis* (1516), Paulus Ricius's Latin translation of Joseph Gikatilla's *Sha'arei Orah* — the image that fixed the now-canonical 'Tree of Life' arrangement of the sefirot in the European imagination.

## Iconography
A bearded sage holds a tree formed of ten labelled spheres — the [[motif:sefirot|sefirot]] — linked by paths and crowned by *Keter*. Each sphere carries a Hebrew divine name and attribute, descending from the hidden crown through wisdom and understanding to the kingdom (*Malkhut*) at the base. The figure presents the diagram as a map of the godhead's self-revelation.

## Significance
Gikatilla's *Sha'arei Orah* (late 13th c.) is the great systematic treatise on the divine names attached to each sefirah. Ricius's 1516 Latin version made it a foundational text of Christian Kabbalah, and this woodcut — not any medieval Jewish source — is the direct ancestor of the schematic Tree of Life used by every later occultist. Gershom Scholem and Moshe Idel are the standard guides to the underlying Kabbalah.

## For artists & game designers
The master 'skill-tree' diagram: ten labelled nodes joined by paths, instantly legible as a system of progressive emanation or attribute-unlocks.

citations.text: Joseph Gikatilla, *Sha'arei Orah*; Latin *Portae Lucis*, trans. Paulus Ricius (Augsburg, 1516).

title: *Segulot* (charms) from the *Sefer Raziel*
creator: Anonymous (Sefer Raziel tradition)
summary:
A page of *segulot* — practical charms and remedies — from the *Sefer Raziel HaMalakh*, showing the everyday magic side of the Kabbalistic tradition.

## Iconography
The leaf combines Hebrew instructions with small magical figures: grids of letters, name-squares, and seals prescribed as [[motif:segulot|segulot]] for concrete ends — healing, protection in childbirth, success, safety in travel. Each charm pairs a holy name or letter-arrangement with a directive for how and when to write and use it.

## Significance
*Segulot* (literally 'remedies' or 'efficacious things') form the operative core of practical Kabbalah (*kabbalah ma'asit*), where the manipulation of divine names is held to act directly on the world. The *Sefer Raziel* was the most widely owned handbook of such charms in Ashkenazi and Sephardi homes. Trachtenberg and, more recently, Gideon Bohak study this tradition of Jewish name-magic.

## For artists & game designers
A recipe book of micro-charms: short letter-figures each tied to a single buff — a compact, lore-grounded consumables system.

citations.text: Gideon Bohak, *Ancient Jewish Magic: A History* (2008).
*Sefer Raziel HaMalakh* (printed editions).

title: The Sefirot (Paulus Ricius diagram)
creator: Paulus Ricius (Paulus Israelita)
summary:
A diagram of the ten sefirot associated with Paulus Ricius, the converted Jewish physician and Hebraist whose Latin translations carried Kabbalah into Christian learning.

## Iconography
The ten [[motif:sefirot|sefirot]] are set out as a branching scheme of named spheres, each glossed with its Hebrew title and divine attribute, joined by connective paths that trace the flow of emanation from the infinite down into the created world.

## Significance
Ricius (d. 1541), physician to Emperor Maximilian I, was among the most important transmitters of Kabbalah to Christian Europe; his *Portae Lucis* and *De arte cabalistica* dialogues gave Reuchlin, Agrippa, and later Christian Hebraists their working vocabulary of the sefirot. Diagrams in his orbit standardized the ordered list of emanations later absorbed into Renaissance occult philosophy. A clean alternate Tree layout — useful when you want the ten-node emanation system in a more austere, scholarly register.

title: Magical seals from the *Sefer Raziel HaMalakh* (1701)
creator: Anonymous (attributed to the angel Raziel)
summary:
A page of magical seals and sigils from the 1701 Amsterdam printing of the *Sefer Raziel HaMalakh* (Book of Raziel the Angel), the great compendium of practical Kabbalah.

## Iconography
The page sets out rows of [[motif:magic seals|seals]] — circles, grids, and looped *characteres* filled with Hebrew divine and angelic names — each keyed to a specific protective or curative purpose: guarding the home, easing childbirth, warding off the evil eye. They were meant to be copied onto parchment and worn or hung as amulets.

## Significance
Attributed to the angel Raziel who supposedly gave the book to Adam, the *Sefer Raziel* gathers older Hekhalot and magical material; its 1701 Amsterdam printing made it a hugely popular protective object — owning the book itself was believed to ward off fire and harm. It is the principal Hebrew source behind the Latin *Liber Razielis*. Joshua Trachtenberg's *Jewish Magic and Superstition* is the classic study.

## For artists & game designers
A sheet of distinct, purpose-tagged seals — each one a craftable amulet whose engraved glyph determines its protective effect.

citations.text: *Sefer Raziel HaMalakh* (Amsterdam, 1701).
Joshua Trachtenberg, *Jewish Magic and Superstition* (1939).

title: Circle diagram of the *Sefer Yetzirah*
creator: Monozigote (modern diagram after the Sefer Yetzirah)
summary:
A circular diagram illustrating the letter-cosmology of the *Sefer Yetzirah* (Book of Formation), the earliest and most enigmatic text of Jewish speculative mysticism.

## Iconography
The twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet are arranged around a circle, divided into the three 'mother' letters (Aleph, Mem, Shin), the seven 'double' letters, and the twelve 'simple' letters, mapping the alphabet onto the elements, planets, and zodiac. The figure shows creation as a combinatorial act of [[motif:hebrew letters|letters]].

## Significance
The *Sefer Yetzirah* (composed sometime between late antiquity and the early Middle Ages) teaches that God created the world through the ten *sefirot* and the twenty-two letters — the seed of all later Kabbalistic linguistic mysticism and of the Golem legend, in which letters animate matter. Scholem and, more recently, Tzahi Weiss study its text and reception. (This image is a modern explanatory diagram, not a historical manuscript page.)

## For artists & game designers
A combinatorial 'alphabet of creation' — letters as elemental building-blocks a player arranges to formulate spells or living constructs.

citations.text: *Sefer Yetzirah*; trans. and study by Aryeh Kaplan (1990).
Gershom Scholem, *Kabbalah* (1974).

title: Table of the Sephiroth and *Ain Soph* the Limitless One
creator: Anonymous (occult-revival compiler)
rights: CC BY 4.0 (Wellcome Collection). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A 19th-century table laying out the sefirot and the unmanifest *Ain Soph* (the Limitless), the kind of correspondence-chart that defined occult-revival Kabbalah.

## Iconography
The sheet tabulates the ten [[motif:sefirot|sefirot]] beneath *Ain Soph*, the boundless source above all emanation, listing for each sphere its Hebrew name, divine name, archangel, planetary or elemental correspondence, and attribute — a full grid of associations rather than a pictorial Tree.

## Significance
Such tables crystallize the synthesis worked by the 19th-century occult revival, which drew the historical Kabbalah of the *Zohar* and Luria through Knorr von Rosenroth and recast it as a system of universal correspondences. The Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn made these grids the backbone of their initiatory grade system and of modern ceremonial magic.

## For artists & game designers
A ready-made correspondence table — every node already keyed to a name, planet, and colour, perfect for a tightly-linked magic system.

title: Shiviti plate (Moshe Ganbash)
creator: Moshe Ganbash
summary:
An ornate *Shiviti* plate by Moshe Ganbash, the devotional-magical placard set before the prayer leader and hung in synagogues and homes.

## Iconography
The plate is built around the verse *Shiviti Adonai le-negdi tamid* ('I have set the Lord always before me,' Ps. 16:8) and a great [[motif:menorah|menorah]] whose seven branches are formed from the words of Psalm 67. Around and within it cluster the [[motif:tetragrammaton|Tetragrammaton]], divine names, and protective verses, often in fine Hebrew micrography.

## Significance
The *Shiviti*-menorah composition fuses contemplative focus with apotropaic power: gazing on the Name and the psalm-menorah was a meditative practice, while the accumulated holy names made the plate a protective amulet for the space it adorned. The form flourished in 18th–19th-century Sephardi and Ottoman Jewish communities. Such plates are studied within the literature on Jewish ritual art and *kavvanah*.

## For artists & game designers
A 'focus altar' object: a text-and-light icon that doubles as both a meditation point and a ward protecting the room.

title: The Tetragrammaton (Sephardi script)
creator: Anonymous
summary:
The Tetragrammaton — the four-letter ineffable Name of God, YHWH — rendered in a Sephardi Hebrew hand.

## Iconography
The four [[motif:hebrew letters|letters]] *Yod–He–Vav–He* are set out in formal script. As the *Shem ha-Meforash*, the Name was never pronounced aloud, substituted in reading by *Adonai*; its written form alone carried supreme sanctity and power.

## Significance
The [[motif:tetragrammaton|Tetragrammaton]] stands at the centre of Jewish and Kabbalistic name-mysticism: its letters were permuted, vocalized, and meditated upon (*tzeruf*) as the very engine of creation, and its derivatives — the 42-letter and 72-letter Names — underlie much of practical Kabbalah and the wider Western magical tradition that borrowed the Name as a word of power. Scholem and Moshe Idel examine the speculative mysticism of the Name.

## For artists & game designers
The ultimate 'true name' token — a single unspeakable word that anchors an entire name-based magic system.

title: The Sephirotic Tree of Life
creator: Kabbalistic tradition
summary:
The **Tree of Life** (*Etz Chaim*) — the central diagram of Kabbalah, mapping the ten **Sephirot**, the divine emanations through which the hidden Godhead (*Ein Sof*) brings the cosmos into being.

## Iconography
Ten spheres in three columns (the pillars of Mercy, Severity, and the Mean), joined by twenty-two paths (one per Hebrew letter). From Keter (Crown) to Malkhut (Kingdom) the figure charts the descent of divinity into matter — and the ladder of return.

## Significance
The Tree is the master-key of [[tradition:kabbalah]]: cosmology, psychology, and map of ascent at once. Through Pico and Reuchlin it entered Renaissance **Christian Cabala**, and later the Golden Dawn, where each sphere was assigned colours, gods, and tarot trumps. *(The first printed Christian Tree appeared in the* Portae Lucis, *1516.)*

## For artists & game designers
The ur-'skill tree' — ten nodes, three pillars, twenty-two paths. A natural magic-progression system or ritual diagram.

title: Amphitheatrum Sapientiae Aeternae - Portrait of Heinrich Khunrath
summary:
The engraved author-portrait that fronts Khunrath's *Amphitheatrum Sapientiae Aeternae* - the Hamburg-Hanau physician shown bust-length within an oval cartouche, hand resting on a table of instruments, ringed by a Latin legend and emblematic apparatus.

## Iconography
Khunrath appears in a ruff and scholar's gown, half-turned, his gaze level. The oval frame carries his name, age and titles; below, a base panel bears a motto and the apparatus of his double calling - the praying hands of the theosopher and the vessels of the laborant. The whole is cut in the dense, even line of late-sixteenth-century German copperplate work.

## Significance
The portrait fixes the *persona* on which the entire *Amphitheatrum* depends: the adept who is at once orator and operator, whose *ora et labora* (pray and work) governs the famous laboratory-oratory plate later in the book. It situates the great circular engravings as the visionary output of a named, historical seeker rather than anonymous emblem.

## For artists
A clean model for the 'learned magus' portrait type - oval frame, instruments of the art arrayed below, a Latin band closing the circle. Strip the period dress and it becomes a reusable template for any scholar-mage character card.

title: Amphitheatrum Sapientiae Aeternae - The Gate of Eternal Wisdom (Porta Amphitheatri)
summary:
One of the celebrated plates of the *Amphitheatrum*: a colossal pyramidal **gateway** of eternal wisdom, every surface of its sloping faces packed with engraved Latin and Hebrew sentences, rising from a rocky wilderness toward a radiant Name of God.

## Iconography
The gate is built not of stone blocks but of *words* - tier on tier of inscribed maxims that the eye must climb. Steps lead up to the threshold; flanking crags, distant towers and emblematic vignettes fill the landscape margins. At the apex the Tetragrammaton blazes in a glory, the goal toward which the whole structure ascends.

## Significance
This is Khunrath's *Porta* - the doorway of the amphitheatre of wisdom. Passage is conditional: only the reborn, the man who has joined prayer to labour, may mount the inscribed steps. The fusion of Hebrew divine names with Christian theosophy and alchemical ascent is the signature of Khunrath's Paracelsian-Kabbalistic synthesis.

## For artists
A ready-made 'temple of text' set-piece: a monumental architecture whose walls are legible scripture. Use it as a gated threshold a player must decipher rather than merely open - the obstacle is reading, not a lock.

title: Amphitheatrum Sapientiae Aeternae - The Mountain of the Adepts (Alchemical Landscape)
summary:
A wide engraved **panorama** - a rugged alchemical mountain riddled with caverns, terraces and toiling figures, ringed by the sea, that sets the labours of the *opus* into a single sweeping landscape of the Amphitheatrum.

## Iconography
Seekers climb, dig and gather across a broken massif; ships ride the shore; emblematic scenes nest in every fold of rock. Banners and cartouches carry Latin tags that name the stages. The composition reads as a map of the spiritual-chemical journey, foreground toil giving way to far horizons of attainment.

## Significance
Khunrath casts the great work as a geography to be traversed. The mountain is at once the matter to be mined and the soul's ascent - the *prima materia* dug from the earth and the inner labour that refines it. The crowded margins insist that no single act but a whole pilgrimage of labours is required.

## For artists
An overworld in one frame: a layered quest-map where each rocky niche is a sub-scene. Perfect reference for a hand-drawn region screen whose every crevice hides an encounter.

title: Amphitheatrum Sapientiae Aeternae - The Cosmic Rose and Star-Citadel of Pansophia
summary:
The great seven-pointed plate of the *Amphitheatrum* - a **heptagram star-citadel** enclosing a central rose, its bastioned points crowded with text, the whole laid out as a fortified cosmos of universal wisdom (Pansophia).

## Iconography
Seven angular bastions radiate from a centre where a mystic rose or sun is set; each point and curtain-wall is filled with inscribed sentences. The form quotes the early-modern star-fort even as it doubles as a rose-window and a seven-fold mandala. Emblematic figures and the divine Name occupy the margins and the heart.

## Significance
Seven is Khunrath's governing number - the planets, the days, the steps to wisdom - and here it shapes a *citadel* of Pansophia, the all-knowledge that must be both contemplated (the rose) and defended (the fort). The plate is the visual climax of his claim that sacred geometry, scripture and the great work converge on a single seven-fold figure.

## For artists
One of the most striking sevenfold mandalas in the whole alchemical corpus - a star-fort and a rose in one device. Use it as a level-map, a sigil, or the floorplan of a sanctum whose seven bastions are seven trials.

title: Amphitheatrum Sapientiae Aeternae - The Alchemical Wheel (Rota of the Work)
summary:
A round-format plate dominated by a great spoked **wheel** - the *rota* of the alchemical work - set in a rocky grotto and flanked by tablets of engraved Latin.

## Iconography
The wheel fills the centre, its radiating blades or vanes catching a light that breaks from above; around it, niched in the rock, stand inscribed panels and emblematic figures. The grotto setting frames the device like the mouth of a cave of mysteries.

## Significance
The wheel is Khunrath's emblem of **circulation** - the turning, recurrent labour by which matter is raised and returned, distilled and re-imbibed, until it is perfected. It restates in mechanical form the cyclical nature of the *opus*: the work is not a line but a revolution, repeated until completion.

## For artists
A mechanism that is also a meditation - a turning device whose every spoke is a stage. Good reference for an interactive 'wheel of stages' UI or a grotto puzzle whose solution is rotation.

title: Amphitheatrum Sapientiae Aeternae - The Cosmological Rose-Compass Disc
summary:
A finely cut circular **cosmological diagram** - a rose-compass disc with a radiant centre, concentric bands of inscription and emblematic markers set about its rim like the points of the winds.

## Iconography
A blazing centre throws rays outward through concentric rings; symbols, letters and small figures are ranged around the circumference like a compass-rose or wind-rose. The diagram is read inward and outward at once - periphery to centre, centre to periphery.

## Significance
Here Khunrath renders the doctrine of **correspondence**: the radiant divine centre and the encircling creation are bound in a single wheel, so that the macrocosm can be surveyed at a glance. It is a diagram of how the One disperses into the many and is gathered back - the cosmological grammar beneath the Amphitheatrum's whole programme.

## For artists
A self-contained mandala/compass usable as a navigation rose, a spell-selector dial, or an establishing 'cosmos' graphic. The radial symmetry makes it trivial to recolour and animate.

title: Amphitheatrum Sapientiae Aeternae - The Oratory and Laboratory (Oratorium-Laboratorium)
summary:
The most famous engraving of the *Amphitheatrum* and one of the iconic images of Western alchemy - the **oratory-laboratory** roundel, in which a single vaulted hall holds prayer and chemical work in one space.

## Iconography
On the left, beneath a richly hung tent-oratory, the adept kneels in prayer before an altar inscribed with divine names; on the right a fully equipped **laboratory** crowds the floor - furnaces, alembics, balances, books, a great central table strewn with instruments. A music-strewn table in the middle ground joins the two halves; the whole is held in a perfect circle, the room continuing seamlessly from altar to athanor.

## Significance
This is the visual definition of Khunrath's maxim **ora et labora** - *pray and work*. Spiritual and material operations are not merely allied but housed under one roof: the laboratory is a chapel and the chapel a laboratory. No image states more plainly the Paracelsian conviction that the great work is at once a devotion and an experiment.

## For artists
The definitive 'alchemist's workshop' interior - endlessly mined for game and book art. Use it as a hub-room reference: an oratory half and a furnace half a character can move between, each with its own verbs.

title: Amphitheatrum Sapientiae Aeternae - The Divine-Human Figure (Adam-Androgyne / Filius)
summary:
A broad allegorical plate built around a **central divine-human figure** - Khunrath's reborn Adam or androgyne - enthroned amid witnesses and columns of engraved text, gathering the book's theosophy into a single personified emblem.

## Iconography
A radiant central personage stands or sits at the heart of the sheet, flanked by attendant figures and by tall panels of inscribed Latin that frame the scene like the wings of a triptych. Light descends from above; emblematic devices and divine names crown the composition. The figure unites opposites - spirit and body, male and female, heaven and earth.

## Significance
The plate images the goal of the work as a *person*: the regenerated human, the *filius* in whom the macrocosm is reconciled. Khunrath's Christian-Kabbalistic alchemy ends not in a substance but in a deified, made-whole Adam - the conjunction accomplished in the seeker himself. The flanking text makes the figure a thesis to be read as much as seen.

## For artists
A textbook 'apotheosis' composition - central glorified figure, symmetrical witnesses, scriptural frame. Reuse it for an ascension cutscene or a final-boss/ally reveal where the character *is* the completed work.

title: Frontispiece to the Arca Noë (Noah's Ark)
work: Kircher's Universe — The Baroque Machine of Universal Knowledge
creator: Athanasius Kircher
summary:
The frontispiece of Kircher's *Arca Noë* (1675), his learned reconstruction of Noah's Ark — its dimensions, cargo, and engineering — as a problem in natural history.

## Iconography
The Ark rides the floodwaters beneath a rainbow of covenant, with the procession of animals, the dove, and emblems of the deluge; the title is borne aloft by allegorical figures of providence and the rescued creation.

## Significance
Kircher treated the Ark as a real vessel to be reverse-engineered: he calculated how Noah housed and fed every species, arranged the stalls deck by deck, and used the project to grapple with the new flood of animals reported from the Americas. It belongs to the early-modern effort to reconcile [[motif:natural history|natural history]] with sacred chronology, and pairs directly with his *Turris Babel*.

## For artists & game designers
A blueprint-minded 'great vessel' image — the Ark as an engineered ship full of compartments and creatures, ideal reference for an arcology-on-water or floating-bestiary setting.

citations.text: Natália Lozada Mendieta & others; cf. Findlen (ed.), *Athanasius Kircher* (2004).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Frontispiece to the Ars Magna Lucis et Umbrae (The Great Art of Light and Shadow)
work: Kircher's Universe — The Baroque Machine of Universal Knowledge
creator: Anonymous engraver after Athanasius Kircher
summary:
The allegorical title plate of Kircher's *Ars Magna Lucis et Umbrae* (1646), his sprawling treatise on optics, light, shadow, and the metaphysics of illumination.

## Iconography
Light descends from a radiant divine source at the top, distributed by allegorical figures bearing mirrors and emblems of sacred and natural light, while shadow gathers below. Beams, reflections, and personifications of the powers of light fill the composition.

## Significance
Kircher's optics treatise ranged from sundials and burning mirrors to the [[motif:optics|magic lantern]] and the projection of images, all framed by a Neoplatonic theology in which physical light is the visible trace of divine light. It is a key Baroque text linking natural magic, scientific optics, and Hermetic metaphysics — the book in which Kircher described early image-projection devices.

## For artists & game designers
The definitive 'light vs. shadow' allegory plate — a directly usable emblem for any setting that personifies illumination and darkness as cosmic forces.

citations.text: Daniel Stolzenberg (ed.), *The Great Art of Knowing: The Baroque Encyclopedia of Athanasius Kircher* (2001).
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Horoscopium Catholicum (Universal Sundial), Ars Magna Lucis et Umbrae
work: Kircher's Universe — The Baroque Machine of Universal Knowledge
creator: Athanasius Kircher
summary:
The *Horoscopium Catholicum Societatis Iesu* — Kircher's 'universal sundial,' an emblematic olive tree whose branches tell the hour simultaneously across all the houses of the Jesuit order worldwide.

## Iconography
A spreading tree rises at the center, each of its branches inscribed with the name of a Jesuit province; the tree casts a shadow that functions as a [[motif:gnomon|gnomon]], the dial-lines and place-names converting the single shadow into the local time of provinces from Rome to China.

## Significance
From the *Ars Magna Lucis et Umbrae*, this plate fuses gnomonics (the science of sundials) with Jesuit self-image: the Society of Jesus as a single tree casting one shadow over the whole globe. It exemplifies Kircher's habit of turning a scientific instrument into a theological emblem.

## For artists & game designers
An elegant 'world clock' conceit — one shadow telling many times at once. Reuse it as a map-spanning device that synchronizes distant locations through a single celestial pointer.

citations.text: John Edward Fletcher, *A Study of the Life and Works of Athanasius Kircher* (2011).
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Hanging Gardens / City of Babylon, Turris Babel
work: Kircher's Universe — The Baroque Machine of Universal Knowledge
creator: Athanasius Kircher
summary:
A reconstruction of ancient Babylon and its monuments from Kircher's *Turris Babel*, his attempt to recover the lost grandeur of the first great city.

## Iconography
The walled metropolis of Babylon is laid out in antiquarian detail — the terraced hanging gardens, monumental gates, and towering structures rendered as a Baroque vision of Mesopotamian splendour, drawn from classical descriptions rather than archaeology.

## Significance
Kircher reconstructed Babylon, its [[motif:hanging gardens|hanging gardens]], and the surrounding empire as the cradle of the post-Babel nations and of idolatry. Lacking real archaeological data (Mesopotamia would not be excavated for another two centuries), he synthesized Herodotus, scripture, and his own conjecture into an influential and wholly imaginative cityscape.

## For artists & game designers
A richly imagined ancient megacity — terraces, gardens, and ziggurats — perfect as a reference plate for a fallen Bronze-Age capital.

citations.text: Daniel Stolzenberg, *Egyptian Oedipus: Athanasius Kircher and the Secrets of Antiquity* (2013).
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Tower of Babel (Frontispiece), Turris Babel sive Archontologia
work: Kircher's Universe — The Baroque Machine of Universal Knowledge
creator: after Athanasius Kircher (Rijksmuseum impression)
summary:
The title plate of Kircher's *Turris Babel* (1679), his scholarly reconstruction of the Tower of Babel and the post-diluvian dispersal of nations and languages.

## Iconography
The great tower rises in receding storeys toward heaven amid the bustle of its construction, while above, divine intervention scatters the builders — the moment of the confusion of tongues — and below, the founder Nimrod and the genealogy of nations are set out.

## Significance
In *Turris Babel* Kircher calculated that a tower reaching the moon was physically impossible, using the engineering question as a frame for his theories on the origin of languages, idolatry, and the spread of peoples after the Flood. It connects to his Egyptological work, where he traced [[motif:hieroglyphs|hieroglyphs]] and pagan religion back to a single primordial wisdom corrupted at Babel.

## For artists & game designers
The definitive Baroque Babel: a spiralling mega-structure mid-construction under divine wrath — a complete set-piece for any 'doomed tower' or 'fractured-language' scenario.

citations.text: Daniel Stolzenberg, *Egyptian Oedipus: Athanasius Kircher and the Secrets of Antiquity* (2013).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Frontispiece to China Monumentis Illustrata (China Illustrated)
work: Kircher's Universe — The Baroque Machine of Universal Knowledge
creator: Athanasius Kircher
summary:
The engraved frontispiece of Kircher's *China Monumentis Illustrata* (1667), Europe's most influential early compendium on the marvels, religions, and antiquities of China.

## Iconography
The Jesuit missionaries Matteo Ricci and Adam Schall present a map of China beneath the radiant name of God; emblems of the mission and of Chinese learning frame the scene, asserting the Society of Jesus's role as interpreter of the East.

## Significance
*China Illustrata* shaped the European image of China for generations, mixing reliable Jesuit reportage with Kircher's own theories — including his claim that Chinese characters and religion descended from Egyptian [[motif:hieroglyphs|hieroglyphs]] and the dispersal after Babel. It is a foundational and famously distorting text of early Sinology and of the Hermetic 'universal wisdom' thesis.

## For artists & game designers
A model 'explorer's title page': two scholars unrolling a map of a distant empire under divine sanction — instantly legible as the opening of a voyage to the unknown East.

citations.text: Florence C. Hsia, 'Athanasius Kircher's China Illustrata: An Apologia Pro Vita Sua,' in Findlen (ed.), *Athanasius Kircher* (2004).
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Nestorian Stele of Xi'an, China Illustrata
work: Kircher's Universe — The Baroque Machine of Universal Knowledge
creator: Athanasius Kircher (after the Xi'an monument)
summary:
Kircher's reproduction of the Nestorian Stele of Xi'an — the Tang-dynasty monument recording the arrival of the Church of the East in China — with its Chinese and Syriac text.

## Iconography
The tall stele is shown with its surmounting cross and dense columns of Chinese characters, flanked by lines of Estrangela Syriac script; Kircher's plate transcribes and annotates the inscription for European readers.

## Significance
The stele (erected 781 CE, rediscovered c. 1625) proved that Christianity had reached China nearly a millennium before the Jesuits. Kircher published the first full European transcription and Syriac decipherment in *China Illustrata*, making the monument a centerpiece of debates over the antiquity of the [[motif:church of the east|Church of the East]] and the global reach of the faith.

## For artists & game designers
A real artifact of 'lost early Christianity in the East' — a bilingual stone whose decipherment can anchor a historical-mystery plot about a forgotten church.

citations.text: Michael Keevak, *The Story of a Stele: China's Nestorian Monument and Its Reception in the West, 1625–1916* (2008).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Map of the Routes to Cathay (Tabula Geodoborica), China Illustrata
work: Kircher's Universe — The Baroque Machine of Universal Knowledge
creator: Athanasius Kircher
rights: CC BY 2.0 (Biblioteca de la Universidad de Sevilla). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
Kircher's *Tabula Geodoborica* — a map charting the overland routes by which various travellers reached Cathay (China), compiled for *China Illustrata*.

## Iconography
A broad map of Central Asia and the approaches to China traces the itineraries of Jesuit and earlier travellers across mountains and deserts, with place-names, routes, and cartographic ornament marking the long road to Cathay.

## Significance
Kircher assembled this map from the reports of missionaries such as Bento de Góis and Johann Grueber to demonstrate that Cathay and China were one land — and to display the Jesuit network as a global instrument of knowledge. It belongs to the same encyclopedic impulse as his [[motif:hydrophylacia|hydrographic maps]]: turning correspondence into cartography.

## For artists & game designers
An authentic overland-route map for a perilous journey east — usable as a campaign map of caravan trails through mountains and deserts.

citations.text: Florence C. Hsia, 'Athanasius Kircher's China Illustrata,' in Findlen (ed.), *Athanasius Kircher* (2004).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Portrait of Athanasius Kircher, Aged 53
work: Kircher's Universe — The Baroque Machine of Universal Knowledge
creator: A. Frölich (engraver)
motifs: the last man who knew everything
summary:
An engraved portrait of Athanasius Kircher, the Jesuit polymath, inscribed as 'aged 53' — the man behind this entire encyclopedic universe.

## Iconography
Kircher is shown in three-quarter view in Jesuit habit, set within an oval frame with a Latin inscription naming him *P. Athanasius Kircherus Fuldensis, è Societate Jesu*, in the formal convention of a learned author's portrait.

## Significance
Born in Geisa near Fulda in 1602, Kircher became the most famous scholar of his age — Egyptologist, geologist, musicologist, Sinologist, and inventor — earning the later epithet 'the last man who knew everything.' His vast, often credulous output made him both celebrated and, after the rise of stricter scientific method, a byword for over-ambitious erudition. This likeness fixes the face that presided over the [[motif:musaeum kircherianum|Roman College museum]].

## For artists & game designers
A ready 'archetypal polymath' portrait — the learned friar in an oval frame, instantly castable as the author-figure or quest-giver of an esoteric library.

citations.text: Paula Findlen (ed.), *Athanasius Kircher: The Last Man Who Knew Everything* (2004).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Title Page to the Mundus Subterraneus, Volume Two (1664)
work: Kircher's Universe — The Baroque Machine of Universal Knowledge
creator: after Athanasius Kircher (Rijksmuseum impression)
summary:
The allegorical engraved title page to the second volume of Kircher's *Mundus Subterraneus*, the great encyclopedia of the underground world.

## Iconography
A Baroque architectural frame is animated with personifications of the natural sciences, glimpses of mountains opened to reveal their fiery and watery interiors, and the divine light descending from above to order the subterranean cosmos. The book's title is set within a draped cartouche.

## Significance
Kircher's frontispieces are themselves arguments: they stage the claim that the hidden machinery of the earth ([[motif:geocosmos|the geocosmos]]) is governed by divine providence and legible to the Jesuit natural philosopher. The *Mundus Subterraneus* (1664–65) was Kircher's most influential scientific work, shaping early geology, mineralogy, and the study of volcanoes for a century.

## For artists & game designers
A textbook Baroque title-card: ornate frame, allegorical figures, and a peek at the world-machine behind the curtain — copy the layout for any 'forbidden encyclopedia' cover.

citations.text: Paula Findlen (ed.), *Athanasius Kircher: The Last Man Who Knew Everything* (2004).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Frontispiece to Latium (The Antiquities of Latium)
work: Kircher's Universe — The Baroque Machine of Universal Knowledge
creator: Athanasius Kircher
summary:
The title plate of Kircher's *Latium* (1671), his antiquarian survey of the region of Rome — its ancient sites, ruins, and topography.

## Iconography
An allegorical figure of Latium presides over a landscape strewn with classical ruins, aqueducts, and monuments; river-gods, antiquities, and emblems of the region's mythic past frame the title.

## Significance
*Latium* combined genuine topographical and antiquarian observation with Kircher's taste for myth, tracing the area's history back to a Saturnian golden age. It is part of his broader effort to recover the sacred and esoteric past inscribed in the monuments of Italy, a counterpart to his Egyptological and [[motif:hieroglyphs|hieroglyphic]] researches closer to home.

## For artists & game designers
A model 'allegory of a haunted landscape' — a personified land surrounded by its own ruins, useful as cover art for a region defined by its lost antiquity.

citations.text: Harry B. Evans, *Exploring the Kingdom of Saturn: Kircher's Latium and Its Legacy* (2012).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Frontispiece to the Magnes, sive de Arte Magnetica (The Magnetic Art)
work: Kircher's Universe — The Baroque Machine of Universal Knowledge
creator: Athanasius Kircher
summary:
The title plate of Kircher's *Magnes, sive de Arte Magnetica* (1641), in which magnetism becomes the master-metaphor for the force that binds the whole universe.

## Iconography
A chain of being descends from the divine source above, linking the spheres, the elements, and earthly creatures as if by magnetic attraction; emblems of the loadstone and its powers frame the central title.

## Significance
Kircher generalized the magnet into a universal principle: a *vis magnetica* of sympathy and attraction running through cosmos, society, and soul, ultimately rooted in divine love drawing all things to itself. The treatise blends genuine experiment on loadstones with Hermetic doctrines of [[motif:sympathy|sympathy and antipathy]], and was a key channel for the magnetic philosophy of the seventeenth century.

## For artists & game designers
A strong emblem for a world held together by an unseen attractive force — the 'great chain' rendered as literal magnetism, useful for any cosmology of binding sympathies.

citations.text: Martha Baldwin, 'Magnetism and the Anti-Copernican Polemic,' *Journal for the History of Astronomy* (1985).
Wikimedia Commons

title: A Magnetic Device, Magnes sive de Arte Magnetica
work: Kircher's Universe — The Baroque Machine of Universal Knowledge
creator: Athanasius Kircher
summary:
An engraved demonstration plate from Kircher's *Magnes*, illustrating one of the magnetic apparatuses he used to dramatize the hidden power of the loadstone.

## Iconography
A carefully drawn instrument combines magnetized elements with mechanical parts — figures, dials, or floating pointers driven by concealed magnets, presented in the diagrammatic style of a working demonstration.

## Significance
Kircher delighted in 'magnetic marvels': clocks, oracular statues, and floating figures secretly moved by loadstones, which he used both to entertain visitors to the [[motif:musaeum kircherianum|Roman College museum]] and to argue for a magnetic order of nature. Such devices blur the line between conjuring trick, scientific demonstration, and theological emblem — natural magic in the precise period sense.

## For artists & game designers
Period blueprints for 'automated wonders' — statues and clocks that move by invisible attraction. Excellent reference for a wizard's hall of self-moving curiosities.

citations.text: Paula Findlen (ed.), *Athanasius Kircher: The Last Man Who Knew Everything* (2004).
Wikimedia Commons

title: A Winged Dragon, Mundus Subterraneus
work: Kircher's Universe — The Baroque Machine of Universal Knowledge
creator: Athanasius Kircher
summary:
One of the dragons Kircher catalogued among the genuine inhabitants of the underground world, depicted as a clawed, bat-winged serpent at rest on the ground.

## Iconography
A long-bodied dragon with membranous wings, a crested head, and taloned forelimbs lies coiled across the engraving's foreground, rendered with the sober precision of a natural-history specimen rather than a heraldic flourish.

## Significance
Kircher devoted a serious section of the *Mundus Subterraneus* to *dracones*, treating reports of dragons in Alpine caves and Swiss mountains as credible natural history alongside fossils and minerals. The plates sit at the hinge between Renaissance bestiary and emerging empirical science — the same author who measured Vesuvius also gravely diagrammed the anatomy of dragons.

## For artists & game designers
A period-authentic 'naturalist's dragon': drawn like a real animal, not a mythic monster — ideal for a cryptozoology codex or a bestiary that insists its dragons are simply rare fauna.

citations.text: Daniel Stolzenberg, *The Great Art of Knowing: The Baroque Encyclopedia of Athanasius Kircher* (2001).
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Underground Water-Reservoirs (Hydrophylacium Asiae Majoris), Mundus Subterraneus
work: Kircher's Universe — The Baroque Machine of Universal Knowledge
creator: Athanasius Kircher
summary:
Kircher's map of the *hydrophylacia* of greater Asia — the hidden water-cisterns he imagined locked inside mountains, the source of every river and spring.

## Iconography
A geographical map of Asia is overlaid with great mountain ranges drawn in profile, each cut open to reveal a bulging subterranean lake. From these reservoirs rivers pour out across the continent, while the surrounding ocean feeds the system through underground channels.

## Significance
The watery counterpart to Kircher's fire-chambers: in his living [[motif:geocosmos|geocosmos]], a vast circulatory system drew seawater inland, desalinated it in mountain cisterns, and discharged it as rivers — an early, if fanciful, attempt to explain the hydrological cycle and the perennial flow of springs. Kircher gathered reports from Jesuit missionaries worldwide to populate such maps.

## For artists & game designers
A gorgeous cartographic device: a real-looking continent map whose mountains hide secret inland seas — perfect for a quest that traces a river back to an impossible source.

citations.text: Paula Findlen (ed.), *Athanasius Kircher: The Last Man Who Knew Everything* (2004).
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Subterranean Fire-Reservoirs (Systema Ideale Pyrophylaciorum), Mundus Subterraneus
work: Kircher's Universe — The Baroque Machine of Universal Knowledge
creator: Athanasius Kircher
summary:
Kircher's diagram of the *pyrophylacia* — the great fire-chambers he believed honeycombed the body of the earth, all fed from a central blaze at the planet's core.

## Iconography
A spherical earth is shown in cutaway, its interior threaded with branching ducts and rounded reservoirs of flame. A vast central fire occupies the core, from which smaller fire-pockets radiate outward and vent at the surface as volcanoes spitting smoke and flame across the encircling landscape.

## Significance
In the *Mundus Subterraneus* (1665) Kircher proposed a living [[motif:geocosmos|geocosmos]] whose circulating fire and water mirrored the human body's humors. The central fire connected to surface volcanoes — a theory he claimed to confirm by being lowered into the smoking crater of Vesuvius in 1638. Though pre-Newtonian and wrong in detail, it is a founding image of geology as a systematic science of the earth's interior.

## For artists & game designers
A ready-made 'world's molten heart' schematic: a planet veined with fire-rivers and magma vaults that any subterranean dungeon or volcano-god setting can borrow wholesale.

citations.text: John Edward Fletcher, *A Study of the Life and Works of Athanasius Kircher* (2011).
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Musaeum Kircherianum (Kircher's Museum at the Roman College)
work: Kircher's Universe — The Baroque Machine of Universal Knowledge
creator: Filippo Buonanni (after the Kircher collection)
summary:
A view of the *Musaeum Kircherianum*, the celebrated cabinet of curiosities Kircher assembled at the Collegio Romano, from Filippo Buonanni's 1709 catalogue.

## Iconography
A long gallery is crowded floor-to-ceiling with marvels: obelisks and Egyptian antiquities, hanging instruments, stuffed animals, automata, mirrors, and machines, with visitors dwarfed by the encyclopedic accumulation.

## Significance
The museum was the physical embodiment of Kircher's project — to gather all of creation into one room as a [[motif:wunderkammer|theatre of the world]]. It became a compulsory stop on the Grand Tour and a model for the encyclopedic museum, blending genuine antiquities with magnetic tricks and reconstructed wonders. Buonanni curated and catalogued it after Kircher's death.

## For artists & game designers
The ur-'museum of impossible objects': a single room that contains obelisks, automata, and beasts. Use the engraving directly as a level map for a collector-mage's hall.

citations.text: Paula Findlen, 'Scientific Spectacle in Baroque Rome: Athanasius Kircher and the Roman College Museum,' *Roma Moderna e Contemporanea* (1995).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Frontispiece to the Musurgia Universalis (The Harmony of the World)
work: Kircher's Universe — The Baroque Machine of Universal Knowledge
creator: Anonymous engraver after Athanasius Kircher
summary:
The allegorical frontispiece of Kircher's *Musurgia Universalis* (1650), the encyclopedia in which all of music is read as a reflection of the harmony binding the cosmos.

## Iconography
The heavens open to reveal a celestial choir and the Pythagorean cosmos as a great stringed instrument; personifications of harmony, allegories of the senses, and the music of nature surround a central scene where divine order is tuned like an instrument. Apollo and emblems of the muses appear among the registers.

## Significance
Kircher's *Musurgia* presents the universe as music: the [[motif:harmony of the spheres|harmonia mundi]] in which God composed creation as a fugue, and the world is held together by ratio and consonance. The work contained early experiments in mechanical composition and influential discussions of acoustics, the 'music of the spheres,' and even animal sound.

## For artists & game designers
The canonical 'cosmos as instrument' image — directly usable for any setting where reality is tuned, played, or held together by sacred music.

title: *De Lapide Philosophico* — Third Figure (detail): stag and unicorn
creator: 'Lambspring' (engraver anonymous; text ed. Nicolas Barnaud / Lucas Jennis)
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: per source — cropped detail of the Tertia Figura; Wikimedia/Internet Archive derivative]
rights: Public domain. From the Musaeum Hermeticum. Via Internet Archive.
summary:
A tightly cropped detail of the famous **Third Figure** of 'Lambspring', isolating just the stag and the unicorn within the engraved frame, stripped of the surrounding letterpress. It is the same scene whose motto runs *In Corpore est Anima & Spiritus* — "in the Body are Soul and Spirit."

## Iconography
The close crop fills the field with the two animals on their rocky shelf among trees: the antlered stag at left, the spiral-horned unicorn at right, a wooded landscape behind. Without the Latin verse the image reads purely as a heraldic confrontation of beasts.

## Significance
This is the most reproduced single image from the whole 'Lambspring' series, and such detail-crops are how it most often travels — as a self-contained emblem of [[motif:soul|Soul]] and [[motif:spirit|Spirit]] hidden in the body of the matter, the two volatile principles awaiting their union. Its clean silhouette has made it a favourite source for bookplates, tattoos, and occult design.

## For artists & game designers
The cleanest possible reference for the stag-and-unicorn motif — high-contrast, frameless, ready to drop into an emblem, loading screen, or crest.

title: *De Lapide Philosophico* — Tenth Figure: the salamander in the fire
creator: 'Lambspring' (engraver anonymous; text ed. Nicolas Barnaud / Lucas Jennis)
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: per source — Internet Archive scan of the Musaeum Hermeticum (Frankfurt, 1625)]
rights: Public domain. From the Musaeum Hermeticum. Via Internet Archive.
summary:
The **Decima Figura**: a salamander lying unharmed in a blaze while a near-naked man rakes the fire. The verse runs *Salamandra vivit in igne, / Ignisque hanc mutavit in optimum colorem* ("the salamander lives in the fire, and the fire has changed it to the best colour"); the gloss reads *Reiteratio, gradatio & melioratio Tincturae, vel Lapidis Philosophorum: Augmentatio potius intelligatur* — the reiteration, gradation and bettering of the Tincture or Stone; understand rather its augmentation.

## Iconography
Flames and rolling smoke fill the left of the cut; the spotted salamander rests within the fire while a labourer, loin-clad, leans in with a long rake to tend the blaze. Hills and a tower close the background.

## Significance
The salamander — the creature fabled to live in and feed on fire — is the perfected [[motif:tincture|Tincture]] that not only survives the flame but is improved by it. This plate marks the stage of [[motif:multiplication|augmentation and multiplication]]: the Stone, once made, is strengthened and increased by repeated firing, 'changed to the best colour'.

## For artists & game designers
A fire-dwelling salamander tended by a stoker — a vivid emblem of an item that grows stronger when burned; ready material for a forge-upgrade or fire-immunity icon.

title: *De Lapide Philosophico* — Ninth Figure: the King attains his kingdom
creator: 'Lambspring' (engraver anonymous; text ed. Nicolas Barnaud / Lucas Jennis)
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: per source — Internet Archive scan of the Musaeum Hermeticum (Frankfurt, 1625)]
rights: Public domain. From the Musaeum Hermeticum. Via Internet Archive.
summary:
The **Nona Figura**: a crowned King enthroned upon an arched bridge or pavilion, holding the orb-and-cross. The verse proclaims *Dominus sylvarum potitus est suo regno, / Et ab infimo ad supremum gradum conscendit* ("the Lord of the forests has gained his kingdom, and has climbed from the lowest to the highest degree"). The closing line, *Intellige primum Gradum Tincturae vere apparuisse*, declares that the first true degree of the Tincture has now appeared.

## Iconography
The King sits robed and crowned in a canopied seat raised on a masonry bridge above a river and walled town; he bears the globus cruciger of sovereignty. The whole rises 'from the lowest to the highest', the architecture echoing the ascent named in the verse.

## Significance
With this plate the bestial and avian transformations give way to the human kingly imagery of the later figures: the matter, having passed through death and reconciliation, is exalted to royalty — the first appearance of the [[motif:tincture|Tincture]]. The forest-creatures are mastered ('Lord of the forests'), and the Work crowns its perfected substance as a King.

## For artists & game designers
A coronation/ascension beat — enthroned monarch with orb on a bridge over a town; ideal as a mid-game 'the work bears fruit' tableau or a level-up throne scene.
