title: *De Lapide Philosophico* — Second Figure: the knight and the dragon (Putrefactio)
creator: 'Lambspring' (engraver anonymous; text ed. Nicolas Barnaud / Lucas Jennis)
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: per source — Internet Archive scan of the Musaeum Hermeticum (Frankfurt, 1625)]
rights: Public domain. From the Musaeum Hermeticum. Via Internet Archive.
summary:
The **Secunda Figura** of 'Lambspring': an armoured knight confronts a winged dragon at the edge of a forest. The verse warns *Hic celeriter animadvertite / Nigram feram in sylva* ("here swiftly mark the black beast in the wood"); the single word beneath the cut names the operation — **PUTREFACTIO**.

## Iconography
A man-at-arms in plate armour, sword raised and round shield advanced, lunges at a scaly winged dragon that rears among rocks and trees, a lake and hilltop town beyond. The dragon is the *fera nigra*, the black beast lurking in the green wood of the matter.

## Significance
The dragon here is the [[motif:prima-materia|prime matter]] in its raw, poisonous, undifferentiated state, and the knight's assault is the violence of [[motif:putrefaction|putrefaction]] — the blackening (*nigredo*) by which the old body is broken down so that something new may arise. In the 'Lambspring' grammar the forest is the secret vessel and the dragon the matter that must first be slain before it can be exalted.

## For artists & game designers
A ready-made boss encounter: armoured hero versus a forest dragon, with the alchemical subtext that the 'death' here is a necessary stage of transformation, not a final defeat.

title: *De Lapide Philosophico* — Fourteenth Figure: the King sweating in his bed
creator: 'Lambspring' (engraver anonymous; text ed. Nicolas Barnaud / Lucas Jennis)
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: per source — Internet Archive scan of the Musaeum Hermeticum (Frankfurt, 1625)]
rights: Public domain. From the Musaeum Hermeticum. Via Internet Archive.
summary:
The **Decimaquarta Figura**: the old King lies in a curtained canopy bed, his crowned head on the pillow, sweating profusely. The verse explains *Hic vehementer sudat Pater, / Oleum & recta Tinctura Philosophorum ex eo promanat* ("here the Father sweats vehemently; the Oil and the true Tincture of the Philosophers flow forth from him").

## Iconography
A richly carved four-poster bed dominates the chamber, drapes drawn back; the bearded King reclines beneath the covers, a pair of slippers and a vessel set on the boards below, daylight at the window. The scene is quiet, domestic, convalescent — the sweat itself the precious product.

## Significance
Having devoured his Son, the King falls sick and undergoes the 'sweating cure': from his fevered body issue the *Oleum* and the true [[motif:tincture|Tincture]] of the Philosophers — the dissolution and exudation that yield the medicine. It is the penultimate plate, the death-and-passion of the old king turning at last to the regenerated life of the final figure.

## For artists & game designers
A convalescence/transmutation-by-sweat scene — sickbed of a king from whom a precious essence is distilled; useful for a healing-ritual beat or an alchemical 'extract the cure' moment.

title: *De Lapide Philosophico* — Thirteenth Figure: the King devours his Son
creator: 'Lambspring' (engraver anonymous; text ed. Nicolas Barnaud / Lucas Jennis)
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: per source — Internet Archive scan of the Musaeum Hermeticum (Frankfurt, 1625)]
rights: Public domain. From the Musaeum Hermeticum. Via Internet Archive.
summary:
The **Decimatertia Figura**, one of the most arresting plates of the series: the old crowned King draws his kneeling Son toward his mouth as if to consume him, while the winged Guide stands by, gesturing. The verse states it baldly — *Hic Pater devorat Filium: / Anima & Spiritus e corpore promanant* ("here the Father devours the Son: Soul and Spirit issue forth from the body").

## Iconography
In a curtained, arcaded palace the bearded King sits enthroned on a raised dais and bends to engulf the young King who kneels before him; the grey winged *ductor* presides at left, a townscape framed in the arches. The act is intimate and terrible at once.

## Significance
This cannibal kingship is a famous alchemical topos — the old fixed body reabsorbing the volatile son so that [[motif:soul|Soul]] and [[motif:spirit|Spirit]] may be driven out and the matter reduced once more. It belongs to the same imaginative family as Saturn devouring his children and the 'green lion devouring the sun'; here it is the penultimate death before the sweating cure and the final reunion.

## For artists & game designers
A shocking yet meaningful image — a king consuming his heir as a stage of renewal; potent material for a sacrifice mechanic or a dark transformation cutscene where loss is the path to power.

title: *De Lapide Philosophico* — Fourth Figure: the two lions become one
creator: 'Lambspring' (engraver anonymous; text ed. Nicolas Barnaud / Lucas Jennis)
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: per source — Internet Archive scan of the Musaeum Hermeticum (Frankfurt, 1625)]
rights: Public domain. From the Musaeum Hermeticum. Via Internet Archive.
summary:
The **Quarta Figura**, in which two lions stand together in a forest clearing, their tails seeming to merge into a single intertwined coil. The verse exclaims *Est summum portentum / Ex duobus leonibus unum fieri* ("it is the greatest marvel that from two lions one is made"), and the motto below: *Spiritus & Anima sunt conjungendi & redigendi ad corpus suum* — "Spirit and Soul are to be joined and brought back to their body."

## Iconography
Two lions — one often read as male and one female — pace side by side between framing trees, a wooded landscape behind, their serpentine tails twining toward one. The doubling-into-one is the visual argument of the plate.

## Significance
The two lions restate the central drama of the Work: the [[motif:soul|Soul]] and [[motif:spirit|Spirit]] (the fixed and the volatile) must be reunited and led back into the [[motif:prima-materia|body]] from which they were drawn. The lion is a classic alchemical sign of a fierce, devouring agent — here doubled and reconciled, prefiguring the kingly conjunctions of the later plates.

## For artists & game designers
Twin-lion heraldry with a built-in 'fusion' motif — excellent for a sigil, a paired-boss design, or an emblem signalling the merging of two powers into one.

title: *De Lapide Philosophico* — First Figure: the two fish in the sea
creator: 'Lambspring' (engraver anonymous; text ed. Nicolas Barnaud / Lucas Jennis)
date: 1625 (engraving; first issued 1599, here in the Musaeum Hermeticum)
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: per source — Internet Archive scan of the Musaeum Hermeticum (Frankfurt, 1625)]
rights: Public domain. From the Musaeum Hermeticum. Via Internet Archive.
summary:
The opening plate of the celebrated *De Lapide Philosophico* of 'Lambspring' — the **Prima Figura**, two great fish swimming in a calm sea. The Latin verse above reads *Pisces duos in nostro mari natare* ("two fishes swim in our sea"), and the motto below glosses it plainly: *Mare est Corpus, duo Pisces sunt Spiritus & Anima* — "the Sea is the Body, the two Fishes are Spirit and Soul."

## Iconography
Across a wide bay two large fish glide just beneath the surface, while in the middle distance a sailing-boat and ships ride at anchor before a walled coastal town backed by hills. The engraving is small, square, and set into a letterpress page with its figure-number and printer's signatures showing.

## Significance
The two fish are the foundational pair of the whole sequence: the volatile and the fixed, [[motif:soul|Soul]] and [[motif:spirit|Spirit]], held within the one watery [[motif:prima-materia|Body]] of the Work. The 'Lambspring' tract — a German verse cycle ascribed to a half-legendary author, latinized by Nicolas Barnaud and given these fifteen plates — was among the most reprinted of all alchemical emblem books, gathered into the *Musaeum Hermeticum* of Lucas Jennis. The motif of two fishes in one sea recurs across the tradition as a sign of the dual principles that must be reconciled.

## For artists & game designers
A serene establishing shot — calm bay, ships, twin fish below the waterline — ideal as a title card or the first beat of an alchemical quest where two principles must later be joined.

title: *De Lapide Philosophico* — Eleventh Figure: Father, Son and the grey Guide
creator: 'Lambspring' (engraver anonymous; text ed. Nicolas Barnaud / Lucas Jennis)
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: per source — Internet Archive scan of the Musaeum Hermeticum (Frankfurt, 1625)]
rights: Public domain. From the Musaeum Hermeticum. Via Internet Archive.
summary:
The **Undecima Figura**: three figures walk hand in hand by a shore — an aged, long-bearded Father, a young crowned Son in armour, and a winged grey-robed Guide. The verse reads *Pater, Filius, cum ductore sibi sunt juncti manibus* ("Father, Son, with the guide, are joined to one another by the hands"), glossed *Corpus, Spiritus & Anima, hic subintelligitur* — "here Body, Spirit and Soul are to be understood."

## Iconography
The grey-bearded Father leads at left with a sceptre, the youthful Son between, and the winged Guide (the *ductor*) at right; behind them a castle, the sea with a ship, and a craggy mountain. The three are linked by their joined hands.

## Significance
The human triad makes literal the inner cast of the whole Work: [[motif:prima-materia|Body]] (Father), [[motif:spirit|Spirit]] (Son) and [[motif:soul|Soul]], led by the grey-cloaked Guide — the philosophical Mercurius or inner teacher who conducts the substances through their stages. This figure opens the closing 'family drama' of the series: father and son guided toward death, ascent and reunion.

## For artists & game designers
A three-character party led by a hooded mentor — an archetypal escort/journey grouping with built-in symbolic roles (body, spirit, soul) for a guided-quest sequence.

title: *De Lapide Philosophico* — engraved title page (1677 Frankfurt edition)
creator: 'Lambspring' (engraver anonymous; latinized by Nicolas Barnaud)

shelfmark: title page (Francofurti, apud Hermannum à Sande, 1677)
summary:
The engraved title page of a separate Frankfurt edition of the 'Lambspring' tract — *LAMBSPRINCK, Nobilis Germani Philosophi Antiqui Libellus De Lapide Philosophico, e Germanico versu Latine redditus, per Nicolaum Barnaudum Delphinatem Medicum … Francofurti, Apud Hermannum à Sande. MDCLXXVII.* Recorded as a title page rather than one of the fifteen Figures.

## Iconography
Beneath the letterpress title stands a small engraved vignette: a robed, grey-bearded philosopher holding a tall sceptre or staff beside a domed, arch-mouthed furnace or athanor, ruins at left and a comet or star streaking the sky. The figure is the type of the ancient sage-adept presiding over the Work.

## Significance
This leaf documents the bibliographic frame of the famous emblem cycle: a German verse libellus attributed to 'Lambspring', a noble ancient German philosopher, rendered into Latin by the physician Nicolas Barnaud. The same fifteen plates circulated both here and within Lucas Jennis's *Musaeum Hermeticum* — the gathering that carried 'Lambspring' to its lasting fame.

## For artists & game designers
A period title-page vignette — sage with staff beside an athanor under a comet — handy as an authentic book-cover plate, a loading screen, or a 'master alchemist' character reference.

title: *De Lapide Philosophico* — Fifteenth Figure: Father and Son made one
creator: 'Lambspring' (engraver anonymous; text ed. Nicolas Barnaud / Lucas Jennis)
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: per source — Internet Archive scan of the Musaeum Hermeticum (Frankfurt, 1625)]
rights: Public domain. From the Musaeum Hermeticum. Via Internet Archive.
summary:
The **Decimaquinta Figura**, the closing plate: three figures sit enthroned together beneath a draped canopy — a crowned young King at left, the winged grey Guide at centre, and the old crowned Father-King at right. The verse seals the cycle: *Hic Pater & Filius in unum sunt copulati, / Ut simul in aeternum manent* ("here Father and Son are coupled into one, that together they may abide for ever").

## Iconography
The regained Son, restored after his devouring and the King's sweating cure, is enthroned in equal majesty beside the Father, the Guide between them as the bond of their union; an arcaded hall opens behind. The three sit in calm, frontal symmetry — the resolved triad.

## Significance
The final figure is the *coniunctio* perfected: [[motif:prima-materia|Body]], [[motif:spirit|Spirit]] and [[motif:soul|Soul]] reunited and fixed 'into one' for ever — the completed Stone. Father and Son, after death and rebirth, reign together, mediated by the Guide (Mercurius). The whole 'Lambspring' sequence has carried the reader from the two fish in the sea to this eternal, threefold kingship — among the most quoted resolutions in the emblem-literature of alchemy.

## For artists & game designers
A triumphant 'reunion / completion' tableau — restored heir, elder king and mediating guide enthroned together; a natural finale screen or victory tableau for an alchemical narrative.

title: *De Lapide Philosophico* — Fifth Figure: the wolf and the dog
creator: 'Lambspring' (engraver anonymous; text ed. Nicolas Barnaud / Lucas Jennis)
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: per source — Internet Archive scan of the Musaeum Hermeticum (Frankfurt, 1625)]
rights: Public domain. From the Musaeum Hermeticum. Via Internet Archive.
summary:
The **Quinta Figura**, the wolf and the dog locked in combat before a river town. The verse runs *Lupus & Canis sunt in una domo / Postremo tamen ex his unum fit* ("a wolf and a dog are in one house, yet at last from these one is made"); the motto below names the work: *Mortificatio, & albificatio, corporis conjunctique cum Anima & Spiritu imbibitio* — "the mortification and whitening, and the imbibing of the conjoined body with Soul and Spirit."

## Iconography
Under a tree at the bank of a wide river two beasts grapple — a lean wolf and a domestic dog rearing against each other — with a walled town and church on the far shore. They share, as the verse says, one house.

## Significance
The wolf is the volatile, untamed principle and the dog the fixed, domesticated one — antimony and the metal, or the fierce and the gentle mercury — set at strife so that out of their mortal struggle one purified substance ('whitened', *albificatio*) may emerge. This pairing of grey wolf and dog is one of the most quoted images in later alchemical literature, taken up notably in the Mylius and Ripley traditions.

## For artists & game designers
A dynamic two-animal clash with a clear meaning — opposed natures fighting toward a single outcome; useful for a transformation cutscene or a 'tame the beast' mechanic.

title: *De Lapide Philosophico* — Eighth Figure: the bird of Hermes and its mate
creator: 'Lambspring' (engraver anonymous; text ed. Nicolas Barnaud / Lucas Jennis)
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: per source — Internet Archive scan of the Musaeum Hermeticum (Frankfurt, 1625)]
rights: Public domain. From the Musaeum Hermeticum. Via Internet Archive.
summary:
The **Octava Figura**, the so-called bird of Hermes: a large winged bird in a forest stoops over a smaller one. The verse names them *Duae aves sunt nobiles & magni pretii, / Corpus & Spiritus, alterum consumit* ("two birds are noble and of great price, Body and Spirit, the one consumes the other"). The long gloss directs that the body be set again 'for digestion' in horse-dung or a bath, the white work done and the red prepared by art — *praeparaturque sic Lapis Philosophorum*.

## Iconography
Beneath a broad tree a great spread-winged bird bends toward a lesser bird on the ground, a coastal landscape with sailing ships beyond. One devours the other — the larger nature absorbing the smaller.

## Significance
This is the 'bird of Hermes' motif familiar from the Ripley *Cantilena* — 'eating his wings to make him tame' — here the [[motif:spirit|Spirit]] and [[motif:prima-materia|Body]] in which one consumes the other so that a single, more perfect nature results. The accompanying text explicitly carries the Work toward the white and then the red, naming the goal as the Philosophers' Stone itself.

## For artists & game designers
A dramatic predation image with a redemptive meaning — the greater bird absorbing the lesser to become whole; strong material for an absorption or fusion mechanic.

title: *De Lapide Philosophico* — Twelfth Figure: the ascent to the mountain-top
creator: 'Lambspring' (engraver anonymous; text ed. Nicolas Barnaud / Lucas Jennis)
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: per source — Internet Archive scan of the Musaeum Hermeticum (Frankfurt, 1625)]
rights: Public domain. From the Musaeum Hermeticum. Via Internet Archive.
summary:
The **Duodecima Figura**: the winged Guide and the crowned Son stand together on a high mountain peak beneath a sun, a crescent moon and a field of stars. The verse reads *Alius mons Indiae in vase jacet, / Quem Spiritus & Anima, utpote filius & dux, conscenderunt* ("another mountain of India lies in the vessel, which Spirit and Soul, namely the son and the guide, have climbed").

## Iconography
From a soaring crag the two figures gesture upward; the radiant sun blazes at left, the moon hangs at right amid stars, and a vast landscape of bays, towns and ships spreads far below. The 'mountain of India' is, the verse says, contained *in vase* — within the alchemical vessel.

## Significance
The ascent figures the sublimation and exaltation of the volatile principles: [[motif:spirit|Spirit]] (the Son) and [[motif:soul|Soul]] (or, with the Guide, the conducting Mercurius) rise to the summit. The pointed reminder that the whole cosmic mountain lies 'in the vessel' is the tract's insistence that this grand spiritual ascent is enacted, materially, inside the sealed flask.

## For artists & game designers
A summit-attainment vista — two figures on a peak under sun, moon and stars over a whole world below; an excellent 'ascension' or chapter-climax establishing shot.

title: *De Lapide Philosophico* — Seventh Figure: the two birds in the forest
creator: 'Lambspring' (engraver anonymous; text ed. Nicolas Barnaud / Lucas Jennis)
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: per source — Internet Archive scan of the Musaeum Hermeticum (Frankfurt, 1625)]
rights: Public domain. From the Musaeum Hermeticum. Via Internet Archive.
summary:
The **Septima Figura**: two birds in a great forest tree, one rising in flight and one perched. The verse reads *Duae aves in sylva nominantur, / Cum tamen saltem una intelligatur* ("two birds are named in the wood, though only one is to be understood"); the gloss: *Mercurius saepius sublimatus, tandem figitur, ut non amplius aufugere & avolare per vim ignis possit; Toties enim sublimatio reiteranda, quousque fixus fiat* — mercury, often sublimed, is at last fixed so that it can no longer fly off by force of fire.

## Iconography
A tall oak fills the right of the frame; one bird beats upward through its branches while a second sits below, and a snail creeps across a fallen log in the foreground — the slow, fixed against the swift, volatile. A wooded valley with a church recedes at left.

## Significance
The two birds are one and the same [[motif:mercury|Mercurius]] in two states — volatile (flying) and fixed (perched) — the verse insisting that though *two* are named, only *one* substance is meant. The figure teaches the repeated sublimation by which the volatile spirit is at last 'fixed' so it can no longer escape the fire. The earth-bound snail is a quiet emblem of that final fixity.

## For artists & game designers
A neat 'one thing, two states' visual — bird in flight versus bird at rest, with a snail for slowness; useful where a single resource toggles between volatile and stable forms.

title: *De Lapide Philosophico* — Third Figure: the stag and the unicorn in the forest
creator: 'Lambspring' (engraver anonymous; text ed. Nicolas Barnaud / Lucas Jennis)
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: per source — Internet Archive scan of the Musaeum Hermeticum (Frankfurt, 1625)]
rights: Public domain. From the Musaeum Hermeticum. Via Internet Archive.
summary:
The **Tertia Figura** — one of the best-loved of all alchemical emblems — showing a stag and a unicorn meeting in a wood. The verse instructs *In sylva cervum & unicornu latere* ("in the forest lie hidden a stag and a unicorn"), and the motto below declares *In Corpore est Anima & Spiritus* — "in the Body are Soul and Spirit."

## Iconography
In a clearing fringed with trees an antlered stag stands at left and a long-horned unicorn at right, facing one another across rocky ground, with a glimpse of a pool and distant building behind. The two beasts are emblems of the same hidden pair the fish announced.

## Significance
The stag is the [[motif:soul|Soul]] and the unicorn the [[motif:spirit|Spirit]] (or, in other readings, the reverse) — the volatile powers concealed within the body of the matter, the forest again standing for the vessel. This figure is the source of countless later borrowings; it became a near-heraldic shorthand for the alchemical conjunction of opposites and circulates widely in modern occult and design contexts.

## For artists & game designers
Iconic heraldic pairing — stag and unicorn confronting in a glade — directly usable as an emblem, sigil, faction crest, or the visual key to a 'reconcile the two beasts' puzzle.

title: *De Lapide Philosophico* — Preface leaf with the Lambspring arms (rebus crest)
creator: 'Lambspring' (engraver anonymous; text ed. Nicolas Barnaud / Lucas Jennis)
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: per source — Internet Archive scan of the Musaeum Hermeticum (Frankfurt, 1625)]
rights: Public domain. From the Musaeum Hermeticum. Via Internet Archive.
summary:
The **Praefatio** leaf of the 'Lambspring' tract, carrying its small engraved coat-of-arms above the prose. The verse heading reads *Lambsprinck vocor, natus ex nobili familia, / Et hoc stemma gero cum laude & jure* ("I am called Lambspring, born of a noble family, and I bear this crest with praise and by right"). Recorded honestly as a text page with its heraldic device rather than as one of the fifteen Figures.

## Iconography
A shield bearing a ram or sheep is surmounted, in the crest, by a second lamb standing upon scrolling mantling — a visual rebus on the name 'Lambspring' (Lamm + Sprinck, the leaping lamb). Letterpress preface fills the rest of the leaf, with the page-number and signatures showing.

## Significance
The arms are the device of the half-legendary 'Lambspring', the supposed German author whose name the rebus crest puns upon. The tract claims noble descent and learned authority — *Philosophiam legi, & bene intellexi* ('I have read philosophy and understood it well'). The leaf frames the fifteen emblems that follow and anchors the work's persona of an ancient German *philosophus*.

## For artists & game designers
A period rebus coat-of-arms — leaping lamb crest over a ram shield — usable as an authentic heraldic device, faction crest, or decorated front-matter prop.

title: *De Lapide Philosophico* — Sixth Figure: the dragon devouring its tail
creator: 'Lambspring' (engraver anonymous; text ed. Nicolas Barnaud / Lucas Jennis)
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: per source — Internet Archive scan of the Musaeum Hermeticum (Frankfurt, 1625)]
rights: Public domain. From the Musaeum Hermeticum. Via Internet Archive.
summary:
The **Sexta Figura**: a great winged dragon coiled in a forest, biting at its own tail — the ouroboros. The verse declares *Hoc vere est magnum miraculum & cita fraus, / In venenoso Dracone summam medicinam inesse* ("this is truly a great marvel and a swift deceit, that in the venomous dragon lies the highest medicine"); the gloss below: *Mercurius recte & chymice praecipitatus vel sublimatus, in sua propria Aqua resolutus & rursum coagulatus* — mercury rightly precipitated or sublimed, dissolved in its own water and again coagulated.

## Iconography
A scaly, bat-winged dragon turns its long neck back upon itself amid trees and underbrush, the forest opening to hills beyond. The serpent-circle is the self-consuming, self-renewing matter.

## Significance
The poisonous dragon that nonetheless holds the *summa medicina* is the philosophical [[motif:mercury|Mercurius]] — the agent that destroys and heals, that must be 'dissolved in its own water and again coagulated'. The [[motif:ouroboros|ouroboros]] form makes explicit the circular *solve et coagula* at the heart of the Work: nothing is added from outside; the matter perfects itself by turning upon itself.

## For artists & game designers
A forest ouroboros — the canonical 'venom that is also medicine' symbol; perfect for a cyclical mechanic, a respawn glyph, or an item that harms and heals at once.

A frameless forest ouroboros, high contrast and self-contained — drop-in art for a cyclical glyph, an infinity sigil, or a save/respawn icon.

title: Shiʿi Calligraphy of ʿAlī as the Tiger of God
work: Lettrism — The Esoteric Science of Letters (ʿIlm al-Ḥurūf)
creator: Anonymous (modern redrawing)
summary:
A black-and-white zoomorphic calligram forming a striding big cat (lion/tiger) out of an Arabic invocation of **ʿAlī**.

## Iconography
Interlaced cursive letters compose the head, flank and legs of the animal; the negative spaces between strokes give the impression of dappled fur. The text is a devotional formula naming ʿAlī, the 'Lion/Tiger of God' (*Ḥaydar*).

## Significance
The piece restates the lettrist principle that a holy name can be re-bodied as its emblematic creature. As a clean line drawing it shows the underlying scaffolding of such calligrams better than gilded album leaves, making the letter-to-limb correspondences legible. It belongs to the broad family of ʿAlī-as-lion talismans tied to the *Nād-i ʿAlī* prayer.

## For artists & game designers
Useful reference sheet: the bare linework reveals how to read a creature back into its constituent glyphs.

title: Panjtan — The Five Holy Ones in Calligraphy
work: Lettrism — The Esoteric Science of Letters (ʿIlm al-Ḥurūf)
creator: Kānūn-i Hunar-i Shīʿī (Shiʿi art workshop)
rights: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Kānūn-i Hunar-i Shīʿī). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A calligraphic composition of the **Panjtan-i Āl-i ʿAbā** — the Five Holy Ones: Muhammad, ʿAlī, Fāṭima, Ḥasan and Ḥusayn — woven into a single symmetrical design.

## Iconography
The five sacred names are arranged as an interlaced star or rosette, often in mirror (muthanna) symmetry so the names reflect one another around a central axis. No faces appear; the persons are present purely as their names.

## Significance
In Shiʿi devotion the Panjtan are the locus of divine blessing and protection, and their five names are deployed together as a powerful talismanic formula — inscribed on amulets, banners and the hand-shaped *panja*. As a sacred-name [[motif:mirror calligraphy|mirror-calligram]], the piece exemplifies the lettrist principle that arranging holy names in ordered, symmetrical form concentrates their power.

## For artists & game designers
A five-fold 'patron set' — a single emblem binding five named protectors into one ward.

title: Mirror Image of 'ʿAlī walī Allāh'
work: Lettrism — The Esoteric Science of Letters (ʿIlm al-Ḥurūf)
creator: Ibrāhīm Maḥmūd
summary:
A **muthannā** (mirror) calligraphic panel of the Shiʿi testimony *ʿAlī walī Allāh* ('ʿAlī is the friend/vicegerent of God'), the phrase doubled in perfect reflection.

## Iconography
The inscription is written once and then mirrored across a vertical axis, so the two halves meet like a butterfly's wings; the symmetry makes a single phrase read as a balanced ornamental whole.

## Significance
Mirror calligraphy (*muthannā* or *aynalı*) was prized exactly because the doubling intensifies a sacred phrase into a self-contained, talismanic image. Applied to *ʿAlī walī Allāh* — the distinctive Shiʿi addition to the call to prayer — it produces a devotional sign carrying both confessional identity and protective power, a paradigm case of the lettrist transformation of a [[motif:sacred names|holy phrase]] into diagram.

## For artists & game designers
The mirror technique is a free 'sigil-doubler': reflect any inscription to make it read as an emblem.

title: The Name of God (Allāh)
work: Lettrism — The Esoteric Science of Letters (ʿIlm al-Ḥurūf)
creator: Anonymous (vector, Wikimedia 'Mr100percent')
summary:
The single word **Allāh** — the Greatest Name (*al-ism al-aʿẓam*) — rendered in bold green calligraphy.

## Iconography
The name is built from the doubled *lām* rising as twin verticals, the looping *hāʾ* below, the *alif* and the *shadda* above — a tight, instantly recognisable monogram of four written elements.

## Significance
For the lettrists the Name *Allāh* is the seed of all the others and the supreme object of meditation; its letters (alif-lām-lām-hā) were analysed for their successive disappearance down to the bare *hū* ('He'), and its abjad value computed as a key to the divine. As the [[motif:names of god|Greatest Name]], it is held to be the most powerful of all letter-talismans, the centre around which the ninety-nine Names and every magic square are organised.

## For artists & game designers
The ultimate 'true name' token — the single glyph at the centre of every ward and rosette in the set.

title: The Ninety-Nine Beautiful Names of God
work: Lettrism — The Esoteric Science of Letters (ʿIlm al-Ḥurūf)
creator: Anonymous
summary:
A golden calligraphy board displaying **al-asmāʾ al-ḥusnā**, the ninety-nine Most Beautiful Names of God, each set in its own cartouche.

## Iconography
The Names — al-Raḥmān, al-Raḥīm, al-Malik, and so on — radiate around a central medallion (typically the Name *Allāh*), the whole arranged as an ordered grid or rosette of letter-talismans.

## Significance
The ninety-nine [[motif:names of god|Names]] are the heart of lettrist devotion and magic: each Name has an abjad value, a planetary and elemental correspondence, and a prescribed number of repetitions (*dhikr*) thought to release its specific power. Al-Būnī's *Shams al-maʿārif* tabulates their squares and seals. Displayed together they form a complete map of the divine attributes — a master-diagram of sacred letters.

## For artists & game designers
A 99-entry 'attribute system': each Name a distinct power with its own number, sound and correspondence.

title: Basmala (Naskh)
work: Lettrism — The Esoteric Science of Letters (ʿIlm al-Ḥurūf)
creator: Anonymous (Saddam19, Wikimedia)
summary:
A clean single-line rendering of the **basmala** in a clear naskh hand.

## Iconography
The phrase *bismillāh ar-raḥmān ar-raḥīm* is set out plainly, letter by letter, so the individual graphemes — and thus their abjad values — are easy to count and contemplate.

## Significance
Where display calligraphy dramatises the formula, a plain naskh basmala is the version the lettrist actually meditates on and computes: each letter weighed for its [[motif:abjad|abjad]] number, the totals sought in the divine Names. The legibility makes this a useful reference for the very alphabet on which the whole science of letters operates.

## For artists & game designers
A legible 'reference inscription' — the base text from which stylised and zoomorphic variants derive.

title: Bismillah in Calligraphy
work: Lettrism — The Esoteric Science of Letters (ʿIlm al-Ḥurūf)
creator: Anonymous (Laisurw2020, Wikimedia)
summary:
The **bismillah** — *bismillāh ar-raḥmān ar-raḥīm* — written as a single flowing line of display calligraphy.

## Iconography
The nineteen letters of the formula are drawn out in expansive thuluth, the elongated *sīn* of *bismi* sweeping under the whole phrase as a base-line that gathers the words into one gesture.

## Significance
The basmala opens every chapter of the Quran but one and every blessed act; its nineteen letters became a focus of lettrist numerology (the 'mystery of nineteen'), and the phrase itself is the most common subject of zoomorphic calligrams and talismanic panels. As the door-formula of speech and writing alike, it is the natural seed of the whole [[motif:sacred letters|science of letters]].

## For artists & game designers
The universal 'invocation header' — the phrase that opens every spell, document and journey.

title: Bismillah Roundel (Mirror Composition)
work: Lettrism — The Esoteric Science of Letters (ʿIlm al-Ḥurūf)

summary:
The **bismillah** composed into a circular seal-like medallion, the words folded to fill a roundel.

## Iconography
Black on white, the formula is arranged so its strokes radiate and interlock within a circle, producing a compact emblem rather than a running line — close to a stamp or seal.

## Significance
Compressing the basmala into a roundel is the move that turns a phrase into a [[motif:seal|seal]]: a self-contained sign that can be impressed, worn or hung as a unit of blessing and protection. The circular format aligns the sacred opening-formula with the talismanic logic of the magic-square amulet and the tughra, where holy text becomes a closed, portable device.

title: The Budūḥ Magic Square
work: Lettrism — The Esoteric Science of Letters (ʿIlm al-Ḥurūf)
creator: after Zakariyā al-Qazwīnī
summary:
The **budūḥ** — the classic 3×3 magic square of Islamic letter-magic, here in a manuscript hand associated with the cosmographer al-Qazwīnī.

## Iconography
Nine cells hold the Arabic numerals 2-9-4 / 7-5-3 / 6-1-8 (or their letter equivalents), every row, column and diagonal summing to fifteen. The four corner letters bā-dāl-wāw-ḥā spell the talismanic word *BUDŪḤ*.

## Significance
The 3×3 square (the *wafq* of Saturn, the Chinese Lo Shu) entered Islamic magic as the [[motif:buduh|budūḥ]], invoked as a guardian word on amulets for safe travel, childbirth and protection — its mere name a charm. It is the foundational object where [[motif:abjad numerology|abjad numerology]] and the magic square meet, and it passed into Latin and Hebrew magic alike.

## For artists & game designers
The budūḥ is a portable, drawable ward: a 3×3 grid the player inscribes to seal a door or a journey.

A calligraphic medallion spelling the name and honorific of **al-Shaykh Aḥmad b. ʿAlī al-Būnī** (d. c. 1225), the foundational author of the Islamic science of letters.

## Iconography
White cursive script on black fills a double-ruled roundel: 'the Shaykh Aḥmad ibn ʿAlī al-Būnī, may God have mercy on him', composed as a balanced seal-like emblem.

## Significance
Al-Būnī is the towering figure of lettrist magic, credited with the *Shams al-maʿārif al-kubrā* ('Sun of Great Knowledge'), the encyclopaedia of the [[motif:names of god|divine Names]], magic squares, and the occult properties of the Arabic letters that stands behind centuries of Islamic and, via translation, European talismanic practice. Rendering his very name as a sealed roundel honours him in the medium he theorised.

## For artists & game designers
A named 'grimoire author' emblem — the sigil of a magus the player can quest to study under.

title: The Buraq Worshipped by Two Princes
work: Lettrism — The Esoteric Science of Letters (ʿIlm al-Ḥurūf)
creator: Anonymous
repository: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
summary:
A painting of the **Buraq**, the winged human-faced steed that carried the Prophet on the Night Journey (miʿrāj), here venerated by two kneeling princes; the verso carries calligraphy.

## Iconography
The Buraq, with a woman's face, peacock tail and equine body, is shown crowned and haloed. The pairing of image (recto) and sacred script (verso) is typical of the talismanic album leaf, where the holy beast and the holy text guard one another.

## Significance
The Buraq is itself a frequent subject of zoomorphic calligrams (the bismillah-as-Buraq), and the creature's body is treated, like the lion of ʿAlī, as a vessel for sacred text. This LACMA leaf shows the painted source-image from which the calligraphic Buraq abstracts. It belongs to the devotional, protective image-culture of [[motif:miʿraj|the Night Journey]].

## For artists & game designers
A fully designed mythic mount — human face, peacock tail, equine body, crowned — ready as a steed asset.

title: Nād-i ʿAlī Prayer Cut in the Shape of a Lion
work: Lettrism — The Esoteric Science of Letters (ʿIlm al-Ḥurūf)
creator: Mīr ʿAlī Heravī (attrib.)

An album page on which the **Nād-i ʿAlī** — a celebrated prayer of intercession to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib — is rendered as découpage (cut-paper) calligraphy in the form of a lion.

## Iconography
The entire lion, mounted on a contrasting ground, is built from the cut-out words of the prayer; the medium of paper-cutting turns the text into a solid silhouette. The lion again signals ʿAlī, the *Asad Allāh*.

## Significance
The *Nād-i ʿAlī* ("Call upon ʿAlī, the manifester of wonders") was prized as a protective and talismanic invocation across the Persianate world. Shaping it into the lion fuses the apotropaic power of the words with the iconic force of the image — a high-art instance of letter-mysticism in service of devotion. The leaf is associated with the great calligrapher Mīr ʿAlī Heravī.

title: Hilye-i Şerif (Calligraphic Description of the Prophet)
work: Lettrism — The Esoteric Science of Letters (ʿIlm al-Ḥurūf)
creator: Anonymous (Ottoman)
summary:
A **hilye** (Arabic *ḥilya*) — the formalised calligraphic 'portrait in words' describing the physical and moral qualities of the Prophet Muhammad.

## Iconography
The genre has a fixed architecture: a top panel (*başmakam*) with the basmala, a central medallion (*göbek*) holding the descriptive text, four corner roundels for the Rightly-Guided Caliphs, and a lower panel with a closing verse — all bordered like an icon. No face is depicted; the description *is* the likeness.

## Significance
The hilye answers the prohibition on figural images of the Prophet by substituting a verbal-visual diagram believed to carry blessing (*baraka*); to keep or gaze upon one was held to confer protection. As a sacred design made wholly of words and ordered space, it is a paradigm of lettrist devotion. The form was codified by the Ottoman master Hâfız Osman in the 17th century.

## For artists & game designers
A strict template UI: fixed panels and medallions you can re-skin as a 'relic-card' frame.

citations.text: Faruk Taşkale & Hüseyin Gündüz, *Hilye-i Şerife* (2006).

title: Hilye by Hâfız Osman
work: Lettrism — The Esoteric Science of Letters (ʿIlm al-Ḥurūf)
creator: Hâfız Osman
summary:
A **hilye** by **Hâfız Osman** (1642–1698), the Ottoman calligrapher who standardised the genre's classic layout, now in the Sadberk Hanım Museum.

## Iconography
The sheet follows the canonical scheme: basmala header, a circular central medallion containing the description of the Prophet, four caliphal roundels, and a framing border, executed in disciplined thuluth and naskh.

## Significance
Hâfız Osman's design fixed the hilye as a devotional and quasi-talismanic object reproduced for centuries; owning one was thought to bring blessing and protection. Its geometry — a sacred text organised into concentric and cornered fields — makes the page a [[motif:devotional diagram|devotional diagram]] as much as a piece of writing, the lettrist ideal of word-as-icon.

## For artists & game designers
The authoritative reference for the hilye frame: copy its proportions for an in-game holy-relic document.

An Ottoman **levha** — a single-sheet calligraphic panel made to be framed and hung — signed by Hasan Rıza Şumnu and dated 1886–87.

A sacred phrase is laid out as a balanced symmetrical composition in bold thuluth, with the words interlocking to fill the field as a designed image rather than a line of running text.

The levha brought monumental sacred calligraphy out of the mosque and into the home as a devotional and protective wall-image. A well-made levha of a Quranic verse or holy name was understood to carry blessing into the room it guarded — the everyday face of [[motif:sacred letters|letter-mysticism]], where a phrase becomes a talismanic object simply by being beautifully and deliberately composed.

title: Persian Wafq — a 6×6 Magic Square with Instructions
work: Lettrism — The Esoteric Science of Letters (ʿIlm al-Ḥurūf)
creator: Anonymous
summary:
A 16th-century Persian manuscript page giving a **wafq** (magic square) of order six, with the construction rules written out above and below the grid.

## Iconography
A 6×6 grid is filled with the numbers 1–36 so that every row and column shares a constant sum (111); the surrounding Persian text explains, cell by cell, how the figure is to be built — a working recipe, not just a finished talisman.

## Significance
The order-six square is the *wafq* of the Sun in the planetary series, and its construction was a prized branch of the lettrist mathematical sciences (*ʿilm al-awfāq*). Squares like this were engraved on amulets and astral talismans, their numbers tied through [[motif:abjad numerology|abjad]] to divine names and planetary powers. The inclusion of the method shows the practitioner's craft, descending from al-Būnī and the Brethren of Purity.

## For artists & game designers
A genuine in-world 'spell recipe': the grid plus the step-by-step text for building it.

This is the institutional backbone of the lettrist culture in which writing the [[motif:sacred letters|holy letters]] is itself an act of devotion and power.

title: The Mysterious Letters Ṭā-Hā (Surah 20)
work: Lettrism — The Esoteric Science of Letters (ʿIlm al-Ḥurūf)
creator: Anonymous (modern roundel)
summary:
A roundel displaying **Ṭā-Hā** (طه), the two disconnected 'mysterious letters' (*muqaṭṭaʿāt*) that open the 20th sura of the Quran.

## Iconography
Within a green medallion the word *sūra* and the number 20 frame the large isolated letters Ṭā and Hā, written without the surrounding text — exactly as they stand, enigmatic, at the head of the chapter.

## Significance
Twenty-nine Quranic suras begin with such [[motif:muqattaat|muqaṭṭaʿāt]] — single or grouped letters (Alif-Lām-Mīm, Yā-Sīn, Ṭā-Hā) whose meaning is undisclosed. For the lettrists they were the supreme proof that bare letters carry hidden power: commentators computed their abjad values, sought their secret names of God, and treated them as keys to the cosmos. They are the Quranic charter of the science of letters.

## For artists & game designers
The muqaṭṭaʿāt are canonical 'untranslatable runes' — sacred glyphs whose meaning is a deliberate mystery.

title: Square Kufic Bismillah Page by Ahmed Karahisari
work: Lettrism — The Esoteric Science of Letters (ʿIlm al-Ḥurūf)
creator: Ahmed Karahisari
summary:
A calligraphic page attributed to the great Ottoman master **Ahmed Karahisari** (d. 1556), combining a cursive **bismillah** with two geometric panels in **square (bannāʾī) Kufic**.

## Iconography
At centre a flowing bismillah; above and below, sacred phrases are folded into diamond grids of square Kufic, where each letter is squared off and woven into an interlocking maze that must be 'read' by tracing the path of the strokes.

## Significance
Square Kufic turns sacred text into pure geometry, the closest the Arabic script comes to a [[motif:magic square|magic square]]: the eye decodes a word from a lattice. Karahisari, founder of an influential Ottoman school, exploited this to make text legible as architecture and ornament. Such grid-letters were used on buildings and as talismanic medallions, sitting squarely within the lettrist treatment of writing as occult diagram.

## For artists & game designers
Square Kufic is a built-in 'glyph puzzle' mechanic — a word hidden in a grid the player must trace.

title: Tughra of Sultan Süleyman the Magnificent
work: Lettrism — The Esoteric Science of Letters (ʿIlm al-Ḥurūf)
creator: Ottoman chancery (nişancı)
summary:
The illuminated **tughra** (sovereign monogram) of **Süleyman the Magnificent**, the calligraphic cipher that authenticated every Ottoman imperial decree.

## Iconography
The tughra weaves the sultan's name and titles into a fixed abstract form: a cluster of vertical staves (*tuğ*) on the right, three looping ovals (*beyze*) on the left, and a flourish sweeping outward, here filled with gold floral illumination.

## Significance
More than a signature, the tughra functioned as a quasi-magical sign of presence and authority: to bear it was to bear the sultan's word made visible, and its inimitable design protected documents like a [[motif:seal|seal]] or talisman against forgery. As a sacred-name-form abstracted into pure pattern, it sits at the meeting of calligraphy, heraldry and lettrist sign-magic.

## For artists & game designers
A ready 'royal seal' generator: a personal name compressed into an unforgeable emblem of power.

title: Bismillah in the Shape of a Hoopoe
work: Lettrism — The Esoteric Science of Letters (ʿIlm al-Ḥurūf)
creator: Anonymous
summary:
The **basmala** — *bismillāh ar-raḥmān ar-raḥīm*, 'In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful' — written so that its letters form a **hoopoe**.

## Iconography
A crested hoopoe, gilded and finely scrolled, is composed entirely of the words of the opening invocation: the crest, beak, wing and tail are each carried by a stroke of the phrase. Black calligraphy on a gold ground.

## Significance
The hoopoe (*hudhud*) is the messenger-bird of Solomon and, in ʿAṭṭār's *Conference of the Birds*, the guide of the soul's journey to the divine — a fitting body for the sacred name that opens every act and every Quranic chapter. Bird-calligrams of the [[motif:bismillah|bismillah]] are a favourite of the lettrist tradition, where the formula's letters are also counted and meditated upon for their abjad value.

## For artists & game designers
A model bismillah-bird: a single holy phrase that resolves into a guide-creature.

title: Calligram in the Shape of a Lion (ʿAlī)
work: Lettrism — The Esoteric Science of Letters (ʿIlm al-Ḥurūf)
creator: Vesal Shirazi (attrib.)
summary:
A zoomorphic calligram in which a devotional Arabic phrase honouring **ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib** is bent into the body of a lion.

## Iconography
The whole beast — mane, paw, curling tail — is formed of cursive script, the letters doubling as anatomy. The lion is the standard emblem of ʿAlī, the *Asad Allāh* ('Lion of God'), so the image is both portrait and prayer: the holy name *becomes* the holy animal.

## Significance
Zoomorphic calligraphy belongs to the lettrist conviction that the [[motif:sacred letters|sacred letters]] are living, generative substance. By shaping a venerated name into a lion the calligrapher makes a talisman that is read and seen at once — a practice especially developed in Shiʿi and dervish circles. Such pieces circulated as protective images in 18th–19th-century Iran and India.

## For artists & game designers
A template for 'word-creatures' — sigils whose silhouette spells the spell they cast.

title: Bronze Astragalus (Knucklebone)
creator: Anonymous (Greek or Roman)
rights: CC0 / Public domain. The Metropolitan Museum of Art. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A bronze *astragalus* (knucklebone) of the Greco-Roman world, the four-sided 'die' used both for games and for divination by lot (Metropolitan Museum of Art).

## Iconography
The object is a cast-bronze copy of a sheep's or goat's ankle-bone, with its characteristic four distinguishable faces of unequal value. Real bones, and metal or stone replicas like this one, were thrown in sets; each face counted as a number (commonly 1, 3, 4, 6).

## Significance
The knucklebone is the oldest randomiser of the Mediterranean world. Beyond the game of *astragaloi*, casting them was a recognised oracle: at certain shrines a throw was matched to a verse in an [[motif:astragalomancy|astragalomantic]] table (the *Anatolian dice-oracles*) that delivered a god-sanctioned answer. The astragalus thus stands at the root of the whole dice-and-lot tradition that the medieval and Renaissance lot-books would elaborate into wheels and printed books.

## For artists & game designers
The original four-sided die — an authentic ancient randomiser prop, and the historical seed of every dice-oracle table.

citations.text: On dice-oracles, see J. Nollé, *Kleinasiatische Losorakel* (2007).
The Metropolitan Museum of Art (CC0).

title: Bollstatter Losbuch (Cgm 312)
creator: Konrad Bollstatter
rights: Public domain. Bayerische Staatsbibliothek. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A page of the *Losbuch* of Konrad Bollstatter (Munich, Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, Cgm 312), a German vernacular lot-book of the later fifteenth century.

## Iconography
The leaf combines diagram and rubricated verse: pointing devices, named prophets or kings, and tables route the reader from a question through a chain of intermediaries to a rhymed German answer. The hand is Bollstatter's, a prolific Augsburg scribe who copied several such books.

## Significance
The German *Losbücher* are the northern counterpart of the Italian printed lot-books, descending from antique and Arabic sortilege. The querent generated a number (by dice, by a spun [[motif:wheel of fortune|wheel]], or by pricking) and followed pointers — often a series of prophets, animals, or kings — to a fortune. Bollstatter's manuscripts are key witnesses to this living medieval game of chance-and-counsel, blending entertainment with quasi-prophetic authority.

## For artists & game designers
The northern lot-book's pointer-chains (prophet → animal → answer) are a vivid model for a hand-drawn, manuscript-styled fortune mechanic.

title: Domanda (Question) Pages — Triompho di Fortuna
creator: Sigismondo Fanti
rights: CC0 / Public domain. The Metropolitan Museum of Art. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
An opening of *Domande* (questions) from Fanti's *Triompho di Fortuna* (1526), the index by which a querent enters the lot-book (Metropolitan Museum of Art).

## Iconography
The text is set as numbered *DOMANDA* entries — 'Se il paese della donna haura victoria o sera vinta', 'Se la phisonomia de l'huomo e buona o no' — each followed by an instruction such as *Va alla Fortuna di Libico alla lettera E*, with a small marginal woodcut. The reader finds their question, then is dispatched by letter and name into the wheels and houses that follow.

## Significance
These question-tables are the entry layer of the lot-book's algorithm: a fixed menu of fortunes (love, victory, journeys, character, life and death) cross-referenced into the [[motif:rota|wheels]]. The form descends from the medieval *Losbücher* and Lorenzo Spirito, and shows how thoroughly the genre systematised divination into a branching, page-jumping procedure long before any mechanical computer.

## For artists & game designers
A genuine 16th-century 'dialogue tree': pick a question, follow the letter, jump to the result — a dating-from-1526 template for branching oracle UX.

title: Rota della Charità & Rota della Fede (Triompho di Fortuna)
creator: Sigismondo Fanti
rights: CC0 / Public domain. The Metropolitan Museum of Art. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A double-page opening from Fanti's *Triompho di Fortuna* (1526) showing two answer-wheels, the *Rota della Charità* and the *Rota della Fede* (the Wheels of Charity and of Faith), flanked by attendant sages (Metropolitan Museum of Art).

## Iconography
Each page carries a paired set of [[motif:rota|wheels]]: an upper figured wheel with a virtue personified at its hub, and a lower dense ring of numbered or lettered cells. Worthies and prophets stand in the margins, named in cartouches. The reader, directed here from the question-tables, spins or reads off the ring to find the cell that yields the next step toward an answer.

## Significance
The *rote* are the working machinery of the lot-book: a randomising lookup table dressed as an allegorical wheel of Fortune. By naming the wheels for the theological virtues, Fanti folds a moral cosmology into the mechanics of chance, so that consulting Fortune becomes a passage through Faith, Charity, and the rest. It is a vivid witness to how Renaissance print turned divination into an interactive, navigable system.

## For artists & game designers
A literal spin-the-wheel UI from 1526 — concentric numbered rings with a themed hub, directly usable as a randomiser interface.

title: Triompho di Fortuna — Title Page (Sigismondo Fanti)
creator: Sigismondo Fanti (woodcut after a design attrib. Baldassare Peruzzi)
summary:
The elaborate title-page woodcut of Sigismondo Fanti's *Triompho di Fortuna* (Venice, 1526), one of the great printed fortune-telling lot-books of the Italian Renaissance.

## Iconography
Beneath the red title a vast turning globe or drum dominates the page; the figures *Virtus* and *Voluptas* (Virtue and Pleasure) are named above, while nude genii heave at the wheel of Fortune below. At right rises an astronomical clock-tower with a zodiacal dial; an aged astrologer kneels with his instruments at lower left. The whole composition allegorises the contest of virtue, pleasure, and chance that the book proposes to read.

## Significance
Fanti's *Triompho* is a sortilege book: the reader poses one of a fixed set of questions and is sent, by dice or chance, through a chain of [[motif:wheel of fortune|wheels]] (*rote*), houses, astrologers, and prophets to a versified answer. It belongs to the same family as Lorenzo Spirito's *Libro delle Sorti* but is more lavishly astrological. The design is traditionally connected to Baldassare Peruzzi, and the book is dedicated, in its grandeur, to the courts of Italy.

## For artists & game designers
A ready-made 'oracle engine' frontispiece — globe, named virtues, clockwork zodiac — perfect as the cover of an in-game book of fate.

citations.text: Sigismondo Fanti, *Triompho di Fortuna* (Venice, 1526).

title: Rota del Dio d'Amore — Triompho di Fortuna
creator: Sigismondo Fanti
rights: CC0 / Public domain. The Metropolitan Museum of Art. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A page from Fanti's *Triompho di Fortuna* (1526) bearing the *Rota del Dio d'Amore* (Wheel of the God of Love) above a zodiacal wheel, attended by named sages including Plotino and Eusebio (Metropolitan Museum of Art).

## Iconography
The upper [[motif:rota|wheel]] frames a scene of the God of Love at its hub, its rim a dense band of inscribed cells; a lower wheel is marked with the [[motif:zodiac|zodiac]] and further numbered divisions. In the corners stand authorities — Plotinus, Eusebius, and others — named to lend the oracle classical weight.

## Significance
Naming a wheel for the *Dio d'Amore* and pairing it with the zodiac shows how Fanti distributed the querent's possible fates across a cosmos of love, virtue, and the stars. The summoned philosophers act as guarantors of the answer, a print-era version of consulting the ancients. It is among the most decorative of the book's many wheels and a fine example of the lot-book as an astrological-allegorical machine.

## For artists & game designers
A themed result-wheel (Love) ringed by named 'experts' — a model for flavourful randomiser screens that cite in-world authorities.

title: The Wheel of Fortune (15th-c. French manuscript)
creator: Anonymous (French illuminator)
summary:
A fifteenth-century French manuscript miniature of the *Roue de Fortune*, the Wheel of Fortune, set in a flowered border above a column of text.

## Iconography
A great wooden [[motif:wheel of fortune|wheel]] turns at the right of a verdant scene; a small figure clings at its summit while others are raised and cast down around it. A crowd of courtiers looks on. The image personifies Fortune's indifferent turning, the ascent and ruin of the great — the visual commonplace of medieval *de casibus* literature.

## Significance
The *Rota Fortunae* is the master-image behind every lot-book and fortune-game: Boethius's blind goddess who raises kings only to dash them, a wheel that became the engine-metaphor for divinatory wheels (Fanti's *rote*, the tarot's trump X) and for the moralised histories of fallen princes. This miniature exemplifies its luxurious courtly form in late-medieval France.

## For artists & game designers
The canonical medieval luck-wheel with rising/falling figures — the ancestor of every spin-the-wheel and a clear 'fate turns' icon.

citations.text: Boethius, *De consolatione philosophiae*.
Wikimedia Commons

title: Wheel of Fortune (de casibus tradition)
creator: Anonymous (manuscript illumination)
summary:
A cropped manuscript image of the Wheel of Fortune in the *de casibus* tradition, with crowned figures rising and falling on the turning wheel.

## Iconography
Fortune's [[motif:wheel of fortune|wheel]] carries kings at its four cardinal points — one ascending (*regnabo*, 'I shall reign'), one enthroned at the top (*regno*, 'I reign'), one toppling (*regnavi*, 'I have reigned'), and one crushed beneath (*sum sine regno*, 'I am without rule') — the classic four-king scheme of the medieval Wheel.

## Significance
This four-king *Rota Fortunae* visualises the cycle of worldly fortune that gave Boccaccio's *De casibus virorum illustrium* and Lydgate's *Fall of Princes* their theme. As the governing emblem of chance and mutability, it underwrites the whole lot-book enterprise: to consult Fortune is to step onto her wheel. The image is among the most copied of all medieval allegories.

## For artists & game designers
The four-king wheel (regnabo / regno / regnavi / sum sine regno) is a compact, legible status-cycle device for any rise-and-fall mechanic.

citations.text: Boccaccio, *De casibus virorum illustrium*; Boethius, *De consolatione*.

title: Geomantic Figures in Wellcome MS Arabic 823
creator: Anonymous (Arabic manuscript)
rights: CC0 / Public domain. Wellcome Collection. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A detail from an Arabic geomantic manuscript (Wellcome Collection, MS Arabic 823) showing the dot-figures of *'ilm al-raml* set out in a working table.

## Iconography
Rows and columns of [[motif:geomancy|dot-figures]] are arranged across the page, each a tetragram of single and paired dots, interspersed with Arabic captions. The layout is the practical 'shield' or table by which a geomancer derives the daughter- and resulting figures from the four 'mothers.'

## Significance
The manuscript witnesses *'ilm al-raml* in its home tradition: a learned Arabic art of generating and combining the sixteen figures to answer questions of fortune, illness, travel, and love. Such tables are the direct ancestors of the European geomantic 'shield chart.' The Wellcome holding documents the Islamic-world geomancy that medieval Latin translators carried into Europe, where it became one of the most popular forms of bookish divination.

## For artists & game designers
An authentic Arabic geomancy worksheet — period reference for the 'shield chart' that turns four random figures into a full reading.

title: Geomantic Figure Types (the sixteen figures, named)
creator: Phil wink (modern diagram of the traditional figures)
date: modern diagram of a medieval system
rights: CC BY-SA 3.0 (Phil wink). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A clear modern chart of the sixteen geomantic figures with their Latin names, illustrating the fixed vocabulary of Western *geomantia*.

## Iconography
Each [[motif:geomancy|figure]] is drawn as four rows of one or two dots and labelled — *Via*, *Cauda Draconis*, *Caput Draconis*, *Puella*, *Puer*, *Fortuna Major*, *Fortuna Minor*, *Acquisitio*, *Amissio*, *Carcer*, *Tristitia*, *Laetitia*, *Albus*, *Rubeus*, *Coniunctio*, *Populus*. The two 'Fortunes' and 'Via'/'Populus' pairs show the symmetry of the set.

## Significance
This is the Latin-European canon of the sixteen figures as transmitted from Arabic *'ilm al-raml* through medieval and Renaissance geomancers. Each figure carries planetary, elemental, and zodiacal attributions and a fortune-meaning, so that a generated chart can be read like a horoscope. The diagram is a convenient reference key to the system that underlies European geomantic divination, the *Book of Fate*, and occult revivals.

## For artists & game designers
A labelled cheat-sheet of all sixteen figures and their names — drop-in reference for implementing a geomancy reading system.

citations.text: S. Skinner, *Geomancy in Theory and Practice* (2011).

title: The Sixteen Geomantic Figures (Arabic classification)
creator: Anonymous (Arabic tradition)
summary:
A classification chart of the sixteen geomantic figures of Arabic *'ilm al-raml* ('the science of the sand'), the binary tetragrams from which geomantic readings are built.

## Iconography
The figure arranges the sixteen [[motif:geomancy|geomantic figures]] — each a stack of four rows of one or two dots (e.g. *Via*, *Populus*, *Fortuna Major*, *Acquisitio*) — into a classified table. The one-or-two pattern of each row encodes a binary value; the four rows give 2⁴ = 16 possible figures.

## Significance
Geomancy generates these tetragrams by tallying random marks made in sand (or on paper) into odd or even, then derives 'mothers,' 'daughters,' 'nieces,' and 'witnesses' to answer a question. Born in the medieval Arab world, *'ilm al-raml* passed into Latin Europe as *geomantia* (Hugh of Santalla, Pietro d'Abano), into the Renaissance via Agrippa, and into living African practice as Ifá and *sikidy*. The sixteen figures are its fixed alphabet of fate.

## For artists & game designers
The definitive 16-symbol binary divination set — trivially generated from random bits and historically deep across three continents.

citations.text: S. Skinner, *Geomancy in Theory and Practice* (2011).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Fuxi Order Grid and Circle of the Hexagrams
creator: James Legge (engraving, Sacred Books of the East, 1882)
summary:
The Fuxi (Shao Yong) arrangement of the 64 hexagrams as both a square grid and an enclosing circle, engraved for James Legge's translation of the *Yi King* (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 16, 1882).

## Iconography
Within a great ring of [[motif:i ching|hexagrams]] sits a square block of the same 64 figures; together they display the 'former heaven' (Fuxi) order attributed to Shao Yong. Each hexagram is six yin/yang lines, and the layout makes the binary symmetry of the sequence visible at a glance.

## Significance
This is the diagram (the *Xiantian* or Fuxi arrangement) that underlies the binary reading of the *Yijing* and that reached Leibniz. In divinatory use the *I Ching* is consulted by building a hexagram from chance — yarrow-stalk counts or tossed coins — and interpreting its judgement, image, and changing lines. Legge's careful Victorian engraving made the classical Chinese oracle and its elegant combinatorics widely available to Western readers.

## For artists & game designers
A beautiful ring-plus-grid of all 64 states — usable directly as the selection diagram for a coin- or stalk-cast oracle minigame.

citations.text: James Legge, *The Yî King* (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 16, 1882).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Diagram of I Ching Hexagrams (Leibniz's copy, 1701)
creator: Anonymous (after the Fuxi arrangement); copy owned by G. W. Leibniz
summary:
The diagram of the 64 *I Ching* hexagrams in the Fuxi 'natural' order, in the copy sent to Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz in 1701.

## Iconography
The 64 [[motif:i ching|hexagrams]] — each six stacked lines, solid (yang) or broken (yin) — are arrayed both as a square grid and around a circle in the Fuxi sequence. Read as binary numbers (broken = 0, solid = 1), the arrangement runs in perfect numerical order, which is what so struck Leibniz.

## Significance
The *Yijing* (Book of Changes) is the great Chinese oracle: a hexagram is produced by casting yarrow stalks or coins, then read through its line-texts for guidance. This particular diagram is famous in the West because Leibniz, who had just formulated binary arithmetic, saw in the Fuxi order a Chinese anticipation of the binary system, and corresponded about it with the Jesuit Joachim Bouvet. It is a landmark in the meeting of divinatory and mathematical thought.

## For artists & game designers
A 64-state binary oracle with a ready visual key — the hexagram grid doubles as both fortune-table and an elegant binary-number display.

citations.text: On Leibniz, Bouvet and the Yijing, see studies of the binary correspondence (1701–03).

title: Wahrsagekarten der Mlle Lenormand (fortune-cards)
creator: After Marie-Anne Lenormand (tradition); print after the Lenormand idea
rights: Public domain. Bibliothèque nationale de France. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A sheet from the *Wahrsagekarten der Mlle Lenormand* (the fortune-telling cards of Mademoiselle Lenormand), a nineteenth-century *jeu divinatoire* after the famous Parisian fortune-teller (Bibliothèque nationale de France).

## Iconography
The print presents the emblematic [[motif:lenormand|Lenormand cards]], each bearing a single concrete symbol — the Ship, the Tree, the Tower, the Scythe, the Clover, the Stars — often with a small inset playing-card or verse. The cards are read in combination, each modifying its neighbours, in the grid spread known as the *Grand Tableau*.

## Significance
Marie-Anne Lenormand (1772–1843) was the celebrated fortune-teller of Napoleonic Paris, reputed to have read for Joséphine. The decks issued under her name after her death codified a distinct, accessible system of [[motif:cartomancy|cartomancy]] — simpler and more literal than tarot — that spread across France and the German lands. As cheap printed oracle-sheets, they mark the nineteenth-century mass-marketing of card divination to a popular public.

## For artists & game designers
A compact emblem-deck (about 36 plain symbols) ideal for a readable, combinable card-oracle distinct from heavier tarot iconography.

citations.text: On Lenormand cartomancy, see histories of nineteenth-century fortune-telling decks.

title: Losbuch, Cgm 252 — 'Book of the Twelve Apostles' leaf
creator: Konrad Bollstatter (attrib.)
rights: Public domain. Bayerische Staatsbibliothek. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
Folio 131r of a German *Losbuch* (Munich, Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, Cgm 252), with a red heading opening a new section, 'der zwölf Botten Buch' — the Book of the Twelve Apostles.

## Iconography
The page is laid out as a column of short prose oracles, each opened by a large alternately red-and-green initial. A red rubric introduces a sub-book keyed to the [[motif:twelve apostles|twelve apostles]], one of the named 'guides' through which the querent's lot is read. The answers are practical and worldly — counsel on patience, friendship, and fortune.

## Significance
Dividing a lot-book into sub-books named for apostles, prophets, or planets is characteristic of the *Losbuch* genre: the querent is routed to one 'authority,' then to a numbered answer. Cgm 252 shows the everyday, German-language face of late-medieval divination — a parlour oracle of rhymed and rubricated counsel that borrowed the prestige of sacred names while remaining a game of chance.

## For artists & game designers
Rubricated, initial-led answer columns under a sacred 'guide' heading — an authentic manuscript layout for an in-world oracle book.

citations.text: Munich, Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, Cgm 252, fol. 131r.

title: Losbuch, Cgm 252 — Oracle Answers leaf (132v)
creator: Konrad Bollstatter (attrib.)
rights: Public domain. Bayerische Staatsbibliothek. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
Folio 132v of the German *Losbuch* Cgm 252 (Munich, Bayerische Staatsbibliothek), a further leaf of rhymed oracle answers.

## Iconography
As on the facing leaves, the text runs in a single column of short German fortunes, each headed by a coloured initial. The answers offer terse worldly counsel — on undertakings, friends, and fortune — the kind of reply a querent would reach after following the book's pointers from a chosen question.

## Significance
The leaf illustrates the bulk of any lot-book: not the diagrams but the deep reservoir of pre-written [[motif:fortune|fortunes]] the apparatus selects from. The German vernacular, the rubricated initials, and the practical tone mark this as a household oracle of the later Middle Ages, a genre that flourished in manuscript before passing into the early printed *Losbücher* and the Italian sortilege books.

## For artists & game designers
A bank of short, reusable fortune-texts — exactly the answer-pool a procedural oracle needs behind its wheels and pointers.

citations.text: Munich, Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, Cgm 252, fol. 132v.

title: Ouija Talking Board (Kennard Novelty Company)
creator: Elijah Bond & Charles Kennard (Kennard Novelty Company)
summary:
An early *Ouija* talking board of the Kennard Novelty Company, the spiritualist alphabet-board patented in 1891.

## Iconography
The flat board is printed with the alphabet in two arcs, the numerals 0–9, and the words YES, NO, and GOOD BYE. A heart-shaped [[motif:planchette|planchette]] glides over the surface under the sitters' fingertips, spelling out messages said to come from spirits — in fact produced by the involuntary ideomotor effect.

## Significance
The talking board is the late, commercial flowering of the European lot-and-oracle tradition, born from the Spiritualist craze of the nineteenth century. Where the medieval *Losbuch* selected a pre-written answer by chance, the Ouija appears to compose a free answer letter by letter — a randomiser dressed as a conversation with the dead. Patented by Elijah Bond and marketed by Charles Kennard, it became the archetypal mass-market parlour oracle and a fixture of popular occulture.

## For artists & game designers
The definitive 'spirit interface' — an alphabet board plus sliding pointer, instantly legible as supernatural communication.

citations.text: On the Ouija board's history, see R. Murch and histories of American Spiritualism.
Wikimedia Commons

title: Original Ouija Board
creator: Anonymous (early Ouija manufacturer)
summary:
An early example of the *Ouija* board, the alphabet-and-numbers talking board used for purported spirit communication.

## Iconography
The board carries the full alphabet, the digits, and the words YES, NO, and GOOD BYE, with sun and moon motifs in the upper corners in the familiar period style. A [[motif:planchette|planchette]] (not always shown) is moved across the letters by the sitters to spell out messages.

## Significance
The Ouija belongs to the family of nineteenth-century Spiritualist devices — table-tipping, the planchette, automatic writing — that claimed to give the dead a voice. Functionally it is the modern descendant of the older lot-oracles: a means of obtaining an 'answer' by a process the querent does not consciously control. Its commercial success made the talking board the popular emblem of amateur divination well into the twentieth century and beyond.

## For artists & game designers
A period-styled spirit board (sun/moon corners, yes/no, alphabet arcs) for any séance or haunted-house scene.

citations.text: On Spiritualist divination devices, see histories of the planchette and talking board.

title: The Circle of Petosiris (Sphere of Life and Death)
creator: Anonymous (Greek; tradition ascribed to Petosiris)
date: diagram in a manuscript (Bibliothèque nationale, Ms. grec 2419, fol. 32)
rights: Public domain. Bibliothèque nationale de France. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
The *Circle of Petosiris* (Πετοσίρου κύκλος), a prognostic diagram for predicting life or death from a patient's name and the day of falling ill (Paris, BnF, Ms. grec 2419).

## Iconography
A circle is divided by a cross into quadrants labelled in Greek: *megalē zōē* (great life) and *mikra zōē* (small life) above, *megas thanatos* (great death) and *mikros thanatos* (small death) below, with *mesē zōē* and *mesos thanatos* (middle life, middle death) on the axis. Numbers fill the four sectors. The diviner reduced the sum of the letters of the patient's name to fit one of the numbered cells.

## Significance
This is the classic *Sphere of Life and Death*, an [[motif:onomancy|onomantic]] computus that turned the numerical value of a name (Greek isopsephy) into a verdict on survival. Ascribed to the legendary Egyptian sage Petosiris and to Pythagoras (the 'Sphere of Pythagoras'), it circulated for over a millennium in Greek, Latin, and vernacular manuscripts. It is the purest medical-divinatory lot-table: name plus date in, life or death out.

## For artists & game designers
A real algorithmic oracle — letters-to-number-to-quadrant — that implements in a few lines as a name-based fate calculator.

citations.text: On the Sphere of Life and Death / Circle of Petosiris, see studies of Greek and Latin prognostic spheres.
Paris, Bibliothèque nationale de France, Ms. grec 2419, fol. 32.

title: Roman Dodecahedron (Tongeren)
creator: Anonymous (Gallo-Roman)
rights: CC BY-SA 2.5 (Wim Deprez). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A Gallo-Roman bronze *dodecahedron*, one of the enigmatic twelve-faced objects sometimes proposed as a dice or divinatory device (example associated with Tongeren).

## Iconography
The hollow bronze has twelve pentagonal faces, each pierced by a circular hole of differing diameter, with a knob at every vertex. Roughly a hundred such objects survive from the north-western Roman provinces. Their original purpose is genuinely unknown — proposals range from a surveying or candle-holding tool to a knitting gauge to a gaming or divinatory die.

## Significance
No ancient text names the [[motif:roman dodecahedron|dodecahedron]], so any divinatory use is conjecture; but the twelve faces invite comparison with the twelve zodiac signs and months, and the object is often cited in popular accounts as a possible oracle die. It is included here as the most famous 'maybe-oracle' artefact of antiquity — a caution that not every twelve-fold object is a fortune-machine, and a reminder of how readily we read divination into the unexplained.

## For artists & game designers
A strikingly designed twelve-faced bronze of unknown use — an evocative 'mystery die' prop with built-in ambiguity.

citations.text: On the Roman dodecahedra and the debate over their function, see B. Greiner and related archaeological surveys.
Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 2.5, Wim Deprez)

title: Sibylla Delphica (the Delphic Sibyl)
creator: Published by Guillaume Rouillé (woodcut)
summary:
A sixteenth-century woodcut portrait of the *Sibylla Delphica*, the Delphic Sibyl, from the kind of illustrated compendium published by Guillaume Rouillé of Lyon.

## Iconography
The [[motif:sibyl|Sibyl]] is shown bust-length in a roundel, an emblematic seer of the antique world. In the standard iconography of the twelve Sibyls each is given an attribute and a prophecy; the Delphic Sibyl, associated with the oracle of Apollo at Delphi, is conventionally the first of the series.

## Significance
The Sibyls — Cumaean, Delphic, Erythraean, and the rest — were pagan prophetesses whom Christian tradition adopted as foretellers of Christ, ranking them beside the Old-Testament prophets. Their image saturated Renaissance art, from Michelangelo's Sistine ceiling to printed *Sibyllarum* books. As keepers of fate-foretelling verse they belong to the deep background of the European oracle tradition that the lot-books domesticated into a parlour game.

## For artists & game designers
A clean emblematic 'prophetess' portrait in period woodcut style — a portable seer icon for an oracle interface or character card.

citations.text: On the iconography of the Sibyls, see É. Mâle, *L'art religieux* and studies of the Sibylline tradition.
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Sibyl Offering the Sibylline Books to Tarquin
creator: Dudley Heath (illustration, after the Roman legend)
summary:
A 1912 colour illustration of the legend of the Cumaean Sibyl offering her books of prophecy to the Roman king Tarquin (from *The Story of Rome*, illustrated by Dudley Heath).

## Iconography
A veiled Sibyl, her robe patterned with rosettes, kneels before the enthroned Tarquin and presents an open [[motif:sibylline books|prophetic book]], a stack of further volumes at her feet; an attendant kneels alongside. The scene stages the famous bargain in which the Sibyl burned volume after volume, raising the price until the king bought the remainder.

## Significance
The *Libri Sibyllini* — the Sibylline Books — were Rome's official oracle: collections of Greek hexameter prophecies, consulted by a priestly college in times of crisis to find the rituals that would appease the gods. They are the supreme Roman instance of bookish, lot-like divination, where the answer to calamity was sought in a sealed canon of prophecy. The legend of their purchase from the Sibyl encapsulates the value placed on prophetic text.

## For artists & game designers
The archetypal 'forbidden prophecy book' scene — a seer driving a hard bargain over volumes of fate the ruler dare not refuse.

citations.text: On the Sibylline Books, see H. W. Parke, *Sibyls and Sibylline Prophecy in Classical Antiquity* (1988).
Mary Macgregor, *The Story of Rome* (1912), illus. Dudley Heath.
