title: Sigillum Dei (Seal of God)
creator: After Giorgio Anselmi (Georgius Parmensis)
summary:
A version of the *Sigillum Dei* (Seal of God), the elaborate concentric talisman of divine and angelic names that crowned the Solomonic and Honorian magical traditions.

## Iconography
The seal is built from nested geometry: an outer ring carrying the names of God and his angels, an inner heptagon or heptagram, and a five- or seven-pointed star at the centre. The interstices are packed with [[motif:divine names|divine names]], crosses, and letters, each compartment assigned to a particular spiritual power. The whole forms a closed cosmogram meant to compel obedience from spirits.

## Significance
The Sigillum Dei descends from the *Liber Juratus* (Sworn Book of Honorius, 13th–14th c.) and reached its most famous form as the *Sigillum Dei Aemeth* used by John Dee and Edward Kelley in their angelic scrying. The design encodes the names by which God governs creation; correctly drawn, it was held to grant the operator the vision of God and authority over angels. Studies by Jan Veenstra and Julien Véronèse trace its descent through the Honorian corpus.

## For artists & game designers
The perfect 'master ward' prop: a dense ring of names around a star, instantly readable as a high-tier protective or summoning glyph.

citations.text: Julien Véronèse, *L'Almandal et l'Almadel latins au Moyen Âge* (2012).
Jan R. Veenstra, on the *Liber Juratus* tradition.

title: Post-medieval talismanic pendant (PAS FindID 755270)
creator: Anonymous; photo The Portable Antiquities Scheme
rights: CC BY 2.0 (The Portable Antiquities Scheme). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A post-medieval copper-alloy medallion or amulet-pendant recorded by the Portable Antiquities Scheme — a surviving physical object from the world that grimoires describe.

## Iconography
The pendant is a small disc of copper alloy, pierced for suspension and bearing inscribed marks — names, characters, or a seal of the sort prescribed by grimoires for protective and curative charms. Worn on the body, such a piece carried its inscribed magic continuously with its owner.

## Significance
Grimoires from the *Clavicula* to the *Petit Albert* instruct the operator to engrave seals and divine names on metal *lamens* or pendants, made at elected planetary hours, to attract or repel particular influences. Excavated and metal-detected finds like this one — catalogued through the British Museum's Portable Antiquities Scheme — show that such talismans were not merely textual but actually manufactured and worn.

## For artists & game designers
A grounded reference for craftable charm items: a plain pierced disc whose inscribed sigil determines its passive effect.

citations.text: The Portable Antiquities Scheme database, FindID 755270.

title: Memory-image leaf from an *Ars memorativa* blockbook (p. 44)
work: The Art of Memory: Mnemonic Diagrams of the Western Esoteric Tradition
creator: Anonymous (German workshop)
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: Wikimedia Commons scan of an Ars memorativa blockbook]
summary:
A page from one of the late-fifteenth-century German *Ars memorativa* blockbooks, the cheap printed manuals that spread the classical art of memory to a wide lay public.

## Iconography
The woodcut sets striking, easily-pictured figures into a remembered place so that abstract matter can be recalled through vivid images. Such leaves typically pair an architectural or bodily *locus* with grotesque or active *imagines agentes* — the deliberately memorable pictures the classical rhetoricians prescribed.

## Significance
The *Ars memorativa* tradition descends from the *Rhetorica ad Herennium* and Quintilian, transmitted through medieval preachers and crystallised in these blockbooks. They are the popular face of the [[motif:art-of-memory|art of memory]] that Frances Yates traced from antiquity into the Renaissance occult revival.

## For artists & game designers
A single page that turns a list into a row of bizarre little figures is a perfect template for a 'memorise this' puzzle interface.

citations.text: Frances A. Yates, *The Art of Memory* (1966).

title: Memory-image leaf from an *Ars memorativa* blockbook (p. 43)
work: The Art of Memory: Mnemonic Diagrams of the Western Esoteric Tradition
creator: Anonymous (German workshop)
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: Wikimedia Commons scan of an Ars memorativa blockbook]
summary:
A facing leaf from the same German *Ars memorativa* blockbook, showing a further set of memory-images.

## Iconography
As on the companion page, the woodcut presents a sequence of vivid figures to be lodged in mental *loci*. The repetition across pages reflects how the manuals drilled the reader through ordered series of images, building an internal storehouse one place at a time.

## Significance
These inexpensive blockbooks were the mass-market vehicle of the [[motif:method-of-loci|method of loci]] on the eve of the Reformation. Their crude but forceful imagery shows how the learned ancient art became a practical devotional and pedagogical technique for ordinary clerics and students.

## For artists & game designers
Use a paired-page layout — image, then the thing it stands for — to teach a memory mechanic across successive screens.

citations.text: Frances A. Yates, *The Art of Memory* (1966).

title: *Figura amoris*: a mnemonic seal of Giordano Bruno
work: The Art of Memory: Mnemonic Diagrams of the Western Esoteric Tradition
creator: Giordano Bruno
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: from a printed edition of Bruno's mnemonic works]
summary:
The *Figura amoris* ('figure of love'), one of the rotating mnemonic seals Giordano Bruno designed for his Hermetic art of memory.

## Iconography
Concentric lettered circles are divided into segments, each carrying images and combinations of letters. By turning the rings the practitioner generates an inexhaustible series of composite memory-images, binding the soul's faculties to the wheel of 'love' that draws the mind toward its objects.

## Significance
Bruno reworked the classical [[motif:art-of-memory|art of memory]] into a magical-Hermetic discipline: his seals in *De umbris idearum* (1582) and related works aimed not merely to recall facts but to imprint the cosmos on the imagination and so unify the magus with the world-soul. Frances Yates made these seals central to her account of Bruno's 'Hermetic memory'.

## For artists & game designers
A rotating multi-ring seal that combines images is a literal procedural generator — turn the dials, get a new sigil.

citations.text: Frances A. Yates, *The Art of Memory* (1966).
Frances A. Yates, *Giordano Bruno and the Hermetic Tradition* (1964).

title: Combinatorial wheel from Bruno's *De umbris idearum*
work: The Art of Memory: Mnemonic Diagrams of the Western Esoteric Tradition
creator: Giordano Bruno
summary:
A rotating combinatorial wheel from Giordano Bruno's *De umbris idearum* ('On the Shadows of Ideas', Paris, 1582), his first and most influential treatise on the art of memory.

## Iconography
Nested rings carry letters, images and the names of agents, places and actions. Aligning the rings yields coded 'shadows of ideas' — composite mnemonic images that stand for the intelligible forms behind sensible things. The wheel is at once a memory device and a metaphysical instrument.

## Significance
*De umbris idearum* recasts memory as a Hermetic path: the 'shadows' are the images through which the dispersed human mind can re-collect the divine ideas. Bruno's title plays on Plato's cave — to remember rightly is to ascend from shadow toward the Ideas. The work helped win him an audience at the court of Henri III.

## For artists & game designers
The '[[motif:shadows-of-ideas|shadow of an idea]]' — an image that is a degraded copy of a perfect form — is a rich design conceit for collectible glyphs that hint at hidden truths.

citations.text: Frances A. Yates, *The Art of Memory* (1966).
Giordano Bruno, *De umbris idearum* (Paris, 1582).

title: Art of memory plate I from Fludd's *De praeternaturali* (1621)
work: The Art of Memory: Mnemonic Diagrams of the Western Esoteric Tradition
creator: Robert Fludd; de Bry / Frankfurt workshop
rights: CC BY 4.0 (Wellcome Collection). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
An *Ars Memoriae* plate from the *De praeternaturali utriusque mundi historia* — the second tract of Robert Fludd's *Utriusque Cosmi Historia* (Frankfurt, 1621).

## Iconography
The engraving belongs to Fludd's treatment of the art of memory: a scheme of *loci* — niches, doors and figures of an imagined building — into which memorable images are placed and later 'walked' to recall their contents.

## Significance
Fludd raised the classical [[motif:memory-palace|memory palace]] to Hermetic ambition, holding that the trained imagination could mirror the whole cosmos. Frances Yates devoted a celebrated chapter to these plates, arguing their theatre-form preserves traces of the Elizabethan public stage.

## For artists & game designers
A labelled architectural interior built to be 'walked' for recall is a ready-made level layout for a memory-palace mechanic.

The completeness of Fludd's illustrated programme — multiple plates, round and square arts, theatre and chambers — makes his *Ars Memoriae* the richest pictorial source for the [[motif:art-of-memory|Hermetic art of memory]] before its eclipse by the new philosophy. title: The Guidonian hand: a musical memory diagram
work: The Art of Memory: Mnemonic Diagrams of the Western Esoteric Tradition
creator: Anonymous (after Guido of Arezzo)
summary:
The *Guidonian hand*, the medieval diagram that maps the notes of the musical gamut onto the joints and tips of the human hand.

## Iconography
Each knuckle and fingertip is labelled with a note of the hexachord system (*ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la*) running from *gamma ut* at the thumb-tip up the fingers. A singer 'reads' melodies by pointing to positions on the hand, the body itself becoming a notated instrument.

## Significance
Attributed to Guido of Arezzo, the hand is the archetypal [[motif:memory-hand|memory hand]] — the most enduring of all bodily mnemonics, used to teach sight-singing for half a millennium. It anticipates the 'memory hands' that Romberch and Rossellius would later adapt for letters and memory-places.

## For artists & game designers
Mapping data onto the joints of a hand is a compact, diegetic UI — the player's own hand as a control surface.

A combinatorial figure from Athanasius Kircher's *Ars Magna Sciendi sive Combinatoria* ('The Great Art of Knowing, or Combinatorics', Amsterdam, 1669).

## Iconography
The engraving arranges categories of being and knowledge into a Lullian apparatus of tables and rotating wheels. By combining the lettered terms the system claims to generate, store and recall every possible proposition — a mechanised art of memory and invention.

## Significance
Kircher's *Ars Magna Sciendi* is the great Baroque synthesis of [[motif:combinatorial-wheels|Lullian combinatorics]] with the art of memory: knowledge becomes a finite alphabet of concepts whose permutations exhaust the knowable. It fed directly into Leibniz's dream of a *characteristica universalis*.

## For artists & game designers
A table of concept-letters that recombine into endless statements is a clean model for a procedural lore- or spell-generation system.

The *Arbor scientiae* ('Tree of Knowledge'), Ramon Llull's encyclopaedic tree that organises all the sciences as branches growing from common roots.

A great tree rises from labelled roots (Llull's basic principles or *dignitates*) through a trunk into successive boughs, each branch a domain of knowledge — the elemental, vegetal, sensual, imaginal, human, moral, celestial, angelic and divine trees. Knowledge is pictured as an organically connected whole.

## Significance
Llull's *Ars* and its trees are a foundational [[motif:combinatorial-wheels|combinatorial]] system later absorbed into the art of memory: an ordered structure on which to hang and recall the totality of learning. Paolo Rossi traced the long line from Llull through Bruno to Leibniz that runs through this image.

## For artists & game designers
A literal tree where roots are axioms and branches are disciplines is the original skill-tree — usable almost unchanged.

A miniature from the *Breviculum ex artibus Raimundi Lulli electum*, showing Ramon Llull and his disciple Thomas Le Myésier presenting anthologies of the Lullian Art to the queen.

## Iconography
The illumination depicts the philosopher-mystic Llull, the *Doctor Illuminatus*, handing over books that contain his *Ars* — the combinatorial method whose wheels and figures underlie his whole project. The scene frames the Art as a gift of universal knowledge offered to royal patronage.

## Significance
Though not itself a diagram, the miniature is the portrait-frontispiece of the Lullian tradition that fed the Renaissance [[motif:art-of-memory|art of memory]]. Bruno, Agrippa and Kircher all drew on Llull's rotating figures; this image fixes the human origin of that long combinatorial lineage.

## For artists & game designers
A framed 'master hands the player the system' scene is a clean way to introduce a combinatorial mechanic in-fiction.

title: The combinatorial wheel of Llull's *Ars Magna* (modern recreation)
work: The Art of Memory: Mnemonic Diagrams of the Western Esoteric Tradition
creator: Lliurepensactua (recreation after Ramon Llull)
date: modern recreation of a c. 1305 figure
summary:
A clean modern recreation of the rotating combinatorial wheel (*figura*) at the heart of Ramon Llull's *Ars Magna*.

## Iconography
A circle is divided into lettered segments, each letter standing for one of Llull's basic 'dignities' or attributes (goodness, greatness, eternity, power, wisdom, will, and so on). Concentric rings turn against one another so that the letters combine in every possible pairing, mechanically generating propositions.

## Significance
This *figura* is the engine of the entire Lullian Art and the ancestor of every later [[motif:combinatorial-wheels|combinatorial wheel]] — Bruno's mnemonic seals, Kircher's *Ars Magna Sciendi*, and ultimately Leibniz's logical calculus. Llull intended it as a means to demonstrate the truths of faith by reason. (The diagram shown is a contemporary CC BY-SA reconstruction, not an early print.)

## For artists & game designers
Two rings of symbols that rotate to pair up letters is a complete, self-contained 'combination lock' or spell-mixing mechanic.

A memory diagram from the *Congestorium artificiose memorie* of the Dominican Johann Host von Romberch, one of the most influential printed manuals of the art of memory (Venice, 1520; repr. 1533).

## Iconography
Romberch's woodcuts systematise the art: schemes of *loci* set in an imagined building, an abbey or town used as a memory-place, alphabet-images, and the celebrated **memory hand** on which letters and figures are lodged at the joints. The page presents memory as an architecture to be furnished and read.

## Significance
The *Congestorium* gathered the medieval and classical art of memory into a teachable system that Bruno, Rossellius and others built upon. Frances Yates and Paolo Rossi treat Romberch as a crucial hinge between the monastic [[motif:art-of-memory|ars memoriae]] and its Renaissance Hermetic transformation.

## For artists & game designers
The abbey-as-memory-place — a familiar building repurposed as an index of knowledge — is a strong premise for an explorable 'palace' hub level.

A memory-place diagram from the *Thesaurus artificiosae memoriae* of the Florentine Dominican Cosmas Rossellius (Venice, 1579), using the regions of Hell as a system of mnemonic *loci*.

## Iconography
The woodcut lays out an ordered set of places — here drawn from the Christian otherworld — into which memory-images are to be set. Rossellius furnished his readers with ready-made cosmic *loci* (heaven, hell, the elements) so that the entire moral universe could serve as a filing system for the memory.

## Significance
Rossellius is, with Romberch, the great late-Renaissance compiler of the [[motif:method-of-loci|method of loci]]. His use of Hell and Heaven as memory-places shows how the art fused with devotional meditation on the Last Things — remembering doctrine by walking the afterlife. Frances Yates singled out his *Thesaurus* as a key occult-memory text.

## For artists & game designers
Using the circles of Hell as labelled storage slots is a vivid, thematically loaded inventory metaphor for a dark-fantasy game.

title: A Practitioner of Mesmerism Using Animal Magnetism

A print of a mesmerist at work, directing animal magnetism upon a seated patient through the characteristic passes of the hands (Wellcome Collection).

## Iconography
The magnetizer leans toward a seated subject, hands extended toward the patient's head and torso, fingers spread to project the fluid. The patient's posture — head tilted, eyes closing — signals the onset of the magnetic state.

## Significance
The [[motif:magnetic pass|magnetic pass]] was the basic technique of the operator: slow sweeping motions of the hands along the body, supposed to channel the [[motif:invisible fluid|fluid]] from magnetizer to patient and establish the [[motif:magnetic rapport|rapport]] that bound them. The image distils the whole practice to its essential gesture — the willed, fingertip transmission of an unseen force.

## For artists & game designers
A spell-casting pose ready for animation: hands that emit an invisible influence, the target's reaction keyed to the operator's gestures.

title: Mesmer's Animal Magnetism Therapy (The Baquet)
work: Mesmerism, Animal Magnetism & the Invisible Fluid (1780s–1850s)
creator: Anonymous
rights: CC BY 4.0 (Wellcome Collection). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A scene of Mesmer's collective therapy around the *baquet*, the magnetic tub at the heart of his Paris clinic (Wellcome Collection).

## Iconography
Patients ring a low covered tub from which protrude bent iron rods; sitters press the rods to afflicted parts of the body, some linked by a connecting cord to share the [[motif:magnetic rapport|magnetic rapport]]. Attendants move among them as one or two slump into the convulsive [[motif:magnetic crisis|crisis]].

## Significance
The [[motif:the baquet|baquet]] was Mesmer's machine for distributing the [[motif:invisible fluid|invisible fluid]] to many patients at once — an oak vat filled with 'magnetized' water, iron filings, and glass, its rods conducting the supposed influence into the body. The room, with its dim light, music, and chains of joined hands, staged a powerful collective suggestion that produced fits, trances, and reported cures.

## For artists & game designers
A ritual-machine set piece: a central apparatus that channels an unseen force to a circle of linked participants, with crisis as the visible 'effect'.

citations.text: Robert Darnton, *Mesmerism and the End of the Enlightenment in France* (1968).

A photograph of a surviving *baquet de Mesmer*, a rare physical example of the magnetic tub preserved at the Bibliothèque municipale de Lyon.

## Iconography
A low circular wooden vat, its lid pierced for the jointed iron rods that patients once applied to their bodies. Seen as an object rather than a scene, it shows the plain cooper's construction beneath the era's extravagant claims.

## Significance
Few genuine baquets survive, so this object anchors the mesmeric craze in material fact: an oak tub that, filled with 'magnetized' water, bottles, and iron filings, was held to store and dispense the [[motif:invisible fluid|animal-magnetic fluid]]. Where engravings show the [[motif:the baquet|baquet]] amid swooning crowds, the surviving artefact reveals the modest apparatus that focused so much Enlightenment controversy.

## For artists & game designers
A 'relic' prop: the actual device, weathered and demystified, that a player might recover and study apart from the spectacle that surrounded it.

The title-page of James Braid's *Neurypnology; or, The Rationale of Nervous Sleep* (1843), the book that coined 'hypnotism' (Wellcome Collection).

## Iconography
A plain printed title-page announcing Braid's treatise on 'nervous sleep considered in relation with animal magnetism'. The typography of a sober medical work signals its claim to rescue the phenomena from occultism.

## Significance
The Manchester surgeon James Braid argued that the 'magnetic' trance owed nothing to any fluid passing between operator and subject; it was a physiological 'nervous sleep' induced by fixed attention and the fatigue of the gaze. Renaming it [[motif:hypnotism|hypnotism]] (from Greek *hypnos*), he recast mesmerism as a subject for [[motif:rational physiology|physiology]] and psychology, a decisive step toward modern hypnosis.

## For artists & game designers
The 'rational reframing' beat: the document by which a feared occult power is redefined as a natural, teachable technique.

An engraved portrait of Alessandro, Count Cagliostro (Giuseppe Balsamo, 1743–1795), the most notorious occult adventurer of the mesmeric age (Rijksmuseum).

## Iconography
A bust-length portrait of Cagliostro, presented with the dignity of a man of mystery and learning — the standard engraved likeness that spread his fame across Europe.

## Significance
Though not a magnetizer himself, [[motif:cagliostro|Cagliostro]] was the era's paradigmatic [[motif:magus|magus]]: healer, alchemist, founder of an 'Egyptian' rite of Freemasonry, and purveyor of elixirs and prophecy. He moved through the same fashionable, occult-hungry salons that took up [[motif:animal magnetism|animal magnetism]], and his spectacular rise and disgrace (entangled in the Affair of the Diamond Necklace, dying in a papal prison) made him the symbol of Enlightenment-age occult charlatanry.

## For artists & game designers
The travelling-mystagogue archetype: a charismatic foreign 'count' trailing rumours of immortality, secret rites, and miraculous cures.

A chronophotographic study of hysteria from the circle of Jean-Martin Charcot at the Salpêtrière, where hypnosis and the convulsive 'grand hysteria' were photographed as clinical phenomena.

## Iconography
A sequence or single frame capturing a patient in the postures of the hysterical attack — the contorted, arching body that Charcot's school catalogued in serial images, the heir to the older convulsive [[motif:magnetic crisis|crisis]].

## Significance
In the 1880s Charcot revived hypnotism as a neurological subject, staging hypnotic and hysterical states before audiences and recording them with the new clinical [[motif:clinical photography|photography]]. His celebrated demonstrations — the direct line from Mesmer's crisis through Braid's nervous sleep — shaped the young Freud and made the Salpêtrière the theatre where mind, suggestion, and the body's spectacle converged.

## For artists & game designers
A clinical-spectacle reference: the medical theatre where an altered state is exhibited and documented, blurring science and performance.

A sheet of portraits of the family of Johann Caspar Lavater (1741–1801), the Zurich pastor whose *Physiognomy* made the reading of character from the face a science of the age (Zentralbibliothek Zürich).

## Iconography
A strip of profile likenesses of the Lavater family, the format echoing the silhouette and profile studies that filled his physiognomical works, where the line of brow, nose, and chin was scrutinised for the soul within.

## Significance
[[motif:johann caspar lavater|Lavater]]'s *Physiognomische Fragmente* (1775–78) systematised [[motif:physiognomy|physiognomy]] — the inference of inner character from outer form — and made it a craze parallel to mesmerism in the same decades. A friend of the sympathetic and 'magnetic' currents of the time, he lent the era's fascination with invisible forces a respectable, sentimental face. Physiognomy and phrenology together formed the broader 'science of the invisible self' around animal magnetism.

## For artists & game designers
A face-reading mechanic: profile portraits whose features the player learns to interpret for hidden traits, allegiance, or fate.

An engraved vignette (fleuron) from *Le magnétisme animal, Mesmer ou les sots* — 'Animal Magnetism, Mesmer or the Fools' — by Louis-Nicolas Mareschal.

A small printer's headpiece ornament from the title-matter of a satirical pamphlet, the kind of engraved fleuron set above the text. The very title yokes Mesmer to 'les sots', the fools who follow him.

## Significance
The pamphlet war over magnetism produced not only large caricatures but a stream of cheap printed satire whose [[motif:fleuron|ornamental vignettes]] carried the mockery into the book itself. The title *Mesmer ou les sots* exemplifies the literary [[motif:satire of magnetism|satire]] that, alongside the royal verdict, framed mesmerism as the gulling of the [[motif:credulity|credulous]].

## For artists & game designers
A period typographic asset: an authentic engraved ornament for mocking in-world 'pamphlets' that ridicule a charlatan's movement.

title: The Magnetic Pass, the Mesmeric Sleep
work: Mesmerism, Animal Magnetism & the Invisible Fluid (1780s–1850s)
creator: Anonymous
rights: CC BY 4.0 (Wellcome Collection). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A nineteenth-century print depicting the magnetic pass inducing the 'Mesmeric sleep', the artificial somnambulic state (Wellcome Collection).

## Iconography
The operator makes a downward pass before the face of a subject who has sunk, eyes closed, into trance. The composition isolates the moment of transition from waking to the lucid magnetic sleep.

## Significance
The '[[motif:mesmeric sleep|magnetic sleep]]' or [[motif:somnambulism|artificial somnambulism]] was the deeper state that displaced the early convulsive crisis as the prized phenomenon of magnetism. In it subjects appeared asleep yet responsive, sometimes credited with clairvoyance or insensibility to pain. This 'lucid sleep' is the direct ancestor of the hypnotic trance that Braid would later rename.

## For artists & game designers
A trance-induction beat: the precise gesture and the subject's collapse into a controllable sleep state — a mechanic for charm or interrogation.

rights: CC BY 4.0 (Wellcome Collection). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A French satirical print, *Les Effets du Magnétisme animal*, lampooning the fashionable craze for animal magnetism (Wellcome Collection).

## Iconography
A crowded, comic scene of magnetism's 'effects': sitters around a tub, some swooning, others making free under cover of the trance, the operator presiding over a room of theatrical excess. The crisis is played for ridicule rather than awe.

## Significance
The magnetic vogue drew a flood of [[motif:caricature|caricature]] that mocked the [[motif:credulity|credulity]] of fashionable Paris and hinted broadly at the erotic licence the darkened séances afforded. Such satires, sharpened after the 1784 royal commissions ruled the fluid imaginary, made mesmerism a byword for fraud and folly even as the practice spread.

## For artists & game designers
A comic-relief tableau: the same ritual rendered as farce, exposing the gap between the operator's claims and what the crowd is really up to.

*De magnetiseur* (The Magnetizer) by the Flemish painter Jan Jozef Verhaghen, a genre depiction of a magnetic operator and his subject.

A painted interior in which a magnetizer attends a seated figure, hands engaged in the work of the passes, observers looking on. The treatment is that of eighteenth-century genre painting, lending the new practice the intimacy of a domestic scene.

## Significance
That a Flemish painter took the [[motif:magnetizer|magnetizer]] as a genre subject shows how quickly animal magnetism entered the visual culture of the Low Countries and German lands as well as France. The work records the magnetic encounter not as caricature but as an everyday act of healing, the operator bending his will and hands to the transfer of the [[motif:invisible fluid|fluid]].

title: Portrait of Franz Anton Mesmer
work: Mesmerism, Animal Magnetism & the Invisible Fluid (1780s–1850s)
creator: Anonymous
summary:
A portrait of Franz Anton Mesmer (1734–1815), the Viennese physician whose theory of 'animal magnetism' gave its name to mesmerism.

## Iconography
A half-length likeness of a gentleman-physician of the Enlightenment, in powdered wig and formal coat, gazing out with composed authority. The print is the standard frontispiece type by which Mesmer was circulated to a curious public.

## Significance
Mesmer proposed that an invisible, magnetic-like [[motif:invisible fluid|fluid]] pervaded all bodies and that illness arose from its obstruction; the healer could redirect it by 'magnetizing' the patient. Trained in Vienna and famous in 1780s Paris, he became the storm-centre of a craze that two royal commissions (1784) investigated and dismissed. Whatever the verdict on the fluid, his practice opened the road from magnetic 'crisis' to somnambulism, suggestion, and ultimately hypnosis.

## For artists & game designers
A charismatic-doctor archetype: the authoritative healer whose 'cures' blur the line between medicine, theatre, and the occult.

*Le Mesmérisme Confondu* ('Mesmerism Confounded'), a caricature celebrating the discrediting of animal magnetism (Wellcome Collection).

## Iconography
A satirical composition in which the apparatus and adepts of magnetism are thrown into disarray, the print's title announcing the rout of the doctrine. Figures scatter from the tub as the pretensions of the magnetizers collapse.

## Significance
The royal commissions of 1784 — one including Benjamin Franklin, Lavoisier, and the physician Guillotin — tested magnetism by blinded trials and concluded its effects came from [[motif:credulity|imagination]], not any fluid. Prints like '[[motif:mesmerism confounded|Le Mesmérisme Confondu]]' turned that verdict into popular ridicule, a landmark in the history of placebo and of debunking by controlled experiment.

## For artists & game designers
A 'reveal' panel: the moment a celebrated power is publicly exposed, the believers fleeing as the apparatus is shown to be empty.

citations.text: Robert Darnton, *Mesmerism and the End of the Enlightenment in France* (1968).

title: The Basic Elements of Phrenology, Physiognomy and Palmistry
work: Mesmerism, Animal Magnetism & the Invisible Fluid (1780s–1850s)
creator: Anonymous
rights: CC BY 4.0 (Wellcome Collection). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A composite chart of 'the basic elements of phrenology, physiognomy and palmistry', the popular sciences of reading character from head, face, and hand (Wellcome Collection).

## Iconography
The plate gathers a mapped [[motif:phrenological head|phrenological head]] partitioned into numbered organs of the faculties, physiognomic faces, and a palm divided into its lines and mounts — a one-sheet compendium of the body read as a text.

## Significance
[[motif:phrenology|Phrenology]], devised by Gall and popularised by Spurzheim and the Fowlers, mapped mental faculties onto bumps of the skull, and readily fused with mesmerism as 'phreno-magnetism' — magnetizing a phrenological organ to excite its faculty in a sensitive subject. Together with [[motif:physiognomy|physiognomy]] and palmistry it formed the nineteenth century's confident art of reading the invisible self from visible signs.

## For artists & game designers
A character-stat overlay: a head or hand divided into labelled regions, each tappable to reveal a personality 'faculty' the player can probe.

citations.text: Roger Cooter, *The Cultural Meaning of Popular Science: Phrenology and the Organization of Consent in Nineteenth-Century Britain* (1984).

title: Investigating the Od Rays (Reichenbach's Sensitive)
work: Mesmerism, Animal Magnetism & the Invisible Fluid (1780s–1850s)
creator: Max Nentwich
summary:
An illustration of an experimenter investigating the 'Od rays' with a silver spoon and a gold ring suspended on a thread, after the work of Baron Carl von Reichenbach.

## Iconography
A figure conducts a test of radiation, holding a silver spoon and a gold ring hung from a thread as a kind of pendulum — instruments by which a 'sensitive' was thought to detect emanations from metals and bodies.

## Significance
The industrial chemist Baron Carl von [[motif:reichenbach experiment|Reichenbach]] (1788–1869) proposed an [[motif:odic force|odic force]] (the 'Od'), a vital emanation streaming from magnets, crystals, metals, and living things, visible as a glow to nervous '[[motif:sensitive subject|sensitives]]' in a darkened room. A late, would-be-scientific descendant of Mesmer's fluid, the Od became a touchstone for theosophy and psychical research even as mainstream science rejected it.

## For artists & game designers
A 'detect aura' mechanic: special-sensitive characters who perceive otherwise invisible emanations from objects, revealing hidden properties.

citations.text: Carl von Reichenbach, *Researches on Magnetism, Electricity ... in Relation to Vital Force* (Eng. trans. 1850).

title: Essai sur la théorie du somnambulisme magnétique (Fleuron)
work: Mesmerism, Animal Magnetism & the Invisible Fluid (1780s–1850s)
creator: Tardy de Montravel (T. D. M.)
summary:
An engraved vignette from the *Essai sur la théorie du somnambulisme magnétique* (1785) by Tardy de Montravel, an early theoretical treatise on magnetic somnambulism.

## Iconography
A printed title-page fleuron from a key text of the magnetic literature, the small ornament marking a serious theoretical essay rather than a satire.

## Significance
In 1784 the Marquis de [[motif:puysegur school|Puységur]] discovered that magnetism could induce, instead of convulsions, a calm 'artificial [[motif:somnambulism|somnambulism]]' in which the subject seemed asleep yet lucid. Followers like Tardy de Montravel theorised this lucid sleep and its supposed clairvoyance; this 1785 *Essai* is a document of that pivotal shift from the crisis to the somnambulic trance that reoriented the whole movement.

## For artists & game designers
A 'source text' prop: a credible period treatise whose title alone establishes the in-world science of the lucid magnetic sleep.

citations.text: Adam Crabtree, *From Mesmer to Freud: Magnetic Sleep and the Roots of Psychological Healing* (1993).

title: Codex Borbonicus (Complete Screenfold)
creator: Anonymous (Aztec / Nahua tlacuilo)
date: c. 1500–1525 CE (very early colonial / late pre-Conquest)
summary:
A composite reproduction of the complete *Codex Borbonicus*, the great Aztec ritual-calendar screenfold held in the library of the French National Assembly (Palais Bourbon).

## Iconography
The long folded strip opens with a *tonalamatl* of twenty trecenas, each large compartment ruled by patron deities and the Lords of the Day and Night, followed by sections on the 52-year cycle, the New Fire ceremony, and the eighteen monthly (*veintena*) festivals.

## Significance
The Borbonicus is arguably the finest single Aztec manuscript, painted in pure native style on bark paper just before or just after the Conquest. Its [[motif:tonalamatl|tonalamatl]] is the canonical example used to explain how diviners read the 260-day count, and its New Fire scene documents the *toxiuhmolpilia*, the binding of the years every 52 years. Studied by Francisco del Paso y Troncoso and, more recently, Elizabeth Hill Boone.

## For artists & game designers
A single artifact that scrolls from a fate-almanac into a festival calendar is a model for an in-game "living" ritual book.

citations.text: Elizabeth Hill Boone, *Cycles of Time and Meaning in the Mexican Books of Fate* (2007).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Codex Borgia, Page 20 (Tonalpohualli Almanac)
creator: Anonymous (Central Mexican / Nahua-Mixtec tlacuilo)
rights: CC BY-SA 4.0 (facsimile rendering, Chaccard). Underlying codex public domain. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A page from the *Codex Borgia*, the most splendid surviving Mesoamerican divinatory book, named for Cardinal Stefano Borgia and now in the Vatican Library.

## Iconography
The register packs the bar-and-dot numbers and twenty day-sign glyphs of the *tonalpohualli* into compartments, each ruled by a deity figure rendered in the flat, outlined polychrome "Mixteca-Puebla" style. Day signs such as Crocodile (Cipactli), Wind (Ehecatl) and Death (Miquiztli) interlock with patron gods and directional colours.

## Significance
The Borgia is the eponym of the "[[motif:tonalpohualli|Borgia Group]]" of pre-Conquest ritual screenfolds. Its almanacs let a diviner (*tonalpouhqui*) read the fate of a day, a birth, or an undertaking from the 260-day count, cross-tabulated with the nine Lords of the Night and the directional trees. Eduard Seler's monumental commentary (1904–09) remains foundational; Elizabeth Hill Boone has reframed these books as "narratives of fate."

## For artists & game designers
The compartment grid of day-glyph × deity × direction is a ready-made procedural lookup table for a divination minigame.

citations.text: Elizabeth Hill Boone, *Cycles of Time and Meaning in the Mexican Books of Fate* (2007).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Codex Borgia, Page 56 (Quetzalcoatl)
creator: Anonymous (Central Mexican tlacuilo)
summary:
A page from the central "narrative" section of the *Codex Borgia* featuring Quetzalcoatl, the Feathered Serpent.

## Iconography
The Feathered Serpent appears in his Ehecatl-Quetzalcoatl aspect, marked by the buccal mask of the wind god and a conch-shell "wind jewel" (*ehecailacacozcatl*). Plumed serpent forms, ritual paraphernalia and offerings fill the surrounding field in saturated reds, ochres and turquoise.

## Significance
Pages 29–46 of the Borgia form a celebrated cosmological cycle, and Quetzalcoatl recurs throughout as creator, wind, and Venus. As [[motif:quetzalcoatl|Quetzalcoatl]] he is the priest-god of self-sacrifice and the planet Venus; as Ehecatl he sweeps the roads for the rain gods. The ambiguous, much-debated "narrative" of these pages may depict a night-sea journey or a New Fire / Venus-related rite, as argued by Karl Anton Nowotny and later by Boone.

## For artists & game designers
A single deity with stacked aspects — wind, serpent, morning star, culture-hero — is a model for a shapeshifting patron god.

citations.text: Karl Anton Nowotny, *Tlacuilolli: Style and Contents of the Mexican Pictorial Manuscripts* (1961; Eng. 2005).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Codex Cospi (Bologna Screenfold)
creator: Anonymous (Central Mexican tlacuilo)
summary:
A view of the *Codex Cospi*, a pre-Conquest divinatory screenfold of the Borgia Group, preserved in the University Library of Bologna.

## Iconography
The deer-hide strip is painted on both sides with *tonalpohualli* almanacs: rows of day-signs and dots framed by directional deities and offerings, with one face given over to a Venus-related and ritual sequence.

## Significance
Cospi (formerly Codex Bologna) is one of the five members of the [[motif:tonalpohualli|Borgia Group]] and one of the very few Mesoamerican books to reach Europe in the sixteenth century, entering the collection of Marchese Ferdinando Cospi in 1665. Its almanacs and Venus pages parallel those of the Borgia and Vaticanus B, helping scholars reconstruct a shared Central Mexican divinatory tradition.

## For artists & game designers
A double-sided ritual strip — fate on one face, a planet-god cycle on the other — is a strong concept for a physical in-game relic.

citations.text: Karl Anton Nowotny (ed.), *Codex Cospi* (facsimile, 1968).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Codex Laud, Folio 43
creator: Anonymous (Central Mexican tlacuilo)
summary:
Folio 43 of the *Codex Laud*, a pre-Conquest divinatory screenfold of the Borgia Group, now in the Bodleian Library, Oxford.

## Iconography
Deity figures and day-signs are arranged in vivid compartments against bands of directional colour; death-and-fertility imagery (skeletal and life-giving gods paired) characterises several of the Laud's almanacs, including marriage and offering prognostications.

## Significance
Named for Archbishop William Laud, who gave it to the Bodleian in the 1630s, the Laud is a core member of the [[motif:tonalpohualli|Borgia Group]]. Its almanacs treat themes such as the fate of marriages and the pairing of death-gods with life-gods, illustrating how the 260-day count structured the most intimate life decisions. The reconstruction of its provenance and content owes much to C. A. Burland and Ferdinand Anders.

## For artists & game designers
Paired death/fertility gods governing marriage omens make an elegant dual-aspect card set for a fate deck.

citations.text: C. A. Burland (ed.), *Codex Laud* (facsimile, 1966).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Codex Ríos (Vaticanus A), Day-Sign Malinalli
creator: Anonymous (indigenous painters, colonial Mexico)
place: Mexico / Italy (compiled in New Spain, completed in Italy)
summary:
The day-sign *Malinalli* ("Grass" / twisted grass) as drawn in the *Codex Ríos*, also called *Codex Vaticanus A* (Vatican Library, Vat. lat. 3738).

## Iconography
The twelfth of the twenty day-signs is shown as a stylised skull-and-grass glyph: a death's-head sprouting the curling blades of *malinalli* grass, the emblem of decay turning to new growth.

## Significance
The Ríos codex is an early-colonial encyclopedic manuscript, copied under Dominican supervision (associated with Fray Pedro de los Ríos), that glosses Aztec cosmology, the [[motif:tonalpohualli|day-count]], the heavens and the underworld in Italian. As a glossed copy it is invaluable for decoding pre-Conquest iconography, even as its colonial framing reinterprets it. Malinalli, ruled by Patecatl, was read as an unlucky, death-tinged sign.

## For artists & game designers
A "grass-from-a-skull" glyph is a compact death-and-rebirth icon for a calendar or tarot-style card.

citations.text: Ferdinand Anders & Maarten Jansen, *Religión, costumbres e historia de los antiguos mexicanos* (Codex Vaticanus A facsimile, 1996).

title: Codex Vaticanus B (3773), Page 24
creator: Anonymous (Central Mexican tlacuilo)
summary:
A page from the *Codex Vaticanus B* (Vatican Library, Vat. lat. 3773), a pre-Conquest divinatory screenfold of the Borgia Group.

## Iconography
Dense compartments arrange the day-signs, numerical coefficients and presiding deities of the *tonalpohualli*, with directional and color schemes guiding the diviner's reading. The drawing is more abbreviated and schematic than the Borgia's, prioritising calculational clarity.

## Significance
Vaticanus B is one of the five core members of the [[motif:tonalpohualli|Borgia Group]] (with Borgia, Cospi, Laud and Fejérváry-Mayer). Its almanacs are unusually systematic, making it a key witness for reconstructing how Central Mexican diviners combined the 260-day count with the directions, the Lords of the Night, and Venus. Eduard Seler produced the standard early commentary (1902–03).

## For artists & game designers
The terse, calculational layout is a good reference for designing a readable in-game oracle table that still feels arcane.

citations.text: Eduard Seler, *Codex Vaticanus No. 3773* (1902–03).

title: Dresden Codex — Page with the Month Kankin
creator: Anonymous (Maya scribes)
summary:
A detail from the *Dresden Codex* featuring the glyph for the month *Kankin*, part of the Maya calendrical apparatus.

## Iconography
A framed Maya hieroglyphic block names the Haab month Kankin, set among the bar-and-dot numerals and almanac columns by which the codex's scribes laid out divinatory and astronomical tables.

## Significance
The Dresden Codex interweaves the 260-day *tzolkin* and the 365-day *haab* (whose eighteen named "months" include Kankin) into its almanacs and astronomical tables, including the Venus and eclipse cycles. Such month glyphs anchored omens and rituals to specific points in the solar year. The codex's calendrics were decoded by Ernst Förstemann, librarian at Dresden, whose work founded modern Maya epigraphy.

## For artists & game designers
Named "month" sigils that gate which events can occur are a tidy way to give an in-game calendar texture and lore.

citations.text: Michael D. Coe, *Breaking the Maya Code* (1992).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Dresden Codex — Venus Table (Facsimile)
creator: Anonymous (Maya scribes); facsimile by Lacambalam
rights: CC BY-SA 4.0 (facsimile, Lacambalam). Underlying codex public domain. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A facsimile of the famous Venus pages of the *Dresden Codex*, the finest surviving Maya book, held in the Saxon State Library (SLUB) in Dresden.

## Iconography
Columns of bar-and-dot numbers, Maya glyphs and almanac tables track the 584-day synodic cycle of Venus across its phases, accompanied by deity figures hurling spears — Venus as a malign spear-thrower whose heliacal rising threatened rulers, captives and crops.

## Significance
The Dresden [[motif:venus table|Venus table]] is the most celebrated piece of pre-Columbian astronomy, correlating Venus's appearances with the 260-day *tzolkin* to issue omens. It encodes a strikingly accurate long-term Venus calendar with correction mechanisms. Studied by Ernst Förstemann (who first cracked its numeration in the 1880s), Floyd Lounsbury and others, it proves that Maya divination was inseparable from precise astronomy.

## For artists & game designers
A planet that returns on a fixed clock to deal omen-driven damage is a clean astronomical event mechanic.

citations.text: J. Eric S. Thompson, *A Commentary on the Dresden Codex* (1972).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Codex Fejérváry-Mayer, Page 11 (Centeotl)
creator: Anonymous (Central Mexican tlacuilo)
place: Central Mexico (possibly the Gulf Coast / Mixteca)
summary:
A detail from page 11 of the *Codex Fejérváry-Mayer* showing the maize god Centeotl (Cinteotl), now in the World Museum, Liverpool.

## Iconography
The young maize deity is shown seated, painted with the facial markings and headdress associated with the patron of sustenance, set within a compartment of the divinatory count with its accompanying day-signs and colour fields.

## Significance
The Fejérváry-Mayer is a small, finely painted member of the [[motif:tonalamatl|Borgia Group]], best known for its opening cosmogram of the four directions and the world-tree calendar. Its interior pages, like this one, present *tonalamatl* almanacs assigning patron gods such as Centeotl — god of maize and human sustenance — to segments of the 260-day count, tying agricultural fertility to ritual time.

## For artists & game designers
A crop-god slotted into a calendar wheel ties planting cycles to a fate mechanic — fertility as a turn-based resource.

citations.text: C. A. Burland (ed.), *Codex Fejérváry-Mayer* (facsimile, 1971).
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Maya Codices (Madrid / Tro-Cortesianus)
creator: Anonymous (Maya scribes)
summary:
A display of Maya codex pages including the *Madrid Codex* (Codex Tro-Cortesianus), the longest of the surviving Maya books, held in the Museo de América, Madrid.

## Iconography
The screenfold pages carry dense almanacs: rows of *tzolkin* day-glyphs and red-and-black numerals threaded between vignettes of gods sowing, weaving, hunting with snares, and tending hives, each scene tied to favourable or unfavourable days.

## Significance
The Madrid Codex is the great compendium of everyday Maya [[motif:divinatory almanac|divination]]: its almanacs govern agriculture, rain-making, beekeeping, hunting, weaving and disease, mapping the practical concerns of life onto the 260-day count. Reassembled from two fragments (Troano and Cortesianus), it complements the astronomical Dresden Codex by showing divination at the village level. Studied by Victoria and Harvey Bricker, among others.

## For artists & game designers
An almanac of "good and bad days" for each craft is a ready loot/luck system tied to an in-world calendar.

citations.text: Gabrielle Vail & Anthony Aveni (eds.), *The Madrid Codex: New Approaches* (2004).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Mictlantecuhtli, Aztec Lord of the Dead (Ceramic)
creator: Anonymous (Mexica / Aztec sculptors)
rights: CC0 (photograph, Gary Todd). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A ceramic figure of Mictlantecuhtli, the Aztec lord of the underworld, of the type recovered from the House of the Eagles at the Templo Mayor, Tenochtitlan.

## Iconography
The god stands as a partly skeletal, fleshless figure with a grinning skull, clawed hands, and a liver or other organ spilling from the rib cage — the liver being the seat of the *ihíyotl* soul, drawn to the underworld. Curly hair set with paper rosettes and starry eyes complete the death-lord regalia.

## Significance
[[motif:mictlantecuhtli|Mictlantecuhtli]] ruled Mictlan, the lowest of nine underworlds, where the ordinary dead journeyed for four years. He governs the day-sign Itzcuintli (Dog) and one of the trecenas, and in the *Codex Borgia* he appears back-to-back with Quetzalcoatl in a cosmic life/death pairing. He embodies the Aztec conviction that death and regeneration are inseparable.

## For artists & game designers
A death-god with an exposed liver — the soul-organ — is a vivid, anatomically specific design for an underworld boss.

citations.text: Leonardo López Luján, *The Offerings of the Templo Mayor of Tenochtitlan* (1994).
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Aztec Sun Stone (Calendar Stone)
creator: Anonymous (Mexica / Aztec sculptors)
rights: CC0 (photograph, Gary Todd). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
The *Piedra del Sol* (Sun Stone or Calendar Stone), the most famous Aztec monument, a 3.6 m basalt monolith now in the Museo Nacional de Antropología, Mexico City.

## Iconography
A central face — usually identified as the sun god Tonatiuh (or the earth-monster Tlaltecuhtli) — is framed by the glyph *Nahui Ollin* ("4 Movement"), whose four cartouches name the four previous world-ages destroyed by jaguars, wind, fire-rain and flood. A ring of the twenty day-signs encircles the center, bounded by two Fire Serpents (Xiuhcoatl) meeting at the base.

## Significance
The Sun Stone is a cosmogram of the [[motif:five suns|Five Suns]]: the present age, *Nahui Ollin*, is fated to end in earthquakes. It binds the 260-day count, the solar cycle and the myth of cosmic destruction into one carved disk, probably set horizontally as a sacrificial altar or *temalacatl*. It is the single most reproduced emblem of Aztec religion.

## For artists & game designers
A wheel that encodes both a calendar and a prophecy of the world's end is an iconic doomsday-clock motif.

citations.text: Khristaan D. Villela & Mary Ellen Miller (eds.), *The Aztec Calendar Stone* (2010).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Tlazolteotl, Eater of Filth (Codex Borbonicus)
creator: Anonymous (Aztec / Nahua tlacuilo)
date: c. 1500–1525 CE (very early colonial / late pre-Conquest)
summary:
The goddess Tlazolteotl as depicted in the *Codex Borbonicus*, patroness of one of the twenty trecenas of the divinatory count.

## Iconography
The goddess wears the unspun-cotton headband and spindle-whorl headdress of the spinners and weavers, with black mouth-paint marking her as an "eater of filth." She is shown in the regalia of the *tonalamatl* compartment she governs.

## Significance
[[motif:tlazolteotl|Tlazolteotl]] ("filth deity"), also called Tlaelcuani, "eater of filth," both incited and absolved sexual transgression: she devoured human misdeeds, and a once-in-a-lifetime confession (*neyolmelahualiztli*) to her priests could wipe a person's offenses clean. Goddess of weaving, childbirth, lust and purification, she ruled the trecena beginning 1 Deer and the thirteenth day-sign, binding moral pollution to the diviner's calendar.

## For artists & game designers
A deity who is both the source of sin and its one-time absolution is a rich quest-giver for a confession or atonement mechanic.

citations.text: H. B. Nicholson, "Religion in Pre-Hispanic Central Mexico," *Handbook of Middle American Indians* vol. 10 (1971).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Tzitzimitl, Aztec Star Demon
creator: Anonymous (indigenous painter, colonial Mexico)
summary:
A *tzitzimitl*, one of the Aztec star-demons, drawn in a colonial-period manuscript of the type of the *Codex Magliabechiano*.

## Iconography
The figure is a fearsome skeletal female with clawed hands and feet, a skirt of crossed bones, and severed-hand and heart ornaments. Such star-demons are shown frontally in an aggressive, descending posture.

## Significance
The [[motif:tzitzimitl|tzitzimime]] were stars personified as monstrous beings, associated with the goddess group around Cihuacoatl and Itzpapalotl. They were feared above all during solar eclipses and at the close of the 52-year cycle, when, if the New Fire failed to kindle, they were believed to descend and devour humankind. They thus express the Aztec dread of cosmic darkness and the precariousness of the world-age — the danger the New Fire ceremony was meant to avert.

## For artists & game designers
Sky-monsters that descend only during eclipses or a failed ritual make a perfect timed apocalyptic threat.

citations.text: Cecelia F. Klein, "The Devil and the Skirt: An Iconographic Inquiry into the Pre-Hispanic Nature of the Tzitzimime," *Ancient Mesoamerica* 11 (2000).

title: Sigillum Dei, Giorgio Anselmi
creator: Giorgio Anselmi of Parma
summary:
A fifteenth-century rendering of the Sigillum Dei (Seal of God) by the Parma physician and astrologer Giorgio Anselmi, an earlier and independent witness to a diagrammatic tradition that would reach its most famous form two centuries later in the hands of John Dee.

## Iconography
Concentric circles divided by radiating lines into compartments inscribed with divine and angelic names, letters, and numerological notation — a wheel-form talismanic diagram meant to be inscribed on parchment, metal, or wax and worn or displayed as a protective and power-conferring device.

## Significance
The Sigillum Dei descends from the medieval *Liber Iuratus* ('Sworn Book') attributed to Honorius of Thebes, a foundational text of the learned-magic tradition that Richard Kieckhefer and others situate alongside the Munich necromantic manuals as evidence of a sophisticated clerical underground combining liturgy, astrology, and ritual magic. Anselmi's version predates by roughly a century John Dee's famous *Sigillum Dei Aemeth*, the wax seal central to his Enochian angel-conjuring system with Edward Kelley — demonstrating that Dee was elaborating an existing diagrammatic vocabulary rather than inventing it whole-cloth.

## For artists & game designers
The wheel-and-radiating-names structure is a versatile 'master ward' diagram template, distinct from but compatible with conjuration-circle iconography.

title: *Negromante* (The Necromancer), Attrib. Angelo Caroselli
creator: Attributed to Angelo Caroselli (or 'Pseudo-Caroselli')
summary:
A Baroque genre painting depicting a necromancer at his work, attributed to the Roman painter Angelo Caroselli or his circle, representative of the seventeenth-century vogue for picturesque scenes of magicians, alchemists, and fortune-tellers as subjects of cabinet painting.

## Iconography
A hooded or bearded magus-type figure, surrounded by the genre's standard props — books, instruments, dim candlelight — staged for theatrical effect rather than documentary accuracy. Caroselli and his followers specialized in exactly this kind of shadowy, Caravaggesque scene of occult practice as popular entertainment subject matter.

## Significance
By the time paintings like this were made, the clerical necromancer of the Munich Handbook tradition — a literate priest secretly practicing demon-conjuration using liturgical Latin — had migrated from real ecclesiastical scandal into popular visual stock-type: the necromancer as picturesque rogue, suitable for collectors' cabinets rather than inquisitorial proceedings. This shift from lived clerical practice to genre entertainment marks the cultural distance traveled between Kieckhefer's fifteenth-century manuscript evidence and the seventeenth-century imagination of what a 'necromancer' looked like.

## For artists & game designers
A strong visual reference for 'necromancer as genre archetype' — hood, candlelight, books — the same stock imagery still used in fantasy art today.

title: John Dee's Seal of God (Wax Disc), British Museum
creator: John Dee (commissioned object)
rights: CC BY-SA 4.0. Photo by user:geni, via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A photograph of the surviving physical Sigillum Dei Aemeth — a large wax disc, roughly a foot across, inscribed with the same diagrammatic design recorded in Dee's manuscripts — held today by the British Museum.

## Iconography
The disc shows concentric rings of incised lettering and geometric figures pressed into beeswax, considerably worn but still legible, an object meant to be set beneath Dee's crystal showstone and his 'holy table' during scrying sessions with Edward Kelley.

## Significance
This is among the very few surviving physical ritual objects from the entire medieval-to-early-modern learned-magic tradition discussed alongside Trithemius and the Munich necromantic manuscripts — most of that tradition survives only as text and diagram, never as the object itself. The British Museum's holding (along with Dee's obsidian 'spirit mirror' and crystal ball, also in their collection) makes Dee's magical practice uniquely, tangibly documented compared to virtually any other figure in this corpus, a rare case where the diagram in the manuscript and the thing itself can be compared side by side.

## For artists & game designers
An excellent prop reference for a 'physical magical artifact' that corresponds exactly to an in-fiction diagram — useful for game puzzles requiring matching a drawn sigil to a found object.

title: Sigillum Dei Aemeth, John Dee (Sloane MS 3188)
creator: John Dee
summary:
A page from John Dee's own working manuscript (Sloane MS 3188), recording the design of his Sigillum Dei Aemeth, the wax disc that anchored his angel-conjuring system developed with the medium Edward Kelley in the 1580s.

## Iconography
Dee's own hand sets out the layered circular design — concentric rings of divine and angelic names, pentagrams, and Latin inscriptions — drafted as a working diagram rather than a presentation copy, complete with the marginal notation typical of Dee's meticulous record-keeping.

## Significance
Dee adapted the older Sigillum Dei diagram (already attested in Anselmi's fifteenth-century version and the medieval Sworn Book of Honorius tradition) into the centerpiece of his Enochian system: a physical wax seal, supposedly dictated to Kelley by the angel Uriel, on which the holy table and showstone rested during their scrying sessions. Dee's manuscripts — now scattered across the Sloane, Cotton, and Ashmole collections at the British Library and Bodleian — represent one of the most extensively documented magical operations in European history, a mathematician-philosopher's systematic, almost laboratory-style approach to angelic communication.

## For artists & game designers
Dee's working notebooks are the gold standard for 'magician's actual lab notes' aesthetic — messy, annotated, iterative, in contrast to the polished symmetry of presentation-grimoire diagrams.

title: Dr. Fian Showing Penitence for His Wicked Life, *Newes from Scotland*
creator: Anonymous woodcut artist (associated with King James VI/I's circle)
summary:
A woodcut from *Newes from Scotland* (1591), the pamphlet account of the North Berwick witch trials, depicting John Fian — a schoolmaster accused of necromancy and witchcraft — in a moment of feigned or genuine penitence the night before his attempted escape from custody.

## Iconography
A spare narrative woodcut in the period's documentary-pamphlet style: Fian shown kneeling or gesturing in a domestic or prison interior, captioned to anchor a specific moment in the trial narrative for a literate but image-hungry popular readership.

## Significance
Fian (born John Cunningham) was a real schoolmaster prosecuted as the supposed ringleader of the North Berwick coven that allegedly conspired, through witchcraft and necromancy, against King James VI's voyage to Denmark — the case that drove James to write his own *Daemonologie* (1597) and to take a direct personal interest in prosecuting magical practitioners. Fian's professional identity as a schoolmaster, a literate man capable of writing and reading Latin charms, situates him within exactly the demographic Kieckhefer identifies as the bearers of 'clerical underworld' necromantic practice — educated men whose Latin literacy gave them access to the same textual magic preserved in the Munich Handbook tradition, here criminalized fatally under early modern witch-hunting law.

## For artists & game designers
A grounding reference for the transition from 'clerical necromancer' to 'witch trial victim' — useful for narrative arcs where learned magic collides with judicial persecution.

title: A Magician (Edward Kelly), after Ebenezer Sibly
creator: Engraved by Ames of Bristol, after a drawing by Ebenezer Sibly
summary:
A late eighteenth-century engraving depicting John Dee's scrying partner Edward Kelley in the act of necromantic conjuration, after a drawing by the astrologer-physician Ebenezer Sibly, whose illustrated compendia did much to fix the popular image of Renaissance magicians for a later age.

## Iconography
Kelley is shown performing a conjuration within a marked circle, gesturing toward a spectral or demonic apparition — a dramatized 'raising the dead' or 'spirit summoning' tableau in the gothic-theatrical mode Sibly favored throughout his *Illustration of the Occult Sciences*.

## Significance
Kelley's posthumous reputation diverged sharply from Dee's: where Dee is remembered as a serious mathematician-philosopher whose angel magic was an extension of his cosmological seriousness, Kelley — a man with a criminal past and a documented history of charlatanism — became, in popular print culture like Sibly's, the template for the fraudulent or dangerously reckless necromancer. Sibly's late-Enlightenment engravings, despite (or because of) their dramatic license, became enormously influential reference images, reproduced and re-engraved throughout the nineteenth-century occult revival.

## For artists & game designers
A ready-made 'conjuration in progress' action pose — figure mid-gesture, circle underfoot, apparition forming — directly transferable to game cutscene or card-art composition.

title: *Picatrix* Frontispiece, Istanbul Hagia Sophia MS 2443 (17th c.)
creator: Anonymous
summary:
An illuminated frontispiece from a seventeenth-century Ottoman-era copy of the *Ghayat al-Hakim*/*Picatrix*, held in the historic Hagia Sophia manuscript collection in Istanbul — a decorative opening that signals the prestige and continued scholarly investment placed in the text centuries after its composition.

## Iconography
A formal illuminated frontispiece in the Ottoman manuscript-decoration idiom: geometric and floral border ornament in the style typical of high-status scientific and philosophical manuscripts of the period, framing the text's opening in gold and color rather than figural imagery.

## Significance
That a copy of this magical-astrological compendium received frontispiece-level illumination, and was housed within the Hagia Sophia library collection — one of the major repositories of the Ottoman scholarly establishment — testifies to the text's status as serious philosophical-scientific literature within Islamicate intellectual culture, not marginal or suppressed knowledge. This contrasts instructively with the *Picatrix*'s reception in Latin Europe, where it circulated more furtively, repeatedly condemned by theologians even as it was avidly read by figures like Ficino and Pico della Mirandola.

## For artists & game designers
A strong visual reference for 'prestige edition of forbidden knowledge' — the same content as a battered grimoire, but presented as honored court scholarship; useful for contrasting two cultures' relationship to the same magical text.

title: Late Arabic *Picatrix* Manuscript, Hamidiye Library MS 852, fol. 45v
creator: Anonymous Arabic scribe
summary:
A folio from a late Arabic-language copy of the *Ghayat al-Hakim* ('The Goal of the Sage') — the original Arabic text underlying the Latin *Picatrix* — preserved in the Hamidiye Library collection, demonstrating the text's continued copying and circulation within the Islamic manuscript tradition independent of, and parallel to, its European Latin afterlife.

## Iconography
A page of Arabic manuscript text in a hand typical of later Ottoman-period copying, without illustration on this folio, part of the long chain of scribal transmission that kept the work in active circulation across the Islamicate world for centuries after its likely tenth- or eleventh-century compilation, traditionally (if disputably) attributed to the mathematician Maslama al-Majriti of Cordoba.

## Significance
The *Ghayat al-Hakim* draws together planetary astrology, talismanic image-magic, and Hermetic and Sabian theoretical material into the most comprehensive handbook of astral magic to survive from the medieval Islamic world, the same broad current of image magic that produced Thabit ibn Qurra's more concise *De Imaginibus* roughly a century or two earlier. Its dual transmission — continuing in Arabic manuscript culture across the Ottoman centuries while simultaneously generating an enormously influential Latin offshoot in Europe — makes it a key case study in how a single body of astral-magical theory could sustain two parallel, centuries-long scholarly afterlives.

## For artists & game designers
A useful reference for 'the same forbidden book in two cultures' worldbuilding — a single magical text with divergent regional manuscript traditions and receptions.

title: Manuscript Page of the *Picatrix*
creator: Anonymous (Latin translation tradition; possibly after Maslama al-Majriti)
summary:
A manuscript page from the Latin *Picatrix* tradition, the medieval translation of the Arabic *Ghayat al-Hakim* ('The Goal of the Sage'), the single most influential compendium of astral image magic to reach Latin Christendom.

## Iconography
Dense Latin prose text, the manuscript page showing no illustration here but representing the textual transmission through which the *Picatrix*'s theoretical apparatus — talisman construction tied to precise planetary and stellar timing — entered European intellectual circulation from the thirteenth century onward, commissioned in the orbit of Alfonso X of Castile's translation project.

## Significance
The *Picatrix* systematizes a tradition of astral image magic with deep roots in late antique Hermetic and Sabian (Harranian) practice — the same broad current that produced Thabit ibn Qurra's earlier and more concise *De Imaginibus*. Where Thabit gives compact astrological-talismanic instructions, the *Picatrix* expands the theoretical framework into a full cosmology linking planetary spirits, sympathetic magic, and ritual timing, becoming required (if officially condemned) reading for figures from Marsilio Ficino to Cornelius Agrippa. Its presence in this collection marks the deep prehistory behind Trithemius's own planetary-angel hierarchies, which draw on the same astrological-magical inheritance Christianized and systematized across centuries of Latin transmission.

## For artists & game designers
Useful as 'the textbook' prop for any in-game astral-magic tradition — a manual of method rather than narrative, good for world-building exposition dumps disguised as found documents.

title: Grave Slab of Johannes Trithemius (Riemenschneider Workshop), Neumünster, Würzburg
creator: Tilman Riemenschneider (workshop)
rights: CC BY-SA 4.0. Photo by Holger Uwe Schmitt, via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A detailed view of the carved grave slab (Grabplatte) of Johannes Trithemius, attributed to the workshop of Tilman Riemenschneider, one of the most celebrated sculptors of the German late-Gothic/early-Renaissance transition and a near-contemporary active in the same Würzburg milieu where Trithemius spent his final abbacy.

## Iconography
The slab presents the abbot in low relief, robed and identified by inscription, executed with the refined naturalism and careful drapery characteristic of Riemenschneider's documented output — a far cry from the angel-cipher tables and necromantic name-lists associated with his subject's controversial books.

## Significance
Riemenschneider, renowned for limewood altarpieces and stone tomb sculpture across Franconia, would himself later be imprisoned and tortured for his sympathies with the Peasants' War of 1525 — a reminder that the Würzburg of this period was a site of real institutional and political danger for figures who fell afoul of authority, the same world in which Trithemius's own reputation had to be carefully managed against accusations of demonic dealing. The collaboration (direct or workshop-attributed) between the era's leading sculptor and its most notorious clerical cryptographer is a small but concrete instance of how thoroughly enmeshed in mainstream ecclesiastical culture these 'occult' figures actually were.

## For artists & game designers
Fine detail reference for German Renaissance funerary relief carving — drapery, inscription banding, facial modeling — useful for any tomb or memorial set-dressing in a period-accurate game environment.

title: Theban Alphabet from Trithemius's *Polygraphia* (1518)
creator: Johannes Trithemius (attrib.); digital cleanup by Wikimedia contributor
summary:
A cleaned-up modern reproduction of the so-called Theban alphabet as it first appears in print in Trithemius's *Polygraphia* (1518), one of the most influential occult scripts in the Western esoteric tradition.

## Iconography
A simple table pairing each letter of the Latin alphabet with an angular, rune-like glyph — the 'Theban' characters, characterized by spiky ascenders and looping bodies bearing no genuine relation to ancient Theban (Egyptian or Boeotian) writing systems despite the name.

## Significance
Trithemius attributes the alphabet to one 'Honorius of Thebes,' but no such script or figure is independently attested — the alphabet is almost certainly Trithemius's own invention or a transmission from an unidentified earlier source, presented within the same compendium of cipher systems as the more straightforwardly cryptographic material. Despite (or because of) its murky origin, the Theban alphabet went on to enormous popularity in later magical practice: it became a standard 'witches' alphabet' in twentieth-century Wicca (via Gerald Gardner) and remains one of the most recognizable occult scripts in contemporary popular magic, journaling, and tattoo culture — a striking case of a Renaissance cryptographer's invented code becoming, five centuries later, sincere ritual writing.

## For artists & game designers
The Theban alphabet is instantly recognizable as 'witchy script' to a modern audience — directly usable as a magical writing system in any game needing an authentic-feeling occult alphabet.

title: *De viris illustribus Germaniae* (1495), Trithemius
creator: Johannes Trithemius
repository: Biblioteca Europea di Informazione e Cultura (BEIC)
summary:
A page from the 1495 printing of Trithemius's *De viris illustribus Germaniae* ('Of Illustrious Men of Germany'), one of his major scholarly-bibliographical works, predating the controversial *Steganographia* by several years and establishing his credentials as a serious humanist historian.

## Iconography
A plain typeset incunable page, without illustration — the visual register of careful Latin scholarship rather than esoteric diagram.

## Significance
Before he was notorious for angel-cipher magic, Trithemius was already one of the most productive bibliographers of his generation: his earlier *De scriptoribus ecclesiasticis* (1494) catalogued nearly a thousand Christian authors, and *De viris illustribus Germaniae* extended the project to celebrate German intellectual achievement specifically — part of the broader humanist nationalism that also produced Celtis's editorial projects. This scholarly output is essential context for understanding why the *Steganographia* controversy wounded Trithemius so deeply: he saw himself, correctly, as one of the preeminent librarians and historians of his age, not primarily as an occultist.

## For artists & game designers
A reminder that real-world 'wizard' figures were usually working scholars first — useful for grounding a magician NPC's day job in mundane intellectual labor.

A later, more elaborate engraved portrait of Trithemius from 1666, a century and a half after his death, demonstrating his continued currency as a figure of interest to print culture's appetite for occult biography.

By the mid-seventeenth century Trithemius had become a fixture of compiled 'lives of the philosophers/magicians' print series — his image circulating alongside Agrippa, Paracelsus, and Dee as part of a developing visual canon of Renaissance magi. The Wellcome Collection's holding of this print reflects the institution's broader collecting interest in the history of medicine, alchemy, and the occult sciences as continuous with early scientific culture.

A good reference for 'compiled rogues' gallery of magicians' print aesthetics — oval portrait medallions with decorative cartouches, useful for any in-game codex or bestiary-of-sorcerers framing device.

title: Title Page, *Polygraphia*, Johannes Trithemius
creator: Johannes Trithemius
summary:
The title page of *Polygraphia*, published in 1518 (the year after Trithemius's death), the work that openly and uncontroversially accomplished what the *Steganographia* did under magical disguise.

## Iconography
A standard early sixteenth-century German printer's title page: woodcut border ornament framing the title in large display type, author and publication details below — conservative, scholarly, deliberately unsensational in contrast to the book it follows.

## Significance
*Polygraphia* is widely credited as the first printed book on cryptology, presenting cipher and code systems openly, as a humanist science of secret writing, rather than concealed within occult pretense. Trithemius arranged for its publication specifically to demonstrate — too late to save his own reputation — that his interest was cryptographic technique, not demonic communication. The book includes the famous 'Ave Maria' cipher, in which an apparently pious prayer text encodes a secret message letter by letter, and introduced cipher tables that would influence cryptographic practice for centuries.

## For artists & game designers
A clean reference for period title-page design when a game prop needs to read as 'real scholarly imprint' rather than 'illuminated grimoire.'

creator: Johannes Trithemius
rights: CC0. Photo by Daderot, via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A museum photograph of a physical 1518 copy of Trithemius's *Polygraphiae*, displayed at the U.S. National Cryptologic Museum (operated adjacent to the National Security Agency) under a label identifying it as the first published book on cryptology.

## Iconography
The bound volume sits open in an exhibit case, photographed for documentary rather than artistic purposes — a closed and open spread of dense Latin type and a printer's woodcut device, captured with museum lighting.

## Significance
The object's modern institutional home is itself the story: a Renaissance abbot's cipher manual, written by a man once denounced as a demon-summoner, now sits in the founding-text display case of the agency most responsible for twentieth- and twenty-first-century American cryptography. It is a tidy emblem of Trithemius's posthumous rehabilitation — the same book that helped sink his contemporary reputation is now read straightforwardly as a landmark in the history of secret writing, the occult framing fully stripped away by institutional memory.

## For artists & game designers
A good visual cue for 'ancient magic book reclassified as historical science exhibit' — useful for any narrative beat where a culture's magic becomes a later culture's technology.

title: Portrait of Johannes Trithemius
creator: Unknown engraver
summary:
A posthumous engraved portrait of Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), shown in the cowled habit of a Benedictine abbot, the visual costume that anchors his entire reputation: a churchman who wrote occult philosophy from inside the institution, not against it.

## Iconography
The sitter is rendered in three-quarter view in monastic dress, a standard humanist-portrait convention applied to a man whose actual fame rested on cryptography and angelology rather than theology. No magical paraphernalia accompanies him — the habit alone does the rhetorical work of asserting orthodoxy.

## Significance
Trithemius became abbot of Sponheim at twenty-one and rebuilt its library into one of the great collections of his age, but he is remembered for two notorious books: the *Steganographia*, ostensibly a manual for commanding angelic spirits to carry messages across distance, and the *Antipalus Maleficiorum*, an attack on witchcraft that nonetheless catalogued its practices in damning detail. Agrippa von Nettesheim studied under him and dedicated *De Occulta Philosophia* to him; Paracelsus is traditionally (if loosely) linked to his circle. The *Steganographia* was placed on the Index of Forbidden Books in 1609 — only to be vindicated three centuries later when cryptographers showed its 'angel magic' was an elaborate cipher system, arguably the founding text of Western cryptography.

## For artists & game designers
The cleric-magician archetype: an authority figure whose legitimacy and forbidden knowledge are the same costume. Useful for any NPC whose institutional role conceals esoteric practice.
