title: Alchemical Qualities Jadwal — Degrees of the Four Qualities in Metals and Minerals (f. 4r)
medium: manuscript, ink on paper, ruled grid table
summary:
Folio 4 recto of the Princeton seven-alchemy-texts compendium (figgy 05fc8244, 17c Arabic), bearing a formal alchemical qualities table headed 'جدول اوزان كيفيات فلذات وغيره' (Jadwal Awzān Kayfīyāt Fildhāt wa-Ghayrihi — Table of Proportions and Qualities of Metals and Other [Substances]).

## Iconography
The table occupies the lower two-thirds of the page as a drawn ruled grid: approximately 10–11 columns (one per substance) with 4 data rows plus a header row, and 4–5 empty rows below indicating the table is designed for further extension. Column headers (reading right to left) name specific metals and minerals including نحس (naḥs — copper), and what appear to be sun (شمس — gold), moon (قمر — silver), zaybaq (زيبق — mercury), kibrīt (كبريت — sulphur), ʿUṭārid (عطارد — Mercury/planet), and other substances. Each data cell contains an Arabic numeral — 1, 2, or 3 — indicating the degree of that quality in that substance. The four row labels (right margin) are the four Galenic qualities: hot (حار), cold (بارد), wet (رطب), dry (يابس) — the fundamental categories of Jabirian balance theory (ʿilm al-mīzān). Above the table, a short supplementary index lists page references for specific sections (74, 75, 81, 82 pages, topics including silver operations and compound preparations). This jadwal form — systematic degree-by-substance tabulation of the four qualities — is the visual/analytical hallmark of Jabirian alchemy, derived from Jabir ibn Hayyan's al-Mīzān (The Balance), which held that all transmutation required precise knowledge and manipulation of a substance's quality-profile. The table enables rapid comparison: copper (naḥs) vs. silver vs. mercury to determine which operations will achieve the desired transmutational shift. The ruled grid drawn entirely in ink, with neat numerals in each cell, occupies the preparatory section of the codex immediately before the text of the seven treatises begins.

## Significance
Represents the Jabirian theory of elemental balance (*al-mīzān*) in Islamic alchemy, in which every metal or mineral is composed of the four Galenic qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry) in degrees from 1 to 3. This system, developed in the enormous *Corpus Jabirianum* (8th–10th c., attributed to Jabir ibn Hayyan / Geber), held that transmutation was possible by adjusting a substance's quality proportions — effectively a predecessor to early modern chemical recipes. Paul Kraus's two-volume study (Cairo, 1943) remains the foundational analysis of Jabir's numerical alchemy.

## For artists & game designers
The ruled multi-column quality table, with its systematic grid of Arabic calligraphy in red and black, offers a strong visual template for fantasy alchemical reference diagrams — world-building material that communicates a credible 'science of transmutation' without requiring the viewer to read the script.

citations.text: Princeton University Library, OPenn Islamic Manuscripts. Princeton Digital Library of Islamic Manuscripts.

title: N-W-A Letter Square — Talisman Grid at Opening of First Treatise (Lawh al-Dhahab) (f. 5r)
medium: manuscript, ink on paper, letter grid with diagonal text
summary:
Folio 5 recto of the Princeton seven-alchemy-texts compendium (figgy 05fc8244, 17c Arabic), the opening page of the first treatise Lawh al-Dhahab (The Gold Tablet).

## Iconography
The page is composed of three distinct layers. In the upper right: ownership/library annotations recording later provenance — title references, donor/copyist name ('لاه قاسم بن الفضل' — property of Qasim ibn al-Fadl or similar), and bibliographic notes. In the upper-left portion: a 3×3 ruled grid bearing a repeating letter pattern — four corner cells contain ن (nūn), the four edge-center cells contain و (wāw), and the single center cell contains ا (alif). This ن/و/ا letter square has an abjad value profile: nūn = 50, wāw = 6, alif = 1; the pattern n–w–a (nuwwā) can mean 'kernel/stone' (as in the stone of a fruit), a significant alchemical metaphor for the hidden core of transmutation. Alternatively ن/و/ا may be letter-abbreviations for three alchemical principles or divine names. The number '١٩٣' (193) appears adjacent, possibly recording the leaf count of the volume (190 leaves + 3 flyleaves). In the right and lower portions of the page, the dense diagonal text of the treatise begins — the Lawh al-Dhahab proper — written in the characteristic alternating-diagonal script used throughout this MS. Scattered red-ink rubrications highlight section headings and key terms. This letter grid, positioned at the literal entrance to the text, functions as both a compositional talisman (drawing the abjad power of the letters into the work) and an organizational marker distinguishing the preparatory jadāwil pages (fols. 4r–4v) from the beginning of the treatise content. The combination of letter grid + ownership inscription + colophon note on a single page is characteristic of Islamic scientific MSS in which multiple owners added their marks to the opening recto of the primary text.

## Significance
Represents the Jabirian theory of elemental balance (*al-mīzān*) in Islamic alchemy, in which every metal or mineral is composed of the four Galenic qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry) in degrees from 1 to 3. This system, developed in the enormous *Corpus Jabirianum* (8th–10th c., attributed to Jabir ibn Hayyan / Geber), held that transmutation was possible by adjusting a substance's quality proportions — effectively a predecessor to early modern chemical recipes. Paul Kraus's two-volume study (Cairo, 1943) remains the foundational analysis of Jabir's numerical alchemy.

## For artists & game designers
The ruled multi-column quality table, with its systematic grid of Arabic calligraphy in red and black, offers a strong visual template for fantasy alchemical reference diagrams — world-building material that communicates a credible 'science of transmutation' without requiring the viewer to read the script.

title: Natural Script (al-Qalam al-Tabi'i) — Abjad-Numeric Correspondence Table for Awfaq Construction
medium: manuscript, ink on paper, red-ruled grid
rights: Public Domain. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
summary:
A structurally complex theoretical page from the Princeton Garrett 52B treatise (18th c.

## Iconography
CE) presenting the 'Natural Script' (al-Qalam al-Tabi'i) — the theoretical root alphabet underlying the construction of awfaq (magic squares) in Islamic occult science. The page has three distinct sections. The top shows a 3-row grid labeled 'العدد' (the number/count) with row headers for 'احاد' (units, 1-9), 'عشرات' (tens, 10-90), and 'سابع' (hundreds/sevens?) — each row contains 9 cells with stylized 'natural script' letterforms representing those numeric values as pen strokes (T-shapes, angled lines, ⊢ forms, arrows, and crosses — each a different visual encoding of a number). The middle section is the largest: a 9-row × 10-column grid labeled 'القلم الطبيعي الذي يكتب الطبع والتنزيل الاوفاق' (The Natural Script that writes nature and the composition of awfaq) with rows labeled 1, 3, 4, 8, 9, 7, 'أسرار د بيس الفلك' (secrets of the celestial spheres), and two more — each row showing the Natural Script letterforms for a set of values. Below, additional rows of exotic letterforms complete the display. The Natural Script is the theoretical foundation of awfaq: by converting Arabic letters to their Natural Script equivalents and placing them in a grid, the practitioner creates a wafq in which the rows, columns, and diagonals sum to a constant — the magic square emerges from the script's internal numeric structure rather than from direct arithmetic.

## Significance
Documents the Islamic and Western tradition of magical writing systems — scripts legible only to initiates — including the huruf system (Islamic letter mysticism), parallel Syriac-derived alphabets, and systems analogous to Agrippa's Celestial, Malachim, and Transitus Fluvii scripts (*De Occulta Philosophia*, 1531). Each script encodes talismanic names of angels or divine attributes, invisible to uninitiated readers. Ibn Khaldun discusses the practice of *sīmiyā'* (sympathetic letter magic) in the *Muqaddimah* (vol. 3, ch. 28).

The magic alphabet grids are directly useful to visual worldbuilders: each script looks alien and systematic while being historically documented, making them ideal for fantasy language design, sigil creation, and occult visual identity. title: Astrological Planetary Classification Table — Seven Planets with Symbolic Headers (f. 78r)
medium: manuscript, ink and red ink on paper, ruled table with symbolic headers
summary:
Folio 78 recto of the Princeton Persian astrological compendium (OPenn Islamic MSS, 1670 CE), containing a formal astrological planetary classification table.

## Iconography
The page divides into two zones: the upper half contains dense Persian nastaʻlīq text in the main body with red-ink rubrication for key technical terms, and the lower half presents a ruled table with a red-ink border encompassing the entire grid. The table has approximately 7–8 columns, one for each classical planet (Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Sun, Venus, Mercury, Moon), with the header row of each column bearing a small pictographic or abbreviated symbol identifying the planet — the visual markers visible in the header cells include curved and angular forms consistent with Arabic abbreviations of planetary names (زحل = Saturn, مشتري = Jupiter, مريخ = Mars, etc.) or simplified astrological glyphs. Below the header row are 6 rows of Persian text, each row recording a category of astrological classification for each planet — possibly covering the planet's nature (hot/cold/wet/dry), its domicile (sign it rules), its exaltation, its day/night distinction, its relation to the four elements, or other standard attributes from Persian astrological tradition. Below the table, a red-ink section heading reads 'نتیجه اجزاء' (Natijah-yi ajzā' — Conclusions/Results of the Parts), indicating this table concludes a longer discussion of planetary classification. The formal ruled table with symbolic column headers is a standard format for Persian astrological jadāwil (tables) used to systematize planetary data for practical horoscopy and the astrological judgment of charts (aḥkām al-nujūm).

## Significance
The formal astrological table (*jadwal*) is the standard instrument for systematizing planetary knowledge in the Abu Ma'shar tradition — the most influential Arabic astrological synthesis transmitted to medieval Europe. Abu Ma'shar's *Introductorium Maius* (9th c.) was translated into Latin by John of Seville (1133) and Hermann of Carinthia (1140), making it the astrological textbook of the medieval West. The planetary classification table represents the core of this tradition: each planet's nature, sign rulership, exaltation, and elemental association.

title: Inline Geomantic Figure Notations (Raml Dot Patterns) — Bulugh al-Watar (p. 16)
rights: Public Domain. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
summary:
A page from Bulugh al-Watar (Princeton), a geomancy treatise, showing inline geomantic figure notations embedded within the Arabic text.

## Iconography
At the bottom of the text block, small geomantic figures are written in the standard Arabic notation: each figure is a vertical stack of 4 rows, each row containing either one point (odd) or two points (even), representing a binary code of 4 bits (24 = 16 possible figures). Above each figure group are letter-labels (Arabic letters indicating which figure it is). These inline notations appear throughout Arabic geomancy manuals as both reference marks and worked examples — showing the reader exactly what each figure looks like in the binary dot notation used in practice. In Arabic geomancy, the 16 figures are generated by randomly marking rows in sand, then counting the points: an odd number of marks per row produces one point; even produces two. This page shows the notation system in its most compact, textual-integration mode.

## Significance
Documents the *ashkāl* (figures) of Arabic geomancy (*'ilm al-raml*) embedded within a text, illustrating the divinatory system in its practical context. Savage-Smith and Smith's study of a 13th-century geomantic device demonstrates the same figure-set used instrumentally, showing the continuous tradition between written and material geomantic practice.

471). The grid is a bordered square divided into cells by black ruled lines, with each cell further subdivided diagonally with cross-hatching lines that create X-shaped or four-triangle subdivisions within each cell. summary:
A multi-column reference table from the Princeton Ghāyat al-Murād manuscript (1462 CE), representing a different genre of magical knowledge from the wafq grids that dominate the manuscript.

The page is a red-ruled 4-column table with a header row followed by approximately 30 numbered entries. The four column headers are: 'Ṣūr' (Forms/Figures — descriptions of celestial or talismanic image types), 'al-Asmāʾ' (Names — spirit or angel names), 'al-Bukhūr' (Fumigations/Incenses — the appropriate incense for each operation), and 'al-Afʿāl' (Actions/Effects — the magical operation that can be achieved). The numbered rows list individual entries across all four columns: for example, row 1 gives the visual form description, the name 'Girāṣ al-Ṭasatī' (?), the incense 'Waraq al-Sūs' (licorice leaf), and the magical effect 'ʿIshq al-Nisāʾ lil-Nisāʾ' (women's love for women); row 3 includes 'kī Samṣāl' as the spirit name, 'Sadd Rūs wa-Bisāwsha' as the incense, and 'lil-Nās wa-liḥdah' as the effect. title: Circular Hebrew Talisman Seal — Italian Grimoire (p. 15), De Characteribus et Sigillis
summary:
Under the heading 'De Characteribus et Sigillis' (On Characters and Sigils), an Italian grimoire page presents a large circular seal bearing Hebrew letters arranged in concentric rings — a characteristic format for Solomonic talisman seals in the learned European tradition.

## Iconography
The concentric-ring format places the divine name or spirit name at the center, surrounded by subsidiary angelic names, protective inscriptions, or letter sequences, creating a kind of cosmological map in which sacred language structures space from the divine center outward. This seal type is common in Key of Solomon manuscripts (Clavicula Salomonis) and Agrippa's De Occulta Philosophia: the circle seals the space, the Hebrew letters invoke specific powers, and the drawn seal substitutes for the inscribed metal or parchment version used in ritual. The section title 'De Characteribus et Sigillis' signals a systematic presentation of spirit characters and their seals.

## Significance
Documents the tradition of Solomonic grimoires, which from the 11th century onward spread from the Islamic world into Jewish and Christian European magic. The Hebrew *Sefer ha-Razim* and *Sefer Shimmush Tehillim*, the Arabic *Picatrix* (Ghāyat al-Ḥakīm), and the Latin *Clavicula Salomonis* form a continuous tradition of practical talismanic and spirit-conjuring manuals. Owen Davies's *Grimoires: A History of Magic Books* (Oxford, 2009) traces this transmission. The magical alphabets encoded in grimoires — Celestial, Malachim, Transitus Fluvii — are theorized by Agrippa in *De Occulta Philosophia* III.29–30.

## For artists & game designers

summary:
A page from an Italian 18th-century grimoire presenting multiple rows of magical alphabets — scripts used to write angelic names, divine attributes, and ritual inscriptions in characters inaccessible to the profane reader.

## Iconography
The letter-forms shown include variants of the Celestial (Angelic) script, the Malachim (Angelic Royal) script, and possibly the Transitus Fluvii (Crossing the River) script — all derived from Hebrew letter-shapes transformed into stylized angular forms. These magical alphabets were systematized in Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa's De Occulta Philosophia (1531, Book 3, Chapter 29) and transmitted through the European grimoire tradition into the 18th century. Each letter-form corresponds to a Hebrew letter by position, so that angelic names can be written in code inaccessible to uninitiated readers. In practice, magical alphabets were used to inscribe seals, talismans, and spirit names on ritual objects, making the script itself a visual expression of sacred language.

## Significance
Documents the tradition of Solomonic grimoires, which from the 11th century onward spread from the Islamic world into Jewish and Christian European magic. The Hebrew *Sefer ha-Razim* and *Sefer Shimmush Tehillim*, the Arabic *Picatrix* (Ghāyat al-Ḥakīm), and the Latin *Clavicula Salomonis* form a continuous tradition of practical talismanic and spirit-conjuring manuals. Owen Davies's *Grimoires: A History of Magic Books* (Oxford, 2009) traces this transmission. The magical alphabets encoded in grimoires — Celestial, Malachim, Transitus Fluvii — are theorized by Agrippa in *De Occulta Philosophia* III.29–30.

title: Two Circular Spirit Seals — Italian Grimoire (p. 18), De Signaculis Spirituum

The combination of two distinct seals on one page suggests a comparative or sequential ritual structure — two spirits, or two aspects of the same invocational process. title: SATOR-Type Letter Word-Square — Italian Grimoire (p. 13)
summary:
A triangular SATOR-type word square from an 18th-century Italian grimoire, drawn in ink on paper.

## Iconography
The square ('Figura') uses a Latin magical word arranged so that reading across any row, column, or diagonal produces the same result — a boustrophedon/palindromic structure. Above the figure, the Latin label 'Figura tabis est' (roughly 'the figure of wasting/tabis') indicates its intended magical use: SATOR-style squares in the grimoire tradition functioned as written amulets, typically inscribed on paper, metal, or wood and carried or placed in specific locations. The SATOR square (SATOR/AREPO/TENET/OPERA/ROTAS) — the most famous example — dates to Roman antiquity and was repurposed through the medieval and early modern periods as a Christian-magical protective charm. This variant in an Italian grimoire reflects the long survival of word-square magic into 18th-century folk and learned practice.

## Significance

title: Alif Chapter Wafq Grid — Huruf MS (p. 18)
medium: manuscript, ink on paper, red-ink borders
rights: Public Domain. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
summary:
A red-bordered wafq grid from the opening chapter (Fasl al-Awwal fi Harf al-Alif — First Chapter on the Letter Alif) of the Taysir al-Matalib fi Asrar al-Huruf.

## Iconography
The grid appears in the upper right of the page alongside explanatory text in Arabic, showing the numeric and letter assignments specific to the letter alif in the system of 'ilm al-huruf. In the huruf tradition, each of the 28 Arabic letters has a corresponding wafq (magic square), abjad value, elemental and planetary assignment, and set of divine names. The Alif — the first letter, associated with divine unity (tawhid) — receives the first and most fundamental wafq treatment. The red-ink ruled border follows the standard format seen throughout this MS and connects it to the wider tradition of Buniyan lettrism where red demarcates the operative/diagrammatic elements from commentary text.

## Significance
Documents the wafq tradition's pinnacle: the large-format magic square, in which the square grid is simultaneously a talismanic instrument, a numerological proof of divine order, and a visual mandala. The 8×8 Jupiter square (*muthallath* of 64 cells) represents a specific planetary attribution following the Islamic astrological-talismanic tradition where each of the seven planets governs a specific square size: Moon=9, Jupiter=16, Mars=25, Sun=36, Venus=49, Mercury=64, Saturn=81 cells.

## For artists & game designers
This Islamic occult manuscript image provides historically accurate visual source material for game designers, illustrators, and worldbuilders working with Arabian/Persian fantasy settings, magical systems, or occult aesthetics. The geometric rigor and systematic organization of Islamic magical diagrams translate effectively into game UI elements, talisman props, and magical-system visual design.

rights: Public Domain. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).

medium: manuscript, ink on paper, red-ink borders
rights: Public Domain. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
summary:

title: Circular Astronomical Diagram (Epicycle/Planetary Model) — Tusi Ptolemy MS (p. 86)
medium: manuscript, ink on paper (open book spread)
rights: Public Domain. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
summary:
A circular astronomical diagram from a Princeton manuscript of al-Tusi's commentary on the pseudo-Ptolemaic Centiloquium, shown in the right-hand page of an open book spread.

## Iconography
The circle contains concentric rings and geometric lines — the standard diagrammatic convention for representing planetary epicycles in the Arabic-Persian commentary tradition derived from Ptolemy's Almagest. Labels in Arabic script indicate celestial entities (planets, deferent, epicycle, zodiac positions). Al-Tusi's commentary on the Centiloquium follows Ptolemy's astrological aphorisms with explanatory notes that connect the abstract number-based predictions to actual planetary mechanics; the diagram illustrates the geometric model underlying a specific astrological claim. In the Islamic tradition, astronomical diagrams in manuscripts served both educational and mnemonic functions: a practitioner consulting the text for astrological guidance needed to understand the celestial machinery producing the phenomena. This diagram stands in a tradition of astronomical illustration running from the Almagest through Tusi, Ulugh Beg, and ultimately contributing to Copernicus's heliocentric reform.

## Significance
The Ptolemaic epicycle diagram represents the culmination of the mathematical astronomy tradition transmitted from Greek to Arabic to Latin scholarship — the deferent-and-epicycle model that explained apparent planetary retrograde motion without departing from circular uniform motion. Al-Tusi's commentary on Ptolemy was a key text in this tradition; the Maragha school (13th–14th c.), centered on Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, produced innovations in planetary modeling that were later transmitted to Copernicus.

title: Al-Jadwal al-Awwal — First of Sixteen Jadwal Tables, Large Numeric Grid (Zad al-ashraf, f. 4a)
medium: manuscript, ink on paper, red ink
rights: Public Domain. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
summary:
A spectacular full-page numeric jadwal (table) from the Zad al-ashraf fi wafq al-qaf (Princeton Garrett 335L), labeled at the top 'al-jadwal al-awwal min al-sita 'ashar jadwalan' (The First of the Sixteen Jadwal Tables).

## Iconography
The grid occupies most of the page and contains rows and columns of red Arabic numerals, with the grid ruled in black ink. The 16 jadwal system is a technique for expanding a basic wafq into 16 variant configurations — each derived by a specific systematic transformation (rotation, reflection, digit-manipulation) of the base magic square. In the qaf tradition, the 16 jadwal tables represent the 16 different operative configurations of the qaf-wafq, each corresponding to a different magical purpose or planetary hour. The sheer scale of this jadwal page (16 complete numeric grids are represented across a set of pages in this treatise) demonstrates the computational ambition of the 'ilm al-qaf system — the practitioner is not merely copying a single magic square but has access to the full 16-configuration system for maximum precision in talisman construction. The page below the large grid contains a short explanatory text identifying the tables and their uses.

## Significance
Documents the Zad al-Ashrāf wafq tradition — a text specifically dedicated to the wafq as a spiritual gift for the noble-born. The multi-type display (5×5 numeric and letter variants, 16-cell jadwal, triple-grid page) demonstrates the three main wafq categories: numeric squares (where cell-sums are equal), letter squares (where cells contain sacred names or Quranic phrases), and word squares (where full divine attributes are arranged in grid form).

title: Three Jinn Encounter Miniatures — Demonic Attacks and Apparitions (f. ~195r)
medium: manuscript, opaque watercolor and ink on paper
summary:
A page from the Princeton illustrated Persian Wonders of Creation manuscript (ʿAjāʾib al-Makhlūqāt, 17th-18th c.

## Iconography
CE) containing three distinct miniature paintings arranged in vertical panels alternating with Persian text — all illustrating encounters between humans and jinn (supernatural beings from Islamic cosmology). Top panel (upper left): a turbaned man in blue and a dark-spotted demon with clawed hands face each other in a flower-strewn landscape, the jinn appearing to materialize or speak to the human. Center panel (right side): a dark-brown ape-demon or jinn figure riding a pale horse or beast, attacking or abducting a sleeping human figure. Bottom panel (lower left): a prostrate man in blue robe confronted by a headless white dog-creature and a dark hooded figure — an apparition or nightmare manifestation. The paintings are in fine Persian miniature style with lapis-blue skies, detailed vegetation, and carefully rendered figures. These three scenes likely illustrate specific anecdotes from the jinn section of al-Qazwini's encyclopedia, which catalogs the types, behaviors, and powers of jinn — including their ability to appear in animal forms, attack travelers, and afflict sleepers. The folio number 190 is visible in the upper corner.

## Significance
Illustrates the Solomonic magical tradition fundamental to both Islamic and Jewish/Christian occult thought. Solomon's command over jinn and demons (*shayāṭīn*) is Quranic (Q. 27:17–44, 38:36–38), giving Islamic cosmography its central figure of magical authority. The *ʿAjā'ib al-makhlūqāt* of al-Qazwini (13th c.) was the most widely illustrated Arabic cosmographic text, existing in hundreds of manuscripts; its Solomon/jinn scenes became a standard image-type in Islamic book painting. Amira El-Zein's *Islam, Arabs, and the Intelligent World of the Jinn* (Syracuse, 2009) gives the best English account of this tradition.

## For artists & game designers
The Solomon-commanding-jinn court scene is the canonical image for ruler-of-spirits iconography in Islamic art — directly relevant for game designers working in Arabian/Persian fantasy settings or any system involving bound spirits and magical hierarchy.

Al-Qazwini's encyclopedia discusses the jinn as a real category of creatures, cataloging their types, habitats, and interactions with humans. This miniature visualizes the hierarchical cosmology in which Solomon stands at the intersection of the human, angelic, and jinn worlds.

Reading from top to bottom: alchemical roundels, emblematic figures, and Middle English verses guide the reader through the seven stages of the Great Work. Successive scenes include: the putrefying king in the earth, the Green Lion devouring the sun, the queen with moon and star, the pelican at the tower (nourishing its young with its own blood — an emblem of the Stone multiplying itself), the alchemical king and queen in conjunction, and finally the triumphant red king holding the crowned Stone. The scroll synthesizes Ripley's Compound of Alchymie into a visual programme: the alchemical process is staged as a royal drama of death (nigredo), purification (albedo), and glorification (rubedo). Each roundel is an instruction painted in symbolic code; the verses gloss the images. The Ripley Scroll was used as a practical guide in 16th–17th-century English alchemical workshops and also as an object of courtly display, explaining its high material quality.

## Significance
The Ripley Scroll embodies the tradition of English practical laboratory alchemy (late 15th–16th c.) — the working tradition of 'chymistry' practiced by experimenters who read Ripley's *Compound of Alchymy* as a recipe manual as much as a symbolic poem. Jennifer M. Rampling's *The Experimental Fire* (Chicago, 2020) is the definitive modern study of English alchemy as laboratory practice rather than purely spiritual allegory. The scroll format (rare outside the Ripley tradition) was designed for continuous consultation — unrolling the parchment traces the Great Work from putrefaction to the tincture.

The Ripley Scroll's continuous scroll format is unique in the alchemical tradition — a narrative that unfolds in space rather than pages. The iconographic program (toad/moon/water at bottom → sun/stone at top) gives a complete alchemical visual vocabulary in a single image, ideal for large-format use or as a visual 'map' of a magical system.

title: Geomancy Table of the 16 Figures (Ashkal) — Al-Shajara al-Muthimara (p. 12)
rights: Public Domain. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
summary:
A tabular page from al-Shajara al-Muthimara, a Princeton geomancy treatise, showing systematic mapping of the 16 geomantic figures (al-ashkal) to their properties.

## Iconography
The table is organized in rows and columns with Arabic text headers and figure names in cells, representing the foundational reference chart of the geomantic system. In ilm al-raml, the 16 figures (each a vertical stack of 4 rows, each row containing 1 or 2 points) are generated from a random process (points drawn in sand, or thrown) and then organized into a horoscopic chart of 16 positions. The table allows the practitioner to look up each figure's attributes and interpret the chart accordingly. This page shows the systematic, tabular presentation of geomantic knowledge that characterizes the learned Arabic tradition — contrasting with the more schematic or pictographic presentation in folk and European geomancy traditions.

## Significance
Arabic geomancy (*'ilm al-raml*, 'science of sand') is one of the eight Islamic divinatory sciences systematized in the Islamic occult encyclopaedic tradition. The 16 *ashkāl* (figures: one or two dots in four rows, giving 4² possible combinations) are used to construct a shield-chart of 16 positions by additive processes, from which a horoscope-like judgment is derived. T. Fahd's *La Divination arabe* (Leiden, 1966) is the foundational scholarly study; Emile Savage-Smith and Marion Smith's monograph on an Islamic geomantic device (Undena, 1980) documents the instrumental tradition.

## For artists & game designers
The three geomantic tables (ashkāl, directions, presence) provide a complete visual vocabulary for the Islamic raml system — useful for any design involving consultation/divination mechanics, or as source material for a fantasy geomantic system.

The column headers across the top include zodiac signs (سنبلة / Virgo visible) and other astrological/celestial designations that determine which operation to use based on current celestial conditions. The row labels on the left identify different tactical components or elements of the military operation (types of forces, materials, procedures). Each cell contains the specific formula, incense, or action appropriate to that intersection of tactical goal and celestial timing. This is an unusually explicit table format for military or offensive magic — most Islamic occult compilations frame battlefield operations metaphorically or in general protective terms, but this chapter presents a systematic reference grid for a practitioner undertaking military campaigns. The use of astrological timing (zodiac columns) reflects the fusion of Islamic stellar magic (tanjīm) with the huruf tradition.

Al-Buni's *Shams al-Ma'ārif* (12th/13th c.) is the foundational work of this genre; later 19th-century compilations like this one represent the continued vitality of the tradition in the Ottoman and post-Ottoman world.

title: 5×5 Numeric Jafr Wafq — Imam Jafar Sultan-Court Efficacy Testimony (f. 26b)
medium: manuscript, ink on paper, bordered numeric grid
summary:
A folio from the Princeton Kitāb al-Sirr al-maṣūn (Garrett collection, 17c) combining a 5×5 numeric magic square (wafq) with one of the most vivid first-person testimonial passages in the Jafr manuscript tradition.

## Iconography
The wafq occupies the lower left of the page: a bordered 5×5 grid (25 cells) with Arabic numerals filling each cell, one cell highlighted in red ink. The visible numbers include 1, 18, 10, 33 in the top row and descending values throughout — this is an abjad-derived wafq where the row, column, and diagonal sums encode the numerical value of a specific divine name. The abjad calculation notations below the grid (reading '٨٨٨٥' and other totals) confirm the computational basis: the scribe has verified that the cell sums correspond to the target abjad total. The annotation 'اللوح كما ترى' (The tablet as you see it) identifies this as a direct transcription of the talisman form from an authoritative source. To the right of the wafq, the headings 'كفاية فاعرفه واكتمه' (This is sufficient — know it and keep it secret) and 'صاراليك وهن صفة' (These qualities/descriptions have come to you) frame the revelation of a secret. The main text above contains the extraordinary testimonial: 'قال الإمام الجعفر رحمه الله وحق تربة جدي كتبته وعلقته على عضدي فادخلت به على سلطان وطلبت منه حاجتي فأقضاها وما تحدثت به على أحد من الأكابر وقصدت شيئاً إلا أبلغت مرادي الآمن خيرا وشراً وحلالا وحراماً' — 'Imam Jafar said, may God have mercy on him: By the soil of my grandfather, I wrote it and tied it to my arm and entered upon a sultan and asked for my need and he fulfilled it, and whenever I wanted something from the great ones I achieved my desire whether for good or evil, lawful or forbidden.' This narrative pattern — first-person testimonial by Imam Jafar al-Sadiq vouching for an operation's efficacy — is the defining rhetorical device of the Jafr tradition, linking each wafq to the imam's personal authority.

## Significance
The Kitāb al-Jafr tradition derives from early Shia Islam — attributed to Imam ʿAlī and systematized by the Sixth Imam Jafar al-Sadiq — combining Quranic numerology, Solomonic angel-lore, and a cosmological letter-code (*huruf*) to produce operational talismans and divination. The red-ink talisman here, labeled as the 'Fourteenth Operation,' belongs to a genre of numbered operational diagrams (*aʿmāl*, 'works') found throughout Islamic magical literature. Emile Savage-Smith documents analogous diagrams from the Bodleian and British Library collections.

## For artists & game designers
The red X-talisman ('Fourteenth Operation') is one of the most graphically striking Islamic magical diagrams in the collection — an unusually bold, minimalist geometric composition ideal for use as a symbolic icon or game asset. The contrast of black square with red diagonal crosses is immediately legible as 'magical' without requiring cultural context.

medium: manuscript, ink on paper, two-column format
summary:

## Iconography
ِ وَاصْطِلَاحَاتِ أَهْلِ الصِّنَاعَةِ — On the Names of the Instruments and Technical Terms of the Craft) across the top of the page in a two-column layout. Folio number 40 appears in the top left. The left column contains the Arabic or Ottoman names of alchemical apparatus in a list format: 'Nār-ı Hażnān' (incubating/gentle fire), 'Hurāra yekūn tumsahā bi'l-yad' (heat that can be touched by hand — a Paracelsian temperature classification), 'Hel-i Nedā' (dew dissolution), and further apparatus types with their definitions written to the right. The right-hand block of text describes functional categories of operation: distillation (taqṭīr), calcination (taklis), sublimation, and other spagyric procedures central to Paracelsian pharmaceutical preparation. The passage cites Jabir ibn Hayyan, Roger Bacon, and Albertus Magnus — the intellectual lineage linking Islamic alchemy to Latin Scholastic alchemical transmission — before the chapter shifts to operational description. Documents the Paracelsian influence on Ottoman medical practice via Salih ibn Nasr Allah ibn Sallum (d. ca. 1670s), physician to Sultan Mehmed IV, who synthesized Galenic, Arabic, and Paracelsian chemical medicine in *al-Tibb al-jadīd al-kīmiyāʾī*. This work shows the transmission of Western European alchemy/iatrochemistry into the Islamic world in the 17th century — the reverse direction from the medieval Arabic-to-Latin translation movement. title: Ottoman Water Medicine Formulary — Tabular Multi-Column Recipe Tables (f. 112v)
medium: manuscript, ink on paper, tabular recipe format, multi-column
summary:
A late folio from the Princeton al-Ṭibb al-jadīd al-kimiyāʾī (figgy ff61422c, 17c) showing a densely structured Ottoman pharmaceutical formulary page with multiple compound medicine recipes in a horizontal multi-column table format.

## Iconography
The page is divided into two vertical sections, each headed by a red-outlined recipe title in Ottoman: 'Ṭarīq-ı Miyāh' (طريق مياه — Method of the Waters, i.e., aqueous pharmaceutical preparations) appears at upper right, and 'Ṭarīq' (Method) appears at upper left for a second recipe section. Each recipe section presents ingredients horizontally — ingredient names written above, with quantity numerals (100, 150, 120, 80, 60 — presumably in dram or dirham weight) written below — creating a horizontal ingredient-quantity table that reads across the page. Ingredient terms visible include 'bārūt' (saltpeter/potassium nitrate — a Paracelsian mineral medicine), 'ʿuqāb' (eagle, a pharmaceutical plant name in Turkish tradition), and numbered sub-recipes (ʿAlā, ʿAlā 2, ʿAlā 3 — designating variant concentrations or preparations). The lower half of the folio contains a dense Arabic discussion of the medicinal properties (ṣifat — nature/quality) of these water preparations, including use for dropsy (istisqāʾ), eye conditions (bayāḍ al-ʿayn), and ulcers. The 'waters' tradition in this Ottoman-Paracelsian context bridges the Arabic alchemy of distilled medicinal waters (māʾ al-hayāt, etc.) with the Paracelsian doctrine of the quinta essentia extracted through distillation.

## Significance
Documents the Paracelsian influence on Ottoman medical practice via Salih ibn Nasr Allah ibn Sallum (d. ca. 1670s), physician to Sultan Mehmed IV, who synthesized Galenic, Arabic, and Paracelsian chemical medicine in *al-Tibb al-jadīd al-kīmiyāʾī*. This work shows the transmission of Western European alchemy/iatrochemistry into the Islamic world in the 17th century — the reverse direction from the medieval Arabic-to-Latin translation movement. Emile Savage-Smith's work on attitudes toward dissection and the history of Islamic medicine provides context.

## For artists & game designers
The Ottoman recipe tables with horizontal ingredient lists offer a clean 'alchemical recipe book' aesthetic — systematically organized, visually legible, and immediately interpretable as 'magical formulary' by modern viewers.

title: Angelic Name Abjad Calculation Table — Mīkā'īl, Hasmayīl, and the Planetary Intermediaries (f. 35b)
medium: manuscript, ink on paper, red ink
rights: Public Domain. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
summary:
A compound page from the Sharḥ Manẓūmat Kashf al-Rān fī al-Zāyirjah (Princeton Garrett 542H, 1787 CE) combining prose text with a structured angelic-name abjad calculation table — one of the most distinctive pages in the manuscript.

## Iconography
The left side of the page contains a column listing five or more named angelic/celestial intermediaries (muwakkil, pl. muwakkilūn — 'those appointed over' specific functions or spheres): Mīkā'īl (1100084 or similar), Hasmayīl (5341), Ibfīshā'īl (11473 or similar), al-Khāmis al-Ḥākim (11493 or similar), and related names — each followed by its abjad numerical value and a column-addition sum. The right side contains a 5-column × 4-6 row numeric lookup table with large Arabic numerals (values in the hundreds to thousands: 2270, 2776, 3278, etc.), whose rows and columns correspond to the angelic names listed on the left. The prose text surrounding the table names the muwakkilūn and explains their role in the Zairja procedure: each celestial intermediary governs a specific aspect of the divination, and the practitioner must compute the abjad value of the relevant name and use it as an input to the lookup table. This page thus encodes the theological scaffolding of the Zairja — its angelology — in computational table form, connecting the names of celestial beings directly to numeric values used in divination calculations.

## Significance
The *Sharh Manzūmat Kashf al-rān fī al-zayirjah* is an 18th-century commentary on the classical *zayirja* — the circular divinatory instrument that, by means of letter permutation according to astrological and mathematical rules, generates answers to questions about the future. Ibn Khaldun devotes a famous chapter of the *Muqaddimah* to the zayirja as the most intellectually ambitious of Islamic divinatory arts, noting that its practitioners could generate astrological and cosmological poetry from a questioner's input.

title: Eight 4×4 Numeric Magic Squares (Saturn-Square Grids) for Zairja Computation (f. 38a)
medium: manuscript, ink on paper, red ink borders

summary:

The page is a working reference tool: the practitioner identifies which of the 8 variants applies to their specific query and reads the output from the corresponding grid. title: Inverted Triangle (Muthallath) Colophon — End of Zairja Commentary Text (f. 15b)
medium: manuscript, ink on paper, red and black ink
rights: Public Domain. Princeton University Library (Garrett Collection).
summary:
A page from the Sharḥ Manẓūmat Kashf al-Rān fī al-Zāyirjah (Princeton Garrett 542H, 1787 CE) showing a muthallath — an inverted triangle text layout — at the conclusion of the first text (fol.

## Iconography
15b). The muthallath is a calligraphic format in which lines of Arabic text are arranged so that each successive line is shorter than the one above it, creating a downward-pointing triangle or pyramid shape. The technique is used for colophons, prayers, dedications, or poetic conclusions, where the diminishing lines visually enact the idea of conclusion, narrowing, or a point of arrival. In this manuscript, the muthallath marks the end of the Zairja commentary text (fol. 1a–15b) with a prayer or doxological formula — the text pyramids down to a single word or divine name at its apex. The surrounding page is yellow-green aged paper. The colophon text is written in red and black ink in a neat naskh hand. This calligraphic figure is one of several shaped-text forms in the Arabic manuscript tradition (alongside the inverted triangle, scribes also use square arrangements, circular colophons, and diamond shapes). The muthallath is specifically associated with conclusions and with the Prophet's name (the inverted triangle is said to resemble the shape of the letter mīm, the first letter of Muḥammad).

title: Alchemical furnace of Augustus, Elector of Saxony (Dresden, c. 1575)
creator: Saxon court workshop (Dresden)
repository: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
rights: Public domain. Photograph by Daderot, via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A surviving brass-and-steel furnace built for Augustus, Elector of Saxony, around 1575 — not an emblem of calcination but the literal device in which calcination, and every other fire-operation of the Great Work, was actually performed.

## Iconography
A compact, drum-shaped furnace of brass and steel set on a chamotte (fireclay) base, fitted with the doors, vents, and chambers needed to regulate draft and graduate heat. Its survival and museum-grade construction mark it as a court instrument rather than a common workshop tool.

## Significance
Augustus of Saxony (r. 1553–1586) maintained one of the most lavishly funded alchemical laboratories in the Holy Roman Empire, staffed by court alchemists pursuing both transmutation and practical assaying, dyeing, and pharmacy. A furnace like this one is the physical referent behind every emblem-book picture of a robed philosopher tending an athanor: the graduated, controllable heat that calcination — Ripley's first gate — required to reduce a body to ash without simply destroying it. Where Splendor Solis or the Rosarium render the operation as myth (a king burned and reborn), an object like this shows the engineering that made the myth performable.

## For artists & game designers
A grounding reference for what a working alchemical furnace actually looked like — useful for any game or illustration that wants its 'calcination station' to read as a real piece of 16th-century laboratory apparatus rather than a generic cartoon furnace.

title: The Solar Calcination of Antimony — Le Fèvre's demonstration plate
creator: Nicaise Le Fèvre (1610–1669)
repository: Digital Public Library of America (scan); original in a copy of Le Fèvre's *Traité de la chymie*
summary:
An alchemist stands at a bench where sunlight, focused through a lens or burning-glass, falls onto a heap of antimony and sets it smoking — calcination performed without any furnace at all, fire drawn directly from the sun.

## Iconography
A single demonstrator stands beside a table on which a lettered diagram identifies each part of the apparatus: the mirror or lens that gathers sunlight, the beam it projects, and the antimony specimen visibly fuming as the focused heat strikes it. The plate is captioned (in French) 'La calcination Solaire de l'Antimoine' — the solar calcination of antimony — and belongs to Nicaise Le Fèvre's chemistry textbook, later translated into English as *A Compleat Body of Chymistry*.

## Significance
Calcination is Ripley's first gate: matter given over to fire until it dries, blackens, and reduces to powder or ash, freeing the volatile spirit trapped within the body. Le Fèvre's plate is unusual among the corpus of emblem-book calcinations in being a literal laboratory demonstration rather than an allegorical king-in-the-furnace scene — it records an actual 17th-century experimental method (solar calcination by burning-glass, a technique also used by Lavoisier's predecessors) and ties calcination as firmly to chemical practice as to symbolic theology. Antimony itself carried heavy alchemical freight as the 'grey wolf,' *lupus metallorum*, prized and feared as a violent purifier of gold.

## For artists & game designers
A clean, non-allegorical reference for how period chemists actually performed a 'burning' operation: focused light, smoke, a labelled apparatus — useful where a game wants a calcination minigame or crafting-station visual grounded in real period technique rather than emblem-book symbolism.

title: *Splendor Solis* — the King and Queen of coagulation (Sol above Luna)
creator: attrib. Salomon Trismosin (illuminator anonymous)
rights: CC BY 4.0. Wellcome Collection, via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A watercolour leaf in the *Splendor Solis* tradition: a queen in blue stands beneath a crescent moon, a king in red beneath a radiant sun — the cycle's clearest single image of the two principles that must be brought together and fixed for the Work to succeed.

## Iconography
The queen, robed in lunar blue, occupies the left field under a pale moon; the king, robed in solar red, occupies the right under a golden sun. Each stands as an independent, crowned figure rather than the joined Rebis seen elsewhere in the cycle — this is the pair *before* their union, posed as still, fixed emblems rather than as actors in a narrative scene.

## Significance
The accompanying cataloguing identifies the pair as figures of mercury (the volatile, 'dissolving' lac virginis under Luna) and sulphur (the 'coagulating' masculine principle under Sol). Congelation — *congelatio*, the sixth gate in Ripley's sequence — is exactly this operation: the volatile spirit is checked and coagulated into a fixed body, no longer free to evaporate. Where the Rebis plates show the *result* of that fixing (a single two-headed body), this image isolates the two principles in the moment just before coagulation locks them together — mercury's fluidity held in tension against sulphur's fixing heat. The king-and-queen, sun-and-moon pairing is one of the most reproduced visual shorthands in the entire alchemical corpus precisely because it lets an illuminator show the *whole* opus — dissolution, conjunction, fixation — in a single static diagram.

## For artists & game designers
A ready-made two-character tableau: a blue, lunar, fluid-coded queen and a red, solar, fixed-coded king, useful wherever a game needs to stage 'volatile spirit' and 'fixed body' as opposing forces about to be locked together — a coagulation puzzle, a binding spell, or a stat-pairing screen.

title: Broadsheet on the Terrible Comet of 1577
work: Prophecy & Apocalyptic Figurae: Diagrams of Sacred History
creator: Jiří Jakubův Dačický
rights: Public domain. Zentralbibliothek Zürich. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A 1577 illustrated broadsheet — *Von einem schrecklichen und wunderbarlichen Cometen* — reporting the Great Comet of 1577 as a [[motif:celestial portent|terrible celestial portent]].

## Iconography
A blazing [[motif:comet|comet]] streams across the sky above a townscape or landscape, its lurid tail the focus; the accompanying German text interprets the apparition (seen 'on the Tuesday after Martinmas') as a wonder and a warning from God of coming punishment.

## Significance
The Great Comet of 1577 was observed across Europe and famously measured by Tycho Brahe, who proved it lay beyond the Moon, shattering the doctrine of unchanging celestial spheres. While astronomers studied its parallax, popular broadsheets read it as a [[motif:omen of the end|divine omen]] of war, plague, and the Last Days — a vivid case of the era's double response to the heavens as both natural object and prophetic sign.

## For artists & game designers
The flaming comet over a sleeping town is the archetypal 'bad omen in the sky' establishing shot for a coming-catastrophe beat.

title: The Seven-Headed Dragon (Liber Figurarum)
work: Prophecy & Apocalyptic Figurae: Diagrams of Sacred History
creator: After Joachim of Fiore
summary:
The great red [[motif:seven-headed dragon|seven-headed dragon]] from a manuscript of Joachim of Fiore's *Liber Figurarum*, the album of prophetic diagrams that crystallised his reading of history.

## Iconography
The dragon stretches across the page, each of its seven heads named for a persecutor of the Church and keyed to one of the seven seals of Revelation; the seventh head — the [[motif:antichrist|Antichrist]] still to come — and the lashing tail (Gog) close the sequence. Names and captions thread between the coils, turning the beast into a timeline of sacred history.

## Significance
Joachim (c. 1135–1202), the Calabrian abbot, devised the *figura* as a tool of prophetic exegesis: history unfolds in three *status* toward an Age of the Spirit. The dragon's heads identify successive tyrants from Herod to the final Antichrist, making the apocalyptic timeline legible at a glance. The *Liber Figurarum* shaped [[motif:joachimism|Joachite]] expectation for centuries among Spiritual Franciscans and radical reformers.

## For artists & game designers
A single monster whose seven heads each encode a chapter of a story — a ready device for a 'boss as timeline,' where defeating each head advances an era.

citations.text: Marjorie Reeves & Beatrice Hirsch-Reich, *The Figurae of Joachim of Fiore* (1972).

title: Joachim of Fiore Showing Saints Dominic and Francis
work: Prophecy & Apocalyptic Figurae: Diagrams of Sacred History
creator: Gregorio Vásquez de Arce y Ceballos
summary:
A Spanish-American Baroque painting (1680) of the abbot [[motif:joachim of fiore|Joachim of Fiore]] revealing the portraits of Saints Dominic and Francis — the prophecy that he had foreseen the coming of the two great mendicant orders.

## Iconography
Joachim, in monastic habit, displays or gestures toward medallion portraits of Saint Dominic and Saint Francis, the founders whom later legend held he had prophesied as the spiritual men (*viri spirituales*) of the dawning third age. The composition frames him as an inspired seer rather than a heretic.

## Significance
Though Joachim's own teaching was later condemned in points, his prestige as a prophet survived, especially among Franciscans who identified themselves as the order of the coming Age of the Spirit. The legend that he predicted Dominic and Francis became a staple of Counter-Reformation imagery; here the Colombian master Gregorio Vásquez gives it Baroque dignity. The image documents how Joachite prophecy was domesticated into orthodox devotion.

## For artists & game designers
A seer revealing future heroes as portrait-medallions is an elegant 'prophecy reveal' device that names characters before they appear.

title: Joachim of Fiore — Tree of Humanity (Adam to Second Coming), Liber Figurarum Tav. II
summary: Table II (Tav. II) from Joachim of Fiore's Liber Figurarum (Book of Figures), the Codice Reggiano manuscript (Reggio Emilia, mid-13th century). Depicts the Tree of Humanity as a genealogical-prophetic tree spanning from Adam to the Second Coming of Christ — a schema of all human history organized under Joachim's three-age theology (Age of the Father, Age of the Son, Age of the Holy Spirit). Joachim's concordist method finds structural parallelism between Old and New Testaments; this tree diagram is one of his most distinctive and influential diagrammatic forms, directly shaping later Franciscan Spirituals and apocalyptic movements.

title: Joachim of Fiore — New Monastic Order / Third Age of the Spirit, Liber Figurarum Tav. XII
summary: Table XII (Tav. XII) from Joachim of Fiore's Liber Figurarum, Codice Reggiano (mid-13th century). Depicts the institutional arrangement of the New Monastic Order that Joachim expected to emerge in the Third Age — the Age of the Holy Spirit, which he placed beginning around 1260. This diagram shows the hierarchical circles of the new order alongside the corresponding structures of the first two ages, enacting Joachim's distinctive concordist typology. The Third Age diagrams were enormously influential on Franciscan Spirituals and Spiritual Franciscan apocalypticism, particularly the circles of Gerard of Borgo San Donnino.

title: The Three Estates (Lichtenberger, Prognosticatio)
work: Prophecy & Apocalyptic Figurae: Diagrams of Sacred History
creator: Johannes Lichtenberger (printed by Jacob Meydenbach)
summary:
A woodcut of the three estates from Johannes Lichtenberger's *Prognosticatio*, the most influential astrological-prophetic book of the late fifteenth century.

## Iconography
The figures of the social order — clergy, nobility/emperor, and commons — are arranged to embody the *Ständeordnung*, the divinely-ordained estates whose fortunes Lichtenberger's prophecy charts. Elsewhere in the book, monks, comets, and astrological conjunctions illustrate the coming upheavals foretold.

## Significance
Lichtenberger compiled his *Prognosticatio* (first printed c. 1488) largely from earlier prophecy and astrology, anchoring it in the great Saturn–Jupiter [[motif:great conjunction|conjunction]] of 1484 and a comet. Its forecasts of religious and political turmoil were read as anticipating the Reformation; Luther himself reissued it with a preface in 1527. It ran through dozens of editions and shaped the visual language of [[motif:astrological prophecy|astral prophecy]].

## For artists & game designers
Linking a prophecy to a specific celestial event (a comet, a planetary conjunction) grounds otherwise vague doom in a datable, observable trigger.

title: Mirabilis Liber (title page)
work: Prophecy & Apocalyptic Figurae: Diagrams of Sacred History
creator: Anonymous (compilation)
summary:
The title page of the *Mirabilis Liber*, an early-sixteenth-century anthology that gathered the major medieval prophecies into a single best-selling volume.

## Iconography
The modest printed title page announces the 'wonderful book' of prophecies. Like Nostradamus's *Preface*, the artefact's power lies in the assembled prophetic *texts* rather than figural illustration — a compendium presented as a key to the future.

## Significance
The *Mirabilis Liber* (first printed in France c. 1522) collected the *Sibylline* oracles, [[motif:pseudo-methodius|Pseudo-Methodius]], the prophecies of St Cæsarius, Joachite material, and the legend of the [[motif:last world emperor|Last World Emperor]] and 'Second Charlemagne.' Hugely popular, it shaped French apocalyptic expectation and is widely thought to have influenced Nostradamus. It is a key witness to how diverse prophetic traditions were bundled and marketed in print.

## For artists & game designers
A single in-world 'book of all prophecies' that anthologises many traditions lets you seed a setting's entire mythos of the future in one prop.

title: The Monk-Calf — A Monstrous Birth as Portent
work: Prophecy & Apocalyptic Figurae: Diagrams of Sacred History
creator: Anonymous (after Reformation broadsheet)
summary:
A print of a deformed calf (*mismaakt kalf*), of the kind read in the Reformation era as a [[motif:monstrous birth|monstrous-birth]] prodigy foretelling divine judgement.

## Iconography
The malformed calf is shown in stark profile as a documentary 'wonder,' the deformity itself the message. Such prints typically carried captions decoding the monster's parts as signs — a tradition that produced the famous *Mönchskalb* (Monk-Calf) and *Papstesel* (Pope-Ass) broadsheets of Luther and Melanchthon.

## Significance
Monstrous births, comets, and prodigies were systematically read in the sixteenth century as God's warnings of impending catastrophe or as polemical signs against opponents. Luther and Melanchthon's 1523 pamphlet interpreted a 'monk-calf' and a 'pope-ass' as portents condemning the Roman Church. This visual genre of the [[motif:prodigy|prodigy]] fused natural marvel, prophecy, and confessional propaganda.

## For artists & game designers
A single deformed creature presented as an omen, with each anomaly 'meaning' something, is a compact way to deliver foreboding through a found object.

title: Les Prophéties — Centuries (antedated edition)
work: Prophecy & Apocalyptic Figurae: Diagrams of Sacred History
creator: Michel de Nostredame (Nostradamus)
summary:
A title page of Nostradamus's *Les Prophéties / Centuries* from an antedated edition, illustrating the tangled print history of the prophecies.

## Iconography
The title page announces the *Centuries* of prophecies; its imprint date is one of several that bibliographers have shown to be antedated — printed later but bearing an earlier year, a common ploy to lend prophecies a false pedigree of having predated the events they seem to foretell.

## Significance
The posthumous editions of the *Prophéties* (from 1568, after Nostradamus's death in 1566) added further *Centuries* and were frequently reissued, sometimes with falsified dates. These antedated printings are central to the scholarly debunking of claims that specific quatrains 'foresaw' particular events, since the supposedly prophetic texts were in fact printed afterward. The bibliographic muddle is itself a key chapter in the Nostradamus legend.

## For artists & game designers
A prophecy book with a deliberately falsified date is a fine plot hook — an artefact whose very printing history is a forgery to be uncovered.

title: Portrait of Nostradamus
work: Prophecy & Apocalyptic Figurae: Diagrams of Sacred History
creator: Anonymous (after earlier portraits)
summary:
A portrait of [[motif:nostradamus|Michel de Nostredame (Nostradamus)]], the French physician and astrologer whose quatrain-prophecies became the most famous of the early modern era.

## Iconography
Nostradamus is shown in the conventional seer's guise: bearded, capped, soberly robed as a learned physician, the very image of the Renaissance scholar-astrologer. The likeness descends from portraits associated with his son César's circle and was reproduced endlessly to front editions of his prophecies.

## Significance
Michel de Nostredame (1503–1566) published *Les Prophéties* from 1555, a collection of nearly a thousand four-line *quatrains* grouped in *Centuries*, couched in deliberately obscure, polyglot, anagrammatic language. Patronised by Catherine de' Medici, he became court astrologer to Charles IX. His enigmatic verses — endlessly reinterpreted to 'predict' later events — made his name a byword for prophecy itself.

## For artists & game designers
The archetypal prophet portrait: bearded scholar in a study, instantly readable as 'the one who foresees,' useful as a quest-giving oracle NPC.

citations.text: Peter Lemesurier, *The Nostradamus Encyclopedia* (1997).

title: Les Prophéties — Preface of 1555
work: Prophecy & Apocalyptic Figurae: Diagrams of Sacred History
creator: Michel de Nostredame (Nostradamus)
summary:
A page of the *Préface à César* opening Nostradamus's *Les Prophéties* (Lyon, 1555), the prose letter in which he addresses his infant son and explains his prophetic method.

## Iconography
Dense black-letter / roman type fills the page of the *Preface to César Nostredame*, the dedicatory letter that prefaces the first edition of the *Centuries*. There is no figural image — the artefact is the prophetic *text* itself, the material object through which the prophecies entered the world.

## Significance
In the Preface Nostradamus describes receiving his foreknowledge through 'natural instinct' aided by judicial astrology, while veiling specifics to avoid scandal and persecution. The 1555 Lyon edition (printed by Macé Bonhomme) launched the *Prophéties*; expanded editions followed through 1568. The Preface is the key statement of his self-presentation as a divinely-and-astrologically inspired seer.

## For artists & game designers
A prophet's first-person preface 'to my son' is a strong framing device for delivering cryptic lore as an in-world document rather than narration.

title: The Tiburtine Sibyl and the Emperor Augustus (chiaroscuro woodcut)
work: Prophecy & Apocalyptic Figurae: Diagrams of Sacred History
creator: Antonio da Trento (after Parmigianino)
summary:
An Italian chiaroscuro woodcut by Antonio da Trento of the [[motif:tiburtine sibyl|Tiburtine Sibyl]] showing the Emperor Augustus the heavenly vision.

## Iconography
The Sibyl gestures toward an apparition in the sky while Augustus looks up, the figures modelled in the tonal layers of the chiaroscuro woodcut — a technique using multiple blocks to build light and shadow like a wash drawing. The scene compresses the legend of the [[motif:ara coeli|Altar of Heaven]] into a single dramatic exchange.

## Significance
Antonio da Trento worked with Parmigianino, whose elegant designs he reproduced in chiaroscuro woodcuts; this print carries the Tiburtine Sibyl's prophecy into the sophisticated idiom of Italian Mannerist printmaking. It shows how the pagan-prophetess-foretells-Christ legend remained a prestigious subject for ambitious printmakers in the early sixteenth century.

## For artists & game designers
Chiaroscuro woodcut's two-tone, washed look is a distinctive visual key for 'old prophetic print' assets that read as antique without losing drama.

title: The Delphic Sibyl (after Michelangelo)
work: Prophecy & Apocalyptic Figurae: Diagrams of Sacred History
creator: Engraver after Michelangelo Buonarroti
rights: CC0. The Metropolitan Museum of Art. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A print after Michelangelo's [[motif:delphic sibyl|Delphic Sibyl]], from the series of Prophets and Sibyls on the Sistine Chapel ceiling.

## Iconography
The youthful Delphic Sibyl gazes outward, an unrolled prophetic scroll in her hand and the wind seeming to stir her drapery — the most serenely beautiful of Michelangelo's seeresses. Her open, startled expression suggests the moment of receiving the oracle.

## Significance
The Delphic Sibyl took her name from the great oracle of Apollo at Delphi, the most famous prophetic site of the ancient world. In Michelangelo's program she joins the company of [[motif:sibyl|sibyls]] who, in Christian thought, prophesied Christ alongside the Hebrew prophets. The image fixed an enduring Renaissance type of the youthful, inspired pagan prophetess as a counterpart to the aged Cumaean Sibyl.

## For artists & game designers
Paired with the aged Cumaean type, the youthful Delphic Sibyl shows how to vary a single role (the oracle) across distinct character ages and moods.

work: Prophecy & Apocalyptic Figurae: Diagrams of Sacred History
creator: Anonymous (after a sibyl series)
summary:
An engraving of the [[motif:persian sibyl|Persian Sibyl]] (*Sibylle Persica*) from a printed series of the twelve sibyls, held by the Rijksmuseum.

## Iconography
The Sibyl is rendered as a standing or seated prophetess with her identifying attribute and a Latin motto naming the prophecy ascribed to her. As one plate in a numbered set, she is conceived less as an individual than as a member of the codified company of ancient seeresses who foretold Christ.

## Significance
Such sibyl series — descending from the schemes of Lactantius and the Renaissance compiler Filippo Barbieri — gave each [[motif:sibyl|sibyl]] a fixed prophetic utterance and emblem, turning the pagan prophetesses into a quasi-liturgical sequence parallel to the Hebrew prophets. Their wide diffusion in prints made the sibyls familiar furnishings of churches, books, and decorative cycles across Catholic Europe.

## For artists & game designers
A second, differently-styled Persian Sibyl underscores how a stock prophetic 'type' can be re-skinned by many workshops while keeping the same emblem and meaning.

title: The Cumaean Sibyl (after Michelangelo)
work: Prophecy & Apocalyptic Figurae: Diagrams of Sacred History
creator: Engraver after Michelangelo Buonarroti
rights: CC0. The Metropolitan Museum of Art. Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A print after Michelangelo's [[motif:cumaean sibyl|Cumaean Sibyl]] on the Sistine Chapel ceiling, the most famous of the prophesying sibyls in Renaissance art.

## Iconography
The aged, powerfully built Sibyl turns to a great open book, her muscular arms and intense concentration conveying the strain of reading the future. On the ceiling she is one of five sibyls set among the seven Hebrew prophets, the whole company foretelling the coming of Christ.

## Significance
Michelangelo's inclusion of the pagan [[motif:sibyl|sibyls]] beside the prophets (1508–1512) monumentalised the old belief that the ancient prophetesses — Cumaean, Delphic, Erythraean, Libyan, Persian — had unknowingly foretold the Incarnation. The Cumaean Sibyl, who guided Aeneas to the underworld and (in the *Fourth Eclogue*) was read as predicting a new golden age, became the type of the inspired ancient seeress.

## For artists & game designers
The straining, hyper-muscular prophetess wrestling with a vast book is a memorable way to depict prophecy as physically demanding labour, not serene revelation.

## Iconography
The Persian Sibyl is shown in flowing classical dress, an inscription naming her and (in such series) often quoting the prophecy assigned to her — traditionally that she foretold the trampling of the serpent and the coming of the Saviour. The Mannerist figure-style and ornamental drapery are characteristic of late-sixteenth-century Northern printmaking.

## Significance
The canonical roster of twelve [[motif:sibyl|sibyls]], codified by writers like Filippo Barbieri, assigned each a specific prophecy of Christ and a distinctive attribute. Engraved sibyl series spread these types across Europe as devotional and decorative sets. The Persian Sibyl (sometimes conflated with the Chaldean or Hebrew Sibyl) was held to have prophesied the Virgin Birth and the defeat of the serpent.

## For artists & game designers
A numbered set of twelve distinct prophetesses, each with her own emblem and saying, is a ready-made faction or tarot-like card series.

A Netherlandish panel (named work of the *Master of the Tiburtine Sibyl*) depicting the [[motif:tiburtine sibyl|Tiburtine Sibyl]] revealing to the Emperor Augustus the vision of the Virgin and Child.

## Iconography
The Sibyl points the kneeling Emperor Augustus toward a heavenly apparition of the [[motif:vision of the virgin|Virgin and Child]] enthroned upon the sun. According to legend, asked whether any man was greater than he, Augustus was shown this vision and built the *Ara Coeli* ('Altar of Heaven') on the Capitol where Santa Maria in Aracoeli now stands.

## Significance
The Tiburtine Sibyl's prophecy to Augustus was among the most beloved medieval legends linking pagan prophecy to Christ's coming, making the sibyls honorary witnesses to the Incarnation alongside the Hebrew prophets. The episode appears in countless paintings and in mystery plays; this panel gave its anonymous master his conventional name. It exemplifies the Christianised [[motif:sibyl|sibyl]] tradition.

## For artists & game designers
A prophet revealing a glowing vision to a kneeling ruler is a clean composition for a 'humbling prophecy' scene that redirects a powerful character.

work: Prophecy & Apocalyptic Figurae: Diagrams of Sacred History

summary:
A further plate (p. 48) from the *Vaticinia de Summis Pontificibus*, continuing the emblematic sequence of papal prophecies.

## Iconography
A pope-figure is shown amid the series' recurring symbolic apparatus — angel, beast, banner, or hand emerging from a cloud — beneath a Latin caption. As throughout the *Vaticinia*, the picture withholds a clear referent, inviting the reader to decode which pontiff and which crisis of the Church is foretold.

## Significance
The *Vaticinia* circulated as a closed cycle of fifteen or thirty prophecies, repeatedly re-illustrated as new editions sought to align them with current events and to point toward an [[motif:reform of the church|Angelic Pope]] who would reform Christendom. The expectation of a coming holy pope (*pastor angelicus*) was one of the most potent strands of late-medieval and Renaissance prophecy.

## For artists & game designers
Deliberately ambiguous emblems that 'come true' only in hindsight model how to write prophecies that feel inevitable after the fact without committing to a reading in advance.

summary:
A leaf of an illuminated *Vaticinia Pontificum* in the British Library (Harley MS 1340), a deluxe manuscript copy of the papal-prophecy emblems.

## Iconography
The page presents a richly coloured prophetic emblem — a pope-figure with attendant symbolic animals and objects — set above its Latin verse. The hand-painted manuscript versions render the cryptic [[motif:vaticinia pontificum|Vaticinia]] images with greater finish than the woodcut printings, heightening their air of mystery.

## Significance
Manuscripts such as Harley 1340 carried the *Vaticinia* into princely and curial libraries, where the prophecies were studied for guidance on the fate of the papacy. The cycle's transmission across luxury manuscripts and cheap prints alike shows how a single body of apocalyptic prophecy could serve both elite and popular audiences from the 14th to the 17th century.

## For artists & game designers
The contrast between a crude printed prophecy and its jewel-like manuscript twin is a model for showing the same lore at different 'tiers' of in-world artefact.

title: Vaticinia de Summis Pontificibus (papal-prophecy plate, p. 9)
work: Prophecy & Apocalyptic Figurae: Diagrams of Sacred History
creator: Pseudo-Joachim / Anselm of Marsico (attrib.)
date: late medieval prophecy; early-modern printed copy
summary:
A plate from the *Vaticinia de Summis Pontificibus*, the celebrated series of cryptic papal-prophecy emblems attributed to [[motif:pseudo-joachim|Pseudo-Joachim]].

## Iconography
Each prophecy pairs a half-page emblematic picture of a pope — accompanied by symbolic beasts, angels, banners, or a bear, sickle, or rose — with a terse Latin motto and a brief enigmatic text. The figures are deliberately obscure, designed to be matched retrospectively to particular pontiffs.

## Significance
The *Vaticinia* (also called the *Genus nequam* and *Ascende calve* series) descend from Byzantine *Leo Oracles* and were circulated under Joachim's name from the 13th–14th centuries. Reprinted throughout the 16th and 17th centuries — by Telesphorus, Paracelsus's circle, and others — they fed an enduring appetite for prophecy about the succession and reform of the papacy, akin to the later 'Prophecy of the Popes' of Malachy.

## For artists & game designers
The template — an emblem + a one-line cryptic motto for each ruler in a line of succession — is a perfect 'prophecy codex' UI for a dynastic or papal storyline.

title: The Aldine anchor-and-dolphin device (colophon, 1502)
creator: Aldus Manutius (Aldine Press)
summary:
A page from an Aldine edition (Venice, October 1502) bearing the printer's anchor-and-dolphin device, the hieroglyph that became Europe's most famous publisher's mark.

## Iconography
Beneath a passage of text and the colophon *VENETIIS IN AEDIB. ALDI ROMANI* stands the device: a vertical **anchor** with a **dolphin** coiled about its shaft, flanked by the name **AL·DVS**. The slow, fixed anchor and the swift dolphin together image the proverb of measured speed.

## Significance
Aldus adopted the anchor-and-dolphin from the [[motif:festina-lente|*festina lente*]] frieze of the *Hypnerotomachia* (and ultimately from a Roman coin of Titus). Erasmus, in his *Adagia*, made the mark the emblem of the scholar-printer's union of haste and care, and treated it as a living [[motif:egyptian-hieroglyph|hieroglyph]] of wisdom. The device fixed the Renaissance idea that a single emblematic image could carry a whole maxim.

## For artists & game designers
The canonical 'maker's sigil': a two-element emblem (fast + fixed) that encodes a guild's whole philosophy in one mark.

citations.text: Erasmus, *Adagia* II.i.1 ('Festina lente').

title: The Hermathena (Bocchi, Symbolicae Quaestiones)
creator: Achille Bocchi; engraving by Giulio Bonasone
summary:
The *Hermathena*, Achille Bocchi's emblem of the union of Mercury and Minerva, the device of his Bolognese academy.

## Iconography
The armoured **Minerva** (Athena), helmeted and bearing a Gorgon-faced shield, stands beside **Mercury** (Hermes) holding the winged **caduceus**; between them a small winged genius, and beneath, a **Gorgon mask** on a herm, with the motto **SIC MONSTRA DOMANTVR** — 'thus are monsters tamed'.

## Significance
The **Hermathena** fuses the god of eloquence and the goddess of wisdom into a single [[motif:composite-deity|composite deity]] symbolizing the perfect union of learning and rhetoric — the ideal of Bocchi's academy. Such polymorphic gods were prized by Renaissance Hermetists as living [[motif:egyptian-hieroglyph|hieroglyphs]] of philosophical concepts. The taming of the Gorgon-monster figures how reason masters the irrational. The image is a touchstone of Edgar Wind's *Pagan Mysteries in the Renaissance*.

## For artists & game designers
A blueprint for a fused patron-deity: two gods merged into one figure whose combined attributes state a faction's whole creed.

citations.text: A. Bocchi, *Symbolicarum Quaestionum... Libri Quinque* (Bologna, 1555).
E. Wind, *Pagan Mysteries in the Renaissance* (1958).

title: Atlas bearing the globe (Bocchi, Symbolicae Quaestiones, Symb. CXXXVIII)
creator: Achille Bocchi; engravings by Giulio Bonasone
rights: Public domain (CC0). The Met, via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
An engraved emblem from Achille Bocchi's *Symbolicarum Quaestionum... Libri Quinque* (Bologna): the kneeling Atlas upholding the globe, Symbol CXXXVIII.

## Iconography
A bearded **Atlas** kneels beneath the weight of a great **celestial globe**, banderoles streaming with the mottoes *AD SVMMA*, *TENDENTI TENENDA* and *OMNIA*. The heading reads **SVMMA OMNIA TENET, SCIRE QVI SCIT SE NIHIL** — 'he holds the highest who knows that he knows nothing'.

## Significance
Bocchi's *Symbolicae Quaestiones* (1555), engraved by Giulio Bonasone, is one of the most learned of all emblem books, its 'symbols' conceived as Hermetic [[motif:egyptian-hieroglyph|hieroglyphs]] of philosophical truth. Here the labouring [[motif:allegory-of-the-gods|Atlas]] becomes an emblem of Socratic *docta ignorantia* — the sage who attains the heights only by confessing his own nescience. The work was central to the Bologna academy and is discussed by Elizabeth See Watson.

## For artists & game designers
The burdened-titan icon repurposed as a maxim about humility — image and motto fused into a single 'wisdom card'.

title: Atlas emblem with epigram (Bocchi, Symbolicae Quaestiones, opening)
creator: Achille Bocchi; engravings by Giulio Bonasone
rights: Public domain (CC0). The Met, via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A full opening of Bocchi's *Symbolicae Quaestiones* showing the Atlas emblem (Symb. CXXXVIII) facing its dedicatory Latin epigram.

## Iconography
On the verso, the engraved **Atlas** kneels under the **globe** with its banderole mottoes; on the recto, a verse epigram dedicated to bishop Joannes Hangestus elaborates the lesson that one must, like Atlas, bear the highest while learning to *know nothing*.

## Significance
The opening displays the emblem book's defining structure — *pictura* and *epigramma* read together so that neither is complete alone. Bocchi treats each [[motif:emblem|symbol]] as a [[motif:egyptian-hieroglyph|hieroglyphic]] knot of meaning to be untied by the accompanying poem, embodying the Renaissance theory that images and words together restore a lost sacred wisdom. The Met's clean impressions preserve Bonasone's fine engraving.

## For artists & game designers
The canonical image-plus-poem spread: study how the facing text changes how the picture is read.

title: Caduceus-bearer and a goddess (Cartari, 1608, p. 79)
creator: Vincenzo Cartari (illustrations after the 1571 edition)
summary:
A woodcut from Cartari's *Le imagini de i dei de gli antichi* (1608, p. 79): two divine figures, one bearing a serpent-twined staff, the other holding offerings.

## Iconography
At left a youthful god holds a **caduceus**-like serpent staff and a pine-cone; at right a draped **goddess** carries fruits or a horn of plenty, with a serpent winding at the centre between them. The pairing belongs to Cartari's parade of the attributes that identify each deity.

## Significance
Cartari's purpose was practical: to give artists and poets a correct visual vocabulary of the [[motif:allegory-of-the-gods|gods]] and their attributes — the **caduceus** for Mercury, the cornucopia for abundance — so that pictures could be 'read'. In this sense each plate functions as a [[motif:egyptian-hieroglyph|hieroglyph]] of the divinity. The book's diffusion across Europe made it the standard image-bank of [[motif:mythography|classical mythography]].

## For artists & game designers
An attribute key in one frame: identify deities by their props (snake-staff, cornucopia) — exactly how an icon-driven pantheon communicates role at a glance.

citations.text: V. Cartari, *Le imagini de i dei de gli antichi* (1608 ed.).
J. Seznec, *The Survival of the Pagan Gods* (1953).
