title: Thought-Form: The Music of Gounod (Besant & Leadbeater)
creator: Annie Besant & C. W. Leadbeater
summary:
A plate from **Besant & Leadbeater's** *Thought-Forms* (1901) — the Theosophical attempt to picture the invisible. This figure renders the 'form' allegedly built in the subtle aether by the music of Gounod, rising over a church like an architecture of coloured cloud.

## Iconography
Clairvoyantly-perceived shapes and colours, each keyed to an emotion by the book's colour-code (affection rose, intellect yellow, devotion blue). Music produces towering, building-like forms.

## Significance
*Thought-Forms* is a landmark in the prehistory of **abstract art** — Kandinsky knew it — and crystallises [[tradition:theosophy]]'s claim that consciousness has a directly visible form.

## For artists & game designers
Proto-abstract 'energy' and 'aura' visualisations — reference for spell-effects, sound made visible, or a synaesthetic UI.

citations.text: A. Besant & C. W. Leadbeater, *Thought-Forms* (London, 1901).
S. Ringbom, *The Sounding Cosmos* (Åbo, 1970).

title: Alchimia (Alchemy)
work: Cesare Ripa's Iconologia — Dictionary of Personifications
creator: after Cesare Ripa (Hertel edition engraver)
summary:
The personification of **Alchemy** as engraved for an eighteenth-century edition of Cesare Ripa's *Iconologia*, the only one of Ripa's allegories devoted directly to the chrysopoetic art.

## Iconography
Alchimia appears as an allegorical female figure surrounded by the apparatus of the laboratory — a furnace, distillation vessels, and the instruments of the *opus* — with attributes pointing to the transmutation of metals and the pursuit of the philosophers' stone.

## Significance
Ripa's inclusion of [[motif:transmutation|Alchemy]] among the personified arts records the discipline's recognized, if contested, place in the early-modern map of knowledge. Because the *Iconologia* was the standard reference for designers of allegorical title pages, Ripa's Alchimia helped fix how the art would be embodied on the frontispieces of Hermetic and chymical books.

## For artists & game designers
A ready-made 'alchemist personified' template: a single figure whose furnace, flask, and posture instantly read as the laboratory art.

citations.text: C. Ripa, *Iconologia* (later illustrated edition, 1764).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Harmonia (Harmony / Music)
work: Cesare Ripa's Iconologia — Dictionary of Personifications
creator: after Cesare Ripa (1644 English 'Tempest' edition)
summary:
The personification of **Harmony** from Ripa's 1644 *Iconologia*, embodying both audible music and the cosmic concord of proportions.

## Iconography
Harmonia holds a stringed instrument and other attributes of music and ordered proportion, presenting the abstract idea of agreement and consonance in bodily form.

## Significance
Harmony in Ripa carries the Pythagorean-Platonic charge of [[motif:music-of-the-spheres|cosmic concord]] — the same numerical ratios that order sound were held to order the heavens and the soul. The figure thus links the *Iconologia*'s allegory of music to the wider Renaissance idea of universal harmony cultivated by Ficino and the Hermetic tradition.

## For artists & game designers
Use a single instrument plus geometric proportion to signal 'harmony' as cosmic order, not merely entertainment.

citations.text: C. Ripa, *Iconologia* (English edition, 1644).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Astrologia (Astrology)
work: Cesare Ripa's Iconologia — Dictionary of Personifications
creator: Cesare Ripa
summary:
The personification of **Astrology** from a *Della novissima Iconologia* edition of Cesare Ripa, embodying the science of reading the heavens.

## Iconography
Astrologia is figured as a woman crowned or winged and bearing the diagnostic attributes of her art — a starry mantle, a celestial sphere or astrolabe, and the signs of the zodiac — by which Ripa's reader was to recognize the practice of judging the influence of the stars.

## Significance
Ripa places [[motif:study-of-the-heavens|Astrologia]] within the same allegorical grammar as Astronomy and the liberal arts, reflecting the period's incomplete separation of the two. As the standard attribute-handbook, the *Iconologia* shaped the visual conventions for astral imagery on ceilings, frontispieces, and instruments across Baroque Europe.

## For artists & game designers
The canonical 'star-reader' avatar: globe, zodiac mantle, and upward gaze make a figure legible as an astrologer at a glance.

citations.text: C. Ripa, *Della novissima Iconologia* (Padua, early 17th c.).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Astronomia (Astronomy)
work: Cesare Ripa's Iconologia — Dictionary of Personifications
creator: after Cesare Ripa (1644 English 'Tempest' edition)
summary:
The personification of **Astronomy** from the 1644 English-text edition of Ripa's *Iconologia*, a single-figure line plate.

## Iconography
Astronomia stands crowned with stars and equipped with the instruments of measurement — a celestial globe, compasses, a quadrant — and often wings, marking her as the soaring, mathematical study of the heavens as distinguished from judicial astrology.

## Significance
Ripa's pairing of Astronomia and [[motif:study-of-the-heavens|Astrologia]] documents the gradual early-modern disentangling of the two heavenly sciences. The figure's star-crown and globe became a stock formula for 'Astronomy' in academic frontispieces and in series of the liberal arts.

## For artists & game designers
Distinguish the scientist from the diviner: give Astronomy precise instruments (compass, globe) where Astrology gets the zodiac mantle.

citations.text: C. Ripa, *Iconologia* (English edition, 1644).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Bellezza (Beauty)
work: Cesare Ripa's Iconologia — Dictionary of Personifications
creator: after Cesare Ripa (1644 English 'Tempest' edition)
summary:
The personification of **Beauty** (*Bellezza*) from Ripa's 1644 *Iconologia*, beauty as a reflection of the divine.

## Iconography
Ripa hides Bellezza's head in clouds (her highest part exceeds understanding) and gives her a compass and sphere, signifying that beauty consists in measure, proportion, and a light that descends from above.

## Significance
Ripa's *Bellezza* is overtly Neoplatonic: beauty is the visible radiance of the divine, apprehended through [[motif:divine-proportion|proportion]] yet ultimately surpassing the senses (hence the clouded head). This Ficinian doctrine of beauty as a ladder to God informed Renaissance love-philosophy and the aesthetics of the Hermetic image.

## For artists & game designers
A head veiled in cloud over a figure holding a compass conveys 'beauty as ungraspable divine order' rather than mere prettiness.

citations.text: C. Ripa, *Iconologia* (English edition, 1644).
M. Ficino, *Commentary on Plato's Symposium*.
Wikimedia Commons

title: Cielo (Heaven / Sky)
work: Cesare Ripa's Iconologia — Dictionary of Personifications
creator: after Cesare Ripa (1644 English 'Tempest' edition)
summary:
The personification of **Heaven** or the sky (*Cielo*) from Ripa's 1644 *Iconologia*, the starry firmament made into a figure.

## Iconography
Cielo wears a mantle of stars and bears the celestial sphere or the band of the zodiac, embodying the visible heavens that turn above the sublunary world.

## Significance
Ripa's *Cielo* gives form to the [[motif:firmament|firmament]] whose ordered revolutions governed astrological influence in the period's cosmology. The star-mantle is the same device used for Astrology, Astronomy, and Night, underscoring how Ripa built complex personifications from a shared stock of celestial attributes.

## For artists & game designers
A star-strewn cloak over a single figure is the most economical way to make a body 'be' the night sky.

citations.text: C. Ripa, *Iconologia* (English edition, 1644).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Colerico (The Choleric Temperament)
work: Cesare Ripa's Iconologia — Dictionary of Personifications
creator: after Cesare Ripa (1644 English 'Tempest' edition)
summary:
The **Choleric** temperament (*Colerico*) from Ripa's 1644 *Iconologia*, one of the four humoral complexions.

## Iconography
Colerico is a fiery, martial figure — hot and dry, governed by yellow bile, the element of fire and the planet Mars — often accompanied by a lion and signs of anger and bold action.

## Significance
Ripa's four temperaments visualize the [[motif:four-temperaments|humoral psychology]] inherited from Galen and woven into astrological medicine: each complexion is keyed to an element, a planet, a season, and an age of life. This humour–planet–element web is the connective tissue of Renaissance occult medicine and the doctrine of correspondences.

## For artists & game designers
Fire, lion, and a sword-ready posture make the choleric an instantly readable 'hot-tempered warrior' type within a four-humour set.

citations.text: C. Ripa, *Iconologia* (English edition, 1644).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Consiglio (Counsel)
work: Cesare Ripa's Iconologia — Dictionary of Personifications
creator: after Cesare Ripa (1644 English 'Tempest' edition)
summary:
The personification of **Counsel** (*Consiglio*) from Ripa's 1644 *Iconologia*, the gift of wise deliberation.

## Iconography
Consiglio bears attributes of considered judgment — a book, an owl (Minervan wisdom), and emblems of the heart and deliberation — marking the faculty of giving and taking sound advice.

## Significance
Ripa's *Consiglio* belongs to the family of intellectual and prudential virtues that organize counsel and judgment; the owl attribute ties it to [[motif:wise-deliberation|Minerva]] and the long iconographic tradition of wisdom-as-counsel that informed advice literature and court emblematics.

## For artists & game designers
The owl plus a book is a compact, instantly legible 'wise counselor' attribute set.

citations.text: C. Ripa, *Iconologia* (English edition, 1644).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Conversatione (Conversation / Social Intercourse)
work: Cesare Ripa's Iconologia — Dictionary of Personifications
creator: after Cesare Ripa (1644 English 'Tempest' edition)
summary:
The personification of **Conversation** (*Conversatione*) from Ripa's 1644 *Iconologia*, the bond of human fellowship and exchange.

## Iconography
Conversatione bears emblems of mutual fellowship — joined or clasped hands, myrtle, and signs of pleasant company — embodying the social intercourse and shared discourse that knit human society.

## Significance
Ripa's *Conversatione* personifies the early-modern ideal of civil [[motif:human-fellowship|fellowship]] and exchange. In the esoteric world this mattered concretely: knowledge passed through learned conversation, correspondence, and the sodalities (academies, Rosicrucian fraternities) whose very ideal was a brotherhood bound by shared discourse.

## For artists & game designers
Clasped hands and myrtle make a gentle, period-accurate icon for 'alliance', 'dialogue', or a social mechanic.

citations.text: C. Ripa, *Iconologia* (English edition, 1644).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Cosmographia (Cosmography)
work: Cesare Ripa's Iconologia — Dictionary of Personifications
creator: after Cesare Ripa (1644 English 'Tempest' edition)
summary:
The personification of **Cosmography** (*Cosmographia*) from Ripa's 1644 *Iconologia*, the art of describing and measuring the whole world.

## Iconography
Cosmographia holds the instruments of mapping the universe — an armillary sphere, a globe, and compasses — uniting the celestial and terrestrial in a single science of the cosmos.

## Significance
Ripa's *Cosmographia* embodies the Renaissance discipline (codified by Ptolemy and revived by Apian and others) that bound astronomy, geography, and [[motif:measure-of-the-cosmos|cosmic measurement]] together. It belongs to the same family of celestial sciences as Astronomy and Astrology, mapping the macrocosm that Hermetic thought saw mirrored in the human microcosm.

## For artists & game designers
The armillary sphere is a high-status 'cosmic cartographer' prop, distinct from the plain globe of geography.

citations.text: C. Ripa, *Iconologia* (English edition, 1644).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Curiosità (Curiosity)
work: Cesare Ripa's Iconologia — Dictionary of Personifications
creator: after Cesare Ripa (1644 English 'Tempest' edition)
summary:
The personification of **Curiosity** (*Curiosità*) from Ripa's 1644 *Iconologia*, the restless desire to know.

## Iconography
Curiosità is winged and given attributes of restless attentiveness — Ripa describes her hair standing on end and her garment strewn with ears and frogs, signs of an over-eager appetite to hear and see everything.

## Significance
Ripa treats [[motif:desire-to-know|Curiosity]] ambivalently: the same drive that fuels learning shades into the forbidden 'curious arts' (*curiositas*) condemned by Augustine — a tension at the heart of how the period viewed magic, divination, and prying into nature's secrets.

## For artists & game designers
Ears-and-eyes ornamentation plus wings reads as an insatiable, slightly dangerous inquisitiveness.

citations.text: C. Ripa, *Iconologia* (English edition, 1644).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Divinità (Divinity)
work: Cesare Ripa's Iconologia — Dictionary of Personifications
creator: after Cesare Ripa (1644 English 'Tempest' edition)
summary:
The personification of **Divinity** (*Divinità*) from Ripa's 1644 *Iconologia*, the abstract figure of the divine nature.

## Iconography
Divinità is shown enveloped in radiance and rays of light, with attributes of transcendence — sometimes a triangle or the all-encompassing sphere — signifying the godhead that exceeds all bodily representation.

## Significance
Ripa's *Divinità* gives cautious bodily form to the formless [[motif:divine-light|divine]], leaning on the Neoplatonic and Dionysian theology of God as supereminent light. Such luminous abstractions of divinity stand behind the radiant Tetragrammaton-triangles and glory-bursts of Rosicrucian and Hermetic frontispieces.

## For artists & game designers
Pure radiance and geometric perfection (triangle, sphere) signal 'the divine' without a literal deity figure.

citations.text: C. Ripa, *Iconologia* (English edition, 1644).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Eternità (Eternity)
work: Cesare Ripa's Iconologia — Dictionary of Personifications
creator: after Cesare Ripa (1644 English 'Tempest' edition)
summary:
The personification of **Eternity** (*Eternità*) from Ripa's 1644 *Iconologia*, the figure of endless, undivided duration.

## Iconography
Eternità is given attributes of the unending — a serpent biting its own tail (the ouroboros), a globe or sphere (the perfect figure without beginning or end), and sometimes the phoenix of perpetual renewal.

## Significance
Ripa's use of the [[motif:ouroboros|ouroboros]] for Eternity ties his allegory directly to one of the most charged esoteric symbols: the tail-eating serpent stood for the cyclical, self-renewing unity of the cosmos in Gnostic, Hermetic, and alchemical sources (where it bears the legend *hen to pan*, 'the all is one'). Ripa thus channels a core occult emblem into the standard handbook of allegory.

## For artists & game designers
The ouroboros is the universal 'eternity / infinite loop' glyph — pair with a sphere for timeless perfection.

citations.text: C. Ripa, *Iconologia* (English edition, 1644).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Philosophia (Philosophy)
work: Cesare Ripa's Iconologia — Dictionary of Personifications
creator: after Cesare Ripa (1644 English 'Tempest' edition)
summary:
The personification of **Philosophy** from Ripa's 1644 *Iconologia*, the figure who unites earthly study and heavenly contemplation.

## Iconography
Philosophia is a seated or standing matron crowned and bearing books and a scepter; in Ripa's text her robe is marked with degrees ascending from the practical to the contemplative, recalling the ladder-of-knowledge motif of Boethius's *Consolation*.

## Significance
Ripa's Philosophy embodies the early-modern ideal of [[motif:contemplative-wisdom|wisdom]] that climbs from the natural to the divine — the same vertical scheme that structured Hermetic and Neoplatonic accounts of ascent. As a frontispiece figure she presided over countless learned title pages.

## For artists & game designers
The ascending-degrees robe is a compact visual for 'levels of knowledge' — useful for a sage or skill-tree avatar.

citations.text: C. Ripa, *Iconologia* (English edition, 1644).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Flegmatico (The Phlegmatic Temperament)
work: Cesare Ripa's Iconologia — Dictionary of Personifications
creator: after Cesare Ripa (1644 English 'Tempest' edition)
summary:
The **Phlegmatic** temperament (*Flegmatico*) from Ripa's 1644 *Iconologia*, the cold, watery complexion.

## Iconography
Flegmatico is a slow, heavy figure — cold and moist, governed by phlegm, the element of water and the Moon — marked by sluggishness, sleep, and a placid, dull demeanour.

## Significance
The phlegmatic completes Ripa's [[motif:four-temperaments|humoral quartet]] alongside the choleric, sanguine, and melancholic. The water-and-Moon keying exemplifies the lunar, watery pole of the doctrine of correspondences that linked the human body to the cosmos in astrological medicine.

## For artists & game designers
Water, lunar imagery, and a drowsy posture make a legible 'placid / slow' type for a four-humour character set.

citations.text: C. Ripa, *Iconologia* (English edition, 1644).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Furore Poetico (Poetic Frenzy)
work: Cesare Ripa's Iconologia — Dictionary of Personifications
creator: after Cesare Ripa (1644 English 'Tempest' edition)
summary:
The personification of **Poetic Frenzy** (*Furore Poetico*) from Ripa's 1644 *Iconologia*, the divine madness of inspiration.

## Iconography
Furore Poetico is crowned with laurel, eyes raised in rapture, holding or playing a lyre — the visible signs of one seized by inspiration rather than composing by craft alone.

## Significance
Ripa here personifies the [[motif:furor-poeticus|*furor poeticus*]] of Plato's *Ion* and *Phaedrus*, revived by Ficino as one of the four divine frenzies through which the soul ascends to God. This Neoplatonic doctrine of inspired madness was central to Renaissance Hermetic poetics and to the magus's claim of access to higher knowledge.

## For artists & game designers
Upturned eyes + laurel + lyre is the canonical 'divinely inspired bard' pose — a clear visual for an inspiration or trance state.

citations.text: C. Ripa, *Iconologia* (English edition, 1644).
M. Ficino, commentary on Plato's *Ion* / *De divino furore*.
Wikimedia Commons

title: Historia (History)
work: Cesare Ripa's Iconologia — Dictionary of Personifications
creator: after Cesare Ripa (1644 English 'Tempest' edition)
motifs: writing on the back of time
summary:
The personification of **History** (*Historia*) from Ripa's 1644 *Iconologia*, the keeper of the memory of the past.

## Iconography
Historia is winged and writes in a book supported on the back of the winged figure of Time (Saturn/Kronos), gazing backward — she records events as they recede, looking to the past while borne forward by time.

## Significance
Ripa's celebrated [[motif:memory-of-the-past|History-writing-on-the-back-of-Time]] became the standard emblem of historiography. For esoteric reception it also models the recovery of *prisca theologia* — the recovery of an ancient lost wisdom — which depended on reading history backward to an originary truth.

## For artists & game designers
A scribe writing while looking backward, carried forward by a winged elder, is a vivid 'chronicler / lore-keeper' tableau.

citations.text: C. Ripa, *Iconologia* (English edition, 1644).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Idaea (Idea)
work: Cesare Ripa's Iconologia — Dictionary of Personifications
creator: after Cesare Ripa (1644 English 'Tempest' edition)
summary:
The personification of **Idea** (*Idaea*) from Ripa's 1644 *Iconologia*, the Platonic form or archetypal pattern in the divine mind.

## Iconography
Idaea is figured as a celestial woman, often unclothed or radiant with a flame above her head, signifying the pure intelligible form prior to and exemplar of all material things.

## Significance
Ripa's *Idaea* is a rare directly Platonic personification: the [[motif:divine-pattern|Idea]] is the eternal model after which the artist or the Demiurge shapes matter. The concept was central to Renaissance art theory (Panofsky's *Idea*) and to Hermetic-Neoplatonic cosmology, where the world is made on archetypal patterns held in the divine *nous*.

## For artists & game designers
A radiant, weightless figure with a flame of mind is a strong visual for an 'archetype' or 'platonic blueprint' concept.

citations.text: C. Ripa, *Iconologia* (English edition, 1644).
E. Panofsky, *Idea: A Concept in Art Theory* (1924).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Imaginatione (Imagination)
work: Cesare Ripa's Iconologia — Dictionary of Personifications
creator: after Cesare Ripa (1644 English 'Tempest' edition)
summary:
The personification of **Imagination** (*Imaginatione*) from Ripa's 1644 *Iconologia*, the inner faculty that forms images.

## Iconography
Imaginatione is shown with attributes of mental image-making — a head wreathed in clouds, winged imagery, or fantastic figures issuing from the brow — marking the faculty that the Aristotelian and medical traditions called *phantasia*.

## Significance
Ripa's personification of the [[motif:phantasia|imaginative faculty]] is significant for esoteric thought because *imaginatio* was held to be the medium of magical, astrological, and visionary operation — the power by which the Renaissance magus impressed forms, drew down celestial influence, or received divine images (Ficino, Bruno, later Paracelsus).

## For artists & game designers
Clouds and half-formed figures around the head visualise an active imagination or dreaming mind.

citations.text: C. Ripa, *Iconologia* (English edition, 1644).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Imitatione (Imitation)
work: Cesare Ripa's Iconologia — Dictionary of Personifications
creator: after Cesare Ripa (1644 English 'Tempest' edition)
summary:
The personification of **Imitation** (*Imitatione*) from Ripa's 1644 *Iconologia*, the principle of art copying nature and the masters.

## Iconography
Imitatione holds the painter's brushes and a mask and is accompanied by an ape — the traditional 'ars simia naturae' (art the ape of nature) — signifying the faculty of reproducing models.

## Significance
Ripa's *Imitatione* crystallizes the Renaissance doctrine of [[motif:mimesis|mimesis]]: art as the imitation of nature and of authoritative exemplars. The ape-of-nature motif also carried an esoteric resonance, since alchemy was often described as *imitating* nature's slow generation of metals by art.

## For artists & game designers
The ape-with-brushes is a witty, period-accurate emblem for any 'copy / mimic / forgery' mechanic.

citations.text: C. Ripa, *Iconologia* (English edition, 1644).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Inganno (Deceit)
work: Cesare Ripa's Iconologia — Dictionary of Personifications
creator: after Cesare Ripa (1644 English 'Tempest' edition)
summary:
The personification of **Deceit** (*Inganno*) from Ripa's 1644 *Iconologia*, the vice of fraud and false appearance.

## Iconography
Inganno wears or holds a mask of fair appearance while concealing serpentine, monstrous, or hooked parts beneath — a beautiful face over a venomous tail, the classic emblem of a fraud that lures before it strikes.

## Significance
Ripa's *Inganno* gives form to [[motif:fraud-and-disguise|deceit]], the master-vice of dissimulation that early-modern moralists feared in courts, in false prophets, and in the 'cozening' arts. Its imagery of beautiful mask over hidden serpent supplied the standard visual language for denouncing fraudulent magicians, charlatans, and demonic illusion.

## For artists & game designers
Fair mask + concealed serpent tail is the canonical 'trickster / con-artist' silhouette.

citations.text: C. Ripa, *Iconologia* (English edition, 1644).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Intelletto (Intellect)
work: Cesare Ripa's Iconologia — Dictionary of Personifications
creator: after Cesare Ripa (1644 English 'Tempest' edition)
summary:
The personification of **Intellect** from Ripa's 1644 *Iconologia*, the highest faculty of the rational soul.

## Iconography
Intelletto bears attributes of the illuminated mind — a flame or crown of light and sometimes an eagle (which alone gazes at the sun) — signifying the intellect's power to apprehend pure truth.

## Significance
Ripa's [[motif:light-of-the-mind|Intelletto]] gives bodily form to the Neoplatonic *nous*, the divine spark of understanding central to Hermetic anthropology, where the *mens* or intellect is the part of the human that can know God. The eagle-gazing-at-the-sun motif recurs throughout alchemical emblem books.

## For artists & game designers
The sun-gazing eagle is a high-signal companion attribute for an intellect, sage, or 'seer' figure.

citations.text: C. Ripa, *Iconologia* (English edition, 1644).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Investigatione (Investigation / Inquiry)
work: Cesare Ripa's Iconologia — Dictionary of Personifications
creator: after Cesare Ripa (1644 English 'Tempest' edition)
summary:
The personification of **Investigation** (*Investigatione*) from Ripa's 1644 *Iconologia*, the diligent search after hidden truth.

## Iconography
Investigatione bears attributes of tracking and uncovering — often a hound (the keen scent of inquiry) and a lantern or intent searching posture, signifying the patient pursuit of what is concealed.

## Significance
The figure embodies the [[motif:search-for-truth|investigative]] ideal that underlies both the new natural philosophy and the esoteric quest for hidden (occult) causes. The hunting-dog attribute links inquiry to scent and trace, a fitting emblem for disciplines that read nature's signatures.

## For artists & game designers
A tracking hound plus a lantern makes a clean 'investigation/quest' avatar for a detective or seeker class.

citations.text: C. Ripa, *Iconologia* (English edition, 1644).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Malenconico (The Melancholic Temperament)
work: Cesare Ripa's Iconologia — Dictionary of Personifications
creator: after Cesare Ripa (1644 English 'Tempest' edition)
summary:
The **Melancholic** temperament (*Malenconico*) from Ripa's 1644 *Iconologia*, the cold, dry, Saturnine complexion.

## Iconography
Malenconico is a brooding, earthbound figure — cold and dry, governed by black bile, the element of earth and the planet Saturn — shown pensive, bound, or downcast, with attributes of study and solitude.

## Significance
Ripa's melancholic carries unusual esoteric weight: the Ficinian doctrine, revived from pseudo-Aristotle, held that [[motif:saturnine-melancholy|Saturnine melancholy]] was the temperament of genius, the dark humour that inclined the soul to contemplation, prophecy, and inspired creation. This is the complexion behind Dürer's *Melencolia I* and the magus's brooding self-image.

## For artists & game designers
Earth tones, Saturn, and a hand-to-cheek brooding pose make the canonical 'tortured genius / scholar' within a humour set.

title: Mathematica (Mathematics)
work: Cesare Ripa's Iconologia — Dictionary of Personifications
creator: after Cesare Ripa (1644 English 'Tempest' edition)
summary:
The personification of **Mathematics** from Ripa's 1644 *Iconologia*, the science of number, measure, and proportion.

## Iconography
Mathematica bears compasses and the instruments of measurement, sometimes winged to signify the elevation of abstract reasoning above the senses.

## Significance
Ripa's [[motif:number-and-measure|Mathematica]] stands at the root of the quadrivium and, in Renaissance Hermetic-Pythagorean thought, of the conviction that number is the key to the cosmos. The compass became the master-attribute uniting mathematics, architecture, and the divine 'geometer' imagery later beloved of Freemasonry and Blake.

## For artists & game designers
The compass is the single most legible 'measurer' prop — pair with wings to push toward abstract or divine geometry.

citations.text: C. Ripa, *Iconologia* (English edition, 1644).

title: Mondo (The World), 1613 edition
work: Cesare Ripa's Iconologia — Dictionary of Personifications
creator: Cesare Ripa
summary:
The personification of **the World** (*Mondo*) from the 1613 illustrated *Iconologia* of Cesare Ripa, a high-resolution plate.

## Iconography
Mondo is embodied as a figure bearing or surmounted by the terrestrial and celestial globe, with attributes of the four elements and the encompassing whole of created things.

## Significance
Ripa's *Mondo* personifies the [[motif:macrocosm|macrocosm]], the great universal body whose correspondences with the human microcosm underpin Hermetic and astrological thought. The figure makes visible the totalizing 'World' that the magus, alchemist, and cosmographer each sought to comprehend.

## For artists & game designers
A figure crowned or bearing the globe is the clearest emblem of 'the whole world / the cosmos' as a single character.

citations.text: C. Ripa, *Iconologia* (Padua, 1613).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Mondo (The World), 1644 edition
work: Cesare Ripa's Iconologia — Dictionary of Personifications
creator: after Cesare Ripa (1644 English 'Tempest' edition)
summary:
The personification of **the World** (*Mondo*) from the 1644 English-text edition of Ripa's *Iconologia*, the single-figure line version.

## Iconography
Mondo bears the globe and the signs of the universal whole, rendered in the spare engraved style of the Tempest edition for ready reference.

## Significance
The persistence of the [[motif:macrocosm|World]] personification from the 1613 woodcut to this 1644 engraving illustrates the stability of Ripa's iconographic formulas across editions and languages, and the centrality of the macrocosm–microcosm scheme to the era's cosmological imagination.

## For artists & game designers
A clean line reference for 'the World' as a personified globe-bearer, easy to adapt as a tarot-style World card.

citations.text: C. Ripa, *Iconologia* (English edition, 1644).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Natura (Nature)
work: Cesare Ripa's Iconologia — Dictionary of Personifications
creator: after Cesare Ripa
summary:
The personification of **Nature** (*Natura*) after Cesare Ripa's *Iconologia*, the nourishing mother of all things.

## Iconography
Natura is figured as a woman with many breasts streaming milk (after the Ephesian Artemis / Diana), her body the source of universal nourishment, sometimes accompanied by a vulture and signs of fecundity.

## Significance
Ripa's many-breasted [[motif:natura-naturans|Natura]] is one of the most enduring esoteric images of nature as a living, generative whole — *natura naturans*. The figure stands behind countless alchemical and Hermetic frontispieces (and Goethe's veiled 'Nature'), where the adept seeks to read or assist the secret operations of this nourishing power.

## For artists & game designers
The multi-breasted nourishing figure is the single most recognizable 'Mother Nature' archetype in Western iconography.

citations.text: C. Ripa, *Iconologia*, s.v. 'Natura'.
Wikimedia Commons

title: Prudenza (Prudence)
work: Cesare Ripa's Iconologia — Dictionary of Personifications
creator: after Cesare Ripa (1644 English 'Tempest' edition)
summary:
The personification of **Prudence** from Ripa's 1644 *Iconologia*, the cardinal virtue of right judgment.

## Iconography
Prudenza bears her traditional attributes — a mirror (self-knowledge) and a serpent (Matthew's 'wise as serpents'), and often a double or two-faced head looking to past and future, signifying foresight grounded in memory.

## Significance
The mirror-and-serpent formula codified by Ripa became the standard sign of [[motif:foresight|Prudence]] in Baroque allegory. The two-faced head connects her to the Janus motif and to the broader emblematic theme of reading time wisely, a concern shared by alchemical and astrological 'timing' of operations.

## For artists & game designers
Mirror + serpent + backward-and-forward gaze is the instant-read kit for a foresight or strategy character.

citations.text: C. Ripa, *Iconologia* (English edition, 1644).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Religione (Religion)
work: Cesare Ripa's Iconologia — Dictionary of Personifications
creator: after Cesare Ripa (1644 English 'Tempest' edition)
summary:
The personification of **Religion** (*Religione*) from Ripa's 1644 *Iconologia*, the virtue of right worship.

## Iconography
Religione bears the cross, the book of Scripture, and a flame of devotion, often veiled to signify the awe and hiddenness proper to the worship of God.

## Significance
Ripa's *Religione* models the cardinal religious virtue (*religio*) as the ordered binding of the soul to the divine. The veil — marking sacred concealment — connects the figure to the broader early-modern theme of [[motif:sacred-mystery|veiled sacred mystery]] that esoteric traditions claimed to penetrate.

## For artists & game designers
Cross + flame + veil cleanly distinguishes pious 'Religion' from the more abstract, light-radiant 'Divinity'.

citations.text: C. Ripa, *Iconologia* (English edition, 1644).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Sanguigno (The Sanguine Temperament)
work: Cesare Ripa's Iconologia — Dictionary of Personifications
creator: after Cesare Ripa (1644 English 'Tempest' edition)
summary:
The **Sanguine** temperament (*Sanguigno*) from Ripa's 1644 *Iconologia*, the cheerful, airy complexion.

## Iconography
Sanguigno is a genial figure — hot and moist, governed by blood, the element of air and the planet Jupiter — associated with music, merriment, love, and a ruddy good health.

## Significance
Within Ripa's set of [[motif:four-temperaments|four temperaments]], the sanguine is the most fortunate, keyed to Jupiter and air. The scheme tied bodily humour to planetary rulership and season, the foundation of the astrological medicine and melothesia that governed Renaissance ideas of health, character, and the timing of cures.

## For artists & game designers
Air, a musical instrument, and rosy good cheer give a clear 'optimist / bard' read within a four-humour roster.

citations.text: C. Ripa, *Iconologia* (English edition, 1644).

title: Sapienza (Wisdom), 1611 edition
work: Cesare Ripa's Iconologia — Dictionary of Personifications
creator: Cesare Ripa
summary:
The personification of **Wisdom** (*Sapienza*) from the 1611 illustrated *Iconologia* of Cesare Ripa.

## Iconography
Sapienza appears as a dignified female figure bearing the attributes of wisdom — a book, a flame or light signifying illumination, and a composed bearing that marks her as the embodiment of right understanding.

## Significance
Ripa's *Sapienza* draws on the biblical and Neoplatonic figure of [[motif:divine-wisdom|Wisdom]] (Sophia/Sapientia), the feminine divine knowledge that orders creation. The personification fed directly into the esoteric reverence for Sophia in Christian Cabala, Boehmist theosophy, and later Rosicrucian imagery.

## For artists & game designers
Light + book = wisdom; keep the light a small steady flame rather than a halo to read as inner illumination.

citations.text: C. Ripa, *Iconologia* (Padua, 1611).

title: Sapienza (Wisdom), 1644 edition
work: Cesare Ripa's Iconologia — Dictionary of Personifications
creator: after Cesare Ripa (1644 English 'Tempest' edition)
summary:
The personification of **Wisdom** as rendered in the 1644 English-text edition of Ripa's *Iconologia*, a single-figure line plate.

## Iconography
Sapienza holds the attributes of true understanding — a book and a flame or lamp of intellect — in the spare engraved style of the Tempest edition, where each personification stands alone for ease of reference.

## Significance
The survival of [[motif:divine-wisdom|Wisdom]] across Ripa's editions, from Italian woodcut to English line engraving, shows how stable the attribute-set became: the flame of intellect and the book remained the fixed signs of *Sapientia* for generations of artists.

## For artists & game designers
A clean, copyable line version — good reference for a minimal 'wisdom' icon stripped to flame and book.

title: Scienza (Knowledge / Science)
work: Cesare Ripa's Iconologia — Dictionary of Personifications
creator: after Cesare Ripa (1644 English 'Tempest' edition)
summary:
The personification of **Knowledge** (*Scienza*) from Ripa's 1644 *Iconologia*, sure understanding of causes.

## Iconography
Scienza holds a book and a flame or light and is often winged, with a scepter — signs that true knowledge is certain, illuminating, and elevates the mind above mere opinion.

## Significance
Ripa distinguishes [[motif:ascent-of-the-mind|Scienza]] (demonstrative, certain knowledge) from Opinion and from the practical arts, mirroring the Aristotelian hierarchy of the disciplines that organized the early-modern map of learning within which alchemy, astrology, and natural magic sought their place.

## For artists & game designers
Wings + flame + book reads as 'enlightened knowledge'; remove the wings for an ordinary scholar.

citations.text: C. Ripa, *Iconologia* (English edition, 1644).

title: Theologia (Theology)
work: Cesare Ripa's Iconologia — Dictionary of Personifications
creator: after Cesare Ripa (1644 English 'Tempest' edition)
summary:
The personification of **Theology** from Ripa's 1644 *Iconologia*, the discipline Ripa ranks above the other sciences.

## Iconography
Theologia is shown with a flame above her head (the light of revelation) and frequently a double face — one turned to the contemplation of God, one to the teaching of the world — together with the book of Scripture.

## Significance
Ripa's two-faced, fire-crowned [[motif:divine-and-revealed-knowledge|Theologia]] embodies the medieval idea of theology as the queen of the sciences, knowledge that descends from God. The motif of revealed light over the head recurs in Hermetic and Rosicrucian frontispieces depicting divine illumination of the adept.

## For artists & game designers
Flame-above-the-head is a compact glyph for 'revealed' or god-granted knowledge, distinct from a lamp the figure merely holds.

citations.text: C. Ripa, *Iconologia* (English edition, 1644).

title: Verità (Truth)
work: Cesare Ripa's Iconologia — Dictionary of Personifications
creator: Cesare Ripa
summary:
The personification of **Truth** (*Verità*) from the 1603 *Iconologia* of Cesare Ripa, the 'naked truth' that conceals nothing.

## Iconography
Verità is figured nude (truth has nothing to hide), holding the sun (truth loves the light), an open book, and often the palm of victory or treading on the globe of worldly falsehood.

## Significance
Ripa's [[motif:naked-truth|naked Truth]] holding the sun is the canonical Western image of *Veritas*, drawing on the proverb *veritas filia temporis* ('Truth the daughter of Time'). The image was endlessly reused — from emblem books to political allegory — and supplied the visual logic for 'unveiling' as the disclosure of hidden truth, a metaphor central to alchemical and Hermetic revelation.

## For artists & game designers
Nudity + sun is the immediate sign of unconcealed truth; add a veil being lifted for the 'revelation' beat.

citations.text: C. Ripa, *Iconologia* (Rome, 1603), s.v. 'Verità'.

title: Alchemist holding a flask (Wellcome) — the presiding sage of the scroll
creator: George Ripley tradition (anonymous limner)
summary:
A Wellcome image of an alchemist holding a great flask — the presiding sage who stands at the head of the *Ripley Scroll* and displays the world-containing vessel.

## Iconography
A robed, bearded philosopher grasps an enormous round flask, within which the scenes of the Work are arrayed. He is the genius of the scroll, sometimes captioned as Hermes, sometimes as the alchemist-author, presenting the vessel to the viewer.

## Significance
The figure encapsulates the scroll's central claim: the entire *opus* — and indeed the cosmos — is enclosed within the philosophical glass that the master holds. As an image it became a generic emblem of the alchemist himself, widely reproduced apart from the full roll. The sage's calm display of the flask asserts mastery: the chaos of dragons, toads and lions below is governed from this single contemplative figure at the top.

## For artists & game designers
A portable, ready-cropped 'alchemist portrait' — a robed sage and his world-flask — ideal as an NPC avatar or shopkeeper icon lifted straight from the scroll.

title: Alchemists revealing secrets from the Book of Seven Seals (Ripley Scroll)
creator: George Ripley tradition (anonymous limner)
rights: Public domain. Via Wikimedia Commons / Wellcome.
summary:
A *Ripley Scroll* detail captioned as alchemists revealing the secrets of the "Book of Seven Seals" — an apocalyptic gloss on the scroll's topmost figures and verses.

## Iconography
Robed adepts gather about the scroll's great vessel and verse-panels, gesturing as though disclosing or unsealing hidden matter. The 'seven seals' caption draws on the imagery of Revelation, casting the alchemical secret as a sealed book now opened.

## Significance
The association with the Book of Seven Seals (Revelation 5) frames the Work as an apocalypse in the literal sense — an *unveiling*. Alchemical writers habitually borrowed scriptural and prophetic language to dignify and conceal their craft; the Ripley scroll's adepts 'opening the seals' present transmutation as a revealed mystery reserved for the elect. It typifies the easy traffic between alchemy and Christian eschatology in early-modern England.

## For artists & game designers
A scene of robed figures unsealing a hidden book of power — a strong 'lore reveal' or initiation tableau for an esoteric order.

title: Ripley Scroll (Wellcome) — detail: the dragon at the base
creator: George Ripley tradition (anonymous limner)
summary:
A detail from a Wellcome *Ripley Scroll* showing the great dragon that anchors the foot of the roll — the scroll's emblem of the prime matter and the mercurial serpent.

## Iconography
A winged dragon or coiled serpent occupies the base of the scroll, sometimes biting its tail or set beneath the figures and verses that rise above it. It frequently breathes fire or stands upon a black ground.

## Significance
The dragon is the scroll's *materia prima* — the raw, fiery, mercurial substance from which the Work begins, the "venomous dragon" the verses warn must be killed and tamed. As an [[motif:ouroboros|ouroboros]]-like serpent it also figures the cyclical unity of the *opus*, the matter that devours and renews itself. Placed at the foot of the roll, it is the ground out of which the whole ascent of emblems grows.

## For artists & game designers
A foundational dragon coiled at the base of a tower of symbols — a natural 'root boss' or origin-monster from which a progression visibly springs.

title: Ripley Scroll (Wellcome) — detail: the sphere of the elements
creator: George Ripley tradition (anonymous limner)
summary:
A detail from a Wellcome *Ripley Scroll* showing a banded sphere or philosophers' egg — the cosmos enclosed within the alchemical vessel.

## Iconography
A large orb divided into concentric bands or quarters, suggesting the elements and spheres, set among the scroll's vessels and verses. It reads at once as a globe of the world and as the sealed philosophical egg in which the matter is enclosed.

## Significance
The banded sphere expresses the doctrine of the [[motif:microcosm|microcosm]]: the sealed vessel contains, in little, the whole structure of the cosmos — the four elements and the heavens — so that perfecting the matter within is a re-making of creation. The *ovum philosophicum* (philosophers' egg) is the hermetically sealed flask in which the Work gestates; the scroll renders it as a small world about to hatch the stone.

## For artists & game designers
A banded cosmic egg/globe inside a vessel — a versatile icon for a 'world-seed', incubating artifact, or contained-universe item.

title: Ripley Scroll (Wellcome) — detail: the red and green lion
creator: George Ripley tradition (anonymous limner)
summary:
A detail from a Wellcome *Ripley Scroll* showing the lions of the Work — the green lion and the red lion that figure dissolution and the maturing tincture.

## Iconography
One or two heraldic lions, coloured green and red, set among the scroll's vessels and verses. The green lion is sometimes shown devouring the sun; the red lion stands for the perfected, reddened stage.

## Significance
The [[motif:green lion|green lion]] is among alchemy's most famous emblems: the crude, corrosive *menstruum* (often vitriol or an acid) that "devours the sun," dissolving gold into the philosophical water. Its reddening into the red lion marks the passage from dissolution toward the *rubedo*, the red stone. The colour-coded beasts let the unlettered reader track the Work's progress at a glance — a hallmark of the Ripley scroll's pedagogy.

## For artists & game designers
Two colour-keyed lions — green for corrosive dissolution, red for the finished tincture — a tidy pair of icons for opposed reagents or rival factions.

title: Ripley Scroll (Wellcome) — detail: the verse banderoles
creator: George Ripley tradition (anonymous limner)
summary:
A detail from a Wellcome *Ripley Scroll* focused on its inscribed verses — the bands of English alchemical poetry that run beside the emblems.

## Iconography
Scrolling banderoles and text-panels carry lines of verse in a period English hand, threaded between the painted images down the roll. The lettering is part of the design, curling around vessels and figures.

## Significance
The verses are the scroll's voice: rhymed, riddling instructions attributed to Canon George Ripley that name 'our water', the toad, the bird and the lions, and exhort the reader to patience and secrecy. They make the Ripley scroll a hybrid object — emblem and poem at once — and are the principal evidence by which scholars such as Jennifer Rampling have reconstructed the work's textual history. The deliberate obscurity of the language enacts the alchemists' duty to conceal the Work from the unworthy.

## For artists & game designers
Authentic riddling 'flavour text' wound around imagery — a model for in-world inscriptions that reward close reading without giving the secret away.

title: Ripley Scroll (Wellcome) — detail: the philosophers attending the vessel
creator: George Ripley tradition (anonymous limner)
summary:
A detail from a Wellcome *Ripley Scroll* showing small philosopher-figures grouped around (or standing on the rim of) the great philosophical vessel.

## Iconography
Diminutive robed figures attend the central flask — perched on its lip, gesturing toward its contents, or ranged about its base — within the scroll's column of emblems and verse. They personify the adepts and the principles enclosed in the vessel.

## Significance
The figures-on-the-vessel motif dramatises the idea that the Work is peopled: inside the glass the contending principles (often read as the male and female, Sol and Luna, sulphur and mercury) meet, struggle and conjoin. The watching philosophers also assert a chain of transmission — the wisdom passed from adept to adept, which the Ripley verses claim to preserve. It is a characteristically English elaboration of the Continental coniunctio imagery.

## For artists & game designers
Tiny attendant figures clustered on a giant flask — a charming scale-play motif for a 'homunculus' or 'soul in the bottle' moment.

title: Ripley Scroll (Wellcome) — detail: the sun, moon and stars
creator: George Ripley tradition (anonymous limner)
summary:
A detail from a Wellcome *Ripley Scroll* showing the celestial register — Sun, Moon and stars — that governs the alchemical emblems below.

## Iconography
Personified or rayed faces of the Sun and Moon, with scattered stars, crown a portion of the roll above the vessels and beasts. The luminaries pour their influence down toward the philosophical work arrayed beneath them.

## Significance
The scroll insists that the laboratory mirrors the heavens. [[motif:sol and luna|Sol and Luna]] over the apparatus name the two great principles — solar sulphur and lunar mercury, gold and silver, fixed and volatile — whose marriage is the goal of the Work. The starry band asserts the Hermetic correspondence *as above, so below*, by which the operator's vessel draws down and concentrates celestial virtue.

## For artists & game designers
A compact celestial header — sun, moon and stars feeding power downward — useful as a banner motif above an alchemy or astrology interface.

title: The Ripley Scroll — the full emblematic roll
creator: George Ripley tradition (anonymous limner)
rights: Public domain. Via Wikimedia Commons / Wellcome.
summary:
A view of a complete *Ripley Scroll* — the long vertical alchemical picture-poem of the George Ripley tradition, read from top to bottom as a single continuous emblem.

## Iconography
The roll stacks the genre's whole cast in sequence: at the top the presiding sage with his vast flask; descending from it the philosophical vessels and fountains, the [[motif:red and green lion|red and green lions]], the dragon, the toad swelling with poison, the black and white birds, and the Bird of Hermes, with banderoles of English verse threaded between every stage.

## Significance
The scroll's vertical format is itself meaningful: the Work is a graded ascent and descent, the matter circulating from grossest to most spiritual and back. Each emblem encodes a phase — putrefaction (the toad), the warring fixed and volatile principles (the lions and dragon), volatilisation and fixation (the birds). About two dozen Ripley scrolls survive; they are among the most ambitious visual statements of medieval and early-modern English alchemy.

## For artists & game designers
A ready-made vertical 'skill tree' of alchemy: a single scroll whose stacked emblems map cleanly onto progression stages from rot to gold.

title: The Ripley Scroll (Huntington Library copy)
creator: George Ripley tradition (anonymous limner)
rights: Public domain. Via Wikimedia Commons / Huntington Library.
summary:
The *Ripley Scroll* in the copy held by the Huntington Library — one of the roughly two dozen surviving witnesses to this spectacular English alchemical picture-poem.

## Iconography
The full vertical programme of the genre: the presiding sage and his great flask at the head; below, the fountain, the philosophical vessels, the red and green lions, the dragon, the toad and the Bird of Hermes, threaded throughout with English alchemical verse on banderoles.

## Significance
The survival of the scroll in multiple institutional copies (Wellcome, British Library, Huntington, Yale, Bodleian and others) lets scholars trace how the emblem-sequence was copied, varied and transmitted from the late fifteenth into the seventeenth century. Jennifer Rampling and others have used these copies to reconstruct the textual tradition behind the verses attributed to Canon George Ripley. The Huntington roll is a key American witness to that lineage.

## For artists & game designers
A second complete exemplar of the scroll — valuable when you want to compare variant renderings of the same emblem sequence for authenticity or for picking the cleanest details.

title: Ripley Scroll (WMS 693) — full roll with verses
creator: George Ripley tradition (anonymous limner)
summary:
A reproduction of the Wellcome *Ripley Scroll* (MS 693) as a whole — the long roll of emblems and English verse read continuously from the presiding sage at the top to the dragon at the foot.

## Iconography
The complete vertical sequence: the master and his great flask; the fountain and vessels; sun, moon and stars; the red and green lions; the toad; the black and white birds; the Bird of Hermes; and the dragon at the base — with verse banderoles running the length of the vellum.

## Significance
Seen whole, the scroll is a single synoptic emblem of the *opus alchymicum*: every creature and vessel is a stage, and the eye travels the Work from prime matter to perfected stone in one sweep. The verses, attributed to Canon George Ripley, supply the only sustained text — making the scroll a rare marriage of English vernacular alchemical poetry with monumental painted emblem. Wellcome MS 693 is among the best-preserved and most reproduced of the surviving rolls.

## For artists & game designers
The canonical 'whole scroll' reference: keep it on hand as the master layout when building any vertical, stage-by-stage alchemical interface.

title: Ripley Scroll (WMS 693) — detail: the toad and the putrefaction
creator: George Ripley tradition (anonymous limner)
summary:
A detail from the Wellcome *Ripley Scroll* (MS 693) showing the toad — the scroll's emblem of putrefaction and the black stage of the Work.

## Iconography
A bloated toad, sometimes shown swelling with poison or expiring on the ground, set within the scroll's vertical sequence near a band of verse. In the celebrated 'Tode' verse the creature drinks the juice of grapes until it bursts and rots.

## Significance
The toad is the *nigredo*: the matter killed, blackened and putrefied so that it may be reborn. "A toad full ruddy I saw, did drink the juice of grapes so fast..." — the verse describes the poisoning, death and final dissolution from which the white and red stones arise. The image makes vivid the alchemical axiom that there is no generation without prior corruption.

## For artists & game designers
A grotesque, poison-swollen toad as the 'rot/death' stage marker — a vivid before-image for a rebirth or purification mechanic.

title: Ripley Scroll (WMS 693) — detail: the alchemist with the flask of the verses
creator: George Ripley tradition (anonymous limner)
summary:
A detail from the Wellcome *Ripley Scroll* (MS 693), one of the great emblematic alchemical rolls of the Ripley tradition, showing the bearded philosopher who presides over the scroll's topmost vision.

## Iconography
At the head of the roll a robed, bearded alchemist (often read as Hermes Trismegistus or Ripley himself) holds aloft a monumental flask. Within and below the great vessel unfold the scroll's nested scenes — figures on the rim, the philosophers' egg, the toad and serpents — while bands of English verse run alongside the images down the vellum.

## Significance
The presiding sage and his outsized flask establish the scroll's claim: the whole cosmos of the Work is contained in the philosophical vessel. The verses ascribed to George Ripley (c. 1415–1490), canon of Bridlington, guide the reader stage by stage through the *opus*. The image of the master displaying the vessel became the visual signature of the genre.

## For artists & game designers
A classic 'master and his great work' tableau — a sage lifting a world-containing flask — ideal as a mentor portrait or the framing art for an alchemy questline.

title: Ripley Scroll (WMS 693) — detail: the fountain and the philosophical vessels
creator: George Ripley tradition (anonymous limner)
summary:
A detail from the Wellcome *Ripley Scroll* (MS 693) showing the fountain of mercurial waters and the philosophical vessels that descend from the great flask.

## Iconography
A tiered fountain pours its streams into basins, flanked by emblems of Sun and Moon and by the round glass vessels of the Work. Serpents or a dragon coil at the base of the structure; bands of verse explain the flow of "our water" through the stages.

## Significance
The fountain is the scroll's image of the *aqua philosophorum* — the philosophical mercury, the dissolving and conjoining water of the Work. Sun and Moon over the basins mark the union of the solar (sulphur, the fixed) and lunar (mercury, the volatile) principles in that water. The cascading design literalises *solve et coagula*: matter dissolved into the fountain and gathered again in the vessels below.

## For artists & game designers
A vertical fountain of glowing 'philosophical water' between sun and moon — a strong centrepiece for a mana-spring, scrying-pool, or alchemy-station backdrop.

title: Ripley Scroll (WMS 693) — detail: the black and white birds
creator: George Ripley tradition (anonymous limner)
summary:
A detail from the Wellcome *Ripley Scroll* (MS 693) showing the paired birds — the black bird and the white bird — that mark the colour-changes of the Work.

## Iconography
Within or above one of the scroll's great vessels, birds rise and descend: a dark raven-like bird and a pale dove-like bird, sometimes shown flying up and down the neck of the flask. Verse-bands explain their alternating flight.

## Significance
The ascending and descending birds figure the repeated sublimation and condensation of the Work — the volatile spirit driven up and brought down again until purified. Their colours track the stages: the black bird the *nigredo* (the raven's head), the white the *albedo* (the dove, the white stone). The motion of the birds in the vessel is the scroll's way of showing *circulation*, the patient cycling that perfects the matter.

## For artists & game designers
Paired ascending/descending birds (black down, white up) inside a vessel — a clean animation cue for a purification or distillation loop.

title: Ripley Scroll (WMS 693) — detail: the golden winged bird
creator: George Ripley tradition (anonymous limner)
summary:
A detail from the Wellcome Collection's *Ripley Scroll* (MS 693) showing the golden winged bird — the Bird of Hermes — one of the emblematic alchemical verse-scrolls associated with the English canon George Ripley.

## Iconography
A radiant winged bird, gilded and displayed against the scroll's vertical sequence of emblems and verses. In the Ripley scrolls the bird perches above or within the alchemical vessels and serpents that climb the long roll of vellum.

## Significance
The [[motif:bird of hermes|Bird of Hermes]] is the scroll's emblem of volatility — "the Byrd of Hermes is my name, eating my wings to make me tame," runs the famous verse. It figures the volatile spirit that must be repeatedly sublimed and "fixed" (its wings eaten) until the volatile and the fixed are reconciled in the stone. The Ripley scrolls survive in roughly two dozen copies, prized as the most spectacular objects of English alchemy.

## For artists & game designers
A single iconic creature — a self-devouring golden bird — that reads instantly as 'volatile spirit'; excellent as a summonable familiar or a transmutation-stage emblem.

title: Rosarium Philosophorum - The Mercurial Fountain (woodcut 1)
creator: Anonymous (pub. Cyriacus Jacobus)
summary:
The opening plate of the Rosarium: the *fons mercurialis*, the Mercurial Fountain from which the whole Great Work flows.

## Iconography
A tall, ornate fountain pours three streams (lac virginis, acetum fontis, aqua vitae) into a basin. Above it the Sun and Moon flank a central star, while serpents and a double-headed mercurial dragon coil at the summit; the basin is inscribed with the philosophical waters. The woodcut sits embedded in the running translation, glossed in the verses 'We are the beginning and first nature of metals.'

## Significance
The fountain is the [[motif:prima materia|prima materia]], the undifferentiated mercurial water that is at once source and solvent of the opus. The triple spout, the paired luminaries and the coiled serpents announce the cast of the drama to come - [[motif:sol and luna|Sol and Luna]], spirit, soul and body. C. G. Jung opened *The Psychology of the Transference* on this very image, reading the fountain as the unconscious matrix from which the coniunctio arises.

## For artists & game designers
A self-contained 'source of all power' set-piece: a single fountain that encodes the elements, the luminaries and the lurking serpent - ideal as an origin location or a resource wellspring.

title: Rosarium Philosophorum - The Meeting of the King and Queen (woodcut 2)
creator: Anonymous (pub. Cyriacus Jacobus)
summary:
The crowned King and Queen meet and join left hands - the betrothal that begins the chymical wedding.

## Iconography
Sol and Luna stand crowned and robed, the King upon the sun, the Queen upon the moon, each extending the left hand to the other while their right hands hold flowering branches that cross. A dove descends between them bearing a third branch, knitting the pair into a trinity. The woodcut is set into the running translation.

## Significance
The joining of the *left* (sinister, unconscious) hands marks an instinctual first contact rather than a public marriage; the dove is the *spiritus* that mediates the union of opposites. This is the first movement of the [[motif:coniunctio|coniunctio]], the meeting of the solar-male and lunar-female principles, sulphur and mercury. Jung made this greeting the emblem of the transference bond between two psyches.

## For artists & game designers
The crossed-branches-and-descending-dove composition is a ready icon for a 'pact' or 'alliance' screen between two opposed factions.

title: Rosarium Philosophorum - The King and Queen Disrobed (woodcut 3)
creator: Anonymous (pub. Cyriacus Jacobus)
summary:
Sol and Luna meet again, now naked - the 'naked truth' that must be told before the principles can unite.

## Iconography
The royal pair stand stripped of their robes, again joining hands across a dove that descends between them with a branch. Standing on the sun and moon, they are reduced to their bare natures. The woodcut is embedded in the running text.

## Significance
The disrobing is the alchemical *nuda veritas*: the King and Queen must shed their outer garments (their accidental qualities) to confront one another as pure sulphur and pure mercury. Only in this stripped sincerity can the genuine [[motif:coniunctio|coniunctio]] occur. Jung read the undressing as the laying-bare of the psyche between analyst and patient, the dropping of persona that the transference demands.

## For artists & game designers
The 'remove the armour to reveal the true self' beat - a vulnerability mechanic where power is gained only by giving up protection.

title: Rosarium Philosophorum - The King and Queen in the Bath (woodcut 4)
creator: Anonymous (pub. Cyriacus Jacobus)
summary:
The King and Queen step together into the hexagonal bath - the *balneum* in which the opposites dissolve toward union.

## Iconography
Sol and Luna stand naked, crowned, joining hands within a six-sided fountain-basin filled with the mercurial water; the dove again hovers between them. The vessel is the alchemical bath in which the pair will be conjoined. The woodcut sits within the running translation, glossed 'the conjunction of two bodies.'

## Significance
The bath is *solutio* - the return of the differentiated bodies to the moist, fluid first state where they can merge. Immersion in the mercurial water softens and dissolves the fixed King so he may unite with the volatile Queen. Jung treated the bath as the immersion in the unconscious, the temenos within which transformation is sealed.

## For artists & game designers
The shared vessel of dissolving water is a strong 'enter the crucible together' location - a bounded space where two entities are combined.

title: Rosarium Philosophorum - The Conjunction / Coupling (woodcut 5)
creator: Anonymous (pub. Cyriacus Jacobus)
summary:
The famous *Coniunctio* plate: King and Queen lie united in the bath, the embrace that is the heart of the whole work.

## Iconography
Sol and Luna recline together in union within the waters of the bath, crowned, their bodies merged in the coupling the text titles 'Conjunction or Coupling.' Verses for Sol and Luna and the parable of Gabricus and Beya accompany the woodcut in the running text.

## Significance
This is the [[motif:coniunctio|coniunctio]] proper - the chymical wedding of sulphur and mercury, fixed and volatile, sun and moon, whose consummation must be followed by their shared death. In the allegory of Arisleus, Gabricus is swallowed up in his sister-bride Beya. Jung placed this plate at the centre of *The Psychology of the Transference* as the image of psychic union - and of its peril.

## For artists & game designers
The canonical 'fusion of two elements' moment - the merge animation before the result is sealed; note that in the source it leads straight to death.

title: Rosarium Philosophorum - The Death / Conjoined Corpse (woodcut 6)
creator: Anonymous (pub. Cyriacus Jacobus)
summary:
'Here lie the King and Queen dead': the united pair become a single conjoined corpse in the tomb - the blackness of the *nigredo*.

## Iconography
A two-headed, fused body lies stretched upon a stone sarcophagus, the wedded King and Queen now a single dead thing. The caption reads 'Here lie the King and Queen dead. The Soul is separated with great grief.' The woodcut is set into the running translation.

## Significance
Union is followed at once by death: the conjoined bodies putrefy and blacken in the sealed vessel, the [[motif:nigredo|nigredo]] in which all distinctions rot away. This putrefaction - corruption as the necessary gate to new life - is the darkest and most essential phase of the opus. Jung read the conjoined corpse as the death of the ego-bond, the mortificatio that the deepest transference passes through.

## For artists & game designers
The two-bodies-fused-into-one-corpse is a vivid 'the merge killed them both' result - a death state that is secretly the prerequisite for rebirth.

title: Rosarium Philosophorum - The Extraction of the Soul (woodcut 7)
creator: Anonymous (pub. Cyriacus Jacobus)
summary:
'The Extraction or Impregnation of the Soul': from the dead conjoined body a small soul rises into the clouds.

## Iconography
The conjoined corpse lies in its sarcophagus while a small naked soul-figure floats up from it into a cloud overhead. The verses read 'Here the Four Elements are separated, and the Soul is most subtly severed from the Body.' The woodcut is embedded in the running text under the heading 'Of Blackness.'

## Significance
In the death of the *nigredo* the volatile soul (*anima*) departs from the blackened body, the separation of the subtle from the gross. This *separatio* of soul from corpse is the necessary emptying-out before the soul can be washed, returned and the body revived. Jung read the ascending soul as the spirit leaving the dead union, the loss that precedes renewal.

## For artists & game designers
A clean 'soul leaves the body' visual - the spirit token that detaches on death and must later be reunited with its host.

title: Rosarium Philosophorum - The Ablution / Falling Dew (woodcut 8)
creator: Anonymous (pub. Cyriacus Jacobus)
summary:
'Of the Rejoicing or Springing or Sublimation of the Soul': dew falls from the clouds to wash the corpse white.

## Iconography
Clouds above the sarcophagus release a fall of dew or rain upon the conjoined body, while a bird descends; the caption reads 'Here the Soul descendeth from on high, and revives the putrefied body.' The woodcut is set into the running translation.

## Significance
The falling dew is the *ablutio* / *mundificatio*: the heavenly water that washes the blackened matter and turns it white, the dawn of the [[motif:albedo|albedo]]. Sublimation lifts the purified parts; the descending moisture revives what death had laid waste. This washing-white is the cleansing without which no resurrection follows. Jung saw in the dew the grace that descends upon the deadlocked work.

## For artists & game designers
Falling cleansing light or dew over a corpse is a textbook 'purification phase' effect - the wash that flips a state from black/corrupted to white/clean.

title: Rosarium Philosophorum - The Birth of the Hermaphrodite (woodcut 9)
creator: Anonymous (pub. Cyriacus Jacobus)
summary:
A winged, two-headed androgyne is born standing on the moon beside the flowering Tree of the Philosophers - an early appearance of the Rebis.

## Iconography
A crowned, double-headed winged figure stands upon a crescent; at left rises the philosophical tree hung with sun-and-moon faces, and a bird perches on the ground at right. The verses sing 'Here is born a noble and rich Queen,' with speeches of Luna and Sol. The woodcut is embedded in the running text.

## Significance
From the washed white body the [[motif:rebis|rebis]] - the 'two-thing,' male and female fused in a single winged body - is first brought forth. The Tree of the Philosophers, fruited with luminaries, marks the growth of the Stone; the figure is both the reborn Queen and the seed of the final hermaphrodite. Jung read the androgyne as the union of conscious and unconscious, the self born of the coniunctio.

## For artists & game designers
The winged double-headed body on a crescent is a striking 'fusion result, first form' - an evolution stage before the crowned final Rebis.

title: Rosarium Philosophorum - Fermentation (woodcut 10)
creator: Anonymous (pub. Cyriacus Jacobus)
summary:
'Fermentation': a winged Sol-figure reclines on a hillside, again enclosed with the philosophers' mercury.

## Iconography
A winged figure reclines upon a mound or wing above a rocky ground, captioned 'Here Sol is again included, and is circumpassed with the Mercury of Philosophers.' The woodcut is set into the running translation under the heading 'Fermentation.'

## Significance
*Fermentatio* is the leavening of the Stone: the reborn solar body is once more steeped in mercury so that the ferment may 'raise' it, as leaven raises dough, toward the red. The Rosarium now runs a second, higher circuit of death and revival - inclusion, drowning, blackening - that perfects what the first cycle began. The repetition underlines that the opus is iterative, not a single passage.

## For artists & game designers
A 'second pass / higher difficulty repeat' marker - the same cycle re-entered at a more refined level.

title: Rosarium Philosophorum - Illumination (woodcut 11)
creator: Anonymous (pub. Cyriacus Jacobus)
summary:
'Illumination': the solar figure dies a second time, drowned in the philosophers' mercury upon the tomb.

## Iconography
A winged sun-figure lies stretched on the stone sarcophagus, captioned 'Here Sol plainly dies again, and is drowned with the Mercury of the Philosophers.' The woodcut is embedded in the running text under the heading 'Illumination.'

## Significance
The second death repeats the [[motif:nigredo|nigredo]] at a higher turn: the reborn body must itself be dissolved and 'drowned' in mercury before it can be fixed for good. Paradoxically titled 'Illumination,' the plate teaches that the deepest darkening is the threshold of the greatest light - the rubedo cannot come without this renewed mortification. Jung saw here the repeated dyings the integrating psyche must endure.

## For artists & game designers
A 'death you must repeat, each time deeper' beat - the recurring sacrifice that powers a higher transformation.

title: Rosarium Philosophorum - Nourishment (woodcut 12)
creator: Anonymous (pub. Cyriacus Jacobus)
summary:
'Nourishment': the solar body is made black as pitch upon the tomb - the dark food on which the Stone feeds.

## Iconography
A blackened figure lies on the sarcophagus, a small bird above, captioned 'Here Sol is made black like unto pitch, with the Mercury of the Philosophers.' The woodcut is set into the running translation under the heading 'Nourishment.'

## Significance
*Cibatio* - feeding - is the patient imbibition by which the Stone is repeatedly nourished with its mercurial water. The blackening shows the matter passing once more through corruption; the nourishment is the gentle, drop-by-drop feeding that sustains the growing Stone through its second putrefaction. The cycle of dark feeding must run its course before the red can dawn.

## For artists & game designers
The 'feed the thing in its dark phase' mechanic - resource input during a vulnerable blackened state, no visible payoff yet.

title: Rosarium Philosophorum - Fixation (woodcut 13)
creator: Anonymous (pub. Cyriacus Jacobus)
summary:
'Here ends the life of Luna': from the tomb the soul subtly ascends once more, fixing the lunar body.

## Iconography
The body lies in the sarcophagus while a small soul rises into a cloud above, captioned 'Here ends the life of Luna, and the spirit subtly ascends on high.' The woodcut is embedded in the running text.

## Significance
*Fixatio* binds the volatile spirit fast to the body so it can no longer fly off. The 'death of Luna' is the consuming of the silvery, white principle as the work turns from the [[motif:albedo|albedo]] toward the red; the ascending soul is sublimed and then fixed. This pairing of ascent and fixation - rising in order to be made permanent - is the paradox at the close of the white work. Jung read it as the spirit raised only to be re-embodied for good.

## For artists & game designers
The 'lock it in place' step after purification - a state that, once reached, can no longer be lost.

title: Rosarium Philosophorum - The Dew / Multiplication (woodcut 14)
creator: Anonymous (pub. Cyriacus Jacobus)
summary:
The water is diminished and falls as dew upon the tomb, moistening the earth for the final increase.

## Iconography
Dew descends from clouds onto the sarcophagus and its body, captioned 'Here the water is diminished, and bedeweth the earth with his moisture.' The woodcut is set into the running translation amid extracts from Geber.

## Significance
The falling dew here serves *imbibition* and *multiplicatio*: the measured watering of the calcined earth that swells and increases the Stone's virtue many-fold. The diminishing water and bedewed ground show the alternation of drying and moistening - calcination and solution - by which the medicine is multiplied. The heavenly dew remains alchemy's image of the grace that fructifies the dead matter.

## For artists & game designers
The 'water it and it multiplies' beat - small repeated inputs that compound an asset's value.

title: Rosarium Philosophorum - Reviving (woodcut 15)
creator: Anonymous (pub. Cyriacus Jacobus)
summary:
'Reviving': the soul descends in glory from heaven to raise up the Daughter of Philosophy from the tomb.

## Iconography
A soul-figure floats down from a cloud toward the body in the sarcophagus, captioned 'Here the Soul descendeth gloriously from heaven, and raiseth up the Daughter of Philosophy.' The woodcut is embedded in the running text under the heading 'Reviving.'

## Significance
This is the *reditus animae*, the return of the soul: the spirit that had ascended now comes back to quicken the purified body, reuniting what death had sundered. The 'Daughter of Philosophy' is the new, glorified body of the Stone, raised incorruptible. The descent answers the earlier ascent of the soul - the work's great rhythm of separation and reunion completes itself. Jung read this homecoming of the soul as the integration that crowns the transference.

## For artists & game designers
The 'soul returns to revive the purified body' moment - the reunion that turns a cleansed but inert shell into a living, upgraded entity.

title: Rosarium Philosophorum - The Crowned Hermaphrodite / Rebis (woodcut 16)
creator: Anonymous (pub. Cyriacus Jacobus)
summary:
The crowned, winged Hermaphrodite - the Rebis - stands triumphant on the moon and dragon: the goal of the work made visible.

## Iconography
A two-headed (male and female) figure in a single robe spreads bat-like wings, holds a chalice and serpent-staff, and stands upon a crescent moon above a coiled dragon; the philosophical tree rises at left. The verses are 'The Riddle of the King' and 'The Answer of Luna the Queen.' The woodcut is set into the running translation.

## Significance
This is the fully formed [[motif:rebis|rebis]], the 'two-thing': the King and Queen reborn as one androgynous body that has conquered the dragon of the prima materia beneath its feet. Crowned and winged, fixed yet volatile, it is the reconciled union of all opposites - the near-attained Philosophers' Stone. It is the single most reproduced image of the Rosarium and a touchstone for Jung's symbol of the integrated Self.

## For artists & game designers
The definitive 'final fused form' - a crowned, winged hybrid standing on the monster it was made from; perfect as an ultimate evolution or boss-ally reveal.

title: Rosarium Philosophorum - The Green Lion Devouring the Sun (woodcut 17)
creator: Anonymous (pub. Cyriacus Jacobus)
summary:
'Our Mercury, the Green Lion devouring the Sun': the green lion bites into the radiant solar disc.

## Iconography
A lion clamps its jaws on a rayed, human-faced sun and swallows it, captioned 'I am the true green and Golden Lion without cares, in me all the secrets of the Philosophers are hidden.' The woodcut is embedded in the running text under 'Of Our Mercury which is the Green Lion Devouring the Sun.'

## Significance
The *leo viridis* is the crude, unripe philosophical mercury that 'eats' gold - the corrosive solvent that dissolves [[motif:sol and luna|Sol]] back into the work so it can be reborn. Green for its raw, vegetative power, the lion is both poison and the agent of every solution; devouring the sun, it returns the perfected to the prima materia for a further turn. The motif became one of alchemy's most quoted emblems.

## For artists & game designers
A beast eating the sun is a complete 'devour to dissolve / consume the prize to power the next stage' icon - raw, ominous, instantly legible.

title: Rosarium Philosophorum - The Coronation / Assumption (woodcut 18)
creator: Anonymous (pub. Cyriacus Jacobus)
summary:
An arched, devotional plate of crowning and glorification - the lunar bride received and exalted before the final resurrection.

## Iconography
Within a tablet-shaped frame hung with banderoles, haloed figures attend a central enthroned figure while a dove of the Holy Spirit descends from above. The surrounding text speaks of the woman as 'receptacle and matrix' of the seed and likens Luna to the Virgin (Hermes: 'Sol is her father and Luna her mother'). The woodcut is set into the running translation.

## Significance
The Rosarium borrows the Christian iconography of the Coronation and Assumption to figure the glorification of the purified lunar principle - the [[motif:albedo|white]] body received into heaven as the matrix of the new Stone. The descending dove repeats the *spiritus* that has mediated the work from the first plate. This sacralising of the chemistry is exactly the religious-alchemical fusion that drew Jung to the cycle.

## For artists & game designers
A solemn 'coronation / ascension' tableau - the honoured-and-elevated beat just before the climactic transformation.
