title: The Dorabella Cipher (Edward Elgar, 1897)
work: The Voynich Manuscript & the Tradition of Occult Ciphers
creator: Edward Elgar
summary:
The Dorabella Cipher, a short enciphered note the composer Edward Elgar sent in 1897, still unsolved.

## Iconography
Three lines of an invented shorthand: a string of squiggles each made of one, two, or three semicircular pen-strokes set at varying angles, like rotated letter 'E's or fragments of arcs. Eighty-seven characters in all, with no spacing into obvious words.

## Significance
Elgar sent the note to Dora Penny ('Dorabella'), a young friend, who never managed to read it; it has resisted cryptanalysts ever since. The glyphs appear to be a [[motif:rotated glyphs|rotation cipher]] of a small alphabet of arcs, but the message — too short to give cryptanalysts much purchase — remains undeciphered. Elgar's fondness for puzzles (he also embedded the 'Enigma' in his *Variations*) makes the cipher a beloved minor mystery of [[motif:secret writing|secret writing]].

## For artists & game designers
A tiny rotation-cipher font: arcs at set angles you can use for short, crackable in-game notes.

citations.text: Jerrold Northrop Moore, *Edward Elgar: A Creative Life* (1984).

title: The Holy Table of John Dee (Enochian Tables of Practice)
work: The Voynich Manuscript & the Tradition of Occult Ciphers
creator: John Dee (after his angelic 'actions' with Edward Kelley)
summary:
A rendering of the Holy Table of John Dee, the engraved table of practice bordered and filled with the characters of his 'angelic' Enochian system.

## Iconography
A square table-top is inscribed around its rim with a band of Enochian letters and, across its surface, a grid of small squares each holding a character or number; the central field would have held the wax [[motif:sigillum dei aemeth|Sigillum Dei Aemeth]]. The whole functions as a ritual instrument keyed to Dee's angelic alphabet.

## Significance
John Dee (1527–1608/9), Elizabeth I's mathematician and astrologer, recorded with the scryer Edward Kelley an entire 'angelic' language — [[motif:enochian table|Enochian]] — delivered through grids of letters that the angels supposedly dictated cell by cell, often backwards as a safeguard. Whether mystical revelation or an elaborate constructed cipher, Dee's lettered tables sit squarely in the tradition of [[motif:secret writing|secret writing]] and angelic cryptography that runs from Trithemius onward.

## For artists & game designers
A glyph-grid altar: a board whose squares the player fills letter-by-letter to 'summon' an effect, with reversed entry as a built-in safety puzzle.

citations.text: Deborah E. Harkness, *John Dee's Conversations with Angels* (1999).

title: The Pigpen (Masonic) Cipher Grid
work: The Voynich Manuscript & the Tradition of Occult Ciphers
creator: Anonymous (Masonic / Rosicrucian tradition)
summary:
A key to the Pigpen or Masonic cipher, the geometric grid-substitution code long used in Masonic and Rosicrucian circles.

## Iconography
The diagram shows the construction grids — a pair of tic-tac-toe grids and a pair of X-shaped grids, some dotted — from whose cells each letter takes the shape of the lines (and dots) enclosing it. The resulting 'alphabet' is a set of angular, gate-like glyphs.

## Significance
The [[motif:pigpen cipher|pigpen cipher]] (also 'Freemason's cipher') is a simple monoalphabetic [[motif:grid substitution|grid substitution]] in which letters are replaced by the fragment of grid surrounding them. Used by Freemasons to keep records private and engraved on Masonic gravestones, it appears across [[motif:rosicrucian code|Rosicrucian]] and fraternal contexts. Easily broken, it survives more as a badge of secrecy than as serious cryptography.

## For artists & game designers
The most legible 'secret alphabet' to letter signage with: instantly readable as 'hidden writing' and trivially decodable by an engaged player.

citations.text: David Kahn, *The Codebreakers* (1967).

title: The Rohonc Codex (Undeciphered Hungarian Manuscript)
work: The Voynich Manuscript & the Tradition of Occult Ciphers
creator: Anonymous
summary:
Pages from the Rohonc Codex, an undeciphered manuscript in an unknown script held by the Hungarian Academy of Sciences.

## Iconography
The spread shows dense rows of an unfamiliar, hooked alphabet — far more symbols than any natural script needs — interspersed with simple line illustrations of apparently religious scenes (crosses, figures, churches). The text appears to run right-to-left and bottom-to-top.

## Significance
The Rohonc Codex is the Voynich's eastern cousin: a roughly 450-page book in an [[motif:unknown alphabet|unknown script]], surfacing in nineteenth-century Hungary, that has resisted decipherment. Theories range from a genuine devotional text in a cipher or invented alphabet, to a forgery by the antiquarian Sámuel Literáti Nemes. Recent work by Levente Zoltán Király and Gábor Tokai argues it is an enciphered religious compilation, but no reading is universally accepted.

## For artists & game designers
Another fully-formed mystery script with matching pictures — a model for a 'found' sacred book in an invented faith.

citations.text: Levente Zoltán Király & Gábor Tokai, studies of the Rohonc Codex (2018–2020).

title: The Shepherd's Monument, Shugborough (with the O.U.O.S.V.A.V.V. Inscription)
work: The Voynich Manuscript & the Tradition of Occult Ciphers
creator: Anonymous (after Poussin); Shugborough Estate
summary:
The Shepherd's Monument at Shugborough Hall, Staffordshire, carrying the unsolved O·U·O·S·V·A·V·V cipher inscription.

## Iconography
A carved stone relief — a mirror-reversed version of Poussin's *Et in Arcadia Ego*, in which shepherds gather at a tomb — is set into a rustic arch. Beneath it runs the enigmatic sequence of letters **O U O S V A V V**, framed by a **D** and **M**, that has never been satisfactorily decoded.

## Significance
The [[motif:shepherds monument|Shepherd's Monument]] (c. 1748–1763) pairs an Arcadian tomb scene with a [[motif:cipher inscription|letter cipher]] whose meaning has eluded everyone from casual visitors to professional codebreakers, and even attracted Grail and Templar speculation. Proposed readings — a Latin devotional acrostic, a lover's memorial — remain conjectural, making it Britain's most famous monumental cipher.

## For artists & game designers
A landmark puzzle object: an outdoor carving whose letters seed a quest, with the reversed-painting motif as a built-in visual clue.

citations.text: A. J. Morton, *The Shugborough Inscription* (research surveys, 2010s).

title: Trithemius, *Polygraphiae* (1518) — First Printed Book on Cryptology
work: The Voynich Manuscript & the Tradition of Occult Ciphers
creator: Johannes Trithemius
summary:
A copy of Johannes Trithemius's *Polygraphiae* (1518), held at the National Cryptologic Museum and often called the first printed book on cryptology.

## Iconography
The open volume shows the printed [[motif:cipher table|cipher tables]] for which the work is famous: long columns of substitute words and Latin-prayer alphabets by which a message is enciphered into seemingly pious text, prefiguring the *tabula recta* of the polyalphabetic cipher.

## Significance
*Polygraphiae libri sex* was published posthumously in 1518 and is widely regarded as the first printed book wholly devoted to [[motif:polygraphy|cryptography]]. Its tables — including the famous 'Ave Maria' cipher that hides letters inside columns of devotional words — and the recta table later developed by Bellaso and Vigenère made Trithemius a founder of Western cryptology, the respectable twin of his disguised *Steganographia*.

## For artists & game designers
A period-accurate codebook prop: real Renaissance cipher tables a player can use to encode or crack messages in a historical setting.

citations.text: Johannes Trithemius, *Polygraphiae libri sex* (1518); David Kahn, *The Codebreakers* (1967).

title: Steganographic Chart in the Hand of John Dee (Trithemius's *Steganographia*)
work: The Voynich Manuscript & the Tradition of Occult Ciphers
creator: Johannes Trithemius; chart copied by John Dee
summary:
A cryptographic chart relating to Johannes Trithemius's *Steganographia*, written out in the hand of the English magus John Dee.

## Iconography
The chart sets out a grid of names, letters, and tabulated correspondences in a careful sixteenth-century hand. Trithemius's *Steganographia* presents its cryptography under the guise of conjuring angels and spirits: tables of barbarous spirit-names that, decoded by the hidden key, yield ordinary enciphered messages.

## Significance
Trithemius's *Steganographia* (written 1499, printed 1606) is the foundational work of [[motif:steganography|steganography]] — the art of hiding the very existence of a message. Its disguise as a manual of [[motif:angelic names|angel magic]] was so convincing that the book was placed on the Index and read for centuries as a genuine grimoire, until scholars showed the 'spirit names' were a cover for a real cipher. That John Dee copied this chart links the cipher tradition directly to Renaissance occult philosophy.

## For artists & game designers
The perfect 'spell that is really a code': a page of conjuration that, read correctly, hides a plain-text clue.

The page teems with tiny nude women standing in basins and barrels linked by a plumbing of pipes and channels through which a greenish liquid seems to flow; clusters of stars and looping conduits connect the pools, all annotated in the unreadable script. The effect is part bath-house, part anatomical or alchemical schematic.

The [[motif:nymphs in tubes|biological section]] is the strangest part of the Voynich, variously read as a treatise on women's medicine and balneology (the healing use of baths), as an allegory of the body's inner vessels, or as an alchemical scheme of fluids. The interconnected tubes have invited comparisons to anatomy, to the bath-cures of medieval medicine, and to the *vasa* of alchemical circulation — none confirmed.

A single plant fills the page: a coloured drawing of stem, leaves, and an exaggerated root system, surrounded and labelled by lines of the manuscript's enigmatic script. The largest section of the book, the herbal pages each pair one plant with a block of writing in the manner of a medieval herbal — yet almost none of the species can be securely identified with a real plant.

Large circular rosettes — elaborate roundels filled with cells, spokes, towers, and looping ornament — are joined to neighbouring circles by causeways and tubes, the whole reading like a schematic map of linked places. A detail from folio 72r of the Voynich Manuscript, showing the central figure of one of the astronomical zodiac medallions.

The close-up isolates the heart of a zodiac wheel: a central roundel containing a zodiacal emblem, framed by the inner ring of compartments and curving labels. Folios 70–73 of the manuscript carry the run of zodiac diagrams; this detail from f72r lets the central device be read apart from its crowded rings of figures.

Isolating the medallion shows how the Voynich follows the convention of placing a sign's emblem at the hub of a [[motif:calendar wheel|calendar wheel]]. The folios run through the zodiac from Pisces and Aries onward, several split across paired diagrams. As with every page, the script naming the figure resists all attempts at decipherment, from William Friedman's wartime study groups to modern computational analysis.

work: The Voynich Manuscript & the Tradition of Occult Ciphers
creator: Anonymous (Beinecke MS 408)
summary:
A close detail of the Voynich Manuscript's opening folio (1r), showing the looping, fluent script that no one has been able to read.

## Iconography
The retouched crop isolates a few lines of 'Voynichese': a flowing hand of perhaps two dozen recurring glyphs, written confidently left-to-right with consistent ligatures and word-like groupings, but corresponding to no known alphabet or language.

## Significance
The Voynich [[motif:undeciphered script|script]] is the crux of the whole mystery. Its statistics behave partly like natural language (it obeys word-frequency laws) and partly unlike it, fuelling rival theories — an unknown language, a cipher, an artificial 'glossolalia,' or a meaningless fabrication. From William and Elizebeth Friedman to modern information theorists, the best cryptanalysts of the twentieth century failed to break it, which is why it anchors the tradition of unsolved [[motif:secret writing|secret writing]].

## For artists & game designers
A constructed alphabet ready to copy: a coherent glyph set you can letter signs and scrolls with for an instantly 'unreadable' world.

A large circular diagram dominates the page: a central roundel containing a zodiacal emblem, encircled by concentric bands in which dozens of small nude or robed figures — many holding stars — stand in compartments, each with a brief label in the unreadable script. title: Ripley Scroll (Wellcome b18597762) — Section 1 — Opening Section
creator: English alchemical tradition (Ripley circle)
medium: manuscript on vellum, pen and watercolor
summary:
A second Wellcome Ripley Scroll witness (Wellcome Library b18597762), photographed in 14 IIIF sections via the Wellcome Collection. This parchment roll preserves the Ripley Scroll iconographic tradition — the canonical English alchemical scroll attributed to George Ripley (c.1415–1490) and his circle — in a distinct manuscript copy with variant compositional choices compared to the WT303 copy.

## Iconography

Like all Ripley Scrolls, this manuscript narrates the alchemical Great Work through a sequence of emblematic paintings on parchment: the philosopher-alchemist bearing the scroll of the Work; corrosion scenes (green lion, toad/eagle); the philosophical conjunction of Sol and Luna; the pelican of multiplication; and the progressive stages of the Work through nigredo (black), albedo (white), citrinitas (yellow), and rubedo (red) to the final triumphant Red King. Sections 1–7 (heavier file weights at 145–157KB) preserve the illustrated panels; sections 8–14 are predominantly verse text.

## Significance

This second Wellcome witness allows comparative study with the WT303 copy, illuminating how different scribes and artists adapted the standard Ripley Scroll program for different patrons. Jennifer Rampling (*The Experimental Fire*) has systematically analyzed the corpus of surviving Ripley Scrolls, demonstrating how the tradition transmitted and transformed Ripley's alchemical poetics across a century and a half of English alchemy.

## For artists & game designers

The slightly different proportions (several canvases are notably wider than WT303) suggest variant panel sizing — offering alternative aspect ratios for game card design. The first seven illustrated sections provide a directly usable sequence of emblematic images for character art, level-select screens, or tarot-style card decks.

title: Ripley Scroll WT303 — Opening Section — Philosopher-Alchemist Figure
creator: George Ripley (attributed); English alchemical tradition
medium: manuscript on vellum, pen and watercolor
summary:
The Wellcome Ripley Scroll (WT 303, b18968831) is one of the finest surviving manuscript witnesses in the English alchemical scroll tradition attributed to George Ripley (c.1415–1490). The parchment roll is photographed here in 19 sections via the Wellcome Collection IIIF service.

## Iconography

Ripley Scrolls are vertical parchment rolls, typically 3–5 metres long, that narrate the alchemical Great Work through a sequence of emblematic images accompanied by Middle English verse stanzas. The standard iconographic program begins with a philosopher-alchemist bearing a staff and scroll, then proceeds through: the corrosion and dissolution stages (green lion devouring the sun; toad devouring the eagle); the philosophical conjunction of king (sol/sulphur) and queen (luna/mercury); alchemical vessels and the stages of the Work; and culminates with the crowned, triumphant Red King — the Philosopher's Stone in its final projection form. The verse texts interspersed between imagery are attributed to Ripley's *Compound of Alchymie* (1471) and allied poems.

Key iconographic symbols include: the **green lion** (vitriol/corrosive; dissolution of gold); the **eagle** (volatility/sublimation); the **toad** (fixation; the earth-bound principle); the **pelican** (multiplication; the pelican feeding her young with her blood is the *multiplicatio* stage); **Sol and Luna** (the royal pair, sulphur and mercury, joined in the philosophical marriage or *coniunctio*); the **nigredo dragon** (putrefaction; matter reduced to its prima materia); the **White Queen** (albedo; the purified silver stage); and the **Red King** (rubedo; the completed Stone).

## Significance

The Ripley Scroll tradition was enormously influential in English alchemy from c.1480 to c.1650, surviving in approximately 20–25 manuscript copies held at institutions including Princeton, the Huntington Library, the Getty, Yale, and the British Library. Jennifer Rampling's foundational study (*The Experimental Fire*, Chicago 2020) provides the most authoritative analysis of the scroll's textual tradition and its relationship to Ripley's other alchemical writings. Barbara Obrist (*Les Debuts de l'Imagerie Alchimique*) situates the scroll tradition within the broader medieval development of alchemical illustration. Lawrence Principe (*The Secrets of Alchemy*) provides the general scholarly context for English chrysopoeia.

The Wellcome WT 303 copy is held in the Wellcome Collection and is freely available via IIIF under their open access policy. It is one of the best-preserved colored copies of the scroll.

## For artists & game designers

The Ripley Scroll is a ready-made visual game structure: each painted panel is a stage or encounter, each symbol a game element. The 9-stage iconographic program maps cleanly to a progression system (corrosion → dissolution → conjunction → calcination → albedo → citrinitas → rubedo → multiplication → projection). The personified figures — green lion, white queen, red king — are direct character art templates. The vertical scroll format suggests game map design: a top-to-bottom level progression where the player descends or ascends through stages of transmutation.

title: Golden Eagle on a Sphere (Rotulum hieroglyphicum)
work: Rotulum hieroglyphicum (Wellcome Collection — Ripley Scroll Tradition)
creator: English alchemical tradition, attributed to Ripley circle
medium: manuscript on vellum, pen and watercolor
summary:
The golden eagle perched on a sphere is among the most powerful images in English alchemical iconography. This image from a *Rotulum hieroglyphicum* at the Wellcome Collection shows the eagle at its moment of maximum elevation — wings spread, golden plumage fully visible against the sphere beneath it. The eagle represents *volatile mercury* (or the volatile principle of sulphur, depending on tradition), raised above the terrestrial sphere by the heat of distillation and sublimation.

## Iconography

In the Ripley Scroll tradition, the eagle's visual program unfolds in several stages. First, the eagle attacks and is attacked — in some scrolls it appears in combat with the toad (the fixed principle). Then it ascends, marking the stage of *sublimatio*. Here, the eagle stands triumphant on the sphere, marking the completion of the volatile's ascent before the stage of coagulation or fixation brings it back down into the fixed earth. The golden coloring is significant: this is not a raw eagle (the unrefined volatile principle) but a *gilded* eagle — the volatile principle that has absorbed gold through the process of dissolution and is now ready to transfer it to the Stone. The sphere beneath the eagle is the *orbis* or earth — the fixed principle that grounds the Work.

## Significance

The eagle-on-sphere image is one of the most instantly recognizable motifs in Western alchemical iconography, appearing in the Ripley Scroll tradition, the *Rosarium Philosophorum* (1550), and the *Splendor Solis* (1582), as well as emblematic literature from Maier to the Rosicrucian texts. This Wellcome photograph preserves one of the finest colored examples at high resolution.

## For artists & game designers

The golden eagle is a ready-made boss sprite, faction emblem, or achievement icon. The pose — wings spread wide, perched on a sphere — is heraldically legible and compositionally balanced. The sphere beneath adds architectural grounding. Consider this as: (1) the sublimation stage boss; (2) the faction symbol of a volatile/fire alchemical tradition; (3) achievement art for completing the distillation stage.

title: Green Dragon (Rotulum hieroglyphicum)
work: Rotulum hieroglyphicum (Wellcome Collection — Ripley Scroll Tradition)
creator: English alchemical tradition, attributed to Ripley circle
medium: manuscript on vellum, pen and watercolor
summary:
The green dragon is the most menacing figure in the English alchemical visual tradition. This image from a *Rotulum hieroglyphicum* at the Wellcome Collection shows the dragon with wings spread, green scaled body fully displayed. In alchemical symbolism, the green dragon represents *vitriol* (green vitriol / sulphate of iron) or the volatile corrosive principle (*sulphur philosophicum*) that dissolves even gold — the philosophical solvent that initiates the Work by corroding and destroying the impure metals.

## Iconography

The dragon's green color is crucial: it marks the *viridis leo* (green lion / green dragon interchangeability in some traditions), the corrosive principle active in the first stage of the Work. Green is the color of the metal at its most corrosive — the green patina of copper and iron, the green of fresh growth before calcination, the green of vitriol. The dragon's wings mark its volatile nature: it is the *volatile sulphur*, able to rise and attack. Unlike the toad (fixed, earth-bound), the dragon can fly — making it the active, aggressive principle in the alchemical contest. In the Ripley Scroll tradition, the dragon first appears as a destructive agent (consuming the metals) but is eventually overcome, its body transformed into the fixed earth of the Stone.

## Significance

The green dragon / green lion is one of the most powerful symbols in Western alchemy, appearing in texts from Ripley through Flamel through Newton. This Wellcome *Rotulum hieroglyphicum* version is among the finest colored examples available in public domain, with the full green-on-red or green-on-gold color contrast visible at high resolution.

## For artists & game designers

The green dragon is an immediately deployable enemy sprite or alchemical hazard. Its specific design — green wings, scaled body, aggressive posture — is both historically accurate and visually distinctive from generic fantasy dragons. Deploying it as the 'corrosion encounter' or first-stage boss (equivalent to the dissolution stage in the alchemical Work) gives game narrative immediate symbolic depth.

title: Philosopher Bearing Staff with Scroll (Rotulum hieroglyphicum)
work: Rotulum hieroglyphicum (Wellcome Collection — Ripley Scroll Tradition)
creator: English alchemical tradition, attributed to Ripley circle
medium: manuscript on vellum, pen and watercolor
summary:
The philosopher-alchemist bearing a staff with a scroll coiled around it is the quintessential opening image of the *Rotulum hieroglyphicum* tradition — the figure that introduces the entire visual program of the alchemical scroll. This image from the Wellcome Collection preserves one of the finest colored examples at high resolution. The staff-with-scroll is a *caduceus* variant: the staff as Mercury's rod (the universal instrument of transformation), the coiled scroll as the serpent of wisdom (the *ouroboros* in its knowledge form).

## Iconography

This philosopher-figure synthesizes three roles simultaneously: (1) *author* — he bears the scroll of the written revelation, the textual program of the Work; (2) *practitioner* — the staff is the alchemist's instrument, the stirring rod and the pointer; (3) *magus* — the coiled scroll as serpent marks his mastery of transformation. The figure's dress — typically a robe or tabard — marks him as a learned man, not a simple craftsman. His posture — upright, staff raised, scroll held — is an act of *presentatio*: he presents the Work to the viewer, inviting them into the scroll's visual program. This is the gate-keeper image of the entire *Rotulum hieroglyphicum* tradition.

## Significance

The philosopher-figure is the Ripley Scroll's signature opening image, appearing in virtually all surviving witnesses. Rampling (*The Experimental Fire*) analyzes how this opening figure establishes the scroll's claim to authority — positioning the alchemical practitioner as both scholar (holding written text) and adept (commanding the scroll of the Work). This Wellcome example is particularly well-preserved, with detailed coloring of the philosopher's robes and staff.

## For artists & game designers

The sage-with-scroll is the archetype for the alchemist NPC — the quest-giver, the mentor, the keeper of hidden knowledge. The specific pose (upright, staff raised, scroll prominent) is the classic 'sage presenting knowledge' posture. The staff-as-caduceus detail marks him as master of transformation, not merely a laboratory technician. Use as: (1) opening narrator character; (2) quest-giver NPC portrait; (3) character class art for the 'Scholar' or 'Magister' archetype.

title: Alchemical Fountain on Column — Left Panel (Rotulum hieroglyphicum)
work: Rotulum hieroglyphicum (Wellcome Collection — Ripley Scroll Tradition)
creator: English alchemical tradition, attributed to Ripley circle
medium: manuscript on vellum, pen and watercolor
summary:
The fountain on a column — the *fons philosophorum* or philosophical fountain — is one of the most resonant images in English alchemical iconography. This left-hand panel, from a *Rotulum hieroglyphicum* at the Wellcome Collection, shows the fountain with its column and symbolic accessories; a facing companion panel (M0010603) completes the diptych. The philosophical fountain is the alchemical *bath* where the metals are purified: the fountain's waters are the universal solvent (*menstruum universale*), and the column that supports it represents the axis of the Work, the *columna philosophorum*.

## Iconography

The fountain-on-column motif appears in numerous Ripley Scrolls and was a standard element of English alchemical imagery from c.1480 onward. Its visual sources include: the medieval *fons vitae* (fountain of life) tradition; the Hermetic *Krater* (mixing bowl) of the *Corpus Hermeticum*; and the alchemical bath (*balneum*) described in practical laboratory texts. The fountain here is likely crowned with Sol and Luna medallions (sun and moon), marking the conjunction of masculine and feminine principles in the philosophical water. The column's capitals and decorative elements mark the Work's division into discrete stages.

## Significance

This image is particularly valuable as one of a pair with M0010603 — the two panels together visualize the complete fountain scene, allowing comparison with single-panel versions in other scroll witnesses. The Wellcome Collection's high-resolution photography preserves fine details of the coloring and line work that characterize English workshop production of the period.

## For artists & game designers

The fountain provides a beautiful game environment element: a purification station, healing fountain, or alchemical resource point. The column-and-basin structure is architecturally specific enough to design from — tall central column, wide basin, decorative top with celestial symbols — while remaining emblematic rather than realistic. Works well as a save point or level-transition symbol.

title: Alchemical Fountain on Column — Right Panel (Rotulum hieroglyphicum)
work: Rotulum hieroglyphicum (Wellcome Collection — Ripley Scroll Tradition)
creator: English alchemical tradition, attributed to Ripley circle
medium: manuscript on vellum, pen and watercolor
summary:
The right-hand companion panel to M0010602, completing the diptych representation of the *fons philosophorum* (philosophical fountain). This panel shows the fountain in its full symbolic context, with the decorative accessories — sun and moon medallions, planetary symbols, inscribed text bands — that annotate the alchemical meaning of the bath. The pair of panels forms a panoramic view of the fountain scene, with the fountain's imagery split between two illustrated sections of the scroll.

## Iconography

Together with M0010602, this panel presents the complete fountain of the philosophers: the source of the universal solvent (*aqua mercurialis*), the place where Sol and Luna meet in conjunction. The symbolic accessories visible in this right-hand panel — likely including sun and moon roundels at the top, planetary signs on the column shaft, and verse text at the base — explain the fountain's role in the Work. The diptych structure is characteristic of Ripley Scroll design: complex, wide images are split across two canvases, requiring the scroll to be unfurled to see the full composition.

## Significance

The paired fountain panels (M0010602–M0010603) are among the most compositionally elaborate images in this *Rotulum hieroglyphicum*, demonstrating the sophisticated visual planning that went into the Ripley Scroll tradition. The Wellcome Collection's separate photography of each panel allows digital reunification of the diptych.

## For artists & game designers

The paired panels are ideal for split-screen or diptych game art: two facing pages of a quest journal, two halves of a loading screen, or two panels of a comic-book-style sequence. The fountain motif recurs across alchemical iconography — cross-reference with the *Splendor Solis* bath scenes for variant design templates.

title: Alchemist Holding an Alembic (Rotulum hieroglyphicum)
work: Rotulum hieroglyphicum (Wellcome Collection — Ripley Scroll Tradition)
creator: English alchemical tradition, attributed to Ripley circle
medium: manuscript on vellum, pen and watercolor
summary:
The central figure of the alchemist-philosopher holding an alembic — the glass distillation vessel that is the primary instrument of the alchemical laboratory. This image from a *Rotulum hieroglyphicum* ("Hieroglyphic Scroll") at the Wellcome Collection shows the practitioner fully immersed in the Work, holding the alembic at the moment of distillation. The alembic is simultaneously a literal laboratory tool and an emblem of the Work's spiritualizing process: matter rises through heat, becomes volatile, and descends purified. The alchemist's posture — holding the vessel at eye level — suggests not mere mechanistic labour but contemplative *theoria*: the alchemist observes the spirit rising through glass, becoming visible.

## Iconography

The alembic-holding alchemist belongs to the rich visual tradition of the *philosophus*, the wise adept who both labours and contemplates. In the Ripley Scroll tradition, the philosopher-figure opens the scroll's visual program, establishing the unity of practice and theory. The alembic specifically marks the stage of *distillatio*, one of the twelve operations of alchemy catalogued by Paracelsus and earlier authors. This figure appears to be from the same *Rotulum hieroglyphicum* as M0010602–M0010606, forming a suite of individual illustrations photographed from a single English alchemical scroll.

## Significance

The Wellcome Collection's systematic photography of Ripley Scroll witnesses has produced some of the highest-quality public-domain images of English alchemical iconography. These individual panels from a *Rotulum hieroglyphicum* give artists and scholars direct access to the standard visual vocabulary of the tradition. Rampling (*The Experimental Fire*) traces the alchemist-figure tradition across fifty years of English practice.

## For artists & game designers

The alchemist-with-alembic is the archetypal starting character in any alchemy-themed game. This image provides a high-quality template for the practitioner archetype: precise hand-gesture (holding vessel to eye), scholarly dress, contemplative stance. The alembic's shape — bulbous base, tapering neck — is both historically accurate and immediately legible as "alchemy" to modern viewers.

title: Aurora Consurgens — The Building (Zurich, f.3r)
creator: Anonymous
summary:
An architectural allegory from the celebrated Zurich *Aurora Consurgens*, whose lively watercolours illustrate the rising dawn of the alchemical Work.

## Iconography
A building or structure stands as an emblem within the manuscript's loose, vivid watercolour style — figures and edifices personifying stages of the opus rather than literal apparatus.

## Significance
The *Aurora Consurgens* ("Rising Dawn") is a fifteenth-century alchemical-mystical text once attributed to Thomas Aquinas. The Zurich copy (Zentralbibliothek, Ms. Rh. 172) carries an unusually expressive cycle of images that C. G. Jung and Marie-Louise von Franz made famous as evidence of alchemy's symbolic depth.

## For artists & game designers
The Zurich hand is wonderfully loose and folk-like — a reference for a deliberately naive, hand-painted illustration style.

A fiery bird — phoenix-like — rises in the Zurich *Aurora Consurgens*, emblem of the red rebirth that crowns the Work.

## Iconography
The bird flames against the page in bright watercolour, wings spread in ascent. Its fire marks the final reddening and resurrection of the matter.

## Significance
The [[motif:phoenix|phoenix]] is alchemy's supreme emblem of the [[motif:rubedo|rubedo]]: death by fire followed by glorious rebirth, the Stone perfected. The *Aurora Consurgens* enlists it among its menagerie of transformation-creatures.

## For artists & game designers
A phoenix in mid-ascent is the archetypal resurrection / respawn icon — fire plus upward motion reads instantly.

The many-eyed bird fills the margin in vivid watercolour, its tail a fan of iridescence — the visible sign of the matter passing through its rainbow of hues.

## Significance
The [[motif:cauda-pavonis|cauda pavonis]] marks the transition between blackening and whitening, when the alchemist sees fleeting colours bloom in the vessel. Its appearance in the *Aurora Consurgens* shows how thoroughly such workshop lore had become poetic image.

Sol and Luna confront one another in the Zurich *Aurora Consurgens*, the cosmic pair whose marriage drives the alchemical opus.

## Iconography
A personified sun and moon face off across the page in the manuscript's bright watercolour, embodying the masculine and feminine principles, gold and silver, fixed and volatile.

## Significance
The pairing of [[motif:sol-and-luna|Sol and Luna]] is the central polarity of alchemy, and the *Aurora Consurgens* dwells on their union and strife in language borrowed from the Song of Songs. Von Franz read the cycle as a spontaneous symbolic process, a touchstone for the Jungian theory of alchemy as projected psychology.

## For artists & game designers
The sun-versus-moon face-off is timeless duality iconography — day/night, fire/water, two-player versus screens.

title: Broadside on the Comet of 1618
creator: Anonymous
summary:
A printed broadside depicting the great comet of 1618, sold to a public hungry to read the heavens for signs of war and woe.

## Iconography
A blazing comet streaks across a printed sky above a landscape or map, framed by explanatory text. Such single-sheet prints combined astronomical observation with portentous interpretation.

## Significance
The comets of 1618 coincided with the outbreak of the Thirty Years' War and unleashed a flood of cometary broadsides across Europe. Read as [[motif:celestial-portent|celestial portents]], they fed astrological prognostication even as Kepler and others began to study comets as natural bodies — a moment poised between omen and science.

title: Horapollo, Hieroglyphica (1595 edition)
creator: after Horapollo
summary:
A page of Horapollo's *Hieroglyphica* in its 1595 edition, the late-antique handbook that taught Renaissance Europe to read Egyptian signs as moralised emblems.

## Iconography
Woodcut symbols — animals and objects — accompany Greek-derived explanations of what each Egyptian sign 'means'. The format pairs a pictured emblem with an interpretive gloss.

## Significance
Attributed to a shadowy late-antique "Horapollo," the *Hieroglyphica* was rediscovered in 1419 and printed by Aldus in 1505. Its fanciful decodings — the scarab as the sun, the vulture as motherhood — convinced humanists that hieroglyphs were a wordless wisdom-script, directly inspiring the emblem books of Alciato and the speculations of Athanasius Kircher.

## For artists & game designers
A model for an in-world 'glyph dictionary' — each symbol an icon plus a one-line meaning the player decodes.

The great red dragon of the Apocalypse, its seven heads labelled with persecutors of the Church, from Joachim of Fiore's *Liber Figurarum*.

## Iconography
A serpentine dragon spreads seven crowned heads across the page, each head glossed with the name of a tyrant or Antichrist-figure; the seventh and the dragon's tail point to the final tribulation.

## Significance
The *Liber Figurarum* is the great picture-book of Joachite prophecy, in which the abbot's reading of history as three *status* — of Father, Son and Holy Spirit — is rendered as trees, [[motif:wheels|wheels]] and beasts. The seven-headed dragon maps Revelation 12 onto a timeline of the Church's enemies, a scheme that shaped centuries of apocalyptic expectation.

## For artists & game designers
A labelled seven-headed dragon is both bestiary art and a 'timeline of villains' UI in one — each head a chapter boss.

A plate from the *Vaticinia siue Prophetiae abbatis Ioachimi* (1589), the printed corpus of pope-prophecies attached to the name of Joachim of Fiore.

## Iconography
An emblematic figure accompanies a cryptic prophetic motto, in the manner of the illustrated pope-prophecies. Beasts, popes and symbolic objects encode a forecast of ecclesiastical history.

## Significance
Though the Calabrian abbot [[figure:joachim-of-fiore|Joachim of Fiore]] (c. 1135–1202) did not author these *Vaticinia de summis pontificibus*, they circulated under his prestigious name through the late Middle Ages and were repeatedly printed. Marjorie Reeves's studies traced their immense influence on apocalyptic and reform movements.

Plate 11 of Joachim of Fiore's *Liber Figurarum*, one of the abbot's diagrammatic *figurae* of salvation history.

A geometric diagram — branching or circling forms — encodes a stage of Joachim's tripartite scheme of history. Labels distribute the persons and ages across the figure.

## Significance
The *figurae* are Joachim's distinctive contribution to medieval thought: theology made diagram. The progression of the three [[motif:three-status|status]] toward an age of the Spirit was read by Franciscan Spirituals and reformers as a prophecy of imminent renewal.

## Iconography
A labelled figure — tree, wheel or interlaced form — sets out relations among the divine Persons and the ages of the world in Joachim's characteristic geometric idiom.

## Significance
Together the plates form a coherent picture-theology in which the structure of the Trinity is mirrored in the structure of time. This conviction made Joachim, in Reeves's phrase, the most influential prophet of the later Middle Ages.

A twelfth-century diagram knotting the Trinity to the four-lettered divine Name, an emblem of the medieval theology of trinitarian *figurae*.

## Iconography
Interlaced circles or shields link the Persons of the Trinity, set against the Hebrew Tetragrammaton. The geometry visualises how three are one — the *scutum fidei* tradition of trinitarian diagrams.

## Significance
Diagrams of this kind belong to the same twelfth-century impulse as Joachim of Fiore's trinitarian *figurae*: the conviction that divine relations could be made visible through geometry. Such schemes fed both orthodox theology and later Christian-kabbalistic speculation on the power of the Name.

title: The Lübeck Totentanz (Dance of Death)

summary:
A long frieze in which capering skeletons lead away pope and emperor, merchant and child alike — the famed Lübeck *Totentanz*, the Dance of Death.

## Iconography
Death, figured as grinning skeletons, links hands with representatives of every social estate in an unbroken processional band. Each living figure is partnered by a corpse who draws them into the dance.

## Significance
The Lübeck *danse macabre*, originally painted by Bernt Notke in 1463 for the Marienkirche, was the most influential of all Death-dances; this image preserves Anton Wortmann's 1701 copy, the original having perished in the 1942 bombing. The [[motif:memento-mori|memento mori]] insists that Death levels every rank — a profoundly democratic terror.

## For artists & game designers
The estates-procession structure is a ready cast list: every social type paired with its mortality, ideal for a parade or roll-call of characters.

title: The Dark Sun (Splendor Solis, plate 19)
creator: Anonymous
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: copy unidentified; cf. British Library, Harley MS 3469]
summary:
A black sun broods over a dim marshy landscape — the *sol niger*, emblem of the blackening that opens the alchemical Work.

## Iconography
A darkened solar disc hangs above swampy ground within the painted border. Where other plates blaze gold, here the light is quenched: the sun of putrefaction.

## Significance
The [[motif:sol-niger|sol niger]] or black sun is the visual sign of the [[motif:nigredo|nigredo]], the death and rotting of the matter that must precede all rebirth. It became one of the most evocative images in the whole alchemical corpus, taken up by Jungian and later esoteric writers as a symbol of psychic descent.

## For artists & game designers
The black sun over a dead marsh is a complete environment mood-board: a cursed or corrupted-zone sky in a single image.

title: The Drowning King (Splendor Solis, plate 7)
creator: Anonymous
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: copy unidentified; cf. British Library, Harley MS 3469]
summary:
A crowned king flounders in dark water, crying out as a figure reaches to haul him from the flood — the alchemical *solutio*, the dissolving of the old body.

## Iconography
The king's head and arm break the surface of a pool; a rescuer leans to grasp him. The painted border frames the drama of a sovereign nearly lost beneath the waters.

## Significance
The drowning king is one of alchemy's most arresting images of [[motif:dissolution|dissolution]]. The fixed, regal body must be undone in the philosophical water (*solutio*) before it can be reborn purified. C. G. Jung treated the motif at length in *Psychology and Alchemy* as a figure of the ego's necessary death.

## For artists & game designers
A potent peril-tableau: a king sinking in black water, half-rescued. Reads as a sacrifice or a near-death turning point.

citations.text: C. G. Jung, *Psychology and Alchemy* (1944).

repository: [PLACEHOLDER: copy unidentified; cf. British Library, Harley MS 3469]

A robed philosopher holds aloft a sealed flask of golden liquid, the adept presenting the matter of the Stone at the threshold of the Work.

## Iconography
The sage stands within an ornamental border, lifting a round-bottomed flask whose contents gleam gold. A motto-scroll names the secret of the art.

## Significance
The flask-bearing philosopher is the cycle's emblem of the operator himself. In the *Splendor Solis* the held vessel announces the prima materia and the promise of the [[motif:opus|opus]]; the alchemist becomes both witness and vessel of transformation.

## For artists & game designers
The quintessential 'alchemist NPC' pose — robed figure presenting a glowing reagent flask. Reusable as a shopkeeper or quest-giver silhouette.

title: The Solar King and Lunar Queen Meet (Splendor Solis, plate 4)
creator: Anonymous (school of Nuremberg)
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: copy unidentified; cf. British Library, Harley MS 3469]
summary:
A crowned solar king in red meets a silver lunar queen, the alchemical bride and bridegroom whose union begins the Great Work.

## Iconography
Two regal figures clasp hands within a richly painted Renaissance border of vines and grotesques. The king bears the red of sulphur and the sun; the queen the white of mercury and the moon. Their meeting stages the [[motif:coniunctio|coniunctio]] — the wedding of opposites.

## Significance
The *Splendor Solis* is the most lavishly illuminated of all alchemical treatises, ascribed to the legendary Salomon Trismosin and surviving in several painted copies from the 1530s onward. Its twenty-two plates narrate the opus as a sequence of allegorical tableaux. The royal marriage of [[motif:sol-and-luna|Sol and Luna]] is the first conjunction, dissolving the fixed and the volatile into a single body. Joscelyn Godwin and others read the cycle as a meditation manual as much as a recipe.

## For artists & game designers
The painted architectural border is itself a design system — treat each plate as a framed tarot-like card and the borders become a unifying UI motif across a deck.

## Significance
Harley MS 3469, dated 1582, is the most reproduced witness of the *Splendor Solis*. The frontispiece knight is read as the alchemist-as-champion who must master the [[motif:red-and-white|red and white]] waters. The double fountain echoes the *Rosarium philosophorum*'s fons mercurialis.

## Significance
The anthropomorphic [[motif:rising-sun|rising sun]] signals the *rubedo*, the perfected red stone and the dawning of the philosophers' gold. In the *Splendor Solis* the sun-over-city closes a narrative that began with the king and queen meeting; the achieved Work shines on the ordinary world.

summary:
A cropped portion of the third plate of the *Splendor Solis*, attributed to the legendary Salomon Trismosin.

## Iconography

## Significance
The attribution to Salomon Trismosin — supposed teacher of Paracelsus — is itself legendary; no such historical author can be securely identified. The *Splendor Solis* circulated as a prestige object among Northern European collectors of the sixteenth century. Detail crops like this one preserve passages of the painter's hand.

## For artists & game designers
Useful as a texture or inset: a single allegorical figure liftable from its plate for a card frame or codex page.

citations.text: Salomon Trismosin (attrib.), *Splendor Solis* (16th c.).

title: The Hermaphrodite with the Egg (Splendor Solis, plate 9)
creator: Anonymous
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: copy unidentified; cf. British Library, Harley MS 3469]
summary:
A two-headed androgyne — the *rebis* — holds a philosophical egg, the perfected union of male and female in a single body.

## Iconography
The standing figure bears two heads, male and female, on one trunk, cradling an egg. The painted border encloses this emblem of completed conjunction.

## Significance
The [[motif:rebis|rebis]] ("two-thing") is alchemy's signature image of the achieved [[motif:coniunctio|coniunctio]]: Sol and Luna fused into the philosophical hermaphrodite. The egg it holds is the sealed vessel of generation, the *ovum philosophicum* from which the Stone hatches.

## For artists & game designers
The double-headed androgyne is iconic shorthand for 'fusion' or 'final form' — a transformation reward or a boss in its perfected state.

citations.text: Joscelyn Godwin (intro.), *Splendor Solis* (1981 facsimile).
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Sun Rising over the City (Splendor Solis, plate 22)
creator: Anonymous
repository: [PLACEHOLDER: copy unidentified; cf. British Library, Harley MS 3469]
summary:
The golden sun rises in glory over a town and its river — the closing plate of the *Splendor Solis*, the dawning of the perfected gold.

## Iconography
A great radiant sun ascends above rooftops, walls and water, flooding the whole scene with gold inside the painted border. This is the cycle's final tableau of achieved completion.

## Significance
The sun-over-city seals the narrative begun with king and queen: the [[motif:rubedo|rubedo]] has dawned and the philosophers' gold illumines the everyday world. Many copies place this as the twenty-second and last plate, a deliberate echo of cosmic renewal.

## For artists & game designers
A serene golden-hour finale — pair with the dark-sun plate (plate 19) as before/after bookends for a corruption-and-cleansing arc.

citations.text: Joscelyn Godwin (intro.), *Splendor Solis* (1981 facsimile).
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Bewitched Groom
creator: Hans Baldung Grien
summary:
Hans Baldung Grien's late woodcut *The Bewitched Groom* (c. 1544), a tour-de-force of foreshortening and one of art's most enigmatic witchcraft images.

## Iconography
A groom lies sprawled on his back in dramatic foreshortening across a stable floor, a currycomb and pitchfork beside him. A great horse looms over him, and an old hag thrusts a flaming torch through a window at upper right. Whether the man is bewitched, dead, or dreaming is left unresolved.

## Significance
The print is read as a meditation on the artist's own mortality and on the disordering power of the [[motif:hag at window|witch]] — the hag intruding from outside the rational world. The Stocker coat of arms on the wall and Baldung's monogram have fed interpretations as a self-portrait-in-allegory. Scholars such as Linda Hults treat it as the summa of Baldung's witch imagery.

## For artists & game designers
Extreme foreshortening of a fallen figure, viewed from its feet, instantly conveys collapse, death, or supernatural defeat.

citations.text: Linda C. Hults, *The Witch as Muse* (2005).
Metropolitan Museum of Art, object record.
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Witches (Witches' Sabbath)
creator: Hans Baldung Grien
summary:
Hans Baldung Grien's *The Witches* (1510), a celebrated chiaroscuro woodcut and one of the defining images of the witches' sabbath.

## Iconography
Nude witches cluster around a steaming pot from which fumes and a forked stick rise; one rides a goat backwards through the air above. Bones, a raised covered dish belching vapour, and wildly streaming hair fill the scene. The tone block lends the print a lurid, nocturnal glow.

## Significance
Baldung, a pupil of Dürer, fused eroticism, the grotesque, and learned demonology into the era's most influential [[motif:witches sabbath|sabbath]] image. The cooking pot and rising vapours allude to weather magic and the ointments said to enable flight. Linda Hults and Charles Zika emphasize how Baldung's witches express anxieties about female sexuality and disorder as much as any literal belief.

## For artists & game designers
Vapour as a compositional device — smoke that carries objects and figures upward — turns a static coven into a scene of active, churning magic.

citations.text: Linda C. Hults, *The Witch as Muse* (2005).
Charles Zika, *The Appearance of Witchcraft* (2007).
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Four Witches
creator: Albrecht Dürer
summary:
Albrecht Dürer's engraving of 1497, traditionally called *The Four Witches*, showing four nude women gathered in a chamber.

## Iconography
Four idealized nude women stand in a tight circle; a small devil with flames peers through a doorway at lower left, and a skull and bone lie on the floor. A sphere overhead bears the date 1497 and Dürer's AD monogram. The women's purpose is deliberately ambiguous — the title is a later tradition rather than Dürer's own.

## Significance
The print fuses the classical motif of the [[motif:nude women|grouped nudes]] (echoing the Three Graces or a Judgement of Paris) with the menacing devil and bones that invite a witchcraft reading. It exemplifies how Dürer translated humanist study of the nude into images charged with moral and demonic suggestion. Art historians continue to debate whether the four are witches, goddesses, or an allegory of discord.

## For artists & game designers
Ambiguity is the lesson: a single small demon and a skull reframe an otherwise classical group as something sinister.

citations.text: Erwin Panofsky, *The Life and Art of Albrecht Dürer* (1943).
Charles Zika, *The Appearance of Witchcraft* (2007).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Witch Riding Backwards on a Goat
creator: Albrecht Dürer
summary:
Albrecht Dürer's engraving (c. 1500–01) of an old witch riding backwards on a he-goat, hair streaming against the wind, accompanied by tumbling putti.

## Iconography
A wizened, naked woman sits astride a horned goat facing its tail, brandishing a distaff. Her hair and the goat's coat blow forward — opposite to her direction of travel — signalling that she generates her own storm. Four winged putti scramble below; Dürer's monogram appears reversed, reinforcing the theme of inversion.

## Significance
The [[motif:goat|goat]] is the Devil's beast and the witch's mount; riding it *backwards*, against the wind, encodes the world-turned-upside-down logic of witchcraft. The distaff marks the figure as a woman whose domestic tool has become an instrument of malefice. Charles Zika reads the print as crystallizing the gendered, weather-making witch of German art.

## For artists & game designers
Reversed motion — hair and cloth blowing the 'wrong' way — is a subtle visual cue that a figure bends natural law.

citations.text: Charles Zika, *The Appearance of Witchcraft* (2007).
Linda C. Hults, *The Witch as Muse* (2005).
Wikimedia Commons

title: A Witches' Kitchen
creator: Frans Francken the Younger
summary:
*A Witches' Kitchen* by Frans Francken the Younger (early 17th century), a crowded cabinet painting of witches at their preparations.

## Iconography
In a vaulted interior lit by candle and fire, witches young and old mix potions, consult open magical books, and tend a cauldron amid skulls, bones, and oddments of the occult. Demons and monstrous creatures lurk in the shadows; figures stream up toward a chimney for the flight to the sabbath.

## Significance
The Antwerp 'witches' kitchen' became a popular cabinet-picture genre that let collectors enjoy the demonic as exotic spectacle. Francken assembles an inventory of magical apparatus — the [[motif:grimoire|book]], cauldron, and skulls — that codified what a witch's workshop should contain. The genre reflects both real demonological literature and the art market's taste for the marvelous.

## For artists & game designers
A single room packed with labelled occult props — book, cauldron, skull, candle — is an efficient way to establish a 'witch's workshop' location at a glance.

citations.text: Charles Zika, *The Appearance of Witchcraft* (2007).
Jane P. Davidson, *The Witch in Northern European Art* (1987).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Buen viaje (Bon Voyage), Caprichos 64
creator: Francisco Goya
summary:
Plate 64 of Goya's *Los Caprichos* (1799), *Buen viaje* ("Bon voyage"), depicting a winged demonic figure speeding off into the night with companions.

## Iconography
A cloaked, winged being launches through pitch darkness, trailed by a knot of indistinct flying figures. The aquatint plunges most of the sheet into black, isolating the airborne shapes against the void.

## Significance
The plate belongs to the cluster of *Caprichos* (60–66) devoted to witches and demons departing for or returning from nocturnal mischief. Its ironic farewell salutes the [[motif:night flight|night-flight]] of malign spirits — Goya using the rich blacks of aquatint to evoke the unknowable dark into which superstition projects its terrors. As with the series generally, the target is human folly, not real demons.

## For artists & game designers
Near-total darkness with only edges of a figure catching light is a powerful way to render menace 'departing' — the unseen is scarier than the shown.

citations.text: Francisco Goya, *Los Caprichos* (1799).
Metropolitan Museum of Art, object record.
Wikimedia Commons

title: Linda maestra! (Pretty Teacher!), Caprichos 68
creator: Francisco Goya
summary:
Plate 68 of Goya's *Los Caprichos* (1799), *Linda maestra!* ("Pretty teacher!"), showing an old witch and a young one flying together on a single broom.

## Iconography
Two nude witches, one aged and one youthful, ride a broomstick through a dark sky; an owl flies alongside. The ironic title casts the hag as a 'teacher' instructing her pupil — the broom-flight as a lesson in vice.

## Significance
The plate satirizes procuresses and the corruption of the young under the guise of [[motif:broomstick flight|witch initiation]]. Like the rest of the *Caprichos*, it uses the inherited iconography of the night-flying witch as a vehicle for moral and political commentary rather than belief. The pairing of old instructress and young initiate became one of Goya's most reproduced witch designs.

## For artists & game designers
Pairing a mentor and apprentice on one mount compresses a whole relationship — teaching, corruption, lineage — into a single silhouette.

citations.text: Francisco Goya, *Los Caprichos* (1799).
Rijksmuseum, object record RP-P-1921-2089.
Wikimedia Commons

title: Volaverunt (They Have Flown), Caprichos 61
creator: Francisco Goya
summary:
Plate 61 of Francisco Goya's *Los Caprichos* (1799), *Volaverunt* ("They have flown"), a satirical etching of bewitched flight.

## Iconography
A serene young woman rises into the air, balanced on the heads of three crouching, bat-cloaked figures, a butterfly-like shape at her own head. She floats with eerie composure against a blank aquatint sky.

## Significance
Goya turns the old [[motif:flight|witch-flight]] into Enlightenment satire: the image mocks credulity, vanity, and the giddy 'flightiness' of fashionable society as much as any literal witchcraft. The *Caprichos* deploy witches and demons as instruments of social and political critique, a key moment when witch imagery is repurposed against superstition itself. Scholars read *Volaverunt* alongside Goya's other sabbath and flight plates as ironic, not credulous.

## For artists & game designers
Goya shows that supernatural levitation reads most uncannily when the figure is calm and the background empty — restraint, not spectacle.

citations.text: Francisco Goya, *Los Caprichos* (1799).
Janis Tomlinson, *Goya: A Portrait of the Artist* (2020).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Matthew Hopkins, Witch Finder Generall
creator: Anonymous (publ. Richard Royston)
summary:
The woodcut frontispiece to Matthew Hopkins's *The Discovery of Witches* (1647), in which the self-styled "Witch Finder Generall" presides over two confessing witches and their named familiar spirits.

## Iconography
Hopkins stands at left in cloak and hat; two seated old women name their familiars, which are depicted as small animal imps with grotesque labels — "Holt," "Jarmara," "Vinegar Tom" (a greyhound with an ox's head), "Sack & Sugar," "Newes," "Pyewacket," and others. Each creature is captioned.

## Significance
The image documents the distinctively English theory of the witch's [[motif:familiars|familiar]] — an animal imp suckled at the witch's mark — that drove Hopkins's East Anglian campaign of 1645–47, the deadliest in English history. The labelled menagerie turned demonology into something like a folk bestiary and remains the iconic image of the English witch-hunt.

## For artists & game designers
Naming and captioning each familiar creature individualizes a coven's 'pets' and is a tidy template for a companion/summon roster.

citations.text: Matthew Hopkins, *The Discovery of Witches* (1647).
Malcolm Gaskill, *Witchfinders* (2005).
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Burning of Witches (Malleus Maleficarum tradition)
creator: Anonymous
summary:
A woodcut of witches being burned, reproduced in connection with the *Malleus Maleficarum* (Montague Summers's edition), representing the lethal end of the witch trial.

## Iconography
Condemned witches are consumed by flames at the stake while officials and onlookers attend. The crude woodcut belongs to the broadsheet tradition that illustrated executions for a popular audience.

## Significance
The *Malleus Maleficarum* ("Hammer of Witches," 1486/87) by Heinrich Kramer codified the procedures of witch-hunting and, with the new printing press, spread the persecuting mentality across Europe. Execution woodcuts like this one supplied the public face of that machinery — the [[motif:burning at the stake|stake]] as the inevitable conclusion of accusation. (This particular plate is a later reproduction associated with the text rather than an original 1487 title-page.)

## For artists & game designers
The stake-and-crowd composition is the visual shorthand for institutional persecution — the human cost behind the more decorative sabbath fantasies.

citations.text: Heinrich Kramer (Institoris), *Malleus Maleficarum* (1486/87).
Montague Summers (ed.), *The Malleus Maleficarum* (1928).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Witches in Flight (Molitor, De lamiis)
creator: Anonymous woodcutter, for Ulrich Molitor
summary:
A woodcut from Ulrich Molitor's *De lamiis et phitonicis mulieribus* ("On Witches and Diviner Women," first printed 1489), depicting witches in flight, partly transformed into animals.

## Iconography
Figures ride through the air on a forked cooking-stick; their heads have become those of beasts, illustrating the belief that witches travelled to the sabbath transformed or in animal guise. The crude woodcut line is typical of early German incunabula.

## Significance
Molitor's treatise was one of the first printed books on witchcraft and the first to be illustrated, so its woodcuts became the foundational visual vocabulary for the witch. Notably, Molitor himself was sceptical that such flights and transformations were real, treating them as diabolical illusion — yet the pictures, reprinted for decades, hardened the very stereotype the text questioned, as scholars including Charles Zika have shown.

## For artists & game designers
Partial animal transformation — a human body with a beast's head mid-flight — is a vivid, readable way to depict shapeshifting in progress.

citations.text: Ulrich Molitor, *De lamiis et phitonicis mulieribus* (1489).
Charles Zika, *The Appearance of Witchcraft* (2007).
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Witches' Weigh House, Oudewater
creator: Photograph (Martinvl)
rights: CC BY-SA 4.0 (photo by Martinvl). Via Wikimedia Commons.
summary:
A photograph of the historic balance scale at the *Heksenwaag* (Witches' Weigh House) in Oudewater, where suspected witches were weighed to disprove accusations.

## Iconography
The great wooden beam balance and weighing platform of the Oudewater weigh house, the institution at the centre of the Dutch 'weighing of witches'.

## Significance
Folk belief held that witches were unnaturally light — able to fly — so weighing could expose them. Uniquely, Oudewater issued official certificates that an accused person's weight was *normal*, effectively clearing them; reputedly no one weighed there was ever condemned. The [[motif:weighing of witches|weighing ordeal]] thus became, in the Dutch Republic, a tool of exoneration rather than persecution, a notable counter-current in the European witch panic. (This item is a modern photograph of the surviving site, under CC BY-SA, not a historical print.)

## For artists & game designers
A giant public balance scale is an evocative ordeal-device prop: trial by weight makes for a tense, legible game mechanic.

citations.text: Hans de Waardt, on the Oudewater Heksenwaag and Dutch witch trials.
Museum de Heksenwaag, Oudewater.
Wikimedia Commons

title: Witches at their Incantations
creator: Salvator Rosa
summary:
Salvator Rosa's *Witches at their Incantations* (c. 1646), a horizontal nocturne of necromantic rites, now in the National Gallery, London.

## Iconography
Across a frieze-like nocturnal landscape, witches and demons perform grisly rites: a hanged corpse, a skeleton, dismembered limbs, candles, scrolls inscribed with charms, and figures bent over books and instruments. Torchlight picks out the macabre incidents against deep shadow.

## Significance
Rosa, a poet and rebel as well as painter, made witchcraft and necromancy signature themes, cultivating a reputation for the sublime and the sinister. The scattered apparatus — [[motif:scroll|charm-scrolls]], corpses, and bones — draws on classical necromancy (Lucan's Erichtho) as much as contemporary witch-belief, appealing to learned patrons' taste for the dark and erudite.

## For artists & game designers
A wide, friezelike composition lets you string many small rituals across one canvas, reading like a sequence of vignettes in a single nocturnal scene.

citations.text: National Gallery, London, object record.
Jane P. Davidson, *The Witch in Northern European Art* (1987).
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Witches' Sabbath (after Teniers)
creator: Follower of David Teniers the Younger
summary:
*The Witches' Sabbath*, a 17th-century painting by a follower of David Teniers the Younger, in the Flemish demonic-genre tradition.

## Iconography
An old witch reads from a magical book within a candlelit chamber swarming with grotesque hybrid demons, toads, and flying monsters. Smoke and apparitions rise around her as a conjuration unfolds, the picture given over to inventive monstrosity.

## Significance
Teniers and his circle made a speciality of demonic and witchcraft cabinet pictures, descending from Bosch and Bruegel. These scenes treat the [[motif:witches sabbath|sabbath]] as a stage for fantastical invention rather than documentary demonology, satisfying collectors' appetite for the bizarre. The 'follower of' attribution reflects how successful compositions were repeated by the workshop and imitators.

## For artists & game designers
The lone reader at a book surrounded by swarming small monsters reads instantly as 'summoning gone large' — quantity of creatures conveys the spell's power.

citations.text: Jane P. Davidson, *The Witch in Northern European Art* (1987).
Christie's sale catalogue (2012).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Witches Riding Brooms (Les Vaudoises)
creator: Martin Le Franc (text); anonymous illuminator
summary:
A marginal illumination in a manuscript of Martin Le Franc's poem *Le Champion des Dames* (c. 1451), showing two women flying on a broom and a stick — among the earliest images of broomstick flight.

## Iconography
Two women in long gowns and head-coverings are borne aloft, one astride a household broom, the other on a plain wooden staff. The marginal caption labels them *Vaudoises* — "Waldensians" — the heretical sect onto which the new crime of diabolical witchcraft was being projected.

## Significance
The image predates the witch-hunt's great print era by half a century and shows the [[motif:broomstick flight|flying broom]] already fixed as the visual sign of the witch. Its identification of witches with the Waldensian heresy (*vauderie*) reflects the fifteenth-century fusion of heresy-hunting and the emerging stereotype of the night-flying sabbath, documented by historians such as Norman Cohn and Richard Kieckhefer.

## For artists & game designers
The humble broom plus an ordinary woman in everyday dress is the most economical witch signifier there is — no warts or pointed hat required.

citations.text: Martin Le Franc, *Le Champion des Dames* (c. 1440–42; ill. ms. c. 1451).
Norman Cohn, *Europe's Inner Demons* (1975).
Wikimedia Commons

title: Description and Figure of the Witches' Sabbath
creator: Jan Ziarnko, for Pierre de Lancre
summary:
Jan Ziarnko's large engraving *Description et figure du Sabbat des Sorciers* (1613), the fold-out plate added to Pierre de Lancre's *Tableau de l'inconstance des mauvais anges et démons*.

## Iconography
A panoramic, numbered scene of the sabbath: the horned Devil enthroned receiving homage, a banquet of the damned, a ring of dancers, a queen and great lords, children offered up, cauldrons, and witches departing through the air on brooms and beasts. A printed key letters and numbers each episode.

## Significance
De Lancre, a magistrate who conducted ferocious witch trials in the Basque Labourd, commissioned the plate to make the [[motif:witches sabbath|sabbath]] systematically visible — a near-encyclopedic catalogue of its alleged components. As Stuart Clark notes, such images lent the learned demonology of the sabbath a spurious documentary authority.

## For artists & game designers
A numbered 'map-key' overlay turns a busy scene into a legible diagram — useful when a single image must convey many simultaneous events.

citations.text: Pierre de Lancre, *Tableau de l'inconstance des mauvais anges et démons* (1613).
Stuart Clark, *Thinking with Demons* (1997).
Wikimedia Commons

title: The Witches' Sabbath (Hans Baldung Grien)
creator: Hans Baldung Grien
summary:
**Hans Baldung Grien's** chiaroscuro woodcut of 1510 — the founding image of the early-modern **witch**.

## Iconography
Naked hags gather around a steaming, fuming cauldron in a night wood; one rides a goat backward through the air; bones, a fork, and conjured weather-vapours swirl around them. Baldung, a pupil of Dürer, gives the scene a learned, eroticised, deliberately disturbing charge.

## Significance
Made as the witch-hunt theory was hardening (the *Malleus Maleficarum* was a generation old), Baldung's print helped *invent the visual stereotype* — cauldron, night-flight, sabbath assembly — that print culture spread across Europe (Iconclass 13B3). It marks the moment **witchcraft becomes an image**. Charles Zika traces exactly this machinery.

## For artists & game designers
The template witches' coven: cauldron, goat, night-flight, conjured storm.

citations.text: Charles Zika, *The Appearance of Witchcraft* (Routledge, 2007).
L. Hults, 'Baldung and the Witches of Freiburg', *Art Bulletin* 69 (1987).
